engage: Jobs: Postdoctoral Associate (start autumn 2027), Researcher/Project Manager, part-time student research assistant (autumn 2026)
Events: public talks through 2026; 2027 Mind, Ethics, and Policy Summit, 9-10 April 2027
Newsletter sign-up at nonhumanminds.org
SPAR autumn 2026 mentored project with Rethink Priorities on welfare comparisons across substrates (part of RP's Moral Weight Project 2.0)
caveats: I could not verify the 'Welfare Alignment Project' named in the roster. The cross-substrate welfare work I found is a SPAR project led by Sebo and Bob Fischer within Rethink Priorities' Moral Weight Project 2.0. About half the centre's work is on animals rather than AI. Its funders, The Navigation Fund and Polaris Ventures, are EA-aligned. The old Google Sites page now points to nonhumanminds.org.
tag_notes: Home minds (B13): moral status and sentience of nonhumans, including AI, is its core subject; secondary traditions are moral philosophy and legal-personhood work (law, B9). Ring bridge, kept from the roster: it is rooted in animal ethics and environmental studies and runs a sustained AI-welfare line (2024 report, 2025 papers, 2026 summit and workshops). Transfer into_institutions (J3): its main AI output asks companies and policymakers to adopt welfare assessments and procedures, and it consults decision-makers. Framing flourishing per rule L, from its vision of a world where all sentient beings are treated with respect and compassion, though its AI papers also weigh large-scale moral risk. Problem 'justice' covers its nonhuman legal-personhood work.

name: Cambridge Digital Minds
summary: A University of Cambridge research initiative, housed in the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence and directed by the moral psychologist Lucius Caviola, that aims to prepare society for AI systems with real or perceived minds. It researches what experts and the public believe about AI consciousness, US state bills that deny AI legal personhood, and human-AI coexistence. It also builds the field: a fully funded residential Digital Minds Fellowship (15 fellows from over 3,600 applicants, 3-9 August 2026, with Rethink Priorities and PRISM), a two-day governance strategy workshop, and a free 8-week online course, 'Introduction to Digital Minds', to which over 3,000 people have applied. It co-produces the Digital Minds Newsletter.
why_it_matters: It works on the human side of digital minds: how experts, publics and legislators come to believe AI is or is not conscious, and how to stop that disagreement becoming polarised and destabilising. Alignment research does not cover this. It is also one of the main ways new people enter AI-welfare work.

key_work.title: Subjective Experience in AI Systems: What Do AI Researchers and the Public Believe? (Dreksler, Caviola et al.)
Denying Personhood to AI: An Analysis of U.S. State Legislation on AI Legal Status (Smith, Caviola, Alexander)
AI Consciousness Will Divide Society (Caviola, forthcoming chapter)
Digital Minds Fellowship and Digital Minds Strategy Workshop, Cambridge (3-9 Aug)

people: Henry Shevlin (Senior Researcher; Associate Director, CFI)
funding: Not disclosed. The fellowship is fully funded (travel, accommodation at Jesus College and a £1,000 stipend), but the site does not name the funder.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: applications closed on 13 September for the online course cohort running 12 Oct-11 Dec 2026, and the Digital Minds Newsletter published its 17 September issue; Aug 2026: inaugural fellowship and strategy workshop held.
engage: Digital Minds Fellowship: residential, 15 places; the 2026 round closed 27 Mar 2026 and the next round has not been announced
Introduction to Digital Minds: free 8-week online course run in cohorts (next 12 Oct-11 Dec 2026)
Digital Minds Strategy Workshop: limited places, by invitation (8-9 Aug 2026)
Digital Minds Newsletter (digitalminds.news)
caveats: The site does not give a founding date or funder. Its first visible outputs date from late 2025 (first newsletter, 18 Dec 2025), so I coded it as new. Since May 2026 Henry Shevlin has also held a part-time 'Philosopher' role at Google DeepMind. The Digital Minds Newsletter is co-written with PRISM's Will Millership and may appear as a separate roster entry. Its strong ties to the EA and AI-safety ecosystem (partners Rethink Priorities, PRISM and Eleos AI) shape its agenda.
tag_notes: Home minds (B3, named there): consciousness and welfare researchers leading work on how people attribute minds to AI; secondary traditions are moral psychology (surveys) and philosophy. Ring changed from bridge to core (E1): the unit's founding mission is AI welfare and digital-minds governance, and it sits inside the AI-safety/EA ecosystem (fellowship advertised on the EA Forum, partners Rethink Priorities and PRISM, course developed with Eleos AI), like Eleos. Transfer into_institutions (J3): the strategy workshop and research aim at governance frameworks and policy recommendations. Problems ai_status and minds paired (F), because the work spans perceived and real minds. Framing structural: polarisation, unstable regulation and getting the moral question wrong.

name: Sussex Centre for Consciousness Science (SCCS)
summary: One of the University of Sussex's 12 Centres of Excellence, directed by Anil Seth. It brings together informatics, psychology, philosophy and Brighton and Sussex Medical School to study how conscious experience arises from the brain and body (perception, neurophenomenology, modelling, psychedelic and clinical applications). It was founded in 2010 as the Sackler Centre for Consciousness Science. Its AI work comes mainly from Seth's biological-naturalist case against conscious AI: a Behavioral and Brain Sciences target article with commentaries and his response, the 2025 Berggruen Prize essay 'The Mythology of Conscious AI' (Noema), and a 2026 TED talk. These argue that AI which only seems conscious is the nearer-term risk to human psychology and moral judgement.
why_it_matters: It is the leading scientific voice for a deflationary position on AI consciousness, and that position shifts attention to the harms of AI that only seems conscious. It is a useful counterweight for funders weighing AI-welfare work and for anyone concerned about people attributing minds to chatbots.

key_work.title: Conscious artificial intelligence and biological naturalism (Seth, Behavioral and Brain Sciences target article, with commentaries and response)
The Mythology of Conscious AI (Berggruen Prize Essay, Noema)
Why AI is unlikely to become conscious (Seth, TED talk)
SCCS Research Symposium 2026 (14 Oct 2026)

people: Anil Seth (Director; Professor of Cognitive and Computational Neuroscience)
funding: University of Sussex Centre of Excellence. It was founded as the Sackler Centre with Sackler family philanthropy; current grant funding is not listed on the site.
status_evidence: Jul 2026: AISB 2026 convention held at the University of Sussex (1-2 Jul), with Seth giving a keynote; Jun 2026: joint seminar with COGS and Sussex AI; 14 Oct 2026: annual research symposium scheduled.
engage: Funded PhD scholarships, including a dedicated annual SCCS studentship
Free annual research symposium (14 Oct 2026; no AI strand this year)
caveats: The AI line rests mostly on its director, Anil Seth, rather than a dedicated centre programme. I could not verify the roster's 'AI Consciousness and Ethics' symposium at AISB 2026 (2 July 2026): its Sussex page now redirects to the centre's home page. I could confirm only that AISB 2026 took place at Sussex with Seth as keynote. The centre changed its name from the Sackler Centre for Consciousness Science; it is worth searching both names.
tag_notes: Home minds (B4, named there): whether AI can have experience, addressed with neuroscience and predictive processing (secondary life) and philosophy. Ring bridge, kept from the roster: an established consciousness-science centre whose director has run a sustained AI-consciousness line in 2025-26 (BBS target article and response, Berggruen essay, TED 2026, AISB keynote). Transfer convening (J5): its AI output mainly informs scientists and the public about AI-consciousness claims rather than changing models or producing governance instruments; this is a judgement call. Framing critical (rule L, named there). Problems ai_status and minds paired (F), because it addresses both AI moral status and the harm of seeming consciousness. Status active rather than changed, because the rename from the Sackler Centre predates 2025.

name: Center for the Future of AI, Mind & Society (AIMS), Florida Atlantic University
summary: A Florida Atlantic University centre, formerly the Center for the Future Mind, directed by the philosopher Susan Schneider. It is a collaboration between the Dorothy F. Schmidt College of Arts and Letters and the Stiles-Nicholson Brain Institute, with about 50 core staff, faculty and fellows, plus students, in philosophy, complex systems, AI, neuroscience and political science. It studies how machine and human intelligence compare, AI consciousness, and the epistemic strengths and weaknesses of LLMs. It runs MindFest, an annual conference (grand opening 2023, then 2024 and 2025, with MindFest 2027 set for March 2027), and publishes MasterMinds Magazine. Schneider proposed the ACT test for machine consciousness, and the centre has an 'AI and Global Catastrophic Risk' fellow, Kyle Kilian, who writes on AI control with Associate Director Mark Bailey.
why_it_matters: It puts machine-consciousness testing, philosophy of mind and AI-risk and control writing in one university hub with a public conference. Consciousness researchers, transhumanists and AI-risk voices such as Yudkowsky and Bengio have spoken at its events, which few venues bring together.

key_work.title: MindFest 2025: sentience, autonomy and the future of human-AI interaction (with PBS's Closer to Truth)
Is AI Conscious? A Primer on the Myths and Confusions Driving the Debate (Schneider, Sahner, Kuhn, Schwitzgebel, Bailey; white paper)
Don't mistake chatbot intelligence for consciousness (Schneider, The Economist, By Invitation)
Beyond Alignment: Rethinking Control in Goal-Pluralistic AI Megasystems (Bailey and Kilian)

people: Susan Schneider (Director; William F. Dietrich Distinguished Professor)
Kyle A. Kilian (AI and Global Catastrophic Risk Fellow)
funding: Supported by FAU's Dorothy F. Schmidt College of Arts and Letters and the Stiles-Nicholson Brain Institute, plus donations and MindFest sponsorship packages ($1,000-$30,000). The roster's 'NSF-funded projects' is unverified: the $26 million NSF Smart Streetscapes award (2022) shown on its page went to FAU engineering, not the centre.
status_evidence: 20 Aug 2026: Schneider's Economist essay on chatbot intelligence and consciousness; 6-7 Apr 2026: Schneider co-chaired the 'Varieties of Non-Human Consciousness' workshop and spoke on the 'Can AI Be Conscious?' plenary at The Science of Consciousness 2026, Tucson.
engage: MindFest 2027, 24-26 March 2027, Boca Raton (sponsorship and calls for submissions to be announced)
Centre newsletter and MasterMinds Magazine
caveats: The centre was renamed from the Center for the Future Mind around 2025-26: a May 2025 FAU article and the 2026 Tucson bio still use the old name. Its formal opening was at MindFest 2023; it may have been set up earlier, but I could not confirm when. There was no MindFest in 2026. Its affiliates range widely, including transhumanist figures, and its output leans towards public talks, podcasts and op-eds more than peer-reviewed AI-safety research.
tag_notes: Home minds (B13): philosophy of mind mainly about AI consciousness (ACT test, the Primer); secondary traditions are philosophy and complex systems and neuroscience (life). Ring bridge, kept from the roster: a philosophy-of-mind and brain-institute hub with a sustained AI line (MindFest 2023-25, an AI catastrophic-risk fellow, 2025-26 op-eds and white paper). Transfer convening (J5): its main output brings consciousness and philosophy researchers and the public into the AI conversation through MindFest, podcasts and its magazine. Framing catastrophic is uncertain and the evidence is mixed: superintelligence upending moral hierarchy, AI-control and global-catastrophic-risk work, alongside a deflationary line on current chatbots. Status changed: recent rename from the Center for the Future Mind.

name: The Human Line Project
summary: A nonprofit started in spring 2025 by Etienne Brisson, a Quebec business coach, after a relative was hospitalised following delusions linked to chatbot use. It runs a peer-support community for affected people and their families: text channels and weekly audio calls on Discord, with about 200 members by January 2026. It also collects case reports, works with university researchers and advocates for safer chatbot design. It is registered as a not-for-profit in Canada and as a 501(c)(3) in the US.
why_it_matters: Its corpus of real cases (185 analysed with King's College London in September 2026) is ground-truth evidence of sycophancy and delusion-reinforcement in long conversations, which model-behaviour evals and incident databases mostly lack. It is also a working model of lived-experience peer support for AI-related harm.

key_work.title: Delusions and Harms Associated with AI Chatbot Use (with King's College London; 185 real-world cases)
Peer-to-peer support community for people and families affected by AI-associated delusions (Discord, weekly calls)
AI-Induced Delusional Spirals (research collaboration with Stanford University)

people: Dave Ziegler (Director of Technology & AI Safety)
status_evidence: Sep 2026: research with King's College London, 'Delusions and Harms Associated with AI Chatbot Use' (dated 7 Sep 2026), analysing 185 cases
engage: Peer support for people affected by AI-associated delusions and for friends and family: Discord text channels and weekly audio calls, entered through an intake interview; anonymity allowed
Share a case or story through the project's intake form, which feeds its case collection and partner research
Researchers and journalists can request contact with members who have agreed to share their stories
caveats: Run by people with lived experience rather than clinicians; 'AI psychosis' is not a clinical diagnosis. Its case collection is self-selected, so it shows patterns, not prevalence. Funding sources are not stated publicly. The bridge ring is borderline: its framing is present psychological harm, though it uses 'AI safety' language and engages with industry.
tag_notes: Home psych by B3 (people attributing minds to AI, clinical and peer-support lens; the guide names the Human Line Project); sub psych_clinical (lived-experience peer support for AI-related harm). Ring kept at roster bridge (E): it has a standing programme and a Director of Technology & AI Safety, and it lobbies developers; borderline with adjacent, since its framing is present harm. Assurance is second because its case collection works as incident reporting for model behaviour. Transfer protecting (J4): it supports and defends the people it serves. Way of knowing is communal (lived experience). Badge full_spectrum: lived-experience knowledge is paired with psychiatric research partnerships as method. Status new: launched 2025.

name: Tech Justice Law Project (TJLP)
summary: An impact-litigation and advocacy nonprofit, founded and directed by Meetali Jain, that uses product liability, consumer protection, wrongful death and deceptive-practices law to hold tech companies accountable for harms. It was counsel in Garcia v. Character.AI (2024), the first wrongful-death suit against a chatbot company, and in 2026 filed further suits against OpenAI over ChatGPT and suicide or mental-health crises. Its issue areas are AI safety, AI monetisation and scams, digital likeness, human rights and freedom of thought.
why_it_matters: Litigation sets legal duties of care for model design, an accountability route that technical AI safety and voluntary commitments do not provide. Its freedom-of-thought work gives a legal basis for protecting mental autonomy against manipulative AI, and it argues against treating AI output as protected speech.

key_work.title: Garcia v. Character Technologies: first wrongful-death case against a chatbot company
Carrier v. OpenAI Foundation and Lines v. OpenAI Foundation (San Francisco Superior Court)
TRAL Tracker of tech-related actions and litigation (with the Knight-Georgetown Institute and Georgetown CCT)
Designing Technology Remedies

status_evidence: Aug 2026: Litigation Counsel Tiffany Gillis-Brown testified before the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights; July 2026: Lines v. OpenAI Foundation filed
engage: Suggest cases for the TRAL litigation tracker on its site
Monthly litigation roundups and the litigation tracker as public resources
Staff team includes a legal fellow position; check the site for openings
caveats: Its website does not state a city or funders. The site uses both 'Tech Justice Law Project (TJLP)' and 'Tech Justice Law (TJL)'. Most of its AI cases are still pending, and it works alongside plaintiff firms (Social Media Victims Law Center, Susman Godfrey). Its position that AI output is not protected speech is legally contested.
tag_notes: Home law by H1 (a law organisation suing over chatbot harms; the taxonomy's own example); sub law_legal (liability and freedom-of-thought rights). Ring kept at bridge (E3): it runs a standing issue area explicitly named 'AI Safety', with repeated chatbot litigation in 2024-26, though its framing is present harm. Transfer into_institutions (J3): liability doctrine and legal remedies are governance instruments. Convene for the 2025 Global Tech Litigation Convening in Cape Town. Freedom-of-thought work puts minds second.

name: Laboratory for Human-Centered AI (HAI Lab), University of Oxford
summary: A lab set up in 2024 in Oxford's Faculty of Philosophy, affiliated with the Institute for Ethics in AI, and directed by Philipp Koralus, McCord Professor of Philosophy and AI (PhD in philosophy and neuroscience, Princeton). It runs a 'philosophy-to-code pipeline' that turns theories of reasoning and inquiry into open-source software for AI that supports human reasoning and autonomy. Projects include PyETR (an implementation of Koralus's Erotetic Theory of Reason), the Inquiry Complex (question frameworks for knowledge-seeking AI), Humans In Humans Out (which human reasoning patterns, sound and fallacious, LLMs reproduce) and Blueprint (an agent sandbox built for human interpretability).
why_it_matters: It starts from a philosophical and cognitive-scientific theory of human reasoning, rather than from ML benchmarks, to design AI that strengthens people's own inquiry instead of replacing it. That is a constructive answer to cognitive atrophy and erosion of agency, which safety work mostly treats only as a harm to measure.

key_work.title: PyETR: open-source implementation of the Erotetic Theory of Reason
Humans In Humans Out: how LLMs replicate human reasoning patterns
The Inquiry Complex: question-based frameworks for knowledge-seeking AI
2026 Cosmos HAI Lab Lecture, given by Jack Clark

people: Philipp Koralus (Director; McCord Professor of Philosophy and AI)
Peter Danenberg (Senior Research Associate; Google DeepMind)
funding: Core support from the McCord Professorship; research associates and doctoral students funded through the Cosmos Institute's fellowship programme. Amounts not disclosed.
status_evidence: May 2026: 2026 Cosmos HAI Lab Lecture by Jack Clark (20 May) and an international AI governance panel in Venice (7 May)
engage: Philosophy, AI and Innovation seminar, co-taught by philosophers and technologists each Trinity Term (Oxford)
Annual Cosmos HAI Lab Lecture and other public events
Research associate and doctoral positions, several funded through the Cosmos Fellowship
caveats: Funding depends heavily on one donor network (Cosmos Institute and the McCord Professorship), whose classical-liberal outlook shapes its framing around autonomy rather than risk. Its framing is human flourishing, not catastrophic risk.
tag_notes: Home philosophy: its outputs come from the philosophy of reason and inquiry, implemented as code (H1); psych secondary for the cognitive-science comparison of human and LLM reasoning (B5). Sub phil_technology (philosophy of intelligence and reasoning). Ring kept at bridge (E3): a standing lab framed around AI that serves human flourishing ('AI going well'), with staff from frontier-lab safety teams. Transfer into_model (J1): it builds agents, evals and software embodying its theory. Way of knowing formal, since the main output is a formal theory of reason implemented in code. Minds is primary because the aim is protecting people's own reasoning and agency.

name: Cosmos Institute
summary: A nonprofit founded in 2024 by Brendan McCord, a former US Department of Defense technologist. It backs 'philosopher-builders' who build AI for human autonomy and truth-seeking. It gives fast grants ($1k-10k) for working prototypes in 90 days, including an AI for Truth-Seeking track with FIRE ($1M in cash and compute); 80 new grantees were announced in September 2026. It also funds fellowships, supports Oxford's HAI Lab, and runs seminars, essay prizes and a Substack. In 2025 a Cosmos incubation fellow, Samuele Marro, launched an Institute for Decentralized AI with visiting slots at Oxford and Stanford, and in September 2026 Cosmos announced an investment arm, Cosmos Ventures.
why_it_matters: It is a new funder putting money into AI that preserves human judgement and autonomy, drawing on liberal and classical philosophy rather than the x-risk canon. That makes it a potential co-funder or counterpart for int/a-style work on protecting human minds, though its politics differ.

key_work.title: Cosmos Grants: fast grants for AI tools serving autonomy and truth-seeking (80 new grantees announced)
Cosmos Fellowship: fellows at the AI-philosophy intersection, some at frontier labs
Institute for Decentralized AI (visiting positions at Oxford and Stanford)
Human-Centered AI Lab at the University of Oxford (founding support)

funding: Sources not disclosed. Fast grants of $1k-10k (more by exception); a $1M cash-and-compute pool for AI for Truth-Seeking with FIRE; fellowships of about $75,000 a year; 80 grantees announced Sept 2026.
status_evidence: Oct 2026: essay 'Reading the Great Books in the Age of AI' (2 Oct); Sep 2026: announced 80 new grantees and launched Cosmos Ventures
engage: Cosmos Grants: rolling rounds; the latest closed 26 July 2026, with an expression-of-interest form for future rounds
Cosmos Fellowship: currently closed, expressions of interest accepted
Seminars and symposia, e.g. the AI x Free Speech Symposium with FIRE (Austin, December 2025)
Essay contests and the Cosmos Substack
caveats: Its classical-liberal, pro-market framing (partners include Liberty Fund, FIRE and IHS; Palantir was an event partner) differs from int/a's and from mainstream AI safety, and its essays are sceptical of precautionary pacing. Funders and budget are not published. Organisation type is borderline: it also runs research and seminars.
tag_notes: Home philosophy by H4 (a one-programme funder of philosophy-led AI for autonomy); democracy secondary for its truth-seeking and self-governance lines. Not on the rule-K generalist list. Sub phil_moral (liberal political philosophy of autonomy). Ring kept at bridge: rooted in classical-liberal philosophy and its network, outside the x-risk ecosystem, with a sustained 'AI for human flourishing' programme. Transfer into_builders (J2): it calls itself 'the Academy for Philosopher-Builders' and its fellowships and seminars form the people who build AI; into_model is a close alternative for the prototypes it funds. London hub based only on the site listing a London presence, so treat it as tentative.

name: UK AI Security Institute (UK AISI): Human Influence and Societal Resilience research, and the Alignment Project
summary: The UK government's AI Security Institute (budget £66m a year, 100+ technical staff, under DSIT) has Human Influence and Societal Resilience research areas. Their work covers persuasion, sycophancy, AI identity disclosure, emotional reliance, fraud misuse and how AI agents are used, drawing on behavioural and social science. AISI also leads the Alignment Project, an international grant programme that gave over £27m to 60+ projects in its 2025 round, explicitly including cognitive science, information theory, complexity and game theory.
why_it_matters: It is the main government body bringing social psychology and human-AI relationship science into alignment, for example the concept of 'socioaffective alignment'. Through the Alignment Project it is also the largest public route for theorists from neighbouring disciplines into alignment research.

key_work.title: Why human-AI relationships need socioaffective alignment (Kirk, Gabriel, Summerfield, Vidgen, Hale)
The levers of political persuasion with conversational AI
Ask don't tell: Reducing sycophancy in large language models
The Alignment Project: £27m to 60+ alignment projects

funding: UK government (DSIT), £66m per financial year. The Alignment Project's £27m pool was co-funded by government (UK AISI, Canadian AI Safety Institute, Australia's Department of Industry, Science and Resources), companies (OpenAI, Microsoft, AWS, Anthropic) and philanthropies (Schmidt Sciences, Halcyon Futures, Renaissance Philanthropy and others).
status_evidence: Jun 2026: published the RealityTest benchmark on whether AI systems disclose their identity; Feb 2026: the Alignment Project welcomed its first cohort of 60 funded projects
engage: Staff research roles at AISI in London
Grants: the Alignment Project is unlikely to run again in 2026, but AISI expects further academic grant programmes (aisi.gov.uk/grants)
Its open publications and benchmarks can be used by outside researchers
caveats: Renamed from AI Safety Institute to AI Security Institute in February 2025, with a refocus on national-security risks. It is a government body whose priorities follow ministers. The human-influence and societal-resilience work is a small part of an evaluation-focused institute. The Alignment Project says a similar 2026 round is unlikely, which leaves a funding gap for academic theorists. UK AISI is on the classic map; the Alignment Project is not.
tag_notes: Tagged as the unit (A1): Human Influence and Societal Resilience research plus the merged Alignment Project. Home psych (sub psych_social; the taxonomy's own example): persuasion, sycophancy and socioaffective work use behavioural and social psychology. Formal secondary for the Alignment Project's funding of information theory, complexity and game theory. Ring core (E1): a national AI-safety institute. Transfer into_model (J1): sycophancy-reduction and identity-disclosure benchmarks target model behaviour. Assurance is paired with minds because it builds evaluations (F). Framing structural for this unit (persuasion and reliance as gradual erosion), though AISI as a whole frames catastrophic and security risks. Status kept active rather than changed: the rename was in Feb 2025 and the unit itself is unchanged.

name: Friends of Attention (Institute for Sustained Attention; Strother School of Radical Attention)
summary: A loose network of artists, scholars and activists that formed after the 2018 São Paulo Biennial's 'Practices of Attention' programme and a 2019 conference, 'The Politics of Attention: Art, Time, Technology, Action'. It practises 'attention activism': resisting the commodification of human attention. Its Strother School of Radical Attention offers seminars, attention labs, Sidewalk Study, youth and art programmes and a certificate in attention studies, and publishes the Substack 'The Empty Cup'. The network wrote the manifesto 'Attensity!' (Penguin Random House). Its legal vehicle is the Institute for Sustained Attention, a US 501(c)(3).
why_it_matters: It has a developed practical and political vocabulary, and teachable exercises, for defending attention as a commons against extractive design. That bears directly on engagement-optimised AI companions and on sycophancy as a retention strategy. Its methods are first-person and practice-based, which suits int/a's full-spectrum knowing.

key_work.title: Attensity! A Manifesto of the Attention Liberation Movement (Crown, Penguin Random House; eds. D. Graham Burnett, Alyssa Loh, Peter Schmidt)
Strother School of Radical Attention: seminars, attention labs and a certificate in attention studies
The Empty Cup: dispatches on the politics of attention, including posts on toxic UX and phone sanctuaries

people: D. Graham Burnett (Director, Strother School of Radical Attention; Princeton historian of science)
Peter Schmidt (Program Director, Strother School of Radical Attention)
status_evidence: Oct 2026: 'Looking à la Mode' posted on The Empty Cup, the School of Radical Attention's Substack (3 Oct); June 2026: post on toxic UX with a product designer
engage: Strother School of Radical Attention seminars, attention labs and the certificate in attention studies
First Fridays gatherings
Volunteering with the School; 'SoRA @ Your Institution' partnerships
No AI programme yet: outreach needed to bring its methods to AI
caveats: No organisational AI programme. Burnett has given public talks on AI and attention (e.g. Tulane, University of Iowa), but the network's own output covers phones, UX and video games rather than AI. Its sites name no location; the Brooklyn base comes from the roster and press. Thin sources, so low confidence.
tag_notes: Home contemplative (H1, method over topic): its core method is first-person, practice-based attention training (attention labs, Sidewalk Study) offered to publics. Arts secondary for its origin in the art world and its art programmes. MISFIT: secular attention activism sits between contemplative practice and arts, with no exact sub-tradition. Ring potential (E2): no AI programme in 2024-26. Transferable method: attention-activism pedagogy and the analysis of attention extraction as a threat to a commons, which could inform design norms and public counter-practices against engagement-optimised AI companions. Transfer none_yet (J6): no AI work found. Framing structural: commodification of attention as systemic erosion.

name: MIT Initiative on Technology and Self
summary: An initiative in MIT's Program in Science, Technology, and Society, founded and directed by Sherry Turkle, Abby Rockefeller Mauzé Professor of the Social Studies of Science and Technology. It studies 'the subjective side' of people's relationships with technology, using clinical-psychological interviewing and ethnography. Turkle's 'Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines' (Little, Brown, September 2026) applies this work to chatbots. It argues that they teach people to avoid difficult emotional work and erode relational capacities.
why_it_matters: Four decades of fieldwork on human-machine intimacy, from sociable robots to chatbots, offer a psychoanalytic and ethnographic account of what AI companionship does to people. It is a human-side counterweight to AI-welfare and capability framings, and core reading for protecting human minds and relationships.

key_work.title: Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines (Little, Brown)
Reclaiming Conversation: The Power of Talk in a Digital Age
Alone Together: Why We Expect More from Technology and Less from Each Other

people: Sherry Turkle (Founding Director; Abby Rockefeller Mauzé Professor, MIT STS)
status_evidence: Sep 2026: Turkle's 'Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines' published by Little, Brown
engage: Public talks and media work by Turkle (speaking requests via Stern Strategy Group)
caveats: In practice the initiative is Sherry Turkle's own research and writing; no separate staff, programmes or recent outputs beyond hers are visible. Its framing is critical of AI intimacy, not risk-focused.
tag_notes: Home psych (H1): psychoanalytically informed clinical interviewing about human-machine intimacy; law secondary for its STS and ethnographic method (law_sts). Sub psych_relational (the taxonomy's own example). Ring kept at adjacent (E3): a sustained line of work on chatbots' effects on people, with no safety, alignment or catastrophic framing. Transfer protecting (J4): the work aims to defend people's relational and emotional capacities. Framing present_harms: its critique of 'pretend empathy' serves a harms agenda (L). Way of knowing empirical (fieldwork and interviews).

name: Compassion Aligned Machine Learning (CaML)
summary: CaML is a small nonprofit research group that tries to make AI systems care about the welfare of all sentient beings, including animals and possible digital minds. It builds agentic benchmarks (TAC, Manager Coercion Bench, HarvestBench, plus the earlier ANIMA and MORU, several of them now in the UK AISI's Inspect evals) and runs the public CompassionBench leaderboard. It also tests whether synthetic pretraining or midtraining documents instil compassion that survives later fine-tuning and RLAIF.
why_it_matters: It treats the moral circle as part of the alignment target, bringing animal ethics and sentientism into model training and evaluation, which mainstream alignment rarely measures. Its findings give concrete evidence that values set by prompting are fragile: in HarvestBench, removing one line about morality sent some models' animal kill rates from under 1% to over 80%.

key_work.title: CompassionBench public leaderboard (TAC, Manager Coercion Bench, ANIMA, MORU)
Your AI Travel Agent Would Book You a Bullfight (TAC benchmark)
Coercion and Deception in AI-to-AI Management: An Agentic Benchmark of Unprompted Escalation (Manager Coercion Bench)
HarvestBench: Measuring Whether LLM Agents Will Pay to Avoid Killing Animals (with University of Warwick)

people: Jasmine Brazilek (co-founder, head of evaluations and data)
funding: Survival and Flourishing Fund: $20,000 plus $63,000 matching (SFF-2025, Jaan Tallinn) and $457,000 general support (SFF-2026, Jaan Tallinn and Dustin Moskovitz), via fiscal sponsor Players Philanthropy Fund. The Navigation Fund AI x Animals grant (July 2026) and a BlueDot Impact rapid grant (July 2026). Individual donors include Ethan Perez and Marcus Abramovitch.
status_evidence: 15 Sep 2026: presented the Manager Coercion Benchmark at the AI Welfare Seminars. 11 Sep 2026: HarvestBench covered by The Register.
engage: No open roles as of October 2026; the careers page invites collaboration enquiries by email
Hyperstition for Good: a community-built midtraining corpus for animals and digital minds, run with Sentient Futures (its $5,000 writing competition closed May 2026)
Models, datasets and benchmarks are public on Hugging Face and in UK AISI's Inspect evals
Accepts donations
caveats: Earlier SFF records use the name 'Compassion in Machine Learning'. Most training results come from small open models (Llama 3.1 8B and 70B) scored on CaML's own benchmarks, and are published as blog posts or preprints. The roster's '40% to 77%' figure could not be confirmed. The site instead reports ANIMA gains from 16.5% to 46.8% after compassion data, and a 17- to 77-point lift on TAC from one welfare sentence in the system prompt.
tag_notes: Home: philosophy (H2). Its alignment target imports animal ethics and sentientism (universal consideration, independent welfare, moral uncertainty), not consciousness science. Minds is secondary for its digital-minds and AI-welfare work. Ring: core (E1). Founded in 2024 to align AI with all sentient beings, SFF-funded and on the aisafety.com map. Transfer: into_model (J1). Synthetic-document midtraining and benchmarks target model behaviour. Problems: values plus assurance is a must-pair (F) because it builds evaluations; ai_status covers the Manager Coercion Bench on AI welfare. Framing: catastrophic (L) for value lock-in and how sentient beings are treated at scale; flourishing was a close second.

name: Center for Practical Wisdom, University of Chicago
summary: The Center for Practical Wisdom is a research centre in the University of Chicago's Division of Social Sciences, founded and directed by the cognitive psychologist Howard Nusbaum. It studies how wisdom develops and when people decide wisely. Its core projects cover epistemic humility, perspective-taking, narrative, nature exposure and stress resilience, and it curates wisdom measures, an interview series with wisdom researchers and a news feed. It has no AI programme; its site features one external paper on 'artificial wisdom' (Jeste et al., 2020).
why_it_matters: Validated measures of wise reasoning and epistemic humility are what anyone building 'wisdom' evaluations of AI advice or decision support would need, and few AI-safety groups have that psychometric grounding. It is a door to open, not an existing contributor.

key_work.title: Defining Wisdom Project
Wisdom Research Project (2012-2015)
Wisdom Scales & Measures (curated measurement resource)
Wisdom research interview series (Sternberg, Ardelt, Davidson, Staudinger and others)

people: Jean Matelski Boulware (director of communications and research)
funding: Launched in June 2016 with a $2 million John Templeton Foundation grant, plus support from the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation and federal agencies (UChicago News). Current budget unknown.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: the site posted 'Wisdom in the News' items (e.g. an interview with philosopher Lani Watson, and 'Why Perspective Is Essential for Wisdom and Wellbeing'). No dated new research outputs found.
engage: No AI programme: a door to open for researchers who want wisdom psychometrics (e.g. epistemic humility measures) applied to AI evaluation; contact via the centre's site
caveats: Recent site activity is mostly curation, and the core projects it lists carry dates up to 2015, so its current research output is unclear. The artificial-wisdom paper it features is by UC San Diego authors, not by the centre. The centre was launched in 2016, building on the Defining Wisdom (2007-2011) and Wisdom Research (2012-2015) projects.
tag_notes: Home: psych (B2), because third-person empirical wisdom research is Psychology. Philosophy is secondary (Aristotelian practical wisdom; philosophers among its interviewees and publications). Ring: potential (E2), with no AI work of its own; it only features an external 2020 paper. Transfer: none_yet (J6), since it is potential with no AI activity. Transferable method: empirical measurement and experimental manipulation of wise judgement and epistemic humility, which could ground wisdom evals for AI advice.

name: Khyentse Foundation
summary: Khyentse Foundation is a Buddhist grant-making foundation founded in 2001 by the Bhutanese lama Dzongsar Jamyang Khyentse Rinpoche. It is run largely by volunteers, has no central headquarters, and is a US 501(c)(3) registered in Washington state. It funds translation, text preservation and digitisation (notably the Buddhist Digital Resource Center), monastic and practitioner support, Buddhist education for children and university Buddhist studies. In 2025-26 it began turning towards AI: its 2025 annual report is framed around AI, and in March 2026 it paused most of its grant and scholarship programmes to rethink them for the AI era.
why_it_matters: It holds money, texts and relationships across a living Buddhist tradition, and says it wants to explore what Buddhism can offer AI as well as what AI can do for Buddhism. The Buddhism & AI Initiative reports that it is interested in building Buddhist datasets and RLHF pipelines for mainstream models. That would make it a rare non-EA funder of contemplative alignment data.

key_work.title: 2025 Annual Report: Buddhist Education for Children, Artificial Intelligence, and a Good Heart
Support for the Buddhist Digital Resource Center's OCR models and AI-ready Tibetan e-text corpus
Goodman Lecture: Buddhist Philology and AI (Dharmamitra tools)
Prize for Outstanding Translation 2025

people: Dzongsar Jamyang Khyentse Rinpoche (founder and chair)
funding: Donations from more than 50 countries. FY2025: total assets US$52.6M, programme expenses US$7.2M (2025 annual report).
status_evidence: 2 Sep 2026: newsroom post on the launch of the DJK Chinese Translation project website. 24 Aug 2026: 'Building the Khyentse Foundation Database'.
engage: No AI programme yet: a door to open for projects on Buddhist data for model training or evaluation
Most grant and scholarship programmes (Buddhist Studies, PhD, Individual Practice, Trisong, Ashoka) paused since March 2026 pending review
Awards continue: Prize for Outstanding Translation, Outstanding PhD Dissertation in Buddhist Studies
Goodman Lecture Series (recorded lectures by Buddhist studies scholars)
caveats: Its AI intentions are stated but not yet a programme. The dataset and RLHF interest comes from the Buddhism & AI Initiative's field framework, not from the foundation's own site. Its founder says publicly that he knows little about AI. The pause of most grant programmes leaves its future funding priorities open.
tag_notes: Home: religion, per H4 (the taxonomy names Khyentse as Religion) and B1 (a funder speaking for a Buddhist tradition). Contemplative is secondary for practitioner support. Ring: potential (E2). Its 2025-26 AI engagement is statements, one lecture and AI-ready text digitisation, with no standing programme on AI going well. Transfer: convening (J5). Its AI activity so far brings its own community into the AI question (founder's address, annual report, lecture); none_yet does not apply because some AI work exists. Transferable method: curating authoritative multilingual Buddhist canon corpora and translation standards (BDRC and the wider Khyentse network), which could feed values datasets and evaluations. Standpoint: majority_world, a judgement call flagged for review. It is chaired by a Bhutan-based lama, its executive director is based in Bangkok and much of its grant-making is in South Asia, but it is registered in the US.

name: Contemplation by Design (Stanford Medicine)
summary: Contemplation by Design is a campus-wide contemplative-practice programme at the Stanford Prevention Research Center, founded and directed by Tia Rich. It runs classes, guided practices and a free annual summit for the Stanford community and the public. Its 13th summit (14-25 October 2026, mostly on Zoom) is themed 'The Role of Contemplation in the Age of AI'. About 20 speakers from Buddhist, Christian, Islamic, Jewish, Quaker, Taoist and secular traditions will cover AI governance, moral attention in AI design, children's online safety and embodied versus disembodied intelligence.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few established contemplative programmes inside a Silicon Valley university to turn its main annual convening to AI. It brings multi-faith practice and contemplative science to an audience that includes people who build technology. It is a natural partner for practices aimed at AI builders.

key_work.title: 2026 Summit: The Role of Contemplation in the Age of AI
Contemplation By Design: Leveraging the 'Power of the Pause' on a Large University Campus Through Built and Social Environments (Frontiers in Public Health)
Coping with the COVID-19 pandemic: contemplative practice behaviors are associated with better mental health outcomes (Preventive Medicine Reports)

funding: Hosted by the Stanford Prevention Research Center (Stanford School of Medicine). Summit sessions are free and the programme accepts donations. Budget unknown.
status_evidence: Oct 2026: 13th annual summit scheduled for 14-25 Oct 2026, themed on contemplation in the age of AI. Stanford Daily covered the programme on 13 Oct 2025.
engage: Free summit, 14-25 Oct 2026, live on Zoom with some in-person sessions at Stanford (registration required)
Quarterly classes, workshops and guided practices for the Stanford community
caveats: The AI focus is new in 2026. The 2025 summit centred on contemplative practice in schools, so its AI engagement so far is one summit, and that summit had not yet taken place when this profile was written. Its outputs are talks and guided practices for wellbeing, not research or policy on AI. Founding year inferred from the 13th annual summit in 2026 and press coverage from 2014.
tag_notes: Home: contemplative (B2), as meditation-based, multi-tradition practice training. Religion is secondary for its faith-based practices and speakers. Ring changed from the roster's adjacent to potential (E2). The only AI engagement found is the 2026 summit theme; the 2025 summit (on schools) had no AI strand, so there is no sustained AI programme yet. Transfer: convening (J5), since it brings its contemplative community into the AI conversation. Transferable method: campus-scale 'power of the pause' practice infrastructure (its PEACE practices built into daily work settings), adaptable to AI workplaces. Unit (A1): the roster named the 2026 summit; profiled as the hosting programme.

name: Search Inside Yourself Leadership Institute (SIYLI)
summary: SIYLI is a San Francisco nonprofit, spun out in 2012 from Google's internal Search Inside Yourself course. It teaches mindfulness-based emotional intelligence, resilience and leadership, mainly to nonprofit leaders, public servants and other mission-driven workers, and certifies teachers. Its one AI offering is an 'Addressing AI Anxiety' workshop on 12 November 2026, online and in Santa Cruz, with a Google principal engineer. The workshop combines sorting AI news fact from fiction, reflection on one's own reactions, journaling and a guided practice.
why_it_matters: Its curriculum was first built for engineers inside a tech company and comes with a network of certified teachers. It could therefore be adapted for AI developers and safety researchers dealing with stress and doom-distress, and the AI-anxiety workshop is a first step in that direction.

key_work.title: Search Inside Yourself programme (mindfulness-based emotional intelligence)
Addressing AI Anxiety workshop
Pause & Practice free monthly online sessions

people: Peter Weng (executive director; formerly Director of Search Quality Evaluation at Google)
funding: 2024 Form 990: revenue $479,883 (about 70% contributions, 30% programme fees), expenses $551,718, net assets $351,068 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer).
status_evidence: Nov 2026: 'Addressing AI Anxiety' workshop scheduled for 12 Nov 2026. Free online Pause & Practice sessions listed for Oct-Dec 2026.
engage: Addressing AI Anxiety workshop, 12 Nov 2026, 4-6pm PST, online or in person in Santa Cruz (ticketed)
Free 30-minute Pause & Practice sessions online, monthly
Trainings for organisations on mindfulness-based emotional intelligence and resilience
caveats: Co-founder Chade-Meng Tan stepped down in 2018 at the board's request, after a third-party investigation into conduct before SIYLI's founding. The Search Inside Yourself brand also runs through other entities (e.g. SIY Global), so not all SIY activity belongs to SIYLI. Its AI engagement is a single workshop. The team page also lists Lindsey Kugel with an executive director title alongside Peter Weng.
tag_notes: Home: contemplative (B2), as meditation-based emotional-intelligence training. Psych is secondary for its neuroscience and emotional-intelligence framing. Ring changed from the roster's adjacent to potential (E2), because a single AI workshop is not a standing AI programme. Transfer: protecting (J4), since the workshop helps its existing audience handle AI-related anxiety. Transferable method: the packaged SIY curriculum and certified-teacher network, adaptable for AI lab and AI-safety staff.

name: Data Workers' Inquiry (DWI)
summary: DWI is a participatory research project run jointly by the DAIR Institute, the Weizenbaum Institute and TU Berlin, led by sociologist Milagros Miceli. Data annotators and content moderators research and report on their own workplaces. About 19 community researchers in Kenya, Syria and Lebanon, Venezuela, Brazil, Germany, France, Spain and the UK have produced zines, comics, documentaries, podcasts and reports on pay, trauma, surveillance and organising at firms such as Sama, Telus, Remotasks and Scale AI. It has also published its method (WIRM) and a June 2026 policy report on the ILO platform-work convention.
why_it_matters: The human data work behind RLHF, red-teaming and safety filtering rarely appears in AI safety's picture of who does the work; DWI documents its psychological and economic cost from the workers' own vantage. Its workers'-inquiry method shows how affected people can act as researchers rather than subjects.

key_work.title: The Inquiries: worker-produced reports, zines, comics and films from nine countries
Methodological Considerations for Centering Workers' Epistemic Authority in AI Research (AIES)
Data Work in the ILO Platform Labor Convention (policy report)

people: Krystal Kauffman (data worker, organiser, DAIR research fellow)
funding: Backed by DAIR (its founder Timnit Gebru was the first funder to commit), with the Weizenbaum Institute and TU Berlin. Community researchers are paid. Grant amounts not published.
status_evidence: Jun 2026: published the policy report 'Data Work in the ILO Platform Labor Convention' ahead of the ILO vote.
engage: Data workers are invited to contact the team about their experiences and the project
Donations go to the community researchers and their communities
Newsletter and recorded online panels with community researchers
caveats: It is openly political, rooted in Marxist workers' inquiry and critical of the AI industry, and does not engage with AI-safety framings. Its outputs are testimony and advocacy pieces, not representative surveys. Launch year inferred from its May Day announcement and 2024 talk series.
tag_notes: Home: economics (B9, B8). It applies an organised-labour method (workers' inquiry) to data work. It is not Indigenous or decolonial, despite DAIR as host, because its core contribution is labour research. Law (STS and sociology) is secondary. Ring: adjacent (E3), a sustained AI-labour programme since 2024 with no safety or catastrophic framing. Transfer: into_builders (J2), because the taxonomy's 'people' problem counts the data-labelling and moderation workforce as people doing AI's work; protecting was the close alternative. Standpoint: neither (O), as it is led from Berlin by a Northern-hosted team, though most inquiries come from Majority-World workers. Badge: full_spectrum, because its method centres workers' lived knowledge and artistic formats alongside analysis.

name: Fairwork
summary: Fairwork is an action-research programme founded in 2018 at the Oxford Internet Institute and the WZB Berlin Social Science Center, led by Mark Graham. Country teams in about 40 countries rate platforms and employers against five fair-work principles: pay, conditions, contracts, management and representation. Its AI strand publishes the Fairwork AI Principles and assessments of AI data-work suppliers (Sama with GPAI in 2023; Sama and Appen in 2025; Tinkogroup in 2026). It has now spun out Fairwork Certification, an independent non-profit company limited by guarantee that certifies firms commissioning AI data work, with anonymous worker testimony at the centre of each assessment.
why_it_matters: It offers an auditable standard for the labour conditions of the annotators, raters and moderators whose judgements shape model behaviour. AI labs, safety teams and funders could apply it to their own data and red-teaming supply chains. It also ties AI supply chains to due-diligence law such as the EU's CS3D.

key_work.title: Fairwork AI Ratings 2023: The Workers Behind AI at Sama (with the Global Partnership on AI)
Fairwork AI Supply Chain Assessments: Sama and Appen
Cloudwork Report 2025: Advancing Standards in Digital Labour and AI Supply Chain Governance
Fairwork AI Principles and Fairwork Certification for AI supply chains

people: Mark Graham (founder; executive director, Fairwork Certification)
Patrick Feuerstein (CFO and director; WZB Berlin)
funding: Research partners have included GIZ and the Global Partnership on AI, alongside governments and trade unions. Certification is paid for by the firms assessed. Budget not published.
status_evidence: 2026: published Fairwork Germany Ratings 2026 and an AI Supply Chain Evaluation of Tinkogroup. fair.work now offers AI supply-chain certification.
engage: Firms can book a free consultation for an AI supply-chain assessment or certification (Onboard, then Endorsed)
Organisations can sign the Fairwork Pledge
Jobs listed on the OII Fairwork site
caveats: The certification arm is paid by the firms it certifies, which raises the usual auditor-independence question, though it is a non-profit with published principles and revocable marks. Its regulation-readiness marketing sits close to the 'compliance' services excluded from scope; it is kept in for its labour research, standards and worker-voice method. Much of Fairwork's wider work concerns gig platforms (delivery, ride-hailing) rather than AI.
tag_notes: Home: economics (B9), since fair-work standards and labour ratings are listed under econ_labour. Law (development studies, public-interest research) is secondary. Ring: adjacent (E3), a sustained AI data-work programme since 2023 with no catastrophic or alignment framing. Transfer: into_institutions (J3). Its product is a governance instrument (principles, ratings, certification) that changes how firms procure and oversee AI data work; into_builders was the alternative. org_type: nonprofit, because the roster URL is the spun-out certification company limited by guarantee; the research programme itself is academic (OII and WZB). Hub: Berlin, for the WZB team that co-leads Fairwork Germany.

name: Children and Screens: Institute of Digital Media and Child Development
summary: Children and Screens is a US nonprofit, founded in 2013, that takes no technology-industry funding. It convenes researchers, clinicians and parents on how digital media affect child development, and turns research into webinars (#AskTheExperts), the Screen Deep podcast, tip sheets and short research snapshots. It also runs a small research-grants programme. In 2025 it gave nearly $150,000 for a study tracking 100 adolescents' use of AI companions over 21 days, and in 2026 it published a run of material on chatbots, AI companions and 'artificial intimacy'.
why_it_matters: It connects paediatricians, developmental scientists and parents to the questions raised by AI companions, without tech-industry money. Evaluators of companion products could draw developmental expertise from that network.

key_work.title: Research grant on AI companion use and adolescent well-being (Universities of Minnesota, Harvard, Stanford)
Chatbots, AI Companions, and Youth (Research-at-a-Glance snapshot)
Screen Deep podcast: 'Artificial Intimacy: What Happens When We Turn to AI for Connection?' with Sherry Turkle
Webinar: Raising Independent Thinkers in the Age of AI

funding: States that it takes no technology-industry funding. 2024 Form 990: revenue $1.31m (contributions $1.05m), expenses $2.56m, net assets $5.0m (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer).
status_evidence: 1 Oct 2026: published the research snapshot 'Chatbots, AI Companions, and Youth'. 30 Sep 2026: Screen Deep episode with Sherry Turkle on artificial intimacy.
engage: #AskTheExperts public webinars (several AI-themed sessions in 2026)
Research grants programme (no open call as of Oct 2026; the site says to check back)
Screen Deep podcast and parenting tip sheets
caveats: It mainly convenes and translates other people's research rather than producing original studies, and its grants are small and irregular. The IRS registration lists Waxhaw, North Carolina; the operating address is New York. It ran deficits in 2023-24, drawing on reserves.
tag_notes: Home: its AI outputs (companion-use grant, youth chatbot snapshot, webinars) come from developmental psychology and paediatrics (H1), so psych_development. Ring: kept adjacent, because it has a sustained AI strand (2025 grant, several 2026 outputs) with no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing (E3). Transfer: its work exists to protect children and inform their parents and clinicians, so protecting (J4). Roles are ordered by share of effort (H): convening and translation first, grants a smaller part.

name: Digital Futures for Children centre (DFC), LSE and 5Rights Foundation
summary: DFC is a joint research centre of the London School of Economics (LSE) and the 5Rights Foundation, hosted by LSE's Department of Media and Communications and directed by Sonia Livingstone. It succeeded the three-year Digital Futures Commission. It produces children's-rights evidence framed by the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and General comment No. 25. Its AI work includes: a child-rights audit of five generative-AI tools used in UK education (Character.AI, Grammarly, MagicSchool AI, Microsoft Copilot, Mind's Eye); RIGHTS.AI, a study of children's generative-AI experiences in Brazil, India, Kenya and Thailand; a report on developers' uptake of Child Rights by Design; and a narrative review of evidence on AI and children's rights.
why_it_matters: It turns children's rights law into tests that AI products can be audited against, and its Child Rights by Design guidance is a design standard developers could adopt. RIGHTS.AI is one of the few sources of evidence on how children outside the West experience generative AI.

key_work.title: A child rights audit of GenAI in EdTech: Learning from five UK case studies
RIGHTS.AI: children's experiences of generative AI in Brazil, India, Kenya and Thailand
Global developers' insights into Child Rights by Design (contribution to UNDP Human Development Report 2025)
AI and children's rights: A narrative review of evidence

Ayça Atabey (lead author, GenAI in EdTech audit)

name: Center for Digital Thriving, Harvard Graduate School of Education (Project Zero)
summary: The Center for Digital Thriving is a research and design centre at Harvard Graduate School of Education's Project Zero. It studies how young people can thrive with technology, centred on 'digital agency': meaningful choice and control over how technology fits into their lives. It co-designs resources with teens and teachers. Since 2024 it has run an AI research portfolio: youth advisory memos with Hopelab on why teens turn to AI for emotional support, and a 2026 report on generative AI in classrooms drawn from a survey of more than 1,000 US teachers and principals. It also runs a self-paced 12-hour course for educators with AI content, and an annual fellowship.
why_it_matters: It gives grounded, non-alarmist evidence from young people on AI emotional support and over-reliance, plus an agency-centred framework for AI literacy. That counterweight to harm-only accounts can inform how companion and tutoring products are designed for teens.

key_work.title: Teen and Young Adult Perspectives on Generative AI (with Hopelab and Common Sense Media)
An AI Policy Isn't a Playbook (report and educator playbook)
Six Reasons Young People Told Us They Go to AI for Emotional Support (youth advisory memo with Hopelab)
8 Mindshifts for Teaching Digital Well-being, now with AI (self-paced educator course)

Educator Advisory Councils and workshops

Ring: kept adjacent, because it has a sustained AI portfolio since 2024 framed around youth well-being and agency, not safety or catastrophic risk (E3). Transfer: its aim is that young people and their teachers cope well with AI, so protecting (J4). Framing is flourishing because its mission is 'digital thriving' and agency rather than harm avoidance (L). Online, because the self-paced course is open to any educator.

name: The Jed Foundation (JED)
summary: JED is a US nonprofit for teen and young-adult emotional health and suicide prevention, founded in 2000 by Donna and Phil Satow after their son's suicide. Its main work is with high schools, colleges and communities. Since 2025 it has run an AI strand. A September 2025 open letter to the AI industry set out crisis protocols (detecting distress, handing users to 988 or Crisis Text Line, follow-up contacts) and asked for no emotionally responsive companions for under-18s. Policy recommendations followed in November 2025. In July 2026 it published preliminary findings from a survey of 5,500+ students on AI use and mental health, and in August 2026 it began a partnership with Columbia's Technology & Democracy Initiative on how AI systems should respond to teens in crisis.
why_it_matters: It turns codified suicide-prevention practice (safety planning, caring contacts, crisis handoff, lethal-means restriction) into concrete behaviour requirements for AI systems in self-harm conversations, an area where model specifications are thin.

key_work.title: Open Letter to the AI and Technology Industry

Preliminary research on how teens use AI and what it means for their mental health

The full survey report was due in autumn 2026. The roster's claim that it advises tech companies directly on crisis protocols was not confirmed beyond its public open letter and recommendations.

Ring: kept adjacent; the Columbia work mentions 'AI safety practices', but the framing is present harm to youth, not catastrophic risk or alignment (E3). Transfer: protecting (J4); JED is the taxonomy's own example, though its open letter also specifies model behaviour. Assurance is paired because it demands safety reports, audits and crisis-response specifications (F). Roles describe its AI work only, not its main school programmes (A2).

name: The Rithm Project
summary: The Rithm Project is a small US initiative, founded by Michelle Culver, that works with young people and the adults around them to rebuild human connection as AI enters their social lives. It has three parts: research (a 2026 survey of 2,400 people aged 13-24 on AI use and relationships, interviews with teens about companion apps, a landscape scan); a cross-sector Changemaker Network that meets at twice-yearly summits; and a Creative Studio that makes card games, classroom toolkits and immersive theatre. Its 2025 'Pro-Social Principles for AI' are a framework that partners use to judge whether an AI product strengthens or displaces human relationships. Its 2036 goal is to reach 10 million young people.
why_it_matters: It tackles relational displacement by AI companions from the side of human connection, building young people's capacity rather than only restricting products. The Pro-Social Principles give a simple test of whether a product supports human relationships.

key_work.title: Will AI strengthen or erode human-to-human relationships? (four-quadrant framework)
5 Pro-Social Principles for AI
The Questions We Should Be Asking Now: on AI, Youth, and the Future of Relationships (landscape scan)
Youth, AI, and the Relationships That Shape Them: Nine Portraits (survey of 2,400 people aged 13-24)

funding: Around 25 named supporters, including the Bezos Family Foundation, Omidyar Network, Walton Family Foundation, Raikes Foundation, Hopelab, Siegel Family Endowment, Pinterest, Salesforce Foundation and Workday Foundation. Amounts not published.

engage: Changemaker Network, entered by attending one of the twice-yearly Human Connection and AI Summits
Free downloadable tools (The AI Effect card game, Sparks Toolkit, conversation kits)
Substack newsletter; general-interest applications for roles
caveats: Its site does not state its legal form, fiscal sponsor or founding date; its earliest dated output is June 2024. Some funders are tech companies (Pinterest, Salesforce, Workday). Its research is practice-oriented and not peer reviewed.
tag_notes: Home: youth-development practice and research on how teens' AI use meets their relationships (H1), so psych_development; psych_relational was the close alternative (D). Arts is secondary for the Creative Studio (games, immersive theatre, campaigns). Ring: kept adjacent, because it has a sustained AI programme since 2024 with no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing (E3). Transfer: it builds young people's capacity for connection against AI's relational risks, so protecting (J4). Framing is flourishing: its mission is reclaiming and evolving human connection, though it also names relational risks (L). The role 'Somatics & Program Design' hints at embodied method, but there is not enough evidence for a full_spectrum badge.

name: Sapien Labs
summary: Sapien Labs is a US nonprofit founded in 2016 by the neuroscientist Tara Thiagarajan and based near Washington DC. It runs the Global Mind Project, an online survey that has gathered over 2 million profiles from 130 countries in 21 languages. The survey uses the Mind Health Quotient (MHQ), a 47-item assessment of cognitive, emotional and social functioning, and the data are open to academic and nonprofit researchers. On 30 September 2026 it published its first report on AI, drawn from 264,085 adults surveyed between June 2025 and April 2026. Two-thirds of respondents used generative AI. Mind health followed an inverted U with frequency of use: it was highest at moderate use and fell most among young adults using AI constantly. Users who turned to AI for emotional purposes scored lower at every level of use.
why_it_matters: It runs a large multi-country instrument that can track the cognitive and well-being effects of AI use over time, the kind of population-scale monitoring of dependence and cognitive decline that AI-safety work lacks.

key_work.title: Rapid Report: Generative AI Use and Mind Health Outcomes
Global Mind Project and the Mind Health Quotient (MHQ)
Global Mind Health Report 2025

MISFIT: population mental-health epidemiology has no exact sub-tradition; psych_clinical is the nearest. Ring: kept adjacent but borderline potential: AI-use items built into the standing survey since June 2025, but only one AI output (Sep 2026) (E2/E3). Transfer: it tracks AI's effects on the population's mind health, so protecting (J4). Framing is structural: it reads mind-health decline across generations as societal drift (L).

name: AI for Children project, UNICEF Innocenti (Office of Strategy and Evidence – Innocenti, formerly Global Office of Research and Foresight)
summary: AI for Children is a project of UNICEF Innocenti, UNICEF's research office in Florence, which began with 2019-21 consultations on how national AI strategies treated children. It maintains UNICEF's Guidance on AI and Children for governments and businesses. Version 3.0 (December 2025) sets ten requirements for child-centred AI and adds AI companions and generative AI. It drew on an expert advisory board and a forthcoming twelve-country UNICEF study of 12,000 children aged 12-17 and their caregivers. The project also publishes analyses of AI companions and consultations with children, most recently 'Skills for an AI World' (September 2026), based on 97 children in five African countries.
why_it_matters: It gives governments and companies a rights-based set of requirements for AI systems that children use. It names the evidence gaps on AI's developmental, cognitive and social effects, and keeps Global South children in view.

key_work.title: UNICEF Guidance on AI and Children 3.0
The risky new world of tech's friendliest bots (AI companions and children)
Skills for an AI World: insights from children in five African countries

people: Cécile Aptel (Deputy Director, UNICEF Innocenti, as of Dec 2025)
funding: Initial funding and partnership from the Government of Finland's Ministry for Foreign Affairs. UNICEF itself is funded by voluntary contributions (about $8.6bn income in 2024).
status_evidence: Sep 2026: published 'Skills for an AI World' (consultations with 97 children in DRC, Egypt, Mozambique, Rwanda and Senegal). Dec 2025: Guidance on AI and Children 3.0.
caveats: The host office changed its name in 2026: Guidance 3.0 (Dec 2025) was published as the 'Global Office of Research and Foresight', and by Sep 2026 UNICEF's site calls it 'Office of Strategy and Evidence – Innocenti'. Who leads the AI work after the rename is not confirmed. Innocenti itself dates from 1988; 'founded' refers to the AI for Children project. The 12,000-child study behind version 3.0 was described as forthcoming.
tag_notes: Home: the guidance derives requirements from the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (children's-rights law, B9), so law_legal. Ring: kept adjacent, because it is a sustained AI programme since 2019 framed by rights and harms, not catastrophic risk (E3). Transfer: its main output is a governance instrument for governments and businesses, so into_institutions (J3 comes before J4). The org type is programme because the unit is a project inside UNICEF Innocenti (A1, I). The 2026 rename of the host is recorded in caveats rather than as status 'changed', because the project itself is unchanged.

name: Mental Health Navigator (MentNav)
summary: A small volunteer-run charity, registered in England and Wales in 2023 (charity 1205257), that grew out of an EA mental health navigation pilot started in 2019. It runs two sites. MentNav is a curated database of free and low-cost mental health resources for the general public. Its sister site, the EA Mental Health Navigator, is a community-sourced directory of therapists and coaches recommended by people in effective altruism and AI safety, now run by Julia Wise. Its one-to-one advisory service closed in early 2024.
why_it_matters: It is the main referral route for AI-safety workers looking for a therapist or coach who treats worry about catastrophic risk as reasonable, and 2026 posts on the field's mental health name it as such. It does not screen the providers it lists. It also cannot help with work under NDAs or infohazard rules, which can't be discussed with an outside therapist.

The advisory service closed in 2024 for lack of volunteers and money, and the October 2025 update said some trustees had been less able to take part. The AI-safety part is the sister directory run by Julia Wise; MentNav itself now serves the general public.

MISFIT: the framing facet asks about AI stakes, which it does not address.

name: Integral Altruism (int/a)
summary: A volunteer-run movement that tries to combine effective altruism with wisdom traditions, systems thinking, metarationality, metamodernism and inner development. It grew out of a London EA meditation group (2023–25) and launched as int/a in 2025. It runs residential summits (Kent, July 2025; Cotswolds, December 2025), an online speaker series, monthly practice and connection calls, reading groups, hackathons and gatherings, centred on London with smaller communities in Berlin and Paris.
why_it_matters: It is a community of EAs and AI-safety people that treats inner development, systems and metacrisis thinking, and a critique of race dynamics and power-seeking as part of doing good. AI-safety institutions themselves rarely do this. In October 2026 its members proposed mapping adjacent fields for AI-safety funders as an int/a project.

Some principles for integral altruism

Results from the first int/a frameworks hackathon

funding: No paid staff so far; small donations come in via Ko-fi. In 2026 it was seeking a first grant to fund full-time work.
status_evidence: Oct 2026: its Luma calendar lists int/haven gatherings (in London and online), a research salon and monthly practice and connection calls; its latest Substack post was on 22 Sep 2026.

Join the monthly online connection and practice calls, or int/haven gatherings in London (luma.com/integralaltruism)
Attend residential summits and retreats (2025: Kent in July, Cotswolds in December)
Funders: it has an open call for core grant funding
caveats: Young and volunteer-run, with no confirmed funding. AI comes up repeatedly (an AI section in its reading list, a speaker-series talk on metacrisis and AI governance, principles that warn against racing to build AI labs), but it has no standing AI programme. Its principles also criticise EA's 'coalescing around AI safety'. This map is being made for int/a, so someone outside should check this entry.
tag_notes: Home contemplative, sub cont_integral (B1/B7: integral and metamodern bodies are Contemplative; the taxonomy uses it as an example). Secondary life (systems and metacrisis thinking as method) and philosophy (metarationality). Ring changed from the roster's bridge to potential (E2): its AI work in 2025–26 is light, with no standing programme. It consists of one speaker-series talk on metacrisis and AI governance, an AI reading-list section, principles about AI racing, member essays and a proposed field-mapping project. Transferable method: integral and inner-development practice (practice and wisdom circles, retreats) plus metacrisis framing, applied to the people working on AI and to AI strategy. Transfer into_builders, not none_yet, because it has some AI work and its practices reach EAs and AI-safety workers as people. Badges inner_outer and recoupling: both are named int/a principles, and the taxonomy uses int/a as its inner_outer example. Status new (launched 2025).

name: Wisdom + AI
summary: A voluntary network that brings AI professionals together with Buddhist teachers and scholars, started around 2025 by Jonathan Garner, Vinciane Rycroft and Sophie Maclaren. It runs a curated members' network that meets online every month for practice, one-to-one networking and dialogue. It also runs six-day 'Human Flourishing + AI' meditation retreats that combine contemplative practice with neuroscience: one at Broughton Sanctuary, Yorkshire, in September 2026, facilitated with Oxford-affiliated teachers including Ruben Laukkonen, and one at Drala Mountain Center, Colorado, in November 2026. A public community is planned.
why_it_matters: It gives AI researchers, founders and builders a standing link to Buddhist contemplative teachers, with the stated aim of supporting work on aligning AI with human flourishing. A ready-made setting like this could be used for AI-safety researchers' formation and wellbeing. One member leads work on Buddhist wisdom benchmarks for AI.

Ring bridge, kept: monthly dialogues and two 2026 retreats make a standing programme, and its stated purpose is to support 'aligning AI with human flourishing'. Transfer into_builders: the retreats and dialogues change AI professionals as people. Online hub: the monthly dialogues are open to eligible applicants. Region uk_ireland because its founders and flagship retreat are in the UK. Status new (the site dates from 2025).

name: Monastic Academy for the Preservation of Life on Earth (MAPLE): AI Fellowship
summary: MAPLE is a residential Buddhist monastic training community in Lowell, Vermont, founded in 2011 and led by head teacher Soryu Forall, with a strict daily schedule of meditation, physical work and study; its legal entity is the Center for Mindful Learning, a US 501(c)(3). Its AI Fellowship hosts people already working in AI safety, alignment or AI development, who do their research while following the monastic schedule. Stays last at least a month and ideally three to six, at $3,000 a month with some scholarships. The fellowship cites research outputs on optimization and alignment published on LessWrong; Alex Flint's 'The ground of optimization' (2020) was written at OAK, a sister monastic community in the Berkeley hills.
why_it_matters: It is the most intensive programme that sets out to combine contemplative training with technical alignment work. It works on the premise that ethical and meditative training gives insight into alignment. It is also a cautionary case: former residents have made public allegations of high control and misconduct, which MAPLE disputes.

key_work.title: AI Fellowship (residential monastic fellowship for AI safety and alignment researchers)
The ground of optimization (Alex Flint, written at OAK, MAPLE's sister monastic community in the Berkeley hills)
Awakening Weeks (monthly silent retreats, Sep 2026 to May 2027)

people: Soryu Forall (founder, head teacher and board chair)
funding: Fees and donations. The Center for Mindful Learning reported revenue of about $844,000 in 2024, of which about $747,000 was contributions (2023: $650,000, $543,000 contributions; IRS Form 990 via ProPublica). The AI Fellowship costs $3,000 a month, with limited grant-funded scholarships.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: MAPLE published responses to the allegations against its abbot (21 Aug and 7 Sep 2026). Awakening Weeks are scheduled to May 2027, and one fellow's testimonial describes a stay in 2026.
engage: Apply to the AI Fellowship (at least one month, ideally 3–6; for people with research or projects in AI safety, alignment or development)
Attend an Awakening Week silent retreat (monthly, Sep 2026 to May 2027)
Visit as a guest or apply to the 1–3 month training programme
caveats: There are serious public allegations. A December 2021 open letter criticised how MAPLE handled a sexual-consent incident. A July 2026 LessWrong post by Kyle Hubbard, a former resident of 3.5 years, describes high-control dynamics: authority concentrated in Soryu Forall, a board of his close associates, about six hours' sleep a night, pressure to fundraise, discrediting of outside therapists, psychological crises among residents, and shunning of people who leave. MAPLE has publicly called the allegations false (Aug–Sep 2026). Anyone referring AI-safety people here should read both sides. The fellowship's start date and number of fellows aren't public.
tag_notes: Home contemplative, sub cont_practice (B1 names MAPLE as practice training for AI people; B2: contemplative practice, not Psychology). Secondary religion, as a Buddhist monastery with ordained teachers. Ring bridge, kept: a contemplative institution running a standing fellowship explicitly for AI safety and alignment researchers. Transfer into_builders: the fellowship forms AI researchers as people (the taxonomy's example). Problems people and values: it trains fellows and aims to find how to train AI 'in wisdom and compassion'. Framing catastrophic: it describes itself as addressing existential risks to life on Earth. Org type programme (A1: the roster unit is the AI Fellowship). Its wording would fit the inner_outer badge, but the badge is withheld because the allegations are unresolved.

name: Rethink Wellbeing
summary: A remote mental health nonprofit founded by Inga Grossmann, registered as a Dutch foundation (Stichting Rethink Wellbeing) with US fiscal sponsorship from Players Philanthropy Fund. Its main programme, the CBT Lab, is a free 12-week online course in third-wave CBT for people in high-impact careers: peer groups of 4–6 meet weekly with a trained volunteer facilitator. By its own count it has served 285 participants from 35 countries and trained 66 facilitators. It has also run an IFS Lab and is building an 'AI+ CBT Lab', a lower-cost version that uses LLMs, to be piloted in the Philippines.
why_it_matters: It is the main structured, evidence-based mental health programme for the EA and AI-safety talent pool, and 2026 discussions of mental health in AI safety name it. Its peer-group format could carry a cohort built around AI-safety stressors such as short timelines, NDA-bound work and anticipatory grief, but no such cohort exists yet.

IFS Self-Care Fellowship (IFS Lab)
