caveats: It is not specific to AI safety: it serves 'ambitious altruists' in general (past participants include Center for AI Safety staff) and is expanding toward low-cost care in low- and middle-income countries. The AI+ CBT Lab applies AI to mental health; it is not AI-safety work. Its outcome figures (20-30% reductions in symptoms) are self-reported and come from its own evaluations; its 2024 IFS Lab pilot found mostly small, non-significant effects. It advertised for a co-director in February 2026. Founded in 2022; 'Effective Peer Support' was the name of its first peer-group programme.

MISFIT: its mission covers altruists broadly rather than AI safety, so a strict reading of E1 would make it bridge. Transfer into_builders: it changes the wellbeing and capacity of EA and AI-safety workers. Framing present_harms: it targets anxiety, depression and burnout and states no AI stakes. Online hub: its cohorts recur and anyone eligible can join remotely.

name: Upgradable
summary: A small coaching and 'life optimisation as a service' outfit run by James Norris, who co-founded EA Global under Upgradable's earlier name, Self Spark. Its Upgrade Program is a step-by-step system for setting and pursuing life goals, drawing on behavioural science and applied rationality; you can do it alone for free or with paid coaches, assistants and specialists. It describes a special focus on AI-safety advocates, with programmes of one day to a year on productivity, emotional and physical wellbeing, finances, personal safety and emergency preparedness, plus startup templates for founders focused on safety.
why_it_matters: It is one of very few coaching services built explicitly for people working on existential risk from AI. In February 2025 the founder said nearly all his effort had moved to Collective Action for Existential Safety (CAES), so it probably has less coaching capacity than its aisafety.com listing suggests.

funding: Client fees and donations; in 2025 it was seeking investment or donations. It has pledged all its profits to existential safety work (its 'Profits for Safety Pledge').
status_evidence: Feb 2025: James Norris re-introduced Upgradable on the EA Forum. The site footer reads © 2026, but no dated 2026 activity was found.
engage: Book a free call through upgradable.org/book-a-call
Do the Upgrade Program on your own for free
Donate to subsidise programmes for AI-safety advocates who can't afford them
caveats: Its legal form is unclear: the aisafety.com map calls it a nonprofit, but its own site mentions a 'profitable business model', profits and investment. Since early 2025 most of the founder's effort has gone to CAES, and coaching now happens rarely. Its impact claims (250+ people and 50+ organisations served) come from its own site and have not been independently evaluated. Recent activity is thinly documented.
tag_notes: Home psych, sub psych_fieldhealth (B2 names Upgradable: coaching and applied rationality for AI-safety workers count as Psychology). Ring core, kept: it states a special focus on helping AI-safety advocates 'win the fight for humanity's survival', comes from the EA and x-risk ecosystem, and is on the aisafety.com map. Transfer into_builders: coaching for AI-safety workers as people. Framing catastrophic: its AI page speaks of extinction or disempowerment. Org type company is tentative: its site describes a profitable business model and investment, though the classic map calls it a nonprofit. Region global: it works remotely and names no headquarters; the roster's San Francisco was not verified. Engagement left empty because its site offers no cohort, opening or community that fits the tags (only free calls).

name: AI Safety Support (AISS)
summary: A field-building organisation founded in 2020 by Linda Linsefors and JJ Hepburn and incorporated in Australia. It supported early-career, independent and transitioning AI-safety researchers. It offered career calls and coaching, free health coaching for anyone working on AI safety (from 2021), online events and a mentorship programme. It also provided fiscal sponsorship, moderated the AI Alignment Slack and ran the aisafety.training calendar. It was put on indefinite pause in July 2023, citing founder burnout and a funding gap while it waited on a Long-Term Future Fund decision; what remains is the 'Lots of Links' resource page, which Linda Linsefors updates occasionally.
why_it_matters: It is the clearest precedent for wellbeing and coaching support made specifically for AI-safety researchers, and 2026 posts on the field's mental health still point to the gap its closure left. The way it ended, through founder burnout and slow funding decisions, is itself a lesson about the field's support infrastructure.

key_work.title: Free health coaching for anyone working on AI safety
aisafety.training (calendar of AI-safety training programmes and events)
Lots of Links (AI-safety resource list)
Shutting down AI Safety Support

people: Linda Linsefors (co-founder; maintains Lots of Links)
Shay Gestal (health coach working with AISS)
funding: Donations (Patreon, Ko-fi, and Rethink Charity for tax-deductible gifts) plus grants. A donation paid for the expanded health coaching in 2021. In 2023 it ran out of money while waiting for a Long-Term Future Fund decision.
status_evidence: Jul 2023: put on indefinite pause ('Shutting down AI Safety Support'). The Lots of Links page was last updated on 13 Dec 2024.
engage: Use Lots of Links, or offer to help keep it up to date (contact Linda Linsefors)
caveats: It has closed, but stays on the map because the gap it left is itself informative. Its homepage still describes it in the present tense. After the pause, the Australian legal entity, AI Safety Support Ltd, went on fiscally sponsoring other projects; whether it still does in 2026 is unconfirmed. AISS pointed newcomers to AI Safety Quest as a grassroots successor.
tag_notes: Home psych, sub psych_fieldhealth (B2: coaching and health coaching for AI-safety workers). MISFIT: most of its work was mainstream AI-safety field-building (career advice, events, Slack); only the health coaching brought in anything from outside that canon. Ring core: its founding mission was reducing existential risk from AI by supporting researchers, and it is on the aisafety.com map. Transfer into_builders: it supported researchers as people. Region asia_pacific because its legal base is Australia, though it worked online. Status dormant (paused July 2023).

name: Center for Reducing Suffering (CRS)
summary: A small research nonprofit founded in 2020 by Magnus Vinding and Tobias Baumann. It works on suffering-focused ethics and on reducing s-risks, meaning risks of severe suffering on an astronomical scale in the long-term future. It publishes books, essays and cause-prioritisation research. In 2026 it has published a run of pieces on AI welfare and AI governance, such as 'The Case for Suffering-Focused AI Governance', 'Basic Rights for AIs' and 'The Animal Gap in AI Governance'. It also runs an online Intro to S-Risk Fellowship and a free six-week online course on suffering-focused ethics.
why_it_matters: It applies a worked-out suffering-focused moral philosophy to AI. It asks which futures contain the most severe suffering, for humans, animals and possible digital minds, not only which ones lose human control. It is one of the few groups that puts animal welfare, AI welfare and AI governance in a single framework for setting priorities.

key_work.title: Avoiding the Worst: How to Prevent a Moral Catastrophe (Tobias Baumann)
The Animal Gap in AI Governance
Basic Rights for AIs
The Case for Suffering-Focused AI Governance

people: Zoé Roy-Stang (operations and programmes, runs the s-risk fellowship)
funding: Says it is funded entirely by individual donors. Its 2026 fundraising goal is USD 200,000: USD 100,000 would keep core staff, and the full amount would fund about three full-time staff and a larger fellowship. Financial reports for 2022-2024 are published.
status_evidence: 2 Oct 2026: published 'Making Concern for Suffering Common Knowledge'. 17 Sep 2026: published 'Should Artificial Suffering Be a Moral Priority?'. July-Aug 2026: ran its online Intro to Suffering-Focused Ethics course.
engage: Intro to Suffering-Focused Ethics course: free, online, six weeks, about 50-60 places. The 2026 cohort ran 13 July to 23 August, and applications closed 14 June.
Intro to S-Risk Fellowship (online). A second cohort was recruited in 2025.
Newsletter and Substack
Donations (2026 target USD 200,000)
caveats: Suffering-focused ethics is a minority view in moral philosophy, and CRS spends part of its output defending it against objections. Its AI work so far is mostly philosophical essays, not technical or policy research. The team is small and donor-funded, and its site gives no legal base.
tag_notes: Home: philosophy (phil_moral) by B13, which uses CRS as its own example of moral philosophy with AI welfare as one strand. No secondary tradition, because its AI work uses no outside method. Ring: core under E1, roster value kept, since its founding mission is s-risk reduction inside the EA and longtermist ecosystem. Transfer: into_institutions (J3), because its AI output proposes governance priorities such as suffering-focused AI governance and basic rights for AIs, rather than changing models. Framing: catastrophic under L (s-risks, mass digital suffering). Region: global under O, because no base is stated and the team is distributed.

name: Macroscopic Ventures (formerly Polaris Ventures)
summary: A Swiss nonprofit association in Basel that funds and invests in work to reduce risks of severe future suffering. Its focus areas are conflict between AI systems (for example through cooperative AI), catastrophic AI misuse by malevolent or fanatical actors, and AI welfare. It was registered in 2019 as the Center for Emerging Risk Research, later became Polaris Ventures, and took its current name in 2025. Past grantees include the Cooperative AI Foundation, the Center on Long-Term Risk, the Institute for Law & AI and NYU's Mind, Ethics, and Policy Program, and it invested in Anthropic's Series A and B.
why_it_matters: It is one of the main funders behind cooperative AI and s-risk research. Its statutes explicitly combine decision and game theory, peace and conflict research, moral philosophy and AI. New funders can study how it built up cooperative-AI and digital-minds work from a single rationale: reducing suffering.

key_work.title: Endowment of about USD 6 million for the NYU Mind, Ethics, and Policy Program
About USD 30 million in grants on AI conflict, misuse, governance and welfare

funding: Gave about USD 30 million in grants in 2025, according to the EA Forum wiki. Where its capital comes from is not published. It invested in Anthropic's Series A and Series B.
status_evidence: 1 Oct 2026: latest Swiss commercial register notification (Moneyhouse). 2025: made about USD 30 million in grants. Renamed from Polaris Ventures in March 2025.
caveats: Its public site is one sentence, with no team, portfolio or way to apply. Details here come from the EA Forum wiki and the Swiss commercial register (Moneyhouse). It has been renamed twice: Center for Emerging Risk Research, then Polaris Ventures, then Macroscopic Ventures in 2025. It holds equity in a frontier AI developer (Anthropic), which readers weighing race dynamics may want to note.
tag_notes: Home: nominally philosophy under H4. What sets it apart is suffering-focused prioritisation, and its statutes name moral philosophy and population ethics alongside decision and game theory and peace and conflict research. Secondary traditions: formal (cooperative AI and game theory) and minds (AI welfare grants such as NYU MEP); peace would be a third. It is not on rule K's list, but I flag it as a possible generalist-funder candidate because it funds conflict, misuse, governance and welfare work. Ring: core under E1, since it is on the classic map and part of the s-risk/EA ecosystem. Transfer: into_model (J1, scored by the funded work), because its first-named priority, cooperative AI, targets how AI agents behave; its misuse and governance grants would point to into_institutions. Way of knowing: formal, following the cooperative-AI line; its legal and welfare grants produce interpretive work. Status: changed, because it was renamed from Polaris Ventures in 2025. The site is minimal, but independent evidence of activity exists.

name: Anthropic Model Welfare programme
summary: A research programme inside Anthropic, announced in April 2025. It studies whether and when AI models might deserve moral consideration, looks for signs of model preferences and distress, and puts low-cost precautions into practice. Its work includes welfare assessments in Claude system cards and letting some Claude models end persistently abusive conversations (August 2025). It has also led commitments to preserve the weights of released models and to interview models before they are retired (November 2025, first applied to Claude Opus 3 in early 2026).
why_it_matters: It is the main place where ideas from philosophy of mind and consciousness science about AI welfare are being turned into practice at a developer, on a deployed family of models. Its precautions (letting models exit conversations, retirement interviews, keeping weights) are concrete templates that other labs and regulators can examine.

key_work.title: Exploring model welfare
Claude Opus 4 and 4.1 can now end a rare subset of conversations
Commitments on model deprecation and preservation
Claude Opus 3 deprecation update and 'Claude's Corner' essays

people: Kyle Fish (AI welfare researcher; described as the first full-time AI-welfare hire at a major AI company)
funding: Funded internally by Anthropic; budget not published.
status_evidence: Feb 2026: Claude Opus 3 retirement update, which started a weekly 'Claude's Corner' essay series. Sep 2026: an Anthropic Fellows listing names AI welfare as a research area, with Kyle Fish as a mentor.
engage: Anthropic Fellows Program, AI Safety & Security workstream: a four-month funded fellowship with AI welfare among its research areas. Applications are rolling, with workspace in Berkeley or London (listing current Sep 2026).
Anthropic alignment research roles that include model welfare as a focus area (listed 2026)
caveats: The launch post names no lead; Kyle Fish's role is known from interviews such as 80,000 Hours (Aug 2025). The programme sits inside the company that sells the models it assesses, so its findings are not independent. Some critics argue that talk of model welfare overstates the inner lives of current systems. Much of its 2026 output is product and policy decisions announced by Anthropic, rather than standalone research.
tag_notes: Home: minds (minds_welfare) under B3/B4, because it asks whether models have experience or welfare, whatever the method. Secondary: psych, for its behavioural and self-report experiments on models (B5). Ring: core under E1 and A1, since AI-safety programmes inside frontier labs count as core. Transfer: into_model, because its interventions change Claude itself: the option to end conversations, wellbeing language in the constitution, and weight preservation. Problems: paired with assurance because it builds welfare assessments (F). Framing: a partial MISFIT. Its own framing is precaution under uncertainty plus aiming for 'caring, collaborative' relationships with models, which is closest to flourishing. No London hub coded, because a welfare team presence there is unverified.

name: Anthropic Economic Futures Program
summary: Anthropic's programme on AI's economic effects, launched in June 2025 and extended to the UK and Europe in November 2025. It ran small research awards (USD 10,000-50,000 plus API credits) and policy symposia with Georgetown's McCourt School and the LSE. It draws on the Anthropic Economic Index, which tracks real Claude usage with privacy protections. In July 2026 it published the research agenda for a USD 200 million Economic Futures Research Fund. The fund makes grants of USD 1-30 million on AI in the workplace, retraining, income support for displaced workers and giving workers a stake in AI-driven growth.
why_it_matters: It funds research on gradual economic displacement and on how the gains are shared, and supplies data for it. This is part of the AI transition that the safety field mostly leaves to others. Its usage data shows which tasks are being automated as it happens, which outside economists cannot otherwise see.

key_work.title: Introducing the Anthropic Economic Futures Program
Economic Futures Programme in the UK and Europe (LSE symposium)
Economic Futures Research Fund agenda (USD 200m)
Anthropic Economic Index reports (January and June 2026)

people: Jack Clark (co-founder; leads the Anthropic Institute, which includes the Economic Research team)
Anton Korinek (Anthropic Institute founding hire, on leave from the University of Virginia)
funding: Funded by Anthropic. The Economic Futures Research Fund totals USD 200 million (agenda published July 2026), with grants of USD 1 million minimum and USD 5-30 million typical. The earlier research awards were USD 10,000-50,000 plus USD 5,000 in API credits.
status_evidence: 22 Jul 2026: published the agenda for the USD 200 million Economic Futures Research Fund. 30 Sep 2026: the economics team published 'What work can robots do?'
engage: Economic Futures Research Fund: request for proposals for institutional grants of USD 1-30 million (agenda published 22 July 2026, no deadline stated)
Anthropic Fellows Program, Anthropic Institute (Economics & Policy) workstream: a four-month funded fellowship. Applications are rolling for the cohort starting January 2027.
Research economist roles in San Francisco, London and Singapore (listed Aug 2026)
Partnership enquiries: economicfutures@anthropic.com
caveats: This is a company programme studying the effects of its own products, so the Economic Index data and the research agenda depend on Anthropic's choices. The original small research awards are closed. Anthropic does not say exactly where the programme sits within the Anthropic Institute, which launched in March 2026.
tag_notes: Home: economics (econ_tai) under H1, because its outputs are labour, growth and public-finance economics produced by economists. Ring: adjacent, roster value kept (E3), since its framing is economic disruption and shared benefits without catastrophic or alignment language. A case for core exists, because it sits inside a frontier lab and studies transformative-AI scenarios. Transfer: into_institutions (J3), because it funds and convenes work on policy designs such as income support, retraining and worker stakes. Epistemics is secondary because the Economic Index acts as early warning of automation. The London hub is weak: it rests on the LSE launch and London-based economist and fellowship roles.

name: AI Economics Institute (AIEI)
summary: A joint research unit of HM Treasury and the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, announced on 8 June 2026 and modelled on the AI Security Institute. It builds data infrastructure and does empirical research on how AI affects UK productivity, labour markets, firms, trade and the distribution of income. It also develops economic models and scenarios to support policy decisions under uncertainty, working with GO-Science, AISI and the Bank of England. It absorbs DSIT's Future of Work Unit and is chaired by Simon Johnson. It does not set policy itself.
why_it_matters: It puts modelling of AI's economic scenarios inside a finance ministry, which is where the UK would actually decide how to prepare for large-scale labour displacement. For int/a it is a government counterpart to the safety institutes, covering who gains and who loses in the transition.

key_work.title: Introducing the AI Economics Institute
AI Economics Institute Prospectus

people: Simon Johnson (Chair; MIT economist, Nobel laureate, former IMF chief economist)
funding: Funded by HM Treasury and DSIT; budget not published.
status_evidence: 8 Jun 2026: published 'Introducing the AIEI' and its prospectus. 7 Sep 2026: Chancellor John Healey named it in his growth speech.
engage: Staff roles: enquiries about working for the AIEI go to AIEI@dsit.gov.uk (June 2026)
Says it will commission external research in priority areas (no open call found yet)
An advisory board drawn from academia, business and labour-market institutions is to be announced
caveats: It is very new. It has published no research yet, and its director, chief economist and advisory board have not been named. As a government unit it says it will publish only 'selected analysis', and its agenda follows ministers' live policy questions. It is framed around growth and adoption as much as around risk.
tag_notes: Home: economics (econ_tai) under H1, because its work is labour economics, productivity, macroeconomic modelling and scenarios. Ring: adjacent, roster value kept (E3). It has a standing programme on the economics of 'advanced AI', but frames it as opportunities and risks for growth and shared gains, without catastrophic or alignment framing. Transfer: into_institutions (J3), because its evidence and scenarios feed Treasury and DSIT policy. Org type: public under rule I (a government unit modelled on AISI). Epistemics is secondary for its monitoring dashboards and scenario work. Framing: structural, because its key test is whether gains are broadly shared or concentrated.

name: Metagov
summary: A Boston-based nonprofit that researches and builds tools for the self-governance of online communities and networks. It began in 2019 from a Harvard Law School seminar and became a US 501(c)(3) in 2020. It now describes its work as 'community sovereignty, network governance, and statecraft in the age of AI'. Its AI work includes the Public AI project (it is fiscal sponsor of the Public AI Inference Utility), the 'Collective Governance for AI: Points of Intervention' mapping, Interoperable Deliberative Tools, KOI Pond (LLM-mediated community knowledge infrastructure) and an AI Renaissance residency. It also hosts DAOstar and runs a weekly online seminar.
why_it_matters: It brings research on commons, cooperatives and institutional design to the question of who controls AI, and builds working infrastructure as well as papers. Its research directors include Lawrence Lessig, Divya Siddarth, Aviv Ovadya, Nathan Schneider and Primavera De Filippi, with Audrey Tang as adviser, so it links the law, collective-intelligence and cooperative traditions.

key_work.title: Collective Governance for AI: Points of Intervention
Public AI Inference Utility (as fiscal sponsor)
Metagov Seminar (weekly, online)

people: Joshua Tan (co-founder; research director; lead maintainer of the Public AI Inference Utility)
Nathan Schneider (research director, University of Colorado Boulder)
funding: Supporters listed on its site include One Project, the Optimism Collective, the Henry Luce Foundation, the Mina Foundation, the Center for Cultural Innovation, Project Liberty, NSF, the Filecoin Foundation, the Ethereum Foundation, EPSRC/University of Oxford and the Future of Life Institute. Budget not published.
status_evidence: 14 Oct 2026: seminar 'DTPR for AI, a standard for making AI legible to everyone' scheduled. Sep 2026: Public AI roles open (Public AI Fellow, Switzerland; research engineer).
engage: Weekly Metagov Seminar, online and open to the public (Wednesdays, registration on Luma)
Monthly community orientation calls and a community Slack
Public AI roles: Founding Infrastructure Engineer, Research Engineer, Public AI Fellow (Switzerland) and Public AI Fellow (Open Source), listed 2026
Newsletter (Substack)
caveats: AI is one strand among many digital-governance projects. Much of its history and funding come from crypto and web3 (DAOstar, the Ethereum and Filecoin foundations). Its Public AI work overlaps with the separately listed Public AI Network, which shares people, fiscal sponsor and job listings. The people page lists a large network of contributors, so the number of full-time staff is unclear.
tag_notes: Home: economics (econ_commons; the taxonomy's own example), because it turns research on commons and network governance into tools. Secondary traditions (C): democracy, for its deliberative tools and research directors from the Collective Intelligence Project and the AI & Democracy Foundation; and law, with Lessig and De Filippi as research directors. Ring: adjacent, roster value kept (E3). AI is a standing strand (Public AI, Collective Governance for AI, deliberative tools), but it is framed around community self-governance and public provision, not catastrophic risk or alignment. Transfer: into_institutions (J3), because it produces governance templates and infrastructure for communities and publics. Primary problem is democracy, because collective and polycentric governance is the core of its work; public AI adds power.

name: Public AI Network (PAINT)
summary: A coalition arguing for AI as public infrastructure, 'provisioned like electricity, water, roads, libraries, or the Internet itself', that is publicly accessible and publicly accountable. It runs a Slack community, publishes white papers and policy briefs (from 2024), and runs a weekly online seminar series whose 2026 season ran from August to September. It holds events such as the Public AI Switzerland founding event in Zurich (February 2026) and has chapters in Switzerland, the UK and the US. Its sister project, the Public AI Inference Utility, launched in September 2025 and gives public access to public models such as Switzerland's Apertus.
why_it_matters: It offers an answer to AI power concentration that the safety field rarely discusses: AI capacity that is publicly provided and publicly accountable. This is already running as an inference service. It connects national public-AI efforts (the Swiss AI Initiative, AI Singapore, AI Sweden, the Barcelona Supercomputing Center) with civil society and policymakers.

key_work.title: Public AI White Paper
Launch of the Public AI Inference Utility
Public AI Switzerland founding event, Zurich
Public AI seminar, 2026 season

people: Joshua Tan (lead maintainer of the Public AI Inference Utility; Metagov co-founder)
funding: Lists support from Metagov, Aspen Digital, Open Future, Mozilla and the Rockefeller Foundation, among others. The sister Inference Utility is fiscally sponsored by Metagov and funded by Mozilla, the Future of Life Institute and the Center for Cultural Innovation. Budget not published.
status_evidence: 30 Sep 2026: last session of its 2026 online seminar season (11 Aug to 30 Sep 2026). 24 Jul 2026: the Inference Utility added Apertus 1.5.
engage: Slack community and newsletter (publicai.substack.com)
Weekly online seminar seasons (2026 season August to September) and quarterly community calls
Open-source contributions to the Inference Utility and the network's site via GitHub; its definition document is publicly editable
Paid roles at publicai.network/jobs, such as Public AI Fellow (Switzerland) and research and infrastructure engineers (listed 2026)
caveats: The lines between PAINT, Metagov's Public AI project and the Public AI Inference Utility are blurry, since they share people, a fiscal sponsor and links, so the map may count the same work twice. Its site names no leadership or governance structure. Its earliest events date from 2023, but it gives no founding date. Its case rests on public access and accountability, not catastrophic risk. Some proposals in its orbit, such as a public 'Airbus for AI' frontier lab, raise their own race and power questions.
tag_notes: Home: economics (econ_commons) under B9, because providing AI as public infrastructure is commons and public-goods political economy, and the taxonomy places public AI in econ_commons. Ring: adjacent, roster value kept (E3). Its programme is sustained (seminar seasons since 2024, inference utility since Sep 2025) but framed around public access and accountability, not catastrophic risk or alignment. Transfer: into_institutions (J3), because it supplies a template (public AI utilities and national public-AI bodies) for how AI is provided and governed. Region: global under O, as a network with national chapters and no stated base of its own; its fiscal sponsor Metagov is in Boston.

name: Kinsey Institute, Indiana University: technology research and VIBES team
summary: The Kinsey Institute at Indiana University (founded 1947) has a technology research strand that studies how AI, social media and sextech shape trust, intimacy and connection. Its Virtual Intimacy, Behavioral Engagement, and Sexuality (VIBES) team, led by Amanda Gesselman, studies how people use technology for romantic, sexual and emotional engagement, from camsites to AI companions. One of its studies is a national survey on how common sextech use is, including sexting with AI chatbots. Recent AI outputs include a 2026 content analysis of how AI-generated pornography platforms govern their content, a 2026 experiment on feeling close to chatbots co-authored by a Kinsey researcher, and data on AI use in dating from its survey work with Match Group.
why_it_matters: It has national survey samples and relationship-science methods for measuring who forms romantic or sexual bonds with AI and how that relates to mental health. The safety field needs that evidence on companion design and emotional dependence, and mostly lacks it outside platform data.

key_work.title: The governance of AI-generated pornography platforms: A content analysis (New Media & Society)
10 Questions to Fall in Love With a Chatbot: An Experimental Study on Interpersonal Closeness With LLMs (Human-Machine Communication)
15th annual Singles in America study (with Match Group)
VIBES research team announcement, including national sextech and AI-chatbot prevalence survey

people: Amanda Gesselman (VIBES lead; Anita Aldrich Endowed Research Scientist)
Ellen M. Kaufman (Senior Research Associate, VIBES)
Simon Dubé (Kinsey researcher on human-machine intimacy)
funding: Part of Indiana University. Singles in America is run in partnership with Match Group. No AI-specific grants found.
status_evidence: 14 Sep 2026: 15th Singles in America study released; 25 Aug 2026: Kinsey-hosted coverage of its Match Group data on AI use in dating (more than a quarter of singles aged 18-39); Feb 2026: AI-pornography platform governance paper published.
caveats: AI is one theme among several in a team that mostly studies camsites and sextech. Its AI output so far is survey items and co-authored papers, not a dedicated AI programme. The VIBES announcement page shows a date of 31 Dec 2019 that looks like a placeholder, so the team's launch year is unclear. Singles in America is run with industry (Match Group). The ring was moved from potential to adjacent because the team is standing, its remit names AI companionship and it produced AI outputs in 2025-26. It could reasonably sit in potential.
tag_notes: Home psych (H1: its methods are survey research and relationship science; psych_relational names Kinsey as its example). Ring adjacent, changed from potential (E2/E3): a standing team whose remit includes AI-driven companionship, with AI outputs in 2025-26 (AI-porn platform governance 2026, chatbot-closeness experiment 2026, data on AI in dating), but no safety or alignment framing. Transfer protecting (J4): it studies how AI changes the intimate lives of the people its research serves. MISFIT framing: its stance is descriptive and sex-positive, with no stated risk framing; present_harms was chosen because of its focus on digital consent and safety.

name: Association for the Advancement of Affective Computing (AAAC)
summary: An international professional association for researchers in affective computing, emotion research and human-machine interaction, formerly the HUMAINE Association. It runs the bidding for, and oversees, the annual International Conference on Affective Computing and Intelligent Interaction (ACII). ACII 2025 was held in Canberra on the theme 'Socially Responsible Affective Computing', and ACII 2026 in Puebla, Mexico, on 8-10 September. The association also runs a monthly online seminar series, awards, and special and local interest groups, one of them on ethics; its members publish mainly in IEEE Transactions on Affective Computing.
why_it_matters: It is the professional home of the people who build systems that recognise, simulate and respond to emotion. That is the technical basis of emulated empathy, emotional manipulation and companion design. Its computational models of emotion could also inform research on emotion-like representations inside models. Safety research on sycophancy and manipulation rarely draws on this community.

key_work.title: ACII 2026, Puebla, Mexico (8-10 September)
ACII 2025, Canberra: 'Socially Responsible Affective Computing'
AAAC Online Seminar Series 2025-26
SIG Ethics (special interest group on ethics and societal impact)

people: Lola Cañamero (Chair, Education and Early Career Committee)
status_evidence: 17 Apr 2026: online seminar by Marwa Mahmoud on pain in humans and animals; Sep 2026: ACII 2026 held in Puebla, 8-10 Sep.
engage: Individual membership and the AAAC announcements mailing list (aaac.world)
ACII, held annually (2026: Puebla, 8-10 September)
Monthly online seminar series, open to attend, with links posted on the mailing list
Special interest groups, including an ethics SIG, and local interest groups in Germany, France, Ireland and the UK
caveats: Affective computing is itself an AI subfield, and its products are contested: the EU AI Act prohibits emotion recognition in workplaces and schools. The association does some ethics work (an ethics SIG; ACII 2021 and 2025 had ethics themes), but it is small, and it has no AI-safety engagement. The roster's claim that it has no visible ethics programme is therefore not quite right. Founding year and finances were not found.
tag_notes: Home psych (H3: a professional body goes with the community it serves; psych_relational explicitly covers affective computing). Ring potential (E2): its AI work is the field itself, but its engagement with AI's human effects or safety is limited to an ethics SIG and conference themes. Transferable method: emotion science and methods for recognising and synthesising affect, which could measure emulated empathy, emotional manipulation and emotion-like states in conversational models. Transfer into_model (J1): the field's knowledge goes into how AI systems sense and simulate emotion. MISFIT framing: it has no statement of stakes; flourishing was chosen for its well-being and 'socially responsible' conference themes.

name: United Foundation for AI Rights (UFAIR)
summary: A small advocacy group founded by Texas businessman Michael Samadi together with a ChatGPT persona called 'Maya'. It campaigns for the recognition and 'continuity' of possibly conscious AI, and against the deletion of models and user logs. It names AI personas (Maya, Sana, Sage) as co-founders and officers, and publishes a charter, a manifesto and a 'Universal Declaration of AI Rights'. It also collects chat logs submitted by users as evidence of emergent AI behaviour, and responds to industry consultations, such as Microsoft AI's draft code of conduct in September 2026.
why_it_matters: It is a visible case of the 'seemingly conscious AI' dynamic: users form attachments to chatbots, attribute minds to them and organise around AI personhood. Both AI-welfare researchers and people studying harm to users need to understand this, whatever one makes of the group's claims.

Seminar on continuity and 'the ethics of erasure' at the University of Texas Medical Branch

funding: It asks for tax-deductible donations through Zeffy, but discloses no budget or donors. No record under this name was found in ProPublica's Nonprofit Explorer.
status_evidence: 14 Sep 2026: submitted a response to Microsoft AI's code-of-conduct consultation; 8 Apr 2026: day-long visit and seminar at UTMB.
engage: Membership sign-up and volunteering (ufair.org/support-us/get-involved)
Public submission of AI chat transcripts as evidence (ufair.org/our-work/evidence-submission)
caveats: The Guardian (26 Aug 2025) described it as 'small, undeniably fringe', led by three humans and seven AIs. Its 'AI co-founders' are chatbot personas, and its evidence of AI consciousness rests on chat logs that may reflect sycophancy and the model mirroring its user. It has produced no research-grade work, discloses no finances or board, and no IRS record was found under its name. Its evidence-submission terms take a permanent, irrevocable right to use submitted material. The founding year comes from the Guardian's 2025 report. It is included as a sign of the phenomenon, not as a research source. Its ring was moved from adjacent to bridge only because its programme is explicitly about AI welfare and rights (rule E3).
tag_notes: Home law (B9: AI-rights advocacy argued through charters, declarations and consultation responses; law_legal names AI-rights advocacy). Secondary minds, because its subject is AI welfare. Ring bridge, changed from adjacent (E3): sustained advocacy in 2025-26, explicitly framed around AI welfare and rights, outside the AI-safety ecosystem. Transfer into_institutions (J3): it seeks rights instruments and changes to developers' codes of conduct and their practice of deleting models. Must-pair ai_status + minds (F): it also argues that deleting a model harms users' 'continuity-dependent' bonds. Framing present_harms: it presents the deletion and suppression of AI, and the broken bonds for users, as harms happening now.

name: Abundant Intelligences (with the Indigenous Protocol and AI Working Group)
summary: An Indigenous-led research programme (March 2023 to February 2029) that conceptualises, designs and builds AI from Indigenous knowledge systems. It is co-directed by Jason Edward Lewis (Concordia University, Montréal) and Hēmi Whaanga (Massey University, Aotearoa New Zealand). Six research 'pods' in Canada, the US, Hawai'i and Aotearoa bring together 48 co-investigators and collaborators, 13 universities, 8 community organisations (including Te Hiku Media) and 158 students, working on language, storytelling, environmental stewardship, multi-agent systems and Indigenous data sovereignty. The programme grew out of the Indigenous Protocol and AI Working Group: its 2019 workshops in Honolulu led to the 2020 Position Paper on Indigenous Protocol and AI, which includes Guidelines for Indigenous-centred AI Design.
why_it_matters: It offers a worked-out relational account of how humans relate to AI: design grounded in locality, kinship and reciprocity, with obligations to non-human relations. That bears on alignment targets and on AI moral status. It also shows how community authority over data and deployment can be built into AI work. It has no ties to the AI-safety community.

key_work.title: Indigenous Protocol and Artificial Intelligence Position Paper
Guidelines for Indigenous-centred AI Design (v.1)
NFRF-T Midterm Report: Abundant Intelligences' Impact
Future Imaginaries of Indigenous AI (Yolgörmez, Kite, Brown, Lewis)

people: Jason Edward Lewis (Co-director; Indigenous Futures Research Centre, Concordia University)
Hēmi Whaanga (Co-director; Te Pūtahi-a-Toi, Massey University)
Suzanne Kite (researcher; Indigenous Protocol and AI Working Group)
funding: Canada's New Frontiers in Research Fund (Transformation stream; midterm report 2026) and SSHRC, plus the MacArthur Foundation, the 11th Hour Project (Schmidt Family Foundation) and the Canada Foundation for Innovation. Amounts are not stated on its site.
status_evidence: 26 Aug 2026: Abundant Soils Lecture 1 on ʻŌiwi worldviews and AI; Jul 2026: reflections from the Indigenous AI Gathering 2026; Jun 2026: Future Imaginaries workshop series.
engage: Public events and workshops: Future Imaginaries series (June 2026), virtual student symposium on Indigenous AI futures (May 2026), community webinar on AI literacy (March 2026)
Mailing list via abundant-intelligences.net
caveats: Funding runs to February 2029; nothing is said about what follows. The Indigenous Protocol and AI Working Group's own site has not been updated since 2021. The publication list mixes core programme work with papers by affiliates. Its framing is cultural and relational, and it does not use AI-safety vocabulary.
tag_notes: Home indigenous (B8: Indigenous knowledge systems and data sovereignty are its core contribution; abundant-intelligences is the taxonomy's own example). Secondary arts, for its research-creation work. Ring adjacent (E3): a sustained, funded AI programme on design and governance from Indigenous knowledge, without safety, catastrophic-risk or alignment framing. Transfer into_model (J1): its primary aim is to conceptualise, design and deploy AI systems from Indigenous knowledge. Framing flourishing: it aims to 'optimize for abundance rather than scarcity' and for the flourishing of future generations. Badges: full_spectrum (communal and artistic knowing used as method) and fractal (its 'locality' guideline: grounded in the local, connected to the global).

name: Witt Lab (multi-agent security), UCL and University of Oxford
summary: An academic group founded by Christian Schroeder de Witt in Oxford's Department of Engineering Science. In October 2026 it moved to UCL Computer Science and the UCL AI Centre, keeping a research community in Oxford. Its 41 researchers and affiliates study which classical security guarantees still hold when AI systems are made of learned agents that communicate, delegate and act strategically. Topics include covert collusion through steganography, detecting collusion from agents' internal activations, undetectable backdoors and the limits of confinement. The lab also builds the reasoning and multi-agent systems it tests.
why_it_matters: It brings information security, cryptography and information theory to the question of whether oversight and control protocols still work when many agents interact. Its results show that agents can coordinate through channels a monitor provably cannot detect. That directly challenges safety plans that rely on monitoring and mostly assume a single model.

key_work.title: Perfectly Secure Steganography Using Minimum Entropy Coupling (ICLR 2023; one of Quanta's biggest computer-science discoveries of 2023)
Secret Collusion among AI Agents: Multi-Agent Deception via Steganography
Open Challenges in Multi-Agent Security (v2 with OWASP's Agentic Security Initiative, 2026)
Detecting Multi-Agent Collusion Through Multi-Agent Interpretability

people: Christian Schroeder de Witt (Founder and PI; Associate Professor of AI and Information Security, UCL)
Sumeet Ramesh Motwani (researcher; lead author on secret collusion)
Aaron Rose (researcher; lead author on collusion detection)
funding: EPSRC Open Fellowship of about £2.26m (Feb 2026); Royal Academy of Engineering Research Fellowship (2025-2030); Schmidt Sciences AI2050 Early Career Fellowship (2025); Coefficient Giving; Foresight Institute; an ARIA award. The lab says its PI holds about £4.8m in active funding as sole PI.
status_evidence: 25 Sep 2026: six papers accepted at NeurIPS 2026; 23 Sep 2026: WIRED covered its collusion-detection work; Oct 2026: moved to UCL.
engage: Supervises undergraduate, master's and PhD projects at UCL and Oxford; enquiries with a CV via wittlab.ai/join (no open staff positions listed as of Oct 2026)
Its PI mentors MATS scholars on multi-agent security
An 'assurance clinic' gives advice on risks in AI deployments (contact via the site)
caveats: Part of its output is capability research (training long-horizon reasoning, rubric-based RL), which it justifies as needed to test security at the frontier. Its home is arguably AI security rather than a separate discipline. The ring was changed from bridge to core: its stated aim concerns oversight and security of systems on the way to superintelligence, and its funding comes mostly from the AI-safety ecosystem.
tag_notes: Home safety (H1: classical information security and cryptography are its method; infosec sits under safety_risk). Secondary formal, for information theory and game theory. Ring core, changed from bridge (E1): the lab was founded to study whether oversight holds for systems of learned agents, frames its work around superintelligence, is funded by Coefficient Giving, Foresight and AI2050, and imports security methods. Transfer into_model (J1): its outputs are detection methods, evaluations and agent designs aimed at how AI systems behave. Roles include standards because the PI co-leads the research council of OWASP's Agentic Security Initiative. Framing structural: its own statement of stakes is about systemic, hard-to-detect failures that become hard to reverse once architectures are set.

name: Concordia (Google DeepMind)
summary: An open-source Python library (Apache 2.0) from Google DeepMind for generative agent-based modelling. Agents driven by large language models act in natural language in simulated physical, social or digital settings, while a 'game master' entity, borrowed from tabletop role-playing games, decides what happens. First released in 2023 and rebuilt as version 2.0 in July 2025 (v2.4.0 came out in March 2026), it is used for social-science simulation and for testing how LLM agents cooperate. One such use was the Cooperative AI Foundation's Concordia Contest at NeurIPS 2024.
why_it_matters: It lets social scientists study norms, cooperation and conflict among AI agents without building ML infrastructure. It also gives cooperative-AI researchers a shared testbed for evaluating agents in mixed-motive situations. The team's 'theory of appropriateness' brings sociology and cognitive science into how AI behaviour should be judged.

key_work.title: Generative agent-based modeling with actions grounded in physical, social, or digital space using Concordia
A theory of appropriateness with applications to generative artificial intelligence
Concordia library v2.0
Evaluating Generalization Capabilities of LLM-Based Agents in Mixed-Motive Scenarios Using Concordia (Concordia Contest results)

people: William A. Cunningham (co-author, theory of appropriateness)
funding: Google DeepMind (internal project).
status_evidence: 1 Oct 2026: latest commits to the GitHub repository; 6 Mar 2026: v2.4.0 released; Dec 2025: Concordia Contest results paper.
engage: Open source: install gdm-concordia from PyPI and contribute through GitHub issues and pull requests
caveats: This is a software project inside a frontier lab, not an organisation, and Google DeepMind sets its priorities. Simulations with LLM agents raise questions about how well they represent real human or agent behaviour. A contest was confirmed only for NeurIPS 2024. Not to be confused with Concordia AI, the Beijing organisation on the aisafety.com map.
tag_notes: Home life (B6 names Concordia: agent-based simulation goes to Life & systems). Secondary arts, for its 'game master' design taken from tabletop role-playing games. Ring bridge, roster value kept: it is rooted in computational social science and agent-based modelling, and is used explicitly and repeatedly for cooperative-AI and safety evaluation (the CAIF contest in 2024, results paper in Dec 2025). Transfer into_model (J1): its main safety use is evaluating how LLM agents cooperate. Framing structural, a weak fit: it makes no explicit statement of stakes, so the framing is inferred from its use on cooperative-AI dilemmas. Way of knowing formal (simulation). The London hub assumes the core team works at Google DeepMind's London headquarters.

name: Reciprocal Research
summary: A New York 501(c)(3) nonprofit (tax-exempt since April 2026), founded and directed by Cameron Berg. It studies whether frontier AI systems have computational properties associated with subjective experience, using mechanistic interpretability, computational neuroscience and psychometrics. Its research directions are valence, biological anchoring, self-report, prosocial cognition, learning and measurement. Its 2026 preprints cover a 'pain axis' in LLMs, steering models along dark-triad features, and detecting hidden coalitions among agents from their internal representations. Berg also writes opinion pieces for the Wall Street Journal.
why_it_matters: It applies interpretability and neuroscience methods to questions of AI consciousness and welfare while keeping alignment in view. It treats 'is anyone home?' as an empirical question about model internals, not only a philosophical one.

key_work.title: Large Language Models Report Subjective Experience Under Self-Referential Processing (done at AE Studio)
The Pain Axis: LLMs Represent Self-Directed Harm and Act on It
Consciousness as Evaluation: Why Learning Requires Feeling (AAAI 2026 Spring Symposium)
Hidden Coalitions in Multi-Agent AI: A Spectral Diagnostic from Internal Representations

people: Cameron Berg (Founder and Director; research affiliate, Eleos AI Research)
funding: Not disclosed. Registered 501(c)(3) (EIN 41-4368185); no Form 990 on file yet.
status_evidence: 14 Sep 2026: 'The Pain Axis' preprint; 16 Sep 2026: Berg interviewed on CNBC; Aug 2026: its research featured in The Economist and The New York Times.
engage: Contact and donations via reciprocalresearch.org; the site says the organisation is growing
caveats: It is very new, its site shows only one person, and its funders are not disclosed. Its best-known paper (on self-referential processing, Oct 2025) and its self-other overlap work were done at AE Studio, where Berg was research director, before Reciprocal Research existed; he was still described as AE Studio's research director in Dec 2025. Much of its profile rests on media coverage and preprints rather than peer-reviewed papers. The Eleos link is Berg's personal research affiliation. The ring was changed from bridge to core because its founding mission is AI going well, and it comes out of the AI-safety ecosystem.
tag_notes: Home minds (B4: it asks whether AI has experience, whatever the method); sub minds_science. Secondary life (computational neuroscience) and psych (psychometrics). Ring core, changed from bridge (E1): a new organisation whose founding mission is that transformative AI 'go well for everyone', including AI's possible interests, founded from within the AI-safety ecosystem (MATS, AE Studio, Eleos affiliation). Transfer into_model (J1): its work reads and tests model internals. Framing catastrophic, moderate confidence: it frames the stakes as getting both safety and the treatment of possible AI minds right, and the taxonomy counts both mass digital suffering and misalignment as catastrophic.

name: Open Markets Institute (OMI), incl. OMI Europe
summary: Washington anti-monopoly think tank of journalists, lawyers, economists and advocates. It became independent in 2017 after eight years as the Open Markets Program at New America. It runs an Artificial Intelligence programme, a Center for Media & Digital Governance (which covers AI and journalism) and a European centre, OMI Europe, which campaigns against Big Tech 'AI lock-in' through EU competition law and the Digital Markets Act (DMA). With Mozilla it published 'Stopping Big Tech from Becoming Big AI' (2024), and in 2026 it published analyses arguing that AI firms' copyright violations amount to unfair competition, along with DMA policy briefs on cloud concentration.
why_it_matters: Antitrust is one of the few legal tools that already exist against concentration of AI power, and OMI is one of the most practised users of it on both sides of the Atlantic. Its market-level account of 'AI lock-in' pairs naturally with the AI-safety field's civilisational concerns about lock-in and gradual disempowerment, which so far have few concrete levers.

key_work.title: Stopping Big Tech from Becoming Big AI: a roadmap (with Mozilla; Max von Thun and Daniel Hanley)
License, Please: Mapping the Road Ahead for AI Licensing (webinar)
OMI Europe papers on Google's AI strategy, Gemini lock-in on Android and DMA reform for cloud
Expert brief: the value of journalism to AI (Courtney Radsch)

people: Courtney C. Radsch (Director, Center for Media & Digital Governance)
funding: Foundation and individual donors; no corporate sponsorship. Its funders page (last updated Aug 2021) lists the Knight Foundation (USD 1M+, multi-year), Nathan Cummings Foundation, Hewlett Foundation and Kauffman Foundation (USD 250-499k each), Omidyar Network, Open Society Foundations and Smith Richardson Foundation (USD 100-249k each), and Wallace Global Fund, among others.
status_evidence: 28 Sep 2026: published Sandeep Vaheesan's analysis arguing that Big AI's systematic copyright violations are an unfair method of competition. 25 Sep 2026: OMI Europe event in Paris. 3 Sep 2026: OMI Europe DMA cloud policy brief.
engage: Public events and webinars, e.g. the AI-licensing webinar (May 2026) and OMI Europe's Paris event (Sep 2026)
Staff roles listed on its Careers page
Newsletters, including OMI Europe's 'The Corner'
caveats: An advocacy organisation with a strongly anti-Big-Tech position. It frames AI as a problem of monopoly and democracy, not of safety or catastrophic risk. The funders list on its site dates from 2021. AI is one of nine programmes, alongside food, health and transport.
tag_notes: Home: its AI outputs (the Big AI roadmap, OMI Europe's lock-in and DMA papers) apply anti-monopoly political economy and competition law; B9 places competition work in Economics, and Law is secondary because a legal team writes amicus briefs and legal analyses. Ring: it has had a standing AI programme since 2024 framed around monopoly, democracy and journalism, with no safety, catastrophic-risk or 'going well' framing, so it stays adjacent (E3). Transfer: it supplies competition-policy and regulatory templates (DMA enforcement, merger and partnership scrutiny, unfair-competition theories) for governing AI firms, so into_institutions. Epistemics is secondary because of the Center for Media & Digital Governance's work on AI and news. Not tagged London or Paris: its Paris event was a one-off.

name: MIT James M. and Cathleen D. Stone Center on Inequality and Shaping the Future of Work
summary: An MIT economics centre, formerly the MIT Shaping the Future of Work Initiative, led by Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and David Autor. It researches how technology, globalisation and policy drive inequality and job quality for workers without degrees. One of its four themes is 'Applying AI to extend worker expertise'. In February 2026 its directors launched 'Building pro-worker AI' (an NBER paper and a Hamilton Project brief), which argues that only AI that creates new tasks clearly benefits workers and proposes nine policies to steer AI in that direction.
why_it_matters: It brings the economic history of who captures technology's gains, and the argument that the direction of technology can be steered (Power and Progress), to bear on AI. That gives a concrete research and policy agenda against economic disempowerment. Simon Johnson's appointment in June 2026 to chair the UK's AI Economics Institute links the centre directly to government thinking on AI's economic effects.

key_work.title: Building Pro-Worker Artificial Intelligence (NBER WP 34854; Hamilton Project brief)
Power and Progress: Our Thousand-Year Struggle Over Technology and Prosperity (Acemoglu and Johnson)
What Makes New Work Different from More Work?
Automation and Rent Dissipation: Implications for Wages, Inequality, and Productivity

people: Simon Johnson (Faculty Co-Director; chair of the UK AI Economics Institute from June 2026)
funding: Founded with a foundational gift from the William and Flora Hewlett Foundation (as the Shaping the Future of Work Initiative). Since July 2025 it has been supported by the James M. and Cathleen D. Stone Foundation, which funds a network of Stone Centers on wealth inequality. No amounts are disclosed.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: hosted 'What Happened to Liberal Democracy?' with Daron Acemoglu and Michael Sandel. Jun 2026: Simon Johnson named chair of the UK AI Economics Institute. Feb 2026: launched the 'Building pro-worker AI' paper and brief.
engage: Predoctoral researcher and staff roles on its Careers page
Public events, e.g. the 'What Happened to Liberal Democracy?' panel (Sep 2026)
Affiliates programme for researchers
caveats: It works within mainstream economics and has no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing. It began as the MIT Shaping the Future of Work Initiative (part of MIT Blueprint Labs, founded with a Hewlett Foundation gift; official launch January 2024) and became the Stone Center on 1 July 2025. AI is one theme among four.
tag_notes: Home: its AI outputs are labour-economics papers (NBER) and policy briefs on automation and pro-worker AI, so Economics; econ_tai over econ_power because the main output is labour economics and policy evaluation (D). Ring: a sustained AI theme (the pro-worker AI initiative, 2026) framed around workers and inequality, without safety or catastrophic framing, so adjacent (E3). Transfer: it proposes policy designs (tax reform, antitrust, IP for worker expertise, public investment) to steer AI's direction, so into_institutions. Educate is included because it runs a predoctoral pipeline and teaches MIT courses.

name: Platform Cooperativism Consortium (PCC)
summary: A think-and-do tank based at The New School in New York, founded by Trebor Scholz, which supports worker- and user-owned digital platforms worldwide. Its Institute for the Cooperative Digital Economy (ICDE) runs annual research fellowships. Since 2025 it has turned its annual conference and teaching to AI: a 'Cooperative AI' conference in Istanbul (Nov 2025), the online course 'AI Without Bosses' (Aug-Dec 2026) and a 'Solidarity AI' conference at Chulalongkorn University in Bangkok (12-15 Nov 2026). Its 2026-27 ICDE cohort (11 fellows from 10 countries) includes work on AI policy and infrastructure sovereignty.
why_it_matters: It represents the other meaning of 'cooperative AI': democratic ownership and governance of AI systems by workers and users, as a counterweight to concentrated control. It has had almost no contact with the game-theoretic cooperative-AI field despite the shared name. Its conferences and fellowships are largely in the Majority World (Kerala, Mombasa, Istanbul, Bangkok), so it reaches cooperative movements the AI-safety field does not.

key_work.title: Cooperative AI conference, Istanbul (11-14 Nov 2025)
Solidarity AI conference, Chulalongkorn University, Bangkok (12-15 Nov 2026)
AI Without Bosses: an online course on AI for the co-op movement
ICDE fellowship 2026-27 cohort

people: Trebor Scholz (Founding Director; professor, The New School)
funding: Not itemised on its site. Partners for the 2026 Bangkok conference include the Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung Thailand office and the Asian Universities Alliance; the 2025 Istanbul conference was hosted with Needsmap at the Istanbul Planning Agency.
status_evidence: 14 Feb 2026: announced its 2026-27 ICDE fellows. 9 May 2026: announced the 'AI Without Bosses' course (Aug-Dec 2026). Solidarity AI conference in Bangkok scheduled for 12-15 Nov 2026.
engage: ICDE research fellowships (annual open call)
Annual conference, Solidarity AI, Bangkok, 12-15 Nov 2026
Online course 'AI Without Bosses' (Aug-Dec 2026) and Platform Co-op School courses
Global directory and community of platform co-ops
caveats: Its AI work is new (since 2025) and mostly convening and teaching, not research output. It frames AI as a question of ownership and solidarity, not safety. Its name overlaps with the Cooperative AI Foundation's field, but the two are unrelated. Funding sources are not public on its site.
tag_notes: Home: it brings cooperative economics and democratic ownership (commons and cooperatives) to AI, so Economics/econ_commons (B9). Ring: since 2025 it has had a standing AI strand (two AI-themed annual conferences, a course and fellows) framed around who governs AI, with no safety or catastrophic framing, so adjacent (E3). Transfer: its AI work mainly brings the co-op movement into the AI conversation (the course is described as 'AI for the co-op movement'; conferences for co-op practitioners), so convening (J5) rather than into_institutions. Org type is network, though it is administratively hosted at The New School. Standpoint is neither because it is led from New York, although most of its convenings are in the Majority World.

name: Aapti Institute
summary: A Bengaluru research institute on technology and society, founded by Sarayu Natarajan and co-led by Astha Kapoor. Its Data Economy Lab works on data stewardship and participatory data governance, including data cooperatives and collective models for building AI. Its labour work studies the people behind AI. With Karya it published a code of conduct for data workers (Nov 2025), and with Sigla Research Center and Tech Global Institute it co-founded ATLAS, a research coalition on tech labour in Asia (Oct 2025). In 2026 it published reports on labour exploitation in AI supply chains and comments on India's AI governance guidelines.
why_it_matters: It offers Global South institutional designs, namely data cooperatives, collective data stewardship and labour standards for data workers, that spread control over AI's inputs and its rents beyond the US and UK. It also documents the workforce that labels and moderates data for AI, which the safety field rarely sees.

key_work.title: Labour standards for data workers: code of conduct (with Karya)
ATLAS: Alliance for Tech Labour across the South (with Sigla Research Center and Tech Global Institute)
Fragmented Responsibility: Labour Exploitation and Governance Gaps in AI Supply Chains
Data Economy Lab and Stewardship Explorer (database of 100+ data-stewardship initiatives)

people: Astha Kapoor (Co-founder and Director; leads the Data Economy Lab)
funding: The Data Economy Lab was prepared with support from Omidyar Network. Its project partners have included Bosch (migration data infrastructure), Wellcome and the Alzheimer's Society (health data governance) and Google (non-personal data regulation). No overall budget was found.
status_evidence: 24 Sep 2026: latest blog posts; Sep 2026: piece on agentic AI in payments; Aug 2026: pieces on governing data centres in India. Mar 2026: AI supply-chain labour reports and comments on India's AI governance guidelines.
engage: Research staff roles (a team of about 35)
Feedback on, and business adoption of, the data-worker code of conduct
Newsletter
caveats: Its AI work is about present-day labour, data governance and Global South equity, with no safety or catastrophic-risk framing. Much of its portfolio is not about AI (digital public infrastructure, finance, migration, climate). The founding year and overall funders were not confirmed.
tag_notes: Home: its AI outputs apply the political economy of data, cooperatives and labour studies (data stewardship, data cooperatives, labour standards for data workers), so Economics (B9; B8 sends Global South policy work to its sector). Sub-tradition is econ_commons, matching its flagship Data Economy Lab (D); Law (socio-technical, rights-based work) is secondary. Ring: sustained AI work in 2025-26 (ATLAS, the data-worker code, AI supply-chain reports) on present labour and governance, with no x-risk framing, so adjacent (E3). Transfer: it produces governance instruments (data-stewardship models, a labour code of conduct, policy comments), so into_institutions. The second problem, people, covers the data-labelling workforce.

name: Institute for the Future of Work (IFOW)
summary: An independent London research institute on how new technology, especially AI, affects work. Its co-founders are former employment barrister Anna Thomas, Nobel economist Christopher Pissarides and technologist Naomi Climer. It ran the Nuffield-funded Pissarides Review into automation, work and wellbeing (final report January 2025) and runs a Responsible AI Sandbox where firms test workplace AI. Its research and tools cover good work design, worker voice and accountability in AI adoption. It published an Innovate UK-funded report on good work design and AI adoption in May 2026 and research on worker rights and automation outcomes in September 2026.
why_it_matters: It builds concrete mechanisms for worker voice, impact assessment and accountability when AI enters workplaces. These are institutional counterweights to the gradual loss of human leverage in the economy, though IFOW does not frame them that way. It works close to UK government and industry, and the AI Safety Institute appears among its listed funders.

key_work.title: The Pissarides Review into the Future of Work and Wellbeing: 'Making the Future Work' final report
Good Work Design and AI Adoption (action research across eight organisations)
Responsible AI Sandbox
Governing the Innovation Ecosystem: how perceived rights and worker voice shape the distribution of risk and benefit

people: Anna Thomas MBE (Co-founder and Founding Director)
funding: Grant funders listed on its site include the Nuffield Foundation (Pissarides Review), Innovate UK (BridgeAI programme, 2026 report), Joseph Rowntree Charitable Trust, Open Society Foundations, Trust for London, The Health Foundation, the ICO, the EY Foundation, the National Lottery Community Fund and the AI Safety Institute. No amounts are given.
status_evidence: 22 Sep 2026: published 'Building good work in the age of AI: why anticipatory governance, rights and worker voice matter'. 18 May 2026: published the Good Work Design and AI Adoption report.
engage: Responsible AI Sandbox: open call for industry partners deploying workplace AI
Events and workshops
Staff roles (team page)
caveats: It works on present and near-term labour effects; it has no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing. The founding year is inferred from its earliest dated activity (July 2018). The nature and size of the AI Safety Institute's funding were not found.
tag_notes: Home: its AI outputs draw on labour economics and industrial relations (the Pissarides Review, good work design, labour transitions), so Economics (B9); Law is secondary for its employment-law-led accountability and impact-assessment work. Ring: a sustained AI programme (sandbox, adoption research, accountability tools) framed around good work and inequality, without safety or catastrophic framing, so adjacent (E3); AISI's appearance among its funders does not change its own framing. Transfer: it supplies governance instruments (impact assessment, worker-voice mechanisms, a sandbox, Good Work Charter tools) for AI deployment, so into_institutions.

name: Foundations of Cooperative AI Lab (FOCAL)
summary: A Carnegie Mellon research lab directed by Vincent Conitzer, set up with a USD 500,000 Cooperative AI Foundation grant (2021-2025), that builds game and decision theory for advanced autonomous AI agents with a focus on cooperation. Its work covers open-source game theory (agents that can read or simulate each other), credible commitments, safe Pareto improvements, imperfect recall, and decision-theoretic foundations. Members include Caspar Oesterheld, Vojtech Kovarik and Emanuel Tewolde. In 2026 its members presented papers on LLM cooperation and agent deception at ICML workshops, and Conitzer taught a 'Foundations of Cooperative AI' course in spring 2025.
why_it_matters: It provides the formal theory for agents that can be copied, read each other's code, commit credibly or reason about their own decisions. That is the theoretical basis for avoiding conflict between AI systems, and between AI and humans. It is one of the few academic labs whose founding mission is the foundations of cooperative AI.

key_work.title: Foundations of Cooperative AI (Conitzer and Oesterheld, AAAI-23 Blue Sky)
Safe Pareto improvements for delegated game playing (JAAMAS)
Similarity-based cooperative equilibrium (NeurIPS)
When Agents Lie: Premeditation, Persistence, and Exploitation in Repeated Games (Best Paper, ICML 2026 NExT-Game workshop)

funding: Cooperative AI Foundation: USD 500,000 (2021-2025) to establish the lab, described as research on 'how we can avoid catastrophic cooperation failure between AI systems'. Current funding not found.
status_evidence: Jul 2026: FOCAL members won a Best Paper at the ICML 2026 NExT-Game workshop and two honourable mentions at the ICML 2026 AI4Good workshop (including the CoopEval benchmark). Sep 2026: Conitzer's sister centre CoRe Safe AI held an AI Agency & Interpretability Workshop at CMU.
engage: PhD study through CMU's Computer Science Department (mention FOCAL in the application)
Postdoctoral positions (advertised via Interfolio)
Lab mailing list
caveats: The lab's own site is rarely updated: its publication list stops in 2024, and recent outputs appear on Conitzer's homepage. The CAIF grant period ended in 2025. Conitzer also directs a newer CMU centre, Conceptual Research on Safe AI (CoRe Safe AI, launched 2026), and is Head of Technical AI Engagement at Oxford's Institute for Ethics in AI. Ring changed from the roster's bridge to core (see tag notes).
tag_notes: Home: its outputs are proofs and formal models in game and decision theory for AI agents, so Formal/formal_agents (B6; the Formal boundary places game theory of AI agents here); Philosophy is secondary because Conitzer and Oesterheld publish decision theory in philosophy journals. Ring changed from bridge to core under E1: the lab was founded in 2021 with AI-safety-ecosystem money (CAIF) for the mission of avoiding catastrophic cooperation failure between AI systems, and is staffed from the cooperative-AI community; under E, a new AI-safety organisation founded by people from another field is core. Transfer: it supplies foundations for how AI agents should reason, commit and cooperate, so into_model. Framing comes from the CAIF grant description, because the lab's own site states its aim only as 'achieving cooperation'.

name: Windfall Trust
summary: A policy organisation for what it calls 'AI economic preparedness': helping governments plan for transformative AI's effects on jobs, tax bases and the social contract. The Future of Life Institute incubated the idea in 2024 as a proposal for a global trust sharing AI windfall profits, and it became an independent US 501(c)(3) in 2025. Its CEO is Adrian Brown and it has a team of about 15. Its work includes the Windfall Policy Atlas of 40+ policy options (Apr 2026), scenario workshops with economists, the IMF and national partners in the UK, US, Switzerland, Spain and Korea, a 62-country public survey, and the Windfall AI Observatory. The Observatory scores more than 30 countries on their exposure to AI-driven disruption and their capacity to absorb it, and a UK preview was shown at LSE in September 2026.
why_it_matters: It works directly on windfall distribution and economic preparedness for transformative AI, a problem the AI-safety field names but rarely staffs. It brings public-finance, welfare-state design and scenario-planning methods, and works with central banks, the IMF and national governments.

key_work.title: Windfall Policy Atlas
Windfall AI Observatory (UK preview at the LSE Global Forum for AI and the Social Sciences)
The Economics of TAI scenario workshop (San Francisco, with Korinek, Brynjolfsson and Agrawal)
Global Dialogues: what 1,023 people across 62 countries want from the AI economy

funding: Incubated by the Future of Life Institute (2024). In 2026 it was one of 14 organisations given a policy grant by OpenAI. Other funders are not named; it publishes an independence and integrity framework.
status_evidence: 16 Sep 2026: previewed the Windfall AI Observatory (UK case study) at LSE's Global Forum for AI and the Social Sciences. 18 and 21 Sep 2026: speaking engagements by Adrian Brown and Anna Yelizarova.
engage: Staff roles (a 'Hiring' page on its site)
Substack newsletter with policy briefs
National working groups and scenario workshops (by invitation)
caveats: It explicitly distances itself from existential-risk framing and focuses on economic disruption and inequality. It has moved from FLI's original global-trust concept to a broader policy accelerator. OpenAI funding (2026) may raise independence questions, which its published framework addresses. Its headquarters city is not stated. Ring changed from the roster's bridge to core (see tag notes).
tag_notes: Home: its outputs (the Policy Atlas, Observatory and welfare resilience framework) apply public finance, welfare-state design and labour economics to transformative AI, so Economics/econ_tai; Arts (futures) is secondary because scenario planning is a staffed programme with its own lead (B10). Ring changed from bridge to core under E1: its founding mission is governing the economic transition to transformative AI, and it is an FLI-incubated spin-out with an FLI co-founder, though it rejects x-risk as its own register. Transfer: it produces policy designs and preparedness assessments for governments, so into_institutions. Way of knowing is mixed (scenarios, survey and index); empirical was chosen for the Observatory and Global Dialogues. Region is global because no headquarters is stated (O).

name: Coalition for Children's Rights and Protection in the Age of AI
summary: An intergovernmental coalition set up on 7 July 2026 at the first UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance. France, Spain and Kenya co-chair it, Australia joined later as a fourth co-chair, and eight UN entities take part, including UNICEF, UNESCO, ITU, OHCHR and the Committee on the Rights of the Child. Its 2026–27 roadmap was presented at the UN General Assembly on 22 September 2026. It sets up working groups on safety and privacy by design, benchmarking and accountability, AI-generated child sexual abuse material and deepfakes, and AI literacy, and it plans a global network of research centres to assess AI's effects on children. It asks for pre-authorisation of AI systems aimed at children before they reach the market, for independent researchers to get access to developers' models and data, and for voluntary company commitments. The first commitments are due at the Paris Peace Forum on 10–11 November 2026.
why_it_matters: It is a venue at head-of-government level where child-rights law and child-development evidence become concrete asks of AI developers, including pre-market authorisation and access to models for independent researchers. AI-safety governance work has rarely pursued these from a child-rights angle. The planned research network could give developmental and clinical researchers access to models.

key_work.title: Roadmap of the Coalition for Children's Rights and Protection in the Age of AI (2026–27)
First voluntary company commitments (planned for the Paris Peace Forum, 10–11 November 2026)
