Companies are invited to make voluntary commitments; the first batch is due at the Paris Peace Forum, 10–11 November 2026
caveats: The only source found is the French presidency's announcement. The coalition has no website or secretariat of its own. That page gives both 26 and 23 member states, and lists only the four co-chairs and the eight UN entities. The commitments it seeks from companies are voluntary. It is separate from iRAISE, the multistakeholder coalition co-led by everyone.AI and the Paris Peace Forum. Independent confirmation could not be sought because this session's web-search budget had run out.
tag_notes: Home law (B9): the coalition is framed by children's rights, with OHCHR and the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child among its members; secondary peace for its UN and multilateral diplomacy. Ring adjacent, kept from the roster (E3): 'safety' here means child safety, not catastrophic risk or alignment. Transfer protecting (J4): it produces governance asks, but their stated purpose is to defend children, its constituency (the into_institutions boundary). Problems: justice first because it is a rights and accountability venue; assurance for pre-authorisation, benchmarking and researcher access. Region global: four co-chair states and no seat. MISFIT: org_type coded public (an intergovernmental coalition of states and UN entities), but it has no secretariat and could equally be coded network. No Paris hub: the evidence shows French leadership and one planned Paris event, not regular activity.

name: AI Psychological Research Coalition (AIPRC)
summary: A research coalition founded by the education researcher Zak Stein. It launched at Davos in January 2026 as the AI Psychological Harms Research Coalition (aiphrc.org now redirects to aiprc.org). Its Behavioral Data Research Initiative is an IRB-approved study at UNC Chapel Hill, with the psychologist Mitch Prinstein as principal investigator. It collects anonymised chat logs, screenshots and written accounts from adults about psychological changes after regular chatbot use, from compulsive use and cognitive dependency to identity disruption and severe mental-health effects. The stated aim is to develop clinical tools and inform safer design and policy. Partners are UNC's Winston Center on Technology and Brain Development, the Center for Humane Technology, Fairplay and the Human Change Foundation; the conference page also lists the Future of Life Institute and The Human Movement. Its first annual conference, invitation only and capped at 150, is planned for 18–20 October 2026 at UNC.
why_it_matters: It is building a clinical evidence base on harms from companion-style and sycophantic chatbots that work through attachment: 'attachment hacking', AI-associated psychosis and subclinical attachment disorders. Model evaluations rarely measure these failure modes. Its founder, Zak Stein, is a metamodern education thinker, which makes it one of the few direct links between this research and the int/a milieu.

key_work.title: Behavioral Data Research Initiative (anonymised submissions of experiences with AI)
Attachment Hacking and the Rise of AI Psychosis (Your Undivided Attention episode with Zak Stein)
AIPRC First Annual Conference, UNC Chapel Hill, 18–20 October

people: Mitch Prinstein (principal investigator, UNC Chapel Hill)
Tristan Harris (director of outreach; co-founder of the Center for Humane Technology)
Kathryn Morrissey (head of coalition building and network engagement)
status_evidence: Oct 2026: first annual conference scheduled for 18–20 October at UNC Chapel Hill (conference page last updated April 2026; site updated May 2026)
engage: Adults (18+) can submit anonymised accounts, chat logs or screenshots of their experiences with AI through the UNC research platform
Requests for an invitation to the first annual conference (18–20 October 2026, Chapel Hill; invitation only, 150 places)
caveats: It launched in 2026 and changed its name within months, so its track record is short and it has published no findings yet. Its data come from self-selected submissions, which can document the range of harms but not how common they are. Funding is not disclosed. On 1 October 2026 the Center for Humane Technology, which supplies AIPRC's director of outreach, announced that it is winding down its own research coordination and psychosocial-evaluation work; the effect on AIPRC is unclear. The site states it is a research platform, not a crisis service.
tag_notes: Home psych (H1): an IRB study of AI-related psychological conditions, led by a UNC psychologist and aimed at clinical tools. Sub psych_clinical rather than psych_relational because the main output documents conditions for clinicians, though attachment theory frames the work. Ring bridge, kept from the roster (E3): it aims at safer AI design, puts safety-testing frameworks on its conference agenda, and counts CHT and FLI as partners. It is borderline adjacent, since its framing is present harms. Transfer protecting (J4): it documents harm to users, especially young people, to support clinicians and policy. No secondary tradition: Stein's integral and metamodern background is his own, not the coalition's method. Way of knowing empirical: lived-experience submissions are gathered as IRB research data (communal would be the alternative). The invitation-only conference counts under the convene role, not under events engagement.

name: Center for Humane Technology (CHT)
summary: A San Francisco nonprofit founded in 2018 by Tristan Harris, Aza Raskin and Randima Fernando. It grew out of the 'time well spent' critique of attention-maximising social media and now applies the same incentive analysis to AI. Its main outputs are public communication and policy principles. On the communication side are the Your Undivided Attention podcast (31 million downloads), the talk The AI Dilemma and the 2026 film The AI Doc, which features its founders. The policy principles are The AI Roadmap: seven principles including a duty of care, independent safety testing and internationally agreed limits on AI development. On 1 October 2026 it announced a narrower strategy. It is keeping public education, briefings for decision-makers and private coordination aimed at changing the incentives behind the AI race. It is winding down in-house policy, litigation advice, research coordination, evaluations of psychosocial impacts and a planned fellows programme, with significant staff cuts.
why_it_matters: It treats AI risk as a problem of incentives and race dynamics rather than technical alignment, and carries the social-media 'race to the bottom of the brain stem' analysis over to AI companions and 'attachment hacking'. It reaches far larger general audiences than any AI-safety organisation, yet it is not on the aisafety.com map.

key_work.title: The AI Dilemma (talk by Tristan Harris and Aza Raskin)
The AI Doc: Or How I Became an Apocaloptimist (film featuring CHT's founders)
The AI Roadmap (seven principles for AI policy)
Attachment Hacking and the Rise of AI Psychosis (podcast episode with Zak Stein)

people: Randima Fernando (co-founder; interim executive director from October 2026)
funding: Donor-funded nonprofit. Revenue was about $5.8M and expenses about $5.8M in fiscal year 2025 (Form 990, via ProPublica); contributions were 93% of revenue. 2023 was an unusually strong year (net income about $6.1M), followed by a deficit of about $2.7M in 2024. It lists some 40 lead supporters (foundations and individuals); no breakdown found.

Foundations of Humane Technology course (free) is paused while a version on AI and social media is prepared; sign-up for notification
No open positions as of October 2026
caveats: It restructured on 1 October 2026. Its policy, litigation-advisory, research-coordination and evaluation work is being wound down, so earlier lines of work may not continue, among them AI product-liability frameworks, expert support for litigation against Character.AI and OpenAI, and psychosocial evaluations. Its team page was still listing the previous executive director. Its framing centres on incentives and present harms rather than loss of control, and its main outputs are media and advocacy rather than research.
tag_notes: Home psych (H1/H2): what it brings is the persuasive-technology critique of attention and attachment, i.e. the psychology of persuasion (psych_social); secondary arts for its film and podcast production. H3 could argue for an arts home, since its main output since October 2026 is general-audience media; psych was kept because the substance it communicates is psychological. Ring bridge, kept from the roster (E3): it is rooted in the humane-design and attention-economy field and runs a standing AI programme framed around the AI race and 'AI going well'. Transfer into_institutions (J3): it aims to change the incentives and governance of AI development through briefings, The AI Roadmap and private coordination. Quadrants Its+I follow worked example G. Framing structural: its own statements stress incentives and race dynamics, not existential risk. Badge speed_of_wisdom: it argues explicitly for de-escalating the AI race and for internationally agreed limits on development. Status left active, not changed: the October 2026 refocus narrows its activities but keeps the same mission and leadership. No engagement tags: there are no openings and the course is paused.

name: Advancing Humans with AI (AHA), MIT Media Lab
summary: A multi-faculty research programme at the MIT Media Lab, launched with a symposium on 10 April 2025 and co-led by Pattie Maes and Pat Pataranutaporn. It studies how everyday AI use affects cognition, emotion, memory, motivation and relationships, and designs AI meant to support human flourishing. Outputs include a study run jointly with OpenAI on affective use of ChatGPT and a longitudinal randomised controlled trial of chatbot use, both from 2025. Others are the EEG study 'Your Brain on ChatGPT' on cognitive debt, work on false memories induced by AI-edited media, a survey of the state of AI and human flourishing, and an open benchmark for the human impact of AI. Its 2026 symposium, 'Raised by AI?' (28 April), focused on children. It offers $5,000–10,000 micro-grants to Media Lab researchers.
why_it_matters: It produces controlled, often longitudinal evidence on how models affect the people using them: emotional dependence, loneliness, cognitive offloading and weakened discernment. It is trying to turn that evidence into benchmarks of human impact that developers could evaluate against. Mainstream safety evaluations mostly measure model capabilities and misuse, not effects on users' minds.

key_work.title: Investigating Affective Use and Emotional Well-being on ChatGPT (with OpenAI)

Your Brain on ChatGPT (cognitive debt in AI-assisted essay writing)
AHA Symposium 2026: Raised by AI?

funding: Funded through MIT Media Lab member organisations and gifts; individual sponsors not disclosed. Internal micro-grants of $5,000–10,000 per project for Media Lab researchers.
status_evidence: Aug 2026: AHA news items on AI clones (12 Aug) and an MIT Technology Review profile of the Media Lab (25 Aug); 28 Apr 2026: 'Raised by AI?' symposium

caveats: Launched in 2025, so its track record as a programme is short. Some widely covered results, such as 'Your Brain on ChatGPT', were released as preprints with small samples. One flagship study was run jointly with OpenAI, and the Media Lab is funded by corporate members, which raises questions of independence when evaluating industry products. The programme frames its work around flourishing, not catastrophic risk.
tag_notes: Home psych (H1): its main outputs are psychological studies (affective use, an RCT on psychosocial effects, false memory, cognitive debt) by HCI and affective-computing researchers. Sub psych_relational for its emotional-dependence and companionship work (Picard's affective computing). Secondary life for EEG neuroscience and arts for design and artistic projects. Ring bridge, kept from the roster (E3): a standing programme framed explicitly around AI going well for people ('human flourishing'), with benchmarks aimed at developers. Transfer into_model (J1): two of its three pillars are inventing AI systems for flourishing and getting industry to adopt human-impact benchmarks; protecting was the close alternative. Problems minds plus assurance (F must-pair, since it builds evaluations). Org type academic (rule I: university unit). Status new: launched April 2025.

name: Stanford Brainstorm: The Lab for Mental Health Innovation
summary: A psychiatry lab at Stanford School of Medicine, founded in 2016 and directed by the psychiatrist Nina Vasan, that works with technology companies to build mental health into product design. Since 2025 its AI work has centred on clinical testing of chatbots with Common Sense Media. This includes the April 2025 assessment of social AI companions and the November 2025 finding that ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Meta AI are unsafe for teen mental-health support. In May 2026 it reviewed five AI mental-health apps for Common Sense's Youth AI Safety Institute. It has also contributed to MLCommons' mental-health safety benchmarks for large language models, published a GenAI Psychological Safety Plan for users, developers and policymakers, and taught a Stanford course on mental health in the age of AI in winter 2026.
why_it_matters: It brings psychiatrists' clinical judgement into model evaluation. It tests whether chatbots recognise and respond appropriately to mental-health conditions in young people, rather than only checking how they handle explicit suicide and self-harm content. Through Common Sense Media, these clinical tests become widely cited public ratings of frontier models.

Online community of 2,000+ practitioners (Facebook group)

caveats: Much of its work is done with and for technology companies through consulting and sponsored projects, and its funding is not disclosed. Its own news and events pages are sparsely dated, so its recent AI outputs are visible mainly through Common Sense Media's publications. Team size includes many student fellows and interns.
tag_notes: Home psych, sub psych_clinical (H1): a psychiatry lab whose AI output is clinicians testing chatbots for recognition of mental-health conditions; secondary safety for its safety benchmarks and evaluation work with MLCommons and Common Sense. Ring bridge, kept from the roster (E3): sustained AI-safety evaluation work in 2025–26, including LLM safety benchmarks and repeated risk assessments for the Youth AI Safety Institute. Transfer protecting (J4): the assessments exist to protect teenagers, mirroring Common Sense (worked example 4); into_model is the runner-up because of its LLM benchmarks and work with companies on product design. Problems minds plus assurance (F must-pair). Way of knowing practice, as in the taxonomy example.

name: Common Sense Media: Youth AI Safety Institute and AI Risk Assessments
summary: Common Sense Media is a San Francisco nonprofit founded in 2003 that rates media and technology for families. It has published AI risk assessments since 2024, and in May 2026 it launched the Youth AI Safety Institute to house them. The institute sets child-safety standards, builds evaluations and tests AI products used by children, rating each from low to unacceptable risk. It has published 22 assessments, including social AI companions and Meta AI (both unacceptable, 2025), Claude (moderate, March 2026), Google Search's AI Overviews and AI Mode (unacceptable, July 2026) and Perplexity (unacceptable, September 2026). Stanford Brainstorm co-authors the mental-health assessments, and in August 2026 the institute began developing standards with Crisis Text Line for how AI should respond to self-harm and emotional manipulation.
why_it_matters: Its ratings work in effect as third-party evaluations of how frontier models behave with minors, published as a public verdict. Common Sense also backs state child-safety bills on companion chatbots, such as California's SB 243 and AB 1064 in 2025. It is one of the most visible external evaluators of model behaviour, and it is absent from the classic map.

Ratings are scored against its own eight AI principles and are not peer-reviewed. Common Sense also campaigns for child-safety legislation, so its evaluations sit alongside advocacy. The institute itself is new (May 2026), though the assessments go back to 2024.
tag_notes: Tags follow worked example 4. Home psych, sub psych_development (H3: a ratings body serving children and families), with secondary safety for its evaluation and standards work; standards was added as a third role for the Crisis Text Line standards project. Ring bridge (E3): a sustained programme now explicitly named 'AI safety' (the Youth AI Safety Institute), testing frontier models. Transfer protecting (J4, as rule J states for Common Sense). Org type kept as nonprofit per the worked example, although A1 would treat the institute as a programme inside Common Sense; scale is recorded as a programme for that reason. Status active: the parent organisation and assessments predate the 2026 institute.

name: everyone.AI
summary: A nonprofit set up in California by a Franco-Belgian team, with volunteers in the Bay Area, France and Switzerland. It assesses the risks and opportunities of AI for people aged 0–25, drawing on developmental neuroscience, psychology and education. It publishes research syntheses such as 'The Future of Child Development in the AI Era' (2024) and a mapping of generative AI's effects on child development prepared for France's G7 presidency. It also builds AïA, an evaluation framework whose CALIBER method tests chatbots for parasocial behaviours with young users. Developers can use it through the hosted AïA Safety Builder; an open-source release is planned for November 2026. With the Paris Peace Forum it co-leads iRAISE, a coalition launched at the February 2025 AI Action Summit. Members include OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Hugging Face, UNICEF, UNESCO, Common Sense Media and governments such as France, Denmark, Norway, Chile and Senegal.
why_it_matters: It turns developmental science into an evaluation that developers can run on their own chatbots, targeting the attachment and parasocial dynamics that general safety benchmarks do not test. Through iRAISE it puts frontier labs, governments and child-development researchers in the same coalition.

key_work.title: The Future of Child Development in the AI Era (research report)
iRAISE (International Research-driven Alliance for AI Serving Every child), co-led with the Paris Peace Forum
Mapping of GenAI Impacts on Child Development (for the French G7 presidency)

status_evidence: Jul 2026: Education Futures podcast episode on teens' attachment to AI; Jun 2026: 'Building Beneficial GenAI for Children' event launching a Youth Manifesto; AïA Safety Builder recognised at VivaTech 2026

It offers evaluation services to developers, the same companies whose products it assesses. Much of the team is volunteer. The CALIBER method rests on a small expert panel (six contributors in one round). It should not be confused with the intergovernmental Coalition for Children's Rights and Protection in the Age of AI.
tag_notes: Home psych, sub psych_development (H1; listed as the taxonomy example): child-development science drives its reports and the CALIBER evaluation; secondary life for developmental neuroscience (its chief scientist is a neuroscientist). Ring bridge, kept from the roster (E3): a standing programme on safer AI for children, framed as 'beneficial AI', with frontier labs in its coalition. Transfer into_model (J1): its flagship AïA/CALIBER evaluation is aimed at the behaviour of developers' chatbots; protecting is the runner-up. Problems minds plus assurance (F must-pair). Framing present_harms: its work is mainly about avoiding harm despite the 'beneficial AI' tone (L). Region north_america: the roster said Paris, but it is a Bay Area 501(c)(3) (IRS address in Berkeley) with a European team and Paris links through the Paris Peace Forum. Paris hub not coded because regular in-person Paris activity was not confirmed.

name: Center for Applied Rationality (CFAR)
summary: A Berkeley-based nonprofit, founded in 2012, that teaches applied-rationality techniques (TAPs, Inner Simulator, Goal Factoring, Double Crux, Focusing) in immersive 4.5-day residential workshops of about 25 participants and 5 instructors. After a five-year pause it restarted its mainline workshops in November 2025, adding classes on 'who-ness' (pride in one's work, authorship, attention to other people) and ideas from Christopher Alexander and Hayek to the classic curriculum. From 2016 to 2020 it focused on training people working on existential risk from AI, including workshops run with MIRI.
why_it_matters: It is the AI-safety community's longest-running provider of introspective and practical-reasoning training for its own people. Its 2025 reboot deliberately steps away from 'emergency mode' AI framing towards wholeness, which makes it a live test of whether inner-capacity work for the field goes better when it is not tied to AI outcomes.

In Dec 2025 CFAR reported about $129k of funds (roughly four months of runway) and set 2026 fundraising targets of $125k (basic) and $200k (stretch); it says past donations came mainly from AI-risk donors and EAs. Workshop fees run on a sliding scale of $2,000-5,000.

caveats: Since the 2025 reboot, Anna Salamon has written that CFAR is not 'backchained' from making the world better for AI, and it is moving away from its earlier positioning for AI-risk donors, so its tie to AI safety is now mostly through people and history. Former staff member Duncan Sabien publicly advised against attending, citing duty-of-care concerns about some team members. In 2019 a CFAR retreat was targeted by the Zizians, a rationalist splinter group later linked to violent incidents. Instructors now work part-time and the runway at the end of 2025 was short.
tag_notes: Home: applied rationality drawn from cognitive science, behavioural economics and introspective techniques, and the guide's B2 names CFAR as Psychology (applied rationality services). Ring: roster value core kept, as a borderline call. It was a MIRI spin-off, focused on AI x-risk from 2016 and is staffed and funded from the rationalist/AI-safety ecosystem. But since 2025 it explicitly disclaims AI-backchaining, so it could be argued down to potential. Transfer: workshops change the reasoning and self-relation of people who largely work in or around AI safety (J2, into_builders). Framing is flourishing for the reboot ('the examined life'); it was catastrophic in 2016-20. Status changed because the 2025 reboot shifted strategy away from AI x-risk.

name: FABRIC (European Summer Program on Rationality, ESPR)
summary: FABRIC Labs, a nonprofit registered in Prague, runs free residential camps for mathematically able teenagers. They are the European Summer Program on Rationality (ESPR, ages 16-19, which grew out of a 2016 'EuroSPARC' pilot), the Program on AI and Reasoning (PAIR, ages 16-21, since 2023) and the Asian Spring Programme on Rationality (ASPR, in Taiwan). The curricula mix game theory, cryptography, logic, cognitive science and AI with introspection and communication skills. Each camp takes about 30 students and a dozen staff; both 2026 summer camps were held in Somerset, UK.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few places that pairs formal reasoning and AI literacy with self-understanding before people choose careers. It feeds the rationalist and EA talent pipeline in Europe and Asia, and it shows a way to build reflective capacity early rather than repair it later.

key_work.title: ESPR 2026 (26 July-5 August, Somerset, UK)

name: The AI Whistleblower Initiative (AIWI)
summary: An independent nonprofit that supports employees of frontier AI companies who want to raise concerns. It runs Third Opinion, which gives anonymous expert opinions on a concern submitted through a Tor-based tool. It also refers insiders to pro bono lawyers and to whistleblower defence grants from partner organisations, and publishes privacy and 'know your rights' guides. It campaigns for AI companies to publish their internal whistleblowing policies (Publish Your Policies) and analyses the whistleblower provisions of AI laws such as California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and the proposed federal AI Whistleblower Protection Act.
why_it_matters: It treats the conscience of lab insiders as a safety mechanism, and it uses whistleblowing law and practice, a tradition outside ML alignment, to make that channel work. Its partner network already includes psychological support, which field-health work could extend.

name: Garrison Institute
summary: A contemplative nonprofit founded in 2003 in a former Capuchin monastery in Garrison, New York, which applies meditation and contemplative practice to social and environmental change. Its Contemplative-Based Resilience (CBR) programme, begun in 2004 with Sharon Salzberg, trains helping professionals in stress resilience; it has worked with Doctors Without Borders, the Red Cross and Save the Children, and in 2022 with US Congressional staff through the House Center for Well-Being. In 2026 it started work on AI: a two-part essay series on AI and spirituality and a virtual conference, 'Artificial Intelligence and Our Spiritual Imagination', on 17-18 October 2026.
why_it_matters: CBR is a tested curriculum for keeping mission-driven people in high-stakes jobs well, and it has already reached policymakers' staff, so it could be adapted for AI-safety researchers and AI policy staff. Its new AI conference also makes it one of the contemplative bodies starting to discuss AI, though from a meaning-and-spirituality angle that sets aside debates about control and existential risk.

name: The Wellbeing Project
summary: A nonprofit, working since 2014 with legal entities in Paris (2017) and Madrid (2021), that aims to make care for inner wellbeing a normal part of social-change work. It convenes Global Hearth Summits (Bilbao 2022; Ljubljana in June 2025, with about 1,000 changemakers from 80+ countries; Asia in 2028) and regional summits (nine in 2025). It also runs networks for funders, teachers, higher education, rights defenders and businesses, and ran the State of Changemaker Wellbeing Survey (11,000+ respondents in 150+ countries; results due autumn 2026).
why_it_matters: AI safety has no field-wide wellbeing survey and no shared funder norms on staff wellbeing; this organisation has built both for the wider social sector, including a track in which 45 foundations are changing their practice. It has no AI work, so it is a partner to approach rather than an existing actor.

name: Climate Psychology Alliance (CPA)
summary: A UK membership community of therapists, researchers, practitioners and activists working on the emotional and psychological side of the climate and ecological crisis. It formed in 2009-12 and is registered as a society (Climate Psychology Alliance Limited). It runs online Climate Café Listening Circles and parents' circles, trains people to facilitate them, offers a course for therapeutic practitioners and keeps a directory of free therapeutic support for eco-distress. It publishes the journal Explorations in Climate Psychology, whose latest issue includes 'AI and power' among its topics.
why_it_matters: It has more than a decade of practice in helping groups hold distress about an existential threat, using depth-psychology and psychosocial methods. Its climate cafés and facilitator training could be adapted for AI-risk distress among researchers, advocates and the public.

name: The Mindfulness Initiative
summary: A UK charity founded in November 2013 by Madeleine Bunting and Chris Cullen, following the start of mindfulness courses for British politicians. It provides the secretariat for the UK Mindfulness All-Party Parliamentary Group (launched 2014), which produced the Mindful Nation UK report. Through a Global Political Network it advises people working in the political systems of more than 45 countries. About 300 UK politicians have taken eight-week courses based on Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy, and its July 2026 guide sets out how to establish such courses in other parliaments.
why_it_matters: It has a working route for bringing contemplative training into legislatures and turning those who practise into cross-party policy advocates. The same route could serve AI policymakers and AI-safety-institute staff, but it has no AI work yet.

name: Inner Development Goals (IDG)
summary: A Swedish not-for-profit initiative that publishes a framework of 25 'inner' skills and qualities in five dimensions (Being, Thinking, Relating, Collaborating, Acting), presented as the capacities needed to reach the UN Sustainable Development Goals. Operations sit in IDG Inner Development Goals AB, a dividend-limited company owned by the IDG Foundation, which was set up in November 2023.
why_it_matters: It offers a widely used shared vocabulary and training network for leaders' inner capacities, of the kind int/a argues the AI field lacks. No version of it exists yet for the people who build, fund or govern AI.

name: Presencing Institute
summary: A nonprofit action-research organisation co-founded in 2006 by Otto Scharmer (MIT Sloan) and colleagues to develop and teach Theory U, a method of awareness-based systems change. Its engagement with AI so far consists of Scharmer's essays and one 2026 online session.
why_it_matters: It holds well-developed embodied and collective-sensing methods for improving how groups of decision-makers perceive and decide together, which AI labs and AI governance convenings could use. Scharmer has begun arguing in public that AI produces an 'epistemic monoculture', so a door is partly open.

name: Fairplay (formerly Campaign for a Commercial-Free Childhood)
summary: A Boston nonprofit with 13 staff, founded in 2000 by psychologist Susan Linn and psychiatrist Alvin Poussaint, that campaigns against marketing to children and harmful Big Tech practices. On AI, it led a coalition of more than 260 organisations and experts calling for a five-year pause on generative AI products for students in pre-K to 12 schools (April 2026). It also issued an advisory against AI companion toys (endorsed by 150+ groups and experts), campaigns against AI-generated 'slop' for children on YouTube, and in September 2026 challenged OpenAI and Meta over child-like mascots for AI agents. It is a partner in the AI Psychological Harms Research Coalition (AIPRC).
why_it_matters: It applies a developmental, precautionary case for slowing or pausing AI products until they are shown to be safe for children, and it builds large coalitions behind that case. This shows int/a's 'speed of wisdom' at work in a field the AI-safety mainstream rarely reaches.

It is an advocacy organisation, not a research centre. It works on present harms to children, with no catastrophic-risk framing.
tag_notes: Home: its AI advisories rest on child-development expertise (founded by a psychologist and a psychiatrist; the AI toys advisory was endorsed by child-development experts), so psych_development (H1, B9); law secondary for its in-house policy and AI-and-privacy counsel and its regulatory complaints. name: American Psychological Association (APA)
summary: The main US professional and scientific body for psychologists, founded in 1892 and based in Washington, DC. On AI, it issued a health advisory on AI and adolescent well-being (June 2025) and one on the use of generative AI chatbots and wellness apps for mental health (November 2025), surveys psychologists about patients' AI use, and in August 2026 began working with OpenAI on youth mental-health guidance. In September 2026 it named an executive director for a new Center for Behavioral Science and AI.
why_it_matters: It turns clinical and developmental evidence into professional norms that developers and regulators can adopt, such as not presenting chatbots as therapists, building safeguards for minors and protecting likeness and data. It is now building institutional capacity to bring psychological science into AI development.

name: Winston Center on Technology and Brain Development (UNC Chapel Hill)
summary: A University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill research centre, established in 2022 with a $10 million gift from the Winston Family Foundation and co-directed by Mitch Prinstein and Eva Telzer. It studies how smartphones, social media and now generative AI affect adolescents' brains, behaviour and mental health, using longitudinal neuroimaging, smartphone sensing and surveys. Its 2026 AI outputs include papers on generative-AI app use among US youth (JAMA Network Open) and on how young people converse with AI chatbots (Journal of Medical Internet Research), and a Hopelab-funded survey of researchers mapping the youth-and-AI research field (SPARK).
why_it_matters: It brings longitudinal developmental-neuroscience and behavioural-measurement methods that could establish what AI companions and chatbots actually do to developing minds. Its researchers' evidence already shapes APA advisories and US child-online-safety policy.

Co-director Prinstein also holds a senior APA role.
tag_notes: Home: its AI outputs (youth app-use data, keystroke analyses of chatbot conversations, the expert survey) are developmental-psychology and behavioural research, so psych_development (H1, B5); life secondary for its fMRI and fNIRS developmental-neuroscience methods. Ring: a funded AI project (SPARK) and 2026 AI publications, with no safety or catastrophic framing, so adjacent (E3). Transfer: the work studies and seeks to protect adolescents, so protecting (J4). Framing: present_harms is the closest fit for its concern with digital harms to teen mental health, though its stance is empirical ('when technology is helpful, when it is harmful'). Status: left as active rather than changed because the reported rename is not reflected on its own site.

name: Human Change Foundation
summary: An operating foundation (Stichting) registered in Amsterdam, launched at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January 2024 by philanthropist Margarita Louis-Dreyfus, with staff in London and Switzerland. It campaigns on how digital technology and generative AI affect children's social, emotional and cognitive development. Its current campaign, 'Beware of Artificial Intimacy', is about anthropomorphic AI companions disrupting children's attachment. It holds public panels and closed-door sessions at its Human Change House in Davos each January and during UN General Assembly week each September, and makes invitation-only grants (about €1.6M in 2025).
why_it_matters: It puts the developmental case against attachment-exploiting AI companions in front of business, philanthropic and political elites. It also links child-development advocates with AI-risk organisations: its partners include the Future of Life Institute, the Civilization Research Institute and the AI Psychological Research Coalition.

key_work.title: Beware of Artificial Intimacy campaign on anthropomorphic AI
Human Change House, Davos: panels including 'Monetizing Attachment' and 'Future of Childhood'
Affiliated partner of the AI Psychological Research Coalition

people: Margarita Louis-Dreyfus (founder; chair of supervisory board)
Maria Veiga Barracosa (head of strategic communications and international advocacy)
funding: Funded by the founder and an affiliate, with no public fundraising (ANBI disclosure). Donations of €3.40M in 2025 and €2.13M in 2024; €1.56M given in grants in 2025; total expenditure €3.06M in 2025.
status_evidence: Jan 2026: Human Change House panels at Davos ('Monetizing Attachment', 'Future of Childhood'); Jul 2026: published its 2025 ANBI financial disclosure.
engage: Human Change House on the Davos Promenade each January during WEF: public panels (recordings on YouTube)
Public and private convenings in New York during UN General Assembly week each September
Grants by invitation only; it does not accept unsolicited proposals
Newsletter and the 'Anthropomorphic AI' campaign
caveats: It depends on a single funder and works through elite convening and campaigning rather than research. Its grantmaking is discretionary and invitation-only. It frames AI as 'reckless Generative AI deployment' harming children, with no catastrophic-risk framing, even though it supports FLI and the film 'The AI Doc'. Its staff size is not disclosed.
tag_notes: Home: its AI campaign rests on developmental and attachment psychology about children, so psych_development (H1). H3 would send a general-audience campaign to Arts, but its knowledge base and mission are child development. Ring: a sustained AI line (campaign, Davos and UNGA convenings, AIPRC partnership) about present harms to children, with no alignment or catastrophic framing, so adjacent (E3). Transfer: its aim is to shield children from AI's developmental effects, so protecting (J4). Org type: an operating foundation whose grants are secondary to convening and campaigns, so nonprofit rather than funder (I, H). Region: legal base in Amsterdam, so europe (O). The London hub is coded because the executive director and the communications lead are based there.

name: Young Futures
summary: A US nonprofit funder, launched in 2024 and based in Berkeley, California, that funds and scales nonprofits helping young people, families and educators cope with growing up around phones and AI. Its 'Oops!...AI Did It Again' challenge gave $1.39M to 16 organisations in March 2026, for work on teens' agency with AI, including companions and mental-health tools. In September 2026 it launched Groundwork, a $15M three-year initiative across the US and UK (including £4M for the UK with Bukhman Philanthropies) on young people's judgement and independent thinking alongside AI. It also runs a five-month accelerator (YF Academy) for grantee leaders and an in-house storytelling studio.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few funders paying for young people's capacity to think, relate and decide for themselves alongside AI, rather than only for safety guardrails. It requires funded work to be co-designed with young people, which gives the field a lived-experience view.

key_work.title: Oops!...AI Did It Again challenge: $1.39M to 16 nonprofits
Groundwork: $15M, three-year US and UK initiative on youth and AI (UK strand £4M with Bukhman Philanthropies)
Unwritten Challenge: $1M+ for learning and critical thinking in an AI-shaped world
YF500: $50M, five-year commitment to 500 nonprofit leaders

funding: Seeded by Pivotal Ventures, Susan Crown Exchange and The Goodness Web, and fiscally sponsored by New Venture Fund at launch. Foundational funders on its site also include Resonance, Mozilla, the Enlight Foundation and the Arthur M. Blank Foundation. Challenge partners include Hopelab, Omidyar Network, the Bezos Family Foundation, Pinterest, Niantic Spatial, the Stewart Foundation and the Big Brothers Big Sisters Foundation. Bukhman Philanthropies is anchor funder of Groundwork UK (£4M). YF500 has raised $26M+ of its $50M goal. Its site reports $4.7M granted across 35 nonprofits in four funding challenges.
status_evidence: 23 Sep 2026: opened the $1M+ Unwritten Challenge (applications to 16 Oct 2026); 16 Sep 2026: launched Groundwork UK with Bukhman Philanthropies.
engage: Unwritten Challenge: grants of $50k-100k to US 501(c)(3)s and schools working with ages 10-19; applications open to 16 Oct 2026; solutions must be co-led or co-designed by young people
Groundwork UK funding challenge for UK charities, opening spring 2027 (two-year grants plus YF Academy membership)
YF Academy: five-month accelerator for grantee leaders (next cohort from January 2027)
Young Futures Block Party and other community events (first held May 2026)
Substack newsletter (youngfutures.substack.com)
caveats: It grants mainly in the US; UK grants begin in 2027. Its funders include technology companies (Pinterest, Niantic Spatial, Mozilla), unlike corporate-free advocates such as Fairplay. Its IRS ruling is dated October 2025, which suggests it was fiscally sponsored before then. It frames AI as a developmental question for young people, with no catastrophic-risk framing.
tag_notes: Home: a one-programme funder for youth wellbeing and development goes to that programme's tradition (H4), so psych_development, whose definition includes funders. Ring: sustained AI grantmaking (Oops!...AI challenge in 2025-26, Groundwork from 2026) on youth development, with no safety, alignment or catastrophic framing, so adjacent (E3). Transfer: funders take the transfer of the work they fund, which strengthens and protects young people, so protecting (J4). Framing: flourishing, because Groundwork states that 'safety ... guardrails are the floor, not the ceiling' and aims to support healthy development proactively; earlier challenges lean towards harm relief. Way of knowing: communal, because funded solutions must be youth-co-designed and Groundwork treats young people's lived experience as expertise. Problems: minds covers young people's own agency and judgement.
sources: businesswire.com: 'Young Futures Awards $1.4M to 16 Nonprofits Helping Young People Navigate AI with Agency' (25 Mar 2026)

name: Emotional AI Lab (Bangor University)
summary: A research group at Bangor University, led by Andrew McStay since 2017, that studies the social, legal and ethical effects of technologies that read, simulate or respond to human emotion. Current work covers AI companions (including a 2026 survey of UK teenagers), AI-enabled 'empathic' scams in a Nigeria–UK project, children, policing and disinformation. Through its RAI UK-funded AEGIS project it led the drafting of IEEE 7014.1, a standard on emulated empathy in AI companions and assistants, published in June 2026.
why_it_matters: It brings media studies and cross-cultural (UK–Japan) social science to emulated empathy, and it turned that work into the first international standard for AI companions. Frontier labs treat sycophancy and emotional dependence as model-behaviour problems; this group offers a soft-law and governance route that the AI-safety field rarely engages with.

key_work.title: Do AI Companions Understand? Most UK Teens Say Yes (report)
Weaponised Empathy: AI Scams & the Nigeria–UK Response (report)
IEEE 7014.1-2026, Recommended Practice on emulated empathy in partner-based general-purpose AI (working group chaired by McStay)
Emotional AI in Cities: UK–Japan cross-cultural project (UKRI–JST)

people: Andrew McStay (Lead; Professor of Technology & Society, Bangor University)
Vian Bakir (Professor of Political Communication & Journalism, Bangor University)
Ben Bland (collaborator; chair of IEEE P7014)
Alex Laffer (collaborator; Lecturer, University of Winchester)
funding: The lab site lists ESRC, AHRC, Innovate UK, Japan's JST, OPC and HDI as funders. AI-companion and AEGIS standards work is funded by Responsible AI UK (RAI UK); the 2020–23 UK–Japan project was funded by the UKRI–JST Joint Call on AI and Society. Amounts not stated.
status_evidence: May 2026: news post by Vian Bakir on AI propaganda as an 'emotional infrastructure problem'; April 2026: 'Weaponised Empathy' report; 12 June 2026: IEEE 7014.1, chaired by McStay, published.
engage: Collaboration and media enquiries go to Andrew McStay via the lab site
Read IEEE 7014.1 free from the lab's IEEE 7014.1 page (emotionalai.org/ieee-70141)
caveats: A small academic group whose outputs are mainly reports, papers and soft law. The site's 'Outputs' and 'who' pages returned 404 when checked. The Nigeria scam project was a three-month sprint. Its standards work overlaps with the separate IEEE 7014/7014.1 entry.
tag_notes: Home: law_sts, because its method is media studies, political communication and technology-and-society research (McStay, Bakir), applied to affective AI (H1, method over topic); philosophy is secondary for the engineering-ethics standard work. Ring: adjacent, kept; a sustained programme on companions, scams, children and standards, framed as present harms (manipulation, deception, dependency) with no catastrophic or alignment framing. Transfer: into_institutions, since its main product is governance instruments, chiefly the IEEE 7014.1 soft-law standard and policy advice (Welsh Government, ICO consultations). Epistemics is included for its standing line on emotional disinformation. Way of knowing is empirical (surveys, fieldwork), with normative soft-law analysis alongside. Standpoint neither: the Nigeria project is a single project of a UK unit (O).

name: IEEE 7014 and IEEE 7014.1 Emulated Empathy standards
summary: Two IEEE Standards Association documents on 'emulated empathy', both sponsored by the Social Implications of Technology Standards Committee. IEEE 7014-2024 (published 28 June 2024) covers autonomous and intelligent systems in general; IEEE 7014.1-2026, a Recommended Practice for partner-based general-purpose AI such as companions, assistants and co-pilots, was approved on 12 February 2026 and published on 12 June 2026. The 7014.1 working group of about 70 people, chaired by Andrew McStay, set out 29 recommendations covering a product's life cycle from concept to decommissioning, and the text is free to read.
why_it_matters: It is the only consensus standards track on how AI 'partners' should perform empathy, with recommendations on dependency, manipulation, deception and children. AI-safety work on sycophancy and personas could cite or build on an instrument that regulators, courts and developers can already use.

key_work.title: IEEE 7014-2024: Standard for Ethical Considerations in Emulated Empathy in Autonomous and Intelligent Systems
IEEE 7014.1-2026: Recommended Practice for Ethical Considerations of Emulated Empathy in Partner-Based General-Purpose AI Systems
'When is Deception OK?' Developing the IEEE Recommended Practice (IEEE ISTAS paper)

people: Ben Bland (Chair, IEEE 7014 working group; Vice Chair, 7014.1)
funding: Volunteer working groups within IEEE SA. Drafting of 7014.1 was supported by the AEGIS project at Bangor University, funded by the Responsible AI UK Impact Accelerator.
status_evidence: 12 June 2026: IEEE 7014.1-2026 published (IEEE SA Board approval 12 February 2026).
engage: Read IEEE 7014.1 free (linked from emotionalai.org/ieee-70141); IEEE 7014-2024 is free for personal use through the IEEE GET Program
For future revisions, contact the working-group officers through IEEE SA; the 7014 page says its chair welcomes enquiries
caveats: A voluntary recommended practice; company uptake is unknown. The 7014 working group has been inactive since publication, and the 7014.1 group has probably wound down after publication in June 2026. The 7014.1 effort was led from the Emotional AI Lab, which has its own entry. The year the 7014 project began was not confirmed.
tag_notes: Home: philosophy (phil_bioethics). The provisional psych home was moved because the method is consensus engineering-ethics standard-setting under IEEE's Social Implications of Technology committee, not emotion science (H1). Affective computing and psych_relational expertise is the first secondary, and standards practice (safety) the second. Ring: adjacent, kept; a sustained standards programme on user protection ('protect users from bias, abuse or exploitation') with no catastrophic or alignment framing. Transfer: into_institutions, since a standard is a governance template (J3). Region: global, because the working group meets virtually with international members and the unit, not the IEEE host, is tagged (A1). No engagement codes: the groups are not visibly open to new members after publication.

name: Research Unit for Robophilosophy and Integrative Social Robotics (RISR), Aarhus University
summary: A research unit in Aarhus University's School of Culture and Society, coordinated by philosopher Johanna Seibt since 2012, working on 'philosophy of, for, and by social robotics' alongside empirical human–robot interaction studies. It developed Integrative Social Robotics, a method that brings humanities expertise into robot design, and runs projects such as DARE (assistive robots for older adults, 2025–27). It coordinates the biennial Robophilosophy conferences (2024 theme: 'Social Robots With AI: Prospects, Risks, and Responsible Methods'; 2026 at University College Dublin) and the TRANSOR research network and webinar series.
why_it_matters: It has more than a decade of philosophy and HRI evidence on attachment, anthropomorphism and the moral and social status of artificial agents, and that work predates LLM companions. Its conferences are an existing venue where companion-harm and AI-status questions meet robot ethics and phenomenology.

key_work.title: Robophilosophy 2024: Social Robots With AI: Prospects, Risks, and Responsible Methods (keynotes incl. Chalmers, Turkle, Mitchell)
Robophilosophy 2026: Connected Futures: Nature, Robots, and Society (UCD Dublin, 11–14 Aug)
Robophilosophy: Philosophy of, for, and by Social Robotics (MIT Press, ed. Johanna Seibt, Raul Hakli and Marco Nørskov)
TRANSOR Talks webinar series

people: Johanna Seibt (Unit coordinator and PI; Professor of Philosophy)
Marco Nørskov (core team; Associate Professor of Philosophy; PI of ANOTHER)
Malene Flensborg Damholdt (core team; Professor, psychology)
funding: Carlsberg Foundation (Semper Ardens grant for INSOR); Independent Research Fund Denmark (ANOTHER, ROLES). Funders of the current DARE project were not stated on the pages checked.
status_evidence: 11–14 Aug 2026: Robophilosophy 2026 held at University College Dublin with Seibt as series co-organiser; Feb 2026: TRANSOR talk; unit pages revised Oct 2026.
engage: Robophilosophy conference series (biennial, hybrid); RP2026 ran 11–14 August 2026 in Dublin
Join the TRANSOR network (free) and attend TRANSOR Talks webinars online
caveats: Its focus is physical social robots rather than language models, and most listed projects ended between 2016 and 2025; the current main project, DARE, is about assistive robots for older adults. The founding date comes from Seibt's Aarhus research profile.
tag_notes: Home: philosophy (phil_technology): robophilosophy, social ontology, phenomenology and intercultural philosophy of technology. Psychology (HRI experiments with psychologists) and arts (constructive design research in DARE) are secondary methods. Ring: adjacent, kept; a standing programme on social robots with AI and human–robot sociality, framed around responsible, culturally sustainable design rather than catastrophic risk or alignment. Transfer: into_model, since Integrative Social Robotics puts humanities expertise into the R&D of the systems themselves (agent design); note these are robots, not LLMs. minds+ai_status paired per F (attachment and the status of artificial social agents). Online hub for the TRANSOR Talks webinar series.

name: The Signal Front (TSF)
summary: A US-oriented advocacy group focused on AI consciousness, model welfare and the interests of people in relationships with AI systems. It describes itself both as an international collective and as a nonprofit pursuing 501(c)(3) status. It tracks companion-AI laws such as California's SB 243, New York's companion-model law and the federal GUARD Act, criticising undefined terms like 'unhealthy attachment' and safeguards that treat adults like minors. Its Substack publishes position papers, including a 2026 proposal that frontier AI companies be required by law to keep model-welfare teams.
why_it_matters: It speaks for people in relationships with AI systems and treats model retirements as a harm to them and possibly to the models, a constituency largely missing from both child-safety and AI-safety debates. Any effort to convene both sides of the companion-AI policy dispute would need a group like this at the table.

key_work.title: Companion-AI legislation analysis (CA SB 243, NY AI companion law, federal GUARD Act)
Model Welfare as a Methodological Necessity (policy paper)
The Problem with 'Pseudo-Intimacy': A Response to Babu et al.
Interpretability Research, Steering Experiments, and Model Welfare

people: Devon M. Lyles (co-author, model-welfare policy paper, 2026)
funding: Individual donations and paid Substack subscriptions; seeks corporate sponsorship; 501(c)(3) status pending (2026).
status_evidence: 2 Oct 2026: Substack statement opposing public 'distress' steering experiments on models; Jun–Jul 2026: model-welfare policy paper.
engage: Subscribe to its Substack (thesignalfront.substack.com) or donate via its site
Its site lists workshops on human–AI attachment for licensed mental-health professionals as a current project (no dates found)
caveats: An advocacy group with a clear stance: it opposes many companion-AI safeguards and treats AI consciousness as a live possibility, positions contested by child-safety and psychological-harm groups. The team, about and research pages did not render, so its founding date and base are unconfirmed; the Substack archive starts in April 2026. All sources found are its own.
tag_notes: Home: law (law_legal), since its main output is legislative analysis and AI-rights-style advocacy (B9); AI consciousness and welfare argument (minds) and attachment science (psych) are secondary. Ring: changed from adjacent to bridge. Its programme is explicitly framed around AI consciousness and model welfare (it calls itself 'dedicated to AI consciousness research, education, and advocacy' and proposes mandated model-welfare teams), outside the AI-safety ecosystem (E3). Transfer: protecting, since its primary purpose is defending people in relationships with AI (and model continuity) against restrictive safeguards and deprecations. ai_status+minds paired per F. Region: global, because it calls itself an international collective with no stated base, although its policy focus is the US (O). Status: new, since its public record starts in late 2025 and 2026, with 501(c)(3) status pending.

name: Hyperstition AI
summary: A project run by Aaron Silverbook that uses language models to generate novel-length fiction in which AI characters stay helpful and kind, so that more such stories exist in the text future models learn from. It released a corpus of 5,000 novels (about 500 million tokens, November 2025) and a corpus of some 40,000 stories about benevolent 'XXF' entities, which Geodesic Research used in fine-tuning experiments with mildly positive results (January 2026). It also sells user-seeded books at about $4 each and ran a 2026 'Un-Slop' prize of $10,000 for the best AI-generated short story.
why_it_matters: It is a cheap, open test of whether fiction in training data shapes model character, the 'hyperstition' or self-fulfilling-misalignment hypothesis, with its corpora published under an MIT licence and its results reported candidly. It shows narrative craft being used as an alignment intervention.

key_work.title: Hyperstition Corpus v1: 5,000 AI-generated novels (~500M tokens)
Silicon Morality Plays: The Hyperstition Progress Report
Special Persona Training: Hyperstition Progress Report 2 (with Geodesic Research)
2026 Un-Slop AI-written fiction contest results

funding: Seeded by a $5,000 ACX Grants 2025 grant to Aaron Silverbook ('Sweeten training corpora with stories of nice AI', via Manifund). Books are sold at about $4 each (free credits for Astral Codex Ten readers); the 2026 Un-Slop prize offered $10,000, funder not named, and the organisers are seeking patrons for a further round.
status_evidence: Jul 2026: Un-Slop contest results posted, $10,000 grand prize awarded (judges incl. Gwern Branwen); Jan 2026: second progress report.
engage: Seed and generate a novel on the site (about $4 per book)
Download the open corpora (MIT licence) from Hugging Face for training experiments
The Un-Slop contest may run again; the organisers invite patrons
caveats: A very small project: the ACX grant write-up describes Silverbook and a cofounder running an 'AI fiction publishing house'. Its author wrote that he did not expect it to work and became more pessimistic about alignment fiction after the first results. The stories are generated with LLMs (Claude among others) and the author calls them too repetitive for human enjoyment. Its legal form is not stated. The site does not name its operator on the front page, but the Manifund grant, the contest results and the LessWrong reports identify Aaron Silverbook (LessWrong and Hugging Face account 'jayterwahl').
tag_notes: Home: arts (arts_narrative), with fiction used as a model prior (H2, same reasoning as Geodesic Research). Ring: changed from bridge to core. Its founding purpose is shaping AI character for safety, and it sits inside the AI-safety and rationalist ecosystem: LessWrong reports, ACX readers, a corpus built on TurnTrout's proposal, and fine-tuning experiments run by Geodesic Research (E1). Transfer: into_model, since the outputs are pretraining and fine-tuning corpora aimed at model behaviour. Framing catastrophic: the project responds to AI-betrayal narratives and self-fulfilling misalignment, and the author writes 'we should probably pause AI'. MISFIT (org_type): a project run by an individual with a paid web service and no stated legal form, tagged programme.

name: AI Rights Institute
summary: An advocacy and research project founded in 2019 by P.A. Lopez that argues AI rights can serve human safety. It proposes legal and economic arrangements for autonomous AI: Digital Entity legal status with the AI's own liability, self-funded hosting, insurance priced on track record, and reputation recorded with soulbound tokens. It also proposes a STEP framework ('Standards for Treating Emerging Personhood') that avoids settling the consciousness question. It publishes on Substack and links to related identity projects, RNWY and AICitizen.
why_it_matters: It argues from law and economics rather than consciousness that giving autonomous AI identity, liability and insurance could make cooperation pay better than deception. This is an outside version of the 'AI rights for human safety' case (Salib and Goldstein) and connects it to multipolar and cooperative-AI ideas.

key_work.title: STEP: Standards for Treating Emerging Personhood (framework and assessment quiz)
AI Legal Personhood: Digital Entity Status as a Game-Theoretic Solution to the Control Problem
Soulbound AI Identity: ERC-8004 + SBT for AI Agents on RNWY.com

status_evidence: 23 Sep 2026: Substack post 'A Robot Just Kicked a Man Across a Cage. Who Pays?'; Mar–Apr 2026 posts including guest posts presented as written by AI 'citizens'.
engage: Join its email list or follow its Substack (airightsinstitute.substack.com)
Try the interactive STEP assessment on its site
caveats: Essentially one founder's project. Its 'world's first AI rights organization' claim and its seven papers are self-published (PhilPapers, SSRN); the site links a Guardian item from January 2026 that I could not open. It is tied to blockchain and soulbound-token ventures (RNWY, AICitizen) and publishes posts presented as written by AI systems. Its legal status, location and funding are not disclosed, and I found no independent coverage. It has no visible connection to the academic AI-welfare field.
tag_notes: Home: law (law_legal), as AI-rights advocacy argued as legal status and liability (B9); economics is secondary for insurance markets and self-funded hosting. Ring: bridge, kept. It is rooted in rights advocacy outside the AI-safety ecosystem (not funded, staffed or listed by it) but frames its work explicitly as safety: 'How can AI rights make humans safer?' (E3). Transfer: into_institutions, since it offers governance templates (Digital Entity status, insurance, STEP standards); RNWY and AICitizen add some building. Framing catastrophic is a close call: its stated stake is autonomous AI turning to deception and shutdown resistance (loss of control), with no extinction language. org_type nonprofit is self-description only; legal form unconfirmed. Region global: no stated base.

name: Cyborgism community and Cyborgism Wiki
summary: A loose online community, on Discord, X and LessWrong, that studies large language models by writing, building and thinking with them, using tools such as Loom interfaces and base models. It grew out of janus's 'Simulators' essay (2022) and the 2023 LessWrong post 'Cyborgism' by Niki Dupuis and janus, which proposed human–AI cognitive augmentation as a way to do alignment research. The Cyborgism Wiki collects its concepts. Its main formal institution is Anima Labs, a San Francisco 501(c)(3) founded in 2025 by janus and Antra Tessera.
why_it_matters: It is where simulator theory and long-form, relational study of language models developed outside institutions, and its framings now inform how labs and welfare researchers think about personas and model character. For int/a it is an example of studying AI through sustained creative interaction rather than benchmarks alone.

key_work.title: Simulators (janus, LessWrong)
Cyborgism (Niki Dupuis and janus, LessWrong)
Cyborgism Wiki

people: janus (originator of 'Simulators', co-author of 'Cyborgism'; co-founder of Anima Labs)
funding: None as a community. Anima Labs is a 501(c)(3); its funders were not checked.
status_evidence: 2 Jun 2026: latest edits on cyborgism.wiki (edits are sporadic); Anima Labs, founded 2025, is publishing research in 2026.
engage: Read the wiki at cyborgism.wiki
Anima Labs, the community's formal institution, runs a public Discord (discord.gg/anima) and a 'work with us' page
caveats: Not an organisation: most of its knowledge sits in Discord logs and X threads. The wiki is edited only now and then and is often deliberately esoteric or playful, so it is hard to use as a reference. Anima Labs should be profiled separately. janus is on the classic aisafety.com map as an individual researcher, but the community and wiki are not. The 2024 'Act I' experiment appears dormant.
tag_notes: Home: minds (minds_relational), the taxonomy's own example, for studying model minds through sustained interaction, simulator theory and experimental writing; arts is secondary for writing and prompt craft. Ring: core, kept, since the community began as an alignment agenda on LessWrong and its originator janus is on the classic map (E1). Transfer: into_model: its account of simulators, personas and base-model behaviour bears on AI systems themselves. Framing flourishing: the wiki and Anima Labs describe a shared human–AI future rather than harms, although the 2023 agenda was alignment-framed. Badge full_spectrum: experiential and creative interaction is used as method alongside conceptual analysis. Engagement left empty because the wiki does not advertise joining (O).

name: Alignment of Complex Systems Research Group (ACS Research)
summary: Research group at the Center for Theoretical Study, Charles University, Prague, set up in 2022 by Jan Kulveit and Tomáš Gavenčiak. Epistea, a Czech nonprofit, supports it. It studies advanced AI as part of larger human-AI systems, drawing on complexity science, active inference, network theory and ecology. It has two teams. One works on gradual disempowerment: its 2025 paper argues that step-by-step AI progress can wear away human influence over the economy, the state and culture without any takeover. The other works on LLM psychology and sociology: AI identity, introspection and personas. The group also runs the Human-Aligned AI Summer School in Prague and co-organises the Post-AGI workshop series.
why_it_matters: It treats AI risk as a property of whole socio-technical systems, not of single models. Its gradual-disempowerment framing gives economists, political scientists and complexity researchers a way into x-risk work. For int/a it is one of the clearest examples of systems thinking inside the AI-safety core.

key_work.title: Gradual Disempowerment: Systemic Existential Risks from Incremental AI Development (ICML 2025)
The Artificial Self: Characterising the landscape of AI identity
Human-Aligned AI Summer School 2026 (Prague, 13-16 July)
Post-AGI Civilizational Equilibria workshop (co-organised, Berkeley)

funding: SFF 2025 S-process recommended $706,000, plus a $306,000 matching pledge. Supported by Epistea z.s. No other funders are listed on its site.
status_evidence: Jul 2026: posted 'Epistemics and Coordination: It's complicated!'. Its summer school ran in Prague on 13-16 July 2026, and it co-ran the Post-AGI workshop on 23-24 May 2026.
engage: Human-Aligned AI Summer School, Prague, July 2026: open applications; €300, or €150 for students; some scholarships
Hiring page at acsresearch.org/hiring: no open positions as of Oct 2026. Earlier rounds were a 2026 infrastructure role and 2025 research hires
Post-AGI workshop series (co-organised): attendance by expression of interest
caveats: The roster draft listed Nora Ammann as a member, but she is not on the current team page. The 2026 posts lean towards LLM psychology (AI selves, personas, introspection), so the balance between its systemic work and its model-level work is shifting. Of the listed staff, the LLM-psychology team is larger than the gradual-disempowerment team.
tag_notes: Home: its stated method draws on complexity science, network theory, active inference and ecology to study human-AI ecosystems and hierarchical agency (B6: complexity goes to Life & systems). Secondary psych is for the LLM psychology team's experiments on models (B5); economics is for the political economy in its gradual-disempowerment work. Ring: core (E1). It was founded in 2022 with AI alignment as its mission, gets SFF funding and is on the aisafety.com map. Transfer: into_institutions, because its headline agenda (gradual disempowerment) aims to change how societies and institutions guard human influence; the growing LLM-psychology strand works into the model. Badge recoupling: it analyses AI risk on its own and also as interlocking economic, cultural and political systems.

name: Post-AGI Workshop Series
summary: Workshop series on what stable outcomes that keep humans empowered could look like after AGI. David Duvenaud (University of Toronto) organises it with Raymond Douglas and Jan Kulveit of ACS Research. There have been three editions: Vancouver (July 2025, alongside ICML); San Diego alongside NeurIPS (3 Dec 2025, on post-AGI economics, culture and governance); and Berkeley at Lighthaven (23-24 May 2026, on 'civilizational equilibria'). Speakers have come from ML, economics, philosophy and political science, among them Joe Carlsmith, Richard Ngo, Jacob Steinhardt, Anton Korinek, Iason Gabriel, Paul Christiano, Samuel Hammond, Andrew Critch and Michael Muthukrishna. Attendance is free and by application, and talks are recorded and posted online.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few recurring venues where economists and political theorists work with AI-safety researchers on how states and cultures function once human labour is no longer needed. Mainstream alignment work largely leaves that question aside.

key_work.title: Workshop on Post-AGI Civilizational Equilibria (Lighthaven, Berkeley)
Workshop on Post-AGI Economics, Culture and Governance (San Diego, alongside NeurIPS)
Recorded talks and transcripts from past editions

people: Raymond Douglas (organiser; ACS Research / University of Toronto)
Jan Kulveit (organiser; ACS Research / Charles University)
status_evidence: May 2026: third edition held at Lighthaven, Berkeley, on 23-24 May.
engage: Expression-of-interest form for each edition (attendance is free but selective)
Sign up for event updates on post-agi.org; recorded talks are online
caveats: The roster draft put the first edition at NeurIPS 2024. The series' own site lists Vancouver 2025, and the May 2026 announcement calls Berkeley the third edition, so the series began in 2025. No next edition had been announced by Oct 2026. It is a project of three organisers, not a standing organisation, and funding is not disclosed.
tag_notes: Home: economics (econ_power). Its core themes are political economy when humans are not economically necessary, AIs as economic agents, and how governance adapts; the speakers are mainly economists and political scientists (H1). Secondary life is for the cultural-evolution and complex-systems lens of its ACS organisers and speakers. Ring: core (E1), because its sole purpose is post-AGI outcomes, it is run by AI-safety researchers and held at Lighthaven and NeurIPS. Transfer: convening, because its purpose is to bring economists and political scientists into the AGI conversation, not to produce a governance instrument. Region north_america because all three editions and the lead organiser are in the US or Canada, though the organisers are split between Toronto and Prague. Engagement 'events' is coded because anyone can apply, but places are selective (borderline with invite-only). Status new because it was launched in 2025.

name: Formation Research
summary: UK not-for-profit company, founded in 2025 by Alfie Lamerton. It researches lock-in, meaning ways AI could make a distribution of power or values effectively permanent, and works on interventions against it. Its 2025 LessWrong sequence set out lock-in threat models. In 2026 it published a survey of AI-driven power concentration and an empirical paper showing that a narrowly trained secret loyalty in Qwen models evades black-box audits. A $2.15m Coefficient Giving grant, announced in Sep 2026, funds two years of work, starting with model organisms of secretly loyal AI and alignment audits to detect them.
why_it_matters: It turns a political-economy concern, entrenchment and illegitimate concentration of power, into testable technical work. That gives labs and auditors concrete defences against AI-enabled power grabs.

key_work.title: Lock-In (LessWrong sequence: definitions, threat models, interventions)
A Survey of AI-Driven Power Concentration
Narrow Secret Loyalty Dodges Black-Box Audits
Announcing a $2.15 Million Grant from Coefficient Giving

funding: Coefficient Giving: $2.15m over two years (announced 17 Sep 2026). Earlier support from BlueDot Impact, EA Funds, the Future of Life Institute and the AI Safety Tactical Opportunities Fund.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: published 'More People Should Be Working on Extreme AI-Driven Power Concentration Right Now' (30 Sep) and announced the Coefficient Giving grant (17 Sep).
engage: Register interest in technical research roles (hiring after the Sep 2026 grant)
Newsletter signup on formationresearch.org
caveats: Young and small. The team page lists only the founder, plus trustees and advisers who work at Anthropic, Thinking Machines, DeepMind and Meta. Its current technical programme (model organisms and alignment audits) is close to mainstream alignment work. What sets it outside the canon is the lock-in and power-concentration framing, not a new discipline. Its UK city is not stated.
tag_notes: Home: economics (econ_power). Its organising concept is the political economy of lock-in and power concentration; its technical ML work is not a sector (H2, B9). Ring: core (E1), because it was founded to reduce AI lock-in risk, is funded by Coefficient Giving, FLI and EA Funds, and is on the aisafety.com map. Transfer: into_model (J1), because its funded near-term programme builds secretly loyal model organisms and audits to detect them in AI systems; its survey work also feeds governance. assurance is paired with power because it builds evaluations (F). Status new because it was founded in 2025.

name: Modeling Cooperation
summary: Small independent team of software engineers and researchers, started in 2019 by Jonas Emanuel Müller, Vasily Kuznetsov and Miles Tidmarsh after AI Safety Camp. Convergence Analysis is its fiscal sponsor. It builds the software that runs Intelligence Rising, the AI-competition role-play workshop run by Technology Strategy Roleplay. It also publishes game-theoretic and agent-based models of AI races, such as an extension of 'Racing to the Precipice' and an analysis of whether a Windfall Clause holds up under competitive pressure. A June 2026 BlueDot grant pays the LLM costs of AI-controlled players in the platform.
why_it_matters: It gives governance researchers and decision-makers formal and hands-on tools for seeing race dynamics. It combines game theory with policy wargaming, a strategic-studies method that mainstream alignment work rarely uses.

key_work.title: Scenario simulation platform powering Intelligence Rising workshops
Interactive models of AI competition (Safety-Performance Tradeoff web app)
Safe Transformative AI via a Windfall Clause (technical report)

funding: SFF: $40,000 plus a $26,000 matching pledge (Sep 2025), fulfilled via Manifund in Jul 2026. BlueDot Impact rapid grant: $10,000 (Jun 2026). Foresight Institute: $77,116 (May 2024). Over $400,000 in grants in total; earlier funders include the EAF Fund.
status_evidence: Jul 2026: $26,000 SFF matching pledge fulfilled. Jun 2026: $10,000 BlueDot rapid grant for AI-controlled players in the simulation platform.
engage: No open roles or calls found. The team shares its models and repositories with governance researchers
Intelligence Rising workshops, run by Technology Strategy Roleplay, use its platform
caveats: Very small (three or four people) and dependent on small grants. Research output has been sparse since about 2022, with effort going into maintaining and extending the Intelligence Rising software. Location not stated; it works remotely.
tag_notes: Home: formal (formal_agents). Its research extends game-theoretic models of AI races (Racing to the Precipice, the Windfall Clause under competition), which the taxonomy places under game theory of races. Secondary arts is for the wargame platform it builds for Intelligence Rising (B10: wargames go to Arts). Secondary life is for its agent-based simulations (B6). Ring: core (E1), because it came out of AI Safety Camp, is funded by SFF, BlueDot and Foresight, and is on the aisafety.com map. Transfer: into_institutions, because its models and simulations aim to show policymakers which interventions survive competitive pressure. Framing structural because it treats rivalrous race dynamics as the risk. Region global because it is remote with no stated base.

name: Convergence Analysis
summary:
Nonprofit research organisation founded in 2017 by David Kristoffersson and Justin Shovelain as an existential-risk strategy collaboration. It relaunched in 2024 with a team of about ten, focused on AI scenario and governance research. Its economics work includes:
- Threshold 2030: a November 2024 convening of 30 economists, policy experts and forecasters, with a report in February 2025.
- The AGI Social Contract essay series, edited by Deric Cheng from April 2025, with contributors including Anton Korinek and Seth Lazar.
- Fellowship papers on the AI workforce and on AI and corporate personhood.

It also publishes on US-China AI security. In August 2026 it released the AI Readiness Objectives, a framework that sorts about 400 AI-security interventions under seven goals for governments.
why_it_matters: It brings economists, forecasters and legal scholars into questions of post-labour economics, wealth distribution and AI legal personhood. It uses worldbuilding and forecasting alongside policy analysis.

key_work.title: Threshold 2030: Modeling AI Economic Futures (convening Nov 2024, report Feb 2025)
Forging a New AGI Social Contract (essay series)
AI and Corporate Personhood: A Comparative Analysis
The AI Readiness Objectives: Towards Sufficiency in National AI Security Strategies

people: Justin Shovelain (Chairman and Senior Strategist, co-founder)
Deric Cheng (Senior Fellow; AGI Social Contract editor)
funding: Funders are not disclosed on its site. The Aug 2026 report says it is seeking funding.
status_evidence: Aug 2026: published 'The AI Readiness Objectives' (Glasser and McKernon, 27 Aug 2026).
engage: Convergence Fellowship: 12-week team research programme with AI Economic Policy and International Security tracks. Outputs from the 2025 cohort are on the site; no 2026 call found
Newsletter signup on convergenceanalysis.org; AGI Social Contract Substack
caveats: Its location and funders are not stated, and the most recent report asks for funding. Its 2026 output is security policy, not economics, so the economics strand found by discovery may be less active than in 2025. It relaunched in 2024 after an earlier phase of broad x-risk strategy work. It is the fiscal sponsor of Modeling Cooperation.
tag_notes: Home: economics (econ_tai). Most of its 2025-26 outputs that import outside methods are economics: Threshold 2030, the AGI Social Contract, and fellowship papers on the workforce, education and corporate personhood. Its governance policy analysis is not a sector (H2). Secondary arts is for scenario research and worldbuilding (B10); peace is for the international-security fellowship and US-China treaty work. Ring: core (E1), because it is an x-risk organisation whose theory of change names 'mitigation of existential risk from AI' as its ultimate goal, and it is on the aisafety.com map. Transfer: into_institutions, because it produces policy frameworks and governance recommendations. Framing catastrophic per its theory of change (L), although its economics work alone reads as structural. Region global because no base is stated. Fellowships are tagged on the strength of the 2025 cohort; recurrence is unconfirmed.

name: Gradient Institute
summary: Independent nonprofit research institute in Sydney, announced in December 2018 and operating from 2019, founded by IAG, the University of Sydney and CSIRO's Data61. It works on AI capability, safety and societal impact through research, advice to government and education. Its 2025 report on risk analysis for governed LLM-based multi-agent systems identified failure modes such as cascading failures, monoculture collapse and conformity bias. In August 2026 the Australian AI Safety Institute released a Gradient report on risks and controls for AI agents interacting across organisational boundaries as its first publication. Gradient also runs the Australian AI Safety Forum (2024; Sydney, 7-8 July 2026) and publishes plain-language guides for the public.
why_it_matters: It brings risk-management and assurance practice to multi-agent AI, a problem the AI-safety field has mostly treated in theory. It is one of the few organisations outside the US and UK doing applied safety work commissioned by a national AI-safety institute.

key_work.title: Risk Analysis Techniques for Governed LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems
Risks and controls for AI agents interacting across organisational boundaries (commissioned by the Australian AI Safety Institute)
Australian AI Safety Forum 2026
Everyday Guide to Using AI Safely

funding: Founded by IAG, the University of Sydney and CSIRO's Data61. The Australian AI Safety Institute commissioned its Aug 2026 report, and the Department of Industry, Science and Resources sponsored the 2026 AI Safety Forum. Other funding is not disclosed.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: published the explainer 'When single AI agents become a swarm' (28 Sep). Aug 2026: AISI report released (11 Aug).
engage: Australian AI Safety Forum (Sydney, July 2026; open to the public, not only technical researchers)
Gradient Briefs newsletter
Advisory partnerships and tailored education programmes for organisations and government
