caveats: It comes from responsible-AI and data-science work, not the x-risk community, and it is not on the aisafety.com map. Its framing is calibrated trust and practical risk control, not catastrophic risk. The provisional home (Life & systems) was not adopted: its method is risk analysis, not complexity science. Funding beyond its foundation members and government commissions is not disclosed.
tag_notes: Home: safety (safety_engineering). Its main AI outputs import risk-management and assurance methods: risk identification and analysis, staged validation, and controls by governance tier. Its central claim is the systems-safety idea that safe components do not make a safe system (H2). The roster's provisional home was life. Ring: core is kept from the roster (E). Its mission is 'Safe and Responsible AI for Public Benefit', it runs the Australian AI Safety Forum and it works for the national AISI. It could arguably be bridge, since its roots are responsible AI, not x-risk. Transfer: into_institutions, because its reports give organisations and government controls and governance tiers for multi-agent deployments. Framing present_harms is the closest fit to its practical, calibrated-trust stance; borderline with structural.

name: Longview Philanthropy: Extreme Power Concentration RFP
summary:
Longview Philanthropy was founded in 2018 by Natalie Cargill and is led by CEO Simran Dhaliwal, with offices in London, Washington DC and San Francisco. It advises major donors and runs grant programmes on AI and nuclear risk.

Its Extreme Power Concentration RFP opened in May 2026 and closed on 2 July 2026, with proposals assessed on a rolling basis. It offered grants of roughly $100k-$2m a year for 6-18 months, plus career-transition funding, for work on the risk that AI lets a small group gain durable control over everyone else. The twelve priority areas include:
- foundational research
- AI integrity and secret loyalties
- law-following AI
- oversight of AI in government
- autonomous weapons and mass surveillance
- political economy
- AI tools that empower citizens
- compute in democracies

A parallel Digital Minds RFP closed on 24 July 2026.
why_it_matters: It is one of the largest funding calls to treat power concentration as a distinct problem. It explicitly invites lawyers, political scientists, economists, national-security veterans and journalists to move into the field, which gives people from adjacent disciplines a direct route in.

key_work.title: Request for proposals on extreme power concentration
Request for Proposals: Research and Applied Work on Digital Minds
Frontier AI Fund

funding: The RFP offered typical grants of $100k-$2m a year for 6-18 months, plus career funding (course buy-outs, post-docs, transition stipends). The Digital Minds RFP offered grants of $50k-$2m and fellowships of $55k-$150k a year. Longview's money comes from major donors (it advises those giving over $1m a year) and from its pooled funds.
status_evidence: Jul 2026: the power-concentration RFP closed on 2 July, with rolling assessment; the Digital Minds RFP closed on 24 July 2026.
engage: Extreme Power Concentration RFP: grants and career funding, now closed (deadline 2 July 2026); questions to the RFP inbox
Digital Minds RFP: project grants, research fellowships and career-development fellowships, now closed (deadline 24 July 2026)
Staff roles via Longview's careers contact
Donor advising and pooled funds (Frontier AI Fund) for major donors
caveats: Both 2026 RFPs are closed and no further rounds have been announced. Longview otherwise does not accept unsolicited proposals. Longview Philanthropy is on the aisafety.com map; the RFP is not listed separately. It operates as two entities, a US 501(c)(3) and a UK company limited by guarantee. Its homepage lists Washington DC first among its offices, so its centre of gravity may have moved from London. The roster entry is the RFP, profiled within Longview.
tag_notes: Home: economics (econ_power). Under H4 a one-programme funder takes its programme's tradition; this RFP funds work against AI-enabled power concentration and lock-in, which B9 places under political economy. Secondary law covers law-following AI and model legislation; peace covers autonomous weapons and oversight of national-security AI. Ring: core (E1), because Longview is an AI-safety and GCR funder on the aisafety.com map and the RFP is aimed at transformative-AI risk. Transfer: into_institutions (J, funders take the work they fund), because most priority areas are oversight, legal, policy and civic instruments. Framing structural, since durable concentration and lock-in are named under the structural framing. Longview funds AI, nuclear and bio risk, so it is a possible generalist-funder candidate under K, but it is not on the K list; flagged for review.

name: Habermas Machine (Google DeepMind)
summary: A Google DeepMind research system in which a language model acts as a 'caucus mediator': it drafts group statements on contested questions, and a personalised reward model ranks them by predicted agreement. The work was published in Science in October 2024. In experiments with 5,734 UK participants, including a virtual citizens' assembly, people preferred its statements to those of human mediators 56% of the time, and groups came out less divided. The code (a fine-tuned version and a prompted Gemini version) and the dataset are open source.
why_it_matters: It is the most-cited empirical test of AI-mediated consensus, so anyone designing AI-assisted deliberation for AI governance starts from it. It also shows the risks the field needs to address: no fact-checking, and possible homogenisation or steering of views.

key_work.title: AI can help humans find common ground in democratic deliberation (Science)
Habermas Machine code and dataset (open source)
Fine-tuning language models to find agreement among humans with diverse preferences (NeurIPS; precursor work)

people: Michael Henry Tessler (lead author, Google DeepMind)
Christopher Summerfield (senior author; Google DeepMind and University of Oxford)
funding: Internal Google DeepMind research project
status_evidence: 21 Jan 2025: last code commit to the repository; Oct 2026: cited as evidence in an EA Forum 'state of the field' review of AI for epistemics and coordination. No follow-up programme found.
engage: Open-source code and dataset on GitHub (software Apache 2.0, other materials CC-BY 4.0), usable for replication or extension
caveats: A finished research project, not an organisation: the repository has had no commits since January 2025 and no follow-up DeepMind programme was found (my web search budget ran out, so later work by the authors may exist). The paper notes that the system does no fact-checking, and critics have raised the risk of homogenising or steering group views.
tag_notes: Home democracy (H1, H2): its output is an AI tool for group deliberation, built on Habermasian deliberative theory and social choice, so it is dem_tools; psych is secondary because the team and the experimental method come from computational cognitive science. Ring kept as bridge (E): a cognitive-science-led project on aligning AI to the preferences of diverse groups. MISFIT: it is a finished project inside a frontier lab, so it could also be read as core (an AI-safety programme in a lab) or as having no sustained programme now. Transfer into_institutions (J3): it offers a template for AI-mediated deliberative processes. Status dormant: a finished project inside an active host (status definition); no hub is coded because the project is over.

name: Allen Lab for Democracy Renovation (Harvard Ash Center), incl. GETTING-Plurality
summary: Danielle Allen's lab at the Harvard Kennedy School's Ash Center (it joined the Ash Center in 2023). It researches and designs governance innovations to 'renovate' constitutional democracy, and works to make democracy a central consideration in technology and AI policy. It hosts the GETTING-Plurality research network of about 40 philosophers, social scientists, computer scientists, legal scholars and technologists. The network's outputs include a roadmap for governing AI through 'power-sharing liberalism', policy primers on public AI, and a 2026 framework for evaluating the ethical-moral intelligence of AI models.
why_it_matters: It brings democratic theory and political philosophy to questions of who governs AI and how power over it is shared, through a network spanning universities and labs (members from Microsoft, OpenAI, Meta and the Santa Fe Institute). Its fellowships and Harvard platform reach policymakers that the AI-safety field rarely reaches.

key_work.title: A Roadmap for Governing AI: Technology Governance and Power-Sharing Liberalism (AI and Ethics)
Crocodile Tears: Can the Ethical-Moral Intelligence of AI Models Be Trusted? (Hubbard, Kidd, Stupu)
Policy 101: Public AI (policy primer)
Reboot Democracy: Designing Democratic Engagement for the AI Era (workshop series with The GovLab and InnovateUS)

people: Allison Stanger (co-director and co-investigator, GETTING-Plurality, Feb 2024 to Jan 2026)
Sarah Hubbard (associate director for technology and democracy)
status_evidence: Sep 2026: announced a Digital Civic Infrastructure Initiative; Apr 2026: GETTING-Plurality paper 'Crocodile Tears' on the ethical-moral intelligence of AI models.
engage: Allen Lab Fellowships: policy and research fellows appointed for AY2025-26 and AY2026-27, including in AI governance
Public events, e.g. Voter Experience Summit (Mar 2026) and book talks
Tech & Democracy Weekly Roundup newsletter (The Renovator, from Sep 2025)
caveats: AI is one strand among several (electoral reform, civic infrastructure, municipal partnerships). The listed GETTING-Plurality co-directorship ran from February 2024 to January 2026, so it is unclear whether the network continues in the same form. Funders not found. The lab existed before it joined the Ash Center in 2023, so '2023' marks that move rather than its origin.
tag_notes: Home democracy (H2, H5): its AI work applies democratic theory and democratic-renovation concepts to AI governance, so the closest sub-tradition is dem_deliberation; philosophy (Allen's political theory) and economics (power-sharing, public AI) are secondary. Ring kept as bridge (E3): an older Harvard democracy lab with a standing, funded network on governing AI for democracy and on AI models' moral reasoning. Transfer into_institutions (J3): roadmaps, policy primers and testimony on governance designs.

name: Collective Intelligence Project (CIP)
summary: A nonprofit R&D lab, founded in 2023, that runs public-input processes for AI and builds the tools for them. Global Dialogues surveys about 1,000 people in 64-69 countries each round on how AI affects them and what they want from it, and publishes the data openly. Weval is an open platform where more than 1,000 contributors write qualitative evaluations of models. It also runs Alignment Assemblies (with Taiwan's Ministry of Digital Affairs from May 2023, and with Anthropic on Collective Constitutional AI), Community Models, and Jhilmil regional and cultural benchmarks.
why_it_matters: It turns public and community input into things labs actually use, such as a model constitution, evaluation blueprints and open datasets. This makes democratic participation part of the alignment pipeline, not only of policy debate. It is not on the aisafety.com map.

key_work.title: Collective Constitutional AI (with Anthropic) and Alignment Assemblies (with Taiwan's Ministry of Digital Affairs)
Roadmap for Democratic AI
Global Dialogues (rounds in Jun 2025, Oct 2025, Feb 2026, May 2026)
Weval community evaluations platform

people: Saffron Huang (co-founder; now a research scientist on Anthropic's Societal Impacts team and adviser to CIP)
funding: Robert Wood Johnson Foundation and Omidyar Network named as major funders on its site; Weval partners include Anthropic, Microsoft and Stanford
status_evidence: 1 Oct 2026: latest dated Weval evaluation runs; May 2026: Global Dialogues round with 1,024 participants in 69 countries.
engage: Write or contribute evaluation blueprints on Weval (open source)
Submit questions for Global Dialogues respondents via its public form
Careers page on cip.org (no specific openings confirmed)
Annual reports published for 2023, 2024 and 2025
caveats: The team page could not be read, so leadership is based on prior knowledge; check before citing. Whether its outputs change model behaviour depends on labs choosing to use them. Its funders come from philanthropy outside the x-risk community, which may explain why it is missing from the classic map.
tag_notes: Home democracy (H1): its method is collective intelligence and participatory input (assemblies, global dialogues, community evals), so it is dem_tools, which the taxonomy illustrates with CIP. Ring kept as core (E1): its primary mission is steering transformative AI well, and it works directly with frontier labs, although it is not on the classic map. Transfer into_model (J1): public input feeds model constitutions, evaluations and Community Models. Problems use the F must-pairs: values with democracy (public input yields model specs) and assurance (it builds evaluations).

name: AI Objectives Institute (AOI)
summary: A nonprofit research lab founded by the late Peter Eckersley, working to make sure that AI and future economic systems are 'built and deployed with genuine human objectives at their core'. Its main product is Talk to the City, an open-source LLM tool that turns surveys, interviews and social-media posts into maps of opinion clusters. The tool has been used by Taiwan's Ministry of Digital Affairs, in Tokyo election polling, at UN climate talks and in an Australian youth-voice study. Its research covers governance with AI, aligning markets and other optimisers, gradual disempowerment, and AI's effects on labour.
why_it_matters: It treats markets and bureaucracies as misaligned optimisers alongside AI, a framing taken from economics and mechanism design. Talk to the City is one of the few deliberation tools in real government use. It also co-authored early work on gradual disempowerment as a systemic risk.

key_work.title: Talk to the City (open-source broad-listening tool; site 2.0 launched mid-2026)
Gradual Disempowerment: Systemic Existential Risks from Continuous AI Development
Generative AI and Labor Market Outcomes: Evidence from the United Kingdom
What Jobs Can AI Learn? Measuring Exposure by Reinforcement Learning

people: Deger Turan (president; formerly first CEO, led Talk to the City; now CEO of Metaculus)
funding: Survival and Flourishing Fund grants (per Longterm Wiki; amounts not confirmed); individual donations and corporate matching via Benevity
status_evidence: 29 Jun 2026: two blog posts on AI, automation and expertise; Aug 2026: commits to Talk to the City after its site relaunch in May-Jun 2026.
engage: Talk to the City code is open source (Apache 2.0)
Donations, and a quarterly newsletter
caveats: Leadership has changed: Colleen McKenzie was announced as executive director in April 2024 but is now listed as an adviser, and the president, Deger Turan, is also CEO of Metaculus, so who runs it day to day is unclear. Blog output is thin (two posts in 2026). The founding year (2021) is from prior knowledge, not confirmed on its site.
tag_notes: Home democracy (H2): its flagship output, Talk to the City, is a collective-intelligence tool, so it is dem_tools (the taxonomy's own example); economics is secondary for its work on market alignment and labour. Ring core (E1): on the aisafety.com map, SFF-funded, with a mission about aligning AI and other optimisers. Transfer into_institutions (J3): it supplies broad-listening processes to governments and research on governing through markets.

name: AI & Democracy Foundation (AIDF)
summary: A San Francisco nonprofit (legally Thoughtful Tech Project Inc, a 501(c)(3)) led by Aviv Ovadya. It works to keep democratic systems fit for an AI-transformed world, and to use representative deliberation, such as citizens' assemblies, in the governance and alignment of AI. Its outputs include the Democracy Levels framework for grading how democratically AI decisions are made, Case Law for AI (turning deliberative input into precedents for model behaviour), a deliberative-tools access programme, and the ARIA-funded Democratic Capabilities Gap Map (democracy.build). It also offers funders strategic prioritisation and regranting.
why_it_matters: It takes deliberative-democracy practice into AI alignment itself, by specifying model behaviour through representative deliberation. Its gap map of capabilities, research questions and product gaps is a ready agenda for founders and funders who want to widen the field.

key_work.title: Democracy Levels framework for AI decision-making
Case Law for AI: judicial-style grounding of deliberative input into alignment
Democratic Capabilities Gap Map (50 capabilities, 253 research questions, 16 product gaps; ARIA-funded)

funding: ARIA (UK Advanced Research and Invention Agency) funds the Democratic Capabilities Gap Map and a 'Deliberative AI Specifications and Infrastructure' grant; other funders not disclosed
status_evidence: Jun 2026: data version of the Democratic Capabilities Gap Map on democracy.build.
engage: Deliberative-tools access programme for practitioners
democracy.build lists high-impact tools to build, open problems and funding needs
Strategic prioritisation, coordination and regranting for funders of democratic AI governance
Substack newsletter
caveats: The founding year comes from the roster and was not confirmed on its own site; the legal entity's name suggests an earlier vehicle. Longterm Wiki reports a partnership with ARIA's Safeguarded AI programme on specifying safety through deliberation; ARIA's funding of democracy.build is confirmed on that site, but the Safeguarded AI link was not confirmed on ARIA's pages. Funders other than ARIA are not disclosed.
tag_notes: Home democracy (H1): its method is representative deliberation and process design (the team has run 30+ intensive deliberative processes), so it is dem_deliberation; law is secondary for the judicial reasoning in Case Law for AI. Ring kept as core (E1): its founding mission is democratic governance and alignment of AI, funded by ARIA's AI-safety-adjacent work. Transfer into_institutions (J3): democratic processes and frameworks for AI decisions; it also reaches the model through alignment specifications, so problems pair values with democracy (F must-pair).

name: Democracy X (formerly the Danish Board of Technology / Teknologirådet)
summary: A Danish non-profit-distributing foundation formed in 2023 by merging Teknologirådet (the Danish Board of Technology, active since the 1980s and known for consensus conferences and the World Wide Views global citizen consultations) with DeltagerDanmark, a community-organising group. About 50 staff run citizen panels, deliberations and local organising on three themes: planetary boundaries, technological acceleration and democratic strengthening. Its main AI work is the National Youth Dialogue on Generative AI (361 young people, autumn 2024), reported in January 2025 with the Danish Data Ethics Council and TrygFonden.
why_it_matters: It holds some of the longest institutional experience in participatory technology assessment, the practice of having citizens deliberate on emerging technologies before they spread. That method applies directly to public deliberation on frontier AI, though Democracy X has not yet aimed it there.

key_work.title: De unges stemme i samtalen om generativ AI (National Youth Dialogue on Generative AI report, with Dataetisk Råd and TrygFonden)
Visioner for fremtidens digitale fællesskaber (citizen visions for future online communities)
World Wide Views global citizen consultations (Danish Board of Technology method)

people: Lise Bitsch (co-author of the youth AI report)
Sigrid Vedel Neuhaus (project lead, technology and digital communities)
funding: Commissioned work for ministries, regions and municipalities; EU research grants (it says it is among Denmark's ten largest recipients of EU research funding); TrygFonden partnership through the 'Viden & Demokrati' programme
status_evidence: Jul 2026: Bo Trygt's backbone secretariat moved to Democracy X; Jun 2026: published 'På sporet af det tavse flertal'; Apr 2026: citizen panel's eight recommendations on pig welfare.
engage: Commissions and partnerships for citizen panels, deliberations and stakeholder processes (Danish and EU projects)
caveats: A renamed and merged successor of the Danish Board of Technology; the old tekno.dk site now points to Democracy X. Its AI engagement is light: one youth dialogue and some work on digital communities. The roster's 'June 2026' date for the youth report is wrong; the report is dated January 2025. Most material is in Danish.
tag_notes: Home democracy (H1): its method is citizen deliberation and participation, so it is dem_deliberation; arts is secondary for its participatory technology assessment heritage (B10). Ring kept as potential (E2): its AI work in 2024-26 is a single youth dialogue, not a standing programme. Transferable method: participatory technology assessment (consensus conferences, World Wide Views) applied to frontier AI. Transfer into_institutions (J3): the youth dialogue fed young people's recommendations to policymakers with the Data Ethics Council. Status changed: renamed successor formed by a 2023 merger, active in 2026.

name: People Powered
summary: A member-driven global hub for participatory democracy, incorporated as a nonprofit in the US and Ireland, with staff and members around the world. It grew out of a Global Participatory Budgeting Hub (2019) and was set up in its current form in 2020 by 58 practitioners from 28 countries. It runs training, mentorship, accelerators and resource centres on participatory budgeting, citizens' assemblies and digital participation. Its AI work so far includes AI criteria in its ratings of 30 digital participation platforms, accelerator funding for European universities where students co-wrote AI policies, and a September 2026 webinar and workshop series with the OECD and Bertelsmann Stiftung on AI in citizen participation.
why_it_matters: It is a main channel to local governments and practitioners worldwide, so safeguards for AI-mediated participation (against exclusion, skewed summaries and simulated public opinion) could spread through it. It also holds practical know-how on running participatory processes, which AI governance could borrow.

key_work.title: Digital Participation Platform Ratings and Guide (AI usage among the criteria; refreshed 2025)
Who Should Decide the Future of AI? These Universities Put Students in Charge (AI Aware Universities, supported by its Digital Democracy Accelerator)
AI is changing citizen participation: are we ready? (webinar and workshop with OECD and Bertelsmann Stiftung)

people: Matt Stempeck (lead author, Guide to Digital Participation Platforms)
hq: Distributed (incorporated in the US and Ireland)
funding: Funding partners and individual donors (IRS Form 990s for 2021-24 published); named funders not found
status_evidence: 16 and 30 Sep 2026: webinar and workshop on AI in citizen participation with the OECD and Bertelsmann Stiftung; 7 Sep 2026: case study on students co-writing university AI policies.
engage: Membership for organisations, government practitioners, researchers and advocates
Online digital participation training courses
Digital Democracy Accelerator and mentorship programmes
Webinars and workshops, e.g. the AI and participation series (Sep 2026)
Democracy Stories Lab (awards up to $1,000)
Staff roles (e.g. Resource Mobilization Director, applications closed Sep 2026)
caveats: Its AI engagement is mostly about AI as a tool inside participation processes, not about governing frontier AI, and there is no standing AI programme or page. Its long-standing co-executive director stepped down in July 2026.
tag_notes: Home democracy (H3): a member body serving participatory-democracy practitioners (participatory budgeting, citizens' assemblies), so it is dem_deliberation. Ring kept as potential (E2): its AI activity is a few webinars, one accelerator grant and AI criteria in platform ratings, with no standing AI programme. Transferable method: practitioner networks and safeguards for running participatory processes, which could carry AI-governance deliberation to local governments. Transfer convening (J5): it brings its own practitioner community into the AI conversation. Region global (O): incorporated in two countries, with staff distributed worldwide.

name: Equilibria Network
summary: A small Swedish-registered nonprofit research network that studies how groups of people and AI systems come to act together, using complex-systems, cybernetic and social-choice models. It publishes working papers on collective agency, gradual disempowerment and adaptive institutions, and builds the Collective Intelligence Library, an open-source JAX simulation in which markets, networks and democracies are composable mechanisms acting on one population.
why_it_matters: It treats AI risk as a property of the network of humans and AI agents rather than of single models, and tries to make gradual disempowerment measurable in simulation, drawing on Beer's Viable System Model, active inference and Ostrom. That is a multi-agent, institution-level lens the alignment mainstream rarely funds.

key_work.title: Spectral Signatures of Gradual Disempowerment
Collective Intelligence Library (open-source simulation) and whitepaper
A Phylogeny of Agents
System Level Safety Evaluations

people: Markov Grey (Technology and Communication Lead, co-founder)
Jobst Heitzig (advisor, Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research)
status_evidence: Sep 2026: published 'Collective Epistemics: Some Napkin Math on Independent Errors' on its Substack; website repository updated 21 Sep 2026; a paper accepted for IWAI 2026.
engage: Newsletter on Substack (equilibria1.substack.com)
Open-source Collective Intelligence Library on GitHub
caveats: The domain listed on the aisafety.com map (equilibria.network) now redirects to a GoDaddy for-sale page; the organisation continues at eq-network.org. The site's structured data gives Uppsala as its locality and a foundingDate of 2026-06-12, which looks like a recent registration of the nonprofit rather than the start of the work (its Substack and LessWrong output goes back to Aug 2025). Funders are not stated. Much of the research output is working papers and blog posts rather than peer-reviewed work. Two core people plus four advisors.
tag_notes: Home life (B6): its main output is agent-based simulation and complexity/cybernetic models of collective intelligence (roadmap phases named for Wiener, Beer, Ostrom), so life_complexity; formal secondary for social choice and mechanism-design theory, democracy secondary for voting and liquid-futarchy work. Ring core: its founding mission is preventing harmful collective AI behaviour, it sits in the AI-safety ecosystem (on the aisafety.com map, director also organises the AFFINE alignment seminar) and imports complex-systems methods. Transfer into_institutions: the simulations aim to design and test coordination mechanisms and institutions for mixed human-AI societies rather than to change individual models. Framing structural: gradual disempowerment and spreading negative loops.

name: The Vincent and Elinor Ostrom Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis (Ostrom Workshop), Indiana University
summary: Research centre at Indiana University Bloomington founded in 1973 by Elinor and Vincent Ostrom, home of the 'Bloomington School' of institutional analysis, polycentric governance and commons research. It runs programmes on commons governance, environment and natural resources, political economy, food systems, space governance, cybersecurity and internet governance, and data management and information governance, with a weekly colloquium and research series, visiting scholars and affiliates.
why_it_matters: It holds the deepest body of evidence on how many actors govern shared resources without a single sovereign or a pure market, which bears directly on governing compute, data and shared agent infrastructure in multipolar AI scenarios. Its AI engagement so far is light.

key_work.title: Governing the Commons (Elinor Ostrom) and the Institutional Analysis and Development framework
Programme on Data Management and Information Governance, including an AI ethics strand
State of Hoosier Cybersecurity 2025 Report (Cybersecurity and Internet Governance programme)
Talk: 'The Cost of Openness: AI, Extraction, and Scholarly Governance'

people: Scott Shackelford (Director, Cybersecurity and Internet Governance programme; led the Workshop for six years to 2025)
Angie Raymond (Director, Data Management and Information Governance programme)
funding: University funds, donations and external grants (its own description); amounts not published.
status_evidence: Oct 2026: hybrid colloquium and research series running weekly, including a 20 Oct 2026 talk on AI, extraction and scholarly governance; Jan 2026: new executive co-directors announced.
engage: Visiting scholars and practitioners programme
Ostrom Fellowship and research awards
Hybrid weekly colloquium and research series (Teams/Zoom)
Become an Ostrom affiliate; programme mailing lists
caveats: No dedicated AI programme found. AI appears as a strand of the data governance programme (mostly 2022-era activity) and in occasional talks. The site's news section is sparse. Leadership changed in Jan 2026 after Scott Shackelford became IU's associate vice president for research.
tag_notes: Home economics (B9: commons and polycentric governance), sub econ_commons; law secondary for its cybersecurity and data governance programmes led by law scholars, life secondary for social-ecological systems research. Ring potential (E2): no standing AI programme, only an AI ethics strand in the data programme and occasional AI talks. Transferable method: Ostrom's design principles and IAD framework for polycentric self-governance of shared resources, applicable to compute, data and shared agent infrastructure. Transfer into_institutions rather than none_yet because some light AI governance work exists; partner engagement because there is no AI programme yet.

name: OpenResearch
summary: San Francisco nonprofit research lab, set up in 2015 as YC Research and renamed in 2020. It ran the Unconditional Cash Study, a randomised trial in Illinois and Texas in which 1,000 people received $1,000 a month for three years (2,000 controls received $50), and has published its data. It now runs RISE, a rural cash-transfer study with GiveDirectly (2025-27), works on AI-assisted survey methods, and is launching an 'AI & Society' line with a listening study called 'Whose AI?'.
why_it_matters: Its trial is the most detailed US evidence on unconditional income, including moderate falls in paid work and short-lived wellbeing gains. That is a direct input to designing AI windfall or dividend schemes, and it is not yet connected to TAI economics work such as the Windfall Trust's.

key_work.title: Unconditional Cash Study and public-use dataset
The Employment Effects of a Guaranteed Income: Experimental Evidence from Two U.S. States (NBER w32719)
Can AI Help Surveys Keep Up with How People Work Today?
Whose AI? study

funding: National Science Foundation grant #2149344 and private donors (per the NBER paper). Sam Altman, a board member, is widely reported as a main backer of the cash study; I did not verify amounts.
status_evidence: May 2026: published a report on conversational AI surveys (GPT-4o, 2,120 participants); RISE data collection running Nov 2025 to Feb 2027.
engage: Public-use data from the Unconditional Cash Study
'Whose AI?' seeks community and individual partners
Donations
caveats: Its AI & Society line is described as just launching; 'Whose AI?' has no published outputs or dates yet. The AI-survey work uses AI as a research tool rather than studying AI's effects. Close ties to Sam Altman (board member, funder) may matter to some funders. Renamed from YC Research in 2020 and says it is now independent of Y Combinator.
tag_notes: Home economics, sub econ_tai: randomised policy evaluation of cash transfers, the core input to income distribution under AI-driven economic change. Ring potential kept (E2): the AI & Society line is 'launching' with one unpublished study, not yet a sustained programme. Transferable method: large-scale RCT evidence on unconditional income, for designing AI windfall or dividend distribution. Transfer into_institutions (policy evidence) rather than none_yet because light AI work exists; partner because its main method has no AI connection yet. Framing flourishing from its 'shared prosperity' and access language.

name: Connected by Data
summary: UK not-for-profit company, founded in 2022 by Jeni Tennison, that campaigns for communities to have a real say in decisions about data and AI. It designs and promotes public deliberation on AI governance, including the 'Citizens Track' for the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance, ran an action-learning programme with nine education unions and the TUC on worker power over public-sector AI, and convened a community of practice for public-engagement practitioners.
why_it_matters: It brings participatory-democracy and data-justice practice into global AI governance, proposing concrete designs for citizen deliberation alongside AI summits and UN processes. These are channels for public voice that the AI-safety policy world mostly lacks.

key_work.title: Global Citizen Deliberation on Artificial Intelligence: Options and design considerations (Tim Davies)
A Citizens' Track on AI Governance: Agency, Alignment & Accountability (white paper with the University of Sheffield's Centre for Machine Intelligence, Ada Lovelace Institute and ISWE Foundation)
Ten lessons on public sector AI from our work with education unions
Public AI Voices & Engagement (PAVE) Case Book, with the University of Sheffield

people: Emily Macaulay (Head of Delivery and Operations)
funding: Shuttleworth Foundation $275,000 (set-up to Feb 2024); AI Collaborative $270,000; Ford Foundation £160,000 (half passed to the TUC); PAVE Case Book funded by the University of Sheffield's Centre for Machine Intelligence.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: blog posts on trialling a community conversation on AI for the Citizens Track (2 Sep) and on its PAVE booth at the AI for Good Global Summit in Geneva (28 Sep).
engage: Data and AI Civil Society Network
Citizens Track webinars and community conversations
Submitting cases to the PAVE Case Book (2026 round closed 5 June)
caveats: It is a fixed-term organisation: in March 2026 it announced it will wind up in 2027, at the end of its planned lifespan, and is exploring 'regenerations' (fiscal sponsorship of collective initiatives, a consultants' umbrella, a grassroots programme), so engagement windows are short. Registered office is in Epsom; I found no evidence of a London office. The public-engagement community of practice ran monthly from July 2024; a June 2026 post discusses its future. It frames its work around power and participation rather than safety, despite 'Alignment' in the white paper's title.
tag_notes: Home democracy, sub dem_deliberation: its main AI outputs are designs for citizen deliberation in AI governance (global assemblies, Citizens Track); economics secondary for the union power-building programme, law secondary for data-justice advocacy. Ring adjacent kept: sustained AI programme framed around participation, power and accountability, with no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing. Transfer into_institutions: it supplies deliberative templates for UN and national AI governance. Framing structural: who holds power over data and AI decisions.

name: MIT Center for Constructive Communication (CCC)
summary: Centre at the MIT Media Lab, launched in January 2021 and directed by Deb Roy, that designs and tests human-led, AI-assisted systems for listening, dialogue and deliberation in small groups. Its tools include Forage (LLM-assisted sensemaking of conversation data), VoiceTrace (tracing public input through civic decisions) and FaciliTrain (AI-simulated facilitation practice), deployed with communities through its nonprofit partner Cortico and its realtalk programmes. It also publishes LLM research on bias and alignment.
why_it_matters: It brings dialogue and facilitation practice, along with computational social science, to the question of how AI should mediate public conversation. Recent papers show leading LLMs underperform for less-educated and non-US users, and examine aligning models to users' long-term interests rather than stated wishes.

key_work.title: From Delegates to Trustees: How Optimizing for Long-Term Interests Shapes Bias and Alignment in LLMs (EACL 2026)
LLM Targeted Underperformance Disproportionately Impacts Vulnerable Users (AAAI-26)
Forage: Understanding LLM-facilitated sensemaking of conversation data (CHI 2026)
Voice to Vision: participatory data infrastructure for civic decision-making (CSCW 2026, best paper)

people: Dimitra Dimitrakopoulou (Principal Research Scientist, leads Translational Research & Practice)
funding: Launched with over $10M in commitments from foundations, corporations, government programmes and philanthropists; its site names Reid Hoffman (general operating support), the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, Google Jigsaw and Media Lab consortium members. Amounts per funder not published.
status_evidence: Apr 2026: 'Voice to Vision' published at CSCW 2026 (best paper); 2026 CHI papers; Sep 2026 essay by Deb Roy in the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists listed on its site.
engage: Graduate study at the MIT Media Lab
Newsletter
Community partnerships via Cortico and realtalk programmes
caveats: The alignment paper is one line of work among many; most output is civic-technology and HCI research. Its relationship with Cortico, a separate nonprofit co-founded by Roy in 2016 where he is unpaid CEO, runs under a 10-year cooperation agreement with MIT (to Jan 2032) over IP, prototyping and pilots, with funding kept separate. It grew out of the Laboratory for Social Machines (2014).
tag_notes: Home democracy, sub dem_tools: AI tools for listening, bridging and deliberation; psych secondary for social-psychology work on outgroup animosity and agency, arts secondary for design and narrative auditing (Storyline). Ring adjacent kept: sustained AI programme focused on civic communication; one alignment paper does not make the programme safety-framed. Transfer into_institutions: its systems are built to feed public voice into civic decision-making. Its 'speed of trust' and 'small is beautiful' principles come close to the speed_of_wisdom badge but concern communication design, not AI pace.

name: Digital Democracy 2030 (DD2030) and Team Mirai
summary: DD2030 is an open, volunteer civic-technology community in Japan, launched in 2025 by engineer Takahiro Anno. It builds open-source tools for AI-assisted 'broad listening' and deliberation: Kouchou AI (comment analysis adapted from Talk to the City), Idobata (deliberation modelled on vTaiwan and JOIN), Polimoney (political-finance transparency) and Project Coreloop. Team Mirai is the political party Anno founded, which uses the same methods. It won an upper-house seat in 2025 and, by its own account, 11 lower-house seats in the 2026 general election.
why_it_matters: Probably the largest live use of AI-mediated public input in national politics: 8,200+ AI interviews and 9,700 policy suggestions fed into Team Mirai's 2025 platform, with municipalities also using the tools. It is almost invisible in AI-safety circles.

key_work.title: Kouchou AI v4.0 (open-source broad-listening tool)
Idobata deliberation platform
Polimoney political-finance transparency dashboard
Digital Democracy Summit 2026 (with Audrey Tang)

people: Takahiro Anno (founder of DD2030, left its board May 2025; leader of Team Mirai)
Ken Suzuki (DD2030 board member; chairman, SmartNews)
Haruyuki Seki (DD2030 board member; Code for Japan)
Makiko Nakamuro (DD2030 board member; Keio University)
funding: Donations and a CAMPFIRE crowdfunding campaign; Schneier and Sanders (Jan 2026) describe DD2030 as philanthropically funded. Amounts not disclosed.
status_evidence: Aug 2026: Digital Democracy Summit 2026 (2 Aug, Keio University Mita Campus, Tokyo, hybrid with streaming, with Audrey Tang); weekly activity reports from 19 Mar 2025 through April 2026; Kouchou AI v4.0 released 28 Dec 2025.
engage: Contribute as developer, researcher, designer, translator or organiser via the join page, Slack and GitHub
Digital Democracy Summit (free, registration)
Broad-listening guidebook
caveats: DD2030 declares party and procedural neutrality and is not Team Mirai's 'sister' organisation: Anno resigned from its board in May 2025 to preserve neutrality. They are profiled together because they share a founder and methods. Team Mirai's 11 lower-house seats in the 8 Feb 2026 election are confirmed by Japanese press (e.g. J-CAST). Most sources are in Japanese.
tag_notes: Home democracy, sub dem_tools: open-source AI tools for broad listening and deliberation. Ring adjacent kept: sustained AI-for-democracy programme with no safety or catastrophic-risk framing. Transfer into_institutions: tools used by municipalities, parties and the Diet to turn public input into policy. Org type network because DD2030 calls itself a loose participatory community, not an organisation. Standpoint neither (Japan, rule O). Badge fractal: national-scale ambition built from local municipal pilots and volunteer community (taxonomy example).

name: Citizens Foundation
summary: Icelandic nonprofit founded in Reykjavík in 2008, after the financial crash, that builds open-source civic participation software: Better Reykjavík, Your Priorities (used in 50+ countries; the Scottish Parliament's Engage platform since 2019) and All Our Ideas. Its newer framework, Policy Synth, coordinates teams of AI agents that research problems, evolve and Elo-rank candidate solutions, and return them to human review and voting. It has been used with the New Jersey AI Task Force, for skills-first hiring and for the ERIC EU rights assistant.
why_it_matters: It offers a working design for using agentic AI in public decision-making while keeping citizens and officials in charge of every judgement ('AI accelerated the work; people decided'). That is a practical template for human oversight of AI in government.

key_work.title: Policy Synth (open-source multi-agent framework) and research paper
Engage @ Scottish Parliament on Your Priorities
New Jersey AI Task Force: 2,200+ worker voices to AI policy
ERIC: AI rights assistant for EU citizens

people: Hanna Dóra Haraldsdóttir (Chair of the Board)
funding: Not published. Project partners include Democracy Fund and The GovLab (election-subversion crowdsourcing) and the New Jersey AI Task Force; a US affiliate, Citizens Foundation America, has existed.
status_evidence: Jun 2026: impact page on the Scottish Parliament's Engage programme, citing a committee report on ADHD and autism support published in early 2026; OECD 2026 report cited on its site.
engage: Open-source code (MIT licence) on GitHub and npm
Work with us: commissioning platforms or Policy Synth projects
caveats: The Scottish Parliament uses Your Priorities, not Policy Synth, contrary to the roster draft. Policy Synth is a tool for AI-assisted policymaking rather than work on AI safety itself; it belongs here as a design for human oversight of agentic AI in public decisions. The core team is about four people.
tag_notes: Home democracy, sub dem_tools: participation platforms and collective-intelligence tools, now combined with AI agents. Ring adjacent kept: a sustained AI programme (Policy Synth) about keeping people in charge of AI-assisted public decisions, with no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing. Transfer into_institutions: parliaments, state task forces and agencies adopt its processes. Framing flourishing from its mission to help citizens and governments make better decisions together.

name: Dembrane (dembrane B.V.)
summary: Dutch company based in 's-Hertogenbosch. It builds an open-source platform that records, transcribes and synthesises dozens of small-group table conversations happening at the same time, and produces outcome documents that trace back to the original speakers while participants are still in the room. It began with a $100k OpenAI 'Democratic Inputs to AI' grant in 2023. Municipalities and companies use it, and it is a partner in the EU AI4Deliberation project.
why_it_matters: A working test bed for AI-mediated deliberation in small groups. It takes an explicit 'low AI' ethics stance: AI is kept minimal and transparent, and participants can accept, reject or change what it suggests. It also moved to EU-sovereign transcription. It is concrete evidence on how to keep humans in charge of the synthesis step that schemes for collective input into AI depend on.

key_work.title: OpenAI Democratic Inputs to AI grant ($100k)
Ethical whitepaper ('low AI' principles for AI in deliberation)
dembrane is going open source
Why we said goodbye to AssemblyAI (and what we're building instead): EU-sovereign transcription

funding: OpenAI Democratic Inputs to AI grant, $100k (Aug 2023); EU Horizon Europe funding as an AI4Deliberation partner (from Nov 2024); client revenue from municipalities and companies such as ASML. Investors not disclosed (it blogged about 'mission aligned investment' in Apr 2025).
status_evidence: Jul 2026: blog post on replacing AssemblyAI with EU-sovereign transcription; Jun 2026: featured post on using dembrane in dialogues; careers page (Oct 2026) lists open engineering, design and sales roles.
engage: Jobs: full-stack engineer, head of product design, sales lead, and freelance facilitator and translator roles listed at dembrane.com/work (Oct 2026)
Internships and thesis projects (dembrane.com/work)
Open-source platform code on GitHub
caveats: A commercial B.V. Its 2023 framing, a route for democratic input into AI alignment, has since given way to a general stakeholder-engagement product. Its site does not give a founding year (it says the founders came together between 2020 and 2024). A 2023 source places it in Eindhoven; it is now in 's-Hertogenbosch.
tag_notes: Home democracy/dem_tools: builds software for small-group deliberation and synthesis that participants validate (H1; the dem_deliberation boundary sends tool-building to CI tools). Ring adjacent (E3, roster kept): sustained work on AI in deliberation (2024 ethics white paper, AI4Deliberation partner) without safety or alignment framing since its 2023 OpenAI grant. Transfer into_institutions: it supplies deliberative processes to councils and organisations and does not change models. Framing flourishing ('every voice heard'). Knowing practice (facilitation know-how built into the tool).

name: AI4Deliberation (Artificial Intelligence for Institutionalised, Multimodal, Gamified, Mass Democratic Deliberations)
summary: Horizon Europe project (grant 101178806, Nov 2024 to Oct 2027, about €3.0M) building ethical AI tools and guidance to help governments run, institutionalise and evaluate large multimodal and gamified public deliberations, including argument mining and AI-supported summarisation. The coordinator is the Greek IT firm Uni Systems. Partners include TU Delft, CERTH, the University of Bamberg, the University of Dundee (ARG-tech), the Ljubljana Institute of Criminology, Dembrane, ActionAid Italia and the City of Bamberg. It runs four large pilots on climate change and long COVID.
why_it_matters: The main EU-funded test of AI-mediated deliberation inside government, and it studies the failure modes as well as building tools. Its outputs include evidence of an 'AI penalty' (people value AI-assisted deliberation less, which risks a new deliberative divide), comparisons of human and LLM deliberation, and institutional-design and legal-ethics work on where AI belongs in democratic processes.

key_work.title: Artificial Intelligence in deliberation: The AI penalty and the emergence of a new deliberative divide (Jungherr & Rauchfleisch, Government Information Quarterly)
Artificial Intelligence for Mass Democratic Deliberations: The AI4Deliberation Project Objectives and Methodology (Tambouris)
Institutional Design for AI-enabled Deliberation (Nouws, Janssen, Tambouris)
The Open Argument Mining Framework (Gemechu, Reed et al.)

people: Efthimios Tambouris (author of the project's objectives-and-methodology chapter)
funding: Horizon Europe grant 101178806: EU contribution €2,999,500 (the full cost), Nov 2024 to Oct 2027.
status_evidence: 2026: project conference papers listed on CORDIS, including 'Procedural Parity, Outcome Mismatch: Evaluating Human vs LLM Deliberation' and 'AI Agents and the Future of Deliberation'; first-sprint pilot plan and policy brief deliverables submitted.
caveats: No working project website was found: ai4deliberation.org is a parked domain (Oct 2026), so the evidence comes from CORDIS and partner pages. Funding is time-limited and ends in Oct 2027. Earlier descriptions listed specific tools (fact-checking, toxicity detection) that CORDIS's summary does not confirm. HQ is given as the coordinator's location.
tag_notes: Home democracy/dem_tools: builds an AI toolkit for mass deliberation, including argument mining, which B10 places in Democracy (H1). Secondary law: a formal legal-ethics strand and partners from criminology and institutional design. Ring adjacent (E3, roster kept): a funded AI programme on democratic deliberation with no safety or catastrophic framing. Transfer into_institutions: guidance and tools for governments to institutionalise deliberation. Framing structural: its stated motive is institutional distrust and polarisation. Org type programme (I: time-limited funded consortium).

name: Nesta Centre for Collective Intelligence (formerly Centre for Collective Intelligence Design, CCID)
summary: A unit of Nesta, the UK innovation foundation, that designs digital tools and deliberative processes for public engagement, including the Zeitgeist deliberation platform and the Collective Intelligence Design Playbook. Its AI work centres on the AI Social Readiness process. This was developed with the UK Government's Incubator for AI and piloted in May-June 2025 with 144 members of the public in 18 workshops on the government's Consult tool. It also includes public-attitude studies on AI in social work and a 2026 citizens' jury on neurotechnology.
why_it_matters: It turns public deliberation into an AI assurance instrument. Before a government AI tool is deployed, an advisory label records public confidence in it, the risks people see and the safeguards they want. That is a ready template for giving the public a say in deployment decisions, which mainstream AI assurance leaves to experts.

key_work.title: The AI Social Readiness process (advisory label for the Consult tool)
How to manage AI risks: a community-based approach to AI assurance
How does the public feel about social workers using AI?
A citizens' jury exploring public views on neurotechnology and neurodata

funding: Funded through Nesta, a charity originally endowed with £250M from the UK National Lottery. Partners and commissioners include the UK Government's Incubator for AI and the Electoral Commission.
status_evidence: Aug 2026: report on a citizens' jury on neurotechnology and neurodata; Jul 2026: roadmap on rebuilding public trust in politics, commissioned by the Electoral Commission; Dec 2025: reports on AI and public trust.
engage: Staff roles via Nesta's jobs page
Partnership enquiries for public-engagement and AI-assurance projects through the centre's page
Collective Intelligence Design Playbook, a free practitioner toolkit
caveats: Renamed from Centre for Collective Intelligence Design, and older pages still use that name. Much of its work is commissioned engagement on non-AI topics such as climate, politics and social care. The Participatory AI project page has not been updated since 2023. Founding year not confirmed in the sources checked.
tag_notes: Home democracy/dem_deliberation: its main AI output, AI Social Readiness, is public deliberation workshops that yield an advisory label (H1). Secondary arts: the centre names design and arts among its methods. Ring adjacent (E3, roster kept): a sustained AI strand (2025 assurance pilot, 2025 social-work AI study, 2026 neurotech jury) framed as public trust and voice, not catastrophic risk. Transfer into_institutions: the label is a governance instrument for public-sector AI deployment. Status changed: renamed from CCID with the same mission and team. Org type programme (I: unit inside Nesta).

name: AI for Collective Intelligence Research Hub (AI4CI)
summary: UKRI-funded National AI Research Hub (EPSRC grant EP/Y028392/1, Feb 2024 to Jan 2029). It is led from the University of Bristol with Bath, Cardiff, Exeter, Glasgow, UCL and Ulster and more than 40 stakeholder partners. It develops AI that gathers and makes sense of distributed data and supports collective decision-making in healthcare, finance, the environment, pandemics and cities, with cross-cutting themes on human-centred design and governance infrastructure. It also runs a Rapid Response Fund and public forums on AI and society.
why_it_matters: It holds complex-systems and agent-based modelling know-how about how communities of people and AI agents behave together. It funds studies such as AI-facilitated deliberation and LLM resampling of team decisions. That knowledge bears on multi-agent and gradual-disempowerment questions, though the hub treats AI as a tool for collective intelligence rather than a risk to it.

key_work.title: Digital twins and AI for healthy and sustainable cities (Computers, Environment and Urban Systems)
Systemic Risk in DeFi: A Network-Based Fragility Analysis of TVL Dynamics
Rapid Response Fund project AI-F: AI-facilitated deliberation for inclusion and democratic engagement (Southampton, with Involve and Ipsos)
Public forum 'AI and Our Society', Derry~Londonderry

people: Seth Bullock (Hub Director, University of Bristol)
Nirav Ajmeri (Deputy Hub Director, University of Bristol)
Laura G. E. Smith (Human-Centred Design theme lead, University of Bath)
funding: UKRI AI programme via EPSRC, grant EP/Y028392/1 (Feb 2024 to Jan 2029). The draft figure of about £12M was not confirmed on the hub's own pages.
status_evidence: Aug 2026: announced free public forums 'AI and Our Society' (Derry~Londonderry, 10 Sep 2026) and 'AI and the Environment' (Exeter); 2026 publications listed on its outputs page.
engage: Job openings via the hub's 'Join the team' page
Rapid Response Fund for small collaborative projects (no call open in Oct 2026; new rounds announced on its mailing list)
Free public forums on AI and society (Sep 2026)
caveats: Mostly applied AI for health, finance, cities and the environment, close to the 'AI for good' applications the map excludes. It is included for its collective-intelligence modelling and its deliberation-related funded projects. No safety or risk framing. The grant ends in Jan 2029.
tag_notes: Home life/life_complexity, not the provisional democracy: the director's field is complex-systems simulation and the hub's 'AI4CI Loop' is about distributed sensing and decentralised agents. B6 sends complexity and agent-based modelling to Life & systems, and Democracy's CI tools are civic opinion-mapping. Secondary democracy: governance-infrastructure theme and the deliberation projects it funds. Ring adjacent (E3, roster kept): a sustained AI programme with no safety framing. MISFIT: an applied AI hub that builds AI applications rather than studying AI's effects; no cell fits AI-for-collective-intelligence engineering. Transfer into_institutions: decision support and governance infrastructure for public bodies. Org type programme (I: time-limited research-council consortium).

name: Jigsaw (Google)
summary: A technology incubator inside Google, based in New York. It builds tools for censorship circumvention, cyberattack defence, online conversation and, increasingly, AI-assisted civic consultation. Its open-source Sensemaking tools use Gemini to summarise large public conversations and surface statements with broad agreement. They were used in the 'What Could BG Be?' county-wide consultation in Kentucky (nearly 8,000 residents) and in the 'We the People' national conversations with the Napolitan Institute. In Sept 2026 Jigsaw launched a Partner Program to take them to 30 cities, states and countries.
why_it_matters: Jigsaw is shaping the default AI-mediation tools that local governments and civic groups adopt, and it frames AI explicitly in terms of human 'structural agency'. How its summarisation and consensus-finding choices treat minority views and resist manipulation will shape AI-mediated democracy at scale.

key_work.title: Sensemaking tools (open-source library for AI summarisation of public conversations)
What Could BG Be? AI-enabled county-wide town hall, Warren County, Kentucky
We the People national conversations (with the Napolitan Institute)
Helping civic leaders hear every voice: Jigsaw Partner Program

funding: Funded by Google. The 2026 Jigsaw Partner Program is backed by Google.org with Bloomberg Philanthropies and the David & Lucile Packard Foundation, and gives local governments free use of Sensemaking AI.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: launched the Jigsaw Partner Program to bring Sensemaking AI to 30 localities; the sensemaking-tools GitHub repository was updated on 1 Oct 2026.
engage: Open-source sensemaking-tools library on GitHub (Apache 2.0)
Jigsaw Partner Program for policymakers and civic leaders who want AI-assisted consultations (2026)
caveats: A unit of Google, a frontier AI developer, and its civic tools run on Gemini, so it is not independent of the industry whose influence it mediates. Founded in 2010 as Google Ideas and renamed Jigsaw in 2016. Much of its work is not about AI (Outline, spun out to the Outline Foundation in Dec 2025; encryption; cyber defence). Its leadership is not named on its own site, and the CEO was not re-verified for 2026.
tag_notes: Home democracy/dem_tools: AI tools for opinion mapping and finding consensus in civic consultations (H1). Ring adjacent (E3, roster kept): a sustained AI civic programme framed around human agency, with no catastrophic or alignment framing. Transfer into_institutions: its tools change how governments consult the public. Org type programme (I: a unit inside Google; the roster said company). Framing flourishing: using AI to 'strengthen, rather than undermine, human agency'.

name: Council on Technology and Social Cohesion
summary: A coalition of peacebuilders, technologists, researchers and civic groups, run with Search for Common Ground. It works to make 'prosocial' technology design, meaning design that builds trust and reduces polarisation, standard practice. It runs thematic hubs, including Deliberative Tech and LLMs and AI Agents, publishes design-governance blueprints and regulation guides, and holds annual Digital Peacebuilding Expos. Its Substack newsletter increasingly covers chatbots and AI-mediated participation.
why_it_matters: It brings conflict-transformation practice to AI design questions such as chatbot sycophancy, frictionless agreement and AI-facilitated dialogue. Its policy track (prosocial design regulation, EU platform-design governance) could carry those lessons into AI governance. Peacebuilders' know-how about de-escalation is largely missing from AI safety.

key_work.title: Blueprint on Prosocial Tech Design Governance
Mapping LLM Tools for Public Discourse, Pluralism & Social Cohesion (with Plurality Institute and Prosocial Design Network)
LLMs and Public Discourse convening, Berkeley (co-hosted with Plurality Institute)
Digital Peacebuilding Expo 2026: From Harm Mitigation to Intentional Design

people: Lena Slachmuijlder (co-chair; Search for Common Ground)
Ravi Iyer (co-chair; USC Neely Center / Psychology of Technology Institute)
funding: Not disclosed; accepts donations. The 2025 LLM-tools mapping was supported by Google.org, Jigsaw and the John Templeton Foundation.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: Substack posts 'The Disagreement Lab' (30 Sep) and, in Aug 2026, 'What Should Stay Human in AI-Enabled Participation?'; May 2026: Digital Peacebuilding Expo in Kyrgyzstan, Washington DC and online.
engage: Digital Peacebuilding Expo, held annually (May 2026 edition in Kyrgyzstan, Washington DC and online)
Thematic hubs, including LLMs and AI Agents and Deliberative Tech (contact via the council's site)
Substack newsletter (techandsocialcohesion.substack.com)
caveats: A coalition with no stated budget or staff of its own, and its membership criteria are not fully documented. At least one report was funded partly by Google (Jigsaw, Google.org). AI is one strand within broader work on social-media design. Founding year not stated; its earliest public output found is from Dec 2023.
tag_notes: Home peace/peace_building: hosted by Search for Common Ground, runs Digital Peacebuilding Expos, and brings peacebuilders' bridging and deliberative tools to tech (H1, B11). Secondary psych (prosocial design research led by Ravi Iyer's Psychology of Technology Institute) and democracy (Deliberative Tech hub). Ring adjacent (E3, roster kept): a sustained AI strand (LLMs and AI Agents hub, 2025 mapping, 2026 posts on chatbots and sycophancy) framed around polarisation and social cohesion. One cross-posted essay, 'Conflict Superintelligence' (Apr 2026), is not a sustained safety framing. Transfer into_institutions: design-governance blueprints and regulation guides. Hub online: expos and hubs can be joined remotely.

name: Make.org
summary: Paris-based civic-tech company founded in 2016. It is a mission-driven company with an associated Make.org Foundation, and it runs large online consultations for public bodies, EU institutions and businesses, reporting over 10 million participants. Its AI work includes leading the Democratic Commons research programme with Sciences Po, Sorbonne University and CNRS, backed by France 2030, which measures and corrects 'democratic biases' in language models used in participation. It also builds Panoramic, an AI platform deployed for EU institutions and events, and co-founded the Worldwide Alliance for AI and Democracy in 2025.
why_it_matters: Democratic Commons is one of the few funded programmes that tests LLMs against explicit democratic criteria and publishes benchmarks and corpora; for example, it found that models translate speeches from fringe parties less accurately than from centrist ones. Make.org also ran the citizens' consultation for the 2025 Paris AI Action Summit, a direct channel from public input into AI governance.

key_work.title: Democratic Commons research programme (with Sciences Po, Sorbonne University, CNRS)
AI Action Summit citizens' consultation 'shaping AI to serve the public good': 11,661 participants, 649 proposals, 121,325 votes
Worldwide Alliance for AI and Democracy (manifesto and launch at the AI Action Summit)
Eighteen Months In: Democratic Commons progress report on bias-aware AI in democratic participation

people: Alina Schütze (head of the Germany team)
funding: Mission-driven company earning revenue from consultation clients (public institutions, EU bodies, businesses). Democratic Commons is backed by Bpifrance's France 2030 'Digital Commons for Generative AI' call (announced May 2024). The Make.org Foundation, an endowment fund, has funded 84 nonprofit actions.
status_evidence: 1 Oct 2026: post on Europe's Democracy Shield and citizen participation; Jul 2026: Democratic Commons progress report covering Sep 2025 to Feb 2026; Sep 2026: partner in Jigsaw's Partner Program announcement.
engage: Public consultations open to anyone on make.org
Worldwide Alliance for AI and Democracy, which organisations can join
Jobs at Make.org and the Make.org Foundation (listed on about.make.org)
caveats: A for-profit mission-driven company registered in Paris, not a nonprofit, and much of its revenue comes from the institutions and companies whose consultations it runs. Its AI framing is democratic resilience and bias, not catastrophic risk. A Germany team exists, but its office location was not confirmed.
tag_notes: Home democracy/dem_tools: builds and runs mass-participation platforms and bias-aware AI for them (H1; tool-building goes to CI tools). Secondary law: formal partner Sciences Po médialab's STS work on democratic bias. Ring adjacent (E3, roster kept): a sustained AI programme framed around democratic values and resilience. Its homepage talks of 'aligning AI development with democratic values', which is borderline bridge, but it has no safety or catastrophic framing. Problems: democracy plus assurance under the F must-pair rule, since Democratic Commons builds LLM bias evaluations. Transfer into_institutions: its primary purpose is citizen input into public decisions, though Democratic Commons has an into_model strand (debiased LLMs). Org type company: a mission-driven company.

name: Forecasting Research Institute (FRI)
summary: US nonprofit founded in October 2022, with Philip Tetlock as president and chief scientist, Josh Rosenberg as CEO and Ezra Karger as director of research. It develops and tests forecasting methods for high-stakes questions on AI, biosecurity and geopolitics. Its work includes the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament (experts and superforecasters on x-risk), the Longitudinal Expert AI Panel (LEAP) and ForecastBench, a contamination-free benchmark that compares LLM forecasting with superforecasters. 2026 reports cover AI cyber risks (July), the effect of ASL-3 safeguards on biosecurity risk (August) and how accurate past AI-progress forecasts have been (September).
why_it_matters: It brings the science of judgmental forecasting, from Tetlock's superforecasting research, to questions about AI risk. Its structured elicitations show where experts and superforecasters disagree about AI risk and why, and ForecastBench gives a running measure of when LLMs match human forecasters. Funders get tracked, scored forecasts in place of unscored opinion.

key_work.title: Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament (XPT) report
ForecastBench: dynamic benchmark of LLM forecasting against superforecasters
Assessing Near-Term Accuracy in the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament
Forecasting the Impacts of ASL-3 Safeguards on Biosecurity Risks

funding: Transparency page: Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy) about $17.3M since founding, including $5.35M general support (Dec 2022), $1.07M for LEAP (Oct 2024) and $10.08M general support (Mar 2025); Vanguard Charitable on behalf of Craig Falls $1.3M (Sep 2024); GiveWell $200,808 (May 2025); Ought $100,000 (Apr 2026); SFF $10,000 (Jun 2025). The Musk Foundation supported its first project before FRI was formally set up.
status_evidence: 22 Sep 2026: published 'How Accurate Have AI Progress Forecasts Been So Far?'; a ForecastBench superforecaster-LLM tournament is scheduled for 25 Oct 2026.
engage: Remote full-time and part-time roles on its careers page (Oct 2026), e.g. Senior LLM Researcher, Research Analyst, Strategy Fellow
ForecastBench superforecaster-LLM tournament on 25 Oct 2026; its public tournament leaderboard accepts submissions
Substack newsletter
caveats: No headquarters is stated and all advertised roles are remote. Over 90% of its disclosed funding comes from Coefficient Giving. An October 2026 EA Forum field review, which names FRI as an example forecasting organisation, notes that a major funder (identified there as likely Coefficient Giving, FRI's main funder) closed its dedicated forecasting programme, and that getting decision-makers to adopt forecasting remains the field's main bottleneck.
tag_notes: Home: democracy (B10 sends probabilistic forecasting to Democracy, and the taxonomy uses FRI as its dem_epistemics example). Secondary: psych for the judgment psychology of Tetlock, Mellers and Lerner, and economics for Karger, Vivalt and its forecasts of AI's economic effects. Ring: core kept; it forecasts high-stakes AI and bio questions, is mainly funded by Coefficient Giving and is on the classic map. Transfer: into_institutions (J3); its outputs are forecasts and elicitation methods for policymakers, and ForecastBench measures models without changing them. Region: global under rule O (US-registered, all roles remote, no HQ stated); north_america would also be defensible.

name: Quantified Uncertainty Research Institute (QURI)
summary: Nonprofit founded by Ozzie Gooen in 2019 to build tools for forecasting and quantitative estimation. Its tools are Squiggle (a probabilistic programming language) with SquiggleHub and SquiggleAI, the older Guesstimate, the Metaforecast aggregator, and RoastMyPost, which runs several LLM evaluators over documents (December 2025). In June 2026 it moved into maintenance mode. It has no full-time staff and does no new research or software development; Guesstimate, SquiggleHub and RoastMyPost stay online on four years of secured maintenance funding.
why_it_matters: Squiggle and Guesstimate made explicit probabilistic estimation usable by EA researchers and funders, and SquiggleAI and RoastMyPost were early LLM-assisted reasoning tools. Its move to maintenance mode after seven years shows a niche funders have struggled to sustain: epistemic tools for decision-makers. That niche is now open.

key_work.title: Squiggle probabilistic programming language (later SquiggleHub and SquiggleAI)
Metaforecast forecast aggregator
RoastMyPost: LLM evaluators for blog posts and documents
QURI is moving into maintenance mode

hq: San Francisco Bay Area, United States
funding: The June 2026 announcement thanks the Long-Term Future Fund, Survival and Flourishing Fund, Coefficient Giving and the Foresight Institute. Rethink Priorities has been its fiscal sponsor since 2023. Four years of basic maintenance funding are secured.
status_evidence: 20 Jun 2026: announced the move into maintenance mode; 21 Jun 2026: released work-in-progress materials.
engage: Squiggle and SquiggleHub are open source and accept community contributions, maintained on a best-effort basis
Guesstimate, SquiggleHub and RoastMyPost remain online for use
caveats: In maintenance mode since June 2026, with no full-time employees and part-time contractors only. Gooen gave compute-budget constraints and concern about short AI timelines as reasons, and has joined Google DeepMind to work on AI safety. Foretold and Metaforecast are being wound down. The roster's 'active' status is wrong.
tag_notes: Home: democracy (dem_epistemics covers reasoning tools and forecast aggregation); formal secondary for its probabilistic modelling and decision analysis. Ring: core kept; an EA-funded epistemics organisation on the classic map whose mission was framed around the long-term future. Transfer: into_institutions (J3) as the closest fit, since its tools serve the estimates and decisions of funders and organisations, not the models. Framing: flourishing, from its stated aim of improving the long-term future through better reasoning. Status: dormant, as maintenance mode is listed under Dormant (the taxonomy uses QURI as an example).

name: TruthfulAI
summary: Berkeley research nonprofit led by Owain Evans and fiscally sponsored by Rethink Priorities, with about eight staff. It studies situational awareness, deception and hidden reasoning in language models, and how narrow training produces unexpected traits. Its papers include Emergent Misalignment (Nature, January 2026), Subliminal Learning (Nature, April 2026) and Value Leakage (July 2026). Value Leakage shows models letting their own values shape their answers without telling users.
why_it_matters: It treats honesty and truthfulness as normative standards for AI, the agenda Evans and colleagues set out in 2021, and tests models for hidden reasoning and covert value influence. Value Leakage bears directly on users' epistemic autonomy, which int/a also cares about. Owain Evans has mentored more than 40 researchers.

key_work.title: TruthfulQA: measuring how models mimic human falsehoods (Lin, Hilton, Evans; predates TruthfulAI)
Emergent Misalignment (Nature)
Subliminal Learning (Nature)
Value Leakage: covert influence of model values on answers

funding: A fiscally sponsored project of Rethink Priorities; its site does not name funders.
status_evidence: 15 Jul 2026: published Value Leakage; Sep 2026: a Director of Operations joined.
engage: No open roles as of Oct 2026; future openings will be posted at truthful.ai/hiring
Owain Evans mentors researchers through MATS and the Astra Fellowship (40+ mentees to date)
caveats: Its methods are mainstream ML experiments. What it brings from outside is conceptual: truthfulness and honesty norms from philosophy. Its site gives no founding year or funders.
tag_notes: Home: philosophy (H2 names TruthfulAI as Philosophy because it imports honesty and truthfulness norms into ML); sub phil_moral; psych secondary for its machine-psychology-style experiments on models (situational awareness, trait transmission). Ring: core; its founding mission is safe and aligned AI, and it is on the classic map. Transfer: into_model (J1); its experiments and evaluations target model behaviour. Framing: catastrophic, inferred from the deception and hidden-reasoning agenda; its site says only 'safe and aligned AI'. Org type: nonprofit, as fiscal sponsorship by Rethink Priorities is administrative, not a hosted unit.

name: Effective Institutions Project (EIP), incl. the Checks & Balances RFP with the Collective Intelligence Project
summary: US philanthropic advisory nonprofit led by its founder and CEO, Ian David Moss. It grew out of the EA working group on improving institutional decision-making. It advises donors on four areas: governance of transformative AI, institutional resilience and accountability, great-power conflict, and pandemics. With the Collective Intelligence Project it ran the Checks & Balances RFP ('Checks and Balances in an Automated Society'), mostly six-figure grants under three pillars: democratic oversight of AI-enabled power, AI tools for collective reasoning and coordination, and foundational macrostrategy.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few funders in the AI-safety ecosystem that treats institutional design and democratic checks and balances as the main lever, not technical alignment. Through the RFP, expertise in democracy, political economy and collective intelligence can get money from x-risk-aligned donors.

key_work.title: Checks and Balances in an Automated Society (RFP, with CIP)
AI Governance: An EIP Primer
A Funder's Guide to AI Governance and Strategy
Managing Global Catastrophic Risk at the National Security Council

people: Divya Siddarth (Collective Intelligence Project; co-author of the RFP)
funding: SFF-2026 recommended $2,192,000 (Jaan Tallinn $469k, Dustin Moskovitz $1.723M), plus a matching pledge of $336k. The RFP says it has philanthropic partners who can make larger grants. Early grants from EA Funds totalled over $45k by July 2022.
status_evidence: Oct 2026: the Checks & Balances RFP is closed to submissions but still takes expressions of interest; it was listed in a 2 Oct 2026 EA Forum field review. SFF-2026 recommended $2.19M for EIP.
engage: Checks & Balances RFP: submissions closed; expressions of interest still accepted at checks-and-balances.ai (several months to review)
Hiring a Peace and Security Senior Program Associate
Slack community for institutional scholars and reformers
Advisory services for donors
caveats: It began in late 2020 as the EA working group on improving institutional decision-making and later took the EIP name; its site gives no headquarters, and I could not date the RFP's launch or awards. As a donor-advisory body, much of its influence runs through other funders' money. The roster marked it as off the classic map, but EIP is listed there by name. The RFP's authors are Ashwin Acharya, Tyler John (EIP), Joal Stein and Divya Siddarth (CIP); Acharya is not on EIP's staff page.
tag_notes: Home: democracy (H4, one-programme funder); the RFP funds the 'institutional infrastructure of an AI-era democracy' with CIP, and its epistemics pillar funds collective-intelligence tools (dem_tools). Economics secondary for the power-concentration pillar. MISFIT: its native tradition, institutional decision-making and organisational design, has no category. Ring: core; AI governance and catastrophic risk lead its programmes, it is SFF-funded and on the classic map. Transfer: into_institutions (J3); it funds democratic oversight designs and checks on AI-enabled power. Org type: funder (donor advice plus an RFP). Not one of the generalist funders listed in rule K.

name: Full Fact (incl. Full Fact AI)
summary: London fact-checking charity founded in 2009 by Will Moy and Michael Samuel. Its Full Fact AI tools find checkable claims, label claim types and match new claims to earlier fact checks; more than 40 fact-checking organisations in 30 countries use them daily, in three languages. In 2026 it monitored how Gemini, Grok and ChatGPT answered questions about false claims, finding 39 major errors over five months (reported August 2026). It is building a public, auditable benchmark of AI models on factuality, transparency, timeliness, consistency and civic responsibility.
why_it_matters: It has codified fact-checking practice (claim detection, claim matching, human-in-the-loop verification) and is now applying it to how chatbots handle false claims. AI-epistemics projects can use its working verification infrastructure and evaluation criteria instead of rebuilding them.

key_work.title: Full Fact AI: claim detection and claim matching tools for fact-checkers
Full Fact analysis: AI chatbots and misinformation
Public, auditable AI benchmark (in development)

people: Ellie Ashman (Head of AI, from Sep 2026)
funding: 2025 income £3,054,478. Donors above £25k include Google.org via Tides (£443,482 and £205,978, about £649k in total), individual supporters and Gift Aid £426,692, Meta £342,712 and Facebook UK £64,167, EFCSN £259,726, Mohn Westlake Foundation £250,000, Peter Samuel Charitable Trust £210,000, LSE Enterprise £189,854, Google Ireland £154,131, Health Foundation £131,821, Pears Foundation £100,000, Esmée Fairbairn £95,000, Nuffield Foundation £88,005 and IFCN £78,102.
status_evidence: 28 Aug 2026 (updated 2 Sep 2026): published its chatbot misinformation analysis; Sep 2026: a new Head of AI joined.
engage: Careers page (around 50 named staff, including a Full Fact AI team)
Full Fact Training courses
Full Fact AI tools are used by fact-checking organisations in 30 countries
caveats: Most of Full Fact AI applies AI to fact-checking. The parts that bear on AI itself are the 2026 chatbot monitoring and the benchmark, and I could not confirm when the benchmark's first report is due. Part of its funding comes from Meta and Google, whose platforms and models it checks.
tag_notes: Home: democracy (B10 sends fact-checking to Democracy; dem_epistemics); arts secondary for its journalism practice. Ring: changed from potential to adjacent.
