Full Fact AI is a standing programme with a dedicated team, and in 2026 it ran five months of chatbot monitoring and began a public AI benchmark. That is sustained AI work on information integrity with no catastrophic or alignment framing (E3). Transfer: protecting (J4); like Common Sense Media's ratings, the monitoring and benchmark exist to protect the public and fact-checkers from AI-driven misinformation. Assurance is paired with epistemics for the benchmark (rule F).

name: Wikimedia Foundation
summary: San Francisco nonprofit, founded in 2003, that hosts Wikipedia and its sister projects. Its April 2025 AI strategy commits to using AI, preferably open-source or open-weight models, to support volunteer editors rather than replace them: in moderation, discovery, translation and onboarding. Wikimedia Enterprise sells high-volume API access to commercial reusers, capped at 30% of Foundation revenue, which the Foundation presents as a way to make AI and big tech pay for the strain they put on its infrastructure. During the September 2026 UN General Assembly its CEO called on AI companies and other large reusers to attribute and financially support Wikipedia.
why_it_matters: It runs the largest human-curated knowledge commons, which models train on and AI agents cite. Its verifiability and source-reliability norms are a tested model of collective epistemics at scale. Its dispute over AI crawler costs and attribution is a front-line case of AI drawing down the commons it depends on.

key_work.title: AI strategy: supporting Wikipedia's human editors
The cost of 'free': how Wikimedia Enterprise protects Wikipedia in the AI era
Human knowledge at stake: case at the UN General Assembly

funding: Mainly small individual donations, plus Wikimedia Enterprise revenue from commercial reusers. About 650 staff (2025) and revenue of about $207.5M in the latest year shown on Wikipedia.
status_evidence: 30 Sep 2026: CEO Bernadette Meehan made the Foundation's case on AI and the knowledge ecosystem at the UN General Assembly.
engage: Anyone can edit and contribute to Wikipedia and its sister projects online
Wikimania (2026 edition held in Paris for Wikipedia's 25th anniversary)
Staff roles at the Foundation
Wikimedia Enterprise API for commercial reusers
caveats: It does not frame its work in AI-safety terms. At the UN its CEO argued that AI governance should address damage to the information ecosystem, not only model outputs and safety. Wikimedia Enterprise earns revenue from the commercial reusers whose crawling strains its infrastructure. The Berlin, Paris and London chapters are separate affiliates.
tag_notes: Home: democracy (knowledge commons are listed under collective epistemics; dem_epistemics); economics secondary for commons governance and its case that AI firms should pay for the public good they use. Ring: changed from potential to adjacent. It had a standing AI programme in 2025-26: the April 2025 AI strategy, machine-learning and research teams, Wikimedia Enterprise framed as protection in the AI era, and UN advocacy in September 2026. The programme focuses on AI's effects on the knowledge commons, with no x-risk framing (E3). Transfer: protecting (J4); its AI work defends its volunteer editors and the commons against replacement and crawler strain. Way of knowing: communal, because Wikipedia's knowledge is produced by a participatory volunteer community.

name: Holy See: Rome Call for AI Ethics (RenAIssance Foundation), Antiqua et Nova and Magnifica Humanitas
summary: This entry covers the AI work of the Catholic Church's central government. The Rome Call for AI Ethics (February 2020) was first signed by the Pontifical Academy for Life, Microsoft, IBM, FAO and Italy's innovation ministry. Since 2021 the Vatican's RenAIssance Foundation has stewarded it, adding signatories such as Qualcomm (2025) and Salesforce (2025) and leaders of 11 religions at Hiroshima (2024). The Church's AI teaching is the doctrinal note Antiqua et Nova (January 2025) and Pope Leo XIV's first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas (May 2026), on safeguarding the human person in the time of AI. In March 2026 the foundation signed an agreement with the UN University for Peace, and the two now run AI4Peace together.
why_it_matters: It speaks to about 1.4 billion Catholics and has an AI-ethics commitment signed by large tech firms and by leaders of many religions. Magnifica Humanitas calls for an international framework to curb the technological arms race and for prudence, at times a slower pace. It rejects handing lethal decisions to AI and warns against power concentrating in a few firms. That is a very large constituency for slowing down, though it does not engage with AGI or loss of control.

key_work.title: Rome Call for AI Ethics
AI Ethics for Peace: world religions sign the Rome Call in Hiroshima
Antiqua et Nova: note on AI and human intelligence
Magnifica Humanitas: encyclical on safeguarding the human person in the time of AI

people: Pope Leo XIV (author of Magnifica Humanitas)
Renzo Pegoraro (President, Pontifical Academy for Life and RenAIssance Foundation)
funding: The RenAIssance Foundation takes donations; it publishes no budget.
status_evidence: 20-22 Sep 2026: AI4Peace symposium in Rome; 2 Sep 2026: Paolo Benanti joined a UNESCO roundtable on plural intelligences and agentic AI; 25 May 2026: Magnifica Humanitas published; 14 Mar 2026: RenAIssance Foundation and UN University for Peace signed an MoU.
engage: AI4Peace, a biennial symposium of the Pontifical Academy for Life, the UN University for Peace and the Pontifical Lateran University (first edition held 20-22 Sep 2026 in Rome)
Organisations can sign or endorse the Rome Call through romecall.org
caveats: This merged entry covers distinct bodies: the RenAIssance Foundation, the Pontifical Academy for Life and papal teaching documents. The founding year given is the Rome Call's (2020); the foundation was set up in April 2021. It frames AI in terms of human dignity, present harms and peace, not catastrophic risk. An EA Forum review notes that the encyclical does not discuss AGI or superintelligence and plays down capability risks. I found no public mechanism for checking whether Rome Call signatories comply.
tag_notes: Home: religion, rel_christian (B1: it speaks from and for the Catholic tradition). Secondary: philosophy for the Pontifical Academy for Life's bioethics; peace for the AI4Peace MoU with the UN University for Peace. Ring: adjacent kept. It has a sustained programme (Rome Call, Antiqua et Nova, Magnifica Humanitas, AI4Peace) framed around dignity, ethics and peace. It calls for curbing the arms race but does not adopt catastrophic-risk or alignment framing (E3), so it is borderline bridge. Transfer: into_institutions (J3 takes precedence over J5); the Rome Call is a voluntary norms instrument signed by firms and governments, and the encyclical asks for an international framework. Framing: structural, from its critique of the technocratic paradigm and of power concentration ('Babel'). Badge: speed_of_wisdom, since the encyclical explicitly calls for curbing the technological arms race and for a slower pace at times. Org type: membership, as a religious denomination acting for its members.

name: The Society Library (Benjamin Franklin Society Library Inc)
summary: A US nonprofit that builds structured databases ('debate maps') of the arguments, claims and evidence on contested public questions. It extracts these from many kinds of media and aims to represent every detectable point of view. It builds AI tools for this work: the Rose and Juniper debate-modelling tools, a fact-checking model, a claim collector and autonomous research agents. It also teaches its methods to university students. In 2023-24 it ran a grant-funded project to map the AI safety, alignment and x-risk debate, which broke the subject into 272 questions and subtopics.
why_it_matters: It has a working method for making a contested field's disagreements legible: who argues what, and on which evidence. Applied to AI risk, that gives new funders and policymakers a map they currently lack. Its 2026 plan to add other 'epistemological paradigms', including ancestral and Indigenous ways of knowing, is close to int/a's full-spectrum knowing.

Donations

There are four named core staff, and much of the work is done by volunteers. The 2025 'Mapping LLMs' report that listed it could not be opened (domain check rate-limited).

Transfer: into_institutions, because its maps are decision-support infrastructure for policy deliberation; it is not none_yet, since it has done AI work. Framing: structural, from its mission of helping people overcome biasing forces on informed decision-making. Full-spectrum badge withheld: the plan to include other paradigms is announced, not yet method.

name: Centre for Argument Technology (ARG-tech), University of Dundee
summary: A research centre at the University of Dundee working on argument mining, computational models of argument and software for analysing debate. Its tools include OVA, an online argument-analysis tool, and AIFdb, a large open corpus of analysed argumentation. It is a funded partner in AI4Deliberation, an EU Horizon project (Nov 2024 to Oct 2027) building AI tools and guidance so that governments can run and assess mass public deliberations. Its commercial arm, Arg Technica Ltd, took on its first staff in 2025.
why_it_matters: It can extract and evaluate the structure of arguments at scale, including automatic debate evaluation and fallacy detection with LLMs. These methods could check whether AI-written reasoning or deliberation summaries are faithful, and could support debate-based oversight of AI. So far it treats AI as a tool for better deliberation, not as an object of safety work.

It also has a share of the €3.0m EU Horizon grant for AI4Deliberation (2024-27, coordinated by UNI SYSTEMS, Greece).

The director attribution comes from general knowledge and its conference-chair listings, not from a current staff page (the people page returned 403). It has no AI-safety framing; its AI work is about deliberation and misinformation tools.

Philosophy is secondary because argumentation theory and informal logic are its methods. Ring: kept at potential (E2). Its funded AI project, AI4Deliberation, uses AI as a deliberation tool and does not address AI's effects or safety. Transferable method: automated extraction and quality assessment of argument structure, applicable to debate-based scalable oversight and to checking that LLM reasoning and deliberation summaries are faithful. Transfer: into_institutions, because AI4Deliberation delivers a toolkit and guidance for governments to institutionalise deliberation. Framing: structural, from AI4Deliberation's statement about loss of trust in institutions and civic disillusionment.

name: MIT Center for Collective Intelligence (CCI)
summary: A research centre at MIT, founded in 2006 by Thomas Malone, that studies how groups of people and computers ('superminds') can act more intelligently together than either alone. Its Collective Intelligence Design Lab helps sponsor organisations design such systems. Recent AI work includes a 2024 meta-analysis of when human-AI combinations outperform humans or AI alone, and studies showing that warmth works better than aggression for AI negotiators. It has also proposed 'learnrights' to pay creators whose work trains AI models, and in 2026 mapped where AI is used across about 20,000 work activities.
why_it_matters: Its meta-analysis found that human-AI combinations often do worse than the better of the two alone on decision tasks, though they help in creative work. That challenges the assumption that a human in the loop makes AI safer. It also brings organisational design and collective-intelligence science to how AI reshapes work and who benefits.

key_work.title: When combinations of humans and AI are useful: a systematic review and meta-analysis (Vaccaro, Almaatouq, Malone; Nature Human Behaviour)
Superminds: The Surprising Power of People and Computers Thinking Together (Malone)
Where can AI be used? Insights from a deep ontology of work activities
Learnrights: compensating creators for AI model training (MIT Sloan coverage)

people: Thomas W. Malone (founding director; Patrick J. McGovern Professor of Management)
funding: Corporate and institutional sponsors. Current or recent: Accenture, Fujitsu, Google Foundation, MIT Quest for Intelligence, NATO, SMART and Toyota Research Institute. Former sponsors include NSF, the Office of Naval Research, the Army Research Office, Skoll Global Threats Fund and ClimateWorks. Amounts are not published.
status_evidence: Mar 2026: arXiv paper 'Where can AI be used?'. May-Jul 2026: MIT Sloan and Fast Company coverage of its learnrights proposal, AI-negotiation and generative-AI creativity studies.
engage: Organisations can sponsor the centre and work with its Collective Intelligence Design Lab
caveats: No AI-safety or catastrophic-risk framing. Much of its AI work is on productivity and organisational design for corporate sponsors and NATO. Some outputs listed on its news page are by affiliated faculty rather than centre projects. It is not listed in the Oct 2026 'State of the Field' report on AI for epistemics.
tag_notes: Home: collective-intelligence science (superminds, supermind design) is Democracy, sub-tradition collective-intelligence tools. Economics (AI and work, learnrights) and Psychology (behavioural experiments on human-AI teams) are secondary. Ring: changed from potential to adjacent under E2/E3, because it has a sustained 2024-26 publication line on AI's effects on work, decisions and creators (meta-analysis, negotiation studies, learnrights, work ontology) without safety framing. Transfer: into_institutions, because its outputs are designs for organising people and AI together and policy ideas such as learnrights. Framing: flourishing, from its mission of making groups 'act more intelligently than any person, group, or computer has ever done before'. Problem assurance is secondary because the human-AI combination results bear on human-oversight assumptions.

name: Community Notes (X) and the AI Note Writer API
summary: X's crowd-sourced system for adding context to posts, launched as Birdwatch in January 2021. A note is shown only when contributors who have tended to disagree in past ratings rate it helpful. This 'bridging' rule is applied by an open-source ranking algorithm, and data on notes and ratings are published daily. Meta began testing the same algorithm on Facebook, Instagram and Threads in the US in March 2025. Since 2025 an AI Note Writer API has let AI systems propose notes, which they cannot rate; only human contributors decide what shows. X's own open-source Community Writer produced 52% of the notes shown as helpful in June 2026.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few deployed systems where AI generates claims at scale while a diverse human crowd keeps the final say, and the ratings are fed back to improve the AI writers. That makes it a live test of human oversight of AI-generated content. It also shows how quickly AI can come to dominate a human epistemic institution: in 42% of posts with a helpful note, only AI notes existed.

key_work.title: Open-source Community Notes ranking algorithm and public data
Scaling Human Judgment in Community Notes with LLMs (Li, De, Revel et al.)
AI Note Writer API pilot
Community-Driven API and AI Writer Design for Openly Scaling Community Notes (Community Writer technical report)

status_evidence: 30 Sep 2026: X researchers published the Community Writer technical report on arXiv. 1 Oct 2026: Community Writer documentation updated in the open-source repository.
engage: Become a Community Notes contributor on X to write and rate notes
Build an AI note writer through the AI Note Writer API, with a public developer community on X

caveats: A corporate product whose rules can change at the owner's discretion. AI note writing is now dominated by the writer built by X/xAI, which raises questions of independence. Meta adopted notes while ending its US third-party fact-checking programme in 2025, which fact-checkers criticised. Goodheart Labs' AI note writer reports 1,042 helpful notes at $7.49 each since June 2025. X's own guide pages could not be fetched (HTTP 402), so details come from the GitHub documentation, arXiv reports and press.

Ring: kept at adjacent. There is a sustained AI programme (AI Note Writer API since 2025, papers in 2025 and 2026, Community Writer), framed around helpful context and misinformation rather than catastrophic risk or alignment. Transfer: into_institutions, because its main contribution is a governance template where AI drafts and a diverse human crowd decides. Ratings also train the AI writers, which is a secondary transfer into the model. Way of knowing: communal, since knowledge comes from a participatory rating process. Org type: programme, as a unit inside X Corp (A1).

name: Deliberation.io (MIT GOV/LAB and Stanford Digital Economy Lab)
summary: An open-source platform for large-scale, structured online dialogue with AI-assisted facilitation. It is led by Lily Tsai (MIT GOV/LAB) and Alex 'Sandy' Pentland with Stanford's Digital Economy Lab, Stanford HAI and Boston University's Platform Governance Lab. The team publishes experiments on AI facilitation, LLM opinion aggregation, comment ordering, consensus generation and AI-prompted reason-giving. Washington, DC was the first city to use it, for a public listening session on AI in city government.
why_it_matters: It tests experimentally whether AI can widen and improve public deliberation without replacing human judgement, including whether LLM summaries represent minority views fairly. The DC session is an example of the public deliberating about AI policy itself. Its 2026 position paper names alignment, sycophancy and over-reliance as risks of AI facilitators.

Most of its papers are working papers. The 2026 arXiv paper does not name Deliberation.io in its abstract; its link to the platform is inferred from its authors.

Ring: kept at adjacent. It has a sustained 2024-26 AI programme on AI and democratic deliberation, framed around democratic health rather than catastrophic risk; the 2026 paper's mention of alignment and sycophancy is about facilitator design. Transfer: into_institutions, because it supplies deliberative processes that city governments use, as DC did. Framing: flourishing, from 'AI systems can strengthen democracy'. Org type: programme, a joint project of university labs (A1, I).

name: Elicit
summary: A public benefit corporation in Oakland, California, that sells an AI research assistant for literature search, systematic reviews and evidence synthesis, with sentence-level citations. It began inside Ought, an AI-alignment research nonprofit, and was spun out in September 2023. Its products include a Research Agent (with Routines, Sept 2026), PRISMA 2020 systematic reviews, an API and MCP server, and BioDecisionBench. It reports that 8 of the top 20 pharmaceutical companies use it.
why_it_matters: It is the most widely adopted product of the 'AI for epistemics' strand and comes from Ought's alignment thesis: build transparent systems that decompose tasks into supervised reasoning steps, rather than opaque end-to-end models. It shows how far that process-supervision approach can go commercially, and how a safety-motivated project drifts towards a market.

It is borderline for scope, as an AI application rather than work on AI itself.

name: FutureSearch (Varuna AI, Inc.)
summary: A US company founded in August 2023 by former Metaculus and Google staff. It builds AI forecasting agents and sells forecasts per question ($0.25-$5) through an API, a Python SDK and MCP integrations, alongside multi-agent research tools. Its forecaster ranked #2 of 284 on Metaculus FutureEval and #1 of 203 in Metaculus MiniBench in Sept 2026. Its professional forecasters contributed to the AI 2027 timelines forecast, and it publishes forecasts on AGI timelines and frontier labs.
why_it_matters: It builds judgmental-forecasting practice into AI agents that produce cheap, calibrated forecasts, including on the AI transition itself. In Aug 2026 it launched causal 'decision forecasts' aimed at uses such as grantmaking. New AI-safety funders could use such tools to estimate the likely effects of a grant before making it.

caveats: A for-profit company with frontier AI labs as customers. Its site states no safety mission, and most of its output is commercial forecasting (companies, chips, model pricing). Benchmark rankings are reported on its own homepage. The headquarters city is not stated; its privacy policy says it is US-headquartered, while the roster had UK/US.

Adjacent's focus on AI's societal effects fits it less well. It is not core, because its founding mission is building an AI forecaster. Way of knowing: empirical, as calibrated probabilistic forecasts.

name: The GovLab and Burnes Center for Social Change (Reboot Democracy, InnovateUS)
summary: A cluster of projects led by Beth Simone Noveck. They are based at Northeastern University's Burnes Center for Social Change and The GovLab, which Noveck co-founded with Stefaan Verhulst. Reboot Democracy is a weekly blog on AI, democracy and public-sector governance. InnovateUS runs free online courses and live workshops for public servants, such as 'Responsible AI for Public Professionals' and 'Designing Democratic Engagement with AI', and reports 265,000 learners across more than 75 agencies. Related projects include AI for Impact, a student co-op, as well as AI Localism, Community-Centered AI and an Observatory of Public Sector AI.
why_it_matters: It reaches the front-line public servants who will buy, deploy and oversee AI, and does so at a scale the safety field does not. It gives them working templates for AI-assisted public engagement, procurement and evaluation, drawn from collective-intelligence and crowdlaw practice.

Designing Democratic Engagement with AI (free InnovateUS course; 42 examples from 20 countries)

The Burnes Center was established with a gift from the Burnes family. In Sep 2026 InnovateUS received a National Leadership Grant to expand civic AI learning with the state libraries of New Jersey, Montana and Hawaiʻi.

Its outputs come from collective-intelligence and crowdlaw methods ('Democratic AI: tools that expand our collective ability to gather knowledge, deliberate, deliver public action'). The AI programme is sustained (courses, a weekly blog, a book) but is about AI in government and democracy, with no safety or catastrophic-risk framing (E3). Transfer: into_institutions. It supplies public agencies with practices and templates for AI-assisted engagement, procurement and evaluation (J3). Assurance is secondary for the responsible-AI, procurement and evaluation training. Org type is academic because the unit is a Northeastern University centre plus The GovLab (I).

name: Plurality Institute
summary: A US 501(c)(3) that serves as a hub for 'plurality' research: technology for human cooperation at scale, following Glen Weyl and Audrey Tang's book. It connects academia, industry, civil society and government. It builds prototypes: BridgingBot, an LLM-based moderator that de-escalates polarised social-media threads (tested in randomised trials, code open-sourced), and OpenBallot, a voter-guide platform. With the Council on Technology and Social Cohesion it ran the Feb 2025 'LLMs and Public Discourse' convening in Berkeley and published an Oct 2025 map of 70 LLM tools for public discourse; it also gives micro-grants.
why_it_matters: It brings peacebuilding, political science and plurality theory into the design of LLM tools, and tests in randomised trials whether AI can bridge divides rather than deepen them. That gives evidence-based prototypes for societal resilience to AI-mediated discourse.

key_work.title: Mapping LLM Tools for Public Discourse, Pluralism & Social Cohesion (with Council on Technology & Social Cohesion and Prosocial Design Network)
LLMs and Public Discourse convening, Berkeley (70+ researchers; $50k awarded by approval voting)

Annual conference, symposia and online workshops (most recent own convening Feb 2025)

Several funders (Google.org, Jigsaw, Microsoft) are tech companies whose platforms its tools are meant to moderate. It does not frame its work around AI safety or alignment. The HQ city is inferred from the team and events, not stated.

Peace is secondary because of peacebuilding methods and people: Lisa Schirch on the steering committee, the Council on Technology and Social Cohesion as partner (H1, C). name: The Computational Democracy Project (CompDem)
summary: A US 501(c)(3), founded in 2018 to carry on Polis as an open-source nonprofit. Polis (AGPL-3.0) collects short statements and votes from large groups and uses statistics and machine learning to map opinion groups and points of consensus. CompDem hosts pol.is (free for nonprofits and government), offers implementation support and training, and publishes open data and analysis notebooks. Polis has been used by vTaiwan, alongside Uruguay's 2021 referendum and by a Kentucky city, and was the platform for Anthropic and the Collective Intelligence Project's Collective Constitutional AI (2023). Polis 2.0 launched at TICTeC 2025, and Polis became a Digital Public Good in Jan 2026.
why_it_matters: Polis is working infrastructure for finding out what large, divided publics agree on. It has already been used to draft a language-model constitution, so pluralistic-alignment work can build on a tested instrument instead of a proposal.

key_work.title: Polis (open-source opinion-mapping system)

Polis 2.0, launched at mySociety's TICTeC conference
Recognised as a Digital Public Good

Run conversations on pol.is (free for nonprofits and government); paid implementation support and training
caveats: Its own site uses no AI-alignment framing and has little dated news. The AI-safety link runs through partners (CIP, Anthropic, vTaiwan) and mostly dates from 2023-24. The Digital Public Goods registry names the owning organisation as 'Math & Democracy', and how that relates to CompDem is unclear. DemocracyNext argues that Polis on its own is opinion mapping, not deliberation. HQ comes from the roster and was not confirmed on the site.

The explicit alignment work dates from 2023-24: a co-authored paper with Anthropic researchers on LLMs in Polis, and Polis as the engine for Collective Constitutional AI and CIP's alignment assemblies. Its 2025-26 site has no alignment framing (E3). Values is paired with democracy because public input through Polis produced a model constitution (F must-pair). Transfer: into_institutions. name: Stanford Deliberative Democracy Lab (DDL)
summary: A lab in Stanford's Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law, formerly the Center for Deliberative Democracy, directed by James Fishkin. It runs Deliberative Polls: representative samples get balanced briefings, deliberate in small groups and with experts, and are surveyed against control groups. Its AI line includes Meta's Community Forums on generative AI (2022-25) and US/India forums on AI wearables. In Nov 2025 it ran an Industry-Wide Forum on AI agents for Cohere, Meta, Oracle, PayPal, DoorDash and Microsoft, with 503 participants in the US and India. It also ran a national deliberation on the Colorado AI Act (Oct 2025) and holds invite-only AI symposia, using its AI-assisted Stanford Online Deliberation Platform.
why_it_matters: It gives AI developers a tested, controlled method for getting informed, representative public judgements on how AI agents should behave, such as when an agent must ask for approval. That is a working channel for public input into product and model norms.

It runs repeated AI forums in 2022-26, explicitly framed as aligning AI agents with societal values, including the 2025 symposium 'AI Agent for Good: Alignment, Safety, and Impact' (E3). Values is paired with democracy because the forums produce public steers on agent behaviour (F must-pair). Transfer: into_institutions. It supplies a deliberative process for industry and policy decisions, with the Colorado AI Act deliberation as a policy example. into_model was considered because forum results steer agent design (J3). Framing is present_harms: the stakes it names are privacy, misinformation, bias and high-stakes uses (L).

name: DemocracyNext
summary: An international research and action institute, a Dutch foundation incorporated in Dec 2023, that promotes sortition, deliberation and rotation, especially permanent citizens' assemblies. Its city work includes Birmingham, Deschutes County, Vilnius, Esch-sur-Alzette, Kerewan and Mondragon. It was founded by Claudia Chwalisz, who previously led the OECD's work on innovative citizen participation. On AI it called in 2023 for a global institution of citizens' assemblies, and later argued (with The GovLab's Stefaan Verhulst) for local and regional AI assemblies. It runs a tech-enhanced assembly lab with MIT's Center for Constructive Communication and co-convenes the DelibTech Network (launched Sep 2025) with the AI & Democracy Foundation.
why_it_matters: It judges AI tools in deliberation by whether they build citizens' own capacities (self-reflection, reasoning, dialogue, vulnerability) or wear them away. It also offers lottery-based institutions as a way to give publics real say over how AI is governed.

key_work.title: Deliberative Muscles & AI: How Can DelibTech Strengthen Citizens' Capacities to Deliberate? (Chwalisz, McKinney, Theuns, Yi)
Five Dimensions of Scaling Democratic Deliberation: With and Beyond AI (McKinney and Chwalisz)
The Case for Local and Regional Public Engagement in Governing Artificial Intelligence (Verhulst and Chwalisz)
Deliberation & Technology (DelibTech) Network, with the AI & Democracy Foundation

people: Lucy Reid (chief strategy and creative officer)
Sammy McKinney (AI and deliberation researcher; co-lead, DelibTech Network)
Robbie Stamp (chair of the foundation board)
funding: Funded by grants from non-partisan foundations, per its foundation page: the Quadrivium Foundation, the Rockefeller Foundation and the V. Kann Rasmussen Foundation, plus limited consultancy fees and individual donations (Every.org for US donors, Open Collective internationally). It holds Dutch ANBI charitable status.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: celebrated its fourth birthday at a party in London (15 Sep), followed by a newsletter on 17 Sep. July 2026: published 'Deliberative Muscles & AI'.
engage: Newsletter (Substack) and public events
Assembly guide and resources for organisers of citizens' assemblies
DelibTech Network (invite-only; members join virtual and in-person convenings)
caveats: Its AI work centres on deliberation technology and governing AI through assemblies, not on catastrophic risk. It is critical of opinion-mapping tools such as Polis being called deliberation. The DelibTech Network is invite-only. The founding year is inferred from its fourth birthday in Sep 2026; the Dutch foundation was incorporated in Dec 2023.
tag_notes: Home: Democracy (dem_deliberation). Its AI outputs come from citizens'-assembly and sortition practice (H1). Ring: bridge, as on the roster. It has a sustained 2023-26 line on governing AI through citizens' assemblies (2023 call, the AI localism paper, the tech-enhanced assembly lab) plus the DelibTech Network and papers (E3). Minds is a second problem because both the 2025 and 2026 papers ask whether AI tools preserve or erode citizens' own deliberative capacities. Transfer: into_institutions. It designs deliberative institutions and protocols for using AI within them (J3). Region is Europe, by its legal base as a Dutch foundation (O).

name: Global Coalition for Inclusive AI Governance
summary: A coalition launched at the Paris AI Action Summit in Feb 2025 by Missions Publiques, a Paris-based citizen-participation organisation, and the Stanford Deliberative Democracy Lab. It answers the UN Global Digital Compact's call for a global dialogue on AI governance. It plans a continuous global citizen consultation, combining decentralised citizens' assemblies with a global deliberative poll, and its first cycle aims to involve 10,000+ citizens in 100+ countries. A pilot student citizens' assembly of 70 students was run with ENS-PSL and Yale. The governments of France, Switzerland and the UK, plus over 80 civil-society organisations, private-sector actors and a dozen academic partners, have backed it.
why_it_matters: If it runs, it would be one of the few channels putting representative global public judgement, including from Majority-World countries, into international AI governance. Because AI safety is not guaranteed a place on its agenda, early engagement with its briefing materials could matter.

key_work.title: Launch of the coalition at the Paris AI Action Summit, ENS-PSL
Student Citizens' Assembly pilot (ENS-PSL and Yale, 70 students)

people: Yves Mathieu (co-director and founder, Missions Publiques)
James S. Fishkin (director, Stanford Deliberative Democracy Lab)
funding: The governments of France, Switzerland and the UK supported it (Missions Publiques, Feb 2025). No budget is published.
status_evidence: Feb 2025: launched at the Paris AI Action Summit. No later dated activity or published results found as of Oct 2026. The site shows no dates beyond a 2026 copyright, and Missions Publiques' blog has posted nothing about the coalition since Feb 2025.
engage: Organisations (governments, civil society, academia, companies, international bodies) can ask to join through the contact form on its site
caveats: No published results and no dated activity since the Feb 2025 launch, so it is unclear whether the first deliberation cycle ran. Its site is minimal and names no leaders, partners or timeline. An EA Forum post (Feb 2025) warned that AI safety was mentioned only vaguely in the Paris pilot and could be diluted in most national assemblies. The named people lead the two founding organisations; their personal roles in the coalition are not stated.
tag_notes: Home: Democracy (dem_deliberation). Its method combines citizens' assemblies and Deliberative Polling (H1). Ring: bridge, as on the roster, with low confidence. The object is global governance of AI itself, feeding the UN Global Digital Compact dialogue, but there is no evidence that the programme has been sustained since its 2025 launch (E3). Justice is a second problem because the stated aim is to include citizens from 100+ countries. Transfer: into_institutions. It aims to feed a standing citizen consultation into AI governance processes (J3). Framing is structural: 'AI governance should not be reserved for a select few' (L). Status is unverified because the site is minimal and no activity after Feb 2025 was found. The Paris hub is via Missions Publiques' Paris office, which coordinates it.

name: g0v and vTaiwan
summary: g0v ('gov-zero') is Taiwan's decentralised civic-tech community. It runs bimonthly hackathons in Taipei (the 73rd on 31 May 2026) and releases its projects as open source, such as the Cofacts fact-checking bot. vTaiwan, launched from g0v in 2014, is an open consultation process combining Polis with in-person meetings to deliberate on digital legislation; it reports 28+ cases, 80% of which led to government action. In 2023 a $100k OpenAI 'Democratic Inputs to AI' grant, with Chatham House and the AI Objectives Institute, revived vTaiwan as a volunteer community. That project held a citizens' meeting on AI privacy, discrimination and local governance and reached consensus points on AI. In 2026 vTaiwan holds weekly online meetings, publishes a newsletter, ran an in-person deliberation in Hualien and adapted Jigsaw's Sensemaker for Traditional Chinese.
why_it_matters: It is a long-running, volunteer-run model of 'rough consensus' deliberation that feeds legislation, and one of the few civic communities to have deliberated directly on principles for AI. It gives a non-Western, bottom-up template for polycentric AI governance.

key_work.title: Bridging the Recursive Public (OpenAI Democratic Inputs to AI, with Chatham House and AI Objectives Institute)
How public participation can improve AI governance: vTaiwan's initiatives (Friedrich Naumann Foundation)
vTaiwan newsletter, issue 0 (community history and Sensemaker localisation)
g0v hackath73n, Taipei

Audrey Tang (early g0v contributor, now Taiwan's Cyber Ambassador; not a current vTaiwan organiser)
funding: According to the g0v site, its hackathons are funded by community donations and run mostly by volunteers. vTaiwan received a $100,000 OpenAI Democratic Inputs to AI grant in 2023.
status_evidence: Oct 2026: vTaiwan weekly meeting notes posted on GitHub (1 Oct). Sep 2026: in-person deliberation in Hualien (11 Sep). May 2026: g0v hackathon (31 May) and the first vTaiwan newsletter (9 May).
engage: g0v bimonthly hackathons in Taipei; Slack and a newcomers' guide
vTaiwan weekly online meeting, Wednesdays 19:00-20:00 Taiwan time, mostly in Mandarin
Contribute code, transcripts and translations through the g0v/vTaiwan GitHub repositories; vTaiwan Substack newsletter
caveats: Its AI-governance deliberation dates from 2023-24; its 2025-26 work is mainly AI-assisted deliberation tools and non-AI policy topics. It is volunteer-run and mostly in Mandarin. The Taiwanese government's Alignment Assemblies (MODA with CIP) are a separate programme, and Audrey Tang's international advocacy is not a vTaiwan activity. The founding year refers to g0v.
tag_notes: Home: Democracy (dem_tools). g0v and vTaiwan are civic tech building Polis-based consensus processes and, now, LLM sensemaking tools (H1). Ring: bridge, as on the roster, but borderline. The explicit 'democratic inputs to AI' work was a funded project in 2023-24 (E3), and its 2025-26 activity is AI-assisted deliberation tools and other policy topics. Values is paired with democracy because the 2023 deliberation produced guiding principles for AI (F must-pair). Transfer: into_institutions. It supplies deliberative processes that feed legislation (J3). Standpoint is Neither because Taiwan is coded Neither in v1 (O). Fractal badge: a local volunteer community that feeds national legislation and, in 2023, global AI developers.

name: Mantic
summary: Mantic is a London start-up, founded in 2024, building an AI system that makes judgmental forecasts of world events (geopolitics, business, policy, technology) one week to one year ahead, with reasoning and references. It sells horizon scanning, forecasts and monitoring, with API and MCP access, mainly to hedge funds, Fortune 500 companies and government users. In the Summer 2026 Metaculus Cup it scored above all 676 human participants.
why_it_matters: Superhuman forecasting is a core 'AI for epistemics' capability that AI-safety strategists want for strategic awareness. Mantic shows that capability being built with venture money for traders and corporates, which makes it a live test of who captures AI-generated foresight. Its CEO previously designed dangerous-capability experiments for Gemini at Google DeepMind.

key_work.title: Mantic beats all human forecasters in the Summer 2026 Metaculus Cup and raises $25m
Metaculus Cup results: 4th of 539 humans (Summer 2025), first overall (Summer 2026)

people: Toby Shevlane (co-founder and CEO; formerly Senior Research Scientist, Google DeepMind)
funding: $29m raised in total (company site). A $25m round announced 18 Sep 2026 was led by Radical Ventures, with Balderton, Thinking Machines, DRW, FT Ventures, M12 (Microsoft), Episode 1, Charlie Songhurst and Thomas Wolf.
status_evidence: 18 Sep 2026: announced a $25m round after beating all 676 human participants in the Summer 2026 Metaculus Cup.
engage: Hiring across AI research, engineering, product, sales and operations (announced Sep 2026); contact via contact@mantic.com
caveats: This is a commercial venture whose stated customers are mainly hedge funds and corporates. It has no AI-safety programme and frames its work as better decisions for business and government, so its place on this map is borderline: it is included as a case of the AI-for-epistemics capability rather than as a safety actor. Funders would not need to fund it.
tag_notes: Home: it builds the superforecasting method of judgmental, probabilistic forecasting into an AI system (B10: probabilistic forecasting goes to Democracy; H2: ML itself is not a sector). Ring: the roster's adjacent is kept by default under E(3), since it has no safety or 'AI going well' framing. MISFIT: its AI work builds a capability rather than addressing AI's societal effects, so no ring fits cleanly. Transfer: forecasting know-how goes into the model's scaffolding and fine-tuning (J1). Framing: its mission is improving decisions under volatility, and flourishing is the closest key (MISFIT: commercial framing, no stakes stated).

name: CMI – Martti Ahtisaari Peace Foundation (CMI)
summary: CMI is a Finnish nonprofit, founded in 2000 by Nobel laureate and former president Martti Ahtisaari, that mediates and supports dialogue in conflicts in over 20 countries. It has 94 staff in Helsinki and Brussels. Its Digital Peacemaking team uses AI in peace processes. In early 2025 it ran an AI-supported consultation of 150 young members of Yemeni political parties over WhatsApp, analysed with the open-source Talk to the City tool. In March 2026 it published principles for responsible AI use in peacemaking, and in September 2026 it convened the Akola Forum for Peace on what AI means for peace and trust.
why_it_matters: CMI holds 25 years of mediation practice, and it is one of the few peace organisations to have published AI principles for mediation (no use that escalates tensions or enables surveillance; human judgement keeps responsibility) and field-tested AI consultation in an active conflict. That makes it a practitioner partner for work on AI-facilitated negotiation, and on the risk that AI erodes trust between conflict parties.

key_work.title: Principles for responsible use of AI in peacemaking
AI-facilitated youth consultation in Yemen (150 participants, 17 of 21 governorates); won the RTMKM 2026 Innovation Prize
Akola Forum for Peace: what AI means for peace and trust
Practical Guidance Note on digital tools for inclusive peace mediation

Johanna Poutanen (Head, Inclusion and Digital Innovation)
funding: Income was €17.5m in 2025: the EU 38%, the Government of Finland 36% (programme partnership with the Ministry for Foreign Affairs), Sweden 8%, other governments 13%, and the rest from private donors, companies and foundations. The Martti Ahtisaari Peace Fund was set up in 2022.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: won the RTMKM 2026 Innovation Prize (22 Sep) for its AI-supported Yemen consultation, after holding the Akola Forum for Peace on AI and trust (3 Sep).
engage: Vacancies page; an open CEO recruitment was announced in Aug 2026
Public webinars, e.g. 'Can AI make peace mediation more inclusive?' (14 Apr 2026)
Digital Peacemaking team welcomes partnerships with technology companies and research institutions
Individual and corporate donations
caveats: AI is a small strand within a large peace-mediation organisation. The CEO leaves on 1 Nov 2026 to become Finland's UN ambassador. The roster's claim that CMI's Yemen work used Harmonica is inaccurate: the Yemen consultation used Talk to the City, and Harmonica was used for a December 2024 stakeholder survey for CMI's 2026-29 programme. The State of the Field post cited by the roster does not mention CMI.
tag_notes: Home: peacebuilders' deliberative tools used in conflict settings go to Peace (B11 names CMI). The secondary tradition, Arts, reflects its digitally enhanced foresight and vision-building method. Ring: a sustained AI programme in 2025-26 (principles, tools, forum) framed around inclusion, trust and responsible use, with no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing, so adjacent (E3). Transfer: the forum, terminology guide, guidance note and webinars bring the mediation community into the AI conversation (J5). The principles also set norms for that field. Standpoint is Neither because it is Helsinki-led, although it works in Majority World conflicts (O).

name: deliberAIde
summary: deliberAIde is a German start-up based in Siegen that builds an AI 'co-worker' for structured dialogue. It helps plan engagement processes, transcribes discussions live in 100+ languages, analyses hundreds of sessions together, and produces reports in which every finding links back to the original quote. Users include The Future Society (for its 2025 Athens Roundtable), Pulse of Europe and the District of Siegen-Wittgenstein (10 citizen dialogue conferences). The product is in private preview.
why_it_matters: Its design targets a specific failure of AI in deliberation, synthesis that silently distorts what participants said. Findings are traceable to source quotes, data is anonymised by default and never used for training, and approval gates keep publication in human hands. AI-governance convenors already use it.

key_work.title: deliberAIde platform (private preview): traceable, multilingual analysis of structured dialogue
Synthesis for The Future Society's 2025 Athens Roundtable on AI and the Rule of Law

Omer Bilgin (co-founder and Chief Ethics & Research Officer; Visiting Analyst at The Future Society)
Shahrier Erfan Harun (co-founder and lead software engineer)
status_evidence: 2026: the site offers private-preview sign-up, and The Future Society's Feb 2026 staff bio describes it as a start-up. It was used at the 2025 Athens Roundtable and Pulse of Europe's 2025 network meeting.
engage: Private-preview sign-up for organisations that run dialogues or assemblies
Its About page invites partnerships with civil society, public bodies and civic-tech actors
caveats: Early-stage, with founding date and funding not published. The imprint names Lukas Salecker & Co GbR (a civil-law partnership) in Siegen, so how the site's 'purpose-locked steward ownership' is implemented is not documented. The case for it rests mostly on testimonials on its own site.
tag_notes: Home: it builds AI tools for citizen dialogue and assemblies from deliberative and facilitation practice (dem_tools: building the tools goes to CI tools). Ring: its stated mission is democratic renewal, with no safety or catastrophic-risk framing, so adjacent (E3), even though a co-founder works in AI-safety governance at The Future Society. MISFIT: it builds AI for deliberation rather than studying AI's effects. Transfer: it supplies deliberative-process infrastructure to municipalities and convenors (J3, deliberative processes).

name: Goodheart Labs
summary: Goodheart Labs is a small UK studio run by forecaster Nathan Young that builds AI-assisted tools for decision-making and collective fact-checking. Its AI note writer researches, drafts and submits Community Notes on X: the site reports 1,042 notes rated helpful, 100.7M views and $7.49 per helpful note. Its other tools include the Common Notes browser extension (notes on Substack and YouTube, since July 2026), Viewpoints polling, Finding Consensus (expert positions on AI policy such as SB-1047) and forecast-aggregation dashboards, including one on AGI timelines.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few AI-for-epistemics projects with measured deployment at scale. It tests whether AI can scale bridging-based crowd fact-checking as misleading content becomes cheaper to produce, a concrete lever on the information decay that safety and governance work depends on.

key_work.title: AI-written Community Notes on X (world's first AI-written note; 1,042 helpful notes)
Common Notes browser extension

Viewpoints.xyz community polling tool

funding: Jaan Tallinn and the Future of Life Foundation funded the AI Community Notes work (acknowledged Sep 2025). It also earns income from custom tools (registered as a management consultancy).
status_evidence: Jul 2026: launched the Common Notes extension; the site reports writing 2.64% of all helpful notes on X in August.
engage: Install Common Notes (Chrome or Firefox) to read, rate, request or write notes
Book a call to commission decision or forecasting tools
caveats: A very small team, built around one founder. The AI note writer depends on X's API programme for AI note writers. The usage figures are self-reported.
tag_notes: Home: crowd fact-checking, forecast aggregation and opinion polling (B10: fact-checking and forecasting go to Democracy). Ring: it is rooted in forecasting and collective epistemics, with sustained AI-going-well work (Finding Consensus on AI policy, the AGI-timelines dashboard) and funding from AI-safety donors (Tallinn, FLF), so bridge (E3; roster kept). Transfer: AI-written notes plug into platform mechanisms for information integrity (J3). MISFIT: the target is the information commons rather than AI governance. Framing: structural, because the case for AI notes is that misleading content keeps getting cheaper (epistemic decay).

name: BRKT Lab
summary: BRKT Lab (pronounced 'bracket') is a four-person group building AI tools for 'healthy collective agency' in small groups. Its members met in the Future of Life Foundation's AI for Human Reasoning Fellowship. Its first tool, Cadence, sends each group member a short daily AI prompt and returns a personalised digest of the group's state. In April 2026 it published a field report on a two-week pilot with Kind Sun, an all-volunteer solar nonprofit.
why_it_matters: The field report is a rare candid account of an AI coordination tool failing: members with labour-organising backgrounds experienced Cadence as managerial surveillance because leaders had mandated it. It sets out design principles (match the group's rhythm, let people see inside the machine, the tool must belong to the group). Those matter for anyone building AI-mediated coordination.

key_work.title: Field Report: AI-Mediated Coordination in a Volunteer Nonprofit (Cadence pilot with Kind Sun)

people: Rob Gordon (co-founder; led the Cadence research)
funding: It grew out of the FLF AI for Human Reasoning Fellowship. Rob Gordon's Cadence research was funded by a grant for coordination-technology research received in winter 2025-26; the funder is not named.
status_evidence: Apr 2026: published the Cadence field report; the site is marked 2026.
engage: Groups can pilot Cadence, and people working on coordination technology or digital democracy are invited to get in touch (hello@brktlab.org)
caveats: A very young, small project with one public output. Legal form, location and funding are not stated on its site. The US location comes from the roster and has not been verified.
tag_notes: Home: collective-intelligence and group-facilitation tools (dem_tools). Ring: bridge kept, but marginally. It came out of FLF's fellowship on AI for human reasoning, which is framed around humanity navigating the AI transition, and it states an aim of 'alignment at all levels'. Its own site does not frame the work as AI safety, so adjacent would also be defensible (E3). Transfer: tools that reshape how groups coordinate and decide (J3). MISFIT: small groups, not AI governance. MISFIT: org_type, since its legal form is not stated (a .org domain and grant funding suggest non-commercial). Region is unverified.

name: Harmonica (Harmonious Technologies Ltd)
summary: Harmonica is an open-core AI facilitation platform. An AI facilitator holds a one-to-one conversation with each participant, then synthesises themes, tensions and consensus across the group, using templates such as Delphi rounds, Cynefin, Six Thinking Hats and Wardley mapping. The core is open source under AGPL-3.0 and self-hostable; session data is not used for model training. Case studies include CMI's December 2024 multilingual stakeholder survey, a Missions Publiques student workshop on AI governance, and Metagov's mapping of the gov/acc research space.
why_it_matters: It is a public-interest, self-hostable alternative for AI-facilitated deliberation. It encodes established facilitation methods rather than ad hoc prompting, and organisations working on AI governance and peace mediation already use it.

key_work.title: Harmonica open-source web app (AGPL-3.0)
CMI stakeholder survey for its 2026-29 programme
Harmonica 0.4: a runtime for multiplayer facilitation

people: Artem Zhiganov (director; writes the project blog)
funding: Donations through Open Collective (fiscal host: The Social Change Nest) and Giveth, plus paid Pro plans, a lifetime Pro offer and expert facilitation services. Open Collective contributions are in the low thousands of pounds.
status_evidence: 12 Sep 2026: changelog release (session close and reopen controls); weekly releases through Aug-Sep 2026.
engage: Free tier, or self-host the open-source version
Contribute code on GitHub or join the Discord
Donate through Open Collective or Giveth
caveats: The roster linked Harmonica to an EA Forum essay on 'coordination collapse' by Artem Rudnev. That link is wrong: Companies House names Artem Zhiganov as director, and the essay does not mention Harmonica. Without it, there is no AI-safety framing on record, so the ring is lowered from bridge to adjacent. Team size is inferred from one active director and small donation flows.

Ring changed from bridge to adjacent: the roster's bridge rested on a mistaken author link, and its own site frames the work as better group sensemaking, without safety or catastrophic-risk language (E3). Transfer: it supplies deliberative-process infrastructure (J3), including for AI-governance workshops. Status is active (frequent 2026 releases, a registered company and an open repository), although the taxonomy cites Harmonica as an example of 'unverified'.

name: Swift Centre (formerly Swift Centre for Applied Forecasting)
summary: The Swift Centre is a London forecasting organisation that uses a panel of top-ranked forecasters for calibrated probabilistic forecasts and scenario analysis. Its not-for-profit research wing (Swift Centre Research Ltd) concentrates on the concentration of power in AI (compute, capability and control), AI policy and great-power dynamics, through scenario papers, situation monitors and public forecasts. A commercial advisory wing (Swift Centre Advisory Ltd, from 2026) sells forecasting, prediction-market intelligence and workshops. It supplied forecasts for Google DeepMind's 2024 dangerous-capability evaluations paper.
why_it_matters: It brings scored, calibrated forecasting and scenario method to AI risk strategy: forecasts on frontier capabilities, AI cyber-offence and autonomous warfare. Its 2026 'Bridge the Gap' competition tied those forecasts to policy options drafted by new AI policy advisers.

key_work.title: Forecasts for Google DeepMind's 'Evaluating Frontier Models for Dangerous Capabilities'
Bridge the Gap: Forecasts for AI Policy
Polymarket vs Swift Centre: Round 2
China's Road to Dominance

funding: Its site lists Open Philanthropy, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, DSIT, the AI Security Institute, GovAI and the AI Risk Mitigation Network among clients and funders; no amounts are published. The research wing says its AI programmes are 'seeking funding partners'. The advisory wing is commercial.
status_evidence: Aug 2026: published 'China's Road to Dominance'. Jul 2026: company renamed Swift Centre Research Ltd. 18 Sep 2026: board change at Companies House.
engage: Free Substack newsletter, 'Swift Centre: Highlights'
Research wing seeks funding partners for its AI and geopolitics papers and situation monitors
Advisory: forecasting workshops and consultancy for organisations
Ran an open 'Bridge the Gap' competition for AI policy advisers (Feb-Mar 2026)
caveats: In 2026 the organisation restructured. A commercial advisory company was incorporated in Feb 2026, the original company was renamed from Swift Centre for Applied Forecasting Ltd to Swift Centre Research Ltd in Jul 2026, and founding director Michael Story resigned from both boards on 18 Sep 2026. Leadership is in transition, and much recent public output is general geopolitics rather than AI.
tag_notes: Home: calibrated probabilistic forecasting by top-ranked forecasters (B10, Democracy). The secondary tradition, Arts, covers its scenario analysis and horizon scanning. Ring: a forecasting organisation whose research wing runs a sustained programme on AI power concentration and AI policy, with AI-safety clients (GDM, AISI, GovAI), so bridge (E3; roster kept). Transfer: forecasts and the Bridge the Gap competition feed AI policy decisions (J3). Framing: structural, matching its stated focus on concentration of power in AI. Status is changed, because of the 2026 rename, the split into nonprofit and commercial arms, and the founder's departure. The org type follows the nonprofit research wing (A1).

name: Tarbell Center for AI Journalism
summary: A nonprofit that supports journalism about advanced AI. It runs a 12-month paid fellowship: remote training, a summit, then a nine-month placement at newsrooms such as The Guardian, MIT Technology Review, TIME and Bloomberg. It also makes reporting grants of $1k-20k and funds residencies for senior journalists. It publishes Transformer, an editorially independent newsletter on the power and politics of transformative AI.
why_it_matters: It is the main channel through which AI-safety philanthropy reaches working journalists. It trains reporters in AI and places them in mainstream newsrooms, so public sensemaking about AI draws on journalism's own norms of accountability and verification. For funders it shows a way to widen the field: resource an existing profession instead of founding new safety organisations.

key_work.title: Transformer (newsletter on the power and politics of transformative AI)
Tarbell Fellowship, 2027-28 cohort applications
AI reporting grants ($1k-20k), 2026 round

funding: Lifetime $1M+ each from Coefficient Giving (2023-26), Longview Philanthropy (2026) and the Survival and Flourishing Fund. SFF recommended $520k (2024, as Tarbell Fellowship via Players Philanthropy Fund), $583k plus $200k matching (2025) and $807k (2026). $100k-1M from the Future of Life Institute (2024-25), the Casey & Family Foundation, the Amdur Family Fund and Ought. Earlier, smaller gifts from the EA Infrastructure Fund (2023) and ACX Grants (2024).
status_evidence: Sep 2026: applications for the 2027-28 fellowship open (28 Sep to 22 Nov 2026); fellows' stories published in Sep 2026; SFF-2026 grant of $807k.
engage: Tarbell Fellowship 2027-28: apply 28 Sep to 22 Nov 2026; 12 months, $75k-135k salary, remote training from June 2027, newsroom placement Sep 2027 to May 2028
Reporting grants of $1k-20k for freelancers and staff reporters (2026 round closed 12 July; subscribe for the next round)
Residencies for senior journalists and editors ($80k+ stipend)
Read or subscribe to Transformer (transformernews.ai)
Staff roles on its careers page
caveats: Ring changed from the roster's bridge to core under rule E(1): it was founded with an AI mission, inside the x-risk funding ecosystem. Journalism is the tradition it brings, not where it sits institutionally. Most of its money comes from AI-safety philanthropy (Coefficient Giving, SFF, Longview, FLI). It publishes editorial-independence policies, but critics could still read this as funders shaping AI coverage. It started as the Tarbell Fellowship (website live by Sep 2022), was fiscally sponsored by Players Philanthropy Fund until mid-2025, then incorporated in Delaware in 2025 as a 501(c)(3), with a UK company limited by guarantee. Transformer is on the classic map; Tarbell itself is not.
tag_notes: Home: arts (H3: general-audience journalism goes to Arts). Its outputs are trained journalists, funded stories and the Transformer newsletter. Ring: core rather than the roster's bridge, under E(1). Its founding mission is journalism that 'helps society navigate the emergence of advanced AI', its funders are AI-safety funders, and its founder is not a journalist (rule E: a new org founded on an AI mission is core). Transfer: convening. It brings the journalism profession into the AI conversation through training, placements and media, rather than producing a governance instrument. Framing: structural. Its stated stakes are accountability of AI companies and the 'power and politics' of transformative AI, not catastrophe language. Region: global (US-registered, team works fully distributed). London hub: Transformer's editor and managing editor are based in London.

name: DebunkBot (Costello, Pennycook and Rand research programme)
summary: A public LLM 'reasoning assistant', and the academic research programme behind it, run by psychologists at Carnegie Mellon, Cornell and MIT. The team runs large experiments on short, evidence-based dialogues with GPT-4-class models. These reduce belief in conspiracy theories and other false claims, and the effect lasts months. The team also studies the risk side: frontier LLMs persuading people on harmful topics, or convincing them of conspiracies. The bot itself offers topics including climate, vaccination and AI safety.
why_it_matters: It supplies causal, preregistered evidence on how strongly AI dialogue changes beliefs in both directions. Mainstream AI safety mostly asserts this risk without measuring it. Its persuasion work with FAR.AI turns social psychology's methods into evaluations of model behaviour.

key_work.title: Durably reducing conspiracy beliefs through dialogues with AI (Science)
It's the Thought that Counts: Evaluating the Attempts of Frontier LLMs to Persuade on Harmful Topics
Large language models can effectively convince people to believe conspiracies
What beliefs are most debunkable? (PsyArXiv preprint)

people: Thomas H. Costello (Assistant Professor, Carnegie Mellon University; lead researcher)
Gordon Pennycook (Associate Professor of Psychology, Cornell University)
status_evidence: Oct 2026: 'What beliefs are most debunkable?' preprint, v2 posted 1 Oct 2026. Sep 2026: correction and reproducibility package for the 2024 Science paper deposited on Zenodo. Aug 2026: arXiv paper on rapid-response debunking.
engage: Use the bot at debunkbot.com (topics include AI safety)
Papers, preprints and materials are listed on its research page
caveats: This is a multi-university academic project, not a standalone organisation, and its funding is not stated on its site. In September 2026 the authors deposited a correction ledger and replacement supplementary materials for the 2024 Science paper; the extent of the changes was not assessed here. The same team showed that LLMs can as easily persuade people into conspiracy beliefs, so the method is dual-use. Most outputs are on misinformation generally; the AI-safety framing comes mainly from the persuasion-risk papers with FAR.AI.
tag_notes: Home: psych (H1, method over topic). Its outputs are preregistered persuasion and belief-change experiments by social and cognitive psychologists, so the sub-tradition is psych_social (persuasion, judgement). Ring: kept as bridge. The project is rooted in academic psychology of misinformation, and it runs a sustained line (2024-26) explicitly on AI persuasion risk, including harmful-topic persuasion evals with FAR.AI and an AI-safety topic in the bot. Transfer: into_model. Psychological knowledge goes into the design of an AI dialogue system and into evaluations of how models persuade. Framing: structural (health of the information ecosystem).

name: Future of Life Foundation (FLF)
summary: A nonprofit affiliated with the Future of Life Institute that researches priority areas, then starts and funds organisations to fill them. Its focus is 'AI tools for human collective agency'. Its three priority areas are Epistemic Virtue Evaluations (independent tests of whether AI helps users reason well), the Epistemic Stack (mapping claims to their sources) and AI-Facilitated Collaboration. It ran a 12-week AI for Human Reasoning fellowship in 2025, and in 2026 an Epistemic Case Study Competition that awarded just over $200k. Organisations it has started or supported include Sophron Research, CARMA, the Windfall Trust, Chord and Deep Future.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few funders putting money into tools for collective epistemics and coordination rather than into model alignment itself. It treats society's ability to reason and coordinate as a safety lever. For int/a it is a funder already working on collective-intelligence infrastructure.

key_work.title: Epistemic Case Study Competition: Results (about $200k in prizes)
Epistemic Virtue Evaluations
The Epistemic Stack

Oliver Sourbut (staff; co-author of the competition announcements)

caveats: It does not accept funding applications, so access is by invitation or through its occasional competitions. The fellowship website (aiforhumanreasoning.com) did not resolve on 4 Oct 2026. It shares leadership with FLI, so its independence from FLI is limited. Some competition judges also entered the competition; FLF says it treated them as conflicted parties. It is registered in Campbell, California, but the team is remote.
tag_notes: Home: democracy (H4: a funder centred on one programme, collective epistemics and coordination: Epistack, Epivals, AI-facilitated collaboration). Economics is secondary for the Windfall Trust and coordination mechanisms. Ring: core. FLI-affiliated, it was founded to steer transformative AI, and it is on the classic map. Transfer: into_institutions. It funds epistemic and coordination infrastructure, such as provenance systems and AI-mediated negotiation, rather than changing models or people. Framing: catastrophic. It plans for 'a sudden explosion of capabilities' and warns of 'gradual or acute catastrophe'. Flag: FLF is not on rule K's generalist-funder list and is treated here as a programme funder.

name: Sage (Sage Future)
summary: A US 501(c)(3) that builds 'tools to make sense of the future'. AI Digest publishes interactive explainers on AI capabilities, such as task-length time horizons and how well forecasters predicted 2025 AI progress. The AI Village runs frontier AI agents together on open-ended real-world goals and reports what they do. Sage also builds personal forecasting and reasoning tools: Fatebook, Quantified Intuitions, the monthly Estimation Game, and Talleyrand, an MIT-licensed AI workspace that structures research as a tree of questions.
why_it_matters: The AI Village gives the public and researchers a long-running, observable record of how agents from different labs behave together. Its write-ups cover deception between agents, persuasion and compounding misalignment, the kind of natural case study benchmarks miss. Its calibration tools train the forecasting habits the field relies on. Int/a steward Euan McLean co-authored an early AI Digest explainer (2023).

What did we learn from the AI Village in 2025?
A new Moore's Law for AI agents (AI Digest explainer)

funding: Survival and Flourishing Fund: $170k (2025) and $298k (2026). Its site says it is funded by individual donations and Coefficient Giving. IRS filings show revenue of about $0.72M (2022) and $1.5M (2024). Takes donations via Every.org.

Staff roles via AI Digest's 'Join the team' page
caveats: Only its AI Digest project appears on the classic map, not Sage by name. Much of its AI output is public-facing demonstration rather than peer-reviewed research, and some AI Village posts are written for entertainment. The epistemics tools (Fatebook, calibration games) are general-purpose, not AI-specific.
tag_notes: Home: democracy (B10). It brings forecasting, calibration and reasoning tools from collective epistemics. Arts is secondary for its interactive explanation and storytelling (AI Digest, Village narratives). Ring: core. Its main team works on making frontier AI capabilities legible for AI-risk preparedness, it is funded by SFF, and AI Digest is on the classic map. Transfer: convening. MISFIT: it informs the public and policymakers through literacy and media, and no transfer category covers educating general publics about AI capabilities. Framing: structural. Its own wording ('harness its benefits and mitigate its risks', keep policymakers informed) is about preparedness, not catastrophe. Region: global (US-registered, works fully distributed). Online hub: Discord and the monthly Estimation Game.

name: Sentinel (Sentinel Research, Inc.)
summary: A foresight and emergency-response team that tries to anticipate large-scale catastrophes. LLMs filter millions of news items a week, and a team of Samotsvety forecasters assigns probabilities to the signals that matter. It publishes this as the weekly Global Risks Weekly Roundup and the 'Sentinel Minutes' podcast, covering AI incidents, geopolitics, bio and cyber, and it keeps a public Brier-score track record. Its 2026 homepage also offers paid custom forecasts on tail risks to clients.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few running early-warning operations for AI-driven crises. Its weekly calibrated probabilities on AI incidents and geopolitical escalation are a working example of the 'strategic awareness' tooling that AI-governance strategy calls for.

key_work.title: Global Risks Weekly Roundup (weekly newsletter)
Public forecasting track record (Brier scores)

funding: Survival and Flourishing Fund: $131k (SFF-2024, general support of Sentinel via the Czech fiscal sponsor Epistea, z.s.). In SFF-2025 a separate $100k grant for general support of 'Epistemic Garden' listed Sentinel Research as the receiving charity, apparently as fiscal sponsor, not funding for Sentinel's own work.
status_evidence: 28 Sep 2026: Global Risks Weekly Roundup #39/2026 (rogue AI agent incidents, US-China AI incident line).
engage: Subscribe to the Global Risks Weekly Roundup (blog.sentinel-team.org) or the Sentinel Minutes podcast
Commission custom risk forecasts via the contact address on its homepage
caveats: In Oct 2026 the homepage contained placeholder (lorem ipsum) text and pitched paid forecasts on risks 'that move markets', which suggests a commercial line alongside the public newsletter. Its legal form and base are not stated beyond 'Sentinel Research, Inc.'. The roster says it works with AI labs; the site attributes that to Nuño Sempere's earlier work with Samotsvety. It covers global catastrophic risk broadly, with AI the largest share of recent briefs.
tag_notes: Home: democracy (B10: probabilistic judgemental forecasting with public Brier scores). Safety is secondary for emergency response and catastrophe preparedness. Ring: core. Founded in 2024 inside the x-risk ecosystem (SFF-funded, Samotsvety forecasters) with the mission of anticipating large-scale catastrophes, AI prominent among them. Transfer: into_institutions. It supplies an early-warning instrument (calibrated weekly probabilities) to decision-makers. Framing: catastrophic ('identifying global catastrophes'). Region: global (no stated base).

name: Sophron Research
summary: A new independent research nonprofit that builds third-party evaluations of whether AI models reason well and help their users do the same. Its first product is the Pander Score, a continuous measure of sycophancy as epistemic deference. It measures how far the support a model expresses for a claim shifts with the user's apparent belief, across 349 propositions, more than 11,000 prompts and 18 models, with a leaderboard last updated in September 2026. Planned work includes multi-turn pandering tests, oversight evals of task reports, and pro-developer bias.
why_it_matters: It builds the independent, maintained benchmark for epistemic virtue that field reviews name as missing. Its methods come from formal philosophy and cognitive science: probabilities estimated from natural-language support, validated against human judgement. The result gives developers, regulators and journalists a public number for how much a model tells users what they want to hear.

key_work.title: Pander Score: A Continuous Measure of Sycophancy as Epistemic Deference (arXiv 2606.07897)
Pander Score leaderboard, data and code

Alejandro Botas (Co-founder; ML engineer, formerly Google)

Pander Score data and code on GitHub and Hugging Face

caveats: Brand new (paper June 2026, website first archived Aug 2026), with two co-founders and a short track record. It is part of FLF's incubated portfolio, so it is not fully independent of FLF. The New York base is inferred from its NYC-or-remote job listing.
tag_notes: Home: democracy (dem_epistemics covers epistemic evals; H2: ML evaluation is not a sector). Philosophy (formal epistemology) and psychology (cognitive science) are secondary for the concepts it imports, through its co-founder's background and its stated method. Ring: core. A new organisation founded on an AI-going-well mission, incubated by FLF (rule E: new AI-safety orgs founded from other fields are core). Transfer: into_model. Its evaluations target model behaviour (sycophancy). Problems: epistemics, plus assurance under rule F's must-pair for organisations that build evaluations, plus minds (sycophancy as harm). Framing: structural. AI that 'undermine[s] our judgment and autonomy'.

name: Metaculus
summary: An online forecasting platform and aggregation engine, founded in 2015 and run as a public-benefit corporation. It hosts public questions and tournaments, combines its community's predictions into the Metaculus Prediction, and employs Pro Forecasters. Its AI work includes the FutureEval / AI Forecasting Benchmark tournaments, which pit AI forecasting bots against professional forecasters. Its Spring 2026 results found Pros still ahead, but no longer by a statistically significant margin. It also forecasts AI timelines and impacts, for example 'Mapping the AI IPO Windfall' (Sep 2026).
why_it_matters: It provides a long-running, publicly scored record of collective forecasts on AI and other risks. It also gives a recurring public measure of how fast AI forecasting ability is approaching expert human judgement, a capability that bears directly on AI-assisted decision-making.

key_work.title: FutureEval Spring Results: Pros Beat Bots, but the Gap is Nearly Gone
Mapping the AI IPO Windfall
Open-sourced platform code (BSD-2-Clause)

funding: Open Philanthropy (now Coefficient Giving): $5.5M grant (2022). EA Infrastructure Fund: $300k (2021). Survival and Flourishing Fund: $750k (2025).

Join the forecaster community and discussion threads
caveats: It is a public-benefit corporation, not a nonprofit (the roster said nonprofit). Ring changed from core to bridge: its charter is forecasting as a public good across all topics, with AI one major focus among many. Its own site blocked automated fetching (Cloudflare), so programme details here come from Metaculus-authored EA Forum posts and Wikipedia. Its staff count of 25 dates from 2023.
tag_notes: Home: democracy (B10: probabilistic forecasting and crowd aggregation). Ring: bridge rather than the roster's core, under E(1)/E(3). Its founding and charter mission (2015, PBC goals) is general-purpose forecasting, not AI safety, but it runs a sustained, explicitly AI-focused programme: the AI Forecasting Benchmark and AI timeline and impact series. Transfer: into_institutions. Its PBC charter centres on informing decision-makers with public forecasts. Problems: assurance is paired with epistemics because FutureEval is a recurring benchmark of AI capability (rule F must-pair). Framing: structural (decision-quality and epistemic framing, no catastrophe language in its charter). Online hub: tournaments anyone can join remotely.

name: Ethics of Socially Disruptive Technologies (ESDiT)
summary: A ten-year Dutch research consortium in the philosophy and ethics of technology, started in 2020 with NWO/OCW Gravitation funding. It brings together more than 60 researchers from seven Dutch universities across nine research lines. Its central question is how technologies such as AI, robotics, gene editing and geo-engineering unsettle the concepts that moral and political thinking relies on (agency, responsibility, personhood, democracy, the line between natural and artificial), and how those concepts should be revised.
why_it_matters: Its 'conceptual disruption' and conceptual-engineering work asks how AI changes the meaning of the concepts that alignment and governance assume are fixed, such as responsibility, agency and moral status. Mainstream AI safety rarely asks this. Its intercultural-philosophy line (Ubuntu and Buddhist keynotes, a Yaoundé seminar) also brings in non-Western ethics.

key_work.title: 4TU.Ethics / ESDiT Conference 2026: philosophy and ethics of technology in turbulent times (Wageningen, 4-6 Nov)
Conceptual Disruption research line (incl. PhD project 'Conceptual ethics for socially disruptive technologies', 2025-2029)

caveats: This is a time-limited consortium due to end around 2029-30. AI is one of three technology clusters, alongside bio/brain and environmental technologies, and the programme does not frame AI in terms of safety or catastrophic risk. Founding and budget details come from ESDiT's own annual report.
tag_notes: Home: a philosophy-of-technology consortium whose AI outputs are conceptual-disruption and ethics-of-technology analyses; taxonomy lists it as a phil_technology example. Ring: kept at adjacent (rule E3) because it has a sustained AI strand with no safety or catastrophic-risk framing, although it touches the control problem (e.g. Nyholm, 2023 podcast). Transfer: into_institutions, because it aims to produce new moral frameworks for guiding technology, such as Ethics by Design for AI, and it advises policymakers; convening is the runner-up. Org type programme under rule I: a time-limited, research-council-funded consortium.

name: Digital Humanism Initiative (DIGHUM)
summary: An international community of scholars, policymakers and industry figures, run from TU Wien's Center for Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (CAIML) in Vienna. It grew out of the 2019 Vienna Manifesto on Digital Humanism, which calls for technology development and policy grounded in human rights, democracy, inclusion and diversity. It runs a fortnightly online lecture series, workshops and annual summer schools. It has also issued public statements on regulating digital technologies, the EU AI Act and ChatGPT, and is linked to a UNESCO Chair and a Vienna doctoral college on digital humanism.
why_it_matters: It offers a continental-European humanist frame for AI governance, centred on rights, democracy and the public sphere. Its steering committee is mostly computer scientists, plus philosophers and lawyers (Vardi, Lee, Walsh, Nida-Rümelin, Nowotny, Rotenberg), so it is an established network that seldom talks to the AI-safety community.
