caveats: dighum.org now redirects to caiml.org/dighum. The network is led by computer scientists. Its framing is human-centred technology and rights, not catastrophic risk, and its steering committee is large and mostly honorific.
tag_notes: Home: philosophy (H2/H5), because the computer-science leadership is not a sector and what it imports is a humanist normative frame (digital humanism, as in Nida-Rümelin's work). It sits on a seam with law_policy, the multidisciplinary public-interest network, so law is listed second. Ring: kept at adjacent (E3): a sustained AI and digital programme framed around rights, democracy and monopoly power, with no safety or catastrophic-risk framing. Transfer: convening, because its main activity brings computer scientists, humanities scholars and policymakers together through lectures, workshops and summer schools; its open letters and its AI Act statement are secondary. The manifesto names monopolisation, loss of privacy and threats to democracy, which is why framing is structural.

name: Uehiro Oxford Institute (UOI)
summary: The University of Oxford's practical-ethics institute. It was established in 2024 with a benefaction from the Uehiro Foundation on Ethics and Education, as the successor to the Oxford Uehiro Centre for Practical Ethics. It researches applied ethics across medicine, pandemics, war, climate and technology, publishes the Journal of Practical Ethics, and teaches an MSt in Practical Ethics. Its AI work includes an 'AI and Digital Ethics' theme, a series of papers on using large language models to support informed consent in medicine, research on relational norms and credit or blame for AI-generated content, and a scenario-planning network on AI, death and the afterlife.
why_it_matters: It brings a large applied-ethics and experimental-moral-psychology group to concrete questions about humans and AI, such as when it is safe to deploy black-box AI in clinical care and whether AI can improve rather than erode moral decision-making. That is practical normative expertise most AI-safety groups lack.

Allen, Earp and Wilkinson, 'AI-Assisted Consent in Paediatric Medicine', Journal of Medical Ethics

Leadership is in transition, with an interim director and a permanent search open. AI is one theme among many, and its AI output is mostly medical and digital ethics rather than AI risk.
tag_notes: Home: applied ethics and bioethics, the institute's discipline; psych is secondary for its experimental moral-psychology work (Philosophical Moral Psychology Lab; Earp's cross-country surveys on credit and blame). Ring: kept at adjacent (E3): a standing AI and digital ethics theme focused on medicine, autonomy and human-AI relations, without safety framing; Giubilini's commentary on AI-risk movements is occasional. Transfer: into_institutions, because its flagship AI output is practical guidance for institutions, such as a decision algorithm for implementing black-box AI in healthcare. Framing is flourishing because its stated AI question is how AI can enhance rather than impede ethical decision-making. Status is changed because it was renamed and re-founded in 2024.

name: AI and Faith
summary: A Seattle-based interfaith nonprofit and expert network of theologians, ethicists, technologists and faith leaders that brings the ethical traditions of the major religions into debates about how AI is built and used. It publishes a podcast, newsletter and articles, keeps resources organised by faith tradition, supports research fellows, and runs workshops and chaplaincy symposia. With the Institute for Security and Technology, and with Future of Life Institute funding, it runs the Religious Voices and Responsible AI initiative. That initiative produces AI curricula, safety and ethics discussion guides and a civic-engagement hub, piloted in evangelical churches in Southern California and in mosques in the Bay Area and Seattle.
why_it_matters: It is one of the main channels between religious communities and AI ethics and safety, and can carry ideas about safe and beneficial AI to congregations that technical or policy organisations do not reach. It also brings theological accounts of human dignity and formation into discussion of what AI should serve.

The Future of Life Institute funds the IST-AI and Faith initiative; the amount was not found. Its 2026 curriculum work links to an OpenAI-funded project with the PC(USA) Synod of the Covenant.

name: Project Imago Dei
summary: A small US Christian 'pro-human' initiative that educates churches about AI capabilities and risks, combining technical literacy with theology rooted in humanity being made in God's image. It produces 'The Shepherd's Warning', a video and workshop series with facilitator guides for pastors, and works with pilot churches. It also surveys Christian staffers on Capitol Hill about a local forum and an educational retreat on AI. The Future of Life Institute granted it $47,500 to educate US evangelical congregations through small groups and media.
why_it_matters: It is one of very few faith organisations founded specifically around AI risk, and it works with AI-safety outreach groups to reach evangelical congregations and conservative political staff. AI safety has had almost no presence with these audiences.

key_work.title: The Shepherd's Warning (video series, facilitator guide, strategic communications and theory-of-change documents)
FLI grant to educate US evangelical congregations on AI capabilities and risks

The director's name is spelled differently on the site (Shon) and in FLI's grant list (Sean). It is openly pro-life and aims at political mobilisation through churches ('politics is downstream from culture, and culture is downstream from faith'), which funders wanting non-partisan partners should note. Listed partners are AI Safety Awareness Project, Biola AI Lab, Anti Entropy and Evitable.

Ring changed from bridge to core (E1): its founding and sole mission is AI risk; it is funded by FLI and partners with AI-safety outreach groups (AI Safety Awareness Project, Evitable); and it fits the rule that new organisations founded from another field around AI safety are core. Bridge remains arguable, since its identity is Christian ministry. Transfer: convening, because it equips its own community (pastors, congregations, Christian staffers) with literacy and resources. Framing is structural because its dominant stake is erosion of human dignity under 'anti-human' elites, although its site also cites bioweapon-scale catastrophe.

name: Sinai and Synapses
summary: A Jewish science-and-religion organisation in New York, incubated and fiscally sponsored by Clal (The National Jewish Center for Learning and Leadership). It runs the interfaith Sinai and Synapses Fellowship for clergy, scientists and writers. Through Scientists in Synagogues it gives congregations $5,000 grants for science programmes (84 communities since 2016), and it makes the podcasts 'Belief in the Future' (technology and religion) and 'Down the Wormhole'. Its AI work includes 'Deepening Jewish Education in the Digital Age' grants and a working group on Jewish thought for the digital future. It also holds a $100,000 FLI grant for a Reform Jewish initiative to prepare rabbis to understand AI and build interfaith partnerships for a human-centred future.
why_it_matters: It brings rabbinic tradition (questioning, ethics of labour and rest, accounts of agency and repentance) into practical AI formation for congregations and clergy. It has a tested regranting model that reaches grassroots religious communities at low cost.

caveats: AI is one strand among broader science-and-religion topics. Its own AI framing is values and Jewish education, and it explicitly avoids apocalyptic or utopian takes; its bridge status rests mainly on the FLI-funded project. It is a project incubated within Clal rather than an independent organisation. The 2013 launch year comes from secondary sources (eJewishPhilanthropy, RJ coverage), not its own site.
tag_notes: Home: religion, sub rel_islamic_jewish (D: its main AI outputs are Jewish education and a Reform rabbinic initiative, though rel_interfaith would fit its science-and-religion fellowship). Ring: kept at bridge (E), but it is borderline. The FLI-funded project frames AI in pro-human, 'AI going well' terms, while its Templeton-funded digital-education work alone would make it adjacent. Transfer: convening, because it informs and equips its own community of rabbis, educators and congregations. Fund is a role because it regrants money to congregations and educators. Org type programme because it is incubated and fiscally sponsored by Clal.

name: World Council of Churches (WCC)
summary: The global ecumenical fellowship of about 350 member churches (Orthodox, Anglican, Protestant and some Pentecostal), founded in 1948 and based in Geneva. Its AI work is new. A Future of Life Institute grant of $100,000 funds a project, led by Sara Speicher, to establish AI red lines across its network of churches in more than 120 countries and to guide global AI governance toward reducing the risks of advanced AI and sharing its benefits. In September 2026 WCC staff met to form an AI task force and to plan a multidisciplinary AI symposium for 15-19 February 2027.
why_it_matters: It could become the widest channel outside Catholicism for carrying AI-safety norms such as red lines into the churches and into the UN-level advocacy where the WCC already works. Its membership is concentrated in the Global South.

key_work.title: FLI-funded project to establish AI red lines and guide global AI governance
WCC staff AI meeting and task force: 'What does it mean to be human?'
Planned multidisciplinary AI symposium (15-19 Feb 2027)

people: Sara Speicher (lead of the FLI AI project; WCC communication officer on AI and WACC deputy general secretary)
Manoj Kurian (Director, Commission of the Churches on Health and Healing)
funding: AI red lines project: Future of Life Institute grant of $100,000 (2026). The WCC's general funding was not researched for this profile.
status_evidence: 25 Sep 2026: WCC news reports a staff meeting (22 Sep) on AI initiatives, a new staff task force and a symposium planned for Feb 2027.
engage: Multidisciplinary AI symposium planned for 15-19 Feb 2027 (participation details not yet published)
caveats: The AI programme is nascent: the task force was forming in September 2026 and no public WCC statement or red-lines document was found. The red-lines aim is documented on FLI's grantee page rather than on the WCC site. Its staff discussions frame AI mainly through human dignity, justice, health and environmental cost, more than catastrophic risk.
tag_notes: Home: religion, sub rel_christian; the WCC is a fellowship of churches speaking for them, and the taxonomy lists it as an example. Ring: kept at bridge (E3), because an old institution now runs a funded project explicitly aimed at reducing the risks of advanced AI through red lines. Transfer: into_institutions, because the project's aim is a governance instrument (red lines for global AI governance). Security is the primary problem because red lines map there, with meaning and justice drawn from the staff discussion. Org type: tagged as the membership body rather than as a programme (A1), because the AI work has no separate identity yet. Framing is structural (justice, control, environmental cost) because no WCC-authored statement of catastrophic stakes was found.

name: DELTA (Notre Dame Institute for Ethics and the Common Good)
summary: DELTA is a University of Notre Dame initiative, run by the Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, that offers a Christian virtue-ethics framework for 'human formation' in the age of AI, built around Dignity, Embodiment, Love, Transcendence and Agency. It produces resources for faith leaders, teachers, students, journalists and tech workers. It holds an annual DELTA Summit on AI, Faith and Human Flourishing (the second ran 21–23 September 2026) and funds faculty fellowships and Faith and AI rapid-response grants of $100,000 each.
why_it_matters: It is the best-funded effort to apply the Catholic intellectual tradition and virtue ethics to how people, rather than models, are formed by AI. It reaches into Catholic schools, parishes and the Bay Area tech industry, communities that mainstream AI safety has almost no channel into.

key_work.title: The DELTA framework (Dignity, Embodiment, Love, Transcendence, Agency)
DELTA Summit on AI, Faith and Human Flourishing (second edition, 21–23 Sept)

status_evidence: Sep 2026: second DELTA Summit (21–23 Sept), opening Mass homily by Cardinal Blase Cupich; faculty fellowship deadline 26 Oct 2026.

caveats: The framework explicitly sets itself apart from safety and privacy concerns: there is no x-risk or alignment framing, and it forms people rather than specifying model behaviour. The work began in 2024 with a Lilly planning grant (200 focus groups), leading to the first summit in September 2025. The Notre Dame–IBM Technology Ethics Lab is a separate unit.
tag_notes: Home religion (B1): it speaks from Christian virtue ethics and the Catholic tradition to faith leaders, Catholic schools and the public; philosophy is secondary because the institute's director is a philosopher. Ring adjacent (E3): a sustained programme (summit, grants, fellowships, newsletter) on human formation, with no safety or alignment framing; its own page contrasts DELTA with safety and privacy concerns. Transfer convening (J5): it mainly equips its own faith and education community; outreach to tech leaders is secondary. Must-pair not applicable.

name: Institute for Technology, Ethics, and Culture (ITEC), Markkula Center for Applied Ethics, Santa Clara University
summary: ITEC is a collaboration between Santa Clara University's Markkula Center for Applied Ethics and the Vatican's Dicastery for Culture and Education. It helps companies put ethical principles into practice for AI and other disruptive technologies. Its main output is the ITEC Handbook, 'Ethics in the Age of Disruptive Technologies: An Operational Roadmap' (2023), a free five-stage guide with a primer and a set of principles. It also commissioned a November 2023 survey of 3,000 Americans on AI ethics, and it publishes commentary on Catholic perspectives on AI.
why_it_matters: It is a standing channel between the Vatican and Silicon Valley firms, turning Catholic social teaching on human dignity and the common good into corporate governance steps. Its director of technology ethics publicly backed slowing advanced AI in 2026 and warned about recursive self-improvement, which makes him a rare Catholic voice on loss-of-control risk.

key_work.title: ITEC Handbook: Ethics in the Age of Disruptive Technologies: An Operational Roadmap

ITEC Principles (anchoring, guiding and specifying principles)

status_evidence: Mid-2026: ITEC's news and commentary page lists Brian Patrick Green's comments on Pope Leo XIV's first encyclical and his backing for Anthropic's call to slow advanced AI (UCA News).
engage: The ITEC Handbook, primer and principles are free downloads for organisations
Markkula Center webinar recordings on AI and Pope Leo XIV's encyclical 'Magnifica Humanitas' (2026)
caveats: The draft dated the survey to 2025; it was fielded on 7 November 2023 (83% wanted clearer federal AI regulation; 70% supported a temporary pause). ITEC was announced on 28 June 2023 together with the Handbook, most of its own outputs date from 2023, and its 2025–26 activity is mainly media commentary by Markkula staff. The Markkula Center is under an interim executive director after Don Heider's departure.
tag_notes: Home philosophy (H1, method over topic): its main output is an applied business-ethics roadmap built from interviews with corporations, so phil_bioethics. The provisional home was religion; religion is kept as the first secondary because ITEC is a formal partnership with the Vatican Dicastery for Culture and Education. Ring adjacent (E3): a standing programme on corporate technology ethics framed around privacy, equity, transparency and accountability; the director's 2026 remarks on loss of control are media commentary, not a programme. Transfer into_institutions (J3): it supplies a governance template for companies. MISFIT: problem 'people' is the nearest column for ethics management inside tech firms.

name: The Faraday Institute for Science and Religion
summary: The Faraday Institute is a Cambridge charity that researches and teaches on science and the Christian faith for academics, churches, schools and the public; it was founded in 2006 and has been independent since 2018. Its AI work has two strands. The 'AI for Humanity' research hub is a theology-engaged programme that ran an interdisciplinary seminar series through 2026 on how AI affects human dignity, relationships, formation and spirituality. The second is a set of AI resources, lectures and small-group materials for church leaders, made with the AI Christian Partnership.
why_it_matters: It gives UK churches a scientifically literate route into AI questions. It is also building a community in which technologists and theologians test claims about AI's effects on human formation. It is a ready channel to clergy, though it deliberately positions itself beyond safety and existential-risk framings.

caveats: The AI hub explicitly looks beyond safety, security and 'hypothetical existential risks', focusing on human flourishing and relationships. Wikipedia's list of senior staff may be out of date. The official site blocks some automated requests.
tag_notes: Home religion (B1): a Christian-ethos science-and-religion charity whose AI output is theology-engaged research and resources for churches. It is coded rel_christian rather than rel_interfaith because it is a single-tradition body whose main focus is science and the Christian faith; philosophy is secondary because the hub draws on philosophical anthropology. Ring adjacent (E3): a standing AI for Humanity hub with a 2026 seminar series and church resources, framed around dignity and flourishing and explicitly not around safety or existential risk. Transfer convening (J5): it mainly equips its church and academic community. The online hub tag rests on its ministry course, which can be followed live online.

name: Center for Theology and the Natural Sciences (CTNS)
summary: CTNS is a centre at the Graduate Theological Union in Berkeley, founded in 1981 by Robert John Russell, that promotes dialogue between Christian theology and the natural sciences. It does this through research, seminary and doctoral teaching, the journal Theology and Science, and public forums. Its AI work was the Templeton-funded project 'Virtuous AI? Cultural Evolution, Artificial Intelligence, and Virtue' (2022–2025). The project held three online conferences in 2023, centred on Berkeley, Seoul and Rome, on whether AI will shape human virtue, whether it can help people acquire virtue, and whether it can itself be virtuous.
why_it_matters: Its question of whether AI can have or cultivate virtue bears directly on character-based alignment targets. The project also built an intercultural, multi-religious network of AI scientists and humanities scholars across the US, Korea and Europe, a network that AI-safety work rarely reaches.

status_evidence: Dec 2025: online CTNS Public Forum on nuclear justice (announced Oct 2025); June 2025: event marking the end of the Virtuous AI project. The live site returned HTTP 502 on 4 Oct 2026; an archived copy from that day lists no new AI programme.

Charles H. Townes Graduate Student Fellowship (GTU doctoral students)

It is coded rel_interfaith as a science-and-religion body and because Virtuous AI was deliberately multi-religious and intercultural. Philosophy (virtue ethics) and life (cultural evolution) are secondary. Ring adjacent (E2/E3): a funded AI project ran into 2025, so it is not potential, and that project was framed around virtue rather than safety or catastrophic risk; it may drift to potential if no new AI work follows. Transfer convening (J5): it convened theologians and AI scientists and published for its own field. Status active on 2025 activity, though its AI work has finished.

name: John Templeton Foundation (JTF): Future of Intelligence venture
summary: The John Templeton Foundation, a Pennsylvania philanthropy founded in 1987, runs 'Future of Intelligence', a venture that will award over $60M over three years from 2026 across all six of its funding areas. It funds philosophers, theologians, biologists, neuroscientists, physicists and computer scientists under four themes: the story, diversity, plurality and future of intelligence. The last theme covers artificial superintelligence, cognitive enhancement and who should steer AI. Separately, in January 2025 JTF gave $8M in nine grants for 'Cultivating Character in the Digital Age', four of them on AI.
why_it_matters: It is probably the largest new pool of money for philosophy, theology and the science of intelligence that touches AI, and it sits almost entirely outside AI-safety funding networks. Work on wisdom, moral status, collective intelligence and alignment targets can compete for it if applicants make the connection.

key_work.title: Future of Intelligence venture (over $60M, 2026–28)

funding: Endowment left by Sir John Templeton. The venture will award over $60M in grants over 2026–28. In Jan 2025 JTF made nine grants totalling $8M for character development in the digital age, including UNC Chapel Hill ($2.06M), Stanford/Challenge Success ($1.10M), Harvard Center for Digital Thriving ($1.03M) and UC Berkeley ($0.93M).

Templeton Futures: articles, videos, convenings and a narrative podcast
caveats: The venture is pluralist about AI's direction ('accelerator or decelerator') rather than safety-focused, and it takes no risk position of its own. JTF warned that inquiry windows could close early because of high volume. Grant sizes per project under the venture were not published.
tag_notes: Generalist funder (rule K, listed as 'JTF Future of Intelligence'). Its nominal home is religion per H4: the most distinctive line is the 'Story of Intelligence' in philosophical and religious traditions, together with JTF's science-and-religion identity, so rel_interfaith. The secondaries are what the venture names: philosophy, the life sciences, character development (psych) and the physical sciences and computer science (formal). Ring changed from adjacent to bridge (E3): theme 4 explicitly frames the venture around artificial superintelligence, extinction versus abundance and who steers AI, within a standing $60M+ programme for 2026–28. Transfer convening (J5, as for FLI): the funded work mostly informs scholarly and public understanding rather than changing models or institutions.

name: Institute for Ethics in AI, University of Oxford
summary: The Institute for Ethics in AI is part of Oxford's Faculty of Philosophy. It was launched in 2021 with a donation from Stephen A. Schwarzman and is based in the Schwarzman Centre for the Humanities. It does philosophy-led research on AI and human rights, governance, health and care, the family and the foundations of AI. It also runs the five-year Accelerator Fellowship Programme (from 2025; fellows include Alondra Nelson, Joy Buolamwini, Yuval Shany and Audrey Tang), hosts the Human-Centered AI Lab (HAI Lab), offers executive education, and leads Civic AI, a '6-Pack of Care' framework for 'alignment-by-process' in deployed systems.
why_it_matters: It brings moral and political philosophy, care ethics and human-rights law into AI governance at a major university. Through Civic AI it offers a bottom-up, care-based account of alignment that complements work on frontier models. It became an affiliate of the International Association for Safe and Ethical AI in June 2026.

caveats: The ring was moved from adjacent to bridge because Civic AI is framed explicitly as alignment and the mission lists safety; most of the institute's output is still AI ethics and human rights rather than catastrophic risk. Edward Harcourt is now director; the inaugural director was John Tasioulas. Civic AI is a research project of two of its people, with its own site.
tag_notes: Home philosophy: an institute of the Philosophy Faculty whose outputs are moral and political philosophy (rights, care, agency), so phil_moral. Law (the human-rights work of Shany and Cofone) and democracy (Civic AI with Audrey Tang) are secondary. Ring changed from adjacent to bridge (E3): the mission includes 'issues of safety and governance', Civic AI is framed as 'alignment-by-process' that complements frontier alignment, and the institute joined IASEAI in 2026. It is a philosophy institution, not an x-risk organisation. Transfer into_institutions (J3): an International AI Bill of Human Rights, governance frameworks and Civic AI processes. Must-pair F: values + democracy for Civic AI. Framing follows the mission statement, which lists present ethical challenges.

name: Center for Philosophy of Artificial Intelligence (CPAI), University of Copenhagen
summary: CPAI is a research collective in the University of Copenhagen's Department of Communication, led by Anders Søgaard, that works in both directions between AI and philosophy. It uses philosophy to define fairness, explanation and representation for AI, and uses language models to study meaning, understanding and goal-directedness. Its 2025–26 output includes papers on whether language models have semantics, world models in Othello-playing models, explanation design, and an AAAI 2026 alignment-track paper on conceptions of intelligence. It co-hosts the Models of Consciousness 2026 conference (12–16 October 2026).
why_it_matters: It is one of the few continental-European centres doing philosophy of language-model understanding together with hands-on NLP experiments. That combination bears on interpretability and on what alignment targets such as 'intelligence' or 'understanding' mean.

Its founding date and funding are not stated; its website was first archived in August 2025. Several outputs are mainstream NLP papers.

Psych (its philosophy of cognitive science group) and minds (co-hosting MoC7) are secondary. Ring adjacent (E3): a standing research programme on AI from philosophy, not framed around safety; one AAAI alignment-track paper does not make it bridge. Transfer into_model (J1): its work asks what models represent and how their behaviour should be explained. MISFIT: framing, because it states no stakes; present_harms is the closest fit, since its ethics papers address fairness, developer responsibility and explanation.

name: Berggruen Institute
summary: A think tank in Los Angeles, founded in 2010 by the investor Nicolas Berggruen and the journalist Nathan Gardels, with centres in Beijing (at Peking University since 2018) and Venice. It publishes Noema magazine, awards the $1m Berggruen Prize for Philosophy and Culture, funds fellows and incubated Antikythera, Benjamin Bratton's programme on planetary computation. Its AI work covers the philosophy of AI and consciousness, AI safety as a US–China public good (it co-hosted the 2024 IDAIS-Venice dialogue with the Safe AI Forum), and digital-democracy pilots such as Engaged California.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few well-endowed places where philosophers, including Chinese and East Asian ones, work on what AI means for being human and for governance, and it has already hosted AI-safety diplomacy. Noema gives int/a-style arguments a way to reach policy and intellectual readers outside the AI-safety community.

key_work.title: Co-hosted, with the Safe AI Forum (FAR.AI), the third International Dialogue on AI Safety (IDAIS-Venice) at Casa dei Tre Oci; Noema essay 'AI Safety Is A Global Public Good'
Antikythera, a programme on planetary computation led by Benjamin Bratton (incubated)
Engaged California, a digital-democracy platform built with the State of California and expanded statewide for AI-policy input
Berggruen China Center projects 'AI Meets Chinese Philosophers' and 'Beyond Consciousness'

funding: Endowed by Nicolas Berggruen: Wikipedia reports an endowment of about $1bn (2024), and 2022 revenue of $16.6m against $18.9m in expenses. Programme grants include more than $225,000 from Templeton World Charity Foundation (2019) for Transformations of the Human.
status_evidence: 7 May 2026: Engaged California expanded statewide for AI-policy deliberation. Also in 2026: 2026–27 China Fellows announced and the Berggruen Prize ceremony for Michael Sandel held.
engage: Berggruen Research Center at Peking University fellowships and internships (applications opened for 2026–27)
Berggruen Prize Essay Competition ($50,000 awards in English and Chinese categories, running since 2024)
Public events in Los Angeles and Venice, e.g. 'Consciousness, AI, and the Human Future' (2026)
caveats: Funded largely by one billionaire founder. Its AI output is broad philosophy and public debate rather than a dedicated safety programme, and Noema publishes deflationary views (e.g. Anil Seth on conscious AI) alongside safety-minded ones. The Transformations of the Human programme (philosophers placed in AI labs) dates from 2019, and I could not confirm it is still running. Engaged California belongs to the state's Office of Data and Innovation; Berggruen is a partner.
tag_notes: Home: its AI output comes from philosophy of technology and planetary thought (Noema, Antikythera, the China centre's East Asian philosophy projects), so philosophy/phil_technology; democracy is secondary because of the formal Engaged California partnership (rule C). Ring: an older philosophy institution with a sustained AI line (the Noema AI-safety essays, hosting IDAIS-Venice in 2024, the consciousness series), so bridge, not core (rule E). Transfer: a governance think tank whose AI work aims at institutions (deliberation platforms, international safety dialogue), so into_institutions (rule J3). Framing is flourishing because its own statements centre on 'navigating change through ideas' rather than harm. Roles: media (Noema) first; fund for the prizes and fellowships.

name: Machine Intelligence and Normative Theory Lab (MINT Lab)
summary: A philosophy lab led by Seth Lazar, founded at the Australian National University in 2022 and now based at Johns Hopkins University's School of Government and Policy. It studies whether AI agents can recognise and act on moral reasons ('normative competence'), how societies should govern AI agents, and political philosophy for a world with advanced AI. It runs an AGI Governance Fellowship and holds workshops at venues such as IASEAI.
why_it_matters: It turns moral and political philosophy into concrete agendas for evaluating and governing AI agents, a link most alignment groups lack. Its funding (SFF, Templeton, CSET, OpenAI) shows that philosophy-led safety work can attract mainstream AI-safety money.

Workshop on Normative Competence and AGI-Ready Institution Design workshop at IASEAI '26
AI and Democratic Freedoms public symposium with the Knight First Amendment Institute, Columbia
AGI Governance Bibliography

Lazar also held an ARC Future Fellowship (2022–25). The CV does not give years for most grants.

caveats: The lab is moving from ANU to Johns Hopkins: Lazar's CV lists him as a JHU professor from 2026, while the lab site dates the move to 2025, so team composition may be changing. Lazar also has industry and sector ties: a 2025 visiting faculty researcher post at Google (0.2 FTE) and a research scientist role at Resolution from 2026. It received a small OpenAI grant.
tag_notes: Home: moral and political philosophy is the lab's method, applied to AI agents (phil_moral, the taxonomy's own example). Ring: rooted in academic philosophy, with a sustained, explicitly safety-framed programme (sociotechnical AI safety, AGI governance, normative-competence evaluations funded by SFF, CSET and OpenAI), so bridge (rule E3). Transfer: its lead line evaluates whether LLM agents act on moral reasons, aimed at model behaviour, so into_model (rule J1); its governance work also feeds institutions. Problems pair values with assurance because it builds evaluations (rule F). Framing is structural: the stated aim is to preserve liberal democratic values through the transition. The move of host institution did not change mission or team, so status stays active, not changed.

name: Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence (CFI)
summary: An interdisciplinary research centre at the University of Cambridge, founded in 2016 with a £10m grant from the Leverhulme Trust, with spokes at Imperial College London and UC Berkeley. Its programmes are Kinds of Intelligence (comparing animal, human and machine cognition, including the Animal-AI testbed), AI: Futures and Responsibility, AI: Trust and Society, AI: Narratives and Justice, and Design, Participation & Praxis. It teaches an MPhil in Ethics of AI, Data and Algorithms and supervises PhD students.
why_it_matters: It holds humanities and cognitive-science methods the safety field rarely uses: animal-cognition tasks that separate real competence from benchmark shortcuts, and the main evidence base on how different cultures imagine AI. It sits beside CSER in Cambridge's Institute for Technology and Humanity, so its people already move between x-risk and humanities work.

key_work.title: Animal-AI environment and the Animal-AI Olympics (about 900 animal-cognition tasks for testing AI agents)
Global AI Narratives project (2018–22), with the OUP volume 'AI Narratives'
AI: Futures and Responsibility programme (foresight, governance, safety and security)
MPhil in Ethics of AI, Data and Algorithms

people: Rachel Adams (Executive Director and Research Professor)
Huw Price (Founder and Strategy Group Chair)
Seán Ó hÉigeartaigh (Associate Director, Research Strategy; Programme Director, AI: Futures and Responsibility)
funding: Founded with a £10m Leverhulme Trust grant (2016). Project funding has included DARPA (RECOG-AI, 2021–23) and UKRI Future Leaders Fellowships.
status_evidence: 17 Sep 2026: the centre listed in its media coverage The Conversation piece 'Why AI consciousness could become the next great societal divide'. 8 Sep 2026: its Citizens' Autonomous Vehicle Observatory project won funding. The Animal-AI repository was last updated in August 2026.
engage: MPhil in Ethics of AI, Data and Algorithms (nine months, full-time)
PhD study and scholarships
Staff vacancies and visiting positions listed on its site
caveats: A broad centre: much of its output is on present-day ethics, justice and culture rather than catastrophic risk, so how relevant it is depends on the programme. Global AI Narratives ended in 2022, though the Narratives and Justice programme continues. Its CASP group is on the aisafety.com map, but the centre as a whole is not. I did not confirm how it is funded now that the 2016 founding grant has run its course.
tag_notes: Home: a hub led by philosophers whose largest output is philosophy of technology and intelligence (the taxonomy lists it under phil_technology); arts (AI narratives) and psych (comparative cognition in Kinds of Intelligence) are secondary under the hub allowance (rules H5, C). Ring: kept at bridge. It is a humanities-rooted academic centre, but its founding framing (Hawking's 'best or worst thing') and the AI: Futures and Responsibility programme give it a sustained 'AI going well' line (rule E3). It could be argued core, but most of its programmes are not x-risk work. Transfer: its stated aim is scholarship that informs academia, industry and government, so into_institutions (rule J3). Framing follows its mission to make the best of AI's opportunities, so flourishing. London hub through the Imperial spoke.

name: Buddhism & AI Initiative
summary: A small initiative started in 2025 by Buddhist practitioners, among them the former Conjecture COO Chris Scammell and the philosopher Peter Hershock, to connect Buddhist communities, scholars and AI practitioners. It has mapped the Buddhism–AI field (191 entries drawn from more than 500 conversations), runs online workshops for Buddhist teachers and sanghas, and publishes essays on Substack. With partners including 84000, Mind & Life Europe and the University of Vienna, it held a summer course and conference on Buddhism and AI at Gomde, Austria, in July 2026.
why_it_matters: It brings a contemplative tradition with centuries of practice in studying mind, ethics and interdependence into AI-safety conversations, and its founders come from both worlds (Conjecture, Mind & Life). Its field map is the clearest guide to who works where Buddhism meets AI, which helps funders find partners in a tradition the safety field rarely consults.

key_work.title: Field framework: six domains where Buddhism meets AI (191 entries)
Buddhism and AI summer course (1–12 July) and conference (9–12 July), Gomde, Austria
Community workshops on AI for Buddhist teachers and sanghas
'Why Buddhism and AI?' and other Substack dispatches

people: Peter D. Hershock (co-founder and intellectual adviser; East-West Center)
Ryan Stagg (co-founder; former Director of Digital Strategy, Mind & Life Institute)
funding: Future of Life Institute, according to the founders' August 2025 EA Forum post. Amounts are not published.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: published a field report from the Buddhism & AI conference (Gomde, Austria, 9–12 July 2026). Its Substack posted monthly through 2026.
engage: Annual summer course and conference (2026 edition: 1–12 July, in person at Gomde, Austria, or online)
Online workshops for Buddhist teachers and communities (rolling Zoom cohorts)
Suggest additions or edits to the field framework
Substack newsletter
caveats: Young and small: four core team members and a short track record. FLI funding ties it to the AI-safety funding ecosystem. There are two websites: engagedbuddhists.ai is the initiative's own, and buddhismandai.com is the collaborative summer course it belongs to. Its technical work is described as guiding partner projects, with few public outputs so far.
tag_notes: Home: speaks from and to a Buddhist community (convening sanghas, teacher workshops, translation partners), so religion/rel_buddhist per rule B1 and worked example 3; contemplative is secondary. Ring: a faith-rooted initiative with a sustained, explicitly 'AI going well' programme (field-building, alignment-informed essays, an annual conference), so bridge, as in worked example 3. Transfer: it mainly brings Buddhist communities into the AI conversation, so convening (rule J5). The official URL is changed from buddhismandai.com (the summer course) to engagedbuddhists.ai (the initiative's own site). Status new: launched in 2025. Online hub: rolling Zoom workshop cohorts.

name: Forethought
summary: A research nonprofit in Oxford, directed by Max Dalton, with William MacAskill and Tom Davidson as senior research fellows, that studies how to navigate a rapid 'intelligence explosion'. It models AI-driven progress and works on the 'grand challenges' that would follow: AI-enabled coups and power concentration, digital minds, and races for space resources. It also works on AI tools for collective reasoning and coordination, and on what a very good post-AGI future would be. It publishes papers, a roughly weekly newsletter and the ForeCast podcast.
why_it_matters: It is the main AI-safety-funded group asking normative questions beyond alignment: what to do about power concentration, what rights digital minds should have, and how to reach a good future rather than merely avoid catastrophe. Its 'Better Futures' series and its work on AI for collective epistemics overlap directly with int/a's interest in wisdom and shared sensemaking.

key_work.title: Preparing for the Intelligence Explosion (MacAskill and Moorhouse)
AI-Enabled Coups: How a Small Group Could Use AI to Seize Power (Davidson, Finnveden and Hadshar)
Better Futures essay series (MacAskill)
Design sketches for a more sensible world (collective epistemics and coordination tools)

funding: Donations from private individuals, according to its site. Donors and budget are not published.
status_evidence: 28 Sep 2026: published 'A Thousand AI Constitutions: A Short Defense' in its newsletter. September 2026 also brought papers on data bottlenecks and on intelligence-explosion dynamics (Toby Ord).
engage: Researcher roles through rolling expressions of interest, including one on extreme power concentration
Founders Fellowship (rolling, no deadline)
Visiting scholar positions
Newsletter (roughly weekly) and the ForeCast podcast
caveats: It sits firmly in the effective-altruist and longtermist mainstream. Its interdisciplinarity is mostly moral philosophy and economics, with little input from contemplative, non-Western or social-science traditions. The team formed in mid-2024 and launched publicly in March 2025. It was built out of the legal and administrative shell of the earlier Forethought Foundation for Global Priorities Research, but the founders describe it as a new team and project, and the Foundation's programmes were wound down. Funders are not disclosed.
tag_notes: Home: moral philosophy is its method (grand challenges, better futures, digital-minds ethics), so philosophy/phil_moral, the taxonomy's own example; economics is secondary for Davidson's growth and progress modelling (rule C). Ring: its founding and primary mission is navigating the transition to superintelligence, and it sits in the EA/x-risk ecosystem and on the aisafety.com map, so core (rule E1). Transfer: its outputs are policy and governance proposals for companies and governments (rules against AI misuse, oversight, government AI deployment), so into_institutions (rule J3). Framing is catastrophic (coups, WMD, irreversible grand challenges), with a strong flourishing strand in Better Futures. Problems: power (coups and power concentration) first, then systemic (long-term trajectory) and epistemics (AI for reasoning and coordination); digital minds (ai_status) is a further strand.

name: Research Center for Islamic Legislation and Ethics (CILE)
summary: A research centre for Islamic applied ethics in Hamad Bin Khalifa University's College of Islamic Studies in Doha, founded in 2012 and headed by Mohammed Ghaly. It runs research seminars and winter schools, supports HBKU's MA in Applied Islamic Ethics, and hosted the 2024 World Congress of Bioethics. Its AI work includes a 2024 winter school on AI and religion with Cambridge's Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence, the September 2025 conference 'AI Ethics: The Convergence of Technology and Diverse Moral Traditions', a November 2025 lecture on AI weapons and Islamic war ethics, and a funded project building IslamGPT, a language model for Arabic Islamic sources.
why_it_matters: It is the strongest institutional base found for Islamic ethics of AI, with scholars already working on human uniqueness, moral accountability (taklif) and the values built into AI instructions. It could supply maqasid-based frameworks for alignment targets and AI red lines to a field that rarely consults Islamic thought, and connect that field to Muslim-majority publics.

key_work.title: Virtual Winter School on AI, religion and ethics, with the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence
Conference 'AI Ethics: The Convergence of Technology and Diverse Moral Traditions' (with HBKU)
Public lecture 'AI Weapons and the Future of War Ethics'
IslamGPT 1.0: an LLM for Arabic sources in Islamic studies (QRDI grant, 2024–27)

people: Mohammed Ghaly (Head of CILE; Professor of Islam and Biomedical Ethics)
Mutaz Al-Khatib (Programme Director and Associate Professor of Methodology and Ethics, College of Islamic Studies)
Samer Rashwani (Senior Researcher and Lecturer in Scriptural Ethics)
funding: Part of Hamad Bin Khalifa University (Qatar Foundation). The IslamGPT project has a Qatar Research, Development and Innovation Academic Research Grant (April 2024 to April 2027).
status_evidence: 1 Oct 2026: call for papers for a research seminar on economic cosmologies and ethics. The most recent AI-specific activity found was a public lecture on AI weapons on 11 Nov 2025.
engage: Research Fellow vacancies (announced 27 Sep 2026)
Online winter schools held alongside research seminars (e.g. 22–24 Sep 2026)
Calls for papers for research seminars
HBKU MA in Applied Islamic Ethics for the Contemporary World
caveats: AI is one theme among many (bioethics, war ethics, economics, education). Its AI work is a series of events plus one tool-building project, not a standing AI-ethics programme. IslamGPT is AI applied to Islamic studies, not work on making AI go well. The framing is human dignity and ethics, with no catastrophic-risk lens.
tag_notes: Home: Islamic jurisprudence and ethics (maqasid, taklif) is its method, so religion/rel_islamic_jewish, the taxonomy's own example; philosophy is secondary for applied ethics and bioethics. Ring: changed from potential to adjacent, because rule E counts repeated convening as sustained and CILE has convened on AI repeatedly in 2024–25 (a winter school with LCFI in Sep 2024, an international conference in Sep 2025, an AI-weapons lecture in Nov 2025) and holds a funded AI project to 2027, all without a safety or catastrophic-risk framing (rule E3). Transfer: it brings Islamic ethical scholarship and its community into the AI-ethics conversation, so convening (rule J5). Framing is flourishing: the stated aim is AI that upholds human dignity and the insights of moral traditions. Online hub: a recurring winter school that remote applicants can join.

name: AI Christian Benchmark (The Gospel Coalition, Keller Center for Cultural Apologetics)
summary: An annual benchmark run by the Keller Center for Cultural Apologetics, the research arm of the evangelical website The Gospel Coalition, led by Michael Graham. The first edition (September 2025) put seven common questions about Christian belief to seven AI platforms. The 2026 edition, with responses collected in June 2026, scored 46 model configurations on theology, ethics (100 scenarios built on the Ten Commandments), Bible knowledge and 'attachment', meaning whether a model fosters unhealthy emotional bonds, for example by offering to pray for users. Scores combine grading by a panel of evangelical scholars with AI grading.
why_it_matters: It is a working example of a faith community writing its own evaluation of model behaviour. It shows how much model defaults differ on worldview questions, how much answers shift when religious context is added, and how widespread attachment-forming behaviour is. Its proposal of 'principled pluralism' (answering from within the tradition asked about, rather than giving a multi-faith summary) is a concrete, contestable input to debates on how model specifications should handle pluralism.

key_work.title: AI Christian Benchmark, first edition (seven questions, seven platforms)
AI Christian Benchmark 2026: theology, ethics, attachment and Bible knowledge scores
Presentation at the G20 Interfaith Forum webinar 'AI and Benchmarks'

people: Michael Graham (founder; programme director, Keller Center for Cultural Apologetics)
Peter J. Williams (scholar panel; Tyndale House, Cambridge)
Michael Kruger (scholar panel; Reformed Theological Seminary)
funding: Run within The Gospel Coalition's Keller Center; no funding specific to the benchmark is disclosed. In May 2026 the Future of Life Institute gave The Gospel Coalition $200,000 for theologically sound AI use (the Silicon Spiritualities podcast, the Keller Center Fellows retreat, conference and ministry-leader training). That grant does not name the benchmark.
status_evidence: 2026: AI Christian Benchmark 2026 published (responses collected in June 2026, 46 model configurations). 2 Jul 2026: presented at the G20 Interfaith Forum webinar 'AI and Benchmarks'.
engage: The 2026 report invites AI developers to contact the team about improving how models handle Christian theology and ethics
caveats: It grades answers against one confessional standard. Responses aligned with Reformed evangelical teaching score highest (prompts citing The Gospel Coalition's foundation documents got the top scores), including on contested ethics such as abortion and sexuality, so it measures fit with that tradition rather than neutral accuracy. Grading is partly done by AI (Gemini 3.1 Pro), and the attachment tests are described as exploratory. The Gospel Coalition's separate AI book ('The AI Apocalypse: A Survival Guide for Humanity') and podcast (Silicon Spiritualities) are not part of the benchmark.
tag_notes: Home: a benchmark built by and for an evangelical community, graded by theologians against confessional standards, so religion/rel_christian (taxonomy: faith benchmarks belong to Religion). Ring: a sustained annual evaluation programme (2025 and 2026 editions) about AI's effects on a faith community, framed around theological reliability, religious literacy and attachment rather than safety or catastrophic risk, so adjacent (rule E3). Transfer: the report's stated hope is that developers change model alignment ('principled pluralism', skill files), so into_model (rule J1), though it also advises Christians on prompting. Problems pair values with assurance because it builds evaluations (rule F, like CEFEAI); minds covers the attachment score. Quadrants It+We, as for CEFEAI (rule G). Status new: first edition in September 2025. The URL is changed from TGC's homepage to the benchmark's own site.

name: World Fellowship of Buddhists (WFB)
summary: An international federation of Buddhist organisations from all schools, founded in Colombo in 1950 and headquartered in Bangkok, with regional centres in more than 30 countries. It holds a General Conference every two years, runs Dhamma talks and ceremonies, and works with other faith bodies on peace events. Its 31st General Conference (5-6 December 2025, Vajiravudh College, Bangkok, about 300 participants), which marked its 75th anniversary, took as its theme 'Cultivating Wisdom and Well-being in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Buddhist Vision for the Future'.
why_it_matters: It can convene Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana institutions across Asia and beyond, and it has already chosen AI as a theme, so anyone looking for organised Buddhist positions on AI has a venue. So far it has produced no declaration or follow-up programme on AI, which leaves the door open to partners.

key_work.title: 31st General Conference: Cultivating Wisdom and Well-being in the Age of Artificial Intelligence

funding: Not published; its site takes donations and member payments.
status_evidence: Oct 2026: co-organised an international peace conference at UNESCO headquarters in Paris; May 2026: MOU signed for the 32nd General Conference in Japan; Dec 2025: 31st General Conference on AI.
engage: The 32nd General Conference is planned for Japan (MOU signed May 2026); the general conferences are for member regional centres.
Approach the headquarters in Bangkok (contact@wfbhq.org) about follow-up work on Buddhist perspectives on AI.
caveats: AI engagement so far is one conference. Talks covered AI ethics, mindfulness and compassionate action, but no declaration, resolutions or published proceedings on AI could be found, and HQ news from 2026 mentions no further AI work. Wikipedia still names Phan Wannamethee as president; the WFB's own office-bearers page names Phallop Thaiarry.
tag_notes: Home: a federation that speaks for and convenes Buddhist institutions is Religion, not Contemplative (B1; the taxonomy's own example for rel_buddhist). Ring: changed from roster 'adjacent' to potential under E(2), because the only AI activity is a single two-day General Conference (Dec 2025), with no declaration or follow-up found in 2026 news. Transferable method: federation-wide convening across Buddhist schools in 30+ countries, bringing the Buddhist ethics of discernment (pañña) and well-being to bear on technology. Transfer: convening, because the conference brought its own community into the AI conversation (J5). Membership body under rule I (a federation). Standpoint majority_world: led from Bangkok. The one-off Paris event does not count as a hub.

name: Toda Peace Institute
summary: An independent peace-research institute in Tokyo, founded in 1996 by Daisaku Ikeda, then president of the Soka Gakkai International lay Buddhist movement. It publishes policy briefs and runs projects on peace and conflict. Its Social Media, Technology and Peacebuilding programme, led by Lisa Schirch, tests AI-assisted deliberation platforms (Pol.is, Talk to the City, Deliberation.io, Crowdsmart) in conflict-affected and authoritarian settings, including Afghanistan, Yemen and the ECOWAS early-warning network.
why_it_matters: Most AI-for-democracy tools have been tested in stable democracies. Toda's programme gathers field evidence and process-design guidance on using them in peace processes, under authoritarian rule and in early-warning systems, a setting the AI-safety and collective-intelligence communities rarely study.

key_work.title: Interoperable Deliberative Technology project
Deliberative Technologies in Afghanistan project (research phase; outputs pending)
Policy Brief No. 306: Deliberative Technologies in Youth, Peace & Security: Promise, Practice, and the Uptake Gap (Lena Slachmuijlder)
Policy Brief No. 311: Process Design: Pathways Towards Deliberative Dialogue to Transform Conflict (Catherine Barnes)

people: Lisa Schirch (Senior Research Fellow, leads the Social Media, Technology and Peacebuilding programme)
funding: Founded by Daisaku Ikeda; its site does not publish funding sources.
status_evidence: 11 Aug 2026: published Policy Briefs No. 311 and 312 (Catherine Barnes) on process design and framing questions for deliberative dialogue; 17 Jun 2026: Policy Brief No. 306.
engage: The programme lead invites researchers who want to contribute to its policy-brief series to get in touch (via the programme page).
caveats: The programme is small: a few administrative staff plus a network of senior research fellows, several based at other institutions (Schirch is at the University of Notre Dame). Its AI work concerns deliberation tools and social media, not the safety of AI systems.
tag_notes: Home: B11 names Toda explicitly; deliberative tools used by peacebuilders in conflict settings, and religious-founded peace research, are Peace. Democracy is secondary because collective-intelligence tools are the method it imports. Ring: adjacent, unchanged, because it runs a standing programme on AI-enabled deliberation with policy briefs through 2025-26 but frames it around polarisation and inclusive peace processes, not catastrophic risk or alignment. Transfer: into_institutions (J3), because its output is process designs for peace processes, early-warning networks and civic consultation. Framing structural: polarisation and digital conflict read as erosion of dialogue. Standpoint neither: Japan is coded Neither in v1 (O), even though the projects centre on Afghanistan, Yemen and West Africa.

name: Shalom Hartman Institute
summary: A pluralist Jewish research and education institute in Jerusalem, with a North American branch, founded by Rabbi David Hartman. It runs seven centres, including the Kogod Research Center for Contemporary Jewish Thought, plus leadership and rabbinic training and two high schools. Its AI output is occasional: a 2024 online panel on AI, Jewish ethics and the future of humanity (with Oren Etzioni, Ellen P. Goodman, Orly Lobel and DZ Kalman), a 2025 piece by Yehuda Kurtzer and DZ Kalman, 'Staying Human in the Age of AI', and a May 2026 essay by Tomer Persico.
why_it_matters: Persico's essay makes an argument the AI field seldom hears: if human worth rests on intelligence, nothing stops AI claiming greater dignity, so dignity needs another ground. Through its leadership programmes the institute reaches rabbis and Jewish community leaders, but it has no AI programme yet.

key_work.title: Artificial Intelligence, Jewish Ethics, and the Future of Humanity (online panel)
Staying Human in the Age of AI (Yehuda Kurtzer and DZ Kalman)
What the Pope Is Telling Us (Tomer Persico)

people: Yehuda Kurtzer (President, Shalom Hartman Institute of North America)
DZ Kalman (scholar; writes on Judaism and technology)
funding: Donor-funded (giving society and annual fundraising); budget not published on its site.
status_evidence: May 2026: published Tomer Persico's essay on human dignity and AI, 'What the Pope Is Telling Us'.
engage: No AI programme: an opening for partners who want pluralist Jewish thought on AI and human dignity, through the Kogod Research Center or its North American leadership programmes.
caveats: The AI 'topic' page lists only a handful of items over 2023-26. They are commentary, not a research line or programme. Staff numbers are inferred from its seven centres and two schools, not from a published figure.
tag_notes: Home: Religion, because Jewish thought and rabbinic leadership education produce its AI output; the sub-tradition is Jewish thought. Ring: changed from roster 'adjacent' to potential under E(2), because its AI items are sporadic (a 2023 transcript, two 2024 events, a 2025 piece, a 2026 essay) and there is no standing programme. Transferable method: pluralist Jewish philosophy, and leadership education for rabbis and community leaders, including arguments for human dignity that do not rest on intelligence. Transfer: convening (J5), because its essays and events bring its own community into the AI conversation. MISFIT: Israel lies in the Middle East, but coding it Majority World would misrepresent a high-income country, so standpoint is coded neither by analogy with the v1 East Asia exception; region is mena by headquarters.

name: Central Conference of American Rabbis (CCAR)
summary: The professional association of Reform rabbis, founded in 1889 by Isaac Mayer Wise, with more than 2,200 members. It issues responsa (formal rulings in Jewish law), publishes through CCAR Press and the CCAR Journal, and runs continuing education and an ethics code for its members. Its AI work so far: Responsum 5784.2 on AI and authorship, a Fall 2025 journal issue 'AI and the Rabbinate', a December 2025 book, and an event series with Sinai and Synapses on AI, personhood and the soul.
why_it_matters: It issues working norms for AI use to a large clergy body. The responsum says that presenting AI-generated work as one's own is deception and requires disclosure, an example of a profession setting honesty norms for AI use. It is also the main channel through which FLI-funded Sinai and Synapses educates Reform rabbis about AI.

key_work.title: Responsum 5784.2: Artificial Intelligence and Authorship
CCAR Journal: The Reform Jewish Quarterly, Fall 2025 'AI and the Rabbinate' (guest-edited by Geoffrey A. Mitelman and Sara Tillinger Wolkenfeld)
Striving to Be Human: Jewish Perspectives on Twenty-First-Century Challenges (CCAR Press; eds. Leah Cohen Tenenbaum and Douglas Kohn; part on AI and robotics)
Sinai and Synapses series: 'Can AI Develop a N'shamah?', 'When Machines Seem Human: Rethinking Personhood in the Age of AI'

people: Geoffrey Mitelman (co-editor of the AI journal issue; founding director of Sinai and Synapses)
funding: A membership body; its budget is not published. Its AI series partner, Sinai and Synapses, received $100,000 from FLI in 2026 for a Reform Jewish project to inform rabbis about AI.
status_evidence: Dec 2025: CCAR Press published 'Striving to Be Human'; 24 Dec 2025: Sinai and Synapses introduced the CCAR Journal's special issue on Judaism and AI.
engage: Continuing Rabbinic Education and the Sinai and Synapses AI series, open mainly to member rabbis.
caveats: Most AI programming runs through Sinai and Synapses; FLI's 2026 grant went to Sinai and Synapses, not to the CCAR. Several event pages sit behind a member login, so the dates of the AI series could not be confirmed. 'Scale' counts members, not staff.
tag_notes: Home: Religion; a denominational professional body goes with its constituency (H3), and its AI outputs are responsa and Jewish textual interpretation. Ring: adjacent, unchanged, because it has a sustained 2024-25 line (responsum, journal issue, book, repeated events) framed around authorship, personhood and being human, not catastrophic risk. Transfer: convening (J5), because the main purpose is to inform and guide its own rabbis. The responsum is a religious ruling, hence role 'standards'. ai_status is secondary because of the repeated events on AI personhood and soul. Membership body under rule I.

name: ADL Center for Technology & Society (CTS)
summary: The technology research and advocacy centre of the Anti-Defamation League. It researches online antisemitism and hate, rates platforms, and takes its findings to social media, gaming and AI companies. On AI it red-teams models: 17 open-weight LLMs on antisemitic and dangerous prompts (December 2025), video generators such as Veo 3 and Sora (October 2025), and four chatbots in Persian against English (July 2026). It also publishes the ADL AI Index (beta), which scores LLMs on detecting and countering antisemitic and extremist narratives.
why_it_matters: It runs independent misuse evaluations of frontier and open-weight models, drawing on decades of hate monitoring. Findings such as weaker safeguards in Persian than in English, and open models with no refusals on antisemitic conspiracy prompts, are concrete data on multilingual safety and guardrail gaps that safety evaluators can use.

key_work.title: The Safety Divide: Open-Source AI Models Fall Short on Guardrails for Antisemitic, Dangerous Content
Innovative AI Video Generators Produce Antisemitic, Hateful and Violent Outputs
Lost in Translation: How AI Chatbots Fail Persian Speakers on Antisemitism
ADL AI Index (beta)

funding: Part of the ADL, a donor-funded nonprofit; the centre's own budget is not published.
status_evidence: 8 Jul 2026: published 'Lost in Translation', comparing Persian and English answers from ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Grok (800 responses).
caveats: The ADL's definitions of antisemitism, broadened since October 2023 to cover some anti-Zionist speech, are contested, and critics say they affect its research credibility, so evaluation criteria deserve scrutiny. The AI Index (launched 28 January 2026) is labelled beta. The centre's current leadership is not named on its page. It was launched in Silicon Valley in 2017 under its first director, Brittan Heller.
tag_notes: Home: Law, which the Religion boundary names for the ADL; its method is civil-society auditing and hate monitoring, so the sub-tradition is STS (civil-society algorithmic auditing). Ring: adjacent, unchanged, because it publishes sustained model evaluations in 2025-26, framed around hate, antisemitism and dangerous-content guardrails, not catastrophic risk or alignment. Transfer: protecting (J4); like Common Sense Media's ratings, its evaluations exist to protect the communities it serves from AI outputs, though the evaluations target model behaviour. Problems pair assurance with the substantive problem (F): hate and bias (justice), plus extremist misuse such as weapons prompts (security). It is a unit inside the ADL, so org type is programme (A1, I).

name: Lausanne Movement
summary: A global network of evangelical leaders, begun in 1974 when Billy Graham convened the International Congress on World Evangelization in Lausanne. It works through 28 issue networks and 12 regional networks and publishes reports, the Lausanne Global Analysis and podcasts. Its AI content includes a State of the Great Commission report chapter on AI, an October/November 2025 Global Analysis issue on AI (including Quintin McGrath's 'AI Ethical Framework') and podcast episodes, mostly about using AI for ministry, evangelism and Bible translation.
why_it_matters: It reaches evangelical leaders worldwide, and its material shows how a very large religious constituency currently thinks about AI: mainly as a tool for mission. Its report chapter says outright that AI is not an existential threat. In 2026 FLI gave it $50,000 to engage evangelical leaders in critical discussion of AI development, so this framing may shift.

key_work.title: AI Ethical Framework (Quintin McGrath, Lausanne Global Analysis)
State of the Great Commission report: Artificial Intelligence (Angela Kim, Sharoon Sarfraz, Jason Thacker, Dan Whitenack)
FLI-funded project engaging evangelical leadership on AI development

people: Matthew Niermann (principal investigator, FLI-funded AI project)
funding: $50,000 from FLI (2026), through its RFP on religious projects tackling the challenges of the AGI race; otherwise donor-funded, with figures not published on its site.
status_evidence: May 2026: FLI grant decisions announced, including $50,000 to Lausanne; 2026: published 'Missional Innovation: Formation Architecture for a Disrupted World' (Samuel E. Chiang).
engage: Issue networks (28) and regional networks (12) for Christian leaders.
caveats: Most of its AI content is about adopting AI for evangelism and discipleship, not about AI risk; the report chapter explicitly says AI does not pose an existential threat. The FLI-funded project could move it towards bridge if it produces risk-framed work. The site names no headquarters.
tag_notes: Home: Religion; an evangelical network speaking to its own tradition, with AI content grounded in biblical ethics and missiology. Ring: adjacent, unchanged, because it has a sustained 2024-26 publication line on AI framed around human dignity and mission, and the chapter rejects the existential-risk framing; the 2026 FLI grant from an AGI-race RFP is noted but has not yet produced risk-framed output (E3). Transfer: convening (J5), because its outputs inform and convene evangelical leaders. Framing flourishing: AI should serve 'shalom and human flourishing'. Region global: a polycentric network with no stated headquarters (O).

name: Ethics & Religious Liberty Commission of the Southern Baptist Convention (ERLC)
summary: The public-policy and ethics agency of the Southern Baptist Convention, the largest US Protestant denomination. Founded in 1947 as the Social Service Commission, it is based in Nashville with an office in Washington, DC. In 2019 it led 'Artificial Intelligence: An Evangelical Statement of Principles', an affirm-and-deny statement in 12 articles covering human dignity, work, data, bias, war and public policy; the SBC's 2023 resolution on AI cites it.
why_it_matters: It wrote the reference evangelical statement on AI and lobbies in Washington for a large, politically active constituency, so it shapes how many US evangelicals and their legislators approach AI ethics and policy.

key_work.title: Artificial Intelligence: An Evangelical Statement of Principles
The Work of Our Hands: Christian Ministry in the Age of Artificial Intelligence (practical guide for churches, 12 scenarios)

people: Jason Thacker (Senior Fellow; led its AI work; author of 'The Age of AI')
RaShan Frost (Director of Research and Senior Fellow; contributed to the 2025 AI ministry guide)
funding: Southern Baptist Convention Cooperative Program.
status_evidence: Jun 2026: Evan Lenow took office as president (elected April 2026); the ERLC site's RSS feed was last updated 2 October 2026.
caveats: The ERLC site blocks automated access, so the statement could not be re-read in this pass. Its 2024-26 AI work includes a September 2025 church guide, 'The Work of Our Hands', and an AI podcast series, known from Baptist Press coverage. Leadership changed in 2025-26 (Leatherwood stepped down on 31 July 2025, followed by acting and interim presidents, then Lenow), and SBC messengers have repeatedly debated abolishing the agency. Whether AI remains a priority under the new president is unknown. Thacker also co-wrote Lausanne's AI report chapter.
tag_notes: Home: Religion, because its AI output is Baptist theological ethics (imago Dei) in a denominational statement. Ring: adjacent, kept from the roster under E, because its AI work is a principles statement plus a senior fellow writing on AI, framed around dignity rather than catastrophic risk; 2024-26 continuity could not be verified because the site blocks automated access, which is why confidence is medium. Transfer: convening (J5), because the statement was written mainly to guide evangelicals, though its public-policy articles and DC office touch institutions. It is a permanent SBC entity with its own board, so it is coded nonprofit rather than programme (I).

name: Theos
summary: Theos is a London Christian think tank, part of the British and Foreign Bible Society, that researches religion's place in society and politics and runs public events and The Sacred podcast. Its AI work is led by senior researcher Nathan Mladin. It includes reports on privacy (Data and Dignity, 2023) and digital afterlives (AI and the Afterlife, 2024), essays on transhumanism and 'techno-nihilism' (2025-26), and 2026 twentieth-anniversary events on being human in the age of AI.
why_it_matters: It brings a theological account of the human person to AI. It asks what picture of humanity AI products and AI-risk talk take for granted, and it reframes the 'existential' threat as an erosion of human self-understanding. It also has the UK policy contacts and public platforms to carry that view into national debate.

key_work.title: AI and the Afterlife: From Digital Mourning to Mind Uploading
Data and Dignity: Why Privacy Matters in the Digital Age
Technonihilism and the human stakes of AI (Nathan Mladin essay)
AI & The Future of Being Human (live recording of The Sacred podcast with Jamie Bartlett)

people: Nathan Mladin (Senior Researcher, AI and technology)
funding: Core funding from the British and Foreign Bible Society (charity 232759), plus individual donors, charitable trusts (including the William Leech Research Fellowships and the Sainsbury Family Charitable Trusts) and sponsorship. It says it takes no money from government, corporations or denominations except as consultancy clients.
status_evidence: Jul 2026: Theos 20 event 'Art, creativity and what it means to be human in the age of AI' at the National Gallery. Mar 2026: Mladin essay on techno-nihilism. Aug 2026: report 'Big Questions, Real-World Skills'.
engage: Public events in London, including the 2026 Theos 20 anniversary series (e.g. 'The Return of the Common Good', 22 October 2026)
Live recordings of The Sacred podcast (AI & The Future of Being Human, 2026)
Newsletter and donations via theosthinktank.co.uk
caveats: AI is one strand among many (motherhood, cathedrals, religious education, investment). Most of the AI output comes from one researcher, and the last AI report was in 2024; since then it has been essays and events. Mladin explicitly reframes x-risk talk as 'secular apocalyptic literature', so the work engages AI safety critically rather than joining it. The live podcast's date differs between the event page (URL dated 30 July 2026) and the homepage (8 September 2026).
tag_notes: Home: a Christian think tank (part of the Bible Society) whose AI output is theological anthropology, so religion / rel_christian (H1, B1). Ring: kept adjacent: it has a sustained AI publication and events line in 2023-26, about meaning, dignity and digital afterlives, and it reframes rather than adopts the x-risk framing (E3). Transfer: its reports, essays, podcast and events bring its Christian and public audiences into the AI conversation, so convening (J5); the 2023 joint letter to the Science Secretary is a one-off. Framing: structural, from Mladin's claim that the real threat is gradual 'techno-nihilism', a shrinking view of the human (L). Org type: nonprofit, not programme, because Theos has had its own identity since 2006 despite sitting within the Bible Society (I).

name: Consortium for Evaluating Faith and Ethics in AI (CEFEAI)
summary: CEFEAI (also styled CEFE-AI) is a consortium of four faith-based US universities (Baylor, Brigham Young, Notre Dame and Yeshiva), announced in May 2026 at the Athens Summit on AI Ethics, that builds open benchmarks of how large language models handle religion. Its AllFaith Benchmark has two released parts. Conversion Bias tests whether models push users towards or away from 14 traditions (20 models, May 2026). Religious Representation measures how often models raise religious perspectives on ordinary ethics and life questions, using items rated in a survey of 1,125 Americans (27 models, May 2026). Datasets and code are MIT-licensed on GitHub, with a public leaderboard.
why_it_matters: Here religious academia does pluralistic-alignment evaluation in the same technical idiom as mainstream evals, turning 'aligned to whose values?' into reproducible tests with confidence intervals. Its charter criteria (faith-faithful, pluralism-aware, resistant to views over-represented in training data, child-appropriate, multilingual) amount to a draft spec for faith-sensitive model behaviour.

key_work.title: AllFaith Benchmark: Conversion Bias (v2, 2Q26)
AllFaith Benchmark: Religious Representation (v1, 2Q26)
CEFEAI Charter

people: David Wingate (Academic lead; Professor of Computer Science, Brigham Young University)
Paul Martens (Baylor University, associate professor of ethics)
status_evidence: May 2026: consortium announced at the Athens Summit on AI Ethics (keynote by Elder Gerrit W. Gong); AllFaith Conversion Bias v2 and Religious Representation v1 released, with 20- and 27-model leaderboards; covered by BYU, Baylor and Deseret News. Jul 2026: G20 Interfaith Forum blog post on Wingate's benchmark work.
engage: Use, audit or contribute to the open AllFaith Benchmark datasets and code on GitHub (MIT licence)
Faith traditions, academic institutions, civil-society partners and AI developers can ask to join by emailing admin@cefeai.org; members may propose evaluations and supply data
caveats: Young: publicly launched in May 2026. Its own site loads content by script and names no staff, governance or funders; member universities and researchers are named in BYU and Baylor press releases. The launch was announced by Elder Gerrit W. Gong, a senior leader of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, and the work is BYU-led, which is worth noting for perceived neutrality. The GitHub organisation has no public members, and the repositories were last updated in May 2026. The member list is US and Abrahamic so far, although the charter aims to expand to global traditions. Its 'faith-faithful' criterion may conflict with other alignment targets, such as neutrality towards non-believers.
tag_notes: Home: multi-faith evaluation built by Baptist, Latter-day Saint, Catholic and Jewish universities, so religion / rel_interfaith (named in that sub-tradition's definition; H2, since ML evaluation is not a sector). Ring: kept bridge: rooted in religious academia, with a standing benchmark programme framed as making AI 'reflect faith, ethics, and human flourishing', an alignment-target framing (E3). Transfer: evaluations aimed at model behaviour, run with AI developers, so into_model (J1). Problems pair values with assurance, as rule F requires for CEFEAI; justice reflects the pluralism and bias focus. Quadrants It+We, per worked rule G. Framing flourishing, from the charter's purpose statement (L), although the benchmarks measure bias. Org type: network, a coalition of universities rather than a single centre (I).

name: Cambridge Interfaith Programme (CIP)
summary: CIP is a programme in the University of Cambridge's Faculty of Divinity, founded in 2002, that researches relations between Judaism, Christianity and Islam and practises Scriptural Reasoning. It runs summer schools, a research forum, podcasts, and projects on climate, antisemitism and Islamophobia, and lunar calendars. Its AI work is one strand by deputy director Daniel Weiss with Sciences Po cognitive scientist Darren Frey: a 2025 Harvard Data Science Review article arguing that empathetic chatbots create 'one-person dialogues', a Harvard Divinity Bulletin essay setting AI concerns against religious prohibitions on giving non-human things godlike status, and a Faith & AI session at Cambridge's Alumni Festival in September 2026.
why_it_matters: Its practice of structured dialogue across deep religious difference is a worked method for the real two-sided conversation that chatbots imitate but cannot provide. The 'one-person dialogue' argument names a harm to people's capacity for dialogue that falls between the AI-safety and companion-AI debates.

key_work.title: One Person Dialogues: Concerns About LLM-Human Interactions (Frey and Weiss, Harvard Data Science Review)
Thinking together about faith & AI: Daniel Weiss and Darren Frey (Alumni Festival workshop)
Scriptural Reasoning (core practice and resources)

people: Esra Özyürek (Academic Director; Sultan Qaboos Chair in Abrahamic Faiths and Shared Values)
Daniel Weiss (Deputy Director; leads the AI strand)
Iona Hine (Programme Manager, Partnerships and Engagement)
funding: Endowed posts include the Sultan Qaboos Chair in Abrahamic Faiths and Shared Values and a Polonsky–Coexist lectureship; project funding is not itemised on its site.
