Academic summer schools on interfaith relations (check the site for current dates)
Outreach to the deputy director's AI strand for collaboration on dialogue and LLMs
caveats: Ring changed from the discovery draft's bridge to potential. AI is not among CIP's listed research projects, and its AI work rests on one academic's paired publications and a single alumni-festival session. The draft's claim that Weiss and Frey were discussants at CSER's 2026 summer programme ('Historical Dimensions of AI, Power & Catastrophic Risk') could not be confirmed: CSER's programme page names only Yuval Noah Harari and unnamed Cambridge colleagues.
tag_notes: Home: a Divinity Faculty programme on Jewish, Christian and Muslim relations and Scriptural Reasoning, so religion / rel_interfaith (B1, multi-faith). Ring: changed from bridge to potential: there is no standing AI programme, only one article pair (2025) and one alumni session (2026), and no verified x-risk programme (E2). Transferable method: Scriptural Reasoning and structured interreligious dialogue, practices for real dialogue across deep difference that apply to pluralistic alignment and to protecting human dialogical capacity from 'one-person dialogues'. Transfer: its existing AI work brings divinity and alumni audiences into the AI conversation, so convening (J5), not none_yet. Framing structural: slow erosion of dialogical capacity and community relations (L). Engagement 'partner' because it has no AI programme (O).

name: AI Faith & Civil Society Commission (AIFCS)
summary: AIFCS is a commission of senior UK faith and civil-society figures, with commissioners from several faiths, Humanists UK and Big Brother Watch. It was convened by the Abu Dhabi Forum for Peace with Google in October 2023, the week before the Bletchley AI Safety Summit, and supported by the Good Faith Partnership. It sent an open letter to the UK Science Secretary, held an inaugural summit (December 2023), parliamentary roundtables on algorithmic bias and the EU AI Act, an AI APPG session on AI and spiritual life, and a Paris AI Action Summit fringe event. In March 2025 it published recommendations to the UK government.
why_it_matters: It was one of the first attempts to bring organised faith and civil-society voices into the AI Safety Summit process. Its six areas (privacy and freedom, dignity of work, moral autonomy, authentic relationships, cognition and creativity, truth and reality) set out what these communities see as at stake. Its apparent lapse since early 2025 leaves that UK convening role open.

key_work.title: Open letter to the UK Secretary of State for Science, Innovation and Technology ahead of the AI Safety Summit
AI APPG event and report: The Impact of AI on Our Spiritual and Cultural Lives
Paris AI Action Summit fringe event: Ethics in Action
The AIFCS Commissioners' Recommendations to the UK Government

Kate Devlin (Commissioner; Humanists UK, King's College London)
Harris Bor (Commissioner; London School of Jewish Studies)
funding: Convened by the Abu Dhabi Forum for Peace and hosted at its first meeting by Google; it names Google and the Good Faith Partnership as supporters. No budget figures are published.
status_evidence: Mar 2025: recommendations to the UK government (last substantive post). Feb 2025: last listed event (Paris fringe). Oct 2025: obituary of commissioner Kishan Manocha.

caveats: Probably dormant. The last event listed was February 2025 and the last substantive news was March 2025, apart from an October 2025 obituary. The site footer reads '© 2024'. It is tagged dormant under the lapsed-site clause even though it technically had activity in 2025. Its ties to the Abu Dhabi Forum for Peace (a UAE-government-linked body) and to Google are worth noting for independence. Sajid Javid chaired the October 2023 meeting; no standing chair is named.
tag_notes: Home: a multi-faith commission speaking for faith communities, so religion / rel_interfaith (B1); law is secondary because civil-liberties commissioners (Big Brother Watch, Humanists UK) shape its rights-based recommendations. Ring: kept bridge: formed to feed the 2023 AI Safety Summit, with a mission to 'harness the opportunities of AI for human flourishing' ('AI going well') and repeated convening in 2023-25 (E3); borderline with adjacent because its content is rights and present harms. Transfer: its main output is recommendations and roundtables aimed at UK government policy, so into_institutions (J3). Framing flourishing, from its mission statement (L). Status dormant, as no activity has been posted since early 2025 (O).

name: Christians for Impact (Effective Altruism for Christians)
summary: Christians for Impact is a careers-advice charity, registered in England and Wales in 2021 and in the US, that also runs Effective Altruism for Christians; it applies EA-style cause prioritisation within a Christian framework. It offers free one-to-one career advice, problem profiles, a job board and a podcast, and its leaders co-wrote the book All the Lives You Can Change (Eerdmans, 2026). In 2025 it published an AI Risk report by Vesa Hautala covering misalignment, misuse and existential risk and recommending careers in technical safety and governance. Its annual conferences (Washington DC, 13-15 November 2026; London, 27-29 November 2026) list catastrophic risks, including from AI, among their topics.
why_it_matters: It is one of very few faith bodies that take AI x-risk seriously and steer people into the field. It makes the case through stewardship, love and hope rather than secular longtermism, and so widens who sees AI safety as their vocation.

key_work.title: AI Risk: Full Report (Vesa Hautala)
All the Lives You Can Change (book by Dominic Roser, J. D. Bauman and David Zhang; Eerdmans)
Christians for Impact 2026 London Conference
Christians for Impact 2026 DC Conference

hq: London, United Kingdom (also Christians for Impact USA Inc., Delaware)

status_evidence: Nov 2026: DC (13-15 Nov) and London (27-29 Nov) conferences announced, with catastrophic risks including AI among the topics. Jul 2026: book launch event for All the Lives You Can Change (published by Eerdmans, April 2026). Jul 2025: AI Risk report last updated.

caveats: It is an EA-aligned careers service rather than a research body: AI is one of several cause areas (alongside poverty, missions, pandemics, climate, nuclear war and animal welfare), and the AI report is a synthesis of mainstream AI-safety arguments with a Christian framing. The UK charity was registered in August 2021; the Effective Altruism for Christians community may predate it. Contact is through a Gmail address and there is no office address, which suggests a small, distributed team.
tag_notes: Home: an ecumenical Christian body that speaks to Christians about vocation, so religion / rel_christian (H3, B1); EA cause prioritisation is the AI-safety community's own toolkit, so no secondary tradition is added. Ring: kept bridge: rooted in a Christian community, with a sustained explicit AI-risk line (2025 report plus a recurring conference track on catastrophic risk) (E3). Transfer: convening (J5): it informs and advises its Christian community, including routes into AI-safety careers; into_builders was considered but rejected, since most of its audience are not yet people who build or govern AI. Primary problem 'people' because it widens who does AI-safety work (F). Region: uk_ireland, by its earlier legal base (the 2021 England and Wales charity), though it is dual-registered in the US (O).

name: Network for Religious and Traditional Peacemakers (Peacemakers Network)
summary: The Peacemakers Network is a global network founded in 2013, in response to the UN Secretary-General's 2012 report on mediation, that links religious and traditional peacemakers to formal mediation and peace processes. Its secretariat is hosted by Finn Church Aid in Helsinki. It runs training, mediation support, small grants and platforms such as a Faith and Traditional Mediators platform for the Horn of Africa (2026). AI has appeared only occasionally: a 2024 UNGA side event on faith, ethics and AI, a 2026 learning lab on AI and hate speech, and its 2026-2030 strategy, which names AI, drones and surveillance as tools of war and repression.
why_it_matters: It practises insider mediation and track-two dialogue with religious and traditional actors in conflict zones. These methods bear on de-escalating AI races and on bringing faith constituencies into AI governance. It already convenes UN and faith actors (Religions for Peace, the World Council of Churches, UN disarmament staff) who would need to be part of any such process.

Outreach to the Helsinki secretariat to propose AI work under the 2026-2030 strategy's advocacy line on ethical use of emerging technologies
caveats: Its AI engagement is occasional events and strategy language, not a programme. The AI items so far concern present harms (autonomous weapons, surveillance, hate speech) rather than frontier-AI races. The link to AI-race de-escalation is the profiler's inference about how its methods could transfer.

Transferable method: insider mediation and track-two dialogue with religious and traditional actors, applicable to AI-race de-escalation, US-China confidence-building and bringing faith constituencies into AI governance. Transfer: its AI events bring its own network of peacemakers into the AI conversation, so convening (J5), not none_yet. Framing present_harms: AI as a tool of warfare, repression and hate speech (L). Standpoint neither, because the secretariat is hosted in Helsinki by a Northern host, although about a third of members are African-headquartered (O).

name: Global Ethic Foundation (Stiftung Weltethos)
summary: The Global Ethic Foundation is a Tübingen foundation set up in 1995 by theologian Hans Küng to carry forward the Declaration Toward a Global Ethic, adopted by the 1993 Parliament of the World's Religions: a minimal set of ethical principles shared across traditions. It runs Weltethos schools, councils of religions, youth and dialogue programmes and a touring exhibition, and since 2012 has hosted the Weltethos-Institut at the University of Tübingen. Its AI engagement is a few public events: a June 2024 panel, 'Herausforderung KI: zwischen Algorithmus und Ethos', with Peter G. Kirchschläger and Milad Karimi, and a November 2025 talk on deepfakes and trust.
why_it_matters: Its core method is finding an ethic that many religious and cultural traditions can endorse without agreeing on doctrine. That is a worked precedent for alignment's pluralistic 'aligned to whose values?' problem. Its network of schools and interfaith councils could also carry AI-ethics education to the public.

key_work.title: Declaration Toward a Global Ethic (Parliament of the World's Religions)
Herausforderung KI: zwischen Algorithmus und Ethos (panel with Cyber Valley, Milad Karimi and Peter G. Kirchschläger)

status_evidence: Sep 2026: launched a Jewish-Muslim dialogue initiative against prejudice. Nov 2025: public talk on AI, deepfakes and trust.

Weltethos school programme and workshops
Outreach for AI-ethics work built on the Global Ethic method
caveats: Its AI engagement is light: three public events in 2024-25, with no AI project or publication. Its work is mostly in German and focused on south-west Germany. The relevance to alignment rests on the transferable method, not on any current AI work.
tag_notes: Home: an interreligious body built on a cross-faith ethical declaration, running councils of religions and interfaith education, so religion / rel_interfaith (B1), with philosophy secondary for its comparative-ethics method. Ring: kept potential: its AI activity is a few public events (2024, 2025) with no standing programme (E2). Transferable method: deriving a minimal shared ethic that diverse religious and cultural traditions can endorse, a precedent for pluralistic value specification in alignment. Transfer: its AI events bring its own public and interfaith constituency into the AI conversation, so convening (J5), not none_yet. Framing structural: its AI talks centre on eroding trust, dignity and social cohesion (L).

name: Interfaith Center on Corporate Responsibility (ICCR), with the Investor Alliance for Human Rights
summary: A New York coalition of faith-based and values-driven institutional investors (religious orders, denominational pension funds, foundations, asset managers) that files shareholder proposals and engages companies on social and human-rights issues. Its Digital Rights and AI Accountability work, run with its Investor Alliance for Human Rights, presses technology companies to adopt human-rights due diligence and board oversight of AI, publishes investor briefings, and comments on AI policy to the US government, the EU and the UN Human Rights Council.
why_it_matters: It uses a lever the AI-safety field has barely touched: shareholder resolutions and investor engagement at Alphabet, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft asking for board-level AI oversight and human-rights due diligence. Its June 2026 briefing on AI in military targeting shows investor channels can also reach defence AI.

AI in the Kill Chain: The Risk of AI-Enabled Warfare and What Investors Need to Know

name: Abu Dhabi Forum for Peace (Forum for Promoting Peace in Muslim Societies)
summary: An Abu Dhabi forum of Muslim scholars, presided over by the Mauritanian jurist Shaykh Abdallah bin Bayyah, that promotes peace and interfaith cooperation from Islamic jurisprudence. On AI it brought Muslim leadership into the Vatican-led Rome Call for AI Ethics (January 2023), convened the faith and civil-society meeting a week before the 2023 Bletchley AI Safety Summit that set up the AI Faith & Civil Society Commission, and co-organised the multi-faith 'AI Ethics for Peace' signing in Hiroshima (July 2024).
why_it_matters: It is the main Islamic convener in the interreligious AI-ethics process and has a link to the AI-safety summit track. It will co-organise Religions for Peace's December 2027 World Assembly, which lists AI and autonomous weapons as a central objective.

name: Religions for Peace (RfP), incl. Religions for Peace Japan (WCRP Japan)
summary: A multi-religious coalition founded in 1970, made up of national interreligious councils in close to 100 countries, with an international secretariat in New York and offices in Japan, Kenya, Peru and the UK. Its AI engagement so far is light: its Japan chapter co-organised the July 2024 Hiroshima event where leaders of eleven religions signed the Rome Call for AI Ethics, its Secretary General opened a 2024 UN General Assembly side event on faith, ethics and AI, and its 11th World Assembly (Abu Dhabi, December 2027) names AI and autonomous weapons as a central objective.
why_it_matters: Its council network is ready-made infrastructure for carrying AI questions into local faith communities, much of it in the Majority World, and its disarmament advocacy maps onto autonomous weapons. The 2027 World Assembly is a concrete moment for AI-safety and int/a people to engage.

key_work.title: AI Ethics for Peace, Hiroshima (co-organised by Religions for Peace Japan)
Faith, Ethics and AI: Shaping a Future for Global Peace (UNGA side event, opened by the Secretary General)
11th World Assembly announced: 'An Alliance of Virtue for Sacred Flourishing', with AI and autonomous weapons as a central objective
What Faith & Belief have to say about Artificial Intelligence (guest article)

people: Deepika Singh (Deputy Secretary General and Director of Programmes)
status_evidence: Aug 2026: announced its 11th World Assembly (Abu Dhabi, 6-10 Dec 2027) with AI and autonomous weapons among its central objectives; Sep 2026: WCRP Japan announced an interfaith youth summit for October 2026
engage: Door to open: national interreligious councils in about 100 countries, and preparations for the December 2027 World Assembly in Abu Dhabi
caveats: Ring lowered from the roster's adjacent to potential: the global body has no standing AI programme; the Hiroshima event was run with its Japan chapter, and the AI-focused Assembly is still being planned. It should move to adjacent if the 2027 Assembly produces AI commitments. The 2021 AI article on its site is by a guest author from the Religious Freedom & Business Foundation. Recent WCRP Japan news showed no AI items.
tag_notes: Home religion (B1), sub rel_interfaith: a multi-religious coalition speaking for faith communities; peace secondary for its peace and disarmament advocacy. Ring potential (E2), changed from adjacent: AI activity in 2024-26 is one co-organised event, one panel opening and a planned 2027 Assembly, not a standing programme. Transferable method: a federated network of national interreligious councils that can carry norms and dialogue into local faith communities, plus disarmament advocacy relevant to autonomous weapons. Transfer convening (J5), not none_yet, because it has done some AI convening. Framing structural (L): the Assembly speaks of protecting human dignity against technological threats. Region by New York secretariat (O).

name: International Islamic Fiqh Academy (IIFA)
summary: The juristic body of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), established in 1981 and based in Jeddah, whose members are jurists and scholars from across the Muslim world. At its 26th session (Doha, May 2025) it adopted Resolution No. 258, 'Artificial Intelligence: Its Rulings, Guidelines and Ethics', which holds that developing and using AI is permissible by default subject to six conditions (lawful purposes, benefit without harm, no insult to religions, protection of data and rights, no threat to security, honesty and transparency), and recommends a study of whether AI should have legal personality.
why_it_matters: It sets the reference ruling on AI for mainstream Islamic jurisprudence across OIC states, reasoning from the purposes of the law about benefit, harm and accountability. Its call to study AI legal personality is a rare opening from a religious legal body onto questions of AI moral and legal status.

key_work.title: Resolution No. 258: Artificial Intelligence: Its Rulings, Guidelines and Ethics
Scientific session 'Artificial Intelligence: Rulings, Controls and Ethics' at the 26th session (Doha)
Secretary-General chairs 'Coexistence in the Age of AI' at the Fez conference on the future of human civilisation and AI

funding: A subsidiary organ of the OIC; budget not found
status_evidence: Apr 2026: Secretary-General chaired 'Coexistence in the Age of AI' at the Fez conference (27-28 Apr); Sep 2026: division meetings and visits at Jeddah headquarters
caveats: Its rulings are normative religious guidance, not binding law. Its AI output so far is one resolution plus speeches; no sign was found by October 2026 of the recommended study on AI legal personality or the specialised symposia. The resolution's English page is dated November 2025, though the session sat in May 2025.
tag_notes: Home religion (B1), sub rel_islamic_jewish: Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh) and religious rulings. Ring adjacent (E3), kept from roster but borderline: a formal deliberative process (session debate, resolution, follow-up) plus 2026 speeches on AI, framed around permissibility, harm avoidance and ethics rather than catastrophic risk or alignment. Transfer into_institutions (J3): the resolution is a normative standard for OIC member states and Muslim institutions. Org type public (I): OIC subsidiary organ. AI legal personality is only a recommendation, so ai_status not added (F).

name: Islamic World Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (ICESCO)
summary: The OIC's specialised agency for education, science and culture, based in Rabat, with 53 member states. With Saudi Arabia's data and AI authority (SDAIA) it launched the Riyadh Charter on AI Ethics in the Islamic World at the Global AI Summit in September 2024; member states approved it in March 2025. The Charter sets seven principles (including reliability and safety, transparency, accountability and 'humanity') grounded in Islamic-world values, and in December 2025 ICESCO and SDAIA signed an agreement to implement it as a common AI-governance framework for member states. It also runs a Center of Foresight and Artificial Intelligence and many AI education, literacy and Arabic-language activities.
why_it_matters: It is the intergovernmental channel for AI norms grounded in Islamic values, built on the argument that international frameworks failed to reflect those values. It is the obvious counterpart for AI-governance dialogue that wants Muslim-majority states' buy-in beyond the UN and OECD tracks.

key_work.title: Riyadh Charter on AI Ethics in the Islamic World (presented to the IIFA's 26th session, May 2025)
ICESCO-SDAIA agreement to activate the Riyadh Charter
Director-General calls for stronger cooperation on AI governance, arguing legislation alone is not enough (international forum, Riyadh)
'Artificial Intelligence for All' initiative; third edition of the Data and AI Glossary

status_evidence: Sep 2026: Director-General argued at an international AI forum in Riyadh that legislation alone is not enough for AI governance; Sep 2026: launched the third edition of its Data and AI Glossary and explored AI cooperation with the UN
engage: AI masterclasses, trainings and conferences, mostly aimed at member-state educators, media and officials
'Artificial Intelligence for All' initiative (launched May 2026)
caveats: Most of its AI activity is education, literacy and Arabic-language work rather than safety; the Charter is principles-level and its implementation with SDAIA only began in 2025-26. Saudi state involvement (SDAIA) shapes the Charter. Outputs of its Center of Foresight and AI were not found. The Charter's 2024 announcement date comes from discovery notes; its publication page did not load in this check.
tag_notes: Home religion (H1, B1): its distinctive AI output is an ethics charter grounded in Islamic-world values; law secondary for public-interest policy work. MISFIT: an intergovernmental education and culture agency, not a religious body; Religion is the closest home for what it brings. Ring adjacent (E3): standing AI programme (Charter, implementation agreement, AI centre, trainings) with a responsible-innovation framing, not catastrophic risk. Transfer into_institutions (J3): the Charter is meant as a unified AI-governance framework for member states. Problem justice first (F): its rationale is that Islamic-world values are missing from international frameworks (plural voices). Org type public (I): OIC agency.

name: Kalam Research & Media (KRM)
summary: A Muslim theological think tank founded in Dubai in 2009 and chaired by the Libyan theologian Aref Ali Nayed, with offices in Abu Dhabi, Amman, Benghazi, Tripoli, Tunis, Cairo, Toronto and Malaysia. Its AI & Technology programme pairs its theologians and philosophers with AI researchers: it works on 'Artificial Understanding' (what it would mean for a machine to understand), applies Nayed's 'operational hermeneutics' to AI artefacts, and in 2025-26 held workshops and lectures with the University of Guelph's Centre for Advancing Responsible AI (CARE-AI).
why_it_matters: It asks conceptual questions most AI-ethics work skips, such as what machine understanding would be, from an Islamic hermeneutic tradition, and argues that responsible AI needs 'institutional wisdom' rather than compliance alone. It is one of few Islamic institutions doing conceptual rather than permissibility work on AI.

key_work.title: KRM to develop new research on Artificial Understanding (AU)
Workshop with the University of Guelph: Humanities, Artificial Intelligence, and the Future of Responsibility
Dr Nayed at the University of Guelph: Operational Hermeneutics and AI Ethics
Renewed partnership with Rose Castle Foundation and an AI and peace symposium announced for 2026

status_evidence: Feb 2026: renewed its partnership with the Rose Castle Foundation and announced an AI and peace symposium; Feb 2026: Nayed lectured on operational hermeneutics and AI ethics at Guelph; Jan 2026: Guelph humanities and AI workshop
caveats: Its dated AI outputs are mostly lectures, workshops and partnership announcements; substantive publications on Artificial Understanding were not found, and no AI items after February 2026 appeared on its site. Its chairman is also a Libyan diplomatic and political figure, which partners may weigh.
tag_notes: Home religion (B1, H3): an Islamic theology (kalam) think tank whose AI programme is staffed by its theologians; philosophy secondary for hermeneutics and philosophy of technology (C). Ring adjacent (E3): a standing AI & Technology programme with repeated workshops and partnerships in 2025-26, framed around dignity, meaning and institutional wisdom rather than catastrophic risk or alignment. Transfer convening (J5): its main effect is bringing Islamic theological and hermeneutic thought into AI-ethics dialogue with universities. 'agency' added for the Artificial Understanding line, a conceptual account of machine understanding.

name: Al-Mahdi Institute (AMI)
summary: An independent Islamic higher-education and research institute in Birmingham, founded in 1993 by Shaykh Arif Abdulhussain, specialising in Shi'i legal theory, philosophy and theology; it runs a Hawza programme linked to an MA at the University of Birmingham and publishes a series with Brill. Its AI engagement is a few events: a May 2024 research seminar on 'Islam and Artificial Intelligence' and a November 2025 international conference, 'Adaptive Faith: Technology and Religious Change in the Digital Age', held with the Catholic University of America's McLean Center and others.
why_it_matters: It practises a method relevant to AI norms: structured juristic reasoning (ijtihad, including through its International Centre for Collective Ijtihad) for deriving ethical rulings on new questions, alongside cross-faith academic partners. It is a UK Islamic academic node within reach of int/a's London community.

key_work.title: Research seminar 'Islam and Artificial Intelligence' (Mazhar Ali Bari and Biliana Popova)
Adaptive Faith: Technology and Religious Change in the Digital Age (international conference)

funding: Registered UK charity (no. 1191746); the 2025 conference listed the Tajir Trust and the Ansari Institute as partners; budget not found
status_evidence: Sep 2026: published 'Regulative Verses of the Qur'an' with Brill; Nov 2025: technology and religion conference covering AI
engage: Door to open: a Birmingham institute with cross-faith academic partners and a conference series, reachable from London
caveats: AI is a minor theme: two events in 2024-25 do not make a programme, so ring was lowered from the roster's adjacent to potential. A book chapter on AI ethics in Islamic thought by AMI scholar Ali-reza Bhojani, reported by discovery, was not verified here. Its current principal was not named on the pages checked.
tag_notes: Home religion (B1), sub rel_islamic_jewish: Shi'i legal theory and theology; philosophy secondary for Islamic philosophy. Ring potential (E2), changed from adjacent: one seminar (2024) and one conference (2025) are not a standing programme. Transferable method: collective ijtihad, structured juristic reasoning that derives ethical-legal norms for unprecedented cases, which could inform value specification and AI governance. Transfer convening (J5), not none_yet, because it has held AI events. Org type nonprofit (I): independent registered charity, not a university unit. 'values' reflects the 2024 seminar's case for Islamic epistemology in value-aligned AI.

name: The Great Simplification (Institute for the Study of Energy and Our Future, ISEOF)
summary: A weekly podcast and media platform hosted by Nate Hagens and run by ISEOF, a US 501(c)(3) founded in 2008. It covers energy, ecology, economics and human behaviour, and treats the global economy as an energy-hungry 'superorganism'. Besides the interviews it publishes Hagens's solo 'Frankly' episodes and a short course, The Human Predicament, and runs an online Hylo community.
why_it_matters: It places AI inside an energy-and-ecology account of the metacrisis, treating AI as something that speeds up material and energy throughput, and it brings AI x-risk arguments (Schmachtenberger 2023, Yampolskiy 2026) to a large collapse-aware audience that AI-safety organisations rarely reach.

key_work.title: Ep 71: Daniel Schmachtenberger, 'Artificial Intelligence and The Superorganism'
Ep 233: Roman Yampolskiy, 'Don't Build Gods': One AI Risk to Rule Them All
Ep 129: Jonathan Rowson, a metamodern framework for human futures
The Human Predicament (short course)

people: Nate Hagens (Director of ISEOF and host)
funding: ISEOF revenue was $1.86M in 2024, 99.5% of it contributions, up from $905k in 2023 (IRS Form 990 via ProPublica). Named donors are not disclosed.
status_evidence: Sep 30, 2026: released Ep 236 (Zeke Hausfather). Sep 25, 2026: Frankly #160. Sep 9, 2026: Ep 233, Roman Yampolskiy on superintelligence risk.
engage: Online Hylo community: an open dialogue group for systems thinking
The Human Predicament short course
Substack newsletter
caveats: AI is an occasional topic, not a programme. Among the twelve episodes from July to September 2026 only one (Yampolskiy) is about AI, and none of the recent Frankly episodes are. The discovery note put it in Minnesota; ISEOF's IRS filings give Wisconsin. The podcast carries a strong collapse/overshoot worldview, and some of its guests take contested positions.
tag_notes: Home: it diagnoses the metacrisis through systems ecology and energy (the superorganism), so Life & systems/cybernetics under B7, with ecological economics as a secondary and H3 placing the publication with the community it serves. Ring: changed from the roster's bridge to potential under E(2), because the AI episodes are occasional (one in about twelve in mid-2026, plus 2023 Schmachtenberger episodes) and there is no standing AI programme. Transferable method: the energy-throughput/superorganism lens on AI, plus reach into ecology- and collapse-aware audiences. Transfer: convening, because its AI episodes bring its own audience into the AI-risk conversation. Bridge is defensible if one counts recurring AI episodes as a publication line. Badge recoupling: it analyses AI risk explicitly as one thread of the metacrisis.

name: Global Challenges Foundation (GCF)
summary: A Stockholm foundation set up in 2012 by the financier László Szombatfalvy to raise awareness of global catastrophic risks and to strengthen global governance to deal with them. It publishes an annual Global Catastrophic Risks report and runs programmes on climate and sustainability and on common security. It funds work through calls for proposals, including, in 2026, a nuclear-risk call made jointly as a member of the Consortium to Reduce Nuclear Dangers. It ran the $5M New Shape Prize for global governance models in 2016-18.
why_it_matters: It names AI as one of its four concern areas, alongside climate, biodiversity and nuclear weapons, and argues that these risks cannot be governed in silos. That makes it a non-EA catastrophic-risk funder with a global-governance (UN-reform) lens that the AI-safety field seldom draws on.

key_work.title: Global Catastrophic Risks 2026 (includes 'AI in military decision-making: the global governance challenge' by Denise Garcia)
Consortium to Reduce Nuclear Dangers, second call for proposals ($50k-$1M)
New Shape Prize for global governance models

people: Anja Olin Pape (Executive Director from July 2026; previously Head of Programmes)
funding: Endowed in 2012 with about SEK 500 million, roughly half of Szombatfalvy's fortune (Wikipedia). A member of the Consortium to Reduce Nuclear Dangers, hosted by Carnegie Corporation of New York with Longview Philanthropy, PAX sapiens and Founders Pledge, which offers $50k-$1M multi-year grants (2026 call deadline 29 May 2026).
status_evidence: Jul 13, 2026: at London Climate Action Week. Jul 9, 2026: announced Anja Olin Pape as Executive Director. 2026: published Global Catastrophic Risks 2026.
engage: Consortium to Reduce Nuclear Dangers calls for proposals (second call closed 29 May 2026; decisions expected late autumn/winter 2026)
caveats: Its AI work is thin: one chapter on military AI in the 2026 report, and AI listed as a concern area. No AI-specific grants were found, so the bridge ring is borderline with potential. The current grant call is about nuclear risk, not AI. Its library page lists the 2024 report as the latest, and a 2025 report could not be checked.
tag_notes: Home: global-governance and common-security work on nuclear weapons and military AI puts it in Peace. Sub-tradition is arms control because its main AI output, the military-AI chapter, is about IHL and escalation (rule D). Ring: the roster's bridge is kept, because the 2026 announcement names AI as one of four concern areas and the annual catastrophic-risk report carries an AI chapter with an explicit catastrophic framing; but there is no dedicated AI grant line, so it is borderline potential under E(2). Transfer: into institutions, because its output argues for global governance frameworks for military AI (J3). Classed as a funder, not a generalist funder under rule K.

name: Odyssean Institute
summary: A UK charity (CIO 1204794), founded around 2022 by Giuseppe Dal Prá, that combines horizon scanning, decision-making under deep uncertainty (DMDU) and exploratory modelling with citizens' assemblies. Its flagship 2026 project, the Odyssean Process on regulating AI for civilisational resilience, runs from a horizon and solution scan with 300+ AI safety and governance experts, through a Horizon Summit and modelling, to a citizens' assembly of 100 demographically representative Britons. The assembly meets online from September and in person in Manchester on 27-29 November 2026. It also works on global catastrophic risks, nuclear-war supply-chain resilience and a food-security resilience network (GRAIN).
why_it_matters: It is a working template for joining expert foresight and complexity modelling to public deliberation on AI policy. That puts democratic legitimacy and deep uncertainty into AI governance, which mainstream AI-safety policy work mostly leaves to experts.

key_work.title: The Odyssean Process: regulating AI for civilisational resilience (with Involve and House of the People)
Horizon Scan on Global Catastrophic Risks
Governance Under Fallout (Horizon Summit report on second-order nuclear strike impacts)
Why Most Efforts Towards 'Democratic AI' Fall Short (Jacob Haimes)

funding: SFF 2025: $79,000 general support (Freedom track, including a $30,000 speculation grant). The Odyssean Process acknowledges Kristian Rönn, Greg Colbourn, the Survival and Flourishing Fund and King's College Cambridge. It reports that fundraising tripled in 2025.
status_evidence: Sep 3, 2026 (updated Sep 22): blog update on the first Odyssean Process. Citizens' assembly deliberations began 12 Jul 2026, with eight online sessions from 3 Sep and in-person deliberation set for 27-29 Nov 2026 in Manchester.
engage: Donations
Contact form for collaboration and curriculum engagement
caveats: Its site does not give a city or founding date; the founding year is inferred from its '3 years old in 2025' review. Its remit is wider than AI (nuclear, food security, supply chains), and AI became the flagship only in 2025-26. The assembly's outputs (policy report, White Paper 2.0, documentary) were still to come at the time of writing.
tag_notes: Home: its main AI output is a citizens' assembly informed by expert elicitation, so Democracy/deliberation (H1), with DMDU and complexity modelling (Life & systems) and horizon scanning (Arts, futures) as secondaries. Ring: core, since its flagship is AI regulation framed around existential and catastrophic risk, it is SFF-funded with CSER-linked advisers and trustees, and it is on the classic map; its wider GCR remit makes this a judgement call. Transfer: into institutions, because the process is built to produce policy signals for AI regulation (J3). Way of knowing: communal, because the deliberative output is knowledge from a participatory process.

name: GAIA Lab (formerly Gaia Network / Digital Gaia)
summary: The Gaia Network was proposed in 2023-24 by Rafael Kaufmann (Digital Gaia) and Roman Leventov: a decentralised 'web of causal models', built on active inference, that AI decision engines could query to check actions against safety constraints, as an incremental route to davidad's Open Agency Architecture. The work now sits with GAIA Lab in Düsseldorf ('systemically safe AI'), which shares the Digital Gaia GitHub organisation and counts Kaufmann and Leventov among its staff. GAIA Lab develops free-energy risk metrics and 'cybernetic gatekeepers' that take over an agent's behaviour when risk crosses a threshold. It applies neurosymbolic AI and world models to nuclear and energy systems, including two German federal (BMFTR) projects, on AI safety for nuclear decommissioning (Alisa34) and collective intelligence for the energy transition (KIKO), and, since mid-2026, world models for fusion plasma control (PLUME).
why_it_matters: It brings active inference and collective-intelligence ideas into AI oversight: risk metrics that carry uncertainty in both world model and stakeholder preferences, and a distributed rather than centralised gatekeeper. That is an alternative to monolithic safety architectures.

key_work.title: Gaia Network: an illustrated primer (EA Forum, with Roman Leventov)
Gaia: Distributed planetary-scale AI safety (Guaranteed Safe AI Seminars talk)
Free Energy Risk Metrics for Systemically Safe AI: Gatekeeping Multi-Agent Study
The GAIA Tech Tree: A Neurosymbolic AI Framework for Strategic Technological Decision-Making

people: Roman Leventov (researcher, neurosymbolic AI and AI safety)
funding: Two projects funded by Germany's BMFTR, each over three years, within the energy-transition programme: Alisa34, AI safety for nuclear decommissioning (about €2.1M, from Feb 2025), and KIKO, a collective-intelligence platform for the energy transition (about €2M, from Mar 2025).
status_evidence: Sep 2026: preprint 'Active Inference is Optimal Control'. Jun 2026: CRISTAL method preprint. GitHub repos (gaia-os) pushed Oct 2026.
engage: Contact via tk@gaia-lab.de for research partnerships
caveats: Changed: digitalgaia.earth fails with a TLS error, and the work continues as GAIA Lab, whose applied work is now mainly AI for nuclear (decommissioning, fusion) and energy systems rather than a general AI-safety network. The link from Digital Gaia to GAIA Lab is inferred from the shared GitHub organisation (which holds Digital Gaia and gaia_network_prototype repos), the shared people, and GAIA Lab listing the 2024 Gaia talk among its outputs. GAIA Lab's legal form (company or university-affiliated lab) is not stated. Karl Friston is listed as an adviser.
tag_notes: Home: active inference and the free-energy principle are its method (risk metrics, gatekeepers), so Life & systems/NeuroAI, with collective intelligence (pluralistic causal-model networks, stakeholder-defined preferences) as a secondary (H2). Ring: core, because Gaia's founding framing was 'distributed planetary-scale AI safety', presented in AI-safety venues (Guaranteed Safe AI Seminars, EA Forum, LessWrong); the pivot of GAIA Lab's applied work to fusion is flagged. Transfer: into the model, because the gatekeeper acts directly on AI agents' behaviour. Org type 'company' is a guess from the CEO title. MISFIT: legal form unclear.

name: Cascade Institute
summary: A research centre at Royal Roads University in Victoria, British Columbia, led by its founder Thomas Homer-Dixon since 2020. It studies the global polycrisis, meaning how crises in different systems become causally entangled, using causal-loop mapping and a Polycrisis Core Model, and looks for high-leverage interventions. Its programmes cover polycrisis, democracy, scale-up and acceleration, permafrost carbon and ultradeep geothermal. Since 2025 its Polycrisis programme has published a handful of AI pieces, including an integrated assessment of AI and data-centre risks for Canadian financial institutions.
why_it_matters: Its causal mapping of interacting crises could model AI as an amplifier between economic, geopolitical and epistemic stresses, a kind of systemic AI-risk analysis that the AI-safety field has barely done.

key_work.title: Global Systemic Stresses: Understanding the drivers of polycrisis
AI and Data Centre Risks for Canadian Financial Institutions (with Global Risk Institute)
The State of AI Global Governance and Its Implications for the U.S.-China Summit
Artificial Intelligence and Energy Innovation: Submission to NRCan

status_evidence: Sep 21, 2026: published 'The State of AI Global Governance and Its Implications for the U.S.-China Summit'. Sep 2026: 'Navigating a Fragmenting World Order'.
engage: No AI programme; outreach via its Polycrisis programme for partnerships
caveats: AI is a growing but minor strand inside the Polycrisis programme, with no AI staff role or programme. Its funders are not named on the pages checked. Sources date 'Global Systemic Stresses' to both June and November 2025.
tag_notes: Home: a systems diagnosis of the polycrisis using causal-loop diagrams, so Life & systems/cybernetics under B7, with Peace (Homer-Dixon's security studies; geopolitics of AI governance) as a secondary. Ring: the roster's potential is kept under E(2), since its AI outputs are a few papers and op-eds inside the Polycrisis programme, not a standing AI programme; it is edging towards adjacent. Transferable method: causal-loop polycrisis mapping and early-warning analysis applied to AI as a cross-system stressor. Transfer: into institutions, because its AI papers brief financial institutions and the Canadian government (J3). Badge recoupling: it analyses AI risk inside interacting systemic crises.

name: The Long Now Foundation
summary: A San Francisco nonprofit founded in 1996 by Stewart Brand, Danny Hillis and Brian Eno to promote long-term thinking on a 10,000-year timescale. It builds the 10,000-Year Clock, runs Long Now Talks, publishes Long Now Ideas and the Pace Layers journal, and operates The Interval venue. Recent talks have covered planetary computation, intelligence and consciousness. Its new Long Now Labs series with the Protocol Institute includes a commissioned study, 'Epistemic Cycles', of historical epistemic crises as a guide to the one brought on by synthetic intelligence, and a planned 'Interspecies Protocols' lab covering humans, nature and AI agents.
why_it_matters: Stewart Brand's pace-layer model gives a ready vocabulary for the AI pacing problem: a fast technology layer set against slow layers of governance, culture and nature. Its Labs format commissions interdisciplinary, historically grounded work on epistemic resilience in an age of generative AI.

key_work.title: Long Now Labs Series 001: Protocols for the Long Now (Lab 001.2 Epistemic Cycles), with the Protocol Institute
Benjamin Bratton, 'A Philosophy of Planetary Computation' (Long Now Talk)

Pace Layers framework

Membership
