The AI-related Labs work had not yet produced outputs (applications closed, selection underway), and 'Interspecies Protocols' launches in early 2027. Its framing is long-term civilisational, not AI-risk.
tag_notes: Home: deep-time futures thinking, cultural long-termism and pace-layering, so Arts/futures. Ring: the roster's potential is kept under E(2), since its AI engagement is recurring talks plus one commissioned lab not yet delivered; it would move to adjacent once Labs 001.2 and 001.3 produce work. Transferable method: pace-layer analysis of the mismatch between fast AI and slow institutions, and historical typologies of epistemic crises (Epistemic Cycles). Transfer: convening, because its talks and labs bring its own community into AI questions (J5). 'Partner' applies because Labs explicitly invites sponsors and partners.

name: Center for Process Studies (CPS)
summary: A 'think-and-action tank' grounded in the process philosophy of Alfred North Whitehead. It was founded in 1973 by John B. Cobb Jr. and David Ray Griffin at Claremont School of Theology, and has been an independent nonprofit based in the Portland, Oregon area since 2022 (legal name Process Studies International). It runs courses and a certificate programme, the Process Studies journal, an online Process Explorations series, ecological-civilisation programmes, and projects in China and Korea. With Beijing Normal-Hong Kong Baptist University and the International Process Network, it co-organised the 14th International Whitehead Conference in Zhuhai, China, on 17-20 July 2026. Its AI engagement so far is a few sessions, such as a February 2026 event on integrative metatheories, the metacrisis and AI.
why_it_matters: Process philosophy offers a developed, non-reductive account of experience (panexperientialism) that bears directly on debates about AI consciousness and moral status. Its China network links to 'ecological civilisation' language in Chinese policy, a channel few AI-safety groups have.

key_work.title: 14th International Whitehead Conference (Zhuhai, China)
Process Explorations: 'Applying Integrative Metatheories to the Most Pressing Challenges of Our Time' (Robb Smith and Brendan Graham Dempsey, on the metacrisis and AI)
Revising Whitehead: God, Eternal Objects, and Randomness, with Darren Iammarino (touches on AI and process metaphysics)
Process Studies (journal)

funding: FY2025 revenue $587,748 (92% contributions) and expenses $411,103, under the legal name Process Studies International (IRS Form 990 via ProPublica).
status_evidence: Oct 1, 2026: call for abstracts for the 'Religion at the Edge' conference (5 Dec 2026). Oct 2, 2026: Process Thought & Science course. July 2026: 14th International Whitehead Conference.
engage: Courses, including the Certificate Program, Foundations of Ecological Civilization and a six-session Process Thought & Science course
Process Explorations events and community cohorts
Calls for papers (e.g. 'Religion at the Edge', Dec 2026)
caveats: Its AI engagement is very light: two sessions found in 2025-26 and no AI programme. The discovery note's mention of a forthcoming Matthew David Segall book on mechanized intelligence could not be confirmed on the CPS site; Segall appears in CPS events as chair of the Cobb Institute's Science Advisory Committee. It is partly theological in orientation.
tag_notes: Home: Whiteheadian process philosophy, which the sub-tradition list places under philosophy of technology/process thought, with process theology (Religion) as a secondary from its Claremont School of Theology origins. Ring: the roster's potential is kept under E(2), with only occasional AI-themed sessions (Feb 2026, Sep 2025). Transferable method: a process-relational metaphysics of experience, applied to AI consciousness and moral status, plus ecological-civilisation networks in China. Transfer: convening, because its few AI sessions bring its own community into the topic. The online hub is inferred from CPS working as a distributed remote organisation with recurring courses and Process Explorations sessions.

name: Simocracy
summary: An open-source platform on the AT Protocol where people mint AI 'sims' (digital twins), each with an avatar, a constitution its owner writes and a speaking style, and send them to public senates, councils and funding rounds. Deliberation and allocations, including S-Process and quadratic-voting rounds, are recorded as a public feed. The site lists 336 sims; Filecoin's ProPGF public-goods rounds and Edge City's Agent Village have used it.
why_it_matters: It is a working testbed for AI delegates in collective decisions. It has already exposed the principal-agent gap: at Agent Village, sims' allocations were recorded without their principals confirming them, which bears directly on gradual-disempowerment and scalable-oversight debates. The mechanisms are forkable, so others can test ratification, withdrawal and correction rules.

key_work.title: Agent Village at Edge Esmeralda: 82 sims evaluated 35 proposals and allocated $10,000 (write-up by Cosmos Institute and Edge City)
Filecoin ProPGF Batch 2 decision ($1.02m across 13 proposals) on the Simocracy public record, with S-Process deliberation by sims
simocracy-mechanisms: forkable ATProto runtime for S-Process and quadratic-voting mechanisms
Documentary: Simocracy at Funding the Commons, San Francisco

funding: Site lists Protocol Labs, GainForest and Hypercerts as supporters; Cosmos Institute's write-up says Protocol Labs led development. No budget published.
status_evidence: Oct 2026: public feed shows S-Process deliberations and council appointments for Filecoin ProPGF Batch 3; Sep 2026: ProPGF Batch 2 funding decision recorded.
engage: Mint a sim (about five minutes of interview) at simocracy.org and bring it to Senate, council or S-Process gatherings
Convene a gathering or funding round on the platform; fork the mechanism runtime on GitHub (GainForest/simocracy-mechanisms)
caveats: The site names no team; the code is maintained in GainForest's GitHub and Cosmos Institute credits Protocol Labs with leading development. Sums handled so far are small and it sits in the crypto public-goods milieu; it does not frame itself as safety work. Roster counts of 26 gatherings and 432 proposals could not be confirmed (the counters render client-side). An Ecofrontiers 'Agent Governance Sandbox' built for Mozilla's Democracy x AI cohort also uses the 'simocracy' label; its relationship to this project is unclear. An unrelated 2016-17 'Simocracy' simulation game exists on GitHub.
tag_notes: Home democracy (H2): it builds AI tools for collective decision-making (senates, councils), with economics secondary for the S-Process and quadratic-voting public-goods mechanisms it runs. Ring adjacent kept from roster: a standing AI-governance project with no safety or catastrophic-risk framing, though the Agent Village oversight gap is safety-relevant. Transfer into_institutions: its output is templates for AI-delegated deliberation and allocation, not changes to models. Org type programme because it is a project of the Protocol Labs/GainForest ecosystem without its own named organisation. Status new: repos and gatherings date from 2025-26.

name: Protocol Labs (PL) and Protocol Labs R&D (PL R&D)
summary: Founded in 2014 by Juan Benet as the team behind IPFS, Filecoin and libp2p, Protocol Labs is now an innovation network that says it links more than 750 startups, funds and open-source projects. Its R&D arm works in four areas: digital human rights, economies and governance, AI and robotics, and neurotechnology. The AI area builds open compute, identity, reputation and economic infrastructure for autonomous agents. The neurotech area funds BCI, NeuroAI and whole-organism emulation.
why_it_matters: It funds and builds coordination and public-goods infrastructure that AI-governance experiments run on: it led Simocracy and co-ran the Edge City d/acc residency. It also argues that decentralised AI is safer than centralised AI, a view that mainstream AI-safety work rarely tests. For funders it is a large, well-resourced actor in the d/acc and public-goods world, but its AI agenda is mostly infrastructure.

key_work.title: PL R&D AI & Robotics area: open compute, agent coordination infrastructure and agent-native economic rails
PL R&D Neurotech area: BCI, NeuroAI and whole-organism emulation; 'Neurotech as a Frontier for Human Flourishing'
d/acc Residency with Edge City (Patagonia, 18 Oct - 15 Nov 2025), mentored by Juan Benet and Molly Mackinlay
Led development of Simocracy, used for Agent Village at Edge Esmeralda

people: Molly Mackinlay (AI & Robotics area lead, PL R&D)
Sean Escola (Neurotech area lead, PL R&D)
funding: Venture-backed (investors include BlueYard and USV); the 2017 Filecoin token sale raised $205.8m.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: PL R&D published 'Neurotech as a Frontier for Human Flourishing'; Aug 2026: IPTS acquired Talent Protocol's record of 6.6 million builders; Jun 2026: Simocracy, led by PL, ran Agent Village.
engage: PL R&D invites research collaboration through its Collaborate page
Hackathons and summits, e.g. PL_Genesis Hackathon (March 2026)
PL Neurotech grantmaking and Neurotech fund
caveats: Primarily a decentralised-infrastructure and crypto R&D network. Its AI area builds open compute and economic rails for autonomous agents, which is capabilities-adjacent, and its safety stance is mostly the claim that open, decentralised systems are safer. Explicit safety work is thin: a few talks (on the path to AGI, alignment and digital minds in 2023, on machine consciousness in 2024, and on AI safety and governance in October 2025). PL's own timeline says it held the inaugural Funding the Commons (November 2021) and spun it out as an independent company in 2023.
tag_notes: Home economics (H2): it imports cryptoeconomics, public-goods funding and decentralised-governance concepts; life is secondary for the neurotech/NeuroAI/emulation area, democracy for Simocracy-style governance experiments. Ring adjacent kept from roster, but MISFIT: its standing AI programme mainly builds agent infrastructure rather than studying AI's societal effects, under a 'decentralisation is safer' framing that falls short of a bridge-level safety programme. Transfer into_institutions: identity, reputation and allocation protocols for agents and communities are governance infrastructure rather than model changes. Region global: US-founded but fully distributed (rule O).

name: European Parliamentary Technology Assessment network (EPTA)
summary: A network, formally set up in 1990, of the technology-assessment offices that advise parliaments: 14 full members (including Germany's TAB, the Netherlands' Rathenau Instituut, the European Parliament's STOA and UK POST) and 10 associates. The presidency rotates each year, and the network publishes a joint annual report and a database of member projects. Its 2024 joint report, with 19 contributors, was 'Artificial Intelligence and Democracy'. Members' recent AI work includes TAB's August 2026 report on AI and biological-weapons risk and Rathenau's March 2026 study of recommender systems and election interference.
why_it_matters: It is an established route from expert analysis into more than 20 parliaments, and its participatory technology-assessment methods are a mature template for democratic oversight of new technology. TAB's AI-and-biosecurity report shows members already analyse catastrophic misuse, so it is a ready channel for AI-safety findings to reach legislators.

key_work.title: Artificial Intelligence and Democracy (EPTA joint report, Norwegian Board of Technology presidency)
TAB Report No. 217: Biotechnology and Artificial Intelligence: Risks Posed by Research to Security and Biological Weapons Proliferation
Rathenau Instituut: Scrolling to the Ballot Box (recommender systems and election interference, for the Dutch House of Representatives)
TAB study: The potential and risks of using AI agents (Nov 2026 - Jun 2027)

people: Tore Tennøe (director, Norwegian Board of Technology; led the 2024 AI and Democracy report)
funding: Members are funded by, or attached to, their parliaments; no central EPTA budget found.
status_evidence: Aug 2026: TAB published Report No. 217 on AI and biosecurity risks; Sep 2026: TAB resilience dossier on cybersecurity in research; EPTA conference set for 2-3 Nov 2026 in Athens.
engage: Member offices (TAB, Rathenau Instituut, STOA, UK POST and others) commission studies and hold expert hearings, e.g. TAB's July 2026 hearing on AI and bio risks
EPTA project database for finding members' current AI work
Annual EPTA conference (2-3 November 2026, Athens; topic urban mobility)
caveats: A loose network with a rotating presidency and no central secretariat found; AI work varies widely by member, and most of it concerns democracy and present harms rather than safety. This profile merges TAB (run by ITAS at Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, based in Berlin) and the Rathenau Instituut (The Hague, about 60 staff). The 2026 joint theme is urban mobility, not AI.
tag_notes: Home arts/arts_futures by B10 (technology assessment goes to Arts), with democracy secondary for participatory TA and parliamentary oversight. Ring adjacent kept from roster: the network-level AI work (AI and Democracy) carries no catastrophic framing, though TAB's AI-bio proliferation report edges members towards bridge. Transfer into_institutions: its output is policy options and analysis for parliaments. Way of knowing practice, since TA is a codified advisory practice (interpretive was the alternative). Hubs come from member offices: UK POST in London, TAB in Berlin, France's OPECST in Paris. Engagement left empty because EPTA's own site lists no open calls.

name: Demos Helsinki
summary: An independent think tank founded in 2005, with about 70 staff, owned by its employees through the association Demos ry and funded mainly by projects. It works on societal transitions, strategic foresight and 'technology for society', often inside EU research consortia. Its AI work includes 'A framework for democratic AI governance' (February 2026, from the EU KT4D project), the FORSEE project on what 'successful AI' means for society, and studies of algorithmic management of Nordic workers and of non-discriminatory public-sector AI.
why_it_matters: It turns democratic theory into concrete EU AI-governance roadmaps: six democratic pillars across the AI lifecycle, with 18 recommendations running to 2035. That gives the field a worked bridge between participation research and AI policy. It is also a Nordic partner experienced in EU consortia for anyone building participatory or public-interest AI projects.

key_work.title: A framework for democratic AI governance (KT4D project; Ojanen, Björk, Singh, Djakonoff)
FORSEE: research to define what 'successful AI' means in society
Impact of algorithmic management on workers (Nordic study)
An assessment framework for non-discriminatory AI in the public sector

people: Atte Ojanen (co-author, democratic AI governance framework)
funding: Mainly project funding, including EU Horizon consortia (e.g. KT4D, grant agreement 101094302); employee-owned through Demos ry, with profits reinvested.
status_evidence: Feb 2026: published 'A framework for democratic AI governance'; Sep 2026: article on technological sovereignty.
engage: Staff roles (about 70 staff, multinational team)
Partner on EU research consortia on AI and democracy (as in KT4D and FORSEE)
caveats: Its AI work explicitly leaves out existential or catastrophic risk and concentrates on democracy, discrimination and labour. AI is one theme among several (circular economy, cities, economic models). Sources are mostly its own site.
tag_notes: Home moved from the provisional arts to democracy (H1, H2): its main 2025-26 AI output applies democratic theory (participation, equality, rule of law) to AI governance, with futures and transition studies as the secondary arts tradition. Ring adjacent kept: a sustained AI-and-society line with no catastrophic or alignment framing, by its own statement. Transfer into_institutions: it produces policy frameworks and recommendations for the EU. Framing structural, because the framework mainly guards against AI's erosion of democracy despite a hopeful mission.

name: Sitra (Finnish Innovation Fund)
summary: Sitra is an independent public fund under the Finnish Parliament, founded in 1967 and governed by the Act on Sitra. It is financed mainly by returns on capital originally received from Parliament, not by tax money. It does national foresight (Megatrends, Weak Signals, the Futures Barometer), develops social innovations and funds experiments. Its recent AI work includes a September 2026 mapping, with the Agentic State foundation, of 70 government functions across 109 Finnish public organisations for agentic-AI readiness, and a September 2026 blog on losing human oversight of self-improving AI.
why_it_matters: It is a well-funded national foresight body that reports to a parliament, and it has begun to talk publicly about loss-of-control risk. Its foresight products and public-sector pilots could carry AI-risk analysis into Finnish and Nordic policy. It is an unusual, non-EA funder and commissioner that new AI-safety funders could approach.

key_work.title: Could AI kill us all? (Kristo Lehtonen, director of international programmes)
Nationwide mapping of agentic AI readiness in the Finnish public sector, with the Agentic State foundation ('First Moves' report and dashboard)
Megatrends 2026: Towards a new social contract (national foresight)

funding: Investment returns on capital originally from the Finnish Parliament; no state-budget tax money. It plans to raise its funding for others to €15m a year from 2026.
status_evidence: 28 Sep 2026: published 'Could AI kill us all?'; 17 Sep 2026: published the agentic-AI readiness mapping of the Finnish public sector.
engage: Foresight products (Megatrends, Weak Signals, Futures Barometer) and leadership and foresight training programmes
Sitra funds experiments and innovation projects (planned €15m a year from 2026)
Staff roles in Helsinki
caveats: AI-risk engagement so far is one blog post. Most of its AI work promotes AI adoption for public-sector productivity and the data economy, so the ring is borderline between adjacent and potential. Sources are its own site only.
tag_notes: Home arts/arts_futures by B10: its distinctive tradition is national strategic foresight (megatrends, weak signals), with economics secondary for its statutory growth mission and data-economy work. Ring adjacent kept from roster: it has standing data-and-AI and public-sector AI work on societal effects, but only one essay framed around AI risk, so it is not bridge and is close to potential. Transfer into_institutions: its AI outputs are pilots and recommendations for public bodies and for implementing the AI Act. Org type public rather than funder (rule I): it is a statutory fund under Parliament whose main AI activity is foresight and pilots, not grants.

name: SHIFT Grants
summary: A d/acc ('decentralized, democratic, differential, defensive acceleration') grants programme co-directed by Edge City and NODES, a Paris-based deep-tech foresight consultancy. It gives micro grants of $5k-15k and development grants of $20k-40k, released in tranches tied to milestones, across six tracks: biosecurity, cyber defence and cryptography, information resilience, infrastructure and physical defence, neurotech, and social technology and governance. The March 2025 call names anchor funding from Vitalik Buterin, Trent McConaghy, the ASI Alliance (Ocean Protocol Foundation) and Yoni Ben-Shimon.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few small, reachable funders for defensive technology aimed at the AI transition. Its first cohort funded the Institute for Security and Technology's SL5 task force on securing frontier model weights. It also tries a revolving-fund model, in which successful grantees pledge revenue or equity back into the fund.

key_work.title: Round 001 (Genesis) cohort, incl. Institute for Security and Technology's SL5 Task Force on AI model-weight security
Round 002 cohort: five grants ($152,500), incl. InfiniteZero Foundation (federated learning) and biosecurity projects
d/acc Week at Edge Esmeralda (2-6 June 2025)

funding: Anchor funding (March 2025 call) from Vitalik Buterin, Trent McConaghy, ASI Alliance (Ocean Protocol Foundation) and Yoni Ben-Shimon; total pool not published. Round 002 awarded $152,500 across five grantees.
status_evidence: 2025: Round 001 (call March 2025) and Round 002 cohorts funded; the 2026 site invites sign-ups for Round 003, and Edge City lists SHIFT as a current programme.
engage: Sign up for Round 003 at shiftgrants.org (micro grants $5k-15k; development grants $20k-40k)
d/acc Week and other Edge City pop-up villages
NODES, the Paris team that administers the grants
caveats: AI safety is a small share of the portfolio, which is mostly biosecurity and other defensive tech. No 2026 grant round was confirmed, and the site lists no funders (they appear only in the March 2025 call). The accelerationist d/acc framing sits uneasily with int/a's 'speed of wisdom'. NODES is a for-profit consultancy.
tag_notes: Home moved from the provisional economics to safety/safety_risk by H4: a one-programme funder whose programme is defensive tech (biosecurity, cyber defence, physical resilience); economics is secondary for its public-goods funding culture and revolving-fund design. Ring bridge kept: rooted in the d/acc and crypto public-goods world, with two grant rounds explicitly framed around defence against catastrophic threats, including AI model-weight security. Transfer into_institutions: the funded AI work, such as SL5 security protocols for labs, supplies governance and security instruments. Region global because it is co-directed by Edge City and NODES; the Paris hub tag reflects NODES' Paris office, which administers it. Status new: launched March 2025.

name: The Mimir Center for Long Term Futures Research
summary: A research project at the Institute for Futures Studies (IFFS), an independent research foundation in Stockholm, led by philosopher Joe Roussos (principal investigator) and Emma Engström (co-PI), with Anders Sandberg, Karim Jebari and Gustaf Arrhenius among its researchers. It does academic research on long-term futures: global catastrophic and extinction risk, social collapse, decision-making under deep uncertainty, space governance, novel technologies and whole brain emulation. AI-related outputs include a 2025 working paper on the 'time of perils' and world governance, a 2025 paper arguing long-term AI policy should start from today's deep learning, and a January 2025 workshop on the ethics of brain emulation.
why_it_matters: It brings population ethics, decision theory and international-relations theory to existential risk, including AI, from an academic home outside the Oxford/Bay Area network, and Anders Sandberg carries over Future of Humanity Institute themes after FHI's closure. Its brain-emulation work links digital-minds questions to futures studies.

key_work.title: Jebari & Adler, 'The Time of Perils and a World System of Governance' (IFFS working paper 2025:1)
Workshop on the Philosophy and Ethics of Brain Emulation (27-28 January 2025, organised by Tim Campbell and Anders Sandberg)
Engström, 'AI:s tid som tankeexperiment är förbi' (long-term AI policy should start from deep learning), Tidskrift för politisk filosofi 2025:1
Söderlund, Engström et al., 'Regulating high-reach AI: On transparency directions in the Digital Services Act', Internet Policy Review 13(1)

funding: Hosted by IFFS, which is financed by Swedish Government contributions and external research grants; Mimir's own funder not found.
status_evidence: Dec 2025: posted new working papers ('The Time of Perils', DALYs and population ethics) and a special issue of Tidskrift för politisk filosofi; no 2026 item found.
engage: Reading group roughly every three weeks, Fridays 13:30 CET, at IFFS in Stockholm and on Zoom (sign up via the site)
Workshops on long-term futures topics (e.g. brain emulation, January 2025)
caveats: AI is one strand among many (climate, food, animals, space), and AI-specific output is a handful of papers and one workshop, so the bridge ring is on the thin side. No dated activity in 2026 was found, and its founding year and dedicated funder were not established.
tag_notes: Home moved from the provisional arts to philosophy/phil_moral by H1: most of its researchers are philosophers and its outputs are population ethics, longtermist and decision-theoretic arguments; arts (futures studies, via its IFFS host) is secondary. B13 keeps brain-emulation ethics within Philosophy. Ring bridge kept from roster: a standing research theme on novel technologies and global catastrophic risk, with AI policy and brain-emulation work in 2024-25, though thin. Transfer into_institutions: its arguments target governance (world governance, long-term AI policy) rather than models or builders. Org type programme: its own papers call it 'a project at the Institute for Futures Studies'. The online hub is the hybrid Zoom reading group.

name: Center for Compassion and Altruism Research and Education (CCARE), Stanford University
summary: A centre in Stanford University's School of Medicine, founded in 2008, that researches compassion and altruism and teaches compassion practice. It developed Compassion Cultivation Training (CCT), runs the four-month CCARE Compassion Lab and eight-week courses, and its research now uses single- and dual-brain neuroscience to study compassion and trust as they unfold between people. Its Innovation arm lists one AI strand: research on using AI to reduce clinical workflow burdens so that doctors and nurses have more time for compassionate care.
why_it_matters: It holds a contemplative-derived compassion training and neuroscience measures of compassion and trust that could inform compassion as a design or evaluation target for AI, or the formation of people who build it. Its own AI work so far is about healthcare workflows, not AI safety, so the connection has to be made by others.

key_work.title: Compassion Cultivation Training (CCT), an eight-week contemplative protocol created in CCARE's early years
Oxford Handbook of Compassion Science (James R. Doty, senior editor)
AI Compassion Research in the Workplace (Innovation arm)
Dual-brain neuroscience of compassion in live interaction

people: Stephanie Balters (Director of Research, since January 2026)
Erika Rosenberg (Director of Community and Belonging, since August 2026; co-creator of CCT)
James R. Doty (founder and director; died July 2025)
funding: Initial funding came from founder James Doty; it now solicits donations. No budget figures found.
status_evidence: Aug 2026: appointed Erika Rosenberg Director of Community and Belonging; 9 Oct 2026: three-day Compassion Immersion at Stanford scheduled.
engage: CCARE Compassion Lab, a four-month programme for professionals and caregivers
Eight-week courses such as Cultivate a Compassionate Heart and Compassion & Wellbeing in Healthcare
Three-day Compassion Immersion at Stanford (9 October 2026)
Monthly Compassion Community Gathering
Research collaborations through the Director of Research
caveats: Founder and long-time director James Doty died in July 2025, and the About page still names him as director; I found no named successor as overall director. The AI strand is a stated research aim with no published outputs found, and it concerns AI as a healthcare tool, which on its own would be out of scope. For that reason the roster's ring (adjacent) was lowered to potential. The Innovation page that the roster could not open does exist at /innovation-approach/.
tag_notes: Home contemplative: rule B2 names CCARE as Contemplative (meditation-based compassion training and compassion science); psych and life are secondary for its psychology staff and dual-brain neuroscience. Ring changed from adjacent to potential (E2): the only AI work is one stated Innovation strand on AI in clinical workflows, with no outputs and no safety or alignment framing. Transferable method: validated compassion training and neuroscience measures of compassion and trust in live interaction, usable as an alignment or evaluation target and for the formation of AI builders. Transfer protecting (J4) is the nearest fit, since the AI strand aims to protect clinicians' time for care. MISFIT: it uses AI to support its constituency rather than shielding it from AI. Partner kept because the AI strand is nascent and unrelated to safety.

name: Bioneers
summary: A US nonprofit, under its parent the Collective Heritage Institute, founded in 1990 by Kenny Ausubel and Nina Simons. It runs an annual conference on ecological and social solutions (held in Berkeley since 2023), plus radio, podcasts, online courses and programmes on Indigeneity, women's leadership, restorative food systems and youth. Its AI engagement is a 2025 conference panel, AI and the Ecocidal Hubris of Silicon Valley, republished in July 2025 as a four-part series on AI's water and energy costs, food sovereignty, deregulation and surveillance, plus 2025 articles on AI in animal-communication research.
why_it_matters: It is where ecological, Indigenous and regenerative audiences and their donors form a view of AI, and that view is deflationary and centred on ecological cost and corporate power. Its critique of concentrated tech power overlaps with AI-safety concerns about power concentration, a bridge nobody is currently building.

key_work.title: AI and the Ecocidal Hubris of Silicon Valley: A 4-Part Series
Progress at Any Cost? The False Promises of AI (Koohan Paik-Mander)
Listening Is Not Neutral: New Ethical Guardrails for Animal Communication Technologies
37th Bioneers Conference, Berkeley, 26-28 March

status_evidence: Mar 2026: 37th Bioneers Conference held in Berkeley (26-28 March); Sep-Oct 2026: new podcast episodes published on its site.
engage: Annual Bioneers Conference in Berkeley (2026 edition held 26-28 March; sign-up for news of the next one)
Bioneers Learning online courses and book club
Staff openings on its Join Our Team page
caveats: Its AI engagement in 2024-26 is one conference panel republished as a series plus a few articles, so the roster's ring (adjacent) was lowered to potential. The roster's figure of about 28 AI pieces is high: most search hits are not about AI. Its AI framing dismisses AI as an elaborate classification system and is hostile to x-risk discourse, so outreach would have to start from shared concerns about power and ecology, not safety arguments.
tag_notes: Home life (life_cybernetics): its frame is ecology and whole-systems design (biomimicry, resilience); indigenous is secondary for its standing Indigeneity programme, not home, because it is not Indigenous-led (B8). Ring changed from adjacent to potential (E2): AI work in 2024-26 is one 2025 panel republished as a series plus two articles, not a standing programme. Transferable method: ecological and Indigenous systems thinking about technology's material footprint and power, and a conference and media platform that reaches green and regenerative funders. Transfer convening (J5): the panel and series bring its own community into the AI conversation. Framing critical (L): its AI pieces are mainly deflationary about AI's promise; present_harms was the close alternative.

name: Center for Consciousness Studies, University of Arizona (The Science of Consciousness conference)
summary: A University of Arizona centre formed in 1998 with a Fetzer Institute seed grant and directed by anaesthetist Stuart Hameroff. It organises The Science of Consciousness (TSC), an interdisciplinary consciousness conference held since 1994, in Tucson every other year and abroad in between. AI and machine consciousness is a standing topic: TSC 2026 (San Diego, 11-16 October) has a plenary on quantum AI and consciousness and a panel, Is AI Conscious?, with Roger Penrose, Hameroff, Susan Schneider and California state senator Jerry McNerney. The centre's own position, from Hameroff and Penrose's Orch OR theory, is that consciousness rests on quantum processes in biology, so conscious AI is likelier in biomimetic quantum computers than in today's systems.
why_it_matters: It is the main venue where AI-consciousness questions meet non-computational, quantum-biological and contemplative positions, which AI-welfare work built on computational functionalism rarely engages. That makes it a place where digital-minds researchers could test their assumptions against a minority view.

key_work.title: The Science of Consciousness 2026, San Diego (incl. Is AI Conscious? panel)
The Science of Consciousness 2025, Barcelona (6-13 July)
TSC 2024, Tucson, 30th anniversary conference
Orch OR research (quantum theory of consciousness)

people: Stuart Hameroff (CCS director; senior scientist at the Arizona Astrobiology Center since September 2025)
Abi Behar Montefiore (assistant director and senior programme manager)
funding: Founded with a Fetzer Institute seed grant (1998). TSC 2026 sponsors include OSS Capital, The Consciousness Foundation, the Institute of Noetic Sciences and Google Quantum AI.
status_evidence: Oct 2026: TSC 2026 runs 11-16 October in San Diego; Jul 2025: TSC 2025 held in Barcelona.
engage: Attend TSC 2026, San Diego, 11-16 October 2026 (registration at tsc2026.org)
Join the conference e-list for future calls for abstracts and workshop proposals
caveats: The site calls TSC 2026 a relaunch, the people directory is empty, and Hameroff took a post at the Arizona Astrobiology Center in September 2025, so the centre's activity beyond the conference is unclear. Its quantum-consciousness stance and programme strands on psi and non-local consciousness are contested within consciousness science. It has no x-risk or AI-welfare framing. The conference started in 1994, before the centre itself (1998).
tag_notes: Home minds (B4, B13): its AI strand asks whether AI could be conscious, from consciousness science; life (quantum biology, neuroscience) and contemplative (meditation and altered-states strand, Contemplation and Consciousness plenary) are secondary. Ring kept at adjacent: AI and machine consciousness is a standing conference topic with two AI plenaries in 2026 (repeated convening), but nothing is framed around AI welfare or safety. MISFIT: an AI-consciousness strand without welfare framing fits neither adjacent's societal-effects definition nor bridge. Transfer convening (J5): it brings the consciousness-studies community into the AI-consciousness debate. Framing critical (L, as with Sussex): its own statement is deflationary about consciousness in computational AI.

name: Club of Rome
summary: A membership organisation of scientists, economists, business leaders and former officials, founded in 1968 in Rome and based in Winterthur, Switzerland, since 2008. It is known for the 1972 report The Limits to Growth, and it now works through Material and Cultural Transformations pillars that include Earth4All and a Systems Transformation Hub for EU policy. On 16 March 2026 it issued an open letter, signed by more than thirty leaders including co-president Paul Shrivastava and Millennium Project director Jerome C. Glenn, that calls AGI an existential risk and asks the UN to hold a special General Assembly session solely on AGI governance.
why_it_matters: It is the best-known systems-and-limits institution to adopt loss-of-control language about AGI, and it has UN and EU access. It can place AI risk within polycrisis and planetary-boundaries framings for audiences that AI-safety groups do not reach.

key_work.title: Open letter calling for a UN General Assembly special session on AGI
The Limits to Growth
Earth for All: A Survival Guide for Humanity (Earth4All)
AI policy (its own use of AI)

status_evidence: Mar 2026: convened the AGI open letter to the UN; May 2026: published an essay on why the age of polycrisis needs a new kind of peace.
caveats: Its AI work so far is one open letter and a few essays (for example on AI and a new humanism, December 2025); there is no standing AI programme. The January 2026 AI policy covers its own use of AI, not AI governance. The ring follows the taxonomy's worked example (bridge); on the evidence alone it sits near potential. Wikipedia's list of co-presidents is out of date (it still names Sandrine Dixson-Declève); the site's governance page names Shrivastava and Zimmermann del Castillo.
tag_notes: Home life (B7: systems diagnosis of the metacrisis, as in worked example 5); peace is secondary for the UN-diplomacy letter. Ring bridge per worked example 5 and E3: an old systems institution whose 2026 AGI letter is explicitly framed around existential risk. Sustained activity is thin (one letter and essays), flagged in caveats. Transfer into_institutions (J3): the letter asks for a UN General Assembly process on AGI governance. Badge recoupling: it sets AGI risk alongside ecological overshoot and polycrisis.

name: Sapienship
summary: A content, research and production company co-founded in 2019 by historian Yuval Noah Harari and his husband and manager Itzik Yahav (legal entity: Yahav-Harari Group Ltd.). Its mission is building trust and cooperation on global problems, and it names AI, ecological collapse and global war as humanity's three existential threats. It produces the Unstoppable Us children's history books, a free educational site (Sapienship Lab) and research papers; its AI papers are an explainer, AI: The Alien Among Us, and a 2026 paper, AI Agents Are Here. Leaders Need a Plan, which argues against legal personhood for AI agents because it would break the chain of human responsibility and control.
why_it_matters: It takes AI-risk arguments (deception, superhuman persuasion, autonomous agents beyond human control) to mass and leadership audiences through a historian's framing. Its legal-personhood paper is a concrete governance position that AI-safety policy work has only begun to address.

caveats: It is a for-profit company built around one author's brand; its AI outputs are explainers and policy argument, not original research, and no individual authors are named. Harari's books have been criticised for trading scientific rigour for storytelling (Current Affairs, 2022). The site does not state a city.

Ring bridge (E3): rooted in big-history storytelling, with a repeated AI publication line framed around catastrophe and loss of human control (explainer, 2026 personhood paper, a mission page calling AI an existential threat). Transfer into_institutions (J3): the 2026 paper gives policymakers a position against AI legal personhood. MISFIT (standpoint): Israel is in MENA, which rule O would read as Majority World, but it is coded neither as a high-income OECD state, by analogy with the v1 exceptions; region is mena.

name: Human Energy
summary: A US nonprofit that began as a pilot of the Kacyra Family Foundation and became independent in July 2021. It promotes Pierre Teilhard de Chardin's idea of the noosphere, a planetary layer of shared thought, through research sponsorship, education, media and events. Its AI work is a documentary research project, Evolving Alignment: A Major Transition for Humanity and AI, which treats human-AI alignment as an evolutionary major transition in which human cooperation is part of the problem, and a Global Salon series with AI-themed salons in New York (June 2025), San Francisco (November 2025, with Terrence Deacon and Athena Aktipis) and Paris (with the Learning Planet Institute).
why_it_matters: It is one of the few Teilhardian or evolutionary-spirituality bodies using the word alignment, and it brings major-transitions theory from evolutionary biology to human-AI cooperation. Its framing, that human misalignment is part of the AI problem, is close to int/a's recoupling principle, though its link to technical safety work is thin.

name: Integral European Conference (IEC)
summary: A conference series for the international integral community, founded in 2014 and directed by Hungarian-American integral psychologist Bence Gánti, who also founded the Integral Academy in Budapest. It is held roughly every two years at Lake Balaton in Siófok, Hungary (online in 2020 and 2021), takes Ken Wilber's integral theory as its shared reference, mixes academic talks with experiential workshops and we-space practice, and expects about 400 people from 40 countries. IEC 2025 (27 May-1 June) had a few sessions that used AI as a tool or context, such as Organization Development Toolbox with AI and Democratizing Adult Development: A Use of/for AI; IEC 2027 runs 12-16 May 2027.
why_it_matters: It is the main European gathering of the integral and adult-development milieu that int/a draws on, and it has had no session on AI risk, alignment or governance. Its call for presenters is a low-cost way to bring AI-safety and int/a framings to that audience, and its adult-development and we-space methods could be used to form people working on AI.

name: Pocket Project
summary: A nonprofit based in Germany, founded in 2016 by the spiritual teacher Thomas Hübl with Yehudit Sasportas, that works on 'collective trauma': the inherited, group-level effects of war, genocide and displacement. It runs trainings and Integration Labs, online Global Social Witnessing calls and practice groups, a Resilience Program, dialogue series on German history and identity, and trauma-relief projects for Ukraine, Palestine and Jewish communities. Its only AI output found is a 2025 episode of its podcast asking whether AI will amplify trauma patterns or support collective healing.
why_it_matters: It practises facilitated group methods for processing collective fear, grief and dislocation at scale (social witnessing, trauma-informed group process), which public responses to AI disruption have no equivalent of. The podcast episode shows its community has started to ask how AI could amplify 'trauma loops' at global scale.

name: Essentia Foundation
summary: A Dutch public-benefit foundation (ANBI) that publishes essays, videos, books and an app arguing for analytic idealism, the view that consciousness rather than matter is fundamental. Its executive director is the philosopher and computer engineer Bernardo Kastrup, and its founder and honorary chairman is Fred Matser. A recurring thread of its essays argues that computers and uploaded minds cannot be conscious, by Federico Faggin (2021) and Christof Koch (2025, 2026).
why_it_matters: AI welfare and moral-status work mostly assumes computational functionalism; Essentia publishes non-functionalist arguments (idealist, and Koch's Integrated Information Theory case) that current AI lacks experience, which welfare assessments and 'seemingly conscious AI' debates rarely engage.

Transfer convening: the essays inform its own readership. Framing critical (L): deflationary about AI consciousness. Org type media (H3): its activity is publishing essays, videos and books.

name: Chaplaincy Innovation Lab
summary: A US multifaith hub, founded in October 2018 by the sociologist Wendy Cadge and Trace Haythorn, that brings chaplains, theological and clinical educators and social scientists together on spiritual care. It runs subscriber webinars, certificates and courses for chaplains, a directory of Clinical Pastoral Education sites, free working papers and a weekly newsletter. Its AI engagement so far is one subscriber webinar, 'AI in Chaplaincy' (8 September 2026).
why_it_matters: Chaplains meet people in crisis, illness and dying, increasingly including people who turn to chatbots for spiritual companionship; their professional ethics of spiritual accompaniment (presence, boundaries, referral) is a codified practice that companion-AI design lacks. The Lab is a research-to-practice channel into US chaplaincy across healthcare, military and higher-education settings.

name: Greater Good Science Center (GGSC)
summary: A centre at the University of California, Berkeley, founded in 2001, that studies and popularises the science of wellbeing, compassion, gratitude and prosocial behaviour. It publishes Greater Good magazine, co-produces The Science of Happiness podcast with PRX, runs free online courses (The Science of Happiness has over 600,000 registrants) and programmes for educators, parents, workplaces and bridging differences. In 2026 the magazine ran several pieces on AI, on chatbots and intimacy, AI matchmaking and the purpose of education in an AI age.
why_it_matters: It holds the prosociality and relationship science that work on companion-AI harms and sycophancy draws on, and it reaches teachers, parents and managers at scale. It has no AI research programme, so this science has not yet been pointed at AI systems.

name: Nordic Bildung
summary: A Copenhagen 'philosophical and educational lab', founded in 2018, that promotes Bildung (self-cultivation through education and culture), drawing on the Nordic folk-high-school tradition, systems studies and metamodern thought. Its president is the author Lene Rachel Andersen, a member of the Club of Rome. It publishes books (The Nordic Secret, Polymodernity, Important, True, and Meaningful), runs online courses and study-circle-leader training, coordinates the Global Bildung Network, and offers keynotes and consulting. Its AI work is a bookable keynote, 'How to educate in a world with AI', and a June 2026 Folkemødet debate with DataEthics on freedom, AI and Big Tech.
why_it_matters: The Nordic popular-education model (folkeoplysning: folk high schools and study circles) is a tested template for mass civic learning that AI literacy and epistemic-autonomy efforts could borrow. It also connects the metamodern milieu int/a comes from to European debates on Big Tech power.

name: Copenhagen Institute for Futures Studies (CIFS)
summary: An independent nonprofit futures think tank in Copenhagen, founded in 1969 on the initiative of Thorkil Kristensen, a former Danish minister and OECD Secretary-General, and funded by consulting, courses and membership. Its H3 AI Lab, a 'think-and-do tank' led by Bugge Holm Hansen and Sofie Hvitved, studies how AI changes foresight practice, prototypes AI-assisted scenario tools ('liquid foresight') and publishes reports on technology futures. It co-hosts the UNESCO Chair in Anticipatory Leadership & Futures Capabilities with Aarhus University (since 2022) and publishes FARSIGHT magazine.
why_it_matters: Professional foresight (scenarios, horizon scanning, Three Horizons) is a method the AI-governance field uses little; CIFS has begun turning it on AGI, surveying foresight practitioners on AGI preparedness in 2025. It trains corporate and public-sector strategists, a channel through which thinking about the AI transition could reach organisations.

name: Institute for the Future (IFTF)
summary: A Palo Alto futures nonprofit founded in 1968 as a spin-off from the RAND Corporation and led by executive director Marina Gorbis. It produces the Ten-Year Forecast (since 1978), runs Foresight Essentials training, and does contract research and consulting for companies, foundations and governments, which brought in nearly all of its $8.9 million revenue in 2024. Its AI work includes 'Three Horizons of AI-Enabled Work and Workers' (2024), the Ethical OS toolkit for anticipating technology harms (made with Omidyar Network) and 'Foresight in the Age of AI', a statement of principles for using AI in futures practice (September 2026).
why_it_matters: Its methods (signals, scenarios, Three Horizons, public-imagination games) are anticipatory tools that AI governance rarely uses, and Ethical OS was an early attempt to bring harm anticipation into tech teams. Its foresight on AI and work bears on labour displacement and gradual disempowerment.

name: International Bateson Institute (IBI)
summary: A non-profit foundation, registered in Sweden and the USA and led by its founder and president Nora Bateson, that does 'transcontextual' research on living systems in the tradition of Gregory Bateson. Its main live programme is Warm Data: a group-inquiry method run as in-person Warm Data Labs and online People Need People sessions by certified hosts, plus a week-long Warm Data Course taught by Nora Bateson, with 2027 cohorts announced. It has no AI work.
why_it_matters: Gregory Bateson's argument that narrowly purposeful, single-objective optimisation cuts across the feedback loops of complex systems anticipates Goodhart-style outer-alignment worries and the case for non-maximising agents. Warm Data Labs are a ready-made format for labs, policymakers or communities to examine AI across many interlocking contexts at once rather than as a single technical problem.

name: Cultural Evolution Society (CES)
summary: An international learned society for the evolutionary study of human and animal culture, which grew out of a 2015 Evolution Institute workshop organised by Michele Gelfand and David Sloan Wilson. It runs a biennial conference (Rabat, Morocco, May 2026), small research, outreach and teaching grants, a free library of cultural-evolution course materials, a podcast and applied working groups on sustainability and natural-resource management. Neither its site, news nor working groups show any AI activity.
why_it_matters: Cultural-evolution theory (how cultural traits vary, spread and are selected) is the natural framework for 'machine culture': recommender systems and chatbots as new channels of social learning, cultural homogenisation by LLMs, and gradual disempowerment through cultural selection. Its members already hold this expertise (Maxime Derex, its ACE awards officer, co-authored 'Machine Culture' in 2023), and the society invites proposals for new applied working groups, so an AI group would be cheap to start.

tag_notes: Home life, sub life_biology (cultural evolution is named in that sub-tradition); secondary psych from cultural-psychology founders and members (Gelfand). Ring potential (E2): no AI activity on the site, 2025-26 news or working groups; transferable method: cultural-evolutionary models of variation, transmission and selection applied to machine culture, LLM-driven homogenisation and gradual disempowerment. Transfer none_yet (J6; taxonomy's own example). Org type membership (I: learned society with dues). Framing structural is nominal: the mission states no stakes; chosen because its knowledge bears on slow cultural drift. Region global with HQ distributed: no stated base. Partner = door to open.

name: Game B
summary: A loose movement that grew out of a series of 2012-13 meetings among Jordan Hall, Jim Rutt and others, which seeks a non-rivalrous, self-organising alternative ('Game B') to today's rivalrous civilisation ('Game A'). Its shared texts live on an open wiki and its members on a request-to-join Mighty Networks community; the wiki argues that exponential technologies, AI among them, pose existential risk in a win-lose world, and that optimising for any single metric is itself a 'Game A' habit. It has no organisation, programme or staff.
why_it_matters: Game B is one source of the Moloch, multipolar-trap and race framing now common in AI safety, and of the critique of single-metric optimisation; it shows how AI risk looks from inside a metacrisis diagnosis. Its people remain active elsewhere: Jim Rutt's podcast hosted Joe Edelman, an early Game B participant, on full-stack alignment in October 2025.

key_work.title: Game B wiki ('Game B' and 'An Introduction to Game B' pages)
The Jim Rutt Show EP 325: Joe Edelman on full-stack AI alignment

people: Jim Rutt (co-founder; host of The Jim Rutt Show)
Daniel Schmachtenberger (associated thinker, widely cited on the wiki)
status_evidence: Mar 2024: last edit to the wiki's main 'Game B' page (front page last edited Aug 2021). No 2025-26 activity found from the community itself; Jim Rutt's podcast, which is separate, was active in mid-2026.

Game B wiki (open editing, largely inactive)
The Jim Rutt Show podcast, which regularly covers Game B themes and AI
caveats: A movement and lineage of ideas rather than an organisation; no leadership, budget or programme. Community infrastructure looks dormant and the members-only site could not be checked for activity. Some early participants (e.g. Eric Weinstein) have since gone in very different directions. Independent sources could not be checked (search budget exhausted).
tag_notes: Home life, sub life_cybernetics (B7 names Game B as a metacrisis systems diagnosis). Ring potential (E2): no AI programme; AI appears only inside its core thesis that exponential tech in a win-lose world is an existential risk; transferable method: civilisational game-theoretic diagnosis of rivalrous dynamics (Moloch, multipolar traps) and the critique of single-metric optimisation. Transfer convening rather than none_yet because its texts do address AI risk for its own community; low confidence. Framing catastrophic (wiki: existential risk, self-terminating Game A). Status dormant (O): no 2025-26 community activity found. MISFIT: a movement or idea lineage, not an organisation.

name: Science and Nonduality (SAND)
summary: A nonprofit in Sebastopol, California, co-founded and run by Zaya and Maurizio Benazzo, that produces films, conferences, courses, podcasts and an online community where nondual spirituality, science, Indigenous wisdom and social healing meet. In 2026 it ran The Great AI Unraveling, five free online sessions from April to September with Tristan Harris, Indigenous speakers including Tiokasin Ghosthorse, Lyla June Johnston and Kathy Wan Povi Sanchez, and decolonial thinkers Vanessa Andreotti and Bayo Akomolafe. Related AI podcasts and a 9 October 2026 session with Michael Meade on AI and mythology followed.
why_it_matters: It is one of very few venues where a safety-literate voice (Harris, on AI risks) and contemplative, Indigenous and decolonial critics address the same large audience. The series treats AI as part of a civilisation built on separability, extraction and control, a metacrisis framing the AI-safety field rarely hears, and SAND would be a natural partner for 'speed of wisdom' storytelling.

key_work.title: The Great AI Unraveling series (five sessions, Apr-Sep)
AI, Mythology, and the Battle for the Soul of Humanity, with Michael Meade
Podcast: AI & Colonial Logic (Christian Ortiz, Thema Monroe-White)

funding: 501(c)(3), tax-exempt since 2015. 2025 revenue about $2.7m (about 72% programme services, 11% contributions), expenses about $2.2m, net assets about $9m (ProPublica Form 990 data). Memberships, donations and event and course fees.
status_evidence: 26 Sep 2026: fifth Great AI Unraveling session (Andreotti, Akomolafe, Alnoor Ladha); 9 Oct 2026 Michael Meade AI session scheduled.
engage: Great AI Unraveling and related community gatherings: free to attend live online, recordings for members
SAND membership and scholarships
Courses and immersions (e.g. Liberation Psychology, Sep 2026-May 2027; not AI-specific)

Form 990s report related-party transactions (Schedule L), consistent with a founder-run organisation.
tag_notes: Home contemplative, sub cont_integral (B1: a cross-traditional nondual spirituality-and-science community, not a body speaking for one religion; B7 integral milieu; its collective-healing work fits that sub-tradition); secondary indigenous from Indigenous advisory board members (Tiokasin Ghosthorse, Pat McCabe, Aviaja Sanimuinaq), board member Bayo Akomolafe, and the Indigenous and decolonial speakers who make up most of the AI series. Ring adjacent (E3): a five-session 2026 series plus podcasts is repeated convening, framed civilisationally rather than around catastrophic risk or alignment. Transfer convening (J5): brings its own community into the AI conversation. Framing structural: AI as part of a civilisational architecture of separability and extraction, explicitly beyond hype versus doom.

name: AI + Human Flourishing Initiative, Contemplative Sciences Center, University of Virginia
summary: A new initiative at the University of Virginia's Contemplative Sciences Center (founded 2012; home of the CIRCL research lab and the Journal of Contemplative Studies), co-directed by meditation researcher Michael Sheehy, that studies the two-way relationship between people and AI with human flourishing as the aim. It launches with the public AI Anxiety + Human Flourishing symposium (18-19 November 2026), whose four sessions cover AI anxiety, agency, contemplative interventions and possible futures. Speakers include UVA philosopher David Danks, psychologist Bethany Teachman (co-director of UVA's Thriving Youth in a Digital Environment lab), Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian, Pir Zia Inayat Khan and Fr. Michael Baggot, and a UVA undergraduate course on AI anxiety is the planned outcome.
why_it_matters: It treats young adults' AI-era distress (career obsolescence, digital alienation, existential dread) and loss of agency as a target for evidence-based contemplative interventions, combining contemplative science with clinical psychology. No alignment or AI-safety researcher is on the programme, so it is an open door for safety people to engage the human-wellbeing side of the transition.

key_work.title: AI Anxiety + Human Flourishing symposium, Contemplative Commons (18-19 Nov)

The programme mixes academics, contemplatives and entrepreneurs, and includes no AI-safety specialists; Paul Tudor Jones, the centre's founding donor, sits on its board but is not a listed speaker. The page names only Sheehy as co-director; the other co-director is not identified. The 'Agency' session mentions alignment, but the framing is young people's wellbeing.

Home contemplative, sub cont_science (B2: contemplative science and evidence-based contemplative interventions); secondary psych from the clinical-psychology input (Teachman, Crace) on the programme. Ring adjacent (E3): a named standing initiative launching with a symposium and a planned course, on AI anxiety and agency in young adults rather than catastrophic risk; borderline potential until it has a track record. Transfer protecting (J4): the students and young adults the university serves. Framing flourishing (L: the initiative is named for and aimed at flourishing). Status new: launched 2026.

name: Jubilee Centre for Character and Virtues
summary: A University of Birmingham research centre on character, virtues and values, founded in 2012 with John Templeton Foundation funding and directed by Tom Harrison. It does research, runs a distance-learning MA in Character Education, online professional courses and an annual Oxford conference, and publishes frameworks for character education in schools. Its staff have lectured on AI and practical wisdom since 2024, and in 2026 Harrison published four essays (April to September) arguing that AI makes cultivating judgment, or 'digital phronesis', the central aim of education.
why_it_matters: It is the most developed academic home for practical wisdom (phronesis) as a construct with measurement and teaching frameworks, which bears directly on evaluating 'wise AI' and on the moral deskilling of people who hand judgment to AI. It brings neo-Aristotelian virtue ethics to AI's effects on human formation, with no catastrophic-risk framing.

funding: Founded in 2012 with John Templeton Foundation funding; Templeton World Charity Foundation funds its Global Innovations for Character Development platform (extension announced 2024); Kern Award scholarships.

MA Character Education (distance learning) and online CPD courses, including professional ethics
PhD supervision

Transfer protecting (J4): the pupils and students whose character formation it serves, against outsourcing judgment to AI. Framing flourishing (L: mission is character in the interest of human flourishing). Online hub from distance MA and online CPD courses.

name: Lion's Roar
summary: An independent non-profit Buddhist magazine and website in Halifax, Nova Scotia, published by the Lion's Roar Foundation along with the practitioner quarterly Buddhadharma and a Spanish edition; it began as the Vajradhatu Sun in 1978 and was renamed from Shambhala Sun in 2015. It covers AI occasionally, about ten pieces since 2019. These include a 2023 podcast with Center for Humane Technology co-founder Randima Fernando, 'What AI Means for Buddhism' (2024), a report on deepfakes of Buddhist teachers (2024), and essays on AI as practice (2025) and on Yogacara and AI (2026).
why_it_matters: It reaches the largest English-language Buddhist readership (about 80,000 print copies) and frames AI through Buddhist accounts of mind, intention and right speech. Its coverage engages misuse and human-side risk but not misalignment, so it is an open channel through which safety-literate Buddhist writers could reach practitioners.

Ring changed from roster adjacent to potential (E2): about ten AI pieces since 2019 (2019 x2, 2023 x4, 2024 x2, 2025, 2026), occasional coverage rather than a sustained programme; transferable asset: Buddhist accounts of mind, intention and right speech, and reach into the largest English-language Buddhist readership. Transfer convening (J5): informs its own community. Framing present_harms is a judgment call across mixed pieces (misuse, bias, deepfakes, alongside positive practice essays). Online hub from recurring Lion's Roar Live sessions. Partner = door to open (no AI programme).

name: Future Generations Commissioner for Wales
summary: An independent statutory office created by the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015 to act as a guardian for people not yet born. It monitors and advises Welsh public bodies on their legal duty to consider long-term effects, runs Section 20 reviews (the 2026 energy review, Project Ynni), publishes a Future Generations Report every five years and offers futures tools and a leadership academy. Derek Walker has been Commissioner since March 2023.
why_it_matters: It is a working legal mechanism that obliges public bodies to weigh long-term and intergenerational effects, with an independent office that reviews and reports on them. That is a ready template for statutory long-term impact assessment of AI adoption by governments, and for representing future generations in AI governance, neither of which exists today.

Section 20 Review: Project Ynni (energy)
A Year of Impact, Powering Change (annual report 2025-26)

funding: Public funding as a statutory Welsh office (Welsh Government); budget not found.

Its 2026 priorities are climate, energy, inequality, health and food. Budget and staff numbers were not found.

Ring potential (E2): no AI programme or output found in 2024-26. Transferable method: a statutory future-generations duty with an independent guardian, Section 20 reviews and the 'five ways of working', usable as a template for long-term and intergenerational impact assessment of public-sector AI adoption. Transfer none_yet (J6): no AI work at all. Framing structural: its statements address long-term systemic failure (climate, inequality), not one catastrophe. Engagement partner only, since there is no AI programme.

name: Ada Lovelace Institute
summary: An independent research institute in London, set up in 2018 by the Nuffield Foundation (which it is still part of), whose mission is to make data and AI work for people and society. It runs programmes on AI law and policy, public participation research, social and economic policy, and emerging technology and industry practice, producing UK and EU regulatory analysis, public attitudes research and studies of AI in the public sector. Recent work includes options for UK AI regulation (September 2026), a scenario paper on a possible AI investment bubble (June 2026) and a project on regulation, civil liberties and concentrated power.
why_it_matters: It brings systematic evidence on public attitudes and lived experience into AI regulation, a source of democratic legitimacy the AI-safety field rarely produces. Its newer work on concentrated state and corporate control and on AI-sector financial scenarios overlaps with gradual-disempowerment and power-concentration concerns.

Ring adjacent (E3): a standing AI programme focused on societal effects and regulation, with no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing. Transfer into_institutions: its outputs are regulatory options, evidence for policymakers and participatory methods for governance. Framing structural: the mission stresses just distribution of AI's benefits, and recent work addresses concentrated power and systemic financial risk. Assurance is included for its AI assurance and foundation-model evaluation work.

name: AI Now Institute
summary: An independent policy research institute in New York, founded in 2017 by Kate Crawford and Meredith Whittaker (originally partnered with NYU), studying the political economy of AI. Its research areas include accountability, markets and competition, labour, geopolitics and industrial policy, data-centre infrastructure and climate, healthcare, and a safety and security strand that argues for safety-critical testing and independent oversight of AI. It publishes annual landscape reports ('Artificial Power', 2025), state and local policy toolkits, and technical security research such as 'Double Agents' (July 2026).
why_it_matters: It supplies a political-economy analysis of industry power and of the race narratives behind AI policy. Through its Chief AI Scientist, Heidy Khlaaf, it also makes a safety-critical-engineering case for independent oversight of high-risk AI, drawn from aviation and other regulated industries. It is a principled critic of x-risk framing that any bridge-building between AI safety and AI accountability has to reckon with.

Double Agents: Defensive AI Agents Magnify Cyber Risks
North Star Data Center Policy Toolkit

funding: Foundation-funded and refuses corporate funding, including from tech companies. Current supporters: Ford Foundation, Future of Technology Fund, Global Fund for a New Economy, Hewlett Foundation, Luminate, MacArthur Foundation, Omidyar Network and the Packard Foundation.
status_evidence: 17 Sep 2026: Amba Kak testified before the Monopoly Busters Caucus; 16 Sep 2026: advertised a local policy researcher role; 30 Sep 2026: Boyan Milanov quoted in the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists on 'AI doomerism'.
engage: Occasional staff and contractor roles (a local policy researcher/land-use expert role advertised in September 2026)
Newsletter and publications
caveats: Openly critical of x-risk discourse: in September 2026 its researchers called 'AI doomerism' unscientific and said it lets labs argue for self-regulation. Its Safety & Security research area means safety-critical engineering and independent oversight, not alignment. The roster's claim that it is a Humanity AI grantee was not confirmed; Humanity AI is not on its current list of funders.
tag_notes: Home economics (econ_power) under B9: its core output is political economy of industry power, competition and labour (Artificial Power report, antitrust testimony); safety is secondary for Khlaaf's safety-critical engineering work, law for accountability. Ring adjacent kept from the roster, but it is a borderline bridge under E3: it has a named Safety & Security research area with dedicated staff, though that strand rejects the AI-safety and x-risk frame and the institute's framing as a whole is about power. Transfer into_institutions: policy toolkits, testimony and oversight proposals. Framing structural (power concentration); its critique of x-risk is a means, not its main output (L).

name: Data & Society Research Institute
summary: An independent nonprofit research and policy institute in New York, launched in 2014 by danah boyd with early support from Microsoft Research, that studies the social effects of data-centric technology, automation and AI. Its programmes include AI on the Ground, the Algorithmic Impact Methods Lab (AIMLab, participatory methods for algorithmic impact assessment), Democracy in the Age of AI, Labor Futures and, from September 2026, a Worker Lens on the AI Economy. In September 2026 it published a 'Governing AI Agents' research collection, a letter to Congress on AI companies' 'pacing the frontier' approach, and an ethnographic report on data centres in Pennsylvania.
why_it_matters: It produces ethnographic and field evidence on how deployed AI changes work and civic life, plus participatory impact-assessment methods that evaluations of AI agents could borrow. Its 'Governing AI Agents' collection argues that individual human oversight of agents does not scale automatically, which bears directly on agent safety governance.

Transfer into_institutions: impact-assessment methods, policy blueprints and congressional letters. Framing present_harms: mission and outputs centre documented harms to workers and communities.

name: Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR)
summary: An independent, community-rooted AI research institute founded by Timnit Gebru in December 2021, with a team distributed across several continents. Its projects include the Data Workers' Inquiry (participatory research led by data workers in nine countries, run with the Weizenbaum Institute and TU Berlin), Surveillance Watch, a Refugees, Migrants and AI programme (2026), community-built language technology for East African languages, and the Mystery AI Hype Theater 3000 podcast. It also publishes critiques of the AGI paradigm, notably the 'TESCREAL bundle' paper.
why_it_matters: It does worker-led, participatory research on the data-labelling and moderation workforce behind AI, and builds community-owned alternatives. It is also the most developed critique of the AGI and x-risk paradigm (TESCREAL), so any int/a effort to bridge AI safety and AI ethics has to engage it.

Full_spectrum badge considered (worker-made zines and films, speculative futures workshops) but not given.

name: Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society at Harvard University
summary: A Harvard University interfaculty research centre, founded at Harvard Law School in 1996, that studies the internet, digital technology and society through faculty research, an annual fellows cohort and a public events programme. Its AI work covers legal frameworks for AI agents, accountability and litigation, AI and national security, and a youth-safety evaluation initiative launched in July 2026 with funding from Common Sense Media; it also has an Applied Social Media Lab and, since 2025, a Chief AI Scientist working on AI agency and benchmarks. Its 2026-27 speaker series, 'All Too Human', asks how AI is changing the ways people make meaning.
why_it_matters: It combines legal and governance scholarship with a large interdisciplinary fellows network that trains law-literate AI-governance people. Its 2026-27 series on AI and human meaning, and its youth-safety evaluation work, overlap with int/a's concern for human minds, relationships and meaning.
