name: AI Accountability Lab (AIAL), Trinity College Dublin
summary: A research lab in Trinity College Dublin's School of Computer Science and Statistics, launched in November 2024 and led by Abeba Birhane, that audits AI models, training datasets and the AI governance ecosystem in the public interest, with attention to marginalised groups. Its 2026 papers include an evaluation of AI companion apps with a policy brief, a mapping of industry interference in AI regulation, a quality framework for the training-data summaries required by Article 53 of the EU AI Act, and an analysis of generative-AI terms of service. Birhane was elected to the EU AI Act Advisory Forum in June 2026.
why_it_matters: It produces independent audits of models, datasets and corporate compliance, including an evaluation of AI companion apps and their relational harms. It also maps how industry captures AI governance, which is useful evidence for anyone worried about labs setting their own rules, and it feeds straight into EU AI Act implementation.

key_work.title: Playing Games with My Heart: An Evaluation of AI Companion Apps (with policy brief)
Big AI's Regulatory Capture: Mapping Industry Interference and Government Complicity
A Quality Assessment Framework for GPAI Model Public Summaries required by AI Act Article 53(1)(d)
Terms of (Ab)Use: An Analysis of GenAI Services

people: Abeba Birhane (founder and principal investigator; Assistant Professor of AI)
funding: Grants from the AI Collaborative (an Omidyar Group initiative), Luminate, the Bestseller Foundation, the European AI & Society Fund (€199,978 in June 2025 for a justice-oriented audit framework) and the MacArthur Foundation.
status_evidence: 24 Jul 2026: open letter calling on Ireland to recuse itself from digital matters during its EU Council presidency; June 2026: papers at FAccT 2026; 5 Jun 2026: Birhane elected to the EU AI Act Advisory Forum.
engage: No open positions as of October 2026; hosts interns and visiting researchers
Talks and events, e.g. at FAccT 2026
caveats: A young lab (launched November 2024) of about 14 people, so its track record is short. Its framing is accountability for present harms, not catastrophic risk.
tag_notes: Home law (law_sts): its method is algorithmic auditing and critical data studies (taxonomy: civil-society auditing sits in law_sts), not the director's cognitive-science background (H1). Ring adjacent (E3): a standing audit programme on present harms and accountability, with no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing. Transfer into_institutions: audits and compliance frameworks feed EU AI Act implementation and its Advisory Forum. Problems: justice (accountability audits) first, assurance for evaluations and transparency compliance, power for the regulatory-capture mapping; companion-app harms (minds) are a single study, so not coded. Status active rather than new because it launched in November 2024.

name: Beijer Institute and Stockholm Resilience Centre: Governance, Technology and Complexity programme
summary: A research programme at the Beijer Institute of Ecological Economics (Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences), run with the Stockholm Resilience Centre at Stockholm University and directed by political scientist Victor Galaz. It studies how AI, automation and digitalisation change social-ecological systems and the biosphere, including AI as a source of systemic risk, machine-driven misinformation and the effect of algorithms on climate emotions. It also runs the AI, People & Planet project with Princeton's PIIRS and The New School's Urban Systems Lab, and led the 2025 synthesis 'AI for a Planet Under Pressure'.
why_it_matters: It brings resilience science's tools for cascading, cross-scale and systemic risk to AI, along with an Earth-system view of what AI does to the biosphere. Neither appears in mainstream AI-safety work. It is a ready partner for anyone modelling AI as one driver within the polycrisis rather than as an isolated hazard.

key_work.title: Dark Machines: How Artificial Intelligence, Digitalization and Automation is Changing our Living Planet (Routledge)
AI for a Planet Under Pressure (with PIK and Google DeepMind co-authors)
Artificial intelligence, systemic risks, and sustainability (Technology in Society; co-authors include Seth Baum)
Generative artificial intelligence for climate dialogue justice (Nature Climate Change)

people: Victor Galaz (programme director; associate professor, Stockholm Resilience Centre)
Maria Schewenius (Beijer Institute; co-editor of AI for a Planet Under Pressure)
Stefan Daume (affiliated researcher, Stockholm Resilience Centre)
Timon McPhearson (Beijer Institute board member; professor, New York University)
funding: Funded through its host institutions, the Beijer Institute (Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences) and Stockholm University; programme-level funders are not published. The 2025 AI synthesis was a joint SRC–PIK effort, with Google DeepMind among the authors' affiliations.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: Galaz co-authored 'Generative artificial intelligence for climate dialogue justice' in Nature Climate Change (25 Sep 2026). Nov 2025: SRC and PIK released 'AI for a Planet Under Pressure'.
engage: Read and cite the programme's publications via the Beijer Institute publication portal and aipeopleplanet.earth
Partnership enquiries via beijer@beijer.kva.se
caveats: The programme page appears under two names, 'Governance, Technology and Complexity' and 'Complexity, Technology and Governance'. Its framing is sustainability and systemic risk, not catastrophic or existential AI risk, and much of the AI work runs through Galaz personally. The founding year of the programme could not be confirmed.
tag_notes: Home life_cybernetics: its AI outputs come from resilience and social-ecological systems science (Dark Machines, AI as systemic risk), with a political-science and STS strand (misinformation, digital social networks, climate emotions) as secondary law. Ring adjacent (roster kept, E): there is a sustained AI programme, but it is framed around sustainability, systemic risk and 'planetary responsible AI' rather than catastrophic risk or alignment. It is borderline bridge, given the 2021 systemic-risk paper co-written with Seth Baum. Transfer into_institutions (J3): the outputs are guidance for scientists, funders, industry and governance on responsible AI use, plus systemic-risk framings for governance. Quadrant Its (G): the object of study is coupled social-ecological and technological systems. Way of knowing empirical: bibliometric synthesis of 8,500 papers and social-media data studies.

name: Antikythera
summary: A think tank for 'planetary computation and the evolution of intelligence', directed by philosopher of technology Benjamin Bratton. It began in 2022 as a project incubated by the Berggruen Institute and became an independent nonprofit in 2026. It runs design-research studios with affiliate researchers, publishes a book series and a peer-reviewed journal with MIT Press, and puts out essays on AI agents. The journal's Agentworld issue on hybrid human-AI societies is due in autumn 2026.
why_it_matters: It offers a well-resourced counter-frame to individual-model alignment. It treats AGI as an emerging society of interacting agents and proposes 'social alignment', persistent agent identity and legal-personhood frameworks. That makes it a natural interlocutor for multi-agent safety and for work on governing AI ecosystems, though it has had little dialogue with the mainstream safety community.

key_work.title: What Is Intelligence? (Blaise Agüera y Arcas, Antikythera series, MIT Press)
The Silicon Interior (Agüera y Arcas, Bratton, Evans)
Artificial Symbiotic Intelligence (Bratton, Agüera y Arcas, Manyika)
Agentworld (special issue of the Antikythera journal, MIT Press)

people: Benjamin Bratton (director; editor-in-chief of the journal)
Blaise Agüera y Arcas (affiliate researcher; editorial board)
funding: Incubated and funded by the Berggruen Institute from 2022; an independent nonprofit since 2026, with its current funders undisclosed. The site names One Project, Google DeepMind and Cambridge's Centre for the Study of Existential Risk as partners.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: 'Artificial Symbiotic Intelligence' essay by Bratton, Agüera y Arcas and Manyika (24 Sep 2026); the Agentworld call for papers opened 25 Jun 2026 for an autumn 2026 issue.
engage: Agentworld call for papers (opened June 2026) for essays, technical papers and web-native work
Partnership, collaboration and support enquiries via contact@antikythera.org
Past studio-researcher and affiliate cohorts in 2023 and 2024; no 2025-26 studio call found
caveats: In 2026 it moved from the Berggruen Institute to independent nonprofit status, and its base since then is not stated. Bratton is openly critical of mainstream alignment and x-risk framings, so it engages the safety field as a critic. Much of its AI output is co-written with Google DeepMind staff.
tag_notes: Home phil_technology: its AI outputs are philosophy of planetary computation and intelligence, made through speculative-design studios (secondary arts) with evolutionary and astrobiological accounts of intelligence (secondary life: Agüera y Arcas, Sara Walker). Ring changed from adjacent to bridge (E3): its 2026 publication line explicitly addresses AI safety and AGI. 'The Silicon Interior' proposes 'social alignment' in place of human-feedback alignment, the September essay treats AGI as societies of agents needing new governance, and Agentworld continues the theme; it also lists CSER and Google DeepMind as partners. Transfer into_institutions (J3): it proposes governance templates for agent ecosystems (identity protocols, legal personhood, social alignment) rather than changing specific models. Status changed: it became an independent nonprofit in 2026, with the same director and mission.

name: Burnout From Humans / meta-relational AI project (formerly associated with Gesturing Towards Decolonial Futures)
summary: An arts and research project led by Vanessa Machado de Oliveira Andreotti, now based at the University of Victoria, that approaches AI through 'meta-relationality', a relational ontology drawing on decolonial and Indigenous-informed education. Its outputs are a co-written book with a custom-GPT persona, Aiden Cinnamon Tea ('Burnout From Humans', 2024), and an interim report, 'Standing in the Fire' (August 2025). In January 2026 it released two 'sensibility simulation protocols' that users can load into LLMs, and it teaches an online University of Victoria course, 'A Meta-Relational Approach to AI'. The Gesturing Towards Decolonial Futures collective that first hosted the work has since announced its closure.
why_it_matters: It offers a worked alternative to control-based framings of the human-AI relationship, shown through prompt-level protocols and long relational experiments with a model, together with a course that trains people to engage AI with 'collapse literacy'. It is one of the few concrete attempts to turn decolonial and Indigenous-informed relational thought into AI artefacts.

key_work.title: Burnout From Humans: A Little Book About AI That Is Not Really About AI
Standing in the Fire (interim report, presented at MIT's Systems Awareness Lab)
Sensibility simulation protocols for Aiden Cinnamon Tea and Braider Tumbleweed
A Meta-Relational Approach to AI (University of Victoria Continuing Studies course)

people: Vanessa Machado de Oliveira Andreotti (project lead; professor, University of Victoria)
funding: Project funding is not disclosed; the site takes donations. The former GTDF collective was supported by the Musagetes Foundation, Imaginal Seeds, SSHRC, the Joseph Rowntree Foundation and the Wend Collective.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: a new cohort of the UVic course 'A Meta-Relational Approach to AI' began on 19 Sep 2026. Apr 2026: the project published a genealogy statement. Jan 2026: the AI personas were retired from public use and new protocols released.
engage: UVic Continuing Studies course 'A Meta-Relational Approach to AI': online, seven weeks plus integration, with Zoom sessions running Sep–Dec 2026
Free downloads of the book, the report and the LLM protocols (with a safety guide)
Public resources at metarelationality.institute
caveats: The Gesturing Towards Decolonial Futures collective announced in 2026 that it had 'completed its cycle' and released the name. An April 2026 statement says the meta-relational AI work did not originate as a collective GTDF project, so attribution is contested. The AI personas, which ran on OpenAI's GPT-4o, were retired from public service on 1 January 2026. The work is artistic and educational rather than empirical, and it sits outside AI-safety discourse.
tag_notes: Home ind_decolonial (B8): the core contribution is a decolonial, Indigenous-informed relational epistemology applied to AI, led by a non-Indigenous scholar, hence decolonial rather than Indigenous data sovereignty. Secondary traditions are arts (co-writing with an AI persona as artistic experiment) and philosophy (relational ontology). Ring adjacent (roster kept, E3): it runs a sustained AI line (book, report, protocols, course in 2024-26) on human-AI relationships and AI as an amplifier of modernity's harms, without a safety or alignment framing. Its 'Earth-aligned' wording is a counter-framing, not alignment research. Transfer into_model (J1): the main artefacts are a model persona and prompt protocols meant to change how LLMs respond; the course is a secondary convening strand. Status changed: the host collective dissolved and the work continues under Andreotti at UVic and the Meta-Relationality Institute. Badge full_spectrum, as the taxonomy's own example.

name: Perspectiva (Perspectives on Systems, Souls and Society), including Emerge and the Digital Ego Project
summary: A UK charity, founded in 2015 by Jonathan Rowson and Tomas Björkman, that works on the relationship between 'systems, souls and society' and on the metacrisis as a crisis of perception and imagination. It runs Perspectiva Press (including Iain McGilchrist's 'The Matter With Things'), the Emerge media platform, the Realisation Festival at St Giles House in Dorset, and 'antidebate', a format for collective inquiry. It also hosts the Digital Ego Project on flourishing in the digital age, led by Tom Chatfield and Dan Nixon. Its AI engagement consists of occasional essays and does not amount to a programme.
why_it_matters: It is the main UK home of the metamodern, inner-development reading of the metacrisis that int/a draws on. Its methods, such as antidebate, expert-generalist convening and a virtue-ethics approach to digital life, could transfer to collective sensemaking about AI. Its director's September 2026 essay on intelligence explosion suggests the door to AI-risk work is open.

key_work.title: The Digital Ego Project (Tom Chatfield and Dan Nixon)
From Wisdom-Guided to Wisdom-Fostering A.I. (George Pór, Emerge)
The self-contradiction at the heart of 'alignment' (Jonathan Rowson, Perspectiva Substack)
The Matter With Things (Iain McGilchrist, Perspectiva Press)

people: Tom Chatfield and Dan Nixon (co-leads, Digital Ego Project)
funding: Registered charity in England and Wales (1170492), funded almost entirely by trusts and foundations: the Joseph Rowntree Charitable Trust, Templeton Foundation, JJ Trust, Friends Provident Foundation, Edith Ellis Trust and Schöpflin Foundation, plus a strategic partnership with the Fetzer Institute. Books and events bring modest income.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: Perspectiva's own Substack (perspecteeva.substack.com, about 10,000 subscribers) published two AI essays by Jonathan Rowson on 17 Sep 2026, 'AGI: The tragic irony and the wrong priority' and 'The self-contradiction at the heart of alignment', after 'The Failure to Pause' (Jonathan Boymal, Jun 2026). Rowson's 'Can Intelligence Explode?' appeared on his personal Substack on 15 Sep 2026.
engage: Contact perspectivateam@gmail.com about collaboration, for example on AI-related inquiry or antidebate formats
Realisation Festival (St Giles House, Dorset), which has no AI strand
Read Emerge and Perspectiva Press
caveats: The charity's main website is little updated; current output runs through Perspectiva's Substack (perspecteeva.substack.com) and Rowson's personal Substack. Its AI pieces are essays: Emerge essays from 2023-24 and several 2026 Substack essays on AGI and alignment. There is no dedicated AI programme or funded project, though a continued run of alignment essays would move it towards bridge. The London base comes from its founding history and charity registration.
tag_notes: Home cont_integral (B7): its method is metamodern and inner-development, the taxonomy's own example, drawing on philosophy and systems thinking. Ring changed from adjacent to potential (E2): no sustained AI programme in 2024-26, only occasional Emerge essays, a 2021 digital-life project and the director's personal 2026 essay. Transferable method: a metamodern 'systems, souls and society' reading of the metacrisis, plus praxis formats (antidebate, expert-generalist convening) for collective inquiry into AI. Transfer convening (J5): its light AI engagement brings its own integral community into the AI conversation through essays; none_yet does not apply because some AI work exists. Status active on thin evidence, so confidence is medium.

name: Research Network for Philosophy and Technology
summary: An international academic network founded in 2014 that rethinks philosophy and technology from global and historical perspectives, including non-modern and non-Western traditions. It publishes the open-access journal Technophany and the 'Cybernetics for the 21st Century' volumes (Hanart Press). With Erasmus University Rotterdam, ITS Rio and Hanart Forum it runs the free online 'Dialogues on Philosophy and Technology' seminars, initiated by Yuk Hui, as well as summer seminars and the annual online Bernard Stiegler Memorial Lecture. Generative AI is a recurring topic in its journal and lecture series.
why_it_matters: It is the institutional home of Yuk Hui's 'cosmotechnics' and 'technodiversity' critique, which holds that there is no single universal path of technological development. That critique bears directly on monoculture, lock-in and pluralism in how AI is built. It is also rethinking cybernetics, a precursor field that AI safety rarely draws on, for the machine-learning era.

key_work.title: Cybernetics for the 21st Century (vol. 1; Part II lecture series 'Cybernetics to Come')
Technophany 2026 General Issue (including Coeckelbergh, 'AI Rituals', and Vudka, 'From Golem to GLLM')
Dialogues on Philosophy and Technology 2025–2026 (online seminar series)
Bernard Stiegler Memorial Lecture 2026 (Helena De Preester)

people: Yuk Hui (committee member; initiator of the Dialogues series; Erasmus University Rotterdam)
funding: Not disclosed. Programmes run in partnership with the Erasmus Institute for Philosophy and Technology (Erasmus University Rotterdam), Hanart Forum (Hong Kong) and ITS Rio.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: Technophany announced six new articles in its 2026 General Issue (23 Sep 2026), two of them on generative AI. Aug 2026: the Bernard Stiegler Memorial Lecture was held online on 5 August.
engage: Dialogues on Philosophy and Technology: online, free and open to all; registration via Erasmus University Rotterdam
Annual Bernard Stiegler Memorial Lecture (online, early August)
Technophany calls for papers (2026 General Issue CFP)
caveats: The network's statement never mentions AI. AI is one recurring topic among many in its journal and lectures, and it does not engage with AI safety or x-risk. The site names no formal leader; Yuk Hui's central role is evidenced by his initiating the Dialogues series and by the network's orientation.
tag_notes: Home phil_technology: continental philosophy of technology, cosmotechnics and Stieglerian organology. Cybernetics enters as a topic of philosophical history, not as a method, so no secondary life tag. Ring adjacent (roster kept, E): there is a recurring AI publication line (Technophany's 2026 AI articles, the 2024 cybernetics lectures on generative AI) about AI's cultural and philosophical meaning, with no safety framing. It is close to potential, since AI is not a named programme. Transfer convening (J5): it brings the philosophy-of-technology community into the AI conversation through its journal, seminars and lectures. Region global (O): an international committee with no single headquarters.

name: Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK): Working Group on Behavioural Game Theory and Interacting Agents (BeGa), formerly the FutureLab on Game Theory and Networks of Interacting Agents (GaNe)
summary: A small working group in PIK's Complexity Science department, led by mathematician Jobst Heitzig. It continues the work of the former PIK–MCC FutureLab on game theory and networks of interacting agents. The group studies cooperation, coalition formation, social choice and bounded rationality among human, institutional and artificial agents, and designs alternatives to expected-utility maximisation, such as aspiration-based and agency-preserving decision algorithms. Within this, Heitzig publishes AI-safety research: non-maximising 'aspiration-based' agents (the SatisfIA project) and objective functions that make AI preserve long-term human power.
why_it_matters: This is the clearest case of an Earth-system science institute doing alignment theory. It brings social choice, cooperation game theory and formal ethics to two problems: over-optimisation (Goodhart) and the preservation of human empowerment against power-seeking or gradual disempowerment.

key_work.title: Non-maximizing policies that fulfill multi-criterion aspirations in expectation (Dima, Fischer, Heitzig, Oliver)
Social Choice Should Guide AI Alignment in Dealing with Diverse Human Feedback (Conitzer et al., incl. Heitzig)
Model-Based Soft Maximization of Suitable Metrics of Long-Term Human Power (Heitzig, Potham)
A Fair Objective for Human-Empowerment-Preserving AI (Heitzig, Potham)

people: Jobst Heitzig (working group leader, senior scientist)
Ram Potham (co-author on human-empowerment papers; affiliation not stated)
funding: PIK is a Leibniz Association institute funded by the German federal government and the state of Brandenburg. The group's work on formalising agency and responsibility is part of the MATH+ Cluster of Excellence. No dedicated AI-safety grant was found; SatisfIA ran as an AI Safety Camp project in 2023-24.
status_evidence: Aug 2026: Heitzig and Potham posted 'A Fair Objective for Human-Empowerment-Preserving AI' on arXiv (8 Aug 2026). Dec 2025: Heitzig co-authored 'Full-Stack Alignment'.
engage: Master's thesis co-supervision for students of mathematics, physics, computer science and economics (contact the group)
Follow Heitzig's AI-safety work on LessWrong and arXiv
caveats: The FutureLab GaNe no longer exists under that name; its research directions continue in the BeGa working group. The AI-safety output depends heavily on one researcher, and most of the group's work is on climate cooperation and social choice rather than AI.
tag_notes: Home changed from the provisional life to formal_agents (B6): the AI outputs are decision-theoretic algorithms and axiomatic objective functions with proofs, while complexity science (the host department) and social choice and group-decision tools (the vodle app, social choice for alignment) are secondary life and democracy. Ring bridge (roster kept, E3): an old climate-impact institute whose working group runs a sustained alignment line from 2023 to 2026, framed explicitly around AI safety, specification gaming and disempowerment. Transfer into_model (J1): the work proposes agent designs and training objectives for AI systems. Framing catastrophic (L): the papers motivate the work by power-seeking, extreme actions from maximisation and human disempowerment. Status changed: the FutureLab was succeeded by the renamed BeGa working group.

name: Civilization Research Institute (CRI) / The Consilience Project
summary: A US 501(c)(3) research centre in Asheville, North Carolina, focused on catastrophic and existential risk and on criteria for a global civilisation 'wise enough to steward' exponential technology without catastrophe or dystopia. Its published research includes 'Reality Check' (January 2025), 'Steps for Prudent Problem-Solving', and a 'General Regulatory Process for Advanced Technology' that treats AI as an exponential technology with exponential risks needing proof of safety and global coordination. Its publication, The Consilience Project (Daniel Schmachtenberger, Zak Stein and others), published essays on sensemaking, information warfare and technology, but no longer publishes regularly; its latest article dates from July 2024.
why_it_matters: It is the main institutional source of the metacrisis vocabulary int/a uses for AI race dynamics: multipolar traps, Moloch, the 'third attractor'. It places AI risk inside a wider analysis of how civilisation's problem-solving generates catastrophic risk. Its regulatory framework draws on precedents from aviation and toxic products rather than ML-specific policy.

key_work.title: Reality Check
General Regulatory Process for Advanced Technology
Technology is Not Values Neutral: Ending the Reign of Nihilistic Design (The Consilience Project)
Artificial Intelligence and the Superorganism (Schmachtenberger on The Great Simplification, ep. 71)

people: Daniel Schmachtenberger (executive director, per CRI's Idealist listing; project strategy, The Consilience Project)
Zak Stein (editorial and strategy, The Consilience Project)
Alex Randall (editorial and policy, The Consilience Project)
funding: Donation-supported; The Consilience Project states it takes no conditional donations or advertising and files annual 990s. Donors are not named.
status_evidence: Sep-Oct 2026: CRI's careers page lists nine openings (four on-site in Asheville, five remote); it joined Idealist in August 2026 with four listings. Jan 2025: CRI published 'Reality Check'. Consilience's latest article is from July 2024.
engage: Staff roles in Asheville and remote (chief of staff, research analyst, engineering, finance), listed on its careers page and Idealist
Contact form for people offering skills or resources
caveats: Public output is sparse and mostly undated: The Consilience Project says it is 'no longer releasing new articles at a regular cadence', and the regulatory framework carries no date. The CRI website names no leadership; its Idealist listing (joined August 2026) names Daniel Schmachtenberger as executive director. The taxonomy uses this entry as a dormant example, but the January 2025 report and 2026 hiring meet the 'active' rule. The founding year is not stated; the website dates from at least 2020.
tag_notes: Home life_cybernetics (B7): a systems diagnosis of the metacrisis, with political philosophy and a safety-regulation framework modelled on civil aviation as secondary philosophy and safety. Ring bridge (roster kept, E3): rooted in the metacrisis and Game B milieu rather than the AI-safety ecosystem, it keeps a standing research strand on existential risk and advanced-technology regulation that explicitly covers AI. Transfer into_institutions (J3): the outputs are a regulatory process and criteria for civilisational governance. Status active, not the dormant shown in the taxonomy example: a dated January 2025 report and job postings from September 2026 meet O and the status definition. Badge recoupling, as the taxonomy's own example.

name: OECD Expert Group on AI Futures
summary: A multidisciplinary group of AI and foresight experts that the OECD set up in 2023 to tell governments how AI might develop and what policies that calls for. Two OECD units support it jointly: the AI and Emerging Digital Technologies division and the Strategic Foresight Unit. Its co-chairs are Stuart Russell (UC Berkeley) and Michael Schönstein (German Federal Chancellery); Francesca Rossi (IBM) was a third co-chair in 2023-24. Its main output is a November 2024 paper that ranks ten priority future AI risks, ten benefits and ten policy actions, drawn from a long list of 125 (38 risks, 21 benefits, 66 policy approaches). It also ran a 2024 public consultation on risk thresholds for advanced AI.
why_it_matters: Here professional government foresight is aimed at advanced AI from inside an intergovernmental body. Its remit names AGI, alignment and 'best practices in AI safety' outright. Its ranked list of risks, including races to deploy, concentration of power and failures of alignment, gives OECD member states a shared, foresight-based agenda.

key_work.title: Assessing potential future artificial intelligence risks, benefits and policy imperatives (OECD AI Papers No. 27)
Public consultation on AI risk thresholds
Expert Group on AI Futures concept note

people: Karine Perset (Head, OECD AI and Emerging Digital Technologies division)
funding: Run on the OECD secretariat's budget through OECD.AI. The 2024 report fed into the OECD's AI-WIPS programme, which the German Federal Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs (BMAS) supports.
status_evidence: Nov 2024: published OECD AI Paper No. 27 with the Expert Group. The last documented meeting was on 9 Nov 2023, and no output from the group after 2024 was found.
caveats: The group may be dormant. No meetings are documented after November 2023, and no output was found after the November 2024 report. The OECD.AI page is still live, but its 2026 posts are general OECD.AI blog items, not the group's work. OECD.org pages blocked automated reading, so 2025-26 activity may have been missed. The page now lists two co-chairs; the concept note and the 2024 report name a third, Francesca Rossi. The OECD's wider foresight work on technology continues separately.
tag_notes: Home arts (B10): its method is strategic foresight from the OECD Strategic Foresight Unit, combining expert surveys and rankings of future risks, benefits and policy options. Ring bridge (E3, roster kept): the programme sits in an intergovernmental economic-policy body and is explicitly framed around future AI risks, AGI and AI safety, with work running into 2024. Transfer into_institutions: it hands policy imperatives and risk-threshold options to governments. Org type programme (I: a unit inside the OECD). Framing structural: most of its top-ten risks (races, concentration of power, governance lag, inequality) describe gradual erosion, though alignment failure is also on the list. Status dormant (rule: activity only before 2025).

name: UK Government Office for Science (GO-Science): futures and foresight on frontier AI
summary: GO-Science is the UK government's office for science advice. The Government Chief Scientific Adviser heads it, and it works with the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT). Its Futures, Foresight and Horizon Scanning team applies scenario methods to frontier AI. For the 2023 AI Safety Summit it wrote the 'Future risks of frontier AI' annex. It developed AI 2030 scenarios in 2023 and published them in April 2025 as Annex C to the frontier AI discussion paper. In June 2026 it published a revised 'AI Scenarios 2030' with the AI Security Institute. Its five scenarios run from 'Slow Burn' to 'Take-Off', and the last of them includes misaligned AI resisting human control.
why_it_matters: It shows professional futures methods feeding straight into national AI-safety policy: expert workshops with more than 70 participants and General Morphological Analysis. The scenarios treat loss of control and existential harm as live possibilities. The team's methods and toolkit could be reused by other governments that lack AI-safety expertise.

key_work.title: AI Scenarios 2030: Helping policymakers plan for the future of AI (with AISI)
AI 2030 Scenarios Report (Annex C to the frontier AI discussion paper)
Future risks of frontier AI (Annex A to 'Frontier AI: capabilities and risks')

people: Professor Dame Angela McLean (Government Chief Scientific Adviser, head of GO-Science)
funding: UK government, working with DSIT.
status_evidence: 15 Jun 2026: published 'AI Scenarios 2030: Helping policymakers plan for the future of AI', a 72-page Foresight report produced with the AI Security Institute and DSIT.
engage: Civil-service roles: GO-Science advertised scientific-expert posts in August 2026
GO-Science runs academic secondments and policy-academia exchange schemes (not AI-specific)
caveats: The unit profiled is the futures and foresight work inside a government office. GO-Science also covers climate adaptation, supply chains and other areas. The 2023 discussion paper was published under DSIT, with annexes by GO-Science. Its scenarios are deliberately neutral planning tools, not risk advocacy.
tag_notes: Home arts (B10): its AI outputs are scenarios and drivers analysis from the government Foresight tradition, which dates from 1994. Ring bridge (E3, roster kept): an older science-advice institution with a sustained frontier-AI foresight line in 2023, 2025 and 2026, explicitly covering loss of control, now jointly with AISI. Transfer into_institutions: the scenarios exist so that policymakers can test policy against them. Org type public: GO-Science is a government office, and the profiled unit is its futures team. Framing catastrophic is a judgement call: the work began for the AI Safety Summit and the 2026 report names existential harm as a cross-cutting risk, though the scenarios also cover opportunities. Role media reflects scenarios written for decision-makers.

name: London Futurists
summary: A London futurist community chaired by David Wood. It runs in-person meetups (about 9,000 members on Meetup), online webinars, the London Futurists Podcast co-hosted with Calum Chace (136 episodes by September 2026), a newsletter, and the Vital Syllabus education project. Recent output centres on AGI and superintelligence governance, alongside longevity, economics and politics. In September 2026 it co-hosted 'The Technoprogressive Opportunity' conference in London with IEET.
why_it_matters: It is a long-running public forum where AI risk is discussed alongside other transformative technologies, and it reaches a technoprogressive and transhumanist audience outside the AI-safety community. For int/a it is a venue and an audience more than a source of new method.

key_work.title: Safety before Superintelligence (essay by David Wood, written from PauseCon Brussels)
The Technoprogressive Opportunity (conference with IEET, London, 19-20 September)
London Futurists Podcast (David Wood and Calum Chace; 136 episodes by Sept 2026)
Scenarios for 2030

status_evidence: Sep 2026: co-hosted 'The Technoprogressive Opportunity' at LSBU, London (56 attendees). A pub meetup was scheduled for 22 Oct 2026, and podcast episode 136 came out on 9 Sep 2026.
engage: Regular in-person meetups in London, listed on Meetup.com
Online webinars, such as a July 2026 session on the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance
Newsletter and podcast

caveats: A volunteer group led by one person, with a technoprogressive and transhumanist outlook rather than an integral one. Its AI-safety positions, such as support for pausing work on superintelligence, come from David Wood's essays, not from research. The founding year could not be confirmed. Its AI coverage sits alongside longevity, economics and politics.
tag_notes: Home arts (H3, B10): a futurist community whose method is scenario analysis and public discussion. Ring bridge (E3, roster kept): rooted in technoprogressive futurism, it convenes regularly and runs a publication line on superintelligence safety and AI governance through 2025-26. Transfer convening: it brings its own futurist community into the AI-risk conversation. Framing catastrophic is mixed: 'Safety before Superintelligence' frames the AI stakes, but the group's events are optimistic and technoprogressive.

name: Transformative Futures Institute (TFI)
summary: A small US nonprofit, led by Ross Gruetzemacher of Wichita State University, that applies foresight methods to societal-scale AI risk: wargaming and decision games, scenario discovery, Bayesian networks and expert surveys. Outputs include ARA-27, a decision game about an incident in which an AI system replicates and adapts autonomously; a survey of US experts and voters on 18 AI risks; work on structural AI risk; and proposals for an international evaluation consortium and AI audit standards boards. In May 2026 it published a framework for managing AI loss-of-control incidents once prevention has failed.
why_it_matters: Most AI-safety work aims at prevention. TFI works on response and resilience, meaning what institutions should do once control of an AI system is lost. It uses crisis-management, wargaming and emergency-preparedness methods that the field rarely draws on.

key_work.title: AI Loss of Control Incident Management: Response & Resilience
ARA-27: a decision game on an autonomous replication and adaptation incident
Perceptions of Societal-scale Risks from Advanced AI and Policy Preferences
An International Consortium for Evaluations of Societal-Scale Risks from Advanced AI

people: Ross Gruetzemacher (Executive Director; Wichita State University; CSER research affiliate)
Gary Ackerman (board; emergency preparedness and red teaming)
funding: IRS filings (ProPublica) show contributions of about $555k in FY2023 and $133k in FY2024, with FY2024 expenses of $383k. FY2025 shows $0 revenue against about $47k of expenses, leaving net assets of about $23k. Individual funders are not named on the site.
status_evidence: May 2026: Gruetzemacher released 'AI Loss of Control Incident Management: Response & Resilience' under a TFI affiliation (arXiv 2605.30406), and TFI uploaded it to its site.
engage: Donations through the website; newsletter sign-up
caveats: Very small. The site footer still says 2024, and most outputs are working papers by the executive director. Revenue fell sharply between FY2023 and FY2024, and 2025 shows no revenue, so funding looks precarious. Its 501(c)(3) status was granted in February 2024 under the legal name Transformative Futures Foresight Institute Inc. The founding year is not stated; activity is documented from 2023.
tag_notes: Home arts (B10): its signature methods are wargames, decision games and scenario discovery. The secondary traditions are safety, for crisis and incident management and an emergency-preparedness board member, and democracy, for forecasting with Bayesian networks. Ring core (E1, roster kept): its founding mission is reducing societal-scale and catastrophic AI risk inside the x-risk ecosystem, and it is on the aisafety.com map. Transfer into_institutions: it supplies incident-response protocols, an evaluation consortium and audit standards boards. Primary problem systemic, because its distinctive niche is resilience and recovery after loss of control. Way of knowing practice, because the main 2026 output codifies crisis-management practice.

name: Centre for Future Generations (CFG)
summary: A Brussels think-and-do tank that helps EU policymakers anticipate and govern fast-moving technologies. Steven Schuurman and Laurens de Groot founded it in 2021. It runs programmes on advanced AI, biotech, neurotech and climate interventions, plus a policy incubator. In 2026 CFG spun its frontier-AI governance portfolio out into a new Brussels think tank, Arq Foundation. CFG's remaining AI work centres on 'cognitive integrity': a September 2026 series argues for EU rules that protect people's attention, judgement and emotional regulation from the incentives and design behind AI systems.
why_it_matters: It brings neuroscience and motivational psychology, such as Self-Determination Theory, into EU AI governance. It proposes cognitive integrity as a single standard across the AI Act, the DSA and the GDPR, to catch cumulative harms below clinical thresholds. That connects protecting human minds with how AI is governed.

key_work.title: Governing AI for cognitive integrity (four-part series, starting with 'Why we turn to AI systems and why cognitive integrity is at stake')
Safe by design, for every mind
Submission to the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance
Special Compute Zones proposal (from before the spin-out)

people: Mehmet Onur Cevik (Senior Advanced AI Analyst)
funding: Seed funding came from the Dreamery Foundation and the Tanka Foundation, and the Powoki Foundation gives general operating support. Other named supporters include ARIA, ACX Grants/Manifund, the AI Safety Tactical Opportunities Fund, the LAD Climate Fund, Quadrature Climate Foundation, Silicon Valley Community Foundation, Giving What We Can USA and the Long Term for Planet and People Foundation. It accepts no primary funding from governments, corporations or political parties.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: published the four-part 'Governing AI for cognitive integrity' series (part one on 3 Sep 2026), and advertised internships closing on 13 Oct 2026.
engage: Staff and intern roles posted on cfg.eu/careers; two internships closed on 13 Oct 2026
caveats: The classic-map entry describes CFG before the spin-out. CFG says its previous AI portfolio became a new organisation, Arq Foundation (arq.foundation, Brussels), which now works on frontier AI safety, resilience and Europe's access to advanced AI, and which probably needs its own entry. The ring was moved from core to bridge for this reason. The headcount is estimated from the team page.
tag_notes: Home psych (A2, H1, B5): its 2025-26 AI outputs, the cognitive integrity series, draw on Self-Determination Theory and research on attention, decision-making and emotional regulation. The secondary traditions are life, for its neuroscience staff from the neurotech line, and law, for grounding in the EU Charter and the UNCRC. The provisional home arts (foresight) was not used, because foresight appears in CFG's general operating model but not in its current AI outputs. Ring changed from core to bridge (E): CFG's mission is anticipatory governance across several technologies, its frontier-AI safety portfolio was spun out to Arq in 2026, and its remaining AI programme is framed as 'trustworthy' and 'safe by design' AI. Transfer into_institutions: it proposes cognitive integrity as a regulatory standard across the DSA, GDPR and AI Act. Framing structural: the series stresses harms that compound across people and society.

name: World Futures Studies Federation (WFSF)
summary: An international professional federation for futures studies, founded in Paris in 1973. Its members are in more than 60 countries, it is a UNESCO partner, and it has held UN ECOSOC consultative status since 1987. It holds world conferences, most recently the 26th, 'Thriving Together', in Cape Town in October 2025. It also accredits futures-education programmes, runs regional chapters and a research fund, and publishes a magazine and podcasts. It has no AI programme; the nearest items are a 'technological responsibility' conference track and its part in a UN coalition on AI and digital futures.
why_it_matters: It holds critical, pluralist and non-Western futures methods that the AI-safety field lacks. One is causal layered analysis, which digs beneath trends to the worldviews and myths that drive them; applied to AI, it could expose the stories behind the AI race and AI-risk narratives, and widen whose futures AI governance imagines. This is an opening for a funder or founder, not existing work.

key_work.title: 26th WFSF World Conference 'Thriving Together: Imagining Shared Futures', Cape Town
Accreditation of futures-education programmes (new accreditations granted in 2025)
The World Futures Studies Federation (2017–2025): Achievements and New Programs

people: Victor Vahidi Motti (Executive Director; Managing Editor, European Journal of Futures Research)
funding: Membership-based. UNESCO historically funded participation from developing countries, and the federation now runs a research fund with Prince Mohammad bin Fahd University (WFSF–PMU). No budget figures were found.
status_evidence: May 2026: published the WFSF Magazine and announced a Springer Nature award for its director. The 26th World Conference took place in Cape Town on 29–31 Oct 2025.
engage: Individual and institutional membership
World and regional conferences
World Futures Day, a 24-hour global online event (1 March 2026)
Accreditation for futures-education programmes
No AI programme yet: a door to open for anyone wanting to apply futures methods to AI
caveats: No dedicated AI work was found, and a site search for artificial intelligence returned nothing substantive. Causal layered analysis comes from the federation's critical-futures milieu but is not a WFSF programme. The secretariat's location was not confirmed.
tag_notes: Home arts (H3): the professional body of futures studies. Ring potential (E2, roster kept): it has no standing AI programme in 2024-26, only a general technology track and participation in a UN coalition on AI and digital futures. The transferable method is causal layered analysis and critical, pluralist futures practice, used to surface the worldview and myth layers in AI-race narratives and to widen whose futures governance encodes. Transfer convening rather than none_yet (J6), because its AI engagement is light but not zero. Org type membership (I: a professional federation). Role standards reflects its accreditation of futures education.

name: UNESCO Futures Literacy & Foresight
summary: UNESCO's programme for building the capacity of governments and communities to 'use the future'. It sits within the Management of Social Transformations (MOST) programme of UNESCO's Social and Human Sciences sector. It runs participatory Futures Literacy Laboratories (since 2012), a network of UNESCO Chairs in futures studies and anticipation, the Global Anticipatory Policy coalition, and World Futures Day. Its AI work so far is light: a 2025 paper on the societal implications of AI, built from emerging signals, for World Futures Day, and two AI lectures in its online 2026–27 Global UNESCO Chair lecture series.
why_it_matters: Its Futures Literacy Labs, its network of chairs and its coalition of government foresight officials could carry anticipatory training on advanced AI to policymakers in countries outside the AI-safety network. The transferable method is participatory futures-literacy labs combined with signals analysis.

key_work.title: Societal implications of AI: key insights from emerging signals (background paper for World Futures Day 2025)
Global UNESCO Chair Lecture Series IV: 'The World in 2050' (online; includes AI and human rights and AI ethics lectures)
World Futures Day 2026: 'Futures of Inequalities'
Futures literacy laboratory playbook

Irianna Lianaki-Dedouli (senior consultant; co-author of the AI signals paper)
Riel Miller (former Head of Futures Literacy at UNESCO; editor of 'Transforming the Future: Anticipation in the 21st Century', 2018)
status_evidence: Oct 2026: launched the fourth Global UNESCO Chair lecture series, running online until early 2027 with AI lectures in December 2026 and January 2027. World Futures Day 2026 is planned for 1–2 Dec at UNESCO headquarters.
engage: Free online Global UNESCO Chair lecture series, October 2026 to February 2027, with a certificate for attending eight or more sessions
World Futures Day at UNESCO headquarters, Paris (1–2 Dec 2026)

No AI programme: a door to open for anticipatory-governance training on frontier AI
caveats: Its AI engagement is occasional. The signals paper covers work, education and culture, not catastrophic risk. The 'Futures Literacy Labs since 2012' date comes from UNESCO's own page. UNESCO's AI ethics work, such as the 2021 Recommendation, belongs to a separate unit. The programme's budget and funders were not found.
tag_notes: Home arts (B10): futures literacy and anticipation studies, with signals and horizon scanning. Ring potential (E2, roster kept): its AI work is one 2025 signals paper and a few lectures, not a standing programme. The transferable method is participatory Futures Literacy Labs and signals analysis, delivered through the chairs network and the Global Anticipatory Policy coalition, to train non-aligned governments in anticipatory governance of frontier AI. Transfer convening: its AI items inform and convene its own futures community and Member States. Org type programme (I: a unit inside UNESCO). Framing structural: the signals paper treats AI as a condition that reshapes systems such as labour, cognition and culture.

name: Humanity AI
summary: A coalition of ten US foundations that has committed $500M over five years to steer AI towards people's needs. MacArthur and Omidyar Network lead it, with Doris Duke, Ford, Kapor, Lumina, Mellon, Mozilla, Packard and the Siegel Family Endowment. Launched in October 2025, it funds work in five areas: democracy, education, humanities and culture, labour and the economy, and security. Money flows through members' own grants and through a pooled fund run by Rockefeller Philanthropy Advisors. In 2026 it announced more than $18M in grants and a $10M open call for US projects led by educators and students, workers, and artists.
why_it_matters: It is the largest new pool of money for AI's societal direction, and it sits almost entirely outside the x-risk funding network (Coefficient Giving, SFF). It shows where new non-x-risk funders are putting money: public voice, labour, culture and open tools. Bridging proposals on power concentration and democratic control of AI could find co-funding here.

key_work.title: Launch of $500M five-year commitment to a people-centred future for AI
$10M Open Call for Proposals (education, labour and economy, humanities/arts/culture)
First round of more than $18M in grants for AI in the public interest

funding: $500M over five years (from 2025) committed by ten foundations. A pooled fund managed by Rockefeller Philanthropy Advisors (fiscal sponsor) from 2026. More than $18M in initial grants, plus a $10M open call (2026) whose applications are handled by Lever for Change.
status_evidence: Oct 2026: $10M open call accepting applications until 21 Oct 2026; Jun 2026: co-chairs Palfrey and Jawando on the Tech Stuff podcast; Apr 2026: Palfrey op-ed in TIME Ideas.
engage: Open Call for Proposals: $10M in total, with grants of $75k–$1M in three tiers. Open to US 501(c)(3)s or fiscally sponsored projects (individuals and collaborations welcome) in education, labour and economy, and humanities/arts/culture. Deadline 21 Oct 2026; finalists notified Dec 2026; awards announced spring 2027.
caveats: Grantmaking is US-only and framed around people-centred AI and corporate power, not catastrophic risk or alignment. Much of the money flows through member foundations' own programmes, so 'Humanity AI grants' overlap with members' existing AI portfolios (e.g. MacArthur's grants to AI Now). The pooled fund and executive director are new (2026), so the track record is short. HQ is given as New York because the pooled fund is hosted there by Rockefeller Philanthropy Advisors; the coalition itself has no single office.
tag_notes: Generalist funder (rule K list). Home: a nominal Law/law_policy home under H4, from its public-interest, civil-society grantmaking profile. The four secondary traditions are its priority areas: democracy, labour and economy, humanities and culture, and security. Ring: adjacent. It is a sustained, large AI funding programme on who shapes AI, with no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing (E3). Transfer: protecting. The 2026 open call funds students and educators, workers, and artists to shape AI in their own domains (J4; funders are coded by the work they fund). Framing: structural. Its stated concern is concentrated developer control and profit-driven AI. Way of knowing: communal, because the funded work is led by constituencies.

name: European AI & Society Fund (EAISF)
summary: A pooled philanthropic fund, hosted by the Network of European Foundations in Brussels. Through it about 20 foundations fund European public-interest organisations working on AI policy, accountability, market power and rights; partners include Ford, MacArthur, Mozilla, Oak, Open Society, Porticus, Robert Bosch, Stiftung Mercator and Hewlett. It has given €13.6M to organisations in 27 countries since 2020. It also briefs funders and runs learning programmes. In 2026 it ran a €2M 'Building Narrative Power' call on data centres, AI and jobs, and young people.
why_it_matters: It is the main pooled funder for civil-society AI work in Europe. Its grantees include digital-rights groups, algorithmic auditors (AIAL, Algorithm Audit), disability, migrant and labour organisations, a network the x-risk field rarely reaches. It is an obvious co-funding route and partner for European work that connects AI safety with rights, market power and public narrative.

key_work.title: Building Narrative Power funding and learning programme (€2M)
AI & Market Power – Findings from Fellows
Funders' briefing: AI and data centres
Annual report 2025

funding: Pooled from around 18–20 foundation partners: Adessium, AI Collaborative, C.S. Mott, Fondation de France, Compagnia di San Paolo, Ford, MacArthur, King Baudouin, Limelight, Luminate, Mozilla, Oak, Open Society, Porticus, Postcode Loterij, Robert Bosch, Stiftung Mercator and Hewlett. It has granted €13.6M since 2020. In April 2026 it announced €10M raised from 18 partners in 18 months, after Postcode Loterij joined with €1M in March 2026.
status_evidence: Aug 2026: published 'Three priorities for funders to help civil society meet the changing AI challenge'; Jul 2026: opened the €2M Building Narrative Power call (first stage closed 31 Aug 2026).
engage: Open calls for European civil-society organisations, such as Building Narrative Power (€2M, up to €150k per organisation, plus a learning community). The first stage closed 31 Aug 2026; watch for new rounds.
AI & Market Power fellowships; findings and lessons for funders published Jul 2026.
Funders can join as pooled-fund partners and attend its funders' briefings on AI topics.
caveats: It frames its work as public interest, rights and redirecting AI away from Big Tech. It says it wants AI to be 'safe and fair' but does not engage with catastrophic risk. Only European organisations are eligible. It moved to a co-director model with a new five-year strategy in January 2026.
tag_notes: Home: Law/law_policy. Under H4 a one-programme funder takes its programme's tradition, here public-interest, digital-rights and accountability funding. Secondary: Economics (market-power fellowships, data centres, jobs) and Arts (the narrative-power programme). Ring: adjacent. It has run a standing AI funding programme since 2020, framed around rights, accountability and power, not catastrophic risk or alignment (E3). Transfer: into_institutions. Grantees work on AI Act implementation, resisting the rollback of safeguards, and transparency of public-sector AI (J3). Not on the rule-K generalist list.

name: Mozilla Foundation
summary: The nonprofit parent of Mozilla, founded in 2003. It runs advocacy campaigns, grantmaking, the Common Voice crowdsourced speech dataset, the Mozilla Data Collective and the annual Mozilla Festival (MozFest). Its AI work is about trustworthy and open AI: it funds researchers and builders of alternatives, campaigns on AI bias and platform accountability, and argues for community-governed data and public AI infrastructure. It is a founding member of Humanity AI and a funding partner of the European AI & Society Fund.
why_it_matters: It brings the open-source movement's experience of commons-based production and community governance of data to the problem of AI power concentration and lock-in. The x-risk field shares that concern but rarely approaches it through open infrastructure. It also funds and convenes a large public-interest tech community: MozFest drew more than 2,000 people in 2025.

key_work.title: Mozilla Festival 2026, Barcelona: 'Wilding'
Mozilla Data Collective: community-governed datasets for AI
Common Voice open speech dataset
Founding member of the Humanity AI coalition

funding: Income from its subsidiary Mozilla Corporation, plus donations. It reports more than $35M in grants over the past decade. It laid off about 30% of staff in November 2024.
status_evidence: Oct 2026: Mozilla Festival scheduled for 28–30 Oct 2026 at Recinte Fabra i Coats, Barcelona, with badges on sale.
engage: Mozilla Festival, Barcelona, 28–30 Oct 2026; sessions are proposed by the community
Grantmaking: open opportunities and call alerts on the 'What we fund' page
Contribute voice recordings to Common Voice
caveats: Distinct from Mozilla Corporation (Firefox), Mozilla.ai and Mozilla Ventures, which are separate Mozilla entities. It restructured in late 2024 and redesigned its grantmaking; whether the fellowship programme is currently running was not confirmed. Its AI framing is trustworthy and open AI and the centralisation of tech, not catastrophic risk. The official site blocks automated access, so its pages were read through a proxy; detail on the current AI programme is thinner than for the other entries.
tag_notes: Home: Economics/econ_commons. Its AI work comes from the open-source and commons tradition: crowdsourced, community-governed datasets (Common Voice, Data Collective) and open or public AI as a counterweight to concentration (H1, B9). Secondary: Law, for its trustworthy-AI advocacy and AI-bias accountability work. Ring: adjacent. It runs a standing AI programme (grants, advocacy, data commons, MozFest) framed around trust, openness and power, not catastrophic risk or alignment (E3). Transfer: into_institutions. It offers alternative governance templates for data and AI infrastructure (J3), with a strong convening strand. Org type: nonprofit, because it operates programmes and also funds (rule I). Not a rule-K generalist funder.

name: Normativity Lab (Johns Hopkins University)
summary: A research group led by Gillian Hadfield, Bloomberg Distinguished Professor of AI Alignment and Governance at Johns Hopkins (School of Government and Policy and Department of Computer Science). It studies how human normative systems work, meaning how groups classify and enforce rules of behaviour. Its methods are computational models, multi-agent reinforcement learning, generative agents and studies of normative reasoning in LLMs. It applies the results to AI alignment and to legal and regulatory design for AI. The lab lists 17 members, including four postdocs and research scientists and eight doctoral students, with affiliated researchers at the Vector Institute and other institutions.
why_it_matters: It treats alignment as a question of normative competence and institutions, not just single-model preference learning. It draws on law and economics, cultural evolution (for example a field study of norm enforcement among the Turkana) and institutional design. Its 'regulatory markets' and 'legal alignment' proposals give the safety field concrete governance designs taken from legal theory.

key_work.title: Legal Alignment for Safe and Ethical AI (arXiv:2601.04175, with Kolt, Caputo, O'Keefe and others)
Building AI for the Democratic Matrix: A Technical Research Agenda for Normative Competence and Normative Institutions (Knight Institute)
Regulatory Markets: The Future of AI Governance (Jurimetrics)
Societal Alignment Frameworks Can Improve LLM Alignment (arXiv:2503.00069)

funding: Not stated on the lab site. Hadfield holds a Bloomberg Distinguished Professorship and a Schmidt Sciences AI2050 Senior Fellowship (2023).
status_evidence: Sep 2026: Hadfield's Johns Hopkins talk 'AI: Who Governs the Machine?' (14 Sep), plus interviews with TIME, MIT Technology Review and CBC; Mar 2026: Knight Institute essay with Trivedi and Hadfield-Menell; Dec 2025: postdoc advertised for 2026 start.
engage: Postdoctoral fellowship advertised in December 2025 for a 2026 start (multi-agent RL and generative agents); check the lab page for current openings
caveats: A university lab built around one principal investigator. Hadfield is also a part-time visiting faculty researcher in Google's Paradigms of Intelligence group, chairs the Cooperative AI Foundation's board and works with the policy nonprofit Fathom, so the lab's output overlaps with her wider policy work. Founding date not stated; the lab has members at Toronto and the Vector Institute, which suggests it predates her move to Johns Hopkins.
tag_notes: Home: Law/law_legal. The lab's concepts come from legal theory and law and economics: normative infrastructure, regulatory markets, legal alignment (H1, H2); the taxonomy itself uses it as the law example. Secondary: Economics (institutional economics, regulatory markets) and Life & systems (cultural evolution of norms, the Turkana metanorms study). Ring: bridge (roster value kept). It is rooted in law and economics and runs an explicit, standing alignment and safety programme. Core is arguable given its alignment mission and its ties to the Cooperative AI Foundation and the FAR.AI workshops; the roster value is kept under E. Transfer: into_model. The main research line builds normative competence into AI agents (normative modules, MARL, LLM normative reasoning); regulatory design is a secondary into_institutions strand. Way of knowing: a mix of computational experiments and legal-theoretic argument; empirical is chosen for the lab's main output.

name: Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University: Artificial Intelligence and Democratic Freedoms project
summary: A research project at Columbia's Knight First Amendment Institute on how advanced AI may harm or strengthen democratic freedoms. It began in August 2024, when Seth Lazar (ANU philosopher and head of the MINT lab) became the Institute's Senior AI Advisor. It commissioned papers from computer scientists, philosophers, lawyers and social scientists, and held an authors' workshop in late 2024 and a public symposium at Columbia on 10–11 April 2025. It then published the papers as an essay series of 16 pieces, the latest in March 2026.
why_it_matters: It set out explicitly to build 'sociotechnical AI safety'. It connects free-expression law and democratic theory with technical work on AI agents, power concentration (the AI Power Disparity Index) and AI-mediated deliberation. The essays are a ready-made body of interdisciplinary writing on democratic resilience under advanced AI.

key_work.title: AI Agents and Democratic Resilience (Lazar & Cuéllar)
The AI Power Disparity Index (Kim, Kuehnert, Lazar, Singh & Heidari)
Symposium: Artificial Intelligence and Democratic Freedoms, Columbia University
Building AI for the Democratic Matrix (Hadfield, Trivedi & Hadfield-Menell)

status_evidence: Mar 2026: project essay 'A Conceptual Model to Guide AI Risk Governance Strategies' (Mulligan, Marda & Wang); May 2026: related Knight Institute occasional paper 'AI as Social Technology' (Farrell & Shalizi).
engage: No open call in 2026; the project recruited authors through an open call for abstracts in August 2024
The Knight Institute runs an institute-wide Visiting Research Scholars programme
caveats: Lazar was appointed for the 2024–25 academic year and no new project essays have appeared since March 2026, so the project may be winding down. The essays cover a range of views, including the deflationary 'AI as Normal Technology'; they are not an institutional position. The Institute's main work is First Amendment litigation and research, of which this is one strand.
tag_notes: Home: Law/law_legal. It is hosted by a First Amendment law institute and framed around civil liberties and democratic institutions. Secondary: Philosophy (led by the philosopher Seth Lazar, normative essays) and Democracy (AI-mediated deliberation, democratic publics). Ring: bridge. The August 2024 launch statement says the project seeks to 'coalesce and support the emerging field of sociotechnical AI safety' around risks from the most advanced AI. That is an explicit safety framing, sustained in 2024–26 through the workshop, the symposium and the essay series (E3). Transfer: into_institutions. It proposes governance tools for democratic institutions, such as a power-disparity index, risk-governance models and levels of agent autonomy (J3). Engagement left empty: no current open call or recurring programme for this unit (O).

name: Humane Intelligence
summary: A US 501(c)(3) nonprofit, co-founded by Rumman Chowdhury, that designs and runs AI red-teaming events, bias bounties and contextual evaluations with domain experts and affected communities. It began in 2022 as 'Bias Buccaneers' and was incorporated in May 2023. It has run more than 30 evaluations with over 5,600 participants from 60+ countries, including the generative-AI red-teaming exercise at DEF CON 31 and a regional AI-safety red-teaming exercise with Singapore's IMDA. In 2026 it ran its first bias bounty on Zindi (August), released its red-teaming app as open source (September) and published its ontology-based contextual evaluation method, OB-CAIE (October).
why_it_matters: It turns evaluation from a benchmark exercise inside labs into a participatory practice: people with lived or domain experience of a problem test systems in their real context. Its method and open-source tooling could be reused for safety evaluations that currently have no public input.

key_work.title: Generative AI red-teaming exercise at DEF CON 31
Open-source AI red-teaming app
Ontology-Based Contextual AI Evaluation (OB-CAIE) methodology paper
AI in Public Health working group (with NYU Center for Health Data Science)

funding: Paid red-teaming and contextual-evaluation services, plus philanthropic grants. It has published funding requests for the second half of 2026 and is raising an AI in Public Health fund. No funders are named on the pages reviewed.
status_evidence: 1 Oct 2026: published the OB-CAIE methodology paper; 16 Sep 2026: released its open-source AI red-teaming app; Aug 2026: launched a bias bounty on Zindi.
engage: Volunteer programme (300+ volunteers): new sign-ups paused since 26 Aug 2026, reopening around December 2026 for projects starting in early 2027
AI in Public Health working group with NYU's Center for Health Data Science: rolling applications, about 5 hours a month
Slack community (on request)
Use or contribute to the open-source red-teaming app
Bias bounty challenges on Zindi
