Since then the organisation has shifted towards paid evaluation services, open-source tooling and public-health work. Its framing is mostly accountability, bias and fitness for social-good deployments rather than catastrophic risk. Headquarters are not stated; New York is inferred from the executive director's location.
tag_notes: Home: Law/law_sts, because the taxonomy places civil-society algorithmic auditing in law_sts. Secondary: Safety (red-teaming as a safety-testing practice) and Democracy (participatory design of evaluations). Ring: bridge (roster value kept, borderline). Its red-teaming is framed as assessing 'safety and effectiveness' and includes AI-safety exercises (DEF CON 31, Singapore IMDA), but most of its framing is about bias and accountability, so adjacent would also be defensible (E3). Transfer: into_model. Its evaluations target the behaviour of models and systems (J1). Way of knowing: communal. The mission centres people with lived or domain experience as evaluators; the contextual evaluations themselves are mixed-method and empirical. Online hub: Slack community and the remotely joinable public-health working group.

name: AI Incident Database (Responsible AI Collaborative)
summary: An open, editor-curated database of real-world AI harms and failures, modelled on aviation and computer-security incident reporting. It is run by the nonprofit Responsible AI Collaborative. It holds more than 1,700 incidents and over 5,000 annotated reports, takes public submissions, publishes taxonomies (including CSET's) and open-source code, and reached over 400,000 users in 2025. Incidents are added continuously: incidents 1720 and 1721 went in with reports dated 1 October 2026.
why_it_matters: It is the main shared record of deployed-AI failures, used by the OECD, central banks (an IMF report), NIST resources and standards bodies to define and track 'AI incidents'. It brings safety engineering's practice of learning from accidents into AI governance, so risk models and evaluations can rest on observed harms rather than speculation.

key_work.title: AI Incident Database (1,720+ incidents)
CSET AI harm taxonomy applied to AIID incidents
Paper on the challenges of AI incident databasing (arXiv:2409.16425)
Funding the AIID – Part I (sustainability appeal and GRC sponsorship trial)

funding: Substantial programme support from the Digital Safety Research Institute at UL Research Institutes, plus individual donations. In 2026, after hosting costs rose, it began seeking corporate sponsorship and started a one-year partnership trial with governance, risk and compliance (GRC) and AI-safety companies, led by Trustible.ai.
status_evidence: 1 Oct 2026: incidents 1720 and 1721 added; Jan 2026: 'Funding the AIID – Part I' blog post by Sean McGregor.
engage: Submit incident reports through the public submission form
Contribute code to the open-source repository (github.com/responsible-ai-collaborative/aiid)
Donate, or join the inaugural cohort of GRC sponsors
Contact the Collaborative to take part in governance; the board invites contributors
caveats: It depends on a small editorial team and on UL's Digital Safety Research Institute. The January 2026 appeal reported rising hosting costs and a search for long-term funding. Its monthly incident roundups on the blog stopped after mid-2024. Coverage is built from news reports and submissions, so it reflects what gets reported. Incident collection began around 2018; the public database launched in 2020.
tag_notes: Home: Safety/safety_risk. It explicitly imports aviation (FAA, FARS) and CVE incident-reporting practice, and the taxonomy lists it as a safety_risk example. Ring: bridge (roster value kept). It is rooted in safety-engineering incident reporting and has a 'safer world with AI' mission, but it covers present harms broadly and was not founded inside the x-risk ecosystem; borderline with core (E). Transfer: into_institutions. It supplies an incident-reporting system and shared definitions used by the OECD and standards bodies (J3). Framing: present_harms, because it documents harms (rule L). Region: global, as a US-registered nonprofit with a fully distributed team (O).

name: Delft Algorithms, Systems & Safety Lab (DASS), TU Delft
summary: A research group led by assistant professor Roel Dobbe in TU Delft's Faculty of Technology, Policy and Management. It applies system-safety engineering, including System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA), and control theory to AI and algorithmic systems in public services and infrastructure. It pairs hazard analysis with interviews and participatory system-mapping workshops involving officials, civil society and ombudsmen. The group is linked to the Dutch Centre for Hybrid Intelligence and the AlgoSoc consortium.
why_it_matters: It brings decades of system-safety practice for software-intensive systems into AI-safety governance. In a direct reply to the International AI Safety Report, Dobbe argues that safety is a property of whole sociotechnical systems, not of models alone. That gives AI-safety policy a tested engineering method for hazards that sit in organisations and institutions, and the EU AI Act is one place it applies.

key_work.title: AI Safety is Stuck in Technical Terms: A System Safety Response to the International AI Safety Report
Co-constructing sociotechnical AI governance: participatory system mapping using algorithm registers
From Silos to Systems: Process-Oriented Hazard Analysis for AI Systems (with Rismani and Moon)
Concrete Problems in AI Safety, Revisited (with Inioluwa Deborah Raji; ICLR 2020 workshop, posted to arXiv Dec 2023)

people: Martijn Warnier (TU Delft, co-supervisor on the lab's hybrid-intelligence safety postdoc)
funding: A 2024 postdoc on safe hybrid-intelligence systems was tied to the Centre for Hybrid Intelligence and the AlgoSoc consortium, both Dutch NWO Gravitation programmes. No budget figures found.
status_evidence: Aug 2026: arXiv paper (de Troya, Enbergs, Doorn, Dobbe) using participatory system mapping and STPA on a Dutch municipal algorithm register for welfare-benefit decisions.
engage: PhD and postdoc vacancies are advertised through TU Delft and AcademicTransfer; a 2024 example was 'Postdoc System Design and Governance for Safe Hybrid Intelligence Systems' (closed). No current opening confirmed.
caveats: No dedicated lab website was found. The 'DASS' name comes from a 2024 vacancy, and the profile rests mainly on Dobbe's TU Delft page and publications. The framing is sociotechnical and justice-oriented, and critical of narrowly technical AI-safety framings, rather than about x-risk. Web search was unavailable during profiling, so current staffing could not be checked.
tag_notes: Home safety: its main AI outputs apply system-safety engineering (STPA, hazard analysis, control theory) to AI (H1), and the secondary law reflects its STS and public-administration fieldwork. Ring bridge: an engineering-faculty group in an established institution, with a sustained 2023-26 publication line explicitly framed as AI safety (rule E3). Transfer into_institutions: it supplies hazard-analysis and governance templates for public algorithmic systems and the EU AI Act, not changes to models. Framing present_harms: the stakes it cites are concrete harms to citizens, such as wrongful benefit denial and decisions that cannot be contested.

name: AI Safety and Societal Impacts Research Group, Hasso Plattner Institute (HPI)
summary: A research group at the Hasso Plattner Institute, started in September 2026 by Paul Röttger, previously of the Oxford Internet Institute and the UK AI Security Institute. It studies the risks and benefits that arise as capable AI systems enter social and political processes such as communication, coordination and competition. It measures these through model evaluations, computational experiments and human studies, and builds technical mitigations where it can. Its DFG Emmy Noether project is on measuring and mitigating political bias in AI systems.
why_it_matters: It brings computational social science and political-science measurement to AI safety. Its topics are how AI shifts political opinion, what happens when people delegate to autonomous agents, and how misaligned behaviour spreads among competing AI systems, all thinly covered by mainstream safety evaluations. It is one of the few university groups in Germany explicitly framed as AI safety, and it is close to the int/a Berlin community.

key_work.title: Emmy Noether project: AI Methods for Measuring and Mitigating Political Bias in AI Systems
PRISM alignment dataset (Röttger's earlier work; NeurIPS 2024 Datasets & Benchmarks best paper)
SafetyPrompts.com, a catalogue of open LLM safety datasets (Röttger's earlier work)

funding: DFG Emmy Noether Programme, six years, according to a recruitment notice. HPI itself is privately funded by the Hasso Plattner Foundation.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: group launched at HPI. It is recruiting fully funded PhD students, postdocs and research interns on a rolling basis.
engage: Fully funded 3-year PhD, 1–2-year postdoc and 3–6-month full-time research internships, starting from September 2026. Applications are rolling, through an expression-of-interest form linked from paulrottger.com, and the work is in person in Germany.
caveats: Launched in September 2026, so it has no group outputs yet and the profile rests on the leader's track record. No HPI page for the group was found. The Emmy Noether funding is reported by a recruitment aggregator rather than by HPI or the DFG. HPI's campus is in Potsdam, though Röttger describes the move as to Berlin, so whether the group counts as Berlin-based is unclear. It sits close to the AI-safety core through Röttger's UK AISI role.
tag_notes: Home law (law_sts): it imports computational social science and political-science measurement into AI evaluation (H2). The secondary democracy reflects its focus on political processes. MISFIT: political science and computational social science have no sector of their own. Ring bridge kept from the roster: the group is explicitly framed as AI safety, but its host (a CS institute), funding (DFG) and methods sit outside the AI-safety ecosystem, so it is not core even though the leader came from UK AISI (rule E3). Transfer into_model: its main outputs are evaluations of, and mitigations for, political bias and misaligned behaviour in models. Berlin hub not coded because HPI is in Potsdam (rule O).

name: Sociotechnical Safety Lab, University of Washington
summary: An HCI research group led by Emily Tseng, assistant professor in the University of Washington's Department of Human Centered Design & Engineering since spring 2026. It studies how computing mediates harm, from spyware in abusive relationships and workplace surveillance to AI companions. It builds interventions, design principles, community-controlled tools and trauma-informed research methods. In July 2026 it was chosen as one of 18 university groups in Microsoft's External Red Team Alliance (EXTRA) for independent AI-safety research.
why_it_matters: It brings knowledge from tech-facilitated abuse and digital-safety work with survivors, where the threat often comes from someone close, into AI red-teaming and the study of social and emotional uses of AI. That relational harm surface matters for AI companions and assistants, and mainstream evaluations rarely model it.

key_work.title: CHI 2026 workshop on Social and Emotional Uses of AI
Selection for Microsoft's External Red Team Alliance (EXTRA)
Trauma-informed approaches to studying digital-safety harms (CSCW 2025, Impact Recognition)

funding: US$25,000 unrestricted gift from Microsoft through EXTRA (2026). Tseng also received a Google Academic Research Award and a UW Community-Engaged Computing Initiative seed grant in 2025.
status_evidence: Jul 2026: selected as one of 18 university research groups in Microsoft's External Red Team Alliance. The lab is admitting PhD students for the December 2026 deadline.
engage: Admitting 1–2 PhD students to UW HCDE (deadline 2 December 2026) on sociotechnical safety, small and private language models, and social and emotional uses of AI
Occasional undergraduate and Master's research-assistant roles, plus an interest form on the lab page
caveats: Founded in 2026, so its track record as a lab is short. AI safety is one strand among wider digital-safety topics, and 'safety' here means present harms to people, not catastrophic risk. Its EXTRA support is small and comes from a frontier developer.
tag_notes: Home law (law_sts): its methods are sociotechnical and community-partnered HCI research on harm (H1). The secondary safety reflects its computer-security and privacy work for at-risk users and its red-teaming. MISFIT: HCI and digital-safety research has no sector of its own. Ring bridge kept from the roster, though it is borderline with adjacent: the lab is named and funded around AI safety (EXTRA) and runs a sustained strand on AI companions, but its harms are present-day and relational (rule E3). Transfer protecting: its primary purpose is to protect at-risk people and survivors from technology-mediated abuse, including through AI.

name: Global Center on AI Governance (GCG)
summary: A nonprofit research centre in Cape Town, founded in 2023 by Rachel Adams, that works on AI governance aimed at reducing global inequality. It has a core team of about 13. It produces the Global Index on Responsible AI (135 countries in the 2026 edition), runs the African Observatory on Responsible AI, and trains policymakers and regulators. Since 2025 it has co-led the African Hub on AI Safety, Peace and Security with the University of Cape Town's AI Initiative.
why_it_matters: It is building an African and Global-Majority evidence base and agenda for AI safety, such as 'Toward an African Agenda for AI Safety' (2025), in debates otherwise led by Northern institutes. Adams also directs Cambridge's Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence, so the centre links Global South governance work directly with the AI-safety research world.

key_work.title: Toward an African Agenda for AI Safety
African Hub on AI Safety, Peace and Security (with UCT AI Initiative)
Global Index on Responsible AI, second edition (135 countries)
South African public attitudes to AI study (with the HSRC's South African Social Attitudes Survey)

people: Jonathan Shock (UCT AI Initiative, co-lead of the African Hub)
funding: IDRC (Canada) and the UK FCDO, through the AI4D programme, fund the Index, the Observatory and the African Hub. The 2025–26 annual report also lists the Gates Foundation, Luminate, GIZ, the Government of Canada and South Africa's Department of Science, Technology and Innovation.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: Data Governance and AI Foundations webinar. Launch of the Global State of Responsible AI Report 2026 scheduled for 22 Oct 2026.
engage: Certificate short courses on AI governance and ethics at South African universities (UCT, Pretoria, Wits)
Free online course 'Introduction to Responsible AI' (MOOC)
Webinars and launch events, including the Global State of Responsible AI Report on 22 Oct 2026
Research fellows and an embedded-researcher network for the Index
caveats: Most of its work is responsible-AI and human-rights governance rather than AI safety as the x-risk community uses the term. The safety strand began in 2025 and centres on present and gendered harms, security and capacity-building. The CEO also holds a senior post at Cambridge's CFI. Google and Meta are listed as partners, not funders.
tag_notes: Home law (law_policy): human-rights, policy and development research led from the Global South goes to Law, not Indigenous and decolonial (B8, where GCG is the named example). The secondaries are economics (Adams's political economy of global inequality) and peace (the AI Safety, Peace and Security hub). Ring bridge: a governance and development centre with a sustained, funded AI-safety programme since 2025, the African Hub and the African AI Safety agenda (rule E3). Transfer into_institutions: its outputs are an index, policy advice (for example on the AU Continental AI Strategy) and regulator training. Framing structural, from its mission to reduce global inequalities exacerbated by AI. Online hub coded for its free MOOC and webinar series.

name: Digital Futures Lab (DFL)
summary: An independent research studio founded in 2021 by Urvashi Aneja, based in Aldona, Goa, with staff also in Delhi and London. Its political scientists, lawyers, sociologists, technologists and storytellers study technology and society in India and the Majority World through social-science research, systematic foresight and public engagement. Its 2026 work covers AI safety, gendered AI harms, AI in Indian courts, data centres and generative AI's effects on creative workers. It is a founding member of the Global South Network for Trustworthy AI and is writing the network's Global South AI Safety Report.
why_it_matters: It asks what AI safety means where AI is actually deployed in the Global South, tracing real deployment pathways, institutions and everyday experience rather than abstract risk taxonomies, and it adds foresight methods. It is one of the few non-Western think tanks engaging the AI-safety frame directly and feeding it into UN and summit processes.

key_work.title: Global South AI Safety Report (Global South Network for Trustworthy AI; interim output 2026, first edition due for the 2027 Geneva AI Summit)
AI Safety and Gender: policy brief on gendered AI harms in India
Guidelines for ethical AI adoption in Indian courts
Foresight study on generative AI and Indian creative workers

people: Shefali Malhotra (Senior Research Manager, AI & Tech Policy)
funding: Past and present partners on its site include the Gates Foundation, Rockefeller Foundation, Mozilla Foundation, Omidyar Network India, Fondation Botnar, GIZ and BMZ, Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung, Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung, Rohini Nilekani Philanthropies and UN agencies. It does not say which of these fund it, or how much.
status_evidence: May 2026: published an update on the Global South AI Safety Report, with an interim output due before the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance in July 2026.
engage: Staff vacancies on its careers page (a Communications Lead in Goa was open in 2026)
DFL newsletter and Substack
caveats: AI safety is one stream within broader technology-and-society work. Its framing centres structural inequity, rights and present harms rather than catastrophic risk. Funders are listed only as 'partners'.
tag_notes: Home law (law_policy): a multidisciplinary public-interest and development research institute led from the Global South goes to Law, not Indigenous and decolonial, despite its feminist commitments (B8). The secondary arts reflects its systematic foresight method (B10). Ring bridge: a sustained, explicit AI-safety stream in 2025-26, the Global South AI Safety Report and the AI safety and gender brief (rule E3). Transfer into_institutions: its outputs are evidence and recommendations for governments, companies and global governance bodies. Framing structural, from its mission statement about innovation trajectories that deepen global inequity and weaken democratic accountability. The London hub is not coded, since only one staff member is based there.

name: Schwartz Reisman Institute for Technology and Society (SRI)
summary: An interdisciplinary institute at the University of Toronto, founded in 2019 with a gift from Gerald Schwartz and Heather Reisman. It links more than 180 researchers across 20 disciplines. Its 2025–2028 strategic plan centres on AI safety in three areas: safe and secure AI systems, data and integrity, and governance and social reordering. A 'solutions' team turns the research into policy submissions and briefs, and the institute funds chairs and fellowships and runs public seminars and conferences.
why_it_matters: It places law, philosophy, psychology, economics and STS researchers alongside AI-safety researchers such as David Duvenaud, co-author of 'Gradual Disempowerment', and Roger Grosse. It turns that mix into concrete policy instruments, such as its 2026 proposal to treat AI transparency as information infrastructure.

key_work.title: Submission to Canada's federal consultation on AI transparency (transparency as information infrastructure, nine recommendations, drawing on 20 researchers)
Gradual Disempowerment: Systemic Existential Risks from Incremental AI Development (co-authored by SRI chair David Duvenaud)
Policy briefs on regulating AI companions and AI therapy chatbots
SRI 2025–2028 strategic plan

people: Sheila McIlraith (Associate Director and research lead)
David Duvenaud (Schwartz Reisman Chair in Technology and Society)
funding: Founded on a 2019 gift from Gerald Schwartz and Heather Reisman, widely reported as C$100 million, which also supported U of T's Schwartz Reisman Innovation Campus. The institute funds Schwartz Reisman Chairs (2024–29) and fellowships.
status_evidence: 29 Sep 2026: appointed a new Advisory Board (adding Alondra Nelson, Audrey Tang and Shuman Ghosemajumder) and an inaugural Scientific Advisory Committee.
engage: Graduate and faculty fellowships and a faculty affiliate programme (University of Toronto researchers only)
Global Fellow and Scholar-in-Residence programmes for faculty at other institutions
Public seminars and conferences, such as 'The Human Variable: Psychology for the AI Age' on 28 Oct 2026
Public discussion groups and a mailing list
caveats: Many programmes are open only to U of T researchers. Much of its output is mainstream AI policy and governance, though the 2025–28 plan moves it closer to the AI-safety core. Founding director Gillian Hadfield has since left. Scale counts its 180+ affiliated researchers, not core staff.
tag_notes: Home law (law_policy): it is the taxonomy's named example of a multidisciplinary public-interest institute. As a hub it gets three secondaries (H5): philosophy, safety (the director's computer-security work and the 'safe and secure AI systems' focus) and psychology (research lead on AI and relationships, therapy-bot and companion briefs). Ring bridge: a university technology-and-society institute founded before its current AI-safety strategy, which now runs a sustained, explicit AI-safety programme (rule E3). Transfer into_institutions: its solutions stream produces policy instruments for governments. Framing structural, from the plan's 'governance and social reordering' focus and the gradual-disempowerment work.

name: Center for AI and Digital Policy (CAIDP)
summary: A Washington DC nonprofit, incorporated in 2021 and founded by privacy lawyer Marc Rotenberg, that works for AI policy grounded in fundamental rights, democratic institutions and the rule of law. It publishes the annual AI and Democratic Values Index; the sixth edition (April 2026) covers 90 countries in 1,739 pages. It files statements, complaints and amicus briefs with US agencies and courts, and campaigns for the Council of Europe AI treaty and for AI red lines. Its semester-long AI Policy Clinics had produced more than 1,400 graduates from about 130 countries by January 2026.
why_it_matters: It brings human-rights and comparative-law methods to AI governance, including frontier-safety questions such as how to enforce red lines. Its clinic alumni form a large, rights-trained global pool of policy analysts that AI-safety policy work rarely draws on.

key_work.title: CAIDP AI Index 2026: Artificial Intelligence and Democratic Values
Enforcing Red Lines in AI Governance (report presented at a UNGA81 event)
Amicus brief with IASEAI supporting California's training-data transparency law (AB 2013)
No Time for Delay: Identifying Rights-Impacting and Safety-Impacting AI Systems in Federal Agencies

people: Stuart Russell (listed on CAIDP's team as an affiliated expert)
funding: About US$900,000 in contributions and grants in 2024 (total revenue about US$924,000, Form 990). Donors are not itemised on its site.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: presented 'Enforcing Red Lines in AI Governance' at a UNGA81 event and published CAIDP Update 8.37 (28 Sep 2026). The Fall 2026 clinic cohort runs 7 Sep to 27 Nov 2026.
engage: AI Policy Clinics: intensive, semester-long online courses for a global cohort, leading to a CAIDP AI Policy Certificate (Fall 2026 applications closed 15 May 2026)
Events, including side events at the UN General Assembly and conferences
Weekly CAIDP Update newsletter
caveats: Its framing is rights and democratic values; safety and red lines are one strand within broad digital-policy advocacy. Much of the Index is compiled by volunteer clinic participants. It was incorporated in 2021 but published an index for 2020.
tag_notes: Home law (law_legal): its AI outputs come from human-rights, privacy and comparative law, through legal analysis, complaints, amicus briefs and treaty advocacy (H1, B9). No secondary tradition qualifies under rule C. Ring bridge kept: a rights-law organisation with a sustained programme on safety-impacting AI and enforceable AI red lines in 2024-26 (rule E3). Transfer into_institutions: its outputs are treaty support, regulation and legal instruments. Framing present_harms, from its mission about fairness, justice, accountability and fundamental rights. Online hub coded for the recurring, remotely joinable AI Policy Clinics.

name: UN DPPA Innovation Cell
summary: An interdisciplinary team set up in January 2020 inside the UN Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs to pilot and scale new technologies for conflict prevention, mediation and peacebuilding. Its main AI tool is Digital Dialogues, an AI-assisted platform that lets UN officials consult up to 1,000 people at once in their own languages and find areas of consensus on ceasefires, humanitarian measures and peace priorities. It also trains political affairs officers to use generative AI, runs an annual E-Analytics and Innovation course with the Qatar Computing Research Institute (the curriculum covers large language models and agentic AI), and builds tools such as Diplomatic Pulse and the Lisan Arabic-dialect corpus.
why_it_matters: It holds years of field experience running AI-mediated, large-scale consultation in real conflict settings: practical evidence on AI-assisted deliberation and bridging that pluralistic-alignment and collective-intelligence work mostly tests only in the lab. Its anonymity-by-design approach to including women in fragile settings is a transferable lesson for public-input processes on AI.

key_work.title: Digital Dialogues: AI-assisted consultations of up to 1,000 participants in UN peace processes
Lisan: Yemeni, Iraqi, Libyan and Sudanese Arabic dialect corpora (with Birzeit University and the American University of Beirut)
E-Analytics and Innovation Course (annual, with QCRI), including LLMs and agentic AI
Social Media Analysis Guide

status_evidence: Oct 2026: the Innovation page is live and lists a 2025 Social Media Analysis Guide and an E-Analytics course curriculum that now covers agentic AI; no dated 2026 Cell-specific news item found.
engage: Contact: DPPA-Innovation@un.org
Diplomatic Pulse and the Peace and Security Data Hub (psdata.un.org) are publicly available tools
caveats: This is AI applied to peacebuilding rather than work on making AI itself go well; it is included for its method (AI-assisted deliberation in conflict settings). Most of the dated material on the Innovation page is from 2021-2023; Martin Waehlisch and Daanish Masood Alavi co-authored its 2022 research outputs (Lisan, with Mustafa Jarrar and Fadi Zaraket), and the page names no current lead. The platform behind Digital Dialogues has been publicly reported as Remesh, but the DPPA page does not name it. The UN's 2025-26 budget cuts and UN80 restructuring could affect the unit; not verified.
tag_notes: Home: peace by rule B11, since its deliberative AI tools are used by peacebuilders in conflict settings (UN DPPA is the rule's own example); democracy is secondary for the collective-intelligence method. Ring: adjacent, keeping the roster value, because it has a standing AI programme with no safety, catastrophic-risk or alignment framing. Transfer: into_institutions, because Digital Dialogues is a template for large-scale AI-assisted deliberation. MISFIT: the flow runs from AI into peacebuilding more than from peacebuilding into the AI transition. Framing coded flourishing because it presents AI as a means to more inclusive peace; it is a weak fit.

name: Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO)
summary: An independent peace and conflict research institute founded in 1959, with about 80 person-years of staff, that publishes the Journal of Peace Research, Security Dialogue and the Journal of Military Ethics and maintains major conflict datasets. Its AI work includes ERM (Jan 2025 to Jun 2028, Research Council of Norway), a project led by Jovana Davidovic and Gregory Reichberg that builds lifecycle risk-assessment and mitigation tools for AI-enabled weapons with defence practitioners. It also runs AsiaTech (Feb 2026 to Dec 2028, Research Council of Norway) on AI-enabled digital authoritarianism in Asia, and the ERC-funded BRIDGE project (announced Sept 2026, led by Jonas Vestby) on using AI and knowledge graphs to connect conflict data. Its VIEWS early-warning system forecasts conflict with machine learning.
why_it_matters: PRIO brings military ethics and quantitative conflict research to two questions the AI-safety field usually treats in theory: how to manage the risks of AI in targeting across a system's whole lifecycle, and how AI entrenches autocratic power. Its conflict-forecasting infrastructure could become an empirical monitor of AI's effects on organised violence.

key_work.title: Ethical Risk Management for AI-Enabled Weapons: A Systems Approach (ERM)
AsiaTech: Understanding and countering the advance of AI-enabled digital authoritarianism in Asia
BRIDGE: AI and knowledge graphs for peace and conflict data (ERC Starting Grant)
PRIO AI Days (seminars on AI in warfare, early warning and global AI governance)

people: Gregory M. Reichberg (Research Professor; ERM co-lead)
funding: Project-funded: the Research Council of Norway, Norwegian government ministries, the European Commission and international organisations; 2025 budgeted turnover about NOK 160 million. AsiaTech is funded by the Research Council of Norway (2026-28) and BRIDGE by an ERC Starting Grant (2026).
status_evidence: 3 Sep 2026: announced the ERC-funded BRIDGE project; 22 Sep 2026: Acting Director's Nobel Peace Prize list; 29 Oct 2025: ERM commentary on human roles in AI warfare.
engage: Staff and doctoral positions: prio.org/about/careers
Public events and recorded seminars: prio.org/events
Monthly newsletter, The PRIO Update
caveats: AI is a minority strand within a broad peace-research portfolio, and its AI topic page is still marked forthcoming. BRIDGE and VIEWS use AI as a research tool rather than studying AI risk. ERM sits close to the bridge ring (risk management for AI weapons) but has no catastrophic or alignment framing.
tag_notes: Home: peace, because its AI outputs come from security studies, military ethics and conflict research; philosophy is secondary because ERM is led by ethicists (Reichberg, Davidovic) and PRIO publishes the Journal of Military Ethics. Ring: adjacent, keeping the roster value (rule E3): it has funded AI projects (ERM, AsiaTech) on ethical risk and repression with no catastrophic, alignment or AI-going-well framing, comparable to Stop Killer Robots. Transfer: into_institutions, because ERM produces risk-assessment tools and guidance for defence procurement and regulators. Problems: democracy is coded for AsiaTech's work on civil liberties and autocratic stabilisation.

name: Oxford China Policy Lab (OCPL)
summary: A non-partisan research group of researchers in Oxford and London, founded around 2022, that works to reduce global risks from US-China great-power competition, especially risks from AI and other emerging technologies. It publishes policy analysis on Chinese AI governance and US-China AI diplomacy, for example on China's stance on loss of control, China's proposed World Data Organization, and the 2026 Trump-Xi AI talks. It runs a research fellowship (12 fellows in its fourth cohort, with 35 expert speakers) and held its annual conference in Oxford in late May 2026.
why_it_matters: It brings China expertise and international-relations theory, such as status-seeking in the AI race, to a field whose race models are mostly game-theoretic or written from Washington. It also trains a pipeline of US-China specialists for AI governance.

key_work.title: OCPL Research Fellowship (fifth cohort applications open October 2026)
OCPL Annual Conference: great-power rivalry, US-China AI governance and middle powers
China Says It Cares About Loss of Control: But Loss of Whose Control?
Summitry or Status Shift? Unpacking the Trump-Xi AI Talks

status_evidence: 30 Sep 2026: Substack analysis of the Trump-Xi AI talks; 2 Sep 2026: 'China Says It Cares About Loss of Control'; annual conference in Oxford on Friday 22 May 2026 (reported in the 29 May newsletter); fifth fellowship cohort recruitment opens October 2026.
engage: OCPL Research Fellowship: applications for the fifth cohort open October 2026
Newsletter and analysis: ocpl.substack.com
Staff roles have been advertised (for example a Programme Associate in March 2026)
caveats: Its exact institutional status is unclear: the Substack describes it as a research group at the University of Oxford, while the website calls it a community of researchers in Oxford and London. No funding information was found. The founding year (around 2022) comes from a February 2024 newsletter that describes OCPL as two years old. It sits near the core ring through its GovAI connections and its listing on effectivealtruism.org.
tag_notes: Home: peace (peace_diplomacy, which explicitly includes China studies), because its methods are China studies and international relations. Ring: bridge, keeping the roster value: the mission covers global risk from US-China competition in general, with AI as the focus, so AI safety is not its sole founding mission (borderline core under E1). Transfer: into_institutions, because it produces policy analysis and bridging dialogue for US-China AI governance. Framing coded catastrophic from its mission of mitigating global risk and its loss-of-control analysis. London hub from its self-description as based in Oxford and London.

name: United Nations Institute for Disarmament Research (UNIDIR)
summary: An autonomous UN institute in Geneva that does independent research on disarmament, arms control and international security. Its Security and Technology Programme (40+ researchers and fellows) runs the Roundtable for AI, Security and Ethics (RAISE), launched with Microsoft in Bellagio in March 2024, and the annual Global Conference on AI, Security and Ethics; the 2026 edition was held at the Palais des Nations on 18-19 June. Other AI outputs: a Framework of Responsible Industry Behaviour for AI in the Military Domain, an AI Policy Portal mapping national policies, a Centre of Excellence on AI, Peace and Security, and a Women in AI fellowship for diplomats.
why_it_matters: It is a neutral UN venue where militaries, diplomats from all five UN regional groups, AI labs and defence firms discuss military AI risk together, which few AI-safety organisations can convene. Its industry-behaviour framework is an early voluntary norm aimed directly at defence AI companies.

key_work.title: Roundtable for AI, Security and Ethics (RAISE)
Global Conference on AI, Security and Ethics 2026
Framework of Responsible Industry Behaviour for AI in the Military Domain
AI Policy Portal

people: Francesca Bosco (Acting Head, Security and Technology Programme)
Andrea Gronke (Deputy Head, Security and Technology Programme)
Yasmin Afina (contact for the AI, Security and Ethics conference)
funding: Voluntary contributions from donors (states and others); RAISE was launched in 2024 as a partnership with Microsoft.
status_evidence: 18-19 Jun 2026: held the second Global Conference on AI, Security and Ethics at the Palais des Nations, Geneva (hybrid); 2026 publications include faith-based perspectives on AI ethics and translating cyber norms to military AI.
engage: Annual Global Conference on AI, Security and Ethics (hybrid, Geneva)
Women in AI fellowship (UNIDIR Academy)
Staff and fellow roles in the Security and Technology Programme
caveats: As a UN body, its output is consensus-oriented and diplomatic rather than advocacy. Microsoft's partnership in RAISE and the presence of defence firms (Palantir, Helsing) at its conferences may raise questions of industry influence. The roster's claim that the industry framework was co-developed with OHCHR was not verified. The headcount behind the 'large' scale code was not verified.
tag_notes: Home: peace (peace_arms), because it is the UN's disarmament research institute and its AI work comes from arms control and security diplomacy. Ring: bridge (rule E: an older institution with a sustained programme), given RAISE, two global conferences and a centre of excellence explicitly on AI security risks. Transfer: into_institutions, through multilateral dialogue, an industry-behaviour framework and the policy portal. Org type public under rule I. Framing coded structural because it frames AI as a threat to international peace and security without an x-risk framing; this is a weak call.

name: Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI)
summary: An independent institute founded in 1966, with around 100 staff, that does research on conflict, armaments, arms control and disarmament, and publishes the SIPRI Yearbook and arms-transfer and military-expenditure databases. Its Governance of AI Programme, led by Vincent Boulanin, studies military AI, autonomy in weapons, export controls and responsible innovation. A Carnegie-funded project ($500,000, Sept 2024, 24 months) on AI and inadvertent nuclear escalation held a scenario workshop in Stockholm on 22-23 September 2025 with experts from seven of the nine nuclear-armed states. Recent reports cover responsible procurement of military AI (Feb 2026) and AI in Chinese, Indian and US nuclear postures (Feb 2026).
why_it_matters: It brings decades of arms-control practice to AI and nuclear escalation, one of the most concrete catastrophic-risk pathways, and can convene officials from nuclear-armed states, which AI-safety organisations generally cannot. Its work on export controls for models and on military AI procurement translates abstract risk into instruments states already use.

key_work.title: Impact of Military Artificial Intelligence on Nuclear Escalation Risk
Stockholm workshop on military AI and nuclear escalation (experts from seven nuclear-armed states)
Responsible Procurement of Military Artificial Intelligence (Goussac and Boulanin)
AI in Chinese, Indian and US Nuclear Postures, Norms and Systems (Saalman)

people: Vincent Boulanin (Programme Director, Governance of AI)
Alexander Blanchard (Senior Researcher, Governance of AI)
Netta Goussac (Senior Researcher, Governance of AI)
funding: Mainly governments and independent foundations, with funding sources published annually. Carnegie Corporation of New York gave $500,000 (Sept 2024, 24 months) for the AI and nuclear-escalation project and $400,000 (2017) for an earlier project on machine learning and strategic stability.
status_evidence: 17 Sep 2026: hosted a dialogue on state-industry collaboration for lawful military AI; 23 Apr 2026: 'Mapping the military AI industry' backgrounder.
engage: Staff and research vacancies: sipri.org/about/vacancies
Stockholm Forum on Peace and Development and other public events
Armament and Disarmament Summer School (co-hosted, 2026)
caveats: AI is one programme in a large arms-control institute. Its framing is lawful and responsible military use rather than opposition to military AI. Its 2017-2020 work on machine learning and strategic stability was an early example of this line.
tag_notes: Home: peace (peace_arms), from its arms-control and nonproliferation research; it is the taxonomy's own example. Ring: bridge (rule E: an old institution with a sustained AI-safety programme, the case the ring definition names). Transfer: into_institutions, because the project aims at a menu of nuclear-AI risk-reduction measures plus guidance on procurement and export controls. Framing coded catastrophic for its focus on inadvertent nuclear escalation.

name: US-China Track II Dialogue on Artificial Intelligence and National Security (Brookings-Tsinghua CISS)
summary: A non-governmental (Track II) dialogue convened since October 2019 by the Brookings Institution's Foreign Policy programme and Tsinghua University's Center for International Security and Strategy (CISS), bringing US and Chinese experts together on the risks of military AI. Eight rounds had been held by late 2023, alongside a joint AI Terminology Working Group building a shared glossary. In November 2025 delegation members (Melanie Sisson, Colin Kahl, Sun Chenghao and Xiao Qian) jointly published proposals on military AI governance, including a shared failure-mode and incident taxonomy and common definitions of dangerous AI-enabled military actions.
why_it_matters: It is one of very few sustained, expert-level channels on AI risk between the two leading AI powers, and it supplies the confidence-building toolkit of Track II diplomacy (shared terminology, incident taxonomies) to the US-China race dynamic that AI-safety work treats as central but rarely engages directly.

key_work.title: Steps toward AI governance in the military domain (joint US-Chinese delegation piece)
From Geneva: AI, security and US-China dialogue (Edelman and Hass)
AI Terminology Working Group, second meeting (joint glossary)

people: Ryan Hass (Director, John L. Thornton China Center, Brookings)
R. David Edelman (Nonresident Senior Fellow, Brookings)
status_evidence: 1 Jul 2026: Brookings podcast by Edelman and Hass recorded at UNIDIR's AI, Security and Ethics conference in Geneva, discussing the resumed US-China government AI dialogue; 12 Nov 2025: joint delegation publication.
caveats: It is invitation-only, and most of its proceedings are not public. The roster's claim that it laid the groundwork for the May 2026 Trump-Xi agreement to resume government AI talks, and for a US incident-alert proposal, could not be confirmed from the cited sources. The joint glossary planned in 2023 was not found published. This entry overlaps with the separate CISS entry; count them once in aggregates.
tag_notes: Home: peace (peace_diplomacy, Track II), because it is run by foreign-policy and security think tanks. Ring: bridge, because it is a sustained convening (since 2019, 8+ rounds) explicitly on military AI risk and crisis stability, hosted by institutions rooted elsewhere. Transfer: into_institutions, through confidence-building measures, terminology and incident taxonomies offered to governments. Region coded north_america because Brookings is the US convenor; it is co-hosted from Beijing, a MISFIT for a single-base facet. Framing coded catastrophic for its focus on inadvertent escalation and AI-powered military crises.

name: Center for International Security and Strategy, Tsinghua University (CISS)
summary: A university think tank at Tsinghua University working on international strategy and security, which serves China's foreign and security policy and runs on donations. Its 'AI and International Security' project is China's main Track II counterpart on AI security: with Brookings it has convened the US-China Dialogue on AI and International Security since 2019 and a joint AI Terminology Working Group, and in 2023 it held a dialogue on AI security governance with the Centre for Humanitarian Dialogue. On 14 January 2026 it hosted a forum of about 30 Chinese experts on AI militarisation, misuse by non-state actors and international AI security governance rules; in July 2026 it held a workshop on frontier AI safety and critical-infrastructure protection at the World AI Conference, and in 2026 it launched a podcast series, SinoAI Insights.
why_it_matters: It is a working channel into Chinese security thinking on AI risk, and its deputy director also helps lead Tsinghua's Institute for AI International Governance. Western AI-safety efforts aimed at international coordination need counterparts like it, and its framing of AI governance as part of great-power security shows how Chinese experts weigh shared risks against strategic competition.

key_work.title: US-China Dialogue on AI and International Security (with Brookings; eight rounds by late 2023)
CISS-HD dialogue on AI security governance
Forum on Artificial Intelligence and International Security
SinoAI Insights podcast: Can AI Dialogue Rebuild Trust?

people: Da Wei (Director; Professor of International Relations, Tsinghua)
Xiao Qian (Deputy Director; Vice Dean, Institute for AI International Governance)
funding: Its own site describes it as a university think tank that runs on donations, and it invites donations and commissioned research.
status_evidence: 22 Jul 2026: workshop on 'Frontier AI Safety and Critical Infrastructure Protection' at the World AI Conference in Shanghai; 26 May 2026: SinoAI Insights podcast episode 2 on the resumed US-China government AI dialogue; 14 Jan 2026: Forum on AI and International Security.
caveats: It is oriented to serving Chinese state diplomacy and security policy, so its positions should be read as close to official thinking. The founding year is inferred from its 2019 start of yearbooks and copyright and from the dialogue beginning in October 2019. Overlaps with the separate Brookings-Tsinghua dialogue entry.
tag_notes: Home: peace (peace_diplomacy), because it is a security-studies and diplomacy think tank and its AI work runs through Track II dialogue. Ring: bridge, because it has a standing AI and International Security project and repeated convenings (2019-2026) on AI security risks, from a centre rooted in international relations. Transfer: into_institutions, through dialogue, shared terminology and governance proposals for the two governments. Framing coded structural because it frames AI risk inside great-power competition and the reshaping of international order. Standpoint is neither because China is coded neither in v1 (rule O).

name: Partnership on AI (PAI)
summary: A US nonprofit founded in 2016 by Amazon, DeepMind/Google, Facebook (now Meta), IBM and Microsoft, with Apple joining in early 2017. It brings together 148 partner organisations (companies, civil-society groups, universities and media) to write shared guidance on responsible AI. Its programmes cover safety-critical AI (guidance on deploying foundation models safely, and a 2025 report on detecting AI-agent failures in real time), AI and human connection (synthetic media and content authenticity), AI, labour and the economy, and public policy.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few standing venues where frontier labs, labour and civil-rights groups and newsrooms agree shared practice. Its labour, media-integrity and inclusive-engagement work gives safety guidance backers beyond the labs, and it offers a channel for getting outside-field perspectives into industry norms.

key_work.title: Guidance for Safe Foundation Model Deployment
Responsible Practices for Synthetic Media framework
Prioritizing Real-Time Failure Detection in AI Agents
UN Global Dialogue co-leads' call to action on safe, secure and trustworthy AI

people: Claire Leibowicz (Director of AI, Trust, and Society)
funding: Charitable contributions from foundations (Ford, MacArthur, Gordon and Betty Moore, Knight, Luminate, Surdna, MetLife, Casey) and companies (Adobe, Amazon, Apple, DeepMind/Google, IBM, Intel, Intuit, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI). The site gives no amounts; they are in its Form 990s and annual reports.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: announced six new partners (10 Sep) and published 'Planning for More Than One Future' (1 Sep); ten-year anniversary in 2026.
engage: Staff roles via partnershiponai.org/careers (about 40 staff listed in 2026)
Organisations can apply to become Partners
Open research and resource library
caveats: Funded largely by the AI companies it convenes, so how independent its guidance is remains a fair question; civil-society members have left before, citing limited influence. It sits close to mainstream responsible-AI policy, and its outside contribution is mainly labour, civil-society and media perspectives. Its safety programme frames risks as near- and long-term deployment risks, not existential ones. The roster's '200+ partners' is corrected to 148, per its partners page.
tag_notes: Home law, law_policy (the taxonomy's own example for PAI). Under H2, AI policy is not a sector, so PAI is placed by its multistakeholder public-interest/ELSI convening method. Secondaries: economics (AI, Labor and the Economy team) and safety (Safety-Critical AI programme, where the AI Incident Database began). Ring bridge kept (E3): PAI was not founded inside the x-risk ecosystem, but it runs a standing Safety-Critical AI programme with a Head of AI Safety and outputs from 2023 to 2025. Transfer into_institutions (J3): its main products are voluntary frameworks and guidance for companies and policymakers. Framing present_harms rather than flourishing (L): the mission is positive, but most outputs address concrete deployment harms.

name: International Bar Association Artificial Intelligence Institute (IBA AI Institute)
summary: An institute of the International Bar Association, launched on 8 June 2026 under former IBA president Jaime Carey and current president Claudio Visco. Its founding director is Dr Farzana Dudhwala, most recently Global AI Policy & Governance Lead at Meta, who earlier worked on UK government AI strategy and led the AI Futures team at the Centre for Data Ethics and Innovation. It aims to bring the legal profession's expertise into international AI governance, shaping frameworks in line with the rule of law, human rights and democratic integrity. The launch release names frontier AI systems, algorithmic accountability, access to justice, privacy and labour transformation among the challenges it will address, and commits to capacity-building so that under-represented jurisdictions help shape AI governance. It can draw on the IBA's network of more than 80,000 lawyers and 190 bar associations and law societies.
why_it_matters: It gives AI governance a route into bar associations, law societies and courts worldwide, especially in jurisdictions that are usually absent from AI-safety discussions. Frontier AI is on its stated priority list, so it is an early opening for AI-safety governance ideas to reach the global legal profession.

key_work.title: Launch of the IBA AI Institute
IBA AI Working Group project (host's earlier AI work, run by the IBA Section on Public and Professional Interest since mid-2023)

people: Jaime Carey (former IBA President, co-established the Institute)
status_evidence: Jun 2026: Institute launched (8 Jun); the IBA's AI hub page links the launch release.
engage: IBA membership gives access to its committees and annual conference (2026 edition in Copenhagen had AI sessions)
No open calls from the Institute found yet
caveats: Brand new, with no outputs yet. The IBA says the Institute's work is separate from the AI guidance its practice committees produce. The director comes from a senior policy role at Meta. Funding and staffing have not been disclosed.
tag_notes: Home law, law_legal (H3): a unit of the global bar that brings legal-profession and rule-of-law expertise. Ring changed from potential to adjacent (E2/E3): it is a standing institute with a director, building on an IBA AI working group that has run since mid-2023. It is framed around responsible governance, human rights and the rule of law, not safety or catastrophic risk; 'frontier AI systems' is among its priorities, so it may move to bridge once outputs appear. Transfer into_institutions (J3): it aims to shape AI governance frameworks and bring under-represented jurisdictions into them. Org type programme (A1, I). The London hub is from IBA headquarters; the Institute's own staff location is not stated.

name: MIT Partnership for Systems Approaches to Safety and Security (PSASS)
summary: A research group in MIT's Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics, directed by Nancy Leveson with John Thomas as executive director. It develops and teaches STAMP, a systems-theoretic model of how accidents happen, and the methods built on it: STPA for hazard and security analysis and CAST for accident analysis. It runs a research consortium with industry and government partners in aviation, defence, space, healthcare, automotive and energy, and publishes handbooks and free tutorials. It also hosts the annual MIT STAMP Workshop, which is free and typically draws 200-400 people in person and about 2,000 online.
why_it_matters: STPA treats safety as a control problem across the whole sociotechnical structure, from regulators and management to operators and software. That is the kind of hazard analysis that frontier labs and AI-agent deployments currently lack. Roel Dobbe and Simon Mylius have argued for applying it to AI, but the group itself has no AI programme, so it is an open opportunity for partnership.

key_work.title: Engineering a Safer World (Leveson, MIT Press)
STPA Handbook (Leveson and Thomas)
CAST Handbook
2026 MIT STAMP Workshop, including talks on STPA for AI certification (Boeing), STPA-Sec wargaming of AI-enabled capabilities (CMU) and runtime safety for AI robots (Amazon)

people: Nancy Leveson (Director; Professor of Aeronautics and Astronautics)
funding: Sponsored research and membership from industrial and government partners in its consortium; amounts not published.
status_evidence: 2026: MIT STAMP Workshop held, with AI-related talks from Boeing, Carnegie Mellon and Amazon; the site promotes the 2026 workshop.
engage: Annual MIT STAMP Workshop: free, in person or virtual, with an open call for presentations
Free online tutorials on STAMP, STPA and CAST
Online training and certification via the STAMP Institute
Research partnership through its industry and government consortium; graduate internships
caveats: No AI-specific programme: the AI talks on its site are by outside presenters at its workshop. The papers that apply STPA to AI (Mylius 2025, Dobbe 2025) are by others, not the group. No founding year is given on its site.
tag_notes: Home safety, safety_engineering (the taxonomy's example), for STAMP/STPA/CAST systems-theoretic hazard and accident analysis; secondary life for the systems-theory and control-theory basis of STAMP. Ring potential kept (E2): there is no standing AI programme; AI appears only in talks by others at its annual workshop (2024 USAF ML aircraft, 2025 CAST on AI incidents, 2026 Boeing, CMU, Amazon). Transferable method: STPA analyses safety as control across the whole sociotechnical hierarchy, and could be used for hazard analysis of frontier and agentic AI and of lab safety culture. Transfer into_institutions rather than none_yet (J6), because AI applications are already presented at its workshops. Framing catastrophic is a loose fit: its stakes are high-consequence accidents in aviation, nuclear and defence systems, with no AI risk statement. Engagement partner is used because it has no AI programme.

name: Stop Killer Robots
summary: A global coalition of more than 300 NGOs in over 75 countries, set up in October 2012 and publicly launched in 2013. It campaigns for new international law on autonomy in weapons systems, to keep human control over the use of force. A steering committee of NGOs leads it (including Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International, Article 36, ICRAC, PAX and Soka Gakkai International), with a small remote staff under executive director Nicole van Rooijen. In 2026 it lobbied the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) expert group, which agreed a text defining lethal autonomous weapons on 6 September. The November Review Conference will decide whether to open treaty negotiations. Its Interfaith Group's June 2026 statement backed Pope Leo XIV's call to 'disarm AI' and called for a legal ban on autonomous weapons that target people.
why_it_matters: It is a tested model of a civil-society treaty campaign for binding limits on one AI application, with more than a decade of experience moving states through UN processes. Its 'digital dehumanisation' framing and its interfaith group connect AI governance to human-rights and religious communities that AI safety rarely mobilises.

key_work.title: 'Disarming AI, Defending Humanity': Interfaith Group response to Magnifica Humanitas
'Nothing less than negotiations': advocacy at the CCW Group of Governmental Experts, 31 Aug-4 Sep
Youth delegate programme for under-30s at Geneva multilateral meetings

people: Nicole van Rooijen (Executive Director, since Jan 2025)
Clare Conboy (Head of Campaigns and Partnerships)
funding: Republic and Canton of Geneva, City of Geneva and Swiss Philanthropy Foundation, as listed on its site in 2026; amounts not published. Human Rights Watch coordinated the campaign from 2012 to 2021.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: published 'Nothing less than negotiations' after the CCW expert-group session (8 Sep); its director was quoted on the 128-state definitional text (6 Sep).
engage: NGOs can join as member organisations
Youth network; youth delegate programme (applications opened Jun 2026 for the Sep and Nov Geneva sessions)
Petition, e-newsletter, parliamentary pledge and story submissions
caveats: Focused on weapons, with no position on frontier or general-purpose AI risk. Campaign groups called the September 2026 definitional text too weak, and the US, Russia, India and Israel opposed stronger negotiations. The Interfaith Group sub-entry is folded into this profile.
tag_notes: Home peace, peace_arms: a humanitarian-disarmament campaign for a treaty under the CCW. Secondaries: law (human-rights NGOs HRW, Amnesty and Privacy International sit on the steering committee) and religion (its Interfaith Group, merged here, issued 'Disarming AI, Defending Humanity' in June 2026). Ring adjacent kept (taxonomy example): a sustained AI-weapons campaign since 2012, framed around human control, humanitarian law and digital dehumanisation, not catastrophic or alignment risk. Transfer into_institutions (J3): its goal is a legally binding instrument. Badge speed_of_wisdom: it campaigns for prohibitions and against arms-race dynamics, which goes beyond ordinary product precaution. Region global: staff work remotely in Canada, the UK, Ireland and Switzerland, with the director in Geneva.

name: International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC): autonomous weapons and AI
summary: The ICRC, the Geneva-based guardian of international humanitarian law, has a standing legal and policy line on autonomous weapon systems and on AI decision-support systems in military decision-making. It calls for binding rules that prohibit unpredictable autonomous weapons and those designed to target people, restrict all others, and keep human control over life-and-death decisions. In 2026 it issued a joint appeal with UN Secretary-General António Guterres (25 Aug) and a working paper to the CCW expert group (28 Aug) urging negotiations on a legally binding instrument in 2027. It also co-sponsored a forum in New York on 28 Sep calling for treaty talks and submitted a working paper to the UN General Assembly First Committee (Oct).
why_it_matters: Its doctrine of human control over force, and its two-tier model of banning unpredictable or anti-personnel systems while restricting the rest, is the most fully developed legal template for limiting AI systems that take irreversible actions. Its neutrality and its role as guardian of the Geneva Conventions give it access to states that AI-safety organisations rarely reach.

key_work.title: ICRC position on autonomous weapon systems
Limits on Autonomy in Weapon Systems (with SIPRI)
Renewed joint call by the UN Secretary-General and ICRC President to adopt rules on autonomous weapons
Working paper on regulating autonomous weapon systems, CCW Group of Governmental Experts

funding: The ICRC as a whole is funded mainly by voluntary contributions from states and the European Commission, with National Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies and private donors; no budget is published for the autonomous-weapons work.
status_evidence: Oct 2026: working paper to the UNGA First Committee; Aug 2026: joint appeal with the UN Secretary-General (25 Aug) and working paper to the CCW expert group (28 Aug).
engage: Follow its working papers and the Humanitarian Law & Policy blog's autonomous-weapons tag (blogs.icrc.org/law-and-policy)
caveats: Its focus is military and humanitarian; it takes no position on frontier or general-purpose AI risk. The treaty outcome depends on the November 2026 CCW Review Conference, where the US, Russia, India and Israel have resisted negotiations. The founding year is the ICRC's; the autonomous-weapons line is much younger.
tag_notes: Home peace, peace_arms (taxonomy boundary: humanitarian law goes to Peace); secondary law for its legal-interpretation method. Org type programme (A1): the unit is the ICRC's autonomous-weapons and military-AI work, not the whole organisation. Ring adjacent kept (E3): a standing programme framed around humanitarian consequences, IHL compliance and a 'moral red line', not catastrophic or alignment risk. Assurance is the secondary problem because human control and the ban on unpredictable systems are oversight requirements. Transfer into_institutions (J3): prohibitions and restrictions for a binding CCW instrument. Framing present_harms is the closest key for anticipated harms to civilians.

name: Build Up
summary: A peacebuilding collective co-founded by Helena Puig Larrauri, working on conflict in the digital age through three legal entities: a California 501(c)(3), a Kenyan subsidiary and a German association. Its digital-conflict programme studies how platforms and AI drive polarisation and violence. The Polarization Footprint ranks large platforms by affective polarisation (Kenya results in 2025). Phoenix is a free, open-source, AI-enabled social-media listening tool for peacebuilders and mediators, built with datavaluepeople and Swiss foreign ministry support. It also publishes monthly Sudan social-media listening reports. It co-organises the annual Build Peace conference (13th edition, Waterloo, Canada, 13-15 Nov 2026) and offers free online courses in digital peacebuilding.
why_it_matters: It brings conflict-transformation practice, participatory social-media listening and platform accountability measures to AI's effects on social cohesion. Its work comes from conflict settings in Africa and the Middle East, which the AI-safety field rarely hears from. The Polarization Footprint is a working example of measuring one societal harm across platforms.

key_work.title: Polarization Footprint (Kenya results)
Phoenix open-source social-media listening platform
Sudan Social Media Listening monthly reports
Build Peace 2026: 'Enabling Encounters', Waterloo

people: Allan Cheboi (AI ethics and digital peacebuilding)
funding: Phoenix was developed with support from the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs; annual audits are published (latest 2024); other donors are not listed on the site.
status_evidence: Jul 2026: Sudan social-media listening report (monthly reports May-Jul 2026); Jun 2026 webinar on information warfare in Sudan; Build Peace 2026 scheduled for 13-15 Nov in Waterloo.
engage: Build Peace 2026, 13-15 Nov, Waterloo, Canada (with the Kindred Credit Union Centre for Peace Advancement at Conrad Grebel University College)
Free self-paced online courses (Digital Peacebuilding 101 and others, in English, Arabic, French and Spanish)
Webinars, e.g. Mar 2026 on tech governance, peace and security
Phoenix is free for eligible peacebuilders and researchers
caveats: AI is one part of a wider digital-peacebuilding portfolio, and Build Up has no x-risk framing. It runs as a non-hierarchical collective without a listed executive director. The founding year comes from the roster and matches the 13th Build Peace being held in 2026.
tag_notes: Home peace, peace_building (the taxonomy's example); secondary democracy for its participatory inclusive-politics methods. Ring adjacent kept (E3): sustained work on how platforms and AI drive polarisation, including AI tooling (Phoenix), with no safety or catastrophic framing. Transfer protecting (J4): its digital work defends the conflict-affected communities it already serves, though the Polarization Footprint is also an accountability tool for platforms. Standpoint majority_world, flagged for review: its programmes centre on Sudan, Somalia, Kenya and other Majority-World conflict settings and much of the team is in East Africa and MENA, but the co-founder is European and the lead entity is Californian. Region global: a distributed collective with US, Kenyan and German entities.

name: AI for Peace
summary: A small think tank founded and run by Branka Panic, with a network of volunteer advisers. It aims to make sure peacebuilders, humanitarians and human-rights activists understand AI and are heard in how it is developed, with focus areas in human security, humanitarian action, human rights and democracy, and ethics. Outputs include a non-technical AI guide for policymakers (2020), the book AI for Peace (Routledge, 2024, with Paige Arthur), and blog analysis of topics such as generative AI and mass atrocities, conflict-prediction models and the 2025 Paris AI Action Summit.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few organisations dedicated to bringing peacebuilders and humanitarians into AI governance. Its human-security lens covers dual-use risks to vulnerable populations and generative AI's role in mass atrocities, which safety work seldom considers.

key_work.title: AI for Peace (book, Routledge; Panic and Arthur)
AI Explained: Non-technical Guide for Policymakers
Generative AI and Mass Atrocities: A Real Threat We Can't Ignore
Reflections on the Paris AI Action Summit: a peacebuilder's perspective

status_evidence: Mar 2025: blog posts on the Paris AI Action Summit, the latest dated items on its own site. Rotary profiled the founder in Mar 2026 (roster source; the page was blocked when checked).
engage: Newsletter and mailing list
Its blog invites contributions from people working in peacebuilding, humanitarian action and sustainable development
caveats: Very small. Its own site was last updated in March 2025 and gives no founding year, location, legal status or funders. Much of its output promotes AI applications for peacebuilding (early warning, hate-speech detection, a pandemic-policy challenge with Omdena), which is closer to 'AI for good' than to making AI go well. It is included for its human-security risk analysis and its work bringing peacebuilders into AI governance.
tag_notes: Home peace, peace_building: it brings peacebuilders', humanitarians' and human-rights activists' perspectives into AI; secondary law for its human-rights and democracy strand. Ring adjacent kept (E3): AI is its whole remit (guide 2020, book 2024, blog to 2025), framed by human security and human rights rather than catastrophic risk. Transfer convening (J5): its stated aim is that peacebuilders are informed and heard in AI development. Framing flourishing: its vision and book are about AI benefiting peace, with risk analysis secondary. Status active only on the strength of 2025 posts; it could be dormant. Region global because its site states no base.

name: Institute for Security and Technology (IST)
summary: IST is a nonprofit security think tank founded in 2017, with offices in Oakland and Washington DC. It brings technologists, officials and industry together in working groups that produce policy recommendations. Its AI work includes: an AI and NC3 programme on AI in nuclear command, control and communications; a Recursive Self-Improvement Initiative launched with the Future of Life Institute in August 2026; the SL5 Task Force on security standards for frontier models; work towards a US–China AI incident line; and the Andrew Carnegie AI–Nuclear Policy Accelerator for mid-career national-security practitioners. It also runs cyber programmes such as the Ransomware Task Force.
why_it_matters: It applies nuclear risk-reduction practice (hotlines, confidence-building, NC3 safeguards) to frontier-AI problems such as loss of control and recursive self-improvement. It also gives nuclear-security practitioners hands-on AI literacy.

key_work.title: Recursive Self-Improvement Initiative (with the Future of Life Institute)
Andrew Carnegie AI–Nuclear Policy Accelerator, first cohort of 26
SL5 Task Force on frontier-model security standards
Before the First AI Crisis, Washington and Beijing Need a Habit of Talking (US–China AI incident line)

funding: Revenue about $3.6M in 2024, down from $4.8M in 2023 (IRS Form 990). Supporters named in the 2025 annual report include Coefficient Giving (which funded the incubation of the SL5 Task Force), Future of Life Institute, Longview Philanthropy, Founders Pledge, Hewlett Foundation, Craig Newmark Philanthropies, Patrick J. McGovern Foundation, the German and Swiss foreign ministries, Microsoft, Meta, AWS, Mastercard and Zscaler. The AI–Nuclear Policy Accelerator is funded by a Carnegie philanthropic grant.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: launched the Perry-Shultz Center for Technology & Strategic Stability and the Center for Advancing Cybersecurity (10 Sep), and published an essay on a US–China AI incident line (25 Sep).
engage: Andrew Carnegie AI–Nuclear Policy Accelerator: a cohort programme for mid-career national-security professionals (first cohort announced Feb 2026)
Staff roles on its careers page
Public events and webinars on its events page; newsletter
caveats: Its founding mission covers technology security in general, and its cyber programmes are large. AI is one of several lines. Some funders are technology companies (Microsoft, Meta, AWS). Its LinkedIn handle still uses an earlier name, Technology for Global Security. I moved its ring from core to bridge.
tag_notes: Home is peace (H1/H2): its AI outputs come from nuclear risk-reduction and national-security practice (NC3, incident lines, an accelerator for nuclear practitioners). Safety is secondary, for the SL5 security standards and its cyber work. Ring changed from core to bridge (E): IST was founded in 2017 as a broad technology-security think tank, and its September 2026 reorganisation centres strategic stability and cybersecurity, so AI is one line among several; that AI line is explicitly framed around loss of control and catastrophic risk. Transfer is into_institutions (J3): it produces governance mechanisms such as RSI oversight frameworks, a US–China incident line and security standards. Sub-tradition is peace_arms (D).

name: Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative (AIGI)
summary: AIGI is a research centre in the University of Oxford's Martin School, launched in September 2023. It studies the governance of frontier AI from both the policy and the technical side. Its work covers international and China AI governance; the Oxford AI Diplomacy Lab, which supports officials who negotiate on AI; technical and hardware governance (verification, chip and compute-cluster monitoring); and frontier-AI risk-management standards. With the Safe AI Forum it co-hosted the fifth International Dialogue on AI Safety (IDAIS) in London in April 2026, which produced the IDAIS London Declaration.
why_it_matters: It applies international-relations and diplomatic practice to frontier AI: Track II dialogue agendas, verification regimes, and lessons from aviation and nuclear governance. It is one of the few university centres building diplomats' capacity for AI negotiations.

key_work.title: Co-host of IDAIS-London and the IDAIS London Declaration (with the Safe AI Forum)
Promising Topics for US–China Dialogues on AI Safety and Governance
Verification for International AI Governance
Oxford AI Diplomacy Lab

people: Reed Schuler (Co-Director, Oxford AI Diplomacy Lab)
Lucia Velasco (Co-Director, Oxford AI Diplomacy Lab)
funding: Hosted by the Oxford Martin School. Its site does not list other funders.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: published 'Equitable Compute Cooperation and the Role of the G20' (24 Sep). Apr 2026: co-hosted IDAIS-London (17–19 Apr).
engage: Technical AI Governance (TAIG) DPhil studentships
AI Academic Upskilling Program for Social Scientists (call for applications April 2026)
Public events and a newsletter
caveats: Much of its output is conventional AI-governance analysis. The interdisciplinary part is mainly international relations, diplomacy, and comparison with how other safety-critical industries are regulated.
tag_notes: Home is peace (H2): AI-governance analysis is not a sector, so AIGI is placed by the tradition it imports, which is international relations and Track II diplomacy (IDAIS, US–China dialogue topics, the Oxford AI Diplomacy Lab) plus verification regimes. Safety is secondary, for its risk-management standards work and its lessons from aviation and nuclear safety. Ring stays core (E1): it was founded in 2023 to govern risks from frontier AI and is on the classic map. Transfer is into_institutions (J3): it produces dialogue agendas, declarations, and verification and risk-management proposals for governments. Sub-tradition is peace_diplomacy, which matches its main output (D).

name: AI Safety Asia (AISA)
summary: AISA is a nonprofit set up in 2024 to build Asian governments' capacity to govern AI safety. It trains officials (in April 2026, 38 Indonesian officials from 11 ministries), runs regional roundtables and civil-society trainings, and keeps invitation-only channels open between senior officials. It also runs AI crisis tabletop exercises; in 2026 these were held in Geneva, at the Biological Weapons Convention working group, and on the official APEC agenda. In 2025 it announced RAISE-SEA, a scenario platform, at the Paris Peace Forum, and published a Brookings report on AI safety governance in Southeast Asia.
why_it_matters: It brings crisis-diplomacy simulation and Southeast Asian policy perspectives into AI-safety governance, which US, UK and Chinese voices otherwise dominate. It helps middle powers and Global Majority states see their dependencies and secure safeguards in AI procurement.

key_work.title: AI Safety Governance, the Southeast Asian Way (with the Brookings Institution)
Scaling AI Diplomacy: scenario exercises for capacity and readiness (with Chatham House and the University of Geneva)
RAISE-SEA scenario and preparedness platform (Paris Peace Forum)
AI crisis-diplomacy convening at the India AI Impact Summit

funding: A Manifund project for its India AI Impact Summit convening was fully funded at $100,000 (early 2026). Its site names Windfall Trust, Omidyar Network and Founders Pledge as funders, lists the Future of Life Institute among its partners, and says the UK FCDO is a government partner (which commissioned an AI-biosecurity mapping study).
status_evidence: Sep 2026: published 'Scaling AI Diplomacy' with Chatham House and the University of Geneva (4 Sep), and held a middle-powers roundtable at UNGA in New York (24 Sep).
engage: Newsletter on AI governance in Asia
Online public convenings, some co-hosted (e.g. with Chatham House, Jan 2026)

Cooperative AI course, Asia edition (March 2025)
caveats: Its site gives no headquarters. The roster said Manila; its Manifund project lists Hong Kong, the UK and the US, and the CEO is based in Hong Kong. Much of its work is high-level convening, whose effects are hard to verify. Its stated stakes mix sovereignty and lock-in concerns with crisis and catastrophic-risk work.
tag_notes: Home is peace (H1): crisis diplomacy, invitation-only channels between officials, and tabletop exercises, including at the BWC working group. Arts is secondary, for scenario foresight (RAISE-SEA; B10). Ring stays core (E1): it was founded in 2024 with AI-safety governance as its mission, and FLI and Founders Pledge are among its supporters. Transfer is into_institutions (J3): it trains officials and shapes national and regional AI policy; its Indonesia training fed into the country's draft presidential AI decree. Standpoint is majority_world (O) because its work centres Southeast Asia and the Global Majority, although some leaders are based in Hong Kong. Framing is structural, following its mission statement on leverage and on upstream decisions that become irreversible (L).

name: UChicago Existential Risk Laboratory (XLab)
summary: XLab is an interdisciplinary lab at the University of Chicago, founded in 2022 by the physicist Daniel Holz. It researches existential and global catastrophic risks (AI safety and security, nuclear security, biorisk and extreme climate change) and trains students in them. It runs a paid 10-week Summer Research Fellowship on AI safety, nuclear security and where they meet; an AI safety fundamentals course; 'Second Look', which replicates influential empirical AI-safety results; and an open AI Security guide. It supports the Nobel Laureate Assembly for the Prevention of Nuclear War and co-sponsored the July 2026 Rome assembly on AI and nuclear war, which produced the Rome Declaration.
why_it_matters: It ties AI risk to the nuclear-security tradition of the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, whose Science and Security Board Holz chairs. It also trains researchers in the neglected overlap of AI and nuclear risk, including resilience after a nuclear detonation.

key_work.title: Summer Research Fellowship in AI safety and nuclear security
Co-sponsor, Global Nobel Laureates Assembly on AI and Nuclear War (Rome Declaration)
Second Look: replicating empirical AI-safety claims
Nobel Laureate Assembly for the Prevention of Nuclear War (supporter)

funding: Supporters listed on its About page: Coefficient Giving, Future of Life Institute, Hewlett Foundation, Carnegie Corporation of New York, Longview Philanthropy and Survival and Flourishing Fund.
status_evidence: Jul 2026: co-sponsored the Global Nobel Laureates Assembly on AI and Nuclear War in Rome (14–16 Jul). Jun–Aug 2026: ran its Summer Research Fellowship.
