AI Security guide: free self-study material with coding exercises
Mailing list
caveats: Its AI programme is fairly mainstream (an AI risk fundamentals reading group, replications, a security guide); what sets it apart is the link to nuclear and broader existential risk. The team is small and many members are students. The classic map lists its fellowship, not the lab. The fellowship requires US work authorisation.
tag_notes: Home is peace (B12): what it adds is the nuclear-security and arms-control tradition (the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, the Nobel Laureate Assembly). Safety is secondary, for its nuclear programme's work on post-detonation resilience and civil defence, which counts as catastrophe resilience (B12). Ring stays core (E1): it was founded in 2022 to work on existential and catastrophic risk, AI included, and its fellowship is on the classic map. Transfer is into_institutions (J3), based on declarations and policy research aimed at governments; its training of researchers is field-building, which has no exact transfer value. Sub-tradition is peace_arms (D).

name: Geneva Centre for Security Policy (GCSP)
summary: GCSP is an international foundation in Geneva, set up by the Swiss government in 1995 as Switzerland's contribution to NATO's Partnership for Peace. It trains diplomats, military officers and officials in security policy, and also does research, policy advice and dialogue work. Its Transformative Technologies cluster runs an annual online course on emerging technologies and security and publishes on military AI, for example a 2026 Geneva Paper on the security implications of agentic AI. With UN CTED and the Swiss foreign ministry it runs a project on human-rights-centred use of AI in counter-terrorism, and it hosts the Processes of International Negotiation (PIN) research programme.
why_it_matters: It holds decades of negotiation research (PIN) and trains security-policy officials from many states. Both could be used to design international AI agreements and to train the officials who will negotiate them. So far its AI work covers military AI and counter-terrorism, not frontier-AI risk.

key_work.title: The International Security and Military Implications of Agentic AI (Geneva Paper)

Tobias Vestner (Director, Research and Policy Advice Department)

funding: The Swiss government is the main contributor. The foundation is governed by 55 member states and the Canton of Geneva, and partners commission and fund specific projects.
status_evidence: Jul 2026: published an analysis of the first UN informal exchanges on AI in the military domain (31 Jul). Oct 2026: its Transformative Technologies and Security course runs 14–15 October.

Global Fellowship Initiative
Open-enrolment executive courses and a Master of Advanced Studies in International Security

Staff roles (over 90 staff)
caveats: I moved its ring from potential to adjacent. AI is one topic in a broad security-policy portfolio. The link between PIN's negotiation research and AI agreements is a possibility, not current work.
tag_notes: Home is peace (H1): security-policy education, arms control and negotiation research (PIN). Law is secondary, for the rule-of-law and human-rights project on AI in counter-terrorism; arts is secondary, for its foresight work (the Future of Peace and War project, strategic anticipation). Ring changed from potential to adjacent (E2/E3): a standing Transformative Technologies cluster, an annual AI-and-security course and 2026 papers on agentic and military AI make a sustained programme, but none of it is framed around catastrophic risk, alignment or 'AI going well'. Transfer is into_institutions (J3): it trains officials and advises multilateral processes on governing military AI. Org type is nonprofit (I): it is an international foundation under Swiss law, funded by government but independent. Sub-tradition is peace_arms, which matches its AI output (D). The online hub reflects the annual virtual course.

name: African Centre for the Constructive Resolution of Disputes (ACCORD)
summary: ACCORD is a Durban-based civil-society organisation, founded in 1992, that works on conflict prevention, mediation, peacekeeping and peacebuilding across Africa, often with the African Union and regional economic communities. It trains mediators and officials, convenes dialogues, and publishes the African Journal on Conflict Resolution and Conflict Trends. Its AI engagement is light: a few analysis pieces (on AI early warning and surveillance in the Sudan conflict, and on trustworthy AI for African peace and security), and a June 2026 UN Peacebuilding Week session where its director argued that African conflict experience should shape how AI peacebuilding tools are built and governed.
why_it_matters: It holds three decades of African mediation and conflict-transformation practice and working relationships with the AU and regional bodies. AI governance and AI-assisted peacebuilding tools mostly lack that knowledge and an African institutional voice on AI and security.

key_work.title: Session 'Making Artificial Intelligence Work for Trustworthy and Inclusive Peacebuilding', UN Peacebuilding Week
AI-Powered Early Warning Systems and the Governance of Autonomous Surveillance Technologies in African Conflict Zones: Lessons from the Sudan Crisis (2023–2025)
Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence: How does it matter for African Peace and Security?
African Journal on Conflict Resolution

status_evidence: 2 Oct 2026: delivered mediation and negotiation training for Ethiopian public servants.
engage: No AI programme: open to partnerships that bring African peacebuilding experience into AI-and-security governance and AI peacebuilding tools
Staff roles and internships listed on its site
caveats: Its AI work so far is two 2026 analysis pieces (one by an ACCORD researcher, one by an outside contributor from NUPI) and one UN Peacebuilding Week session; I found no AI staff or programme. I could not confirm from its site the roster's description of it as Ubuntu-informed. Funders are not listed.
tag_notes: Home is peace (H1): mediation, peacekeeping and peacebuilding practice. Ring stays potential (E2): its AI engagement is a few analysis pieces and one UN side event, with no standing programme. Transferable method: African mediation, conflict-analysis and early-warning practice, with access to the AU and regional bodies, applied to designing and governing AI peacebuilding tools and to giving Africa a voice in AI-security governance. Transfer is convening (J5): its AI articles inform its own African peace-and-security readers. It is not none_yet because some AI work exists. Sub-tradition is peace_building (D).

name: Kofi Annan International Peacekeeping Training Centre (KAIPTC)
summary: KAIPTC is a training and research centre in Accra. Ghana's Ministry of Defence established it in 1998 and it was commissioned in 2004; it is one of ECOWAS's three peacekeeping training centres of excellence. It trains military, police and civilian personnel for peace operations, runs master's and PhD programmes in peace and security, and does research. Since late 2023 it has offered a fee-paying short course, 'Artificial Intelligence in Peacebuilding', for practitioners in Ghana (the latest edition was 2025). In October 2026 it is running a certificate in cybersecurity, AI and digital resilience that covers AI security and deepfakes.
why_it_matters: Its peacekeeping-training curricula and West African network of security practitioners make it a natural channel for building AI-and-security capacity where that capacity is thin. Its AI courses so far teach people to use AI tools, not to govern AI risks.

key_work.title: Artificial Intelligence in Peacebuilding course
Professional Certificate in Cybersecurity, AI & Digital Resilience (with Cyber1Defense)
Fee-paying public short courses introduced, including AI in Peacebuilding

people: Air Vice Marshal David Anetey Akrong (Commandant)
funding: Norway provides core, non-earmarked funding through a joint financing arrangement. Earmarked funders are Austria, Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Japan, Nigeria, Sweden, Switzerland, the UK and the USA. Institutional partners include ECOWAS, the AU, the UN and GIZ.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: hosted the 2nd UNODC–WIMOWCA regional conference on women, peace and security in the Gulf of Guinea. The AI and digital resilience certificate runs 12–16 Oct 2026.
engage: Fee-paying short courses open to the public, including AI in Peacebuilding (for Ghana-based practitioners) and the Cybersecurity, AI & Digital Resilience certificate (12–16 Oct 2026, Accra)
Master's and PhD programmes in peace and security
No AI-governance programme: open to partnerships on AI-and-security capacity-building
caveats: Its AI engagement is limited to short applied courses on using AI tools and on cyber and AI security, one of them delivered with a private cyber firm. I found nothing on governing AI risk. The AI in Peacebuilding announcement page carries a wrong 2019 date, and the course is aimed at Ghana-based professionals.
tag_notes: Home is peace (H1): peacekeeping training and peace-and-security research. Ring stays potential (E2): its AI engagement is one applied short course on using AI in peacebuilding and one AI and cyber certificate, with no work on AI risk or governance. Transferable method: UN-standard peacekeeping curricula and an ECOWAS training network, applied to building AI-and-security capacity among West African practitioners. Transfer is convening (J5): the courses inform its own community of practitioners. It is not none_yet because some AI work exists. Org type is academic (I), following the roster, because it awards degrees and has a research department, although it is a Ghana Ministry of Defence institution.

name: AlgorithmWatch
summary: A nonprofit (gGmbH) based in Berlin, with a Swiss branch in Zurich, that investigates automated decision-making and AI systems and campaigns for their accountability under EU and Swiss law. It audits deployed chatbots and platforms, for example testing how ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok and Claude answer pregnancy and abortion questions across three languages, and it presses for enforcement of the AI Act and the Digital Services Act. It also runs a recurring fellowship for journalists and researchers who investigate algorithmic systems.
why_it_matters: It has years of practice in auditing deployed AI systems from outside, using personas and multilingual prompt sets, and in turning the findings into regulatory pressure. The AI-safety evals world rarely draws on that kind of external civil-society auditing. It is based in Berlin, close to the int/a community there.

key_work.title: ChatGPT and Co: Are AI-driven search engines a threat to democratic elections? (with AI Forensics, SRF, RTS)
How popular AI chatbots recommend pro-life websites to pregnant people
Algorithmic Accountability Reporting Fellowship (cohort 5 in 2025-26; 34 fellows since 2023)

funding: Funders each giving more than 10% of 2025 income: Alfred Landecker Foundation, Stiftung Mercator, Schöpflin Stiftung and the German federal family ministry (BMBFSFJ). Earlier support came from the Bertelsmann and Hans Böckler foundations. The Swiss branch is funded by Engagement Migros. Supporting memberships start at €5 a month. Annual accounts are published.
status_evidence: Aug 2026: published a chatbot audit on abortion information (22 Aug) and an article on slow regulation of AI-generated child sexual abuse material (20 Aug).
engage: Algorithmic Accountability Reporting Fellowship: six-month paid fellowships for journalists and researchers in Europe, including the UK, Türkiye, Georgia and Ukraine (recurring since 2023)
Staff roles in Berlin and Zurich (careers page at algorithmwatch.org/en/jobs/)
Supporting membership from €5 a month
caveats: Its framing is present-day harms and rights. It does not engage with catastrophic-risk or alignment framings. The Swiss branch, AlgorithmWatch CH, has its own leadership.
tag_notes: Home law/law_sts: civil-society algorithmic auditing and public-interest investigation (chatbot audits, DSA systemic-risk work). Arts is secondary because investigative journalism is one of its methods (the reporting fellowship). Ring adjacent: a sustained AI programme on rights and democratic harms with no catastrophic-risk, alignment or 'going well' framing (E3). Transfer into_institutions: its findings feed AI Act and DSA enforcement and policy (J3). Framing present_harms follows rule L, which names AlgorithmWatch as the example. Problems: justice (accountability audits) first, then epistemics (chatbots and election information, source steering).

name: BRAID: Bridging Responsible AI Divides
summary: A national programme funded by the Arts and Humanities Research Council (AHRC) and led by the University of Edinburgh with BBC R&D and the Ada Lovelace Institute. It embeds arts and humanities research in the UK's responsible-AI ecosystem. It funds fellowships that pair humanities researchers with non-academic partners, artist commissions and challenge funds, and runs a Responsible AI Cultural Leaders Academy with Arts Council England and free online responsible-AI training for small businesses. In 2026 it opened calls for creative commissions to be shown at the 2027 Edinburgh Festivals and is sponsoring a Creators Emergency Summit on generative AI and creative rights.
why_it_matters: It is the largest UK public funding line for placing humanities researchers and artists inside companies, regulators and cultural bodies that work on AI. Its fellowship model, which pairs a researcher with a non-academic partner, is a tested template that a humanities-to-AI-safety programme could copy.

key_work.title: Mapping the Responsible AI Ecosystem: A BRAID Landscape Study (Vallor and Tollon)

Creators Emergency Summit, London, 13 October 2026 (sponsored by BRAID)

Oonagh Murphy (BRAID fellow; leads the Cultural Leaders Academy)
funding: AHRC, more than £18M over 2022-2028 by BRAID's own account. The core grant AH/X007146/1, 'Enabling a Responsible AI Ecosystem', is £11.9M and runs from November 2022 to May 2029 according to UKRI Gateway to Research. Partners co-fund some challenges, for example the National Lottery Heritage Fund and Framestore.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: opened new fellowships, creative commissions and an Edinburgh Festivals accessibility challenge (announced for Thursday 3 September). Its Creators Emergency Summit is scheduled for 13 Oct 2026 in London.
engage: BRAID research fellowships for arts and humanities researchers paired with non-academic partners (calls opened September 2026)
Creative commissions for UK-based creatives, with a showcase at the 2027 Edinburgh Festivals

Responsible AI Cultural Leaders Academy for senior cultural-sector leaders
Free online responsible-AI training for small businesses
Creators Emergency Summit, London, 13 October 2026
caveats: Its framing is 'responsible AI' (humane, equitable, resilient innovation), not safety or catastrophic risk. The words safety, existential and frontier do not appear on its About page. It is time-limited: funded to 2028-29. Funding totals differ between sources (£18M+ claimed overall, £11.9M on the core grant).
tag_notes: Home arts/arts_creative: its distinctive outputs are artist commissions, cultural-sector leadership training and creators' rights work. It funds arts and humanities broadly, so philosophy (Vallor) and law (copyright, Ada Lovelace partnership) are secondary (H4/H5). Ring adjacent: a sustained, funded programme on responsible AI with no safety, catastrophic-risk or alignment framing (E3). Transfer into_institutions: its stated aim is to embed humanities knowledge in industry, policy and regulatory practice (J3); the creators' summit leans towards protecting a constituency. Framing flourishing is borderline: its four themes (humane, inspired, equitable, resilient innovation) are aspirational, while the creators' summit uses a rights and harms framing. org_type programme: a time-limited funded consortium (I). London is not tagged as a hub because the summit there is a one-off event.

name: Centre for Technomoral Futures, University of Edinburgh
summary: A research and teaching centre in the Edinburgh Futures Institute that aims to 'unify technical and moral knowledge' in work on AI and data. It runs the MSc in Data and AI Ethics (44 students in 2024-25), a PhD fellowship programme (18 fellows), an affiliates network and industry training, for example a four-day AI and data ethics course for NatWest. Its research covers AI and human agency, the integrity of knowledge ecosystems, surveillance and rights, and corporate influence on AI policy. A 2026 FAccT paper with partners identified 27 patterns of 'Big AI' policy capture.
why_it_matters: Shannon Vallor's virtue-ethics work, including 'The AI Mirror' (2024), treats AI as something that can erode or cultivate human moral skill. On that view practical wisdom is a human capacity to protect and train, which bears directly on int/a's claims about wisdom and inner development. The centre also forms a steady stream of AI-ethics practitioners through its MSc and PhD programmes.

key_work.title: MSc in Data and Artificial Intelligence Ethics (first cohort graduated October 2023)
Study mapping how 'Big AI' influences AI laws and oversight (FAccT 2026)
Building AI futures worth wanting (feature by Emily Sullivan)
The AI Mirror (Shannon Vallor, Oxford University Press)

people: Shannon Vallor (co-director; Baillie Gifford Chair in the Ethics of Data and AI)
Emily Sullivan (co-director since August 2025; philosophy of science and machine learning)
Zeerak Talat (Chancellor's Fellow in Responsible Machine Learning and AI)
funding: Founded with an initial gift from Baillie Gifford in 2020, which also funds the PhD studentships. A visiting-scholar programme has anonymous donor support. Scholarship partnerships include the Luksic Scholars Foundation and the IAPP. Individual researchers hold external awards, for example a Schmidt Sciences AI2050 fellowship to Atoosa Kasirzadeh.
status_evidence: Aug 2026: published 'Building AI futures worth wanting'. Jun 2026: early-career researcher showcase. Mar 2026: advertised postdoc posts in philosophy of science and machine learning.
engage: MSc in Data and AI Ethics (University of Edinburgh)
PhD fellowships (Baillie Gifford studentships)
Postdoctoral posts, for example in philosophy of science and machine learning (advertised March 2026)
Affiliate programme for scholars, and a Distinguished Visiting Scholar programme
caveats: Folds in a duplicate entry for its own site, technomoralfutures.uk. Vallor's work is generally critical of AGI and x-risk framings, and the centre has no safety programme. Some listed affiliates, such as Kasirzadeh, appear to have moved to other institutions.
tag_notes: Home philosophy/phil_technology: Vallor's philosophy of technology and virtue ethics and Sullivan's philosophy of science of ML produce its AI outputs. The taxonomy lists it as a philosophy example. Law is secondary for its STS and rights work (Talat; the Big AI capture study). Ring adjacent: sustained AI ethics research and teaching with no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing (E3). Transfer into_builders is a judgement call: its main lever is forming practitioners' 'technomoral' skill through the MSc, PhD and industry training (J2). The policy-capture research would otherwise point to into_institutions. Framing flourishing comes from its own slogan, 'AI futures worth wanting' (L). Problems: meaning (AI as a mirror of moral capacities) first, then power (Big AI capture, wealth concentration) and epistemics (knowledge-ecosystem integrity).

name: UN Human Rights (OHCHR) B-Tech Project
summary: A project of the UN Human Rights Office (OHCHR), launched in 2019, that applies the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights to digital technology. It publishes guidance on human-rights due diligence, business models, remedy and a 'smart mix' of regulation. It runs a Community of Practice of large tech companies and a Peer Learning Platform with regional strands in Africa, Asia and Latin America. Its generative-AI project published a taxonomy of human-rights harms across the AI value chain in 2023, and in July 2026 it launched a one-year workstream with BSR on building human-rights due diligence into AI product development.
why_it_matters: It applies established legal machinery to foundation-model developers: value-chain responsibility, due diligence, remedy and regulatory 'smart mix'. That gives AI-safety governance a template backed by UN legitimacy and a working channel to the companies. In September 2026 the High Commissioner began addressing frontier AI directly.

key_work.title: Generative AI foundational papers, including a Taxonomy of Generative AI Human Rights Harms
AI product design workstream with BSR: human-rights due diligence in AI product development
2026 B-Tech Survey on AI and Human Rights
B-Tech scoping paper and foundational papers on four focus areas

people: Volker Türk (UN High Commissioner for Human Rights; head of the host office)
status_evidence: Jul 2026: launched an AI product-design workstream with BSR (8 July) and issued a special newsletter for the UN Global Dialogue on AI. Feb-May 2026: held AI and human-rights events in New Delhi, New York, Seoul and Tokyo, including a High Commissioner roundtable with AI company leaders in Seoul (13 May). Sep 2026: Volker Türk warned governments and frontier AI developers of irreversible change.
engage: B-Tech newsletter (archive on Mailchimp; most recent issue July 2026)
Tech companies can join the Company Community of Practice; OHCHR publishes an FAQ on joining
Periodic calls for input, such as the 2026 B-Tech Survey on AI and Human Rights for industry experts
Contact: ohchr-B-techproject@un.org
caveats: The OHCHR site blocks automated access, so the project description comes from an archived copy and from its newsletters. Staff leads and donors were not confirmed. The September 2026 frontier-AI statement came from the High Commissioner, not from B-Tech itself. If OHCHR builds a standing frontier-AI line on top of B-Tech, this entry would move to bridge.
tag_notes: Home law/law_legal: it applies international human-rights law (the UNGPs) to tech companies (H1). Ring adjacent: a sustained generative-AI programme framed around human-rights harms. It is not framed around safety or catastrophic risk (E3), although the High Commissioner's 2026 frontier-AI statement points towards bridge. Transfer into_institutions: it supplies due-diligence guidance and regulatory designs to companies and states (J3). Assurance is the second problem because human-rights due diligence across the AI lifecycle works as oversight of specific systems. org_type programme: a unit inside OHCHR (A1, I). Way of knowing practice: codified due-diligence guidance and standards. Engagement left empty because the Community of Practice is open only to companies and most roundtables are by invitation.

name: Research ICT Africa (RIA)
summary: A digital-policy think tank in Cape Town, registered as a South African nonprofit company, that has run multidisciplinary research on digital governance, data justice and the digital economy across Africa for about two decades. Its Africa Just AI project (2021-2026) produced policy briefs and submissions on AI ethics within human-rights frameworks, agentic AI responsibility, electoral integrity, surveillance and economic justice. In 2026 it is shaping African input to the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance and publishing on AI's effects on African labour.
why_it_matters: It is an established African evidence base on AI labour, data justice and compute access, and it feeds that evidence into UN and African Union processes. AI-governance efforts that want real Majority-World input, beyond a handful of voices, could partner with it for both legitimacy and evidence.

A pivotal moment for AI for all: how we focus our research and engagement for the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance

Newsletter and events listed on its site
caveats: Its own site says it has operated for 'two decades' (nonprofit registration number dated 2009) but gives no founding year, so the field is left blank. Its 2026 UN recommendations deliberately focus on inclusion, labour and data sovereignty rather than frontier or catastrophic risk. No independent source was retrieved: the founding-year and history pages tried (RIA and IDRC) returned 404s, so this profile rests on RIA's own pages.
tag_notes: Home law/law_policy: a public-interest development and digital-governance research institute (B8: a Global South group working through policy stays in the Law sector, with location shown in region and standpoint). Economics is secondary for its labour and digital-economy research. Ring adjacent: a sustained AI programme (Africa Just AI, UN Global Dialogue engagement) without safety or catastrophic-risk framing; its UN recommendations explicitly leave frontier risk aside (E3). Transfer into_institutions: policy recommendations to African governments, the AU and UN processes (J3). Framing structural: the stakes it names are neo-colonial extraction, labour restructuring and power, rather than documentation of specific harms (L).

name: Derechos Digitales
summary: A Latin American digital-rights nonprofit, based in Chile with staff in more than ten countries, that researches and advocates on human rights in the digital environment. Its AI work covers AI and digital autonomy, AI-enabled devices and privacy (for example Meta's smart glasses), data centres, and the costs of training AI, including the destructive scanning of books. It explicitly rejects both 'destroyer' and 'saviour' narratives about AI. Its co-executive director Jamila Venturini sits on the expert advisory panel of a Global South AI Safety Report.
why_it_matters: It is a main Latin American civil-society voice on AI and rights. Through its seat on the Global South AI Safety Report panel it already links to AI-safety debates, so it is a natural partner for anyone building AI-safety work in a region with no dedicated hub. Its scepticism of x-risk narratives is itself useful information for the field.

key_work.title: Ni destructora ni salvadora: lo que hay en medio del mito de la Inteligencia Artificial
Inteligencia artificial y autonomía digital
Debate on AI, data centres and rights at the University of Buenos Aires
Expert advisory panel member, Global South AI Safety Report

funding: Listed supporters (years not given): Ford Foundation, Omidyar Network, Mott Foundation, National Endowment for Democracy, IDRC Cyber Policy Centres, Inter-American Development Bank, Tides Foundation, New Venture Fund, UNFPA, Internews, Fundatec and MILA. Annual reports from 2017 to 2025 are published.
status_evidence: Oct 2026: published 'Ni destructora ni salvadora' on AI myths (2 Oct). Sep 2026: held a debate on AI, data centres and rights at the University of Buenos Aires (25 Sep) and took part in UNESCO's Global Forum on the Ethics of AI.
engage: Staff team across more than ten Latin American countries (no openings checked)
Runs a separate funds portal (fondos.derechosdigitales.org), whose content could not be read
caveats: It is openly sceptical of existential-risk narratives, which it calls marketing by AI companies, so any engagement on AI safety would need to start from present harms. The founding year (2005) is consistent with the site's 'over 20 years' but was not confirmed directly. Most material is in Spanish.
tag_notes: Home law/law_legal: digital human-rights research and advocacy (B8: a Global South rights group goes to Law, with region and standpoint carrying location). Ring adjacent: a sustained AI line (autonomy, surveillance devices, data centres, training costs) with no safety framing. The Global South AI Safety Report seat is an advisory role, not its own programme (E3). Transfer into_institutions: its main lever is advocacy on public policy and private practice (J3). Framing present_harms: it critiques x-risk discourse in service of a present-harms agenda (rule L). Power is the second problem for its work on data centres, extraction and corporate narratives.

name: 5Rights Foundation
summary: A London-based children's-rights charity, with an EU hub in Brussels, that campaigns for digital services and AI to be designed for children's safety and rights by default. It grew from the iRights campaign started by Beeban Kidron, whose amendment to the Data Protection Act 2018 led to the UK's Age Appropriate Design Code. In March 2025 it published the Children & AI Design Code, a lifecycle checklist for identifying and mitigating AI risks to children. It works on regulation in the UK, EU and elsewhere, and in September 2026 welcomed UK plans to legislate against unsafe digital design.
why_it_matters: It has turned children's-rights law into working design codes, one statutory (the UK AADC) and one for the whole AI lifecycle. Its method of assessing foreseeable risks and setting safety by default is regulatory know-how that model-spec and evals work on companion and chatbot harms rarely draws on.

key_work.title: Children & AI Design Code

Childhood Redrawn campaign
Digital Futures for Children research centre (with LSE)

people: Beeban Kidron (founder; honorary president since June 2025)
funding: States that it has never accepted, and will never accept, funding from technology companies. Its main funders were not identified.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: responded to the UK government's announcement of legislation on unsafe digital design (28 Sep) and launched the Childhood Redrawn campaign.
engage: Staff roles posted on its vacancies page (none open in October 2026)
Youth engagement programmes and public petitions on its site
caveats: It began as a campaign (iRights) around 2012-13 and was registered as a charity in 2018. Its AI work sits within a broader child online-safety agenda and does not engage with catastrophic-risk framings.
tag_notes: Home law/law_legal: children's-rights law and regulation (B9: children's-rights law goes to Law; the taxonomy lists 5Rights as a Law example). Psych is secondary because its codes build on children's developmental stages and it partners with LSE's Digital Futures for Children. Ring adjacent: a sustained AI line (Children & AI Design Code, AI regulation advocacy) framed around child safety, not catastrophic risk (E3). Transfer protecting: its design codes exist to protect children, as with Common Sense Media (J4). Problems: minds (children's development and companion harms) first, with assurance paired because it sets lifecycle standards for AI systems (F). Way of knowing practice: codified design-code and standards know-how.

name: The Elders
summary: The Elders is an independent group of former heads of state, UN officials and Nobel laureates. Nelson Mandela founded it in 2007, and a secretariat in London supports it. Its 2023-27 strategy covers four threats: climate, pandemics, nuclear weapons and conflict. It commissioned a consultancy to scope AI work (December 2025 to May 2026), issued a call to action on AI in March 2026, and has run a dedicated AI programme since July 2026, including a declaration on AI and nuclear weapons. The programme calls on governments to regulate AI, to govern military AI and to negotiate a treaty on autonomous weapons.
why_it_matters: It brings political standing that AI-safety groups lack: former presidents and UN human-rights chiefs who can put catastrophic AI risk in front of heads of government. It also explicitly ties AI to the nuclear, pandemic and climate threats it already works on. A new funder could partner with a voice whose credibility comes from outside the AI-safety community.

key_work.title: Governments must act now to manage AI for the public good (call to action, backed by Bengio and Russell among others)
ProHuman: Governing the Global AI Revolution (eight-part podcast with Foreign Policy and FLI)
The Elders' AI Principles for Leaders
Co-sponsor, with six governments, the ICRC and FLI, of the UN forum calling for treaty negotiations on autonomous weapons

funding: A donor advisory council funds it independently: Virgin Unite, the Peter Gabriel Foundation, the Skoll Foundation, Humanity United, the J Coller Foundation, the Dutch Postcode Lottery and others (per Wikipedia). The Patrick J McGovern Foundation supports its AI work (acknowledged 2026).
status_evidence: Sep 2026: published 'The Elders' AI Principles for Leaders' (21 Sep) and co-sponsored the 28 Sep UN forum in New York calling for treaty negotiations on autonomous weapons.
engage: Secretariat roles and consultancies in London, advertised on its site (for example the AI programme scoping consultancy, Nov 2025)
caveats: The AI programme only launched in 2026. So far its output is statements, a podcast, declarations and co-sponsorship, not research. Its framing mixes catastrophic risk (AI-enabled nuclear and biological weapons) with present harms (rights, inequality, environmental costs). The Elders are retired leaders whose influence runs through access and moral authority, which is hard to measure. Its CEO is not named on the pages checked.
tag_notes: Home peace / peace_diplomacy: its method is elder statesmanship and multilateral advocacy, the case named in the sub-tradition; law is secondary for the human-rights commitment that former UN High Commissioners Robinson and Zeid carry. Ring bridge (E3): an institution from another field with a standing AI programme from July 2026, explicitly framed around existential threats such as AI-enabled nuclear and biological weapons. Transfer into_institutions: its asks are governance instruments (regulation, an autonomous-weapons treaty, binding global AI governance). Recoupling badge: it frames AI as cutting across its climate, pandemic, nuclear and conflict programmes. Standpoint coded neither because it is London-based and Northern-funded, though most Elders, including the Chair and Deputy Chair, come from the Majority World.

name: Andrew Carnegie Foundation (formerly Carnegie Corporation of New York)
summary: Andrew Carnegie founded this US grantmaking foundation in 1911. It has an endowment of about $5bn and grants about $220m a year, and it renamed itself the Andrew Carnegie Foundation in June 2026. Its international peace programme funds work on AI and nuclear risk: SIPRI's study of nuclear escalation in the age of AI ($500k, 2024, after $400k in 2017 on machine learning, autonomy and strategic stability); the Institute for Security and Technology's Andrew Carnegie AI-Nuclear Policy Accelerator (first cohort of 26, 2026); and a Pugwash-Carnegie Fellow for Science and Security (2026).
why_it_matters: It is the main philanthropic backer of the AI and nuclear-risk bridge. Instead of founding new AI-safety organisations, it pays established arms-control institutions to take on AI. A new AI-safety funder could co-fund with it, or fill the gaps it leaves, such as US-China AI dialogue or AI in biological and chemical weapons.

key_work.title: Grant to SIPRI: assessing the risks of nuclear escalation in the age of AI ($500,000)
Andrew Carnegie AI-Nuclear Policy Accelerator at the Institute for Security and Technology

people: Jonathan Tepperman (Vice President, International Program, from May 2026)
funding: Self-funded by its endowment (about $5bn in 2026), with an annual grant budget of about $220m (FY2026). AI-related peace grants found: SIPRI $500k (2024) and $400k (2017), the IST accelerator (2026, amount not found), and Cornell $1.5m (2026) for tracking armed groups' use of drones and autonomous technology.
status_evidence: Jun 2026: renamed the Andrew Carnegie Foundation; Jul 2026: first cohort of the IST AI-Nuclear Policy Accelerator it funds met in Silicon Valley.
engage: No open AI funding call found; past grants are searchable in the grants database at carnegie.org
caveats: AI is not a named focus of its peace programme, whose stated priorities are migration, non-state actors, nuclear and space security and open-source intelligence. Its AI grants are separate projects, not a dedicated portfolio. The Pugwash fellowship is not described as AI-specific. It changed its name in June 2026 with the same mission, so search under both names.
tag_notes: Home peace / peace_arms (H4): its AI funding runs through one programme, international peace and nuclear risk; the taxonomy itself cites 'Carnegie Corporation Peace'. Ring bridge (E3): an old institution funding several AI-nuclear projects in 2024-26 (SIPRI, IST accelerator), framed around nuclear escalation. Transfer into_institutions: for funders, the work they fund, which builds arms-control and policy capacity. Status changed: renamed from Carnegie Corporation of New York in June 2026 with the same mission. Not a rule-K generalist funder.

name: Carnegie Endowment for International Peace: Technology and International Affairs Program
summary: This programme of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace (Washington DC, founded 1910, with centres worldwide) works on the governance and large-scale risks of AI, biotechnology, cyber and the information environment. It has about 20 staff. Its AI strands cover: the geopolitics and security of the race toward advanced AI; AI and international development; AI governance institutions; and a China AI Initiative that studies Chinese AI safety and US-China dialogue.
why_it_matters: It brings international-relations and China expertise, and a century-old institution's access to governments, to questions such as how rival and middle powers should act in an AI race. Its China AI work, for example on China's AI safety and development association, is one of the few close English-language readings of Chinese frontier-AI governance.

key_work.title: If-Then Commitments for AI Risk Reduction (Holden Karnofsky)
How Some of China's Top AI Thinkers Built Their Own AI Safety Institute (Singer, Elmgren, Guest)
AI Breakout Capacity: A Middle-Power Path Between Racing and Dependence (Leicht, Winter-Levy)

people: Scott Singer (Fellow; Co-Director, China AI Initiative)
funding: Funded through the Carnegie Endowment's endowment and donors; programme-specific funders are not listed on its pages.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: published 'AI Breakout Capacity: A Middle-Power Path Between Racing and Dependence' (Anton Leicht and Sam Winter-Levy, 28 Sep).
engage: Research staff roles at the Carnegie Endowment (check its careers page)
Public events and the podcast The World Unpacked
caveats: This is a programme inside a large general-purpose think tank. Not all Carnegie AI output comes from it: AI and democracy work, for example, sits in the Democracy, Conflict, and Governance Program. Its founding year was not found. Its framing is mainly geopolitical competition rather than alignment. The roster's evidence on Scott Singer (a 2024 Lawfare interview) predates his Carnegie role; his current Carnegie profile confirms that role.
tag_notes: Home peace / peace_diplomacy: international-relations and China-studies methods applied to the AI race and US-China dialogue; economics is secondary for its standing strand on AI and international development and economics. Ring bridge (E3): an old peace institution with a sustained AI programme framed around the 'dangers of the break-neck race toward advanced AI' and 'large-scale risks'. Framing coded catastrophic for that language and for work such as the If-Then commitments paper, though a structural reading (race dynamics, middle-power dependence) is close. Transfer into_institutions: its outputs are policy designs for governments and international institutions. Org type programme (I).

name: Stanford Center for International Security and Cooperation (CISAC)
summary: CISAC is Stanford's international security centre, founded in 1983 and now part of the Freeman Spogli Institute. It is led jointly by a social-science and a natural-science co-director. It is known for nuclear-policy research and for Track II talks with China, North Korea, Pakistan and Russia. Its AI work includes two postdoctoral fellowships and Herbert Lin's research on AI and nuclear escalation. The fellowship on AI in strategic stability and military competition builds datasets for nuclear wargaming scenarios and designs experimental wargames on AI in nuclear command and control and force posture. The other fellowship covers the geopolitics of AI, including US-China competition and the tension between speed and safety.
why_it_matters: It brings decades of arms-control and Track II practice, plus wargaming and expert elicitation, to the question of AI in nuclear command and control. That gives the AI-safety field a tested template for US-China dialogue and crisis analysis.

key_work.title: AI in the Information Ecosystem and Its Impact on Nuclear Escalation (Herbert Lin, Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists)
Artificial Intelligence in Strategic Stability and Military Competition Fellowship (AI in nuclear command and control, wargames)
Geopolitics of Artificial Intelligence Fellowship

people: Colin Kahl (FSI Director; supervises the AI fellowships)
funding: Stanford University and the Freeman Spogli Institute (FSI received a $50m gift in 2005), plus fellowship sponsors such as the Motwani Jadeja Family Foundation (India-US fellowship); funders of the AI fellowships are not stated.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: new co-director James Fearon named AI and its international-security implications a research priority; the application for 2027-28 fellowships, including two AI fellowships, opens 7 Oct 2026.
engage: CISAC fellowships, including the two AI fellowships; applications for 2027-28 open 7 Oct 2026
Staff openings listed on its site
Public seminars and events
caveats: AI is a growing strand, not a dedicated CISAC programme. The AI fellowships are supervised through FSI's Program on Geopolitics, Technology, and Governance and involve Hoover Institution staff, so the AI work is spread across FSI and Hoover. Its Track II record is on nuclear, cyber and space; no AI Track II was found. The current natural-science co-director is not named on the pages checked.
tag_notes: Home peace / peace_arms: nuclear policy and security studies applied to AI in nuclear command and control. Ring bridge (E3): an old institution with recurring AI fellowships and a funded project on AI and nuclear deterrence, framed around strategic stability and loss of control. Transfer into_institutions: wargames and expert elicitation are meant to inform nuclear posture and policy. Way of knowing empirical, since the fellowship project builds datasets, experimental wargames and expert interviews; the wargaming method borders on arts_futures (B10).

name: Safe AI Forum (SAIF)
summary: SAIF is a US 501(c)(3) nonprofit with staff in London and San Francisco. It runs the International Dialogues on AI Safety (IDAIS), where senior Western and Chinese scientists (among them Andrew Yao, Yoshua Bengio, Stuart Russell and Zhang Ya-Qin) agree joint statements on extreme AI risks. There have been five dialogues: Oxford 2023, Beijing 2024 (red lines such as autonomous replication), Venice 2024, Shanghai 2025 (deception) and London 2026. The London dialogue in April 2026 was co-hosted with the Royal Society and the Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative, and covered AI-enabled cyberattacks and biological misuse. SAIF also publishes research on international cooperation and technical safeguards, often with Chinese co-authors.
why_it_matters: It applies the Pugwash model of scientist-to-scientist diplomacy to AI, keeping a US-China channel on catastrophic risk open while official dialogue is thin.

key_work.title: IDAIS-Beijing statement proposing red lines for AI development
IDAIS-London statement on AI-enabled cyberattacks and biological misuse
In Which Areas of Technical AI Safety Could Geopolitical Rivals Cooperate?
Technical Safeguards Against Extreme Misuse of AI: Current Landscape and Future Directions (English and Chinese)

hq: London, UK and San Francisco, USA (US 501(c)(3))
funding: Funders are not listed on its site. It was fiscally sponsored by FAR.AI until it became independent in May 2025.
status_evidence: Apr 2026: IDAIS-London and its statement; Oct 2026: hiring a General Counsel (deadline 11 Oct 2026) and a researcher on misuse risks.
engage: Jobs (Oct 2026): (Senior) Researcher – Misuse Risks, General Counsel, Executive Business Partner; in person in London or San Francisco, some remote
caveats: The dialogues are invitation-only and their statements are non-binding, so their influence on governments is hard to trace. The founding year is taken from the first IDAIS (October 2023); SAIF ran under FAR.AI's fiscal sponsorship until May 2025.
tag_notes: Home peace / peace_diplomacy: Track II scientist dialogue on the Pugwash model; the taxonomy uses it as the example. Ring core (E1): its founding mission is minimising extreme AI risk, and it is on the aisafety.com map. Transfer into_institutions: its consensus statements and red lines are offered as templates for governments. Assurance is secondary for its research on technical safeguards and on mitigations for autonomous AI. Region north_america by legal base (O); it has an in-person London office.

name: Concordia AI
summary: Concordia AI is a social enterprise working on AI safety and governance in China and internationally, with offices in Beijing and Singapore; Brian Tse is its founder and CEO. It publishes the annual State of AI Safety in China report (fourth edition, July 2026, covering July 2025 to June 2026), a State of AI Safety in Singapore report, a Frontier AI Risk Management Framework (version 2.0) and an online Frontier AI Risk Monitor. It also runs the AI Safety in China newsletter, convenes safety forums such as one at the World AI Conference in Shanghai, and advises AI companies and Chinese policy consultations.
why_it_matters: It makes Chinese AI-safety policy, research and expert opinion legible abroad, and connects Chinese and international safety researchers. Without that translation, Western safety strategy rests on guesses about China.

key_work.title: State of AI Safety in China (2026), fourth edition, with interactive companion site
Frontier AI Risk Management Framework 2.0
Frontier AI Risk Monitor (update: risk indices rise severalfold)
State of AI Safety in China, first edition

Safety is secondary for its risk-management framework and risk monitor (safety_risk methods). Ring core (E1): its founding mission is AI safety and governance, and it is on the aisafety.com map. Transfer into_institutions: reports, standards input and policy consultations aimed at Chinese and international governance. Standpoint neither (O: China is coded Neither in v1).

name: Simon Institute for Longterm Governance (SI)
summary: A Geneva think tank and Swiss nonprofit, founded in 2021 by Maxime Stauffer and Konrad Seifert, that helps diplomats and international civil servants govern frontier AI. Since narrowing its focus to AI in 2023 it has advised over 100 diplomats from dozens of countries. It supported the design of the UN Independent International Scientific Panel on AI and the Global Dialogue on AI Governance. Since 2025 it has run a workstream on confidence building and crisis preparedness between the US and China.
why_it_matters: It works inside the UN system in Geneva and New York, translating frontier-AI risk for diplomats from many countries, developing countries included. Few AI-safety organisations do this.

key_work.title: Recommendations for the design of the UN Independent International Scientific Panel on AI and Global Dialogue on AI Governance
What is Artificial General Intelligence? (explainer for policymakers)
Frontier AI and emerging biological risks: side event at the UN Biological Weapons Convention working group
When AI Agents Start Interacting at Scale: Implications for AI Governance

people: Konrad Seifert, listed on the site as Konrad Gerosa (Chief Strategy Officer, co-founder)
Renata Dwan (Director of Tech Diplomacy, joined Sep 2025)
funding: It raised CHF 2.3m in 2025 (audited income CHF 1.6m, plus CHF 0.7m deferred to 2026) and grew from 6 to 9 staff. Its 2025 financial report names Good Ventures Foundation (about CHF 1.3m), the Survival and Flourishing Fund (about CHF 444k across several grants), Longview (about CHF 245k), the Astralis Foundation (about CHF 235k) and Open Philanthropy (now Coefficient Giving).
status_evidence: Sep 2026: CEO commentary on governing AI agents that interact at scale (9 Sep); Aug 2026: public side event on frontier AI and biological risks at the UN BWC working group (20 Aug).
engage: Staff roles (no open positions as of Oct 2026)
Public events in Geneva, such as UN side events
Donations (tax-deductible in Switzerland and the US)
