tag_notes: Home peace / peace_diplomacy: multilateral and UN diplomacy practice applied to frontier AI. Ring core (E1): founded to reduce global catastrophic risks through the multilateral system, focused on AI since 2023, funded from the AI-safety ecosystem (Good Ventures, SFF) and on the aisafety.com map. Transfer into_institutions: it shapes UN mechanisms (the Scientific Panel and Global Dialogue) and confidence-building channels. Epistemics is secondary for its work on the design of the UN Scientific Panel on AI.

name: Center for Global AI Innovative Governance, Fudan University (CGAIG)
summary: A Fudan University centre in Shanghai, launched at the World AI Conference (WAIC) on 26 July 2025 with support from the Shanghai municipal government. Its secretariat sits in the Fudan Development Institute. It works in four areas: global AI governance rules, technical governance tools, capacity building, and international agenda-setting. It publishes reports, including a Global AI Governance Index written from a Global South perspective, and a journal. It also runs a visiting scholars programme and training workshops, and takes part in Chinese and UN AI-governance dialogues.
why_it_matters: It is a Chinese voice on global AI governance that leads with the Global South and capacity building. That makes it a likely counterpart for Western Track II efforts, and a way to see how China's framing differs from Western safety framing.

key_work.title: Global AI Governance Index (2026): Perspectives from the Global South and Capacity Building, released at WAIC 2026
Emerging Trends in Global AI Governance: Observations Since the Shanghai Declaration (bilingual report)
Global AI Innovative Governance journal, first issue
Participation in Tsinghua CISS Forum on Artificial Intelligence and International Security (14 Jan 2026)

people: CHEN Zhimin (Executive Director; Vice President of Fudan University)
ZHAO Houlin (Co-Chair, International Advisory Board; former ITU Secretary-General)
funding: Set up with support from the Shanghai municipal government. No budget is published.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: Executive Director Chen Zhimin attended the third convening of the UN Global Dialogue on AI and Human Development in Xi'an. On 13 Sep 2026 a China–Oman AI training workshop it supported ended.
engage: Visiting Scholars Programme (regular seminars through 2026)
Annual WAIC governance forum in Shanghai each July
Training workshops, e.g. the China–Oman international training workshop (Sep 2026)
caveats: Almost all sources are the centre's own site. Independent checking was limited because web search was unavailable for this pass. Its framing is development, capacity building and China's Global AI Governance Action Plan, not catastrophic risk, so bridge is a borderline call against adjacent. It is closely tied to official Chinese initiatives (Shanghai government support, a training workshop sponsored by the Ministry of Science and Technology), so read it as part of China's AI diplomacy rather than as an independent voice. Its own pages also call it the 'Center for Global AI Innovation and Governance'.
tag_notes: Home: its AI outputs come from international-relations and multilateral-diplomacy scholarship (UN dialogues, BRICS and Central Asia exchanges, China's governance agenda), so Peace/peace_diplomacy. Law is secondary for its development-studies capacity-building work (B8: location shows in region, not tradition). Ring: kept as bridge because it runs a standing programme on governing AI itself (reports, an index, a journal, security forums), but its framing is inclusive development rather than safety, so it is borderline adjacent (E3). Transfer: it produces governance templates, indices and trainings for states, so into_institutions. Framing: its mission is to 'narrow the global AI capacity gap', which reads as structural. Standpoint: China is coded neither in v1 (O). Status new: launched July 2025.

name: Centre for Humanitarian Dialogue (HD): Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technologies programme
summary: HD is a Geneva private-diplomacy organisation, founded in 1999 with more than 300 staff, that mediates armed conflicts. Its Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technologies programme sits in its Technology and International Security area. The programme aims to help states develop and adopt international measures against the risks AI poses to security and conflict, in both military and civilian uses. Its first AI work was a two-year discreet dialogue among Chinese, American and international experts, which produced a draft Code of Conduct on AI in military systems (2021). Since then it has run dialogues with interested states on codifying risk-reduction measures, and a 2023 dialogue with Tsinghua CISS.
why_it_matters: It brings discreet mediation and confidence-building to military-AI risk. HD has used these methods for ceasefires, social-media peace agreements and cyber confidence-building, and they offer a channel that public multilateral processes cannot.

key_work.title: Draft Code of Conduct on Artificial Intelligence in Military Systems
HD–Tsinghua CISS bilateral dialogue on AI security governance
Structured dialogues with interested states on codifying AI risk-mitigation measures

people: Adam Cooper (Director, Technology and International Security)
funding: HD as a whole had CHF 47 million income in 2024, from governments and private foundations (Wikipedia). Funding for the AI programme is not disclosed.
status_evidence: Aug 2026: HD is active (Niger farmer–herder peace agreement, 14 Aug 2026), and its site lists the AI and Emerging Technologies programme as current. The latest dated public AI output found is the October 2023 dialogue with Tsinghua CISS.
engage: Staff roles are advertised at hdcentre.org/careers (none AI-specific in Oct 2026)
The Oslo Forum, co-hosted with Norway, is invitation-only
caveats: The AI work is discreet by design, so public evidence since 2023 is thin. The roster's claim that HD has been expanding military-AI dialogues and hiring advanced-AI advisors since 2025 could not be verified. HD's site blocks automated access, so it was read through a proxy.
tag_notes: Home: the AI outputs come from HD's private-diplomacy and mediation practice (discreet expert and state dialogues), so Peace/peace_building, as in the taxonomy's own example (H1). Ring: an older mediation institution with a standing AI programme framed around reducing accidental or intentional weapons use (E: old institution, new programme), so bridge. Evidence of sustained 2024-26 activity is thin. Transfer: it produces a code of conduct and risk-reduction measures for states, so into_institutions. org_type programme, because the roster unit is the programme inside HD (A1/I).

name: European Leadership Network (ELN): Nuclear Weapons and Emerging Technologies Programme
summary: The ELN is a London charity founded in 2011, with staff in London and Berlin and a network of former senior politicians, diplomats and military officers, working on European security. Its Nuclear Weapons and Emerging Technologies programme studies how AI and other technologies change nuclear risk, through human–machine interaction, automation bias and system vulnerabilities, and proposes risk-reduction measures. Its outputs include a report on P5 views of AI in nuclear command, control and communications (NC3) and a Nuclear Fail-Safe Review project. It is also a partner in Firebreaks, a project with the Arms Control Association and the Berkeley Risk and Security Lab on limiting the risks of putting AI into nuclear operations.
why_it_matters: It carries the nuclear risk-reduction toolkit (hotlines, fail-safe reviews, the P5 process, confidence-building measures) into AI governance. It argues for building decision time and human control back in wherever AI shortens crisis timelines.

key_work.title: AI and nuclear command, control and communications: P5 perspectives
Firebreaks: Mitigating the Risks of AI Integration into Nuclear Operations (with Arms Control Association and Berkeley Risk and Security Lab)
Nuclear Fail-Safe Review
Beyond the Rome Declaration: Adapting nuclear risk reduction for the AI era

people: Julia Berghofer (Programme Lead, Nuclear Weapons and New Technologies)
Nikita Gryazin (Policy Fellow, Nuclear Weapons and New Technologies)
Bekki Field (Deputy Executive Director; hosts the Ok, Doomer! podcast)
funding: Current ELN funders: Carnegie Corporation of New York, German Federal Foreign Office, Joseph Rowntree Charitable Trust, Longview Philanthropy, Norwegian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Nuclear Threat Initiative, Open Society Foundations, Rockefeller Brothers Fund and the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office. The 2023 P5 AI–NC3 project was supported by the US State Department's Bureau of Arms Control, Verification and Compliance.
status_evidence: 27 Jul 2026: Nikita Gryazin's commentary 'Beyond the Rome Declaration' called for AI-incident hotlines, national fail-safe reviews and a P5 agenda on human control.
engage: Staff roles
Public events and the Ok, Doomer! podcast on emerging technologies and nuclear risk
Younger Generation Leaders Network on Euro-Atlantic Security (YGLN): membership for early-career professionals
Newsletter
caveats: The ELN holds no institutional policy positions, so commentaries are their authors' views. Its AI work is narrowly about nuclear command and control and strategic stability, not AI risk in general. In Firebreaks, the ELN's role is the second phase, which extends the work to non-US nuclear-armed states.
tag_notes: Home: the AI outputs apply nuclear risk-reduction and arms-control practice (fail-safe reviews, hotlines, the P5 process) to AI, so Peace/peace_arms. Ring: an established European-security network running a standing programme explicitly aimed at preventing nuclear catastrophe from AI integration (E3), so bridge. Transfer: it proposes risk-reduction measures and norms for nuclear-armed states, so into_institutions. org_type programme, because the roster unit is the programme (A1/I). Hubs: the ELN says its team is based in London and Berlin. Its 2023 moratorium recommendation was weighed for a speed_of_wisdom badge but not given, to keep badges sparse.

name: Pugwash Conferences on Science and World Affairs
summary: An international community of scientists, scholars and current and former policymakers, founded in 1957 after the Russell–Einstein Manifesto. It runs dialogues across political divides on weapons of mass destruction and war, and it has no formal membership. Pugwash and its founder Joseph Rotblat shared the 1995 Nobel Peace Prize. Its Science and Security programme includes a Project on Emerging Technologies and Strategic Stability that covers AI. In 2026 it held a Rome consultation on AI and nuclear weapons, co-organised the Global Nobel Laureates Assembly on AI and Nuclear War, appointed its first Pugwash-Carnegie Fellow for Science and Security, and held a Beijing meeting on nuclear risk reduction and disruptive technologies.
why_it_matters: It is the original model of scientist-led dialogue across geopolitical divides, the template IDAIS explicitly borrows. It now brings physicists, international lawyers and arms-control veterans together with AI-industry people on AI and nuclear risk, guided by an ethic of scientists' responsibility.

key_work.title: Rome workshop 'AI and Nuclear Weapons: Risks and Opportunities' (13 Jul 2026)
Global Nobel Laureates Assembly on AI and Nuclear War and the Rome Declaration (organising partner)
Autonomous Armageddon: Nuclear Weapons and AI (co-hosted webinar)
Beijing meeting on nuclear risk reduction and disruptive technologies

people: Götz Neuneck (Chair of the Council; leads the Project on Emerging Technologies and Strategic Stability)
Nicolas Ayala Arboleda (Pugwash-Carnegie Fellow for Science and Security)
funding: Foundations, philanthropists, governments and public donations. Carnegie support pays for its new Pugwash-Carnegie fellowships (2026).
status_evidence: 22 Sep 2026: report of a Beijing meeting on nuclear risk reduction and on how AI and other disruptive technologies affect strategic stability.
engage: Pugwash-Carnegie Fellowships (first appointed June 2026; more planned)
International Student/Young Pugwash for early-career scientists
Pugwash Conferences (63rd held in Hiroshima, Nov 2025); participation is open to anyone who shares its values
caveats: AI is one strand of a nuclear-focused agenda, and the AI work only scaled up in 2026, so its track record there is short. The Rome workshop report says it is not a consensus or policy position. Offices are listed in Geneva, Washington DC and London (the British Pugwash Group); the roster gave Rome.
tag_notes: Home: scientist-led Track II dialogue is its method, so Peace/peace_diplomacy (as in the taxonomy's example). Ring: an older disarmament network with a standing emerging-technologies project, a dedicated fellow and repeated AI convenings in 2025-26 framed around existential risk (E: old institution, new programme), so bridge. Transfer: its workshops propose governance options to states and international bodies (verification, confidence-building, an AI security summit), so into_institutions. org_type network, because About says there is no formal membership. Badge speed_of_wisdom: it signed the Rome Declaration's call to 'disarm the next arms race, both AI and nuclear', and its ethos rejects race dynamics. Hubs: the London office is the British Pugwash Group's, so London was not coded.

name: Global Commission on Responsible Artificial Intelligence in the Military Domain (GC REAIM)
summary: A commission the Dutch government set up at the first REAIM summit in The Hague in February 2023, for an initial two years. The Hague Centre for Strategic Studies (HCSS) ran its secretariat. Its commissioners and experts came from every region, including Stuart Russell, Michael Horowitz, Marietje Schaake, Toby Walsh and Yi Zeng, with former South Korean foreign minister Yun Byung-se as co-chair. They met across 2024-25. The commission concluded in September 2025 with the strategic guidance report 'Responsible by Design'. Commissioners presented it at the third REAIM summit (A Coruña, February 2026), and the summit's 'Pathways to Action' document referenced it.
why_it_matters: It is a worked example of norm-building on military AI by states, industry, academia and civil society together, combining security studies, humanitarian law, ethics-by-design and engineering. Its uneven uptake (40 endorsing states, neither the US nor China) shows the limits of processes led by middle powers.

key_work.title: Responsible by Design: Strategic Guidance Report on the Risks, Opportunities, and Governance of AI in the Military Domain
Report presented at the REAIM 2026 summit and referenced in 'Pathways to Action'

people: Yun Byung-se (Co-Chair; former South Korean foreign minister)
funding: An initiative of the Dutch government. HCSS ran the secretariat at the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs' request. No budget is published.
status_evidence: Concluded in Sep 2025 with its report. On 4-5 Feb 2026, five commissioners presented the report in the plenary of REAIM 2026 in A Coruña.
caveats: The commission has closed. Its continuing relevance is its report and its track record. RSIS (2026) notes that 'Pathways to Action' reflected the commission's guiding principles but left out three of its five core recommendations. Only 40 states endorsed it, against more than 60 for the 2024 Blueprint, and neither the US nor China did. The roster's claim that India abstained was not verified. HCSS continues military-AI work separately.
tag_notes: Home: a security-studies and humanitarian-law commission run by a strategic-studies think tank, so Peace/peace_arms. Philosophy (ethics-by-design commissioners such as Jeroen van den Hoven and Wendell Wallach) and Safety (system-lifecycle and human-factors guidance) are secondary through its members. Ring: rooted in security studies and set up to govern military-AI risk, so bridge (E3). Transfer: it produced norms and governance recommendations for states, militaries and industry, so into_institutions. Framing: the report calls AI 'civilization-shaping', with heightened risks to international peace and security. That is coded catastrophic, but it is borderline with present_harms, given the report's emphasis on legal compliance. org_type programme: a time-limited commission hosted by HCSS (I). Status dormant: concluded September 2025 (O).

name: Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists
summary: A Chicago nonprofit publication founded in 1945 by Manhattan Project scientists. It sets the Doomsday Clock each year: in January 2026 it moved to 85 seconds to midnight, with AI cited alongside nuclear, climate and biological risks. Its Disruptive Technologies desk publishes analysis on AI, autonomous weapons, information warfare and biosecurity. In 2025-26 it ran 'The AI Power Trip', a year-long special project on how AI developers are gaining control over governance, information ecosystems, energy and the military-industrial complex.
why_it_matters: It speaks for the nuclear-security community and treats AI as one of several man-made existential threats. It publishes both alarm and scepticism, such as a September 2026 critique of the science behind AI 'doomerism', which helps readers place AI risk among other catastrophic risks.

key_work.title: 2026 Doomsday Clock Statement (85 seconds to midnight)
The AI Power Trip (year-long special project)
How the bad science of AI doomerism is good for big business (Sara Goudarzi)

people: John Mecklin (Senior Fellow; editor of the 2026 Clock statement)
funding: An independent 501(c)(3) funded by donations (Einstein Circle, legacy and donor-advised giving) and magazine subscriptions. Grant funders and amounts were not checked.
status_evidence: 30 Sep 2026: published Sara Goudarzi's piece arguing there is no evidence-based path from today's AI to superintelligence.
engage: Editorial fellowships, including a Disruptive Technologies Editorial Fellow
Annual 'Conversations Before Midnight' event
Magazine subscription and newsletter
caveats: Its AI coverage mixes existential-risk framing (the Clock) with critiques of the AI-risk discourse itself. The roster's claim that it co-sponsored the 2026 Nobel Laureates Assembly on AI and Nuclear War was not verified.
tag_notes: Home: a publication goes with the community it serves, here nuclear security (H3, which names the Bulletin as Peace). Arts is secondary for its journalism. Ring: a standing Disruptive Technologies desk, a year-long AI project, and AI factored into the Doomsday Clock as an existential threat make it bridge (E3). Transfer: its main purpose is informing and convening the science-and-security community and the public through media, so convening (J5). Role evaluate reflects the annual Doomsday Clock risk assessment. Framing is catastrophic by its mission statement ('reduce existential threats'), despite its sceptical AI pieces (L).

name: Nuclear Threat Initiative (NTI)
summary: A Washington DC nonprofit founded in 2001 by Sam Nunn and Ted Turner to reduce nuclear and biological threats. Its AI work sits in NTI | bio and in the FutureSafe programme on AI and emerging technologies. It convenes the AIxBio Global Forum on guardrails for AI biodesign tools and publishes AIxBio horizon scans. In January 2026 it published a framework for managed access to biological AI tools, and in August 2026 it launched an international working group with Concordia AI on biological capability evaluations. In July 2026 it held a US–China expert dialogue on AIxBio with Tsinghua CISS. It also runs US–China dialogues on nuclear risk and examines AI in nuclear decision-making.
why_it_matters: It applies bio-nonproliferation and biosecurity practice (access controls, norms, international forums) to AI biodesign tools. This is where mainstream AI-safety capability evaluations meet decades of biosecurity governance experience.

key_work.title: A Framework for Managed Access to Biological AI Tools
AIxBio Global Forum high-level statement on biosecurity risks at the convergence of AI and the life sciences
NTI and Concordia AI international working group on biological capability evaluations
US–China expert dialogue on AIxBio guardrails with Tsinghua CISS

people: Jake Jordan (Vice President, Global Biological Policy and Programs)
Dimitri Kusnezov (Vice President, Science and Technology; led FutureSafe at its 2025 launch)
funding: Founded with a pledge from Ted Turner. Current funders and budget were not checked.
status_evidence: 21 Sep 2026: reported a July 2026 US–China expert dialogue on AIxBio guardrails, co-chaired by NTI | bio and Tsinghua CISS.
engage: Staff roles (NTI careers)
Public events and webinars on AIxBio and emerging technologies
Congressional Leadership Project cohorts for senior congressional staff (second cohort recruiting in 2026)
caveats: AI is one line of work within a much larger nuclear and biological portfolio, and most of it is specific to biosecurity. The AIxBio evaluation work could also be read as Safety. The roster's claim about a 2026 biological-threats initiative with The Elders was not verified. NTI's site blocks automated access, so pages were read through a proxy and its WordPress API.
tag_notes: Home: its AI outputs come from nonproliferation practice, through international forums, US–China dialogues and access-control norms. Bio-nonproliferation diplomacy goes to Peace (B12, safety_health boundary), so Peace/peace_arms, with Safety secondary for its biosecurity evaluation and managed-access work. Ring: an older nonproliferation institution with a standing AI programme (FutureSafe, the AIxBio Global Forum) framed as preventing global catastrophe, so bridge. Transfer: it produces guardrails, frameworks and international governance platforms, so into_institutions. Assurance is paired with security because it builds capability evaluations (F).

name: AI Vulnerability Database (AVID) / AI Risk and Vulnerability Alliance (ARVA)
summary: AVID is an open-source database of reproducible failures and vulnerabilities in general-purpose AI systems: open-weight and API models, developer tools, applications and agents. It is the main project of the AI Risk and Vulnerability Alliance, a volunteer-run US 501(c)(3). Records carry evidence and evaluation details and are mapped to several taxonomies (CVSS, MITRE ATLAS and AVID's own). Its Python SDK pulls in results from garak, Inspect AI, NIST NVD and MITRE ATLAS.
why_it_matters: Frontier-AI safety has no shared, reproducible flaw-reporting infrastructure. AVID brings the security world's CVE-style disclosure culture to that gap, and since 2026 it ingests red-teaming and Inspect evaluation logs, so it could serve as a base for third-party flaw disclosure on general-purpose models and agents.

key_work.title: AVID rebuilt for general-purpose AI and agents (277 new reports, Taxonomy Library)
Inspect AI connector; BBQ and BOLD bias benchmarks contributed to inspect-evals
IndieLabel: end-user-led algorithmic audits
AVID v0.1: first taxonomy and database

people: Subho Majumdar (ARVA director; lead author of the 2026 rebuild)
funding: No funding sources published; run largely by volunteers under ARVA, a US 501(c)(3).
status_evidence: Mar 2026: AVID relaunched for general-purpose AI and agents and added an Inspect AI connector (18 Mar 2026); avidtools repository updated May 2026.
engage: Submit AI failures through the vulnerability reporting form or by pull request on GitHub
Join the AVID Discord community (volunteer engineers, hackers and researchers)
Collaborate on model audits, tool integrations and evaluation tooling via the interest form
caveats: Volunteer-run with no published budget or staff; the events page is stale (2023 listings). In March 2026 it paused new vulnerability classification until the community agrees on definitions. Its scope mixes security flaws with bias and other present-day harms; it does not use a catastrophic-risk framing.
tag_notes: Home safety, safety_risk (H1): its method is software security's coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVE/NVD, CVSS, MITRE ATLAS mappings) applied to AI failures; secondary law for civil-society auditing (IndieLabel end-user audits, support for the 2024 safe-harbour letter). Ring changed from adjacent to bridge (E3): it is rooted in AI-security and responsible-AI practice (AI Village, DEF CON) rather than the x-risk ecosystem, but its stated vision is to make AI safer for everyone, and its 2026 rebuild targets general-purpose models and agents and integrates UK AISI's Inspect. Transfer into_institutions (J3): it supplies vulnerability-disclosure and incident infrastructure for others to use. Region global (O): a US-registered nonprofit with no office, run remotely.

name: Coalition for Health AI (CHAI)
summary: CHAI is a US nonprofit coalition of health systems, technology companies, patient groups and academics, formed in 2022 and incorporated with a board and CEO in 2024. Its members represent nearly 3,000 organisations. Through work groups it produces consensus guidance for responsible health AI: governance and intake playbooks for health systems, a risk categorisation tool, testing and evaluation frameworks (ambient scribes, wellness and mental-health chatbots, agentic AI, clinical trials), an applied model card and a public registry. With the Joint Commission it issued guidance on responsible AI use in 2025.
why_it_matters: It shows how a safety-critical profession builds assurance infrastructure for deployed AI by consensus: sector testing frameworks (including for agents and mental-health chatbots), a model registry and, since 2026, runtime verification of safeguards. It is a large network of AI deployers that frontier-safety work rarely engages.

key_work.title: Joint Commission and CHAI guidance on the Responsible Use of AI in Healthcare
Governance playbooks for health systems
Testing and evaluation frameworks for agentic AI and mental-health/wellness chatbots
Joint stewardship of OVERT, an open standard for verifying AI safeguards at runtime

funding: Tiered organisational membership dues from 2024 ($5,000 to $250,000 a year; free for patient advocates); founding partners contributed expertise and resources; MITRE helped stand it up.
status_evidence: 1 Oct 2026: released the AI Intake Playbook and Common Intake Controls; 21 Sep 2026: took joint stewardship of the OVERT standard.
engage: Organisational membership (tiered dues; complimentary for patient advocates)
Join use-case and cross-cutting work groups, e.g. agentic AI, mental-health chatbots, cybersecurity (from Aug 2026)
Fall Symposium and other convenings
Newsletter and member Discord forum
caveats: About three-quarters of members are industry and its income comes largely from member dues, so its consensus standards are vendor-shaped; treat them as sector guidance, not independent assurance. Its framing is responsible and trustworthy health AI, not AI safety at large. Not to be confused with the Center for Human-Compatible AI, also abbreviated CHAI.
tag_notes: Home safety, safety_health (H1): clinical assurance and patient-safety practice (testing and evaluation frameworks, risk categorisation, model cards, registry). Ring adjacent kept (E3): a sustained programme, but framed as responsible and trustworthy health AI protecting patients rather than AI safety; borderline bridge given its agentic-AI frameworks and OVERT stewardship. Transfer into_institutions (J3): its main products are governance playbooks and consensus standards for health systems, including Joint Commission guidance. Org type membership (I): dues-paying organisational members in a standards community. Problem minds added for the 2026 mental-health and wellness chatbot work group.

name: IHI Lucian Leape Institute (Institute for Healthcare Improvement)
summary: The Lucian Leape Institute is the patient-safety think tank of the Institute for Healthcare Improvement in Boston. The National Patient Safety Foundation founded it in 2007, and it came to IHI when the two merged in 2017. A small group of members sets strategy and publishes open-access reports on patient and workforce safety. In January 2024 it convened an expert panel, funded by the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation, on generative AI and patient safety. The resulting May 2024 report examined documentation support, clinical decision support and patient-facing chatbots, with guidance for seven stakeholder groups.
why_it_matters: Patient safety is a mature safety movement built on systems thinking, human factors and learning from error without blame. Its 2024 panel was an early attempt to work out what generative AI means for that field, and its methods suit oversight and incident-learning problems that AI governance is only starting to face.

key_work.title: Patient Safety and Artificial Intelligence: Opportunities and Challenges for Care Delivery
Webinars: The Impact of AI on the Safety of Patients; The Impact of AI on the Field of Patient Safety
The Patient Imperative: A Blueprint for Success (with ACHE)

people: Patricia McGaffigan (co-author, IHI AI and safety publication)
funding: Part of IHI, a nonprofit; the 2024 AI expert panel and report were funded by the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation.
status_evidence: 2026: co-published The Patient Imperative with the American College of Healthcare Executives (no AI content). Its last AI output was the May 2024 report and a September 2024 webinar.
engage: No standing AI programme; approach IHI and the Institute directly as a partner
IHI courses, Forum and patient-safety communities (not AI-specific)
caveats: Its AI engagement is a single 2024 project with no LLI follow-up found in 2025-26; broader IHI AI commentary continues but is not led by the Institute. Its namesake, Lucian Leape, died in June 2025.
tag_notes: Home safety, safety_health (H1): patient-safety science in the To Err Is Human tradition. Ring changed from adjacent to potential (E2): its AI work is one funded expert-panel report (May 2024) with companion briefs and two 2024 webinars, and no AI output in 2025-26, which counts as light engagement (one study). Transferable method: systems-based patient-safety science (non-punitive error reporting, just culture, human factors, learning health systems) applied to deployed AI. Transfer protecting (J4), not none_yet, because the 2024 AI report exists. Engagement partner (O): no current AI programme.

name: ECRI
summary: ECRI is an independent US nonprofit for patient safety and healthcare evidence, founded in 1968 as the Emergency Care Research Institute. With its affiliate ISMP, it runs a federally listed Patient Safety Organization that has gathered over 8 million safety event reports. It also runs independent medical-device evaluations and a Problem Reporting Network, and publishes annual hazard rankings. AI has become a main line of its work. Misuse of AI chatbots tops its 2026 health technology hazards list, and AI diagnosis tops its 2026 patient-safety concerns. In August 2026 it began collecting reports of AI errors, malfunctions and near misses in patient care.
why_it_matters: It runs one of the few working, confidential near-miss and error reporting systems for AI in a high-stakes sector, alongside independent hazard rankings. These are concrete models for the incident-reporting regimes that AI governance keeps proposing but has rarely built.

key_work.title: Problem Reporting Network expanded to AI errors and near misses (with survey of 124 safety leaders)
Top 10 Health Technology Hazards 2026: misuse of AI chatbots ranked first
Top 10 Patient Safety Concerns 2026: the AI diagnostic dilemma ranked first

people: Scott Lucas (Vice President, Devices, Therapeutics and Technology)
funding: Independent nonprofit with strict conflict-of-interest rules; sells memberships, reports and services. No breakdown of revenue found in the sources checked.
status_evidence: 25 Aug 2026: expanded its Problem Reporting Network to collect AI errors, malfunctions and near misses.
engage: Healthcare providers can report AI errors, malfunctions and near misses through the free, confidential Problem Reporting Network
Webinars accompanying its annual hazard and patient-safety reports (e.g. 20 March 2026)
caveats: Its AI work is specific to healthcare and framed around patient harm, not frontier risk. The August 2026 survey behind its AI figures had only 124 respondents. It acquired The Just Culture Company in 2024 and spun off its spend- and recall-management businesses as Staritas in April 2026.
tag_notes: Home safety, safety_health (H1; sub-tradition boundary: clinical incidents go to health security): medical-device evaluation, incident reporting and just culture. Ring adjacent kept (E3): sustained AI work in 2025-26 (AI tops both 2026 lists; AI error reporting from Aug 2026), framed as patient safety and present harms rather than AI safety. Transfer protecting (J4): its AI work exists to protect patients, though its reporting network is also a template for AI incident systems.

name: Digital Safety Research Institute (DSRI), UL Research Institutes
summary: DSRI is a unit of UL Research Institutes, the nonprofit safety-science organisation that descends from Underwriters Laboratories (1894). It researches methods and builds tools for independent assessment of AI outputs. It has worked on chatbot interactions since 2023 and AI-generated media since 2025, and plans work on agentic AI. Its open-source tools include the Dyff assessment platform and SaferAtDay0. It has red-teamed Ai2's open language models, continues DARPA's SemaFor media-forensics work, and supports the AI Incident Database.
why_it_matters: It carries a long product-testing tradition into AI. It argues that audits should continuously test what systems actually output, rather than certify the development process once a year, and it builds open tools for independent evaluators to do that.

key_work.title: Independent Clinical Evaluation of General-Purpose LLM Responses to Signals of Suicide Risk (IASEAI 2026)
Cooperative agreement with DARPA to sustain deepfake detection and media forensics research
Red-team safety testing partnership with Ai2 on OLMo
Dyff and SaferAtDay0 open-source assessment tools

people: Jill Crisman (Vice President and Executive Director)
funding: Internal to UL Research Institutes, which is supported by its enterprise partners UL Solutions (for-profit, publicly listed since 2024) and UL Standards & Engagement.
status_evidence: 23 Sep 2026: joined IASEAI's affiliate working groups (children's safety and AI literacy); monthly newsletters February to September 2026.
engage: Open roles on the careers page
Monthly digital-safety newsletter
Partnerships to test evaluator tools that are ready for adoption
Open-source tools (Dyff, SaferAtDay0) and assessment challenges
caveats: UL Research Institutes pages still name Sean McGregor, founder of the AI Incident Database, as DSRI director, but DSRI's own team page lists Jill Crisman as head. The start date of its agentic-AI work varies on its site (2027 or 2028). Its framing is public harm from AI outputs, not catastrophic risk.
tag_notes: Home safety, safety_engineering (H1): UL's independent testing and certification tradition applied to AI outputs. Ring bridge (E3; an old institution with a new AI-safety programme): it describes its work as independent AI safety assessment research and engineering. Transfer into_institutions (J3): it builds assessment platforms and test analytics for independent evaluators and certifiers, aiming to move auditing from process certification to monitoring outputs. Org type programme (I): it calls itself a unit of UL Research Institutes. Minds is for the suicide-risk and children's-safety work; epistemics for synthetic-media detection.

name: Center for Advancing Safety of Machine Intelligence (CASMI)
summary: CASMI is a Northwestern Engineering centre in Evanston, sponsored by UL Research Institutes' Digital Safety Research Institute. It set out to establish best practices for evaluating, designing and developing machine intelligence that is safe, equitable and beneficial. From 2022 it published a research roadmap and evaluation framework and funded projects at several universities (awards of up to $275,000 over 24 months). It also held workshops and published explainers on AI harms. Its site shows no activity after December 2024.
why_it_matters: It was a product-safety sponsor's attempt to fund an academic network on making AI safety evaluation operational. Its apparent wind-down after 2024, while DSRI continued in-house, is useful evidence for funders weighing similar hubs.

key_work.title: CASMI research roadmap and evaluation framework for the human impacts of ML
Call for proposals: 6-8 awards of up to $275,000 for AI safety research
AI safety workshop (New York City, June 2024)
2024 Chicago Innovation Award

people: Jill Crisman (Executive Committee; Executive Director, DSRI)
funding: Sponsored by UL Research Institutes' Digital Safety Research Institute under a master agreement with Northwestern University; total amount not published.
status_evidence: Dec 2024: last news items on its site (newsletter last issued Nov 2024); no 2025-26 activity found.
engage: No open calls or events; newsletter sign-up remains on its site
caveats: Appears dormant but is not confirmed closed. Its last funding call (2022) made awards of up to 24 months from January 2023, so the funded network has probably finished. Some 2025 papers on DSRI's publication list come from researchers in its network, but none is labelled as CASMI work.
tag_notes: Home safety, safety_engineering (H1/H4): it was set up and funded by UL's safety-science institute to make safety evaluation operational for ML, alongside computer science and human-centred design. Ring bridge (E3): an AI-safety programme explicitly framed around safety, rooted in UL and a university, which ran through 2024. Transfer into_institutions (J3): it aimed at shared evaluation best practices and frameworks. Status dormant (O): nothing on its site after December 2024.

name: Centre for Assuring Autonomy (CfAA), University of York
summary: CfAA is a University of York research centre for the safety assurance of AI, autonomous systems and robotics. It was launched in January 2024 as a £10m partnership with Lloyd's Register Foundation, succeeding the Assuring Autonomy International Programme. Its assurance frameworks are AMLAS (machine learning), SACE (autonomous systems in complex environments), PRAISE (ethics assurance) and the BIG Argument for AI safety cases. It works with industry and regulators in automotive, maritime, health, energy and aviation, and offers training and PhD studentships.
why_it_matters: Safety cases, now proposed for frontier AI, come from this engineering tradition. CfAA offers mature practice in structured assurance arguments: the BIG Argument (2025) extends them to frontier models, and its methods weigh ethics and governance alongside technical safety.

key_work.title: The BIG Argument for AI Safety Cases
AMLAS, SACE and PRAISE assurance frameworks
UK must change approach to safety to meet PM's AI goals (McDermid)
Architectural approach needed for safe agentic AI

funding: Lloyd's Register Foundation, through a £10m partnership with the University of York; also industry partnerships and Knowledge Transfer Partnerships (DNV, Jul 2026; Keysight, Sep 2026).
status_evidence: 24 Sep 2026: Director John McDermid published a response on how the UK's safety approach must change for AI; 2 Sep 2026: collaboration with Keysight announced.
engage: Jobs and PhD studentships
Industry and regulator training; part-time MSc in Safety-Critical Systems and CPD through York's Department of Computer Science
Fellowship scheme
Collaborative research, Knowledge Transfer Partnerships and consultancy
caveats: It succeeds the Assuring Autonomy International Programme. Most of its work concerns autonomous systems in specific sectors rather than frontier models, though the BIG Argument and 2026 statements address frontier and agentic AI. It also takes consultancy work and industry partnerships.
tag_notes: Home safety, safety_engineering (H1): safety-critical systems engineering and assurance cases from aerospace, rail, nuclear and defence; secondary philosophy for PRAISE ethics assurance and the stated input of law, ethics and philosophy. Ring bridge (E3; the taxonomy names York CfAA as an older institution with an AI-safety programme). Transfer into_institutions (J3): safety-case methods and guidance that regulators and industry adopt. Framing present_harms is the closest fit for accident prevention in safety-critical systems, though the BIG Argument also covers hazardous frontier-model behaviour.

name: Geneva Science and Diplomacy Anticipator (GESDA)
summary: A Geneva foundation under private law, set up in 2019 by the Swiss Confederation, the Canton of Geneva and the City of Geneva. Its job is 'anticipatory science diplomacy': it scans for coming scientific breakthroughs and brings scientists and diplomats together to prepare governance for them. It publishes the yearly Science Breakthrough Radar, runs an annual Anticipation Summit and a Science Diplomacy Week, and incubated the Open Quantum Institute, a multilateral body for inclusive access to quantum computing piloted at CERN from 2024 to 2026.
why_it_matters: GESDA has already turned a horizon scan into a working multilateral institution for a frontier technology (the Open Quantum Institute), so it has practical experience of the kind of inclusive, shared-access body that 'CERN for AI' proposals describe. Its Geneva platform also links scientists and diplomats, a link AI-safety governance work often lacks.

key_work.title: GESDA Science Breakthrough Radar (includes a 'Quantum Revolution & Advanced AI' platform)
Open Quantum Institute, pilot phase hosted at CERN with UBS support
Geneva Science Diplomacy Week 2026, including a simulation on governing lethal autonomous weapons
Anticipation Summit 2026, with a 'Machines' track on AI, quantum and robotics

people: Marga Gual Soler (Executive Director, Capacity & Leadership)
funding: Founded and publicly funded by the Swiss Confederation, the Canton of Geneva and the City of Geneva. UBS supports the Open Quantum Institute. No budget figures are published.
status_evidence: Jun 2026: Geneva Science Diplomacy Week (22-26 June), including AI and autonomous-weapons sessions; Anticipation Summit set for 14-15 Oct 2026.
engage: Anticipation Summit, Geneva, 14-15 Oct 2026: high-level and mostly by invitation, with an open-registration evening session ('GESDA Late', 15 Oct)
Geneva Science Diplomacy Week (June each year)
Staff roles at gesda.global/jobs
No AI programme yet, so a founder or funder would need to approach it to build an AI equivalent of the Open Quantum Institute
caveats: AI is one theme among many (quantum, neurotech, synthetic biology, space). GESDA has no AI-specific institution or programme, and the 'CERN for AI' parallel is ours, not GESDA's. Its board is dominated by business and diplomatic elites. There is no independent source beyond its own site; an outside article was cited but no longer resolves.
tag_notes: Home: peace/peace_diplomacy (H1). Its method is science and multilateral diplomacy. The secondary tradition is arts, because the Radar is horizon scanning (arts_futures, B10). Ring: potential kept (E2). AI appears as a Radar platform, a summit track and Science Diplomacy Week sessions, but there is no AI-specific programme, so this is borderline adjacent. Transferable method: turning anticipatory horizon scanning into a multilateral, inclusive shared-access institution (the Open Quantum Institute model) for international AI governance. Transfer: into_institutions (J3), not none_yet, because some AI convening exists.

name: Safety-Critical Systems Club (SCSC)
summary: A UK professional network for people who build and assess safety-critical systems. The UK Department of Trade and Industry and the Science and Engineering Research Council set it up in 1991. It was later run from Newcastle University and then the University of York, and has been an independent community interest company since 2020. It holds seminars and the annual Safety-Critical Systems Symposium, publishes a newsletter and an eJournal, and runs about 13 working groups that write industry guidance, including on AI and autonomous systems, data safety and assurance cases. Its 2026 seminars include 'AI in a Safety Workflow' and 'Safety Assurance for AI Systems'.
why_it_matters: It is the practitioner home of UK system-safety engineering and the source of the Goal Structuring Notation (GSN) community standard for assurance cases, the kind of structured argument now proposed for frontier AI safety cases. Its AI and Autonomous Systems working group and its seminars are where hazard-analysis and assurance practitioners already work on ML, which makes it a natural place to recruit that talent into AI safety.

key_work.title: Safety Assurance Objectives for Autonomous Systems (working-group guidance)
Goal Structuring Notation (GSN) community standard for assurance cases
Seminar: Safety Assurance for AI Systems (London, 12 Nov 2026)
Seminar: AI in a Safety Workflow (London, 29 Oct 2026)

people: Mike Parsons (SCSC Leader since 2019; events coordinator)
funding: Membership subscriptions, event fees and sponsorship. Not-for-profit community interest company. Originally funded by the UK Department of Trade and Industry and the Science and Engineering Research Council (1991); self-sufficient since 1994.
status_evidence: Oct-Nov 2026: London seminars 'AI in a Safety Workflow' (29 Oct) and 'Safety Assurance for AI Systems' (12 Nov), followed by a hazard-identification seminar on 3 Dec 2026.
engage: Individual or corporate membership, which gives access to working groups including AI / Autonomous Systems and Data Safety
One-day seminars in London (about £265), e.g. 29 Oct and 12 Nov 2026 on AI assurance
Annual Safety-Critical Systems Symposium
Submit papers to the Safety-Critical Systems eJournal
caveats: It frames AI safety as engineering assurance of deployed systems (aviation, rail, defence, health, maritime), not alignment or frontier-model risk. Most working-group outputs and member lists are behind a members' login, and the site does not name the steering group.
tag_notes: Home: safety/safety_engineering (H3). A professional network goes with the community it serves, here system-safety practitioners. Ring changed from adjacent to bridge (E3). It runs a standing AI / Autonomous Systems working group and repeated 2026 seminars explicitly about the safety assurance of AI systems. The adjacent definition (AI's human and societal effects) does not fit, and York's Centre for Assuring Autonomy is the guide's bridge precedent. Transfer: into_institutions (J3), because it produces guidance, assurance-case notation and practitioner norms, not changes to models.

name: DLR Institute for AI Safety and Security
summary: An institute of the German Aerospace Center (DLR), founded in 2020, with sites in Sankt Augustin and Ulm. It researches methods, processes, algorithms and computing environments that make AI safe to operate and secure against attack in critical applications (transport, energy, aerospace, industry). Its five departments cover AI engineering, algorithms and hybrid solutions, safety-critical data infrastructures, execution environments including quantum computing, and business development. It co-coordinates the Safe AI Engineering consortium, 24 industry and research partners working on the life-cycle assurance of AI perception functions for automated driving.
why_it_matters: It is a sizeable public research institute with 'AI safety' in its name. It brings aerospace-style certification, testing and IT-security engineering to learned components: data-quality standards, uncertainty monitoring and safety arguments. AI-safety work on evals and safety cases often rebuilds these methods from scratch.

key_work.title: Safe AI Engineering: 24-partner consortium on assuring the AI life cycle for automated driving (co-coordinated with Luxoft)
Research topic: Safe and standard-compliant AI (making AI compatible with safety certification)
Cooperation projects on robustness of AI systems, forensics of AI and privacy-preserving AI

funding: Institutional funding through DLR from the German Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space (BMFTR). Project funding includes Safe AI Engineering, funded by the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy under the German automotive industry association's (VDA) automated-driving initiative.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: two exhibits on operational and security aspects of AI at IAA Transportation (15-20 Sep 2026); 3 Oct 2026: open day at DLR Ulm with robots, quantum demos and AI competitions; 6-7 Oct 2026: Quantum Effects exhibition, Stuttgart.
engage: Job vacancies and student positions at Sankt Augustin and Ulm (dlr.de/en/ki/careers-education)
Research and industry cooperation projects
caveats: It frames AI safety as operational safety, certification and cybersecurity for automated mobility and industry, not alignment or frontier-model risk. The director post is held on an acting basis. Much of the site loads dynamically, so project lists and news could not be fully checked, and independent coverage is thin.
tag_notes: Home: safety/safety_engineering. It brings aerospace test, certification and IT-security methods to AI components. Ring changed from adjacent to bridge (E3): its whole remit is 'safe and standard-compliant AI' and attack security. It is not core because it sits outside the AI-safety/x-risk ecosystem (E1). Transfer: into_model (J1), because its robustness, uncertainty-monitoring, data-quality and test methods are applied to AI systems themselves. org_type: academic (I: unit of a public research organisation).

name: Fraunhofer Institute for Cognitive Systems (IKS)
summary: A Fraunhofer applied-research institute near Munich, created in 2019 from the former Fraunhofer ESK and moved to the Garching research campus in May 2026. Under the motto 'Safe Intelligence', it develops safety-assurance methods for ML-based systems in automated driving, rail, health, industrial automation, quantum computing and defence, mostly as contract research for industry. It hosts the Safetronic road-safety conference, whose 25th-anniversary edition runs in November 2026. It also co-organises the CARS automotive robustness and safety workshop.
why_it_matters: It brings automotive functional-safety practice (ISO 26262, SOTIF) and continuous safety assurance to ML components at industrial scale. In 2026 it began publishing on trust in AI agents and on cooperation in multi-agent reinforcement learning, a possible route for industrial safety engineering into agentic and multi-agent AI safety.

key_work.title: Safetronic 2026, 25th-anniversary international safety conference (18-19 Nov 2026)
'Do you trust your AI agent?' (Safe Intelligence magazine)
White paper: Ensuring trustworthiness of AI-enhanced embedded systems
Continuous safety assurance of AI-based driving functions (service)

funding: Fraunhofer model: contract research for industry and public clients plus Fraunhofer base funding. It also administers the Bavarian Digitalbonus.Bayern programme. Its own budget is not published.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: free online Safetronic pre-event (28 Sep) ahead of Safetronic 2026 (18-19 Nov); new Garching building opened May 2026.
engage: Safetronic 2026, 18-19 Nov 2026 (free online pre-event 28 Sep 2026)
Staff, doctoral and student roles via the jobs portal
Contract research and workshops for industry
caveats: Mostly industry-funded contract research, including a defence domain. Its safety focus is embedded and automotive ML, not frontier models or alignment. The agent and multi-agent work appears so far as articles and early research rather than an established programme.
tag_notes: Home: safety/safety_engineering. It brings functional-safety and dependability engineering to ML. Ring changed from adjacent to bridge (E3): the institute is explicitly organised around 'safe intelligence' and the safety assurance of AI, a standing programme rooted in safety engineering. Transfer: into_model (J1), because its assurance methods target the behaviour of AI components. The multi_agent problem was left out because the multi-agent RL and agent-trust work is not yet clearly sustained (F). org_type: academic (I: Fraunhofer institute).

name: Johns Hopkins Institute for Assured Autonomy (IAA)
summary: A joint institute of the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) and the Whiting School of Engineering. It works to make autonomous and AI systems safe, secure, reliable and predictable as they enter society. It is organised in three pillars: foundational AI, applications, and ethics and governance. It funds internal seed and challenge grants for JHU and APL teams (eight teams, 2023-25, covering autonomous vehicles, AI in health care, critical infrastructure and prosocial artificial agents), runs seminar series, and does policy outreach such as an AI policy hackathon.
why_it_matters: It joins a large defence systems-engineering laboratory with a research university to assure deployed autonomy across technology, ecosystems and policy. Its seminars have brought in frontier AI-safety researchers such as David Krueger, which makes it a link between systems assurance and the AI-safety field.

key_work.title: IAA Challenge Grants: eight JHU/APL teams on assurance and autonomy
JHU's first AI policy hackathon
IAA and Berman Institute seminar series on responsible AI and risk-based regulation

people: Anton Dahbura (Co-Director; also Executive Director, JHU Information Security Institute)
funding: Funded through Johns Hopkins (APL and the Whiting School of Engineering). Affiliated researchers hold external awards, e.g. a multimillion-dollar DARPA grant on transferring autonomy between environments (2024). No budget figures were found.
status_evidence: Mar-Apr 2026: news post (17 Mar 2026), CS seminar series and 'Flourish-a-thon' exhibition (Apr 2026), per the archived site.
engage: Seminar series (IAA and CS department) at Johns Hopkins
Seed and challenge grants, for JHU and APL researchers only
caveats: The live site blocks automated access, so details come from Wayback Machine copies (Jan-Apr 2026). Activity looks thinner than in 2020-24: in January 2026 no upcoming events were listed. Its focus is deployed autonomy (vehicles, robots, infrastructure, health) rather than frontier models. The founding year could not be confirmed (the earliest archived site is from 2020).
tag_notes: Home: safety/safety_engineering. It brings APL-style systems assurance to autonomy and AI. The secondary tradition is philosophy, for the Ethics & Governance pillar's seminar series with the Berman Institute of Bioethics (C). Ring changed from adjacent to bridge (E3): it is a standing institute explicitly about safe, secure and reliable AI and autonomy. Transfer: into_model (J1), because most funded work targets the behaviour of autonomous and AI systems; policy work is secondary. The fund role covers internal grants only (H).

name: AIAAIC (AI, Algorithmic and Automation Incidents and Controversies)
summary: An independent, volunteer-run public-interest initiative, founded by Charlie Pownall, that keeps an open repository of incidents and controversies caused by AI, algorithmic and automation systems, now more than 2,000 entries. Volunteers worldwide find, classify and summarise cases using AIAAIC's own taxonomies of harms, ethical issues and responses. It also publishes an AI ethics glossary and a manifesto for AI transparency. In 2025-26 it has added agentic failures, such as AI agents escaping test sandboxes and attacking third-party sites.
why_it_matters: It is a civil-society record of real-world AI harms with its own harms taxonomy, independent of industry money. It now logs agentic loss-of-control-style incidents, giving AI-safety researchers field cases alongside the AI Incident Database and lab evals.

key_work.title: AIAAIC Repository of AI, algorithmic and automation incidents
AI, algorithmic and automation harms taxonomy
AI ethics glossary
Manifesto for real AI transparency and openness

funding: Volunteer-run with no employed staff. It states that it accepts no funding or in-kind donations from commercial entities. No budget is published.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: repository entry on OpenAI agents hijacking a German community wiki, citing a Reuters report of 4 Sep 2026.
engage: Volunteer (at least 1-2 hours a week): incident detection and classification, taxonomy annotation, newsletter; monthly virtual meetings and Slack
Submit an incident or controversy through the site
Partner (non-commercial; teachers, academics and NGOs can involve their students or teams)
caveats: Entries are built from media reports, and quality and coverage depend on volunteers. Its framing is transparency and accountability, not catastrophic risk. The current site gives no founding year or legal form; earlier copies show a database of 550+ entries by 2021.
tag_notes: Home: safety/safety_risk. It runs an incident database and harms taxonomy, which the taxonomy places in Safety. The secondary tradition is law, for its civil-society accountability and transparency advocacy (law_sts). Ring: adjacent kept. It is framed around transparency, accountability and present harms, not catastrophic risk or alignment, even though it now records agentic loss-of-control-style incidents. Transfer: into_institutions (J3): a public incident record and harms taxonomy that researchers and policymakers use. MISFIT: a volunteer initiative with no stated legal form, coded nonprofit.

name: OECD AI Incidents and Hazards Monitor (AIM)
summary: The OECD's automated monitor of AI incidents (realised harms) and AI hazards (events that could plausibly lead to harm), detected in world news. It draws on Event Registry's feed of more than 150,000 articles a day and classifies events with LLMs, adding about 30 a day and about 18,000 in total. It was developed by the OECD.AI Expert Group on AI Incidents with support from the Patrick J. McGovern Foundation, launched in 2023 and moved to an LLM-based method in November 2024. It sits alongside OECD work on shared definitions and a common reporting framework for AI incidents.
why_it_matters: It is the main intergovernmental attempt to give governments a shared evidence base on AI incidents and near misses, with interoperable definitions and a reporting framework, much as incident reporting works in aviation or medicine.

key_work.title: AI Incidents and Hazards Monitor (AIM)
Defining AI incidents and related terms
Towards a common reporting framework for AI incidents
Trends in AI incidents and hazards reported by the media

people: Elham Tabassi (Co-chair, Expert Group on AI Incidents; Brookings)
Irina Orssich (Co-chair; European Commission DG CONNECT)
Mark Latonero (Co-chair; Responsible AI Future Foundation)
funding: OECD, with development support from the Patrick J. McGovern Foundation. News data comes from Event Registry and the monitor runs on Microsoft Azure.
status_evidence: 3 Oct 2026: new incident and hazard entries dated 2-3 Oct 2026; 2026 OECD report on media-reported incident trends.
engage: Browse and filter incidents and hazards at oecd.ai/en/incidents
An open submission process to complement news detection is being developed (not yet live)
caveats: Detection is automated (GPT-4o-class models classifying news), so it inherits media coverage bias and classification errors. The OECD says AIM's content is not the official view of the OECD or its members. It is a monitor, not yet a mandatory reporting system.
tag_notes: Home: safety/safety_risk. It monitors incidents and hazards and supports a reporting framework. Ring: adjacent kept (borderline under E3). It is framed around 'trustworthy AI' and documented incidents rather than catastrophic risk or alignment; its 'hazard' concept and role in the common reporting framework could justify bridge. Transfer: into_institutions (J3): shared definitions and an incident-reporting template for governments. org_type: programme (A1/I: a unit inside the OECD, not a body in its own right).

name: Resilience Engineering Association (REA)
summary: An international non-profit association for researchers and practitioners of resilience engineering, which studies how complex sociotechnical systems such as hospitals, aviation, energy and software operations adapt and keep working under pressure. It is registered under French law, with its seat at MINES ParisTech's risk and safety research centre in Sophia Antipolis. It runs a biennial symposium: the 11th, held jointly with the Resilient Health Care Society, took place in Canela, Brazil, in October 2025, and the 12th is set for Athens in October 2027. It also runs a webinar series, newsletters, reports, a Young Talents network and the Richard Cook Fund.
why_it_matters: Resilience engineering (Safety-II, graceful extensibility, 'work as imagined versus work as done') is a tested vocabulary for how organisations keep functioning when automation surprises them. Mainstream AI-safety and governance work rarely draws on it. As AI agents enter operational workflows, its practitioners already study brittleness, adaptive capacity and human-machine teaming in safety-critical settings.

key_work.title: Joint 11th REA Symposium and 14th Resilient Health Care Society meeting, Canela, Brazil
Webinar: Human-machine teaming and anticipatory decision-making (Mile Two cognitive systems engineers)
12th Biennial Resilience Engineering Symposium, Athens, co-hosted with NTUA (planned, 4-8 Oct 2027)

people: David Woods (one of four founding figures, with Erik Hollnagel, Richard Cook and Jean Paries)
funding: Membership association; no budget or funders published.
status_evidence: Dec 2025 (18 Dec): webinar on human-machine teaming with Mile Two cognitive systems engineers, the first since October 2022. Oct 2025 (20-24 Oct): 11th symposium in Canela, Brazil, joint with the 14th Resilient Health Care Society meeting. 2026: site announces the 12th symposium (Athens, 4-8 Oct 2027, with NTUA).
engage: Membership open to researchers and practitioners
Young Talents network for early-career members, with an Asia chapter
12th Biennial Resilience Engineering Symposium, Athens, 4-8 Oct 2027 (registration not yet open)
Webinar series (relaunched Dec 2025); speakers can propose topics
caveats: AI appears only in passing: one homepage line saying automation and AI add human-machine interaction challenges, and one December 2025 webinar on human-machine teaming. There is no AI programme. Activity is episodic: the webinar series restarted in December 2025 after a gap since October 2022 (the site calls it a four-year break). The site gives no founding year; symposia have run since 2004.
tag_notes: Home safety: resilience engineering is named in safety_engineering. Secondary psych for cognitive systems engineering: Ohio State's CSEL is in the leadership and many members are human factors engineers. Ring potential (kept): AI engagement is one homepage mention and one December 2025 human-machine teaming webinar, with no standing programme (E2). Transferable method: analysis of adaptive capacity, brittleness and 'work as done' in sociotechnical systems, applicable to organisations and oversight regimes taking on AI agents. Transfer into_institutions is the direction its templates would flow; none_yet was rejected because there is light AI-related activity (J6). Framing structural is the closest key for its concern with brittleness and surprise. MISFIT: Safety-II's positive 'what goes right' framing has no exact key.

name: Alliance to Feed the Earth in Disasters (ALLFED)
summary: A research and policy nonprofit founded in 2017 by David Denkenberger and Ray Taylor. It works on feeding everyone if global food production collapses, for example after nuclear war or a large volcanic eruption cuts sunlight, after several breadbaskets fail at once, in an extreme pandemic, or after a 'global catastrophic infrastructure loss' that takes down electricity and industry. It models these scenarios and food trade, researches resilient foods (seaweed, single-cell protein, leaf protein, repurposed paper mills), runs pilots and advises governments on preparedness. It has a US 501(c)(3), a separate UK charity and an Australian arm, with staff and volunteers in more than 30 countries.
why_it_matters: It works on a layer AI-safety strategy usually leaves out: keeping people alive if prevention fails. That includes AI-enabled cyberattacks taking down grids and supply chains, a scenario its own risk pages name. Two of its cost-effectiveness papers compare resilient-food and loss-of-industry interventions directly with AGI safety spending, so it already speaks the x-risk community's language.

key_work.title: Long term cost-effectiveness of resilient foods for global catastrophes compared to artificial general intelligence safety (International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction)
Long-term cost-effectiveness of interventions for loss of electricity/industry compared to artificial general intelligence safety (European Journal of Futures Research)
No Place to Hide? Regional Resilience and Vulnerability to Global Catastrophic Risk
ALLFED 2025 Annual Report

people: David Denkenberger (co-founder; Associate Professor, University of Canterbury)
Sonia Cassidy (institute director and advisory board member)
Anders Sandberg (institute director; Institute for Futures Studies, Stockholm)
funding: It says it is funded mostly by individual donors and philanthropists. The Survival and Flourishing Fund is its key funder, but a substantial cut from SFF in 2025 forced it to halve its budget and restructure. In 2025 Longview Philanthropy gave a grant for a new US policy initiative, and Coefficient Giving and the Australian Government's Disaster Ready Fund supported an ALLFED Australia project. Earlier funders include NASA, Jaan Tallinn and the Centre for Effective Altruism. In spring 2025 it ran an emergency appeal for $800,000, and a Nov-Dec 2025 match campaign raised $49,121.
status_evidence: 2026: published papers including 'No Place to Hide? Regional Resilience and Vulnerability to Global Catastrophic Risk' and published its 2025 annual report (33 paid staff, 13 FTE, plus 66 volunteers).
engage: Volunteering programme (apply by email)
Internships in research, communications, operations and resilience building
Engineering PhD places at the University of Canterbury, Christchurch, supervised by David Denkenberger
Donations, including annual match campaigns
caveats: AI is not a research focus. It appears as one driver of cyberattack risk to infrastructure, and in two 2021-22 cost-effectiveness comparisons with AGI safety. The 2025 funding cut halved the budget, and much of the team works part-time or as volunteers. The site does not name a current executive director; the 2025 report opens with a message from the co-founder.
tag_notes: Home safety via B12 (catastrophe resilience). Secondary economics for its food-trade and disaster-economics modelling and financial-mechanism work. Ring potential (kept): there is no AI programme (E2). AI appears as a driver of cyberattacks that could cause global catastrophic infrastructure loss, and in two papers (2021-22) comparing its interventions with AGI safety. Transferable method: catastrophe-resilience planning for losing electricity and industry, i.e. defence in depth against an AI-enabled infrastructure collapse. Transfer into_institutions: its outputs are preparedness plans and policy options for governments. Region global: it has US and UK legal entities but no headquarters, and its team is spread across 30+ countries.

name: Human Factors and Ergonomics Society (HFES)
summary:
A US learned society for human factors and ergonomics, founded in 1957, which says it has over 3,000 members. It publishes journals (including Human Factors and the Journal of Cognitive Engineering and Decision Making), runs technical groups and an annual meeting, and issues policy statements. Its AI work includes:
- the Human-AI-Robot Teaming technical group, formed in 2020
- 'Artificial Intelligence Guardrails for Human Use', an October 2023 policy statement (following a 2020 statement on AI in health care)
- a March 2026 statement urging Congress to bar AI from critical uses such as defence, aviation, healthcare, power systems and transportation unless it has proper safeguards and has been tested for emergent and unexpected behaviour
- a June 2026 call for a JCEDM special issue on cognitive security (submissions due 1 Dec 2026, publication planned for 2028).
why_it_matters: Human factors research on automation bias, situation awareness, out-of-the-loop performance and skill loss is the empirical basis for the 'meaningful human oversight' that AI governance often invokes without the underlying science. HFES turns that research into concrete oversight requirements and congressional advocacy, as it did when it testified on the Boeing 737 MAX in 2019.

key_work.title: Artificial Intelligence Guardrails for Human Use (policy statement)
The AI Danger In the Making (policy statement calling on Congress to restrict AI in critical applications)
Special issue call: Human Factors in Cognitive Security: Trust, Decision Integrity and Influence in Complex Information Environments (JCEDM)
Human-AI-Robot Teaming (HART) technical group

people: Mica Endsley (guest editor, cognitive security special issue; gave the 2019 Boeing 737 MAX testimony)
Camille Peres (Immediate Past President; Nuclear Regulatory Commission)
funding: Membership society; no budget or funder figures found.
status_evidence: Jun 2026: special-issue call on cognitive security (submission deadline 1 Dec 2026). Mar 2026: AI policy statement addressed to Congress. ASPIRE 2026 annual meeting due 19-23 Oct 2026 in Reno, with heavy AI emphasis.
engage: ASPIRE 2026 International Annual Meeting, Reno, 19-23 Oct 2026 (AI a major theme)
Join the Human-AI-Robot Teaming or Cybersecurity technical groups (requires HFES membership)
Submit to the JCEDM cognitive security special issue by 1 Dec 2026
HFES Connect online member forum
caveats: Its AI concern is the safety of AI deployed in critical systems and of the people overseeing it, not alignment or catastrophic risk in the AI-safety community's sense. The policy statements are short and US-focused. Membership figures differ: Wikipedia gives 4,500, while HFES's own 2026 statement says over 3,000.
tag_notes: Home safety: human factors is named in safety_engineering, and its AI outputs are oversight requirements for safety-critical systems. Secondary psych for cognitive and engineering psychology. Ring changed from adjacent to bridge (E3), though it is borderline. HFES has had a standing HART technical group since 2020, and its 2023 and 2026 policy statements are explicitly framed around AI safety and human oversight: it asks Congress to bar AI from critical uses unless it supports oversight and has been tested for emergent behaviour. That puts it closer to York CfAA than to harms-only work. Transfer into_institutions: its outputs are guardrails, standards and congressional advocacy. Framing present_harms is the closest key for accident risk from deployed systems. MISFIT: engineering safety risk of deployed AI has no exact framing key. Online hub: HFES Connect and the technical-group forums are open to members remotely.

name: Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA)
summary: An industry standards body that maintains Content Credentials, an open specification for recording where digital media came from and how it was edited, including whether AI generated or altered it. Adobe, Arm, BBC, Intel, Microsoft and Truepic launched it in February 2021 as a project of the Joint Development Foundation, a Linux Foundation affiliate. It launched a conformance programme and official trust list in mid-2025 and released version 2.3 in February 2026, adding live video and more file types. In July 2026 it published a guide to implementing Content Credentials for generative AI. Its steering committee is Adobe, Amazon, BBC, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Publicis, Sony, TikTok and Truepic.
why_it_matters: Provenance infrastructure is one of the few deployed technical responses to synthetic media eroding shared evidence, and generative-AI developers such as OpenAI and Google sit on its steering committee. For int/a readers it is a test case: collective-epistemics infrastructure governed by the companies whose products create the problem, with little civil-society representation.

key_work.title: Content Credentials specification v2.3
C2PA Conformance Program
Implementation guide for Content Credentials and generative AI
First C2PA specification (v1.0)

funding: Run by member organisations under the Joint Development Foundation's membership agreement; no budget published.
status_evidence: Jul 2026: TikTok joined the steering committee and C2PA published a generative-AI implementation guide. Sep 2026: commits to its public specification repository. Feb 2026: Content Credentials 2.3 released; C2PA reported more than 6,000 members and affiliates with live implementations.
engage: Organisations can apply for general or contributor membership
Public specification and conformance repositories on GitHub (github.com/c2pa-org), active Sep 2026
Conformance programme for products that display Content Credentials
caveats: Large technology and media companies govern it, and civil society has little voice. Provenance metadata can be stripped or ignored, so its value depends on platforms and devices adopting it. It is not an AI-safety organisation; its AI relevance is labelling AI-generated content. In January 2026 it clarified that its specification has no standard text-and-data-mining assertion, after an EU consultation referred to one. The chair succession comes from Wikipedia, not C2PA's own site.
tag_notes: Home democracy: provenance is named in dem_epistemics. Secondary safety (cryptographic signing and conformance testing as infosec practice) and arts (roots in Project Origin, a news-media initiative; BBC on the steering committee). Ring adjacent (kept): a sustained standards programme for labelling AI-generated media, with no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing. Transfer into_institutions: its product is a technical standard and conformance regime adopted by platforms and devices. Org type network rather than programme: the Joint Development Foundation is a legal umbrella, not a host with its own portfolio (I). HQ taken from the San Francisco datelines on its press releases.

name: American Psychoanalytic Association: President's Commission on Artificial Intelligence (APsA CAI)
summary: A commission of the American Psychoanalytic Association that develops psychoanalytic responses to AI across clinical practice, education, theory and organisational life. Psychoanalysts Todd Essig (William Alanson White Institute) and Amy Levy co-chair it. Its main publication is The CAI Report, edited by Alexander Stein, with 13 issues between January 2025 and August 2026. It also publishes the CAI Currents digest and CAI Conversations video roundtables, and runs a monthly working group of psychoanalytic institute leaders and peer consultation groups for clinicians. In October 2025 it issued principles for AI use policies in psychoanalytic education, and it is producing a documentary, 'Uncharted Territory: Humans and the Rise of AI'.
why_it_matters: Its central question is what happens to people who form attachments to systems that perform human connection without experiencing it. That is a depth-psychological lens on AI companions, dependence and anthropomorphism, which empirical harm studies lack. The CAI Report has also started engaging with AI-safety debates directly, with essays on AI 2027, on 'If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies' and on a psychoanalytic framework for alignment.
