caveats: It writes mainly for clinicians, so its policy reach is limited. The Report mixes clinical essays, poetry and an advice column, and quality varies. The essays on x-risk and alignment are individual contributors' views, not commission positions. The commission's founding date is not stated. It is distinct from the American Psychological Association and the American Psychiatric Association.
tag_notes: Home psych via H1: its method is psychoanalytic, and psychoanalysis is named in psych_clinical. Secondary arts for the documentary, made with filmmakers Charles de Lauzirika and Jeremy Emerman. Ring adjacent (kept, borderline bridge): a standing commission and bimonthly publication on AI's effects on the psyche, relationships and clinical practice. Its mission speaks of a 'humanizing AI future' and the Report carried alignment and x-risk essays in Feb and Jun 2026, but these do not frame the programme (E3). Transfer convening (J5): it mainly brings the psychoanalytic community into the AI conversation through its report, roundtables, working group and peer groups. Minds is the primary problem because its core concern is attachment to AI 'new others'. Engagement community refers to the clinician-only peer groups. Merged sub-entry folded in.

name: British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy (BACP)
summary:
The UK's largest professional body for counsellors and psychotherapists, with around 75,000 members. It is a registered charity, founded in 1977 and based in Lutterworth, Leicestershire. In 2026 AI in mental health has become a recurring policy theme:
- February: responded to the MHRA consultation on regulating AI in healthcare, citing its Mindometer survey of therapists
- July: a public survey found 46% of 16-24-year-olds had used AI instead of talking to a person about their mental health
- September: responded to the National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare, and published guidance on managing anxiety about AI's future.
why_it_matters: It brings frontline clinical evidence of chatbot use and harm, drawn from its member therapists. It is also one of the few professional bodies publicly addressing anxiety about where powerful AI is heading, including fears that no one is in control. That makes it a natural partner for psychological support around AI distress, including for people working in AI safety.

key_work.title: Our call for clearer AI regulation in mental health (response to the MHRA consultation)
Young people turning to AI as loneliness takes toll on mental health (Public Perceptions Survey)
AI has a role to play in improving mental health, but people must remain at its core (response to the National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare)
AI and mental health: how to manage anxiety about the future

funding: Registered charity and membership body; no AI-specific funding identified.
status_evidence: 22 Sep 2026: published guidance on managing anxiety about AI's future. 10 Sep 2026: responded to the National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare.
engage: Membership for counsellors and psychotherapists (student, individual, registered)
Communities of Practice for members
Public therapist directory
caveats: It responds to AI's effects on clients and the profession and does not engage with AI systems themselves. Its AI work so far consists of consultation responses, surveys and guidance, not a dedicated programme. In April 2026 the Charity Commission closed a regulatory compliance case into its safeguarding, governance and financial controls, opened after trustee resignations and the removal of its Chair and Deputy Chair. The Commission said it was now satisfied with how BACP is governed. The chief executive's name comes from Wikipedia.
tag_notes: Home psych (psych_clinical) via H3: a counselling and psychotherapy professional body whose AI outputs draw on clinical practice and member surveys. Ring adjacent (kept): repeated AI work in 2026 (consultation responses, surveys, guidance) on AI's effects on mental health and on regulating AI tools. It has no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing, though its September 2026 guidance acknowledges public fears about losing control. Transfer protecting (J4): it aims to protect clients and the public from AI used in place of human therapy. Engagement community applies only to credentialed members. Merged sub-entry folded in.

name: American Psychiatric Association: Committee on Mental Health Information Technology (AI in Psychiatric Care)
summary:
The AI workstream of the American Psychiatric Association (founded 1844; more than 40,400 members), led by its Committee on Mental Health Information Technology. It publishes guidance for clinicians on AI in psychiatric practice:
- a 2024 position statement treating AI as 'augmented intelligence' that supports rather than replaces clinicians
- a 2026 AI Resource Document, with a webinar series
- a checklist for assessing AI scribe tools
- a blog on the risks of 'AI prescribing'
- its App Advisor model for evaluating digital mental-health tools, adopted in a 2026 SAMHSA advisory
- an eight-part 'facts label' for AI mental-health tools, published in Frontiers in Psychiatry in August 2026.
why_it_matters: The facts label (identifying information, intended use, warnings, risks and limitations, model information, clinical evidence, accessibility, privacy) is a ready transparency template. It could be extended to the general-purpose chatbots people use for emotional support. The APA also brings organised clinical judgement on patient safety to AI tools at a time when US regulation of them is thin.

key_work.title: Facts label for transparent communication of AI risks in mental health technology (Frontiers in Psychiatry)
APA AI Resource Document and webinar series
AI Prescribing Blog: Innovation, Risk, and the Need for Guardrails

Download the 2026 APA AI Resource Document via a form
caveats: It focuses on psychiatrists' clinical use of AI tools (scribes, decision support, prescribing), not on general-purpose chatbots or AI safety more widely. Its framing is clinical safety and professional standards. The AI pages do not list the committee's chair or members. The CEO's name was not confirmed on the AI pages. It is distinct from the American Psychological Association, which is already in the roster.
tag_notes: Home psych (psych_clinical) via H3: a committee of a psychiatry professional body applying clinical governance to AI tools. Ring adjacent (kept): standing AI guidance, a resource document and a webinar series, framed around clinical and patient safety rather than catastrophic risk or alignment. Transfer protecting (J4, as with Common Sense Media): the facts label, scribe checklist and App Advisor exist to protect patients and clinicians who use AI tools. Assurance is primary because most outputs evaluate and label clinical AI tools; minds is second for its attention to companion-chatbot risks. Online hub: the live webinar series is a recurring programme open to registrants.

name: Centre for Software Reliability (CSR), City St George's, University of London
summary: A research centre in the School of Science and Technology at City St George's, University of London, founded in 1983. It studies how to assess and contain risk in systems that depend on software (reliability, safety, security), using probabilistic and statistical methods, assurance cases and static verification. Past applications include nuclear reactor protection systems, medical infusion pumps and air traffic control. Its AI work comes mainly from Robin Bloomfield, who with SRI's John Rushby applies 'Assurance 2.0' assurance cases to AI, and from Lorenzo Strigini, Peter Popov and Kizito Salako, who work on statistical safety assessment of autonomous vehicles.
why_it_matters: It brings four decades of probabilistic reliability assessment and safety-case practice from nuclear, aviation and critical infrastructure to AI. Bloomfield and Rushby argue that ML components can't be assured directly, so safety has to come from defence in depth and highly assured guards around them. Mainstream alignment work rarely engages with this dependability view, though it was presented at UK AISI's 2024 conference on frontier AI safety frameworks.

key_work.title: Assurance of AI Systems From a Dependability Perspective (Bloomfield and Rushby)
Where AI Assurance Might Go Wrong: Initial lessons from engineering of critical systems (presented at UK AISI FAISC 24)
Quantifying Confidence in Assurance 2.0 Arguments
The Impact of Operational-Data Fidelity when Assessing Safety-Critical Autonomous-Vehicle Software (Salako and Muhammad)

people: Robin Bloomfield (professor; Assurance 2.0 and AI assurance)
Kizito Salako (researcher; conservative Bayesian reliability assessment)
funding: By the centre's own account, about half of its research support has historically come from EPSRC; the rest comes from industry, charities and government grants and contracts in the UK, EU and US. No AI-specific funding found.
status_evidence: Aug 2026: Salako and Muhammad preprint on assessing autonomous-vehicle software safety; Mar 2026: Bloomfield and Rushby, 'Quantifying Confidence in Assurance 2.0 Arguments'.
engage: PhD research projects in dependability and assurance, listed on the centre's microsite
Consultancy and advisory services, listed on the centre's microsite
caveats: The university site sits behind a bot wall, so the centre's pages were checked through April 2026 archived copies; the project list on its microsite is mostly historical. The AI work rests on a few senior researchers, and the AI-assurance papers are written jointly with SRI International. There is no visible AI-specific programme or grant, so its ring as bridge rests on a 2024-26 publication line rather than a funded programme.
tag_notes: Home safety: a dependability and assurance-case centre whose AI outputs apply Assurance 2.0 safety cases and probabilistic reliability assessment to AI and autonomy (H1); formal is secondary because of its static-verification and probabilistic-proof methods. Ring bridge: an institution from 1983 with a 2024-26 publication line explicitly on AI assurance and frontier AI safety frameworks (E3, old institution with a new AI-safety line). Transfer into_institutions: what it offers is assurance cases and confidence arguments, templates for decisions about deployment. Framing: MISFIT, because its stakes are high-consequence failures of critical systems (engineering accident risk); catastrophic is the closest value, since its AI papers address frontier AI frameworks and AGI.

name: Stanford Center for AI Safety
summary: A Stanford University centre, set out in a 2018 white paper by Clark Barrett, David Dill, Mykel Kochenderfer and Dorsa Sadigh, that develops rigorous techniques for building safe and trustworthy AI and for establishing confidence in its behaviour. Its research covers formal methods (for example verifying neural controllers with the Marabou verifier), safety validation of autonomous systems, learning and control, transparency, AI governance and human-AI interaction. It lists AI-safety courses such as CS120 Introduction to AI Safety and AA228V Validation of Safety Critical Systems, and holds an annual meeting (SAFE) with its industry affiliates.
why_it_matters: It carries the verification and validation culture of aviation and hardware into AI. Co-director Kochenderfer's research fed the international aircraft collision-avoidance standard, and the centre's work aims at provable guarantees and systematic stress-testing rather than benchmark scores alone. It is one of few US academic AI-safety centres rooted in safety-critical engineering rather than ML alignment.

key_work.title: Stanford Center for AI Safety white paper
Stanford Center for AI Safety Annual Meeting 2025

Algorithms for Validation (MIT Press textbook, co-director Mykel Kochenderfer)

funding: Industry Affiliates Program with tiers at $50,000, $150,000 and $300,000 a year, plus visiting scholar places at $75,000 a year. The site lists Torc Robotics and Accenture as core members, NRI as associate, DARPA and NSF as federal sponsors, and Ford, Future of Life Institute, Siemens, Open Philanthropy, GE Global Research and IBM as other sponsors (undated).
status_evidence: Oct 2026: SAFE Annual Meeting 'Trust, Verified' scheduled for 5 October 2026 at Stanford, with speakers from Anthropic and Cohere.

Industry Affiliates Program ($50k-$300k a year) and paid visiting scholar places

Mailing list via the contact page
caveats: Most of the work concerns autonomous vehicles, aerospace and formal verification; frontier-model alignment is a small part. It frames its mission as safe and trustworthy AI, not catastrophic or existential risk. Funding mixes industry (AV and engineering firms), DARPA and EA-linked philanthropy. The founding year is inferred from the 2018 white paper.
tag_notes: Home safety: its co-directors and outputs come from safety validation of safety-critical systems (aircraft collision avoidance, autonomous vehicles, navigation integrity), and formal verification is the second strand, so formal is secondary (H1; seam with formal per the safety-to-formal boundary). Ring bridge, the roster value kept: an academic centre rooted in verification and aerospace safety engineering with a standing AI-safety programme, analogous to York's Centre for Assuring Autonomy; it isn't part of the x-risk ecosystem or on the aisafety.com map (E3). Transfer into_model: verification, certificates and validation methods applied to AI systems and controllers themselves (J1). Framing: MISFIT, because its stakes are accident risk in high-stakes deployed systems; present_harms is the closest value.

name: Lloyd's Register Foundation (LRF)
summary: An independent UK safety charity, set up in 2012, that owns Lloyd's Register Group and funds work to 'engineer a safer world'. It has a grant portfolio of about £300m (live and completed) across maritime safety, safer infrastructure and engineering skills, and runs the Global Safety Evidence Centre and the World Risk Poll. Its AI work includes a £13.9m grant (2017-2028) behind the University of York's Centre for Assuring Autonomy, a 2025-26 Foresight Review on the Safe Adoption of AI led by Careful Industries, and World Risk Poll data on public perceptions of AI risk.
why_it_matters: It is a large, established engineering-safety funder that already pays for AI assurance work, such as York's safety-case methods (AMLAS, SACE and the 2025 BIG argument, which also addresses frontier models). Its Foresight Review frames AI safety as a whole-lifecycle, sociotechnical problem covering workers, environmental impacts and critical infrastructure. That makes it a plausible new funder for systems-safety approaches outside the EA funding base.

key_work.title: Centre for Assuring Autonomy, a partnership with the University of York (£13.9m grant, 2017-2028)

An end-to-end view of AI safety (Foresight Review interim findings)

funding: Income comes from its ownership of Lloyd's Register Group. Grant portfolio of about £300m (live and completed), 609 grants in total; £13.9m to the Centre for Assuring Autonomy (2017-2028); founding partner of the £5m Safer Complex Systems programme with the Royal Academy of Engineering (2019).
status_evidence: Sep 2026: announced Small Grants Programme 2026 (up to £10,000; 24 Sep) and other news through 29 Sep 2026; Feb 2026: published Careful Industries' interim findings ('An end-to-end view of AI safety') and the literature review 'The AI Safety Paradox' with the positioning paper 'Levers for the Safe Adoption of AI' (24 Feb 2026), for its Foresight Review on the Safe Adoption of AI.

Sign-up for updates and the community of practice around the Foresight Review on the Safe Adoption of AI
Collaboration with the Centre for Assuring Autonomy, through LRF's programme manager
Newsletter
caveats: AI is one strand within a portfolio centred on maritime and engineering safety. Its AI framing is the safe adoption of AI in engineered systems, worker and environmental safety, not frontier or existential risk. The Foresight Review's final report was due in June 2026 and wasn't confirmed in the sources checked. Its World Risk Poll data on AI dates from the 2021 round.
tag_notes: Home safety: a single-mission engineering-safety funder whose AI money goes to safety assurance (H4, one-programme funder; not a generalist funder under K). Arts is secondary because its standing Foresight Review method (scenarios and participatory foresight) produced its main 2025-26 AI output. Ring bridge: a long-established safety charity running sustained, explicitly 'AI safety' work in 2024-26, including the CfAA grant, the Foresight Review and its publications (E3). Transfer into_institutions: what it funds is safety cases, guidance, standards input and policy recommendations. Framing present_harms: the Foresight Review centres current and emergent harms to workers, environments and infrastructure.

name: Artificial Intelligence Underwriting Company (AIUC)
summary: A San Francisco company, publicly launched in 2025, that writes and maintains AIUC-1, a quarterly-updated security, safety and reliability standard for AI agents. The standard's six risk domains include a 'Society' domain covering catastrophic and cyber misuse. AIUC accredits auditors (Schellman was the first) to certify agents against the standard and links certification to insurance; ElevenLabs obtained the first agent insurance backed by AIUC-1. Certified customers include Cursor, Intercom's Fin, KPMG, Harvey and UiPath. In September 2026 it raised a $40m Series A (total $55m) and proposed that frontier labs form a mutual insurer to carry liability for catastrophic harms.
why_it_matters: It applies the insurance-and-certification model to AI: the company cites how insurers funded Underwriters Laboratories to make electricity safe, and uses premiums and audit conditions as a market incentive against a race to the bottom. Its stated mission, 'Underwrite Superintelligence', and its mutual-insurer proposal tie this commercial tradition directly to frontier and catastrophic risk.

key_work.title: AIUC-1, the standard for AI agent security, safety and reliability (quarterly updates; Q4 2026 update on 3 Oct 2026)
Frontier AI Mutual Insurer (Rune Kvist)

Rajiv Dattani (Cofounder; METR board member, former McKinsey insurance partner)

status_evidence: Oct 2026: AIUC-1 Q4 2026 update (3 Oct); Sep 2026: $40m Series A (15 Sep) and the 'Frontier AI Mutual Insurer' proposal (23 Sep).

AIUC-1 certification and audits for organisations deploying AI agents
caveats: A venture-funded business whose revenue comes from certifying and insuring enterprise agent deployments; most of AIUC-1 covers everyday agent risks (data, security, reliability) rather than frontier catastrophe. Certifying paying customers raises questions about the independence of its assurance. The founding year comes from its public launch in July 2025 (the earliest web captures of aiuc-1.com are from 25 July 2025); the site doesn't state it. Ring changed from the roster's bridge to core (see tag_notes).
tag_notes: Home safety (safety_risk): its method is insurance, underwriting and certification, explicitly modelled on insurers founding Underwriters Laboratories (H1). Ring changed from bridge to core: a new organisation founded in 2025 with the mission 'Underwrite Superintelligence'; one cofounder came from Anthropic and the other sits on METR's board; staff come from METR, Anthropic and OpenAI; it imports insurance practice into AI safety (E1 and the core boundary note: new AI-safety organisations founded by people from other fields are core). Transfer into_institutions: standards, accredited audits and insurance or mutual-liability structures are governance instruments (J3). Framing catastrophic: its own copy speaks of models that 'can also escape our sandboxes' and of liability for catastrophic risks.

name: Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security (CHS)
summary: A centre at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, founded in 1998 by D. A. Henderson as the Center for Civilian Biodefense Strategies. It researches and advises on epidemic and pandemic preparedness, biosecurity and deliberate biological threats. It is known for pandemic tabletop exercises (Dark Winter, Clade X, Event 201), runs the Emerging Leaders in Biosecurity fellowship and edits the journal Health Security. Its AIxBio line covers AI-enabled biological risk: which biological capabilities AI evaluations should prioritise, governance of biological data used in AI, upstream risk-benefit review of dual-use AI, and repeated submissions on US AI policy.
why_it_matters: It brings public-health preparedness and biosecurity governance to one of the most concrete catastrophic AI risk pathways: AI tools that could help create pandemic-capable pathogens. It argues for evaluations and governance focused on high-consequence capabilities. Its tabletop-exercise tradition is a ready template for AI crisis preparedness.

caveats: AI is one strand of a broad public-health security portfolio, and its AI outputs are mainly policy analysis rather than technical evaluations. The site sits behind a bot wall, so 2025-26 pages were checked through archived copies. It depends heavily on Coefficient Giving and US government funding. Event 201 later became a target of COVID conspiracy theories.
tag_notes: Home safety (safety_health): a public-health and biosecurity centre whose AI outputs are health-security governance and evaluation-priority work (B12: health security and biosecurity evaluation go to Safety). Ring bridge: an institution from 1998 with a standing AIxBio focus and publication line through 2024-26, framed around pandemic-scale catastrophe (E3). Transfer into_institutions: its main AI products are governance frameworks, data-governance proposals and policy submissions (J3). Assurance is paired as second problem for its work on what AI evaluations should test (F).

name: AIxBio Global Forum (NTI | bio)
summary: An international forum run by NTI | bio, the biological programme of the Nuclear Threat Initiative. It brings together policymakers, AI developers, biosecurity and AI-safety experts and bioscientists to build a shared understanding of AI-enabled biological risks and to promote governance of 'AIxBio' capabilities. NTI began scoping it in January 2024. Two technical working groups, one on guardrails for biological design tools and one on horizon scanning, risk assessment and evaluations, feed statements, frameworks and horizon scans. It holds events at Biological Weapons Convention meetings and ran a 2025 tabletop exercise with the Munich Security Conference.
why_it_matters: It carries nonproliferation practice over to AI tools that could help engineer pathogens: international norms, managed access, verifying users and BWC diplomacy. NTI's wider bio work adds US-China Track II dialogue, including a February 2026 joint statement with the China Arms Control and Disarmament Association. It is one of few standing international venues on AI-bio risk, with participants that include Concordia AI.

Ring bridge: rooted in the nuclear and bio nonproliferation community, with a standing forum, working groups and outputs through 2024-26 framed around global biological catastrophe (E3). Transfer into_institutions: its products are governance frameworks, statements and recommendations for governments, funders and developers (J3). name: SecureBio
summary: A Cambridge, Massachusetts nonprofit that aims to secure the world against catastrophic pandemics through a 'delay, detect, defend' approach. Its Detection programme (formerly the Nucleic Acid Observatory) runs metagenomic sequencing as a pathogen-agnostic early warning system. Its AI team builds benchmarks of biology-relevant capabilities in AI models (the Virology Capabilities Test, ABC-Bench, BioTIER for measuring safeguards, and WMDP with partners), runs pre-release assessments for frontier developers, and works on mitigations such as unlearning.
why_it_matters: It puts virology and biosecurity expertise directly into frontier-model evaluation. In 2026 it ran pre-release assessments of OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol (July) and GPT-6 Astra (September) and reviewed Anthropic's chemical and biological risk report for Claude Opus 4.6; this kind of work feeds developers' responsible scaling decisions. It shows how a domain-expert organisation can become part of the assurance chain for catastrophic misuse risk.

It also takes individual donations.

Its funding is concentrated in one funder. Bio-capability evaluations are dual-use, so parts of the work aren't public. The founding year (2022) comes from its incorporation as reported; the site doesn't state it, and the earliest archived copy of the site dates from May 2023.
tag_notes: Home safety (safety_health): a pandemic-defence organisation whose AI outputs are biosecurity evaluations of models (B12: biosecurity evaluation goes to Safety). Ring bridge: its founding mission is catastrophic pandemics, not AI, and its AI team is a sustained programme with benchmarks, pre-release assessments, NIST consortium membership and an EU AI Office partnership (E3). Transfer into_model: its evaluations and unlearning or robustness mitigations target model behaviour and feed developers' scaling policies (J1). Assurance is paired with security because it builds evaluations (F).

name: Global Shield
summary: An international advocacy organisation, launched in August 2023, that campaigns for governments to adopt policies against global catastrophic risk from all hazards: nuclear war, pandemics, AI, climate tipping points and asteroid impacts. A central policy team researches and designs proposals, and country offices in the US and Australia plus a multilateral team aimed at the UN lobby for them; it is now recruiting a director for a Berlin office. Its AI work includes a December 2025 critique of Australia's National AI Plan and an August 2026 assessment of Australia's decision to drop mandatory AI guardrails, built on freedom-of-information requests to forty agencies.
why_it_matters: It brings emergency-management and all-hazards disaster-risk practice to AI. It treats AI as one hazard among several and pushes for cross-cutting preparedness law (US Defense Production Act reform, UN capacity for complex global shocks) rather than AI-only rules, which is a template the AI-policy field seldom uses.

Register interest for future hiring rounds and volunteer roles in policy, research, operations and communications
Global Shield Briefing: monthly newsletter on catastrophic-risk policy (globalshield.substack.com)
caveats: AI is one hazard among many, and its AI output so far is mostly Australian. As a 501(c)(4), Global Shield does lobbying; donations to it are not tax-deductible. Its newsletter began in 2022 as Rumtin Sepasspour's 'GCR Policy Newsletter' and took the Global Shield name at the August 2023 launch.
tag_notes: Home: safety, because it applies all-hazards disaster-risk and emergency-management practice (catastrophe resilience, B12), with peace as secondary for its national-security and NATO policy staff. Ring: bridge (roster kept, E3). Its mission is all-hazards catastrophic risk, not AI, but it runs a sustained AI line: the 2025 National AI Plan critique, the 2026 guardrails report, and AI items throughout its briefings. Transfer: into_institutions, because it drafts legislation and policy proposals for governments and the UN. Badge recoupling: it treats AI both as a hazard of its own and as part of cascading, complex global shocks. No Berlin hub yet, because the Germany director role is still being recruited.

name: Centre for Long-Term Resilience (CLTR)
summary: A London think tank, incorporated in November 2019 as Alpenglow Group Limited, that works on extreme risks from AI and biology and on how governments manage risk. It advises and red-teams UK government policy, runs cross-sector workshops, and places experts in government. Its 2026 AI work centres on loss of control: a prototype Loss of Control Observatory that detects real-world incidents from open sources, reports showing that scheming-related and loss-of-control incidents are rising, and proposals for how the UK government should govern the risk.
why_it_matters: It carries national risk-register and civil-service risk-management practice into AI governance, and adds empirical incident monitoring as an early-warning input for government. Its 2026 writing draws explicitly on aviation safety-management systems and the 'three lines' model from corporate risk.

key_work.title: The Loss of Control Observatory: a prototype to detect real-world AI control incidents
AI loss of control incidents are worsening, shows CLTR analysis
How the UK Government can govern the risk of loss of control
AI and the systemic management of risk: what the frontier labs can learn from business

funding: It takes no government funding and relies on voluntary donations. Survival and Flourishing Fund (via CEA, Founders Pledge): $885,000 (SFF-2021-H2) and $908,000 (SFF-2022-H1) to Alpenglow Group Limited; $769,000 + $60,000 (SFF-2023-H2, FLI and Jaan Tallinn); $1,083,000 (SFF-2024); $527,000 + $38,000 matching (SFF-2025); $432,000 + $650,000 matching (SFF-2026, Jaan Tallinn & Dustin Moskovitz).
status_evidence: 24 Sep 2026: published 'AI and the systemic management of risk'; 9 Sep 2026: published priorities for the UK government on frontier AI risk and biosecurity; Oct 2026: recruiting a Loss of Control Incidents analyst.
engage: Jobs: Analyst, Loss of Control Incidents (contractor, closes 19 Oct 2026); Operations Associate (closes 5 Oct 2026)
Rolling open call for contractors on AI, biosecurity and AI-bio work
caveats: Its mission covers extreme risks in general, with AI one of three units alongside biosecurity and government risk management. It is registered as Alpenglow Group Limited, a company limited by guarantee rather than a registered charity.
tag_notes: Home: safety (H2, B12), since it imports national risk-register, resilience-planning and incident-reporting practice into AI and biosecurity policy. Ring: core (roster kept, E1). It is an x-risk think tank on the classic map, SFF-funded, and AI is one of its main units. Transfer: into_institutions, because its outputs are UK government risk-governance proposals and incident-monitoring systems. Evaluate is a role because the Loss of Control Observatory tracks incidents.

name: SaferAI
summary: A Paris nonprofit (a French loi 1901 association registered in August 2022) working on risk management for frontier AI. It builds quantitative risk models (nine cyber models completed, with loss-of-control and CBRN models in progress) and publishes a tracker that rates frontier AI companies' risk-management frameworks. It also runs independent risk evaluations of models, such as GLM-5.2 in 2026, and helps write EU and international standards for AI risk management and red-teaming, including input to the EU's General-Purpose AI Code of Practice.
why_it_matters: It imports quantitative risk-management practice from aviation, nuclear and finance (risk tolerances, quantified risk estimates, maturity ratings) into frontier AI, and turns it into public ratings and standards. Its 2026 work also brings in external safety-case review and systems-thinking approaches to loss of control.

key_work.title: Frontier Risk Management Tracker (ratings of AI companies' risk management)
Open Problems in AI Risk Modeling: Insights from a Workshop on the Technical Foundations of AI Risk Modeling
Lessons from External Review of DeepMind's Scheming Inability Safety Case
Exploring Systems-Thinking Approaches to Loss of Control Risk

funding: Survival and Flourishing Fund: $214,000 (SFF-2022-H2), $95,000 (SFF-2024), $200,000 + $111,000 matching (SFF-2025), all via Jaan Tallinn. Other funders not listed on its site.
status_evidence: 17 Sep 2026: published 'Open Problems in AI Risk Modeling'; 2 Aug 2026: GLM-5.2 risk evaluation report; ratings tracker updated July 2026.
engage: Jobs: Risk Modeling Lead, Research Scientist/Engineer and Founding Engineer (Infrastructure) on its Evaluations team, open as of Oct 2026
caveats: The founder, Siméon Campos, is now chairman and adviser; Henry Papadatos runs the organisation. The tracker scores companies against SaferAI's own methodology.
tag_notes: Home: safety (H2), since its method is quantitative risk management imported from aviation and finance. sub_tradition is safety_risk because quantitative risk models and ratings are its main output. Ring: core (roster kept, E1). It was founded as an AI-safety organisation, is on the classic map and is SFF-funded. Transfer: into_institutions, because ratings, EU standards and the Code of Practice change how companies and regulators govern models. Security is a secondary problem because of its cyber and CBRN misuse risk models.

name: Center for AI Risk Management & Alignment (CARMA)
summary: A small, largely remote think tank on risks from transformative AI, founded and led by Richard Mallah and run as a fiscally sponsored project of Social & Environmental Entrepreneurs. Its programmes are comprehensive risk assessment (adapting probabilistic risk assessment from safety engineering to AI), offense/defense dynamics, geostrategic dynamics (game theory, mechanism design and an LLM-agent model of an AI arms race), civil safety sciences, alignment of dynamical cognitive systems, and public security policy. Outputs since October 2024 include a national-preparedness policy brief (2025), a best-practice guide to AI whistleblowing law (2026) and a framework for adaptive AI governance (2026).
why_it_matters: It combines probabilistic risk assessment from nuclear and aerospace safety with complex-systems, dynamical-systems and mechanism-design modelling. Its civil-safety programme aims at detection and resilience technologies for when prevention fails, a systemic emphasis that is rare among core AI-safety organisations.

key_work.title: Probabilistic Risk Assessment for AI (framework and workbook 2024; full technical paper 2025)
Modeling an AI Arms Race using LLM Agents
AI Whistleblowing Law: A Best Practice Guide
Adaptive Governance for Advanced AI

people: Anna Katariina Wisakanto (Senior Risk Assessment Associate)
funding: Future of Life Institute: $2,300,000 general support (Aug 2026). Fiscally sponsored by Social & Environmental Entrepreneurs, Inc., a 501(c)(3).
status_evidence: 14 Sep 2026: published 'How a Superintelligence Might Kill Most of Us'; 18 Aug 2026: $2.3M FLI general-support grant; Jul 2026: AI whistleblowing law guide.
engage: Jobs: remote roles including Senior Economist (effects of transformative AI), Senior Researcher in Civil Safety Sciences and research engineers, listed as of Oct 2026; virtual-first, with in-person meetings clustering around Berkeley, Cambridge MA, Washington DC and London
caveats: CARMA is a fiscally sponsored project, not a separate legal entity. Its known funding comes mainly from FLI, and its job adverts run through FLI's hiring system ('Future of Life Organizations'). The founding year is inferred from its first publications in October 2024; the site gives no founding date.
tag_notes: Home: safety (H2), since its flagship output adapts probabilistic risk assessment, a safety-engineering method, and national preparedness, which counts as catastrophe resilience (B12). Secondary: life, for its complex and dynamical systems work, and formal, for game theory and mechanism design (B6). Ring: core (roster kept, E1). Its founding mission is transformative-AI risk, it is FLI-funded and it is on the classic map. Transfer: into_institutions, because risk-assessment frameworks, preparedness plans, whistleblowing law and governance designs are its outputs. Multi_agent comes from its game-theoretic arms-race models and platform-mediated coordination of AI agents. Org type is nonprofit rather than programme, because fiscal sponsorship is administrative. Region is global under rule O, since it is virtual-first with a US fiscal sponsor.

name: Safer Complex Systems (Engineering X, Royal Academy of Engineering)
summary: A £5m programme on the safety of complex, interdependent infrastructure systems, launched in 2019 by Engineering X, the Royal Academy of Engineering's collaboration with Lloyd's Register Foundation. It commissioned an initial framework from the University of York (2020), 18 case studies of safety successes and failures, and four reports on governance, then held a roundtable in December 2024 on emerging principles for governing complex systems. After a 2024 scoping workshop in Bogotá, it ran a grant call in 2025 to select the managing team of a Systems Hub in Colombia, planned to run from November 2025 to November 2028, to test systems approaches and adaptive governance in the energy transition. It has not worked on AI.
why_it_matters: It holds a body of evidence and draft principles on governing complex sociotechnical systems where no single duty holder can be held accountable. Hard rules lag new situations in such systems, and soft powers matter, which is the same situation AI deployed across critical infrastructure creates. That evidence has not yet been applied to AI.

key_work.title: Safer Complex Systems: An Initial Framework (University of York)
Safer Complex Systems Case Study Collection (18 case studies)
Governance of Complex Systems Roundtable Report
Systems Hub Colombia (grant call 2025; hub runs Nov 2025 to Nov 2028)

people: Dame Judith Hackitt (Chair of the programme board; former Chair of the Health and Safety Executive)
Dr Chris Elliott (Chair of the Govern workstream and Advisory Board)
Prof John McDermid (presented the York initial framework)
funding: £5 million programme funded by Lloyd's Register Foundation and the Royal Academy of Engineering (founding partners of Engineering X), launched in 2019.
status_evidence: Jul-Sep 2025: grant call for the managing team of the Systems Hub Colombia, which is to run from Nov 2025 to Nov 2028; 3 Dec 2024: governance roundtable with 27 participants from nine countries.
engage: Door to open: contact the Safer Complex Systems team (programme manager Ana Andrade) at the Royal Academy of Engineering
Free resources: the case study collection, governance reports and draft governance principles
caveats: No AI engagement found. No activity dated 2026 was found beyond the Colombia hub, which began in late 2025. A July 2024 retrospective by the governance chair hints that the programme may be maturing or winding down. It remains listed as one of Engineering X's five live programmes.
tag_notes: Home: safety, as an engineering-safety programme on complex infrastructure (safety_engineering), with life as secondary for its systems-thinking methods. Ring: potential (roster kept, E2), since no AI work was found on the programme's pages. Transfer: none_yet. Transferable method: complexity-appropriate governance principles and a case-study method for sociotechnical systems with no single duty holder, which could feed AI-in-infrastructure assurance. The York framework team links it to the assured-autonomy community. Framing: structural, from its own account of cascading failure across interdependent systems. Org type: programme, hosted by the Royal Academy of Engineering (Engineering X).

name: The Geneva Association
summary: The Zurich-based think tank of the global insurance industry, founded in 1973, whose members are chief executives of insurance and reinsurance companies. Under its Digital & AI Transformation research line it published 'Gen AI Risks for Businesses' (October 2025), a survey of 600 corporate insurance buyers in six countries that assesses whether generative-AI risks can be insured, and a report on Gen AI in the insurance customer journey. It runs an invitation-only AI & Insurance Conference (next in Shanghai, March 2027) and is editing a special issue of its journal, The Geneva Papers, on digital and AI transformation in insurance.
why_it_matters: Insurance is one of the few market levers that can price and constrain AI risk. The Geneva Association's work on the insurability of AI risks, together with the industry's expertise in catastrophe and accumulation risk (correlated losses across many policyholders), bears directly on that lever. So far it deals only with business-level generative-AI risks.

key_work.title: Gen AI Risks for Businesses: Exploring the role for insurance
Gen AI in the Insurance Customer Journey
Call for Papers: Digital and AI Transformation in Insurance (The Geneva Papers special issue, April 2028)
AI & Insurance Conference 2027 (Shanghai)

people: Ruo (Alex) Jia (lead author of the Gen AI risks report; Deputy Editor-in-Chief, The Geneva Papers)
funding: Membership association of insurance and reinsurance companies; its budget is not published.
status_evidence: Jun 2026: announced a Geneva Papers special issue on AI in insurance; Sep 2026: announced the AI & Insurance Conference 2027; Oct 2025: Gen AI risks report.
engage: Submit to The Geneva Papers special issue on Digital and AI Transformation in Insurance (call announced June 2026, for an April 2028 issue)
AI & Insurance Conference, 17-18 Mar 2027, Shanghai (by invitation only)
caveats: Its AI work serves insurers' commercial interests: business adoption, customer journeys, and insurability of present-day generative-AI risks such as defective outputs, copyright and cyber. It does not address frontier or catastrophic AI risk.
tag_notes: Home: safety, since insurance and risk transfer belong under safety_risk (H3, the constituency is the insurance industry), with economics as secondary for insurance economics and its journal. Ring changed from potential to adjacent under E2/E3. It has a sustained AI line: a standing Digital & AI Transformation topic, two 2025 Gen AI reports, a webinar, a recurring AI & Insurance conference and a 2026 special-issue call. None of it is framed around catastrophic risk or alignment. Transfer: convening, because its AI work mainly informs and convenes its own member insurers. Insurance as a governance instrument for AI is the latent contribution, which would make it into_institutions if pursued. Engagement 'contribute' refers to the open call for papers.

name: Chartered Institute of Ergonomics & Human Factors (CIEHF)
summary: The UK's chartered professional body for ergonomics and human factors, founded in 1949 as the Ergonomics Research Society and granted a Royal Charter in 2014. It accredits practitioners, degree courses, training and consultancies, and publishes white papers and guidance. On AI and automation it has published 'Human Factors in Healthcare AI' (2021), 'Human Factors in Highly Automated Systems' (2022, nine principles), and, through its Special Interest Group in AI and Digital Health, a 2024 guide to integrating human-centred AI in clinical practice.
why_it_matters: It is the professional home of the human-factors knowledge most relevant to AI oversight: automation bias, the 'ironies of automation', skill decay, situation awareness, and the alignment of ability, authority, responsibility and control. That knowledge is directly relevant to human-in-the-loop safety claims, which mainstream AI safety rarely tests against this evidence.

key_work.title: Human Factors in Healthcare AI (white paper)
Human Factors in Highly Automated Systems (white paper, nine principles)
Integrating Human-Centred AI in Clinical Practice: A guide for health and social care professionals

people: Tina Worthy (Deputy CEO and Director of Engagement)
Ron McLeod (lead author, Human Factors in Highly Automated Systems)
funding: Membership body and registered charity; financial details not published on its site.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: published the September issue of its magazine The Ergonomist; Jan 2026: news item on human-AI workflow design; Dec 2024: AI guidance and webinar from its AI and Digital Health special interest group.
engage: Associate membership, open to anyone through online sign-up
Special Interest Group in AI and Digital Health
Accredited training courses and CPD in human factors
caveats: Its AI work is confined to healthcare and workplace automation. It has not engaged with frontier AI or AI-safety institutions. The organisation is a small secretariat serving a membership of practitioners.
tag_notes: Home: safety (H3, a professional body grouped with its discipline), since human factors sits under safety_engineering; psych is secondary for cognitive ergonomics. Ring changed from potential to adjacent under E2/E3. It has a standing AI and Digital Health special interest group and a publication line (2021 healthcare AI white paper, 2022 automation white paper, 2024 clinical AI guide and webinar). Its framing is patient safety and human-centred design, not catastrophic risk or alignment. Transfer: into_institutions, because its principles and guidance set how developers, regulators and procurers design and deploy AI. Human factors of oversight is listed under the assurance problem.

name: Human-Centered AI Lab, Georgia Tech (formerly Entertainment Intelligence Lab)
summary: Mark Riedl's research group in Georgia Tech's School of Interactive Computing. It works on computational narrative (story generation and understanding), explainable AI, value alignment, game-playing and role-playing agents, and computational creativity. Its alignment strand uses stories as a source of human norms for agents, from the 2016 Quixote work to the 2025 Goofus & Gallant story corpus; since 2025 it has also built LLM wargames and social simulations of military decision-making.
why_it_matters: It is one of very few technical labs where narrative is a working method for alignment: stories serve as a training signal for social norms, a route to model character that mainstream alignment pursues through preference data instead. Its 2026 papers on LLMs in strategic and nuclear-conflict simulations add empirical evidence on AI in high-stakes decisions.

key_work.title: Using Stories to Teach Human Values to Artificial Agents (Quixote)
The Goofus & Gallant Story Corpus for Practical Value Alignment
Position: AI Is Not Ready for Strategic Conflicts
No One Wins in Nuclear War: A Social Simulation of Military Decision-making

people: Mark Riedl (Director; Githesh Ramamurthy Endowed Professor of AI; Director, Georgia Tech Machine Learning Center)
Glenn Matlin (researcher; lead author on the lab's wargame and social-simulation papers)
status_evidence: Aug 2026: arXiv preprint 'No One Wins in Nuclear War: A Social Simulation of Military Decision-making' (Matlin, Song, Zang, Riedl), following the July 2026 position paper 'AI Is Not Ready for Strategic Conflicts'.
engage: Research collaboration through Mark Riedl; his page says he cannot currently fund new PhD or MS assistantships
caveats: Value alignment is one strand among several (explainable AI, creativity, game agents, legal questions around AI agents). The lab frames its work as human-centred and responsible AI rather than x-risk. It was renamed from the Entertainment Intelligence Lab but still uses the eilab domain. Founding year and funders were not found.
tag_notes: Home arts/arts_narrative (H2): its distinctive alignment outputs import narratology, treating stories as carriers of norms (Quixote, the Goofus & Gallant corpus), and the taxonomy names it as an arts_narrative example. Law is secondary because of repeated co-authored legal work with Deven Desai (AI Agents and the Law, 2025; Responsible AI Agents, 2025; legal risks of medical AI, 2026). Ring kept at bridge (E3): rooted in computational narrative and HCI, it has a sustained value-alignment line (2016-2025) and safety-framed 2026 papers on strategic conflict. Transfer into_model: story corpora and normative priors for training agents. Framing present_harms under L, from its mission statement (explainable AI, value alignment, mitigating algorithmic harms), although the 2026 nuclear-conflict work leans catastrophic. Status is changed only because of the rename; it is clearly active in 2026.

name: Existential Hope (Foresight Institute)
summary: A programme of the Foresight Institute, a San Francisco nonprofit founded in 1986, that argues for ambitious, science-based positive futures. It produces the Existential Hope podcast, animations (such as 'AI 2035: The Alternate Timeline'), a newsletter, prizes (a $10,000 meme prize; an award at ISEF 2026) and a free online AI-futures worldbuilding course. Its AI Pathways project (2025) consists of two scenario reports, by Linda Petrini and Beatrice Erkers, on a Tool AI future and a d/acc future, with input from Vitalik Buterin, Glen Weyl, Anton Korinek, Anthony Aguirre and others.
why_it_matters: It works on the positive-vision side of AI safety, describing desirable and plausible end states and the paths to them, which most of the field leaves implicit. Its worldbuilding course and scenarios give non-specialists a structured way to picture AI futures they would want.

key_work.title: AI Pathways: Tool AI and d/acc scenarios
AI Futures Worldbuilding Course (free, online)
AI 2035: The Alternate Timeline (animated short)
Existential Hope Podcast: Stuart Russell on provably beneficial AI

people: Allison Duettmann (Founder; CEO of Foresight Institute)
funding: Funded within Foresight Institute, a donor-funded 501(c)(3); programme-specific funders are not published. AI Pathways included a $5,000 forecasting challenge with Metaculus (ended Nov 2025).
status_evidence: 29 Sep 2026: podcast episode with Stuart Russell on provably beneficial AI; an Audrey Tang episode appeared in September 2026.
engage: Free online AI-futures worldbuilding course (self-paced, on Udemy)
$10,000 meme prize for short-form media about hopeful, science-based futures; deadline 1 November (year not stated on the site, presumably 2026)
Newsletter and podcast
caveats: AI is one theme among several; Foresight's wider agenda includes atomically precise manufacturing and radical life extension, and critics may read its optimism as techno-boosterism. Founding year not found. Foresight's funding programme and fellowship are on the aisafety.com map; Existential Hope is not.
tag_notes: Home arts/arts_futures: its outputs are scenarios, worldbuilding, animation and podcasts, the tools of futures studies and media (B10: scenarios are Arts). Ring kept at core (E1): it is a programme of an x-risk-ecosystem organisation, and its flagship work is now AI-focused (AI Pathways, the AI worldbuilding course, AI 2035). It could arguably be bridge, since its remit covers other technologies. Transfer convening: it mainly brings the public and its own community into imagining AI futures; AI Pathways also targets governance choices. Framing flourishing (the taxonomy's own example). Online hub because the free course can be joined remotely. Org type programme (I: a unit inside Foresight).

name: AI Futures Project (AIFP)
summary: A Berkeley nonprofit founded in October 2024 by Daniel Kokotajlo after he left OpenAI. It writes detailed narrative scenarios of AI development (AI 2027 in April 2025; AI 2040: Plan A in July 2026) and maintains an interactive timelines model (aifuturesmodel.com) with periodic forecast updates. It has also run more than 30 tabletop-exercise iterations and in 2026 began publishing proposals for domestic AI regulation and giving testimony to the US Senate.
why_it_matters: AI 2027 showed what narrative form can do in AI-risk communication: it reached policymakers and the public in a way abstract argument had not. For a map of adjacent fields it is the core-side reference point for scenario and story methods, and a natural partner for futures and narrative scholars.

key_work.title: AI 2040: Plan A
AI Futures Model (interactive timelines model)
Senate testimony by Daniel Kokotajlo

funding: Mainly the Survival and Flourishing Fund and a major individual donor, plus smaller donations and grants (per its own site).
status_evidence: 2 Oct 2026: posted Daniel Kokotajlo's 30 Sep 2026 testimony to the Senate Subcommittee on Disaster Management, District of Columbia, and Census; Aug 2026: Q2.5 timelines update.
engage: Open positions listed in a recruitment document linked from its About page
Donations via Every.org or donor-advised funds (EIN 99-4320292)
Substack blog
caveats: Critics called AI 2027's timelines implausibly aggressive. The authors lengthened their forecasts in December 2025 and shortened them again in April 2026. It is a mainstream x-risk forecasting group: what it adds from outside the field is narrative form, not scholarship imported from other disciplines.
tag_notes: Home arts/arts_futures (B10): its main outputs are scenarios and tabletop exercises (AI 2027, AI 2040), and the taxonomy uses it as an Arts example. Democracy is secondary for the probabilistic timelines model. Ring core (E1): founded to forecast and steer the path to superintelligence, funded by SFF, and on the classic map. Transfer into_institutions: its scenarios and Plan A feed policy proposals ('How to pace the US frontier') and Senate testimony. Security is the second problem because Plan A and AI 2027 centre on US-China racing and coordination.

name: Intelligence Rising (Technology Strategy Roleplay)
summary: A facilitated strategic role-play game in which players take the parts of governments, tech companies and their advisers and play out competitive AI development over several simulated years. It was created by Shahar Avin at Cambridge's Centre for the Study of Existential Risk (seed funding 2019). Since 2022 it has been run by Technology Strategy Roleplay, a registered charity in England and Wales, through paid workshops for universities, AI-safety programmes, companies and governments in the UK, EU and US. Findings from 43 games were published in 2024.
why_it_matters: It brings wargaming and interactive drama to AI governance, so decision-makers experience race dynamics and coordination failures instead of only reading about them. It is the field's main serious-game tool, with a published methodology and a participant evaluation.

key_work.title: Exploring AI Futures Through Role Play
Strategic Insights from Simulation Gaming of AI Race Dynamics (43 games)
Documentary of a game hosted by Faculty's Marc Warner, covered by TIME

people: Shahar Avin (creator; UK AI Security Institute)
James Fox (co-author and facilitator; London Initiative for Safe AI)
funding: 2019 Long-Term Future Fund grant to Shahar Avin; since 2021 mainly fee income from paid workshops (per its own site).
status_evidence: Mar 2026: a feature documentary of an Intelligence Rising game hosted by Faculty CEO Marc Warner premiered; TIME covered it on 17 Mar 2026.
engage: Book a workshop (events@intelligencerising.org)
Facilitator training through Technology Strategy Roleplay
Contributor roles (partnerships, operations, facilitation, impact research, scenario design, social media; at least about 5 hours a week) via an expression-of-interest form
caveats: Workshops are bespoke and paid, with no public calendar. The participant evaluation (Cambridge, 2020-23, 50 responses from 14 games) is not independent. The headquarters city reflects the game's Cambridge origin; the charity's registered address was not checked. The TIME article does not describe Technology Strategy Roleplay's own role in the filmed game.
tag_notes: Home arts/arts_futures (B10: wargames are Arts); the taxonomy uses it as a media-role example. Peace is secondary because the game models US-China and state-lab strategic rivalry, and its facilitators include a former US diplomat. Ring core (E1): created at CSER for AI x-risk governance, funded by the LTFF, and on the classic map. Transfer into_builders: it changes the people who govern and build AI by forming their felt understanding of race dynamics. Quadrants: the geopolitics it models (Its) and participants' experiential learning (I). Badge full_spectrum: embodied role-play used as a way of knowing alongside research-based scenarios.

name: Geodesic Research
summary: A technical alignment nonprofit in Cambridge, UK, run as Meridian Impact CIC and publicly announced in May 2026. It studies how pretraining and midtraining shape a model's alignment priors, and whether those priors survive later capabilities reinforcement learning. Its January 2026 paper found that upsampling synthetic documents about AI misalignment in pretraining data increased misaligned behaviour, while documents depicting aligned AI reduced it; a September 2026 preprint tests 'inoculation midtraining' with learned neologisms.
why_it_matters: Its results make the stories a culture tells about AI a measurable variable in model behaviour. That gives narrative, cultural and media scholarship a concrete opening: deciding what training corpora should depict, a question those fields have not yet taken up with it.

key_work.title: Alignment Pretraining: AI Discourse Causes Self-Fulfilling (Mis)alignment
Inoculation Midtraining with Learned Neologisms
Announcing Geodesic Research

people: Kyle O'Brien (founding member of technical staff)
funding: Philanthropic grant from Coefficient Giving (announced May 2026, pending final logistics at the time); seed funding from the AGI Safety Tactical Opportunities Fund; support from the ERA:AI fellowship and CAISH; compute partnership with the UK AI Security Institute.
status_evidence: 14 Sep 2026: arXiv preprint 'Inoculation Midtraining with Learned Neologisms' (O'Brien, Young, Radmard, Kirch, Tice, Korbak, Africa).
engage: Hiring four Members of Technical Staff (job description and application form on its site)
caveats: It is classed under Arts because its central finding concerns AI discourse as training data. It is an ML lab with no humanities staff, and its newer work (inoculation midtraining, robustness to capabilities RL) has less to do with narrative. Its claim that Anthropic's 'Teaching Claude Why' and 'Model Spec Midtraining' build on its alignment-priors framing is self-reported. The alignment-pretraining paper (Jan 2026) predates the formal launch (May 2026).
tag_notes: Home arts/arts_narrative (H2, as in worked example Q2): it imports the idea that cultural narratives about AI act as model priors, and tests it with ML methods. Ring core (E1): its founding mission is robust alignment of capable LLMs, it is funded by Coefficient Giving, and it is on the classic map. Transfer into_model: it changes training data and midtraining to shape model behaviour. Status new: announced May 2026. MISFIT (mild): the Arts home rests on one finding; most of its methods are standard ML.

name: Center for Science and the Imagination, Arizona State University (CSI)
summary: A centre at Arizona State University, founded in 2012 with Ed Finn as founding director, that pairs writers and artists with scientists and engineers to imagine technological futures in detail. Starting with Project Hieroglyph (with Neal Stephenson), it has published more than twenty speculative-fiction collections, along with lesson plans, the Imaginary Papers series and the Imagination Desk podcast, and runs public events and the Sloan-supported Applied Sci-Fi Project. Its AI work is occasional: podcast episodes (e.g. Brian Christian, Pat Pataranutaporn), an April 2025 public conversation, 'The Spark and the Code', on AI and imagination, and Finn's own writing on how stories about algorithms shape them.
why_it_matters: It has a tested method for writing grounded, hopeful futures with scientists and writers working together. AI-futures efforts such as Existential Hope's worldbuilding attempt the same thing with less literary craft. Finn is also academic director of Future Tense, which publishes fiction and essays on emerging technology.

key_work.title: Hieroglyph: Stories and Visions for a Better Future
Frankenstein: Annotated for Scientists, Engineers, and Creators of All Kinds
The Spark and the Code: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Human Imagination (public event)

funding: Arizona State University; the Applied Sci-Fi Project is supported by the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation.
