Imaginary Papers and the Imagination Desk podcast
Door to open: no AI-futures programme yet
caveats: No dedicated AI programme was found; AI appears in occasional events and podcast episodes. Its 'Imagining Intelligence' project and older AI essays date from 2016-2021. Staff numbers and the full funder list were not verified.
tag_notes: Home arts/arts_narrative: its method is collaborative science fiction and creative writing with scientists. Ring potential (E2): AI engagement is light (a 2025 public event, a few podcast episodes, older essays), with no standing AI programme. Transferable method: structured collaboration between domain scientists and fiction writers to produce detailed, hopeful technology futures (Hieroglyph, the climate-imagination anthologies), ready to apply to AI. Transfer convening, not none_yet, because it has some AI activity, aimed at its public audience. Framing flourishing ('thoughtful optimism').

name: Käte Hamburger Centre for Apocalyptic and Post-Apocalyptic Studies (CAPAS)
summary: An institute of advanced study at Heidelberg University, opened in 2021 and funded through the German federal research ministry's Käte Hamburger Kolleg programme; its second funding period began in 2025. Each year it hosts about 15 international fellows who study how societies imagine and experience the end of the world and what follows, across literature, history, religion, film, politics and the sciences. It also publishes the journal Apocalyptica and a magazine. It names AI among today's apocalyptic threats, and some fellows have worked on it, e.g. Teresa Heffernan on 'Artificial Intelligence and the (Post)Apocalyptic Imaginary' (2022-23) and Elke Schwarz on robo-apocalypse and posthumanism (2022-23).
why_it_matters: AI-risk communication relies heavily on apocalyptic framing, and CAPAS studies how such framings mobilise, paralyse or polarise people. Its scholarship could inform how existential risk is communicated, and could give the field an outside view of its own 'doomer' discourse.

key_work.title: Fellow project: Artificial Intelligence and the (Post)Apocalyptic Imaginary (Teresa Heffernan)
Fellow project: Late-Modern Technology and its biotechno-politics, incl. AI case studies (Jan Cornelius Schmidt)
Apocalyptica special issue 'Vitality and Radical Axé'

funding: German Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space (BMFTR, formerly BMBF), Käte Hamburger Kolleg programme; second funding period from 2025. Amounts are not published on its site.
status_evidence: Jul 2026: fellowship applications for 2027-28 closed (deadline 3 Jul 2026); a distinguished lecture by Alenka Zupančič is announced for Dec 2026.
engage: Fellowships of up to 12 months for international scholars (about 15 a year; the last deadline was 3 Jul 2026, for 2027-28)
Public lectures, the Apocalyptic Cinema film series and arts collaborations in Heidelberg
Door to open for AI-risk communicators and researchers
caveats: It has no AI programme; its AI work comes through individual fellows. Much apocalypse scholarship is critical of apocalyptic rhetoric, which may sit uneasily with x-risk advocacy. Only the centre's own site was available as a source.
tag_notes: Home arts/arts_narrative: it studies apocalyptic imaginaries through literary, cultural and media studies (its director is a literary scholar). Religion is secondary because apocalyptic studies draws on religious studies and eschatology. Ring potential (E2): AI appears only in individual fellows' projects and its general framing, with no standing AI programme. Transferable method: humanities research on how apocalyptic and post-apocalyptic narratives shape public affect and action, applicable to x-risk communication. Transfer convening, not none_yet, because fellows have worked on AI. Framing catastrophic because catastrophe and world-ending are its object of study, not something it advocates about.

name: Superflux
summary: A London design studio, founded in 2009 by Anab Jain and Jon Ardern, that works in design-led foresight, experiential futures, speculative design and immersive installations for governments, foundations and companies. Its AI work runs as occasional commissions: the voice-assistant design fiction Our Friends Electric (2017), a confidential 2019 project for DeepMind on 'alternate ways of thinking about AI systems', the Ecological Intelligence Agency for the UK Policy Lab and DEFRA (2023), and Nobody Told Me Rivers Dream (Design Museum, 2025). That last piece uses sensors and language models trained on weather lore, folklore and Indigenous ecological knowledge.
why_it_matters: Experiential futures make AI scenarios felt rather than only argued. Superflux has sold this method to the UK Cabinet Office, UNDP and the UAE Government, and did a confidential 2019 project for DeepMind on alternative ways of thinking about AI systems. That is a ready method for helping decision-makers take in AI trajectories, in the way Intelligence Rising does with wargames. It also offers a non-extractive picture of what AI could be for.

key_work.title: Nobody Told Me Rivers Dream (Design Museum, More than Human)
The Craftocene, solo exhibition at Weltmuseum Wien
The Ecological Intelligence Agency (with UK Policy Lab and DEFRA)
Our Friends Electric (voice-AI design fiction)

funding: Commissioned work for clients including the UK Cabinet Office, UNDP, the UAE Government, Google AI, DeepMind, Samsung, Sony and IKEA (Ingka Group); EU Horizon 2020 grant (2020); Rivers Dream supported by the Joseph Rowntree Foundation (2025).
status_evidence: Mar-Aug 2026: The Craftocene solo exhibition at Weltmuseum Wien, including the 2025 AI work Nobody Told Me Rivers Dream.
engage: Commissions and collaborations through the studio (Somerset House Studios, London); no open calls found
caveats: AI is one theme among many (climate, care, multispecies futures). Its AI-lab work (DeepMind 2019, Google AI 2020) is confidential or undisclosed. No safety framing. Independent coverage checked in this session was thin.
tag_notes: Home: Arts. Its AI outputs are speculative-design and art installations (Rivers Dream, Our Friends Electric), so the sub-tradition is arts_creative rather than futures (D). Ring: kept at potential (E2). In 2024-26 its only AI output is one artwork (2025, re-shown in 2026), with no standing AI programme. Transferable method: experiential futures and design-led foresight that let decision-makers live inside AI scenarios, already sold to DeepMind, the Cabinet Office and UNDP. Transfer: convening, because exhibitions bring museum and design publics into the AI conversation; it has done some AI work, so none_yet does not apply (J6).

name: Te Hiku Media (Te Reo Irirangi o Te Hiku o Te Ika)
summary: A charitable Māori media organisation in Kaitaia, collectively owned by the five Far North iwi (Ngāti Kuri, Te Aupouri, Ngai Takoto, Te Rārawa and Ngāti Kahu). It runs radio, television and online news for te reo Māori revitalisation. Its technology arm built te reo Māori speech recognition from community-recorded speech, the Papa Reo language platform and the Kaituhi transcription tool. It also wrote the Kaitiakitanga License, which restricts use of its data to those who respect Māori values and share benefits with the community.
why_it_matters: It is a working case of community-governed training data and models: consent-based collection, a stewardship licence, and refusal to hand language data to Big Tech platforms. That is a concrete template for data governance and benefit-sharing which mainstream AI safety and governance rarely look at.

key_work.title: Te reo Māori speech recognition (Papa Reo)
Kaitiakitanga License and practical guide to creating a stewardship licence
Kaituhi transcription tool (find-and-replace release)

funding: Iwi radio is funded largely through Te Māngai Pāho. Te Hiku describes Papa Reo as a $13 million project to build digital capabilities for te reo Māori; the funder of that project was not confirmed in the sources checked.
status_evidence: Oct 2026: broadcaster publishing regional news daily. Jun 2025: Kaituhi transcription tool update from the tech team.
engage: Request use of Te Hiku data or tools under the Kaitiakitanga License (requests from Indigenous communities are prioritised)
caveats: Public output from the tech arm has slowed: one dated tool update in 2025, against a busier 2020-23. The Kaitiakitanga License was last updated in October 2023. The speech-recognition accuracy figures come from 2022 press coverage.
tag_notes: Home: Indigenous. Its language models and licence come from tikanga and kaitiakitanga under iwi ownership (B8), coded as in worked example 6. Ring: adjacent. Its AI programme concerns data sovereignty and language revitalisation, with no safety or 'going well' framing (E3). Transfer: protecting, because the licence and tools exist to keep te reo data under Māori control for its iwi (J4). Fractal badge: a scope-relevant model of data governance that stays rooted in one community, as the taxonomy's own example shows.

name: Old Ways, New
summary: An Indigenous-owned research, design and advisory business in Australia, founded by Professor Angie Abdilla (palawa) with the late Uncle Wayne Mukgrrngal Armytage. It runs Indigenous Protocols for AI, a research line since 2017 that draws on Indigenous knowledge systems and engineering practices to shape how machine-learning systems are governed and designed. It also runs Country Centred Design workshops, AI advisory work for government and art and film projects. Abdilla co-authored the 2020 Indigenous Protocol and AI position paper, and the business is listed as a civil-society reviewer of the International AI Safety Report in 2025 and 2026.
why_it_matters: It is one of very few Indigenous-led organisations inside the AI safety conversation: it reviews the International AI Safety Report and frames Indigenous protocols as 'key to safe and trustworthy AI systems'. Its kinship- and Country-based design methods offer a different source of alignment norms.

key_work.title: Indigenous Protocol and Artificial Intelligence Position Paper (co-author)
Envisioning Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander AI Futures (communiqué with Barrowcliffe, Hutchinson et al.)
Civil-society reviewer, International AI Safety Report
Meditation on Country, in Data Dreams: Art and AI, Museum of Contemporary Art Australia

funding: Fees for workshops, advisory and commissioned cultural projects; no grant funders identified.
status_evidence: Feb 2026: listed as a civil-society reviewer in the International AI Safety Report 2026, and 'Meditation on Country - AI and Art' news item on its site.
engage: Book an Indigenous Protocols for AI or Country Centred Design workshop (oldwaysnew.com/workshops)
caveats: It is essentially one person's practice, and its advisory roles (Services Australia board, International AI Safety Report panel) are Abdilla's. The founding year is not stated; the site says 'almost 10 years', which suggests about 2016. The edited book Indigenous Protocols for AI is listed as forthcoming.
tag_notes: Home: Indigenous. Its AI protocols come from Aboriginal knowledge systems and Indigenous data sovereignty (B8); Arts is secondary for its film and Country Centred Design practice. Ring: changed from adjacent to bridge (E3). Its own pages frame the programme around safety ('key to safe and trustworthy AI systems', 'encoding trustworthiness and safety'), and it is a listed reviewer of the International AI Safety Report in both 2025 and 2026, so the safety work is sustained. Transfer: into_institutions. Its outputs are protocols, workshops and government advisory rather than trained models, despite the language of embedding protocols in ML (J3). Full-spectrum badge: practice-based art and film research alongside technical ML workshops, as method.

name: Global Indigenous Data Alliance (GIDA)
summary: An international alliance of national Indigenous data sovereignty networks, formed at a July 2019 workshop in Oñati, Spain, convened by Maggie Walter and Desi Rodriguez-Lonebear. It publishes and promotes the CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance, supported the IEEE 2890-2025 standard on recording the provenance of Indigenous Peoples' data (published November 2025), and runs the Global Indigenous Data Sovereignty Conference. In February 2026 it convened an Indigenous data sovereignty and AI workshop in Texcoco, Mexico, which produced a communiqué applying Indigenous data rights to AI development and use.
why_it_matters: The CARE Principles and the IEEE provenance standard are ready-made instruments for collective consent and benefit-sharing over training data, an area where AI governance has little to offer. The 2026 communiqué states Indigenous Peoples' terms for AI directly to governments and developers.

key_work.title: CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance
IEEE 2890-2025 Recommended Practice for Provenance of Indigenous Peoples' Data
Indigenous Data Sovereignty and Artificial Intelligence Communiqué (Texcoco workshop)
Global Indigenous Data Sovereignty Conference

people: Maggie Walter (co-convenor of the founding workshop)
Desi Rodriguez-Lonebear (co-convenor of the founding workshop)
funding: The 2026 IDSov and AI workshop was funded by the Catalyst Fund, the 11th Hour Project and the Tauhokohoko project; no core budget found.
status_evidence: Feb 2026: IDSov and AI workshop at COLPOS, Texcoco, Mexico, and AI communiqué published.
engage: Global Indigenous Data Sovereignty Conference (2025 edition)
Newsletter sign-up on gida-global.org
IEEE 2890-2025 standard available free with registration
caveats: The CARE Principles were drafted by the Research Data Alliance's International Indigenous Data Sovereignty Interest Group and released through GIDA. Current leadership is not named on the site.
tag_notes: Home: Indigenous, the taxonomy's own B8 example: Indigenous-led data sovereignty is its core contribution. Ring: adjacent. AI is now a standing strand (the 2026 workshop and communiqué), framed around harms and rights rather than safety (E3). Transfer: into_institutions. Its main products, the CARE Principles and the IEEE 2890 standard, are governance instruments meant for governments, universities and AI developers to apply; this edges out protecting under J3 before J4.

name: Te Mana Raraunga – Māori Data Sovereignty Network
summary: A volunteer network of Māori researchers and data practitioners, founded in 2015 and run by a core working group (Te Pokapū), with about 800 people on its mailing list. It advocates for Māori rights in data through public statements, submissions on legislation and virtual wānanga (gatherings). Its algorithm and AI work includes the Principles of Māori Algorithmic Sovereignty from the Tikanga in Technology team, a 2020 study of Māori trust in automated decision-making for the Digital Council, a 2021 call for NZ Police to open up its facial-recognition use, and presentations from the 2022 Māori AI Wānanga.
why_it_matters: It shows a people claiming governance rights over algorithms trained on or acting on them, and gives principles and a submission practice to match. AI governance usually treats affected communities as stakeholders to consult, not as rights-holders.

key_work.title: Māori algorithmic sovereignty: idea, principles, and use (Brown, Wilson, West et al.)
Māori perspectives on trust and automated decision-making (for the Digital Council)
Statement calling on NZ Police to open its black box on facial recognition
Submission on the Data and Statistics Amendment Bill

people: Kiri West (Te Pae Anamata, core working group)
Daniel Wilson (Te Pae Anamata; University of Auckland computer science)
funding: Volunteer-run; no funders identified.
status_evidence: Apr 2026: submission on the Data and Statistics Amendment Bill. Feb 2026: participant in GIDA's IDSov and AI workshop.
engage: Join the network (open to Māori and iwi data users, researchers, policymakers and others who share its charter)
Seasonal pānui (newsletter)
caveats: Most of its AI-specific material dates from 2020-23. Recent public work centres on census and statistics policy. The algorithmic sovereignty principles came from the separately funded Tikanga in Technology project.
tag_notes: Home: Indigenous. Its principles extend Māori data sovereignty, grounded in tikanga, to algorithms (B8). Ring: kept at adjacent (E). AI work is a continuing line (2023 principles paper, 2026 GIDA AI workshop) with no safety framing, though 2024-26 AI output is thin. Transfer: protecting. Its submissions and statements defend Māori rights and interests in data against state and corporate use (J4).

name: Masakhane (Masakhane Research Foundation and Masakhane African Languages Hub)
summary: A grassroots, pan-African natural language processing community, started in 2019, with over 1,000 participants in about 30 countries. It works on open datasets, models and benchmarks for African languages (machine translation, named-entity recognition, sentiment, question answering), and its stated values include Ubuntu, African-centricity, data sovereignty and participatory research. The Masakhane African Languages Hub, set up in July 2025 under the Masakhane Research Foundation and directed by Chenai Chair, funds community-led data and model projects through rounds of calls for proposals. In February 2026 the Hub became a member of the Global South Network for Trustworthy AI.
why_it_matters: Safeguards and evaluations are weakest in low-resource languages, and Masakhane holds the datasets, benchmarks and community to close that gap. Its open, participatory way of working is a live example of pluralistic, community-led AI development.

key_work.title: Participatory Research for Low-resourced Machine Translation: A Case Study in African Languages
MasakhaNER: Named Entity Recognition for African Languages
Masakhane African Languages Hub launched, with grant calls (Cycle 2 in Jan 2026)
Member of the Global South Network for Trustworthy AI (multilingual safety benchmarks)

people: Chenai Chair (Director, Masakhane African Languages Hub)
Kathleen Siminyu (Chair of the board, Masakhane Research Foundation)
funding: Hub funders listed as the UK FCDO, Canada's IDRC and the Gates Foundation (2025-26). Earlier dataset work was funded by the Lacuna Fund and GIZ, among others.
status_evidence: Feb 2026: Hub joins the Global South Network for Trustworthy AI at the India AI Impact Summit. Jan 2026: second round of grant calls opened.
engage: Join the open community (Slack, Google Groups, weekly meetings; adherence to the Code of Conduct is the only requirement)
Masakhane African Languages Hub calls for proposals (Cycle 2 webinar 14 Jan 2026)
Hub staff openings (e.g. Finance and Grants Officer, Kenya)
caveats: Its core work is NLP capability for African languages rather than safety. The safety link runs through multilingual evaluation and its GSNTA membership. The main masakhane.io pages are only partly current, and Hub details come from hub.masakhane.io.
tag_notes: Home: Indigenous and decolonial. ML is not a sector (H2), so it is placed by what it imports: Ubuntu-guided, African-centric participatory research ('Decolonise Science'), which is a taxonomy example for this home. ind_decolonial was chosen over ind_indigenous because it is a pan-African community, not an Indigenous peoples' movement; this is borderline. Ring: adjacent. It has a sustained AI programme on under-representation of African languages, but its own framing is not safety; GSNTA membership is a step towards bridge (E3). Transfer: into_model. Its datasets, models and benchmarks change AI systems directly (J1). Assurance is paired with justice for its benchmark work (F).

name: Ethics of AI Research Group, Centre for AI Research (CAIR), University of Pretoria
summary: The AI ethics node of South Africa's Centre for AI Research (CAIR), a multi-university network supported by the Department of Science and Innovation and the CSIR. The group sits in the University of Pretoria's Department of Philosophy and is coordinated by Emma Ruttkamp-Bloem, who chaired the UNESCO expert group that drafted the 2021 Recommendation on the Ethics of AI. Its listed topics include machine ethics, artificial moral agency, robot rights, autonomous weapons, data ethics and culturally sensitive AI policy for Africa. It ran the CAIR/UP AI for Society symposium series from 2018 to 2020.
why_it_matters: It brings African relational ethics and epistemic- and data-justice arguments into global AI governance. Through its coordinator it reached the UNESCO Recommendation, a perspective largely missing from Northern AI-safety policy work.

key_work.title: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI (drafting group chaired by Ruttkamp-Bloem)
CAIR/UP AI for Society Symposium series (5th edition)
Relationality and Data Justice for Trustworthy AI Practices in Africa
Africa leading the global effort for AI that works for all (Nature Africa)

people: Emma Ruttkamp-Bloem (group coordinator; head of the Department of Philosophy, University of Pretoria)
funding: CAIR is supported by South Africa's Department of Science and Innovation (DSI) and the CSIR; no group-specific budget found.
status_evidence: The group's own pages show no activity after 2022. Its coordinator co-authored a 2026 Delphi study on prioritising AI risks and a 2025 Nature Africa commentary.
engage: Postgraduate supervision in AI ethics through the University of Pretoria Department of Philosophy (per the coordinator's CAIR profile)
caveats: The group's web presence is stale: the last listed event is from 2020, the last publication from 2022, and only the coordinator is listed as a member. Recent output found is the coordinator's own, so it is unclear whether the group operates as a unit in 2026.
tag_notes: Home: Philosophy. Its outputs are ethical and philosophy-of-technology arguments (artificial moral agency, relational and data justice), and the African tradition places it in phil_technology (D). Ring: kept at adjacent (E). The work concerns ethics, dignity and justice rather than safety; the coordinator's 2026 AI-risk Delphi co-authorship is too light to move it. Transfer: into_institutions, through the coordinator's leading role in the UNESCO Recommendation, a governance instrument (J3). Status: unverified, because the group's site has lapsed while its coordinator stays active.

name: American Law Institute (ALI): Principles of the Law, Civil Liability for Artificial Intelligence
summary: A Principles of the Law project of the American Law Institute, the Philadelphia-based body of elected judges, lawyers and law professors (founded 1923) whose Restatements and Principles are widely cited by US courts. ALI's Council approved it in October 2024 to set out principles, grounded in existing common-law tort doctrine, for assigning responsibility when AI systems cause physical harm (bodily injury and property damage). Reporter Mark Geistfeld (NYU) and Associate Reporter Ketan Ramakrishnan (Yale) work with nearly 60 advisers, including counsel from OpenAI, Google, Apple, Amazon and Anthropic, and a Members Consultative Group of over 400.
why_it_matters: Tort liability is one of the few existing levers that puts the cost of AI risk on developers without new legislation, and an ALI text could become the default reference for US courts deciding who pays when AI causes physical harm. The associate reporter writes on negligence liability for frontier foundation models and has co-authored with Institute for Law & AI researchers, so it is an obvious venue for AI-safety legal scholars.

key_work.title: ALI launches Principles of the Law, Civil Liability for Artificial Intelligence
Project overview on The ALI Adviser (physical-harm scope, supply-chain allocation of responsibility)
Ketan Ramakrishnan, 'Tort Law at the Frontier of Artificial Intelligence' (Yale Journal on Regulation, forthcoming)

people: Mark Geistfeld (Reporter, NYU School of Law)
Ketan Ramakrishnan (Associate Reporter, Yale Law School)
funding: ALI is a 501(c)(3) supported by members and donations (annual fund); no project-specific funding disclosed.
status_evidence: Jun 2026: The ALI Adviser published Associate Reporter Ketan Ramakrishnan's 'Tort Law at the Frontier of Artificial Intelligence'; Mar 2026 project overview post; project listed as ongoing on ali.org.
engage: Participation is limited to ALI members (membership is by election), who can join the project's Members Consultative Group
The ALI Adviser blog publishes project-related scholarship, open to read
caveats: Drafts are visible only to ALI members and project participants, so the content of the emerging principles could not be checked, and no completion date is published. Scope is limited to physical harm; copyright, defamation and privacy are left to other ALI projects. Its advisers include counsel from major AI developers, so industry views are built into the consensus process. ALI Principles are not binding, though courts often follow them.
tag_notes: Home law (H1: common-law tort doctrine is its method), sub law_legal. Ring adjacent kept (E3): a standing project on liability for AI-caused physical harm, framed around tort responsibility rather than catastrophic risk or alignment, though the associate reporter's frontier-model negligence work and LawAI co-authorship put it close to bridge. Transfer into_institutions (J3): the output is a liability framework for courts and regulators. Problem justice only, because the assurance boundary sends liability to Rights. Role policy before standards because Principles are written for courts and legislatures; convene for the consensus process joining judges, academics and industry counsel. Org type programme (A1: a unit inside ALI).

name: World Academy of Art and Science (WAAS)
summary: An academy of more than 560 elected fellows from over 90 countries, founded in 1960 by figures including Robert Oppenheimer, Bertrand Russell and Joseph Needham. It is registered in Napa, California, and holds UN ECOSOC consultative status. Its AI work runs mainly through EXTRA (Existential Threats and Risks to All), a working group set up in 2022 that keeps a directory of several hundred existential-risk reports, issues a monthly newsletter and co-hosts symposia, treating AI and artificial superintelligence alongside climate, nuclear, pandemic and ecological threats as parts of one polycrisis. It also lists an AI Governance project under its 'Technology as Force for Good' programme.
why_it_matters: EXTRA reads AI risk as one strand of a systemic polycrisis rather than in isolation, and convenes voices outside the Anglophone AI-safety community, for example an October 2026 Beijing symposium on existential-risk governance with the Centre for China and Globalisation. It is a ready-made network of senior scholars for the 'AI within the metacrisis' framing int/a holds, though its output is mostly curation and convening rather than original research.

key_work.title: EXTRA InfoHub, directory of existential-risk reports and monthly eNewsletter (e.g. Oct 2025 issue 'Artificial Intelligence: Between Threat and Promise')
Symposium 'Synthetic Societies: Human Vulnerability and Systemic Fragility in a Context of Rising Algorithmic Power' (with CIRET)
Symposium 'Global Existential Risk Governance for Human Survival: Chinese Perspectives on Enhancing Cooperation' (with CCG, Beijing, 15 Oct 2026)
AI Governance project (Technology as Force for Good programme)

people: Thomas Reuter (Trustee; Chair of EXTRA; anthropologist, University of Melbourne)
Kiriti Prasad Choudhury (EXTRA AI, IT and data analytics specialist)
funding: 501(c)(3) public charity supported by member contributions and donations; EXTRA receives some central WAAS funding and administrative support. No budget figures found.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: EXTRA session 'Navigating Existential Risk in an Age of Global Turbulence' at the WAAS@66 conference and September newsletter; symposium with CCG in Beijing scheduled for 15 Oct 2026.
engage: EXTRA monthly eNewsletter (free subscription)
Live-streamed EXTRA symposia and WAAS webinars, e.g. the hybrid Beijing symposium on existential-risk governance, 15 Oct 2026
Events can be submitted to EXTRA's events listing
Fellowship is by nomination and election
caveats: AI is one topic among many, and the output is mainly curation (report directory, newsletter) and convening rather than original AI research. The ring was raised from the roster's adjacent to bridge on the strength of EXTRA; the separate 'AI Governance' project page lists only a few events. The academy is registered in Napa but its leadership and operations are spread across India, Europe and elsewhere. Its October 2026 partner, the Centre for China and Globalisation, was founded by a former State Council counsellor.
tag_notes: Home life (B7: its AI output, EXTRA, is a systems diagnosis that treats existential risks as emergent properties of an interconnected polycrisis), sub life_cybernetics. Secondaries: arts (foresight; EXTRA's team includes futurist Michael Marien, and speakers include Jerome Glenn of the Millennium Project) and peace (its human-security and global-governance programmes). The provisional home, philosophy, was not used: transdisciplinary humanism is WAAS's identity but not the method of its AI output (H5). Ring changed from adjacent to bridge (E3): EXTRA has been a standing working group since 2022 with recurring AI and superintelligence coverage framed as existential threat (Oct 2025 newsletter on AI, Jul 2026 Synthetic Societies symposium, Oct 2026 event naming artificial superintelligence). Transfer convening (J5): it informs and convenes its fellows and the public through its newsletter and symposia. Org type membership (I: a learned academy of elected fellows). Badge recoupling: it explicitly places AI inside a systemic polycrisis (Apr 2026 newsletter 'More than only AI'). Hub online for its live-streamed symposia. WAAS also runs an 'Integral Knowledge' programme, but nothing shows it feeds the AI work.

name: UNI Global Union
summary: The global union federation for service-sector workers, formed in 2000 from four earlier federations and based in Nyon, Switzerland, with affiliated unions representing about 20 million workers in 150 countries. On AI it presses employers to negotiate over deployment, from Davos to sectoral agreements such as the 2024 joint AI declaration between its European region, UNI Europa, and the European banking employers. In April 2025 in Nairobi it launched the Global Trade Union Alliance of Content Moderators, which in June 2025 published eight mental-health protocols for moderation work aimed at TikTok, Meta, Alphabet and OpenAI. It also backs affiliates' AI disputes, such as the July 2025 strike by TikTok moderators in Berlin being replaced by AI and Blizzard workers' first contract (September 2026), which requires the company to bargain over AI.
why_it_matters: It organises the human layer of the AI supply chain: content moderators, data labellers and outsourced BPO workers, whose conditions shape the quality of the data that filters and trains models. The AI-safety field rarely looks at this part of the pipeline. Its global framework agreements with multinationals are a tested template for enforceable supply-chain standards.

key_work.title: Launch of the Global Trade Union Alliance of Content Moderators (Nairobi)
Mental Health Protocols for content moderators and the report 'The People Behind the Screens'
'Labour behind AI' side event at the UN Forum on Business and Human Rights; Protocol for Safe Content Moderation
Blizzard workers ratify first union contract requiring bargaining over AI

funding: Funded by its affiliated unions; no figures found.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: reported Blizzard workers' first contract with AI bargaining (9 Sep) and a meeting of outsourcing workers in Stockholm 'to shape the rules on AI' (18 Sep).
engage: Staff vacancies posted at uniglobalunion.org/about/jobs (none open when checked)
Workers join through affiliated national unions; moderators' unions through the Global Trade Union Alliance of Content Moderators
caveats: AI is one strand of a broad service-sector labour agenda, and it does not engage with frontier or catastrophic AI risk. Much of the AI-related action (strikes, organising) is carried out by affiliates such as ver.di and CWA, with UNI coordinating and amplifying.
tag_notes: Home economics (H3: unions go to Economics), sub econ_labour. Ring adjacent kept (E3): sustained AI work (content-moderator alliance, bargaining over AI, the UN BHR forum) with no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing. Transfer protecting (J4): its protocols and agreements exist to defend the workers it represents. Problems: power (labour as counter-power across sectors), then people (the moderation and data-labelling workforce behind AI). Quadrant I second for its focus on moderators' mental health. Org type membership (I: a federation of unions).

name: SAG-AFTRA (Screen Actors Guild-American Federation of Television and Radio Artists)
summary: The US union of about 160,000 actors, broadcasters, recording artists and other media professionals, formed in 2012 by the merger of SAG and AFTRA, with national offices in Los Angeles and New York. Its AI framework rests on consent, compensation and control over performances. The 2023 TV/Theatrical contract set consent and pay rules for digital replicas, and the 2026 agreement, ratified on 4 June 2026 by 91.42%, adds rules to keep 'synthetic performers' the exception. It also works on AI law: its president testified before a House Judiciary subcommittee in July 2026, it backs the federal NO FAKES Act, and it publicised a California law, in force by September 2026, requiring disclosure of AI-generated performances.
why_it_matters: It has turned public concern about AI copying and replacing people into binding contract terms on consent and likeness, a working model of a membership body governing AI use from the bottom up. Its digital-replica rules are an early template for protecting human identity and presence as generative models improve.

key_work.title: 2026 TV/Theatrical Agreement, with new restrictions on synthetic performers

name: AFL-CIO Tech Institute and Workers First Initiative on AI
summary: The AFL-CIO, the US federation of 65 unions representing about 15 million workers, set up its Tech Institute in 2021 to work on technology in the workplace. In October 2025 the federation launched the 'Workers First Initiative on AI', with the report 'Artificial Intelligence: Principles to Protect Workers', an education and mobilisation programme and a state-level AI task force. In April 2026 President Liz Shuler gave a National Press Club speech on AI, and the Tech Institute sent Congress a letter on AI and workers. The Tech Institute, led by former NLRB chair Lauren McFerran with about a dozen staff, publishes research (for example on electronic shelf labels and grocery wages) and the 'Workers Tech Watch' newsletter.
why_it_matters: It is the largest US labour coalition arguing that tech firms cannot be trusted to self-regulate AI, and it brings electoral and state-legislative reach that AI-governance advocates lack. It shows mass-membership organisations entering AI politics, though its frame is workplace harms and economic power, not frontier risk.

name: European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC)
summary: The European-level trade union confederation, founded in 1973 and based in Brussels, representing about 45 million members through 94 national confederations in 42 countries plus 10 European federations. On AI it campaigns for a dedicated EU directive on algorithmic management and AI at work (circulars in October and December 2025), adopted the resolution 'Artificial Intelligence for Workers, Not Just for Profit' in March 2025, and opposes parts of the AI and Digital Omnibus that it says weaken worker safety and data protection (statements in May and September 2026). It works with the European Trade Union Institute (ETUI), which publishes research on AI and labour.
why_it_matters: It is the main worker-side voice in EU AI law, defending the 'human in control' and precautionary principles as the AI Act is implemented and simplified, which is where much binding AI governance is being decided. Its push for a workplace AI directive is a live test of whether AI rules in Europe are extended or rolled back.

name: Alphabet Workers Union-CWA Local 9009 (AWU-CWA)
summary: A union of Alphabet workers in the US and Canada, organised as Local 9009 of the Communications Workers of America. It went public in January 2021, is open to full-time staff, temps, vendors and contractors, and has about 1,400 members according to press reports. It set up a Committee on Artificial Intelligence in summer 2024, has organised Google's contracted AI raters (through Appen and, from 2025, GlobalLogic) who evaluate Gemini and AI Overviews, and in September 2025 co-published 'Ghost Workers in the Machine', a survey of US AI data workers, with TechEquity. Its elected board has opposed Google's December 2025 Gemini deal with the US Department of War and backed Anthropic's February 2026 refusal to drop safety guardrails for the Pentagon.
why_it_matters: It is organised labour inside the parent company of a frontier AI lab (Google DeepMind) and among the raters who produce human-feedback data. That gives workers a collective channel on military uses of AI and on how alignment data is produced, and makes it one of the few existing structures for worker voice and conscience inside AI developers.

Its positions on military AI come from its elected board and do not speak for all Alphabet staff. The membership figure comes from press reports, not the union's own site.

Problems: people (worker voice in labs and the rater workforce), power, then security (recurring opposition to military AI contracts). Engagement community, though only Alphabet workers, contractors included, in the US and Canada can join.

name: Data Labelers Association (DLA)
summary: A Nairobi-based association of data labellers, annotators and content moderators. It was founded and is run by data workers, and launched officially on 13 February 2025. It reports 878+ members and a wider network of 5,000+, and runs job matching (DLA Connect), mental-health support (DLA Health), training (DLA Academy), and advocacy and collective bargaining (DLA Voice). In 2025-26 it held stakeholder convenings in Nairobi. In September 2026 it published findings from structured interviews with Kenyan labellers and moderators on pay, hours, mental-health support and job security.
why_it_matters: Much of the training, RLHF and content-moderation data behind frontier models is produced by workers like DLA's members, including a lot of the safety-relevant labelling. DLA gives that workforce a standing, worker-run body that AI-safety organisations and labs could consult about the conditions under which safety data is made.

name: Tech Workers Coalition (TWC)
summary: An all-volunteer, worker-led coalition of tech workers, labour organisers and allies. It began in the San Francisco Bay Area in 2014 and organises for worker power through rank-and-file self-organisation and education. It has active chapters in about ten North American cities and in Berlin (since 2019), Italy and the Netherlands. In December 2025 it co-launched workersdecide.tech, a set of organising resources against workplace AI mandates, with DAIR, Turkopticon, the Times Tech Guild and others. It runs the Circuit Breakers tech-labour conference (New York, 17-18 October 2026).
why_it_matters: It is one of the few structures through which rank-and-file tech workers, including some at AI firms, organise across employers. Worker leverage over how AI is deployed, and possibly over how it is built, is a lever the AI-safety field rarely uses. Its Berlin chapter is within reach of int/a's Berlin community.

name: United Tech and Allied Workers (UTAW), with Unite the Union: Google DeepMind recognition campaign
summary: UTAW is the UK's tech workers' union, a national branch of the Communication Workers Union (CWU), formed in 2020 by activists from the London Tech Workers Coalition. On 4 May 2026, its members at Google DeepMind UK, together with Unite members, asked Google for voluntary union recognition. Google refused but agreed to talks through ACAS, saying bargaining should cover only pay, holidays and hours. The members' demands cover AI safety and Google's AI principles, an end to what they call unethical military contracts, and guarantees against AI-led redundancies. Membership has passed the 10% threshold for a statutory recognition claim. On 2 October 2026 UTAW published an AI Workers' Inquiry on how generative AI is changing tech work.
why_it_matters: It was widely reported as the first union drive at a frontier AI lab. A recognised union could give lab staff a legally backed collective channel to bargain over safety and use policies, protect people who raise concerns, and staff safety committees on the model of health-and-safety representatives.

name: International Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War (IPPNW): AI and nuclear weapons work
summary: A federation of national medical organisations in 56 countries campaigning to abolish nuclear weapons. It was founded by US and Soviet physicians in 1980 and won the 1985 Nobel Peace Prize. In October 2025, at its 24th World Congress in Nagasaki, it set up a working group on AI and the nuclear threat. Its position is that the nine nuclear-armed states must keep AI out of nuclear command and control and that humans must stay in control. It co-hosted the January 2025 webinar 'Autonomous Armageddon' with ICAN and Pugwash, made a statement to the UN Secretary-General on autonomous weapons, and in July 2026 was a partner in the Global Nobel Laureate Summit on AI and Nuclear Weapons at Castel Gandolfo, which produced the Rome Declaration.
why_it_matters: It applies four decades of medical campaigning on nuclear catastrophe to AI in nuclear command and control, and ties AI-risk concerns to the established disarmament coalition (ICAN, Pugwash). It is also a working example of a professional body using clinicians' standing to campaign on an extinction-level risk.

IPPNW also argues that nuclear power, including small modular reactors, cannot sustainably power AI expansion, a position not everyone concerned about AI risk shares.

name: Society for Risk Analysis (SRA): 'AI for Risk Analysis and the Risks of AI' special issue
summary: The international learned society for risk analysis, founded in 1980 and based in Herndon, Virginia. It publishes the journal Risk Analysis and runs annual meetings, specialty groups (including Security and Defense) and regional sections. Its journal ran a two-part special issue, 'Artificial Intelligence for Risk Analysis and the Risks of AI', edited by Vicki Bier, Emanuele Borgonovo, Tony Cox and Cynthia Rudin (Part 1 in March 2025, vol. 45 no. 4; second volume in February 2026, vol. 46 no. 3). Most papers apply AI within risk assessment, but the issue also covers reliability assessment of machine learning in safety-critical systems and includes Seth Baum's risk assessment of takeover catastrophe from large language models.
why_it_matters: Risk analysis has mature methods that frontier-AI risk modelling often rebuilds: probabilistic risk assessment, expert elicitation, decision-making under deep uncertainty and risk communication. The special issue gives AI-risk researchers an established venue and reviewer pool in that field.

key_work.title: Artificial intelligence for risk analysis and the risks of artificial intelligence: Part 1 (Risk Analysis 45(4))

Tony Cox (special-issue co-editor; University of Colorado Denver)

Annual meeting, specialty groups (e.g. Security and Defense) and regional organisations such as SRA-Europe
caveats: SRA's AI engagement is concentrated in its journal. Most special-issue papers apply AI to risk analysis rather than assess risks from advanced AI; only Baum's paper addresses catastrophic AI risk. Its site shows no AI specialty group or standing AI programme, and its AI webinars date from 2021 and 2023. The entry sits on the line between bridge and potential.

MISFIT: its framing is neutral risk-analytic (reliability, cyber, takeover); present_harms was chosen as the closest fit, but no framing key fits well.

name: SAE G-34 / EUROCAE WG-114: Artificial Intelligence in Aviation
summary: A joint standards committee of SAE International's G-34 and EUROCAE's WG-114 that writes guidance for developing and certifying aeronautical systems that use machine learning. It has published a statement of concerns (EUROCAE ER-022, 2020; SAE AIR6988, 2021) and a taxonomy (ER-027 / AIR6987, 2024). Its main deliverable, the process standard ED-324 / ARP6983, was finalised in draft at a joint meeting at EUROCONTROL in Brussels in mid-2025 and is due for publication by the end of 2026. Reports on human factors, information security, reinforcement-learning gaps and use cases are due in 2026-27.
why_it_matters: Aviation's design-assurance tradition (DO-178C, assurance levels, statements of concerns) has produced one of the most developed attempts to certify learned systems for life-critical use. Its concepts and process standard bear directly on frontier-AI safety cases, yet they are little known in the AI-safety community.

ER-027 / AIR6987: AI in Aeronautical Safety-Related Systems, Taxonomy

name: UL Standards & Engagement (ULSE): UL 4600
summary: UL Standards & Engagement is the nonprofit standards-development and advocacy organisation of the UL enterprise. It was set up as a separate nonprofit in 2022 and is based in Evanston, Illinois; it has developed more than 1,700 standards and documents and has about 4,000 volunteers. It publishes UL 4600, the Standard for Safety for Evaluation of Autonomous Products, which requires manufacturers to argue safety through structured safety cases backed by evidence. UL 4600 was first published in 2020 and updated in 2023 with safety-case guidance for autonomous trucking. Its Software-Enabled Products, Autonomy and Robotics (SEPAR) programme covers AI-based products, service robots and autonomous vehicles. In July 2026 it argued for safety-case requirements in proposed US federal autonomous-trucking legislation.
why_it_matters: UL 4600 is a published, maintained standard built on structured safety cases and field evidence. That is the structure the UK AI Security Institute and labs now propose for frontier-AI safety cases. ULSE also brings long experience of consensus standards-making and of getting standards written into state law.

key_work.title: UL 4600, Standard for Safety for Evaluation of Autonomous Products (first edition 2020; updated 2023 for autonomous trucking)
Software-Enabled Products, Autonomy and Robotics (SEPAR) standards portfolio, covering AI-based products
'The Safety Questions All Autonomous Truck Companies Need to Answer Before Deployment' (UL 4600 and the BUILD America 250 Act)

funding: Part of the nonprofit UL enterprise. In February 2022 Underwriters Laboratories committed $1.8 billion to safety science, including launching ULSE as a second nonprofit for standards and advocacy.
status_evidence: 8 Jul 2026: published UL 4600 guidance for autonomous trucking tied to the BUILD America 250 Act; 27 Jan 2026: CES 2026 takeaways on AI safety gaps and standards needs
engage: Join a standards technical committee or register as a stakeholder (ulse.org/standards/get-involved-in-a-technical-committee/)

caveats: ULSE is distinct from UL Solutions (the for-profit testing and certification company) and from UL Research Institutes, whose Digital Safety Research Institute is a separate roster entry. UL 4600 covers autonomous products such as vehicles, not general-purpose or frontier AI, and ULSE publishes no frontier-AI standard. Most of its work is outside AI (batteries, fire, home and energy safety). The UL lineage dates to 1894, but the ULSE name and structure date from 2022. The ring was changed from the roster's potential to bridge (see tag notes). The staff-size estimate is inferred, not published.
tag_notes: Home: a product-safety standards body using safety-case methodology, so Safety/safety engineering. Ring changed from potential to bridge (E3): it runs a standing SEPAR programme covering AI-based and autonomous products and maintains UL 4600, which it actively promoted in 2026, all framed explicitly as safety. That is comparable to York CfAA and SAE G-34, not 'light or absent' AI engagement. Transfer: a safety-case standard and policy advocacy for governing autonomous systems, so into_institutions (J3). MISFIT: its framing is accident prevention (it cites AV crash rates); present_harms is the closest key.
