name: INCOSE Artificial Intelligence Systems Working Group
summary: A working group of the International Council on Systems Engineering (INCOSE), set up in 2019 as an outcome of INCOSE's Future of Systems Engineering (FuSE) initiative. It has two strands: applying AI to the engineering of systems ('AI for SE') and developing the systems-engineering methods needed for systems with embedded AI ('SE for AI'). Its stated research objectives include human-AI collaboration, evaluating the safety and security of AI systems, and standards and benchmarks. It is linked to the annual AI4SE & SE4AI workshop held with the Systems Engineering Research Center (SERC).
why_it_matters: Systems engineering treats AI as one component of a larger sociotechnical system, and it brings requirements traceability, verification and validation, and lifecycle assurance, which model-centred alignment work largely lacks. The group is a ready entry point into a large professional community that already engineers safety-critical systems.

key_work.title: Working group established from INCOSE's Future of Systems Engineering (FuSE) initiative
AI4SE & SE4AI Research and Application Workshop series (with SERC; seventh edition 22-23 Sep 2026)
Survey of LLM Applications for Systems Engineering (presentation by the WG chair)

people: Ali K. Raz (Chair; George Mason University)
funding: No separate budget found. It is volunteer-run inside INCOSE, a member-funded not-for-profit professional society.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: SERC's seventh AI4SE & SE4AI workshop (22-23 Sep), a series INCOSE documents tie to the WG; 2026: Ramakrishnan Raman listed as WG co-chair in the INCOSE India MBSE Summit 2026 programme; Sep 2026: SwissED 2026 keynote cites the WG's response to agentic AI.
engage: Take part through INCOSE membership; the WG page links to membership, and enquiries go to AI@incose.net
Attend the annual AI4SE & SE4AI workshop with SERC (autumn, Washington DC area)
INCOSE International Workshop and Symposium sessions
caveats: Most visible output is AI for SE (using LLMs in engineering work) rather than the safety of AI. Evaluating the safety and security of AI systems is a stated objective, but I found no dedicated safety output. The WG page blocks scripted fetches and was read in a browser; its footer is dated 2025. Search access was limited, so the 2025-26 output list is thin.
tag_notes: Home safety (H1): its method is systems engineering and lifecycle assurance applied to AI-enabled systems. Ring changed from roster 'potential' to adjacent (E2/E3): it is a standing AI working group since 2019, so its AI engagement is not light, but the programme is framed around engineering AI systems in general, with safety as one of six objectives, so it is not bridge. Transfer convening (J5): its stated purpose is to identify and communicate AI developments to INCOSE members and establish INCOSE as a resource. MISFIT: adjacent is defined around societal effects, and this is an engineering programme; framing has no stated risk frame, and 'flourishing' is the nearest fit for its enabling, development-oriented stance.

name: The Cybernetics Society
summary: UK learned society for cybernetics, founded at King's College London in 1968 and authorised under the Friendly Societies Act 1974. It awards the MCybS and FCybS credentials and is a member of the International Federation for Systems Research. It runs monthly online 'Cybernetics Live' seminars and an annual conference: in 2026, 'The Cybernetics Conversation' at Loughborough (1-3 July) marked Stafford Beer's centenary and included an Ethics and AI track. It also publishes the open-access journal Enacting Cybernetics. Several 2025-26 seminars dealt with AI, including David Wood on anticipating the social consequences of next-generation AI (May 2026).
why_it_matters: Cybernetics has concepts for whether a regulator can control a system more complex than itself, such as Ashby's law of requisite variety, Beer's viable system model and second-order cybernetics. These bear directly on AI control and on whether institutions can oversee AI. The society's AI engagement is so far occasional, so it is an open door for a cybernetics-and-alignment strand.

key_work.title: The Cybernetics Conversation 2026 (Loughborough; Ethics and AI track; Dan Davies on the 'unaccountability machine')
Cybernetics Live: 'Anticipating the human and social consequences of next generation AI - before it's too late' (David Wood)
Cybernetics Live: 'Emergent Language and Systemic Understanding: AI-Augmented Deliberations Through a Cybernetic Lens' (Kevin Dye)
Enacting Cybernetics (open-access journal)

people: Peter Kawalek (Immediate Past President; Loughborough Business School)
funding: Member subscriptions (from £30 a year). No other funding found.
status_evidence: Oct 2026: Cybernetics Live seminar 'Ashby, Fuzzy, and Me' (Dr Steve Morlidge) scheduled for 15 Oct; Jul 2026: annual conference held at Loughborough University Business School.
engage: Cybernetics Live: monthly online seminars, free registration on Zoom; recordings on YouTube
Annual conference (2026: 1-3 July, Loughborough)
Membership open to anyone with an interest in cybernetics, from £30 a year; MCybS/FCybS credentials
Submit to Enacting Cybernetics (open-access, peer-reviewed)
caveats: AI is one topic among many, and there is no standing AI programme. The society's own framing of AI is ethics, not safety or control. Wikipedia credits Haneef Fatmi as founder and lists Kybernetes as an official journal; I did not verify the current journal arrangement.
tag_notes: Home life/life_cybernetics (H3): a learned society serving the cybernetics community. Ring potential (E2): its AI engagement is a handful of seminar talks and one conference track in 2025-26, not a standing programme. Transferable method: requisite variety and the viable system model for designing regulators and institutions capable of overseeing more complex AI systems. Transfer convening, not none_yet, because it has held AI talks for its members. Online hub: the monthly Zoom seminars are open to the public.

name: System Dynamics Society (SDS)
summary: International professional society for system dynamics, the stock-and-flow and feedback simulation of social, economic and environmental systems. It was formed in 1983 with Jay Forrester as first president. It runs the annual International System Dynamics Conference (2026: TU Delft, 20-24 July; 2027: Cleveland), publishes the System Dynamics Review, and has 21 regional chapters and 17 special interest groups. Its organised AI work is an AI in SD Education Task Force (monthly virtual meetings and a white paper on using AI in teaching). Individual conference papers model AI's effects on labour, software quality and governance.
why_it_matters: Feedback modelling, the method behind The Limits to Growth, suits AI questions that mainstream safety work rarely models dynamically: race dynamics, compute-capability-investment loops, and the gradual loss of human economic leverage. The society offers a community of modellers, a conference and a journal through which such work could be commissioned.

key_work.title: International System Dynamics Conference 2026: 'Navigating uncertainty, managing instability and crafting futures together' (TU Delft)
Using Artificial Intelligence in System Dynamics Education (white paper, AI in SD Education Task Force)
System Dynamics Review (society journal)

funding: Membership dues, conference fees, sponsorship and sales of publications and games; it also runs a 'Strengthening the Field Fund'. Amounts not found.
status_evidence: Oct 2026: blog post 'Building systems literacy from childhood to leadership' (2 Oct); Sep 2026: AI in SD Education Task Force monthly meeting; Jul 2026: conference held at TU Delft.
engage: Annual conference: 2027 in Cleveland (submissions 19 Jan-16 Mar 2027; scholarship applications by 15 Apr)
Membership, regional chapters and special interest groups
AI in SD Education Task Force: monthly virtual meetings, open application
Online course catalogue (80+ options) and webinars
caveats: No SDS group yet works on AI safety or on the dynamics of the AI transition; its AI work is mostly about AI as a tool for modelling and teaching. The presidency rotates; I did not confirm the current president.
tag_notes: Home life/life_cybernetics (H3; system dynamics is named under Cybernetics, systems & ecology): a professional society for system dynamics modellers. Ring potential (E2): its only standing AI activity is about AI in teaching, and its AI-impact work is scattered individual papers, not a programme on AI's effects or safety. Transferable method: stock-and-flow feedback simulation of AI race dynamics, investment-capability loops and labour displacement. Transfer convening: the task force brings its educators into the AI conversation. Way of knowing formal (simulation models).

name: Nuffield Council on Bioethics (NCOB)
summary: Independent UK policy and research centre that identifies, analyses and advises on ethical issues in biomedicine and health. It works through expert working groups, horizon scanning, calls for evidence and public deliberation, including a 2024 citizens' jury on assisted dying. Its AI work has been occasional: 2018 briefings on AI in healthcare, and a joint project with the Ada Lovelace Institute on AI and genomics (2023-24), whose final report advised that the NHS should not yet roll out AI-powered genomic health prediction widely. In July 2026 it launched a project on brain-computer interfaces and their convergence with AI and quantum computing.
why_it_matters: It has decades of practice in anticipatory governance of contested technologies such as genome editing and neurotechnology, using working groups, horizon scans and public deliberation. These methods could be applied to frontier AI or digital minds. Its new BCI project takes it into questions of autonomy, identity and privacy where AI meets neurotechnology.

key_work.title: Predicting: the future of health? (AI and genomics futures, with the Ada Lovelace Institute)
DNA.I. - Early findings and emerging questions on the use of AI in genomics
Neurotechnology in healthcare: brain-computer interfaces and their convergence with AI and quantum computing (project launch)
The big ethical questions for artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare

people: Martyn Pickersgill (Chair, BCI Working Group; University of Edinburgh)
funding: Jointly funded by the Nuffield Foundation, the Medical Research Council and Wellcome, on a five-year rolling basis.
status_evidence: Jul 2026: launched a project on brain-computer interfaces and their convergence with AI and quantum computing (27 Jul), with a working group and a call for evidence.
engage: Respond to calls for evidence, such as the 2026 BCI project's
Follow its annual horizon scans and blog
caveats: The roster said it had been inactive on AI since 2018. That is not right: it ran an AI and genomics project in 2023-24 and launched a BCI/AI project in 2026. AI is still not one of its standing priorities, and its work is health-focused rather than about frontier AI risk.
tag_notes: Home philosophy/phil_bioethics (B13: ethics councils go to Philosophy); secondary democracy for its citizens' juries and public dialogue methods. Ring changed from roster 'potential' to adjacent (E2/E3): a funded AI project ran into 2024 (AI and genomics futures) and a BCI/AI convergence project started in July 2026, framed around ethics and harms, not safety. Transfer into_institutions: its main purpose is ethics advice to policymakers and the NHS. Engagement: 'partner' left out because it now has AI projects, but its deliberative methods remain an outreach opportunity for frontier AI.

name: Center for Digital Narrative (CDN) and ERC project AI STORIES, University of Bergen
summary: A Norwegian Centre of Research Excellence (2023-2033) at the University of Bergen, funded by the Research Council of Norway and the university, for humanities-led research on digital narrative. Its six research groups range from electronic literature and games to computational narrative systems. It hosts AI STORIES: Narrative Archetypes for Artificial Intelligence, an ERC Advanced Grant (2024-2029) led by Jill Walker Rettberg, which studies how narrative patterns in training data shape the stories language models tell. A 2025 paper from the project found that AI-generated stories favour stability over change, and a 2026 preprint by Jessica Witte found that their emotional arcs differ from human stories, with longer endings.
why_it_matters: It studies what language models do to narrative culture: which story shapes they reproduce and how they flatten them. That bears on model character, cultural homogenisation, and work that treats stories in training data as priors for model behaviour. These are humanities methods the alignment field mostly lacks.

key_work.title: AI STORIES: Narrative Archetypes for Artificial Intelligence (ERC Advanced Grant, 2024-2029)
AI-generated stories favour stability over change (Open Research Europe)
Preprint comparing the emotional arcs of AI-generated and human stories (Jessica Witte)
Contemporary Perspectives on AI and Narrative (Open Library of Humanities collection, guest-edited by Scott Rettberg)

people: Jill Walker Rettberg (Co-Director; PI, AI STORIES)
funding: Research Council of Norway Centre of Excellence (SFF) funding for 2023-2033 (project no. 332643), plus the University of Bergen; AI STORIES is funded by an ERC Advanced Grant (2024-2029).
status_evidence: Sep 2026: CDN published the call for papers for Nordic DiGRA 2027 (29 Sep); Oct 2026: 'After Virtual Reality' symposium (19-21 Oct) and BIFF exhibition (15-21 Oct) scheduled; 2026: AI STORIES preprint on emotional arcs.
engage: PhD and postdoc vacancies listed on the CDN site
Public symposia, exhibitions and screenings in Bergen
Calls for papers (e.g., Nordic DiGRA 2027)
Off Center podcast and newsletter
caveats: AI is one strand of a broader digital-narrative centre, and AI STORIES is its most AI-specific part. The work is critical humanities and does not use an AI-safety frame. Staff numbers not found.
tag_notes: Home arts/arts_narrative (H1): narratology, literary and game studies applied to model outputs and training data. Ring adjacent (E3): AI STORIES is a sustained funded programme on AI's cultural effects, with no safety or alignment framing. Transfer convening (J5): its outputs inform scholarly and public understanding rather than changing models directly. 'Values' is secondary because the project treats training-data narratives as shaping model behaviour; framing structural because cultural homogenisation is a gradual erosion.

name: Better Images of AI
summary: A nonprofit collaboration, coordinated by the London charity We and AI and set up with BBC R&D and the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence. It commissions, curates and freely licenses images of AI to replace robots, glowing brains and other science-fiction tropes. Its image library launched in December 2021. It also publishes guides, including a guide for users and creators, a submission handbook and a playbook for making images from archives, alongside artist commissions and a blog.
why_it_matters: Stock imagery shapes what publics and policymakers think AI is, and it hides the people and institutions accountable for it. AI-risk communicators, who often still reach for Terminator-style images, can use the library and its guidance directly.

key_work.title: Better Images of AI image library (launch)
Better Images of AI: A Guide for Users and Creators (Kanta Dihal and Tania Duarte)
Archival Images of AI: a playbook for making better images of AI from digital heritage
The glowing blue brain - the visual myth of AI cognition (blog)

people: Tania Duarte (Founder, We and AI; coordinator)
Kanta Dihal (co-author, Guide for Users and Creators)
funding: At launch it was funded by volunteers at We and AI and by BBC R&D; it invites sponsorship and in-kind support. No budget published.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: blog post 'The glowing blue brain - the visual myth of AI cognition'; Aug 2026: post on its inclusion in We and AI's AI Resist List.
engage: Submit images (submission handbook published Dec 2025)
Use the free Creative Commons-licensed image library
Sponsor an artist commission or partner with the project
caveats: It is coordinated by We and AI, whose wider work (critical AI literacy; the AI Resist List, launched May 2026) is sceptical of corporate AI. The project itself is about representation and does not describe itself in AI-safety terms.
tag_notes: Home arts/arts_creative (H1): visual art and commissioned design are its method. Ring adjacent (E3): a sustained programme since 2021 on how AI is pictured, with no safety or catastrophic-risk framing. Transfer convening: it brings artists into the AI conversation and changes media practice. MISFIT: its real effect is on public discourse and editorial image choices, and no transfer value names that. Framing critical: its main output deflates anthropomorphic and hype imagery ('visual myth of AI cognition'). Org type programme: a collaboration hosted by We and AI.

name: Serpentine Arts Technologies
summary: The art, research and commissioning programme of the Serpentine galleries in London. It supports artists working with AI, blockchain, games and the life sciences, and convenes people from art, technology, law, policy and academia. Its Future Art Ecosystems (FAE) strand, running since 2019, publishes annual strategic briefings (FAE4: Art x Public AI, 2024; FAE5: Art x Creative R&D, 2025). It produced Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst's exhibition The Call (Oct 2024-Feb 2025), which proposed cultural, legal and technical protocols for consent-based AI training data. Since September 2026 it has run a paid R&D fellowship, Art x Convergence, on agentic AI.
why_it_matters: It gives artists a structured route into AI governance questions: data consent, public AI infrastructure, and accountability when agentic systems act. It also connects the art world with AI labs, economists and lawyers; the 2026 fellowship jury includes Google DeepMind's Lila Ibrahim and Mariana Mazzucato. Few art-world programmes engage with AI governance this directly.

key_work.title: Future Art Ecosystems 4: Art x Public AI
Holly Herndon & Mat Dryhurst: The Call (Serpentine North)
Future Art Ecosystems R&D Fellowship: Art x Convergence (2026-27 cohort)
Creative AI Lab (research programme for cultural institutions, artists and engineers)

funding: Part of Serpentine, a London charity; the pages I read do not itemise the programme's funders. The 2026-27 fellowship pays each fellow £10,000 plus travel and accommodation for three London weekends.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: the inaugural FAE R&D Fellowship (Art x Convergence) began with four fellows, running to March 2027; May 2026: launched an online game by Danielle Brathwaite-Shirley.
engage: FAE R&D Fellowship: inaugural cohort 2026-27, £10,000 award, three London weekends plus weekly online sessions
Exhibitions, talks and online commissions at Serpentine, London
Free FAE annual strategic briefings online
Arts Technologies newsletter
caveats: Arts Technologies is a strand of a major public gallery, so its priorities can shift with leadership and sponsors, and AI is one of four technology strands. Its framing is cultural and infrastructural, not safety. The fellowship jury includes industry figures (Google DeepMind, Snap). Founding year left blank: FAE dates from 2019 and Serpentine digital commissions from 2014, but I did not find when the programme took its current name.
tag_notes: Home arts/arts_creative (H1): artist commissions and creative R&D are its method. Secondary law (its Legal Lab and consent-based data protocols) and economics (the Public AI and ownership work, commons). Ring adjacent (E3): a sustained AI strand (FAE briefings, The Call, the 2026 fellowship) on AI's cultural, legal and economic effects, with no safety or catastrophic framing. Transfer convening (J5): its stated purpose is supporting artists and convening art, technology, law and policy people, though The Call also proposed governance protocols. Framing flourishing: it describes its aim as building ecosystems and creative alternatives rather than avoiding harm.

name: ARC Centre of Excellence for Automated Decision-Making and Society (ADM+S)
summary: A national research centre funded by the Australian Research Council from 2020 to 2026. It is hosted at RMIT University in Melbourne, with nodes at eight other Australian universities and about 350 members (investigators, research staff, students and affiliates). Researchers from media and communications, law, sociology, anthropology, design, economics and computer science study automated decision-making in news and media, mobility, social services and health. The centre also writes submissions to Australian governments on AI, privacy and online safety.
why_it_matters: It has a large body of sociotechnical research on how automated systems behave inside welfare, media and public procurement, which AI-safety work rarely draws on. Its September 2026 hackathon, 'The Post Imitation Game: Re-thinking the Turing Test for AI Safety', built around chatbots that imitate dead people, treated 'safety' as a mix of design, social and governance problems rather than a property of models.

key_work.title: The Post Imitation Game: Re-thinking the Turing Test for AI Safety (hackathon, with Swinburne Social Innovation Research Institute)
ADM+S Submission to the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence
AI Procurement in the Victorian Public Sector
Submission on the exposure draft Digital Duty of Care Bill

people: Kimberlee Weatherall (lead author of 2026 AI submissions)
funding: Australian Research Council: A$31.8 million over 2020-2026; about A$71.1 million in total including university and partner contributions (Wikipedia).
status_evidence: 1 Oct 2026: news of Flora Salim's ATSE fellowship; 30 Sep 2026: report on its AI-safety hackathon; 24-28 Sep 2026: submissions on privacy reform and the Digital Duty of Care Bill.
engage: Public events and an annual hackathon (Sep 2026: 'The Post Imitation Game')
Research staff and student positions across nine universities (check the site)
News sign-up and open publications (reports and policy submissions)
caveats: The site says ARC funding runs from 2020 to 2026. I found no public statement on what happens after 2026, so the centre may wind down or change form. Its 'AI safety' framing so far amounts to one hackathon. The main agenda is responsible, ethical and inclusive automated decision-making.
tag_notes: Home: the centre's methods are critical data studies, media and communications, sociology, anthropology and law applied to ADM (H1), so law/law_sts rather than law_policy, since the discipline it brings outweighs its policy outputs (D). Ring: it has a sustained AI programme on societal effects (rights, inclusion, disinformation). The 2026 'AI Safety' hackathon is a single event, so the ring stays adjacent (E3). Transfer: its stated objective is to 'formulate world-leading policy and practice' for governments and industry, and in 2026 it made submissions to parliamentary inquiries, so into_institutions (J3).

name: Knowing Machines
summary: A research project, sponsored by the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation, that studies how machine-learning training datasets are made and how they construct 'ground truth'. It is led by Kate Crawford and Mike Ananny (USC Annenberg) and Jason Schultz (NYU Law). Its team of scholars, lawyers, data journalists and artists has produced papers on deprecating datasets, a critical field guide for working with datasets, an investigation of LAION-5B, legal explainers and amicus filings, a podcast and the Calculating Empires artwork.
why_it_matters: It treats training data as a cultural and legal artefact with a history. That gives alignment and data-provenance work concrete methods for asking whose categories and worldviews end up in a model. It also shows what investigating AI systems from outside ML looks like in practice, combining critical data studies, law and art.

key_work.title: Calculating Empires: A Genealogy of Technology and Power Since 1500 (Crawford and Joler; Silver Lion, Venice Architecture Biennale 2025)
A Critical Field Guide for Working with Machine Learning Datasets
A Framework for Deprecating Datasets (ACM FAccT)

people: Kate Crawford (Lead PI; USC Annenberg and Microsoft Research)
Jason Schultz (Co-PI, NYU Technology Law & Policy Clinic)
Vladan Joler (team member; co-creator of Calculating Empires)
funding: Alfred P. Sloan Foundation (I did not find the amount or grant period).
status_evidence: 2025: Calculating Empires, listed as a Knowing Machines publication, won the Silver Lion at the Venice Architecture Biennale. I found no project outputs dated 2026.
engage: Open resources: the Critical Dataset Studies reading list, the SeeSet dataset tool, a legal explainer and the Knowing Machines podcast
caveats: The founding year and grant period are not confirmed. The earliest listed output dates from 2021, and most research outputs from 2021-24, so the project may be winding down. The 2025 award went to an artwork first shown in 2023. The lead PI also holds a senior post at Microsoft Research.
tag_notes: Home: its outputs come from critical data studies, STS, media studies and legal scholarship (H1), with art (Calculating Empires, artists on the team) as a secondary tradition. Ring: it is a sustained, funded programme on training data and its politics, with no safety or catastrophic-risk framing, so adjacent (E3). Transfer: its field guide and deprecation framework target how training datasets are built and used, so into_model (J1) is the closest fit, though its legal work also feeds institutions. Status is active only on the strength of the 2025 award; no 2026 output was found.

name: AIxDESIGN
summary: A nonprofit community organisation (AIxDESIGN Foundation), founded in 2019 and run from Amsterdam, that brings designers, artists, technologists and researchers together to question dominant AI narratives and prototype alternatives. A core team of five runs open research projects, festivals, workshops and critical AI literacy sessions. It also hosts a Slack community of more than 1,500 members in 65 countries and sends a monthly newsletter to about 6,000 readers.
why_it_matters: Its Slow AI programme (2024-25) and 2025 festival 'On Slow AI' question mainstream AI's assumptions about speed and scale, working from design and art practice rather than policy. It reaches creative practitioners and cultural-heritage institutions, audiences the AI-safety field seldom works with. In 2026 Anthropic commissioned it to run artist projects with Claude.

key_work.title: Slow AI (with Small AI, Ancestral AI and Esoteric AI strands)
AIxDESIGN Festival 2025: On Slow AI (Loods6, Amsterdam)
<please touch the art> with Claude (Nxt Museum; client Anthropic)
Let's Have Better Conversation About AI (with Netherlands Institute for Sound & Vision)

funding: Project grants from Stimuleringsfonds Creatieve Industrie (Slow AI; 2025 festival). The festival was also supported by Elisava, the Netherland-America Foundation, the Netherlands Institute for Sound & Vision, the Netherlands Film Academy, het Cultuurfonds and Jagt Zwolsman Fonds. Sound & Vision supports its 2026 conversations project. It also earns from paid commissions (Anthropic, 2026; earlier workshops for WeTransfer and Ars Electronica) and takes monthly 'AIxD Friends' donations. It describes itself as underfunded.
status_evidence: Jun-Dec 2026: 'Let's Have Better Conversation About AI', with the Netherlands Institute for Sound & Vision; May-Jun 2026: '<please touch the art> with Claude' at Nxt Museum, Amsterdam.
engage: Join the community Slack (open to anyone)
Talks, workshops and community hangouts, listed on Luma
Open calls and roles posted on its Notion page
Monthly newsletter; 'AIxD Friends' membership from EUR 2 a month
caveats: It calls itself underfunded, with a team of five relying on unpaid hours. One 2026 project lists Anthropic (Claude) as its client. It explicitly rejects both AI hype and 'AI going rogue' narratives, so it does not share the x-risk framing. The Amsterdam base is inferred from its Dutch funders and venues; the site describes the community as spread across 65 countries.
tag_notes: Home: design research, art and speculative prototyping (Slow AI essays, festival exhibition, playable artworks), so arts/arts_creative (H1); the taxonomy itself cites aixdesign under arts_creative. Ring: it has run sustained AI programmes since 2019 without safety or catastrophic-risk framing, and it explicitly rejects 'AI going rogue' tropes, so adjacent (E3). Transfer: its main purpose is critical AI literacy and alternative narratives for its own community of designers, artists and cultural institutions, so convening (J5). The framing mixes flourishing ('making AI work for the rest of us') with critique of Big Tech narratives. Badge speed_of_wisdom for the Slow AI programme (P; also the taxonomy's example).

name: Dreaming Beyond AI
summary: A web platform and collective, published in English, German, Spanish, French and Turkish, for critical writing, visionary fiction, speculative art and community organising around AI, centring feminist, queer, Black and decolonial perspectives. It was conceived by Nushin Yazdani and Raziye Buse Çetin and is published with ifa (Institut für Auslandsbeziehungen). It runs artist residencies, an online fellowship and public programme, podcasts and workshops.
why_it_matters: It works on who gets to imagine AI futures: it holds that algorithmic systems reinforce existing structures of oppression, and it uses speculative art and community practice to build alternatives 'from the margins'. For int/a it is a working example of artistic and embodied knowing applied to AI and power, with ties to European digital-rights networks.

key_work.title: Unwired Currents: Imagining Technologies Otherwise (online fellowship and public programme, May-Oct)
Coalition Building in Times of AI: Intersecting Struggles (artist-activist residency)
In the Loop: On Artificial Intelligence and Time (residency, then platform launched 2024 at Kampnagel)
Living Technologies: Knowledge-Making Beyond the Machine (online session)

people: Nushin Yazdani (co-founder; creative direction, concept and curation)
Raziye Buse Çetin (co-founder; idea and concept)
Iyo Bisseck (web design and technical realisation)
funding: ifa (Institut für Auslandsbeziehungen), which publishes the platform; Humanity in Action and the Alfred Landecker Foundation, through the Landecker Democracy Fellowship; mur.at. Past partners include Kampnagel (Hamburg) and Deichtorhallen.
status_evidence: 26 Feb 2026: online session 'Living Technologies: Knowledge-Making Beyond the Machine'. Its exhibition 'Portals Behind the Algorithm' at ifa-Galerie Stuttgart (25 Apr - 30 Aug 2026) is marked cancelled on its site.
engage: Residencies and fellowships through open calls (2023; 2024-25 rounds)
Free online public programmes and lectures (Unwired Currents, 2025-26)
Newsletter; contributors can get in touch through the site
caveats: It is run by a three-person core team who say they 'each work various jobs', and legally it is a project published by ifa (Stuttgart). The founding year comes from the platform's 2022 copyright notice. Its 2026 exhibition was cancelled and I found no activity after February 2026, so continuity is uncertain. It held several Berlin events in 2024, but its 2025-26 activity was online or elsewhere (Barcelona, Vienna). It critiques present-day AI and has no x-risk framing.
tag_notes: Home: decolonial, Black and queer-feminist speculative practice (pluriverse, emergent strategy, design justice) is the core contribution, so indigenous/ind_decolonial rather than arts (Arts boundary: decolonial speculative work goes to Indigenous; B8), with arts as secondary. Ring: it has run sustained residencies, fellowships and publishing on AI since 2022, framed around algorithmic oppression with no safety framing, so adjacent (E3). Transfer: it informs and convenes its own community of artists, activists and marginalised groups through residencies, programmes and media, so convening (J5). Org type is programme because ifa is the legal publisher (I).

name: Critical AI (journal and Critical AI @ Rutgers initiative)
summary: An interdisciplinary peer-reviewed journal, published twice a year by Duke University Press and edited by Lauren M. E. Goodlad at Rutgers University's Center for Cultural Analysis. It grew out of the Critical AI @ Rutgers initiative. Alongside the journal it runs a blog, the 'AI Hype Report', the Design Justice Labs teaching platform and a student guide to critical AI literacies. It also holds workshops and institutes, such as the 2024 Design Justice AI Global Humanities Institute in Pretoria.
why_it_matters: It is a central venue for humanities and social-science critique of AI claims, including claims of AI sentience, so it shows what any attempt to join present-harms scholarship with catastrophic-risk work has to answer. In July 2026 it co-organised 'BATCH: Beyond Alignment', a transdisciplinary workshop at the ACL conference, which is a point of contact with alignment discourse.

key_work.title: Critical AI journal, volume 4 (Duke University Press)
Design Justice AI Global Humanities Institute, University of Pretoria
Critical AI Literacies: A Guide for Students
BATCH Workshop: Beyond Alignment: Transdisciplinary Conversations on Human-AI Futures (ACL 2026, San Diego)

people: Lauren M. E. Goodlad (Editor; Chair, Critical AI @ Rutgers)
Matthew Stone (Co-PI, Design Justice AI; Rutgers Computer Science)
Katherine Bode (Co-PI, Design Justice AI; Australian National University)
Vukosi Marivate (Co-PI, Design Justice AI; University of Pretoria)
funding: Hosted by Rutgers University (Center for Cultural Analysis). The journal is published on subscription by Duke University Press. Its 2021 workshops with the Australian National University were sponsored by the US National Endowment for the Humanities. I could not verify other funders.
status_evidence: 16 Sep 2026: blog review 'sneak preview'; 4 Aug 2026: call for papers for the special series 'AI's Cultures of Value'; 4 Jul 2026: co-organised the BATCH workshop at ACL 2026; issue 4.1 published in 2026.
engage: Submit articles to the journal; Aug 2026 call for papers for the special series 'AI's Cultures of Value'
Contribute posts to the AI Hype Report
Online and hybrid workshops and symposia (e.g. Oct 2025 'Troubleshooting' AI workshops)
Open teaching resources: Design Justice Labs and the Critical AI Literacies guide
caveats: The founding year is the journal's first volume, inferred from volume 4 appearing in 2026 at two issues a year; the Rutgers initiative was active by 2021. It is deliberately sceptical of AI hype, including claims of AI sentience, so engagement with AI-safety framings is likely to be critical. Most journal content is behind a subscription.
tag_notes: Home: the journal comes out of literary and cultural studies (editor in English and Comparative Literature; based at the Center for Cultural Analysis), so arts/arts_narrative (H1, H3), with STS and design-justice work as a secondary law tradition. Ring: it has a standing AI publication line with no safety framing. The 2026 'Beyond Alignment' workshop is a single event, so it stays adjacent (E3). Transfer: it brings the critical humanities community into the AI conversation through a journal, teaching guides and institutes, so convening (J5). The taxonomy cites critical-ai as its example of critical framing and interpretive knowing (L, N).

name: Algorithmic Justice League (AJL)
summary: A nonprofit founded in 2016 by Joy Buolamwini that combines research, art and advocacy to expose bias and harm in AI systems. It is known for the Gender Shades audit of commercial facial analysis (2018), the documentary Coded Bias (2020) and spoken-word 'evocative audits' such as Voicing Erasure. It currently runs the #FreedomFlyers campaign on facial recognition at US airport security and a public platform for reporting AI harms.
why_it_matters: It shows art and testimony working as accountability tools: poetry, film and exhibitions that move publics and legislators, alongside technical audits. Its work on third-party audits and bug bounties for algorithmic harms carries over to AI assurance, though it frames these as present harms rather than frontier risk.

key_work.title: Gender Shades (with Timnit Gebru)
Coded Bias (documentary, premiered at Sundance)
Voicing Erasure (spoken-word piece on speech-recognition bias)
#FreedomFlyers campaign and TSA scorecard

funding: Foundation support from the Ford, MacArthur, Alfred P. Sloan, Rockefeller and Mozilla foundations (Wikipedia). Its November 2026 anniversary event lists the Ford, MacArthur, Heising-Simons and Hewlett foundations as sponsors. Individual donors and merchandise.
status_evidence: Oct 2026: registration open for its 'Decade of Impact Masquerade' (Boston and livestream, 14 Nov 2026; keynote by Alondra Nelson). The #FreedomFlyers campaign is ongoing.
engage: Report AI harms or share an airport face-scan experience at report.ajl.org
Decade of Impact celebration, Boston and online, 14 Nov 2026 (virtual 'Founder's Cut' on 5 Nov)
Newsletter, monthly donations, 'become an agent' volunteer actions
caveats: Its focus is bias, civil rights and present harms; it has no catastrophic-risk framing. Much of its best-known research dates from 2018-22.
tag_notes: Home: it says 'we combine art and research', and its distinctive method is art, film and spoken word used as audit and mobilisation (H1; H3 general-audience film and campaigns go to Arts). The audit and civil-rights advocacy strand gives law as secondary. This is a seam between arts and law_sts. Ring: it has had a sustained AI programme since 2016 on bias and civil rights, with no safety framing, so adjacent (E3). Transfer: its mission is to 'build the voice and choice of the most impacted communities' and protect them from biased AI (e.g. airport face scans), so protecting (J4). Way of knowing is empirical because its main outputs (Gender Shades, the TSA traveller study) are measurement-based.

name: Seismic Foundation
summary: A nonprofit that provides marketing and communications for the responsible-AI movement: audience research and message testing, campaign strategy, commissioned creative work and media buying. In the US it is registered as Seismic Catalyst Foundation, a Delaware 501(c)(3). It is led by Sander Volten, former global CEO of the advertising agency 180. In 2025 it published a poll of 10,000 people in the US, UK, France, Germany and Poland on how AI relates to their wider hopes and fears.
why_it_matters: It brings professional advertising and campaign practice into AI safety, a field that mostly relies on researchers and policy specialists to do its communicating. Its 2025 report found that people expect AI to worsen most of the issues they care about while ranking it low among their concerns, and that fear for human relationships outranks fear of job loss. That is useful for anyone building public support for AI governance.

key_work.title: On the Razor's Edge: Seismic Report 2025
Seismic Thinking (blog on AI public opinion and communication)

funding: Survival and Flourishing Fund 2026 round: US$7,000 in general support, recommended by Jaan Tallinn (paid to Seismic Catalyst Foundation). It says an ethical funding policy keeps it independent of commercial and political interests; other funders are not disclosed.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: blog post 'Why was summer 2026 the season of data centers?'. Mar-Jun 2026: posts on public response to the Anthropic-Pentagon crisis and on the 'Claude Mythos question'.
engage: Civil-society groups can approach it for campaign and communications support (contact on the site)
Donations
caveats: The founding date is not stated: its privacy policy dates from February 2025 and the IRS recognised the US entity in August 2025, so it may be newer than its status suggests. Beyond the report and blog, its campaigns are not publicly documented. Its messaging mixes responsible-AI and present-harm themes with 'controllable' AI and frontier risk. Funding is largely undisclosed, and the only grant I could verify is small.
tag_notes: Home: general-audience campaigns, narrative strategy and audience research from the advertising profession, so arts/arts_narrative (H3). Ring changed from bridge to core: its 501(c)(3) mission is 'to reduce risks from AI by raising public awareness', it was set up for that purpose by advertising professionals, and it has SFF funding. The rule that new AI-safety organisations founded by people from other fields are core applies (E1). Transfer: what changes is public awareness and salience, so convening (J5) is the closest value. MISFIT: there is no transfer value for 'into public opinion' by general-audience campaigns. Region is global because the team is distributed (a US ED for North America, a CEO from Amsterdam's advertising scene) and the Delaware entity is a legal shell address (O).

name: Technecultura
summary: A research institute and policy incubator founded by computer scientist Chinasa T. Okolo. It works on the global AI divide, African AI and data governance, and the geopolitics of AI. It publishes policy research, advises governments and multilateral bodies, and offers sociotechnical model evaluations. In July 2026 it started the AI Governance Catalyst, a three-month mentorship fellowship for 15 scholars of Nigerian descent.
why_it_matters: It brings Black decolonial data ethics and African governance expertise into AI governance. Okolo contributed to the International AI Safety Report 2025 and sits on the Global South AI Safety Report's advisory panel, so the institute connects frontier-safety discussions with Global Majority priorities and trains a pipeline of Nigerian-descent policy researchers.

key_work.title: Institutionalizing AI Diplomacy in Africa (Science)
African Data Ethics: A Discursive Framework for Black Decolonial AI (ACM FAccT)
AI Governance Catalyst (AIGC) fellowship, inaugural cohort
Contribution to the International AI Safety Report 2025

status_evidence: Jul 2026: first AI Governance Catalyst cohort of 15 fellows began; 2026: 'Institutionalizing AI Diplomacy in Africa' published in Science
engage: AI Governance Catalyst: a three-month, time-flexible mentorship fellowship for scholars of Nigerian descent (inaugural cohort July 2026; the site says future rounds will be announced)
Advisory, model-evaluation and speaking requests through the website's contact form
caveats: It looks largely like a vehicle for Okolo's own work. Her about page says she is currently a Legislative AI Fellow in Congress through the AAAS Science and Technology Policy Fellowship; her UN (AI & Emerging Technologies Policy Specialist), World Bank (Africa Fellow) and Brookings roles are listed as past. The research list includes work published under those earlier affiliations. The site gives no founding year, team, funders or address; the Washington, D.C. location is inferred from the founder's profile.
tag_notes: Home: its signature contribution is a Black decolonial framework for African data ethics, and the taxonomy uses it as the ind_decolonial example (B8 test: the epistemology, not the geography); law is secondary for its data-governance policy work. Ring: kept adjacent (E3), because the institute frames its mission as global equity and the AI divide, even though Okolo personally describes her focus as 'AI governance and safety for the Global Majority' and contributed to the International AI Safety Report. Transfer: into_institutions (J3), since its stated aim is to inform policy implementation and advise the African Union, UN bodies and governments. Standpoint majority_world because its leadership and focus are African, although its base is in the US.

name: Centre for Responsible AI (CeRAI), IIT Madras
summary: An interdisciplinary research centre in IIT Madras's Wadhwani School of Data Science and AI, set up in May 2023 and headed by Balaraman Ravindran. Its roughly 40 technical projects cover fairness in Indian contexts, explainability, LLM evaluation (including extending the AILuminate benchmark to multilingual and multicultural settings) and safe deployment of reinforcement-learning agents. Its policy work includes a 2025 paper on voluntary AI risk commitments in India and a 2026 working-paper series on AI and consumer law. It holds an annual AI governance conclave, and as a founding member of the Global South Network for Trustworthy AI it helps write the Global South AI Safety Report.
why_it_matters: It brings Indian legal, linguistic and deployment contexts into AI evaluation and governance, and it has direct lines to Indian regulators and ministries (IndiaAI Mission, MeitY, RBI) and to the global safety community: Yoshua Bengio is an honorary advisor, and Ravindran sits on the UN Scientific Panel on AI.

key_work.title: Making AI Self-Regulation Work: Perspectives from India on Voluntary AI Risk Mitigation
Working-paper series on AI and consumer law in India
Expanding AILuminate: multilingual, multicultural and multimodal benchmarking (project)
Co-writing the Global South AI Safety Report

people: Balaraman Ravindran (Head; member, UN Scientific Panel on AI)
funding: Google gave USD 1 million (May 2023); Ericsson joined as a platinum consortium member (Sep 2023). Listed partners include the Gates Foundation, Roche, American Express, Meta and MeitY. Its host school was set up with a ₹110-crore endowment (2024).
status_evidence: Aug 2026: launched a working-paper series on AI and consumer law in India; Industry Conclave on AI Governance scheduled for 22 Oct 2026
engage: Staff vacancies on its careers page (it says it is hiring)
Summer internships, post-baccalaureate and postdoctoral fellowships
Industry Conclave on AI Governance, 22 Oct 2026, IIT Madras
NPTEL online course 'Responsible and Safe AI' (offered 2024)
caveats: Most of its work is mainstream CS and ML responsible-AI research; the law, humanities and policy strand is a minority. 'Safety' here mostly means robustness, privacy and fairness rather than catastrophic risk. Much of its funding comes from industry (Google, Ericsson, Meta, American Express).
tag_notes: Home: under H2, ML does not count as a sector, so it is placed by what it imports, which is legal and public-interest policy for Indian deployment (consumer-law papers, self-regulation analysis, NALSAR and Vidhi as partners): law_policy, with safety secondary for its benchmarking and evaluation work. Ring: changed from adjacent to bridge (E3) because it runs explicitly safety-framed lines (an 'AI & Safety' research theme, Safe GenAI and RL-safety projects, AILuminate benchmarking, co-writing the Global South AI Safety Report) and has Bengio as an advisor. Transfer: into_institutions (J3), since it aims to be India's body for recommending AI guidelines and policy.

name: Coding Rights
summary: A Brazilian feminist organisation founded in 2015 by Joana Varon. It works on how technology is developed and regulated, from a transfeminist, decolonial and anti-racist human-rights perspective. Its AI work: Not My A.I. (since 2021), a feminist toolkit and map of harmful algorithmic systems in Latin America; a T20 policy brief, written with Sasha Costanza-Chock and Timnit Gebru, on federated, community-controlled AI; the Compost Engineers manifesto for slow, regenerative technologies; TRAMAS (2025-26), which maps data-centre and AI conflicts in Latin American territories; and a May 2026 guide to AI, disinformation and gendered political violence in Brazil's elections.
why_it_matters: It offers worked alternatives to extractive AI development, grounded in Latin American feminist and decolonial thought. It argues explicitly for slower technologies that restore emotional, spiritual and ancestral knowledge, which is close to int/a's 'speed of wisdom', and it links AI to environmental and territorial justice.

key_work.title: Not My A.I.: feminist toolkit and map of harmful AI in Latin America
Compost Engineers: regenerative technologies manifesto (Varon and Egaña Rojas)
Policy brief: Fostering a federated AI commons ecosystem (T20)
Disassembling the Machine: guide to AI, disinformation and political violence in Brazil's 2026 elections

funding: Funders are not itemised on its site. TRAMAS is funded by the Green Screen Coalition's Catalyst Fund and Heinrich Böll Foundation Brazil; the 2025 annual report acknowledges APC, Hivos and the Heinrich Böll Foundation.
status_evidence: May 2026: released 'Disassembling the Machine' with Mulheres Negras Decidem, NetLab UFRJ and others for Brazil's 2026 elections
engage: Free library of publications, the IMAGINE podcast and annual reports (2016-2025)
Lampejo, a popular-education school on technopolitics and digital care (in person, Brazil)
caveats: AI is one strand among its work on digital rights, surveillance, gender violence and the environment. It is critical of mainstream AI development and does not engage with x-risk framings. Much of its output is in Portuguese or Spanish. Neither the site nor the 2025 annual report gives a city; Rio de Janeiro is its long-reported base.
tag_notes: Home: its core AI contribution is decolonial and transfeminist epistemology (feminist categories of oppressive AI, the Compost Engineers manifesto), so it stays ind_decolonial under B8; law is secondary for digital-rights advocacy and arts for speculative fiction (decolonial speculative work stays with Indigenous & decolonial). Ring: adjacent (E3), a sustained AI programme on present harms and alternatives with no safety or catastrophic-risk framing. Transfer: protecting (J4), since its primary purpose is defending women, LGBTQI+ people and territories in Latin America from harmful technology. Badge speed_of_wisdom for its explicit 'slow knowledges' position on technology outside capitalist pace.

name: Global South Network for Trustworthy AI
summary: A civil-society-led coalition of 15 organisations, launched on 20 February 2026 at the IndiaAI Impact Summit in New Delhi and coordinated by Digital Futures Lab. Founding members include the Global Center on AI Governance, ITS Rio, CeRAI (IIT Madras) and International Innovation Corps; other members include Derechos Digitales, Karya, Masakhane African Languages Hub, Khazanah Research Institute, the Collective Intelligence Project and ROOST. Its first-year flagships are multilingual safety benchmarks, research on AI's labour-market effects, a taxonomy of gendered AI harms, and procurement guidance for governments. It is writing the Global South AI Safety Report, co-chaired by Kalika Bali and Vukosi Marivate, with an interim output for the July 2026 UN Global Dialogue and a first full edition due at the 2027 Geneva AI Summit.
why_it_matters: It recasts AI safety around how systems actually fail in Global South languages, institutions and deployments. It also connects frontier-safety bodies (AI Safety Institutes, the UN Scientific Panel) with Global Majority responsible-AI researchers; Cecil Abungu (ILINA) and Divya Siddarth (CIP) sit on the report's advisory panel. Funders who want to widen what 'safety evaluation' covers have a ready-made partner here.

key_work.title: Launch at the IndiaAI Impact Summit
Global South AI Safety Report (announced; interim output for the UN Global Dialogue, full edition 2027)
Grounded, Plural, Accountable: submission to the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance

people: Urvashi Aneja (Founder and Director, Digital Futures Lab; network lead)
Kalika Bali (Report co-chair, Microsoft Research India)
Vukosi Marivate (Report co-chair, University of Pretoria; UN Scientific Panel on AI)
Aarushi Gupta (Digital Futures Lab; report writing team)
funding: Not disclosed. The IndiaAI Mission sits on the steering committee and has pledged support.
status_evidence: May 2026: submission to the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance, and the Global South AI Safety Report announced with its advisory panel and writing team
engage: No public membership process found; enquiries go through Digital Futures Lab
Regional hubs planned in South Africa and Brazil
caveats: It has no website of its own, and almost all information comes from Digital Futures Lab. IDRC's summit programme lists the launch session as the 'Global South Network on AI Safety & Evaluation', hosted by the Global Center on AI Governance and the Government of India; this appears to be the same network under a working name. I could not confirm that the interim report was published in July 2026. Government (IndiaAI Mission) and industry members (Microsoft researchers, Cognizant AI Lab) may affect its independence.
tag_notes: Home: a coalition of public-interest tech-policy and development institutes, so law_policy (B8: Global South policy work goes to its sector, with location carried by region and standpoint); safety is secondary for its multilingual safety benchmarks and evaluation agenda. Ring: bridge (E3), since its flagship is an explicitly titled AI Safety Report and its launch was framed as broadening AI safety beyond technical and speculative framings. Transfer: into_institutions (J3), through procurement guidance, a UN submission and an evidence base aimed at AI Safety Institutes. Region global because it has no single formal base, though Digital Futures Lab (Goa, India) coordinates it.

name: African Hub on AI Safety, Peace and Security
summary: A hub in the University of Cape Town's AI Initiative, co-led with the Global Center on AI Governance and funded by IDRC and the UK FCDO through AI4D. It was announced in September 2025 as the twelfth lab in the AI4D network and the first devoted to policy and governance. It teaches an interdisciplinary AI Safety honours course and a technical AI safety track in applied mathematics, and runs red-teaming workshops, quarterly AI safety hackathons and an AI diplomacy curriculum for African policymakers. It funds 15 honours, 4 master's and 1 PhD places, including a 2026-28 master's fellowship on mapping AI harms. Its stated aims are African representation in global AI safety debates and attention to AI risks for marginalised groups, particularly women and girls.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few places training African students and policymakers in AI safety itself, with public-law, criminology and peace-and-security perspectives alongside a technical track. That widens both who does safety work and which harms get counted.

key_work.title: AI4D announcement of the hub (twelfth AI4D lab)
Master's Fellowship in AI Governance and Harm Mapping (2026-28)
Interdisciplinary AI Safety honours course and technical AI safety track
AI diplomacy curriculum for African policymakers

people: Jonathan Shock (Associate Professor, UCT AI Initiative; co-lead)
Rachel Adams (Global Center on AI Governance; co-lead)
Annette Hübschle (UCT Department of Public Law)
Leah Junck (Global Center on AI Governance)
Mark Gaffley (Global Center on AI Governance)
funding: IDRC and the UK FCDO through AI4D (the 2025-29 AI4D phase totals more than CAD 100 million); the hub's own budget is not published.
status_evidence: 2026: recruited for its Master's Fellowship in AI Governance and Harm Mapping (2026-28); applications now closed
engage: Master's Fellowship in AI Governance and Harm Mapping, 2026-28 (applications closed)
Funded honours, master's and PhD places at UCT
Quarterly AI safety hackathons and red-teaming workshops
Open educational resources (online courses for the continent)
caveats: The hub page lists offerings without dates, so I could not check how many have actually run. The launch date comes from IDRC's 29 Sep 2025 announcement.
tag_notes: Home: peace, because the hub is built around a peace-and-security frame and an AI diplomacy curriculum (H1); law (public law, harm mapping) and safety (red-teaming) are secondary. Close call: the leadership is mixed (physics, governance, criminology), and law would also be defensible. Ring: bridge (E3, and old institutions with new safety programmes are bridge), as an explicitly AI-safety-framed standing programme inside UCT funded outside the x-risk ecosystem. Transfer: into_institutions (J3), through policy development and diplomacy training for African policymakers. Org type programme (I), since it is a funded hub inside UCT's AI Initiative.

name: Equiano Institute
summary: A small research lab, apparently based in Nairobi with a distributed team, that describes itself as working on AI alignment and responsible AI adoption in Africa. Most of its output is policy analysis of how AI capabilities reach Africa and other low- and middle-income countries: the quarterly 'State of AI Diffusion' newsletter (since July 2026), essays on export controls and jurisdiction-bound models, a review of India's AI diffusion charter, and an Interstate AI Policy Playbook (2024). It has also run an 'Evaluations in Residence' call for volunteers to evaluate language models in Sub-Saharan African languages, and has written on ethnographic approaches to AI safety and on benefit sharing.
why_it_matters: It treats access to frontier AI, and who gets its benefits, as an AI-governance problem seen from Africa, which mainstream safety debates on export controls and compute governance rarely do. Its argument for ethnographers in AI labs and ethnographic safety studies names a method the field lacks.

key_work.title: State of AI Diffusion (quarterly newsletter)
Localised AI Models and Centralised Diffusion
Reviewing Progress on Responsible AI Diffusion (India's AI charter)
The Interstate AI Policy Playbook

people: Jonas Kgomo (researcher; lead author of most output)
status_evidence: 30 Jul 2026: State of AI Diffusion Vol. II No. 01, 'Capability Diffusion and Access'
engage: Subscribe to the quarterly State of AI Diffusion newsletter
Evaluations in Residence: an interest form for contributors evaluating language models in Sub-Saharan African languages (posted May 2025)
caveats: Its self-description ('pioneering research in AI alignment', 'a global leader in AI governance') outruns the visible output, which is mostly diffusion and access policy rather than alignment research. Team roles, legal status and funders are not published, and I found little independent coverage. The site lists outside work, such as a GovAI benefit-sharing brief, next to its own without clear attribution; GovAI's page does not credit Equiano. The founding year comes from its GitHub organisation (created Aug 2023, location Kenya). Its base is ambiguous: the 2025 review names Nairobi as its primary hub (with links to Paris and Oxford), while the homepage foregrounds London ties (London Data Week, an Alan Turing Institute partnership).
tag_notes: Home: its main output analyses who gets access to AI and its gains (diffusion, export controls, benefit sharing), so economics, econ_power (political economy: who holds the gains); law is secondary for its ethnographic and STS strand. Ring: kept bridge (E3), since it frames itself around alignment and a 'safe and equitable AI future' while rooted in African development policy; not core, because its practice is not alignment research and it is not clearly part of the x-risk ecosystem. Transfer: into_institutions (J3), through policy playbooks and diffusion-policy analysis aimed at governments. Organisation type nonprofit is assumed; legal form not published.

name: Artificial Intelligence for Development (AI4D), IDRC
summary: A funding programme of Canada's International Development Research Centre that supports locally led responsible-AI research, policy and innovation in the Global South. It began in 2020 as AI4D Africa, a CAD 20 million partnership with Sweden's Sida that funded policy hubs, multidisciplinary university AI labs and nearly 100 innovations. Since 2025 it has run as 'AI4D: Responsible AI, Empowering People' with the UK FCDO (more than CAD 100 million to 2029), extending to Latin America, the Middle East, South and Southeast Asia and the Pacific. In September 2025 it added the African Hub on AI Safety, Peace and Security at UCT and an AI Evidence Alliance for Social Impact, and it convenes an AI4D Funders Collaborative with the Gates Foundation and Germany's BMZ.
why_it_matters: With more than CAD 100 million committed for 2025-29 and a network of 13 labs across 36+ countries, it is a major non-philanthropic funder behind African AI institutions, including UCT's AI-safety hub; three of its research partners were appointed to the UN Scientific Panel on AI in 2026. New funders who want Global South safety capacity could co-fund through it.

key_work.title: AI4D Africa (2020-2025)
AI4D: Responsible AI, Empowering People (2025-2029, with FCDO)
AI4D expands to safety, peace, security and social impact (African Hub at UCT; AI Evidence Alliance)
AI4D research partners appointed to the UN Independent International Scientific Panel on AI

funding: AI4D Africa: CAD 20 million from IDRC and Sida (2020-25). AI4D: Responsible AI, Empowering People: more than CAD 100 million from IDRC and the UK FCDO (2025-29); the AI4D site cites £60 million committed. Further partners: Community Jameel, the Gates Foundation, BMZ and JICA. The AI Evidence Alliance gets more than CAD 5 million, co-financed with Google.org.
status_evidence: 21 Sep 2026: IDRC joined the Gates Foundation-led joint commitment on closing AI's language gap; Feb 2026: three AI4D research partners appointed to the UN Scientific Panel on AI
engage: Open calls posted on ai4d.ai (for example the Master's Fellowship in AI Governance and Harm Mapping, and a Pan-African Sign Language Research & Innovation Survey)
IDRC funding calls, mainly for Global South institutions
The AI4D Funders Collaborative, for funders who want to coordinate
caveats: It frames its work as responsible AI for development (bias, inclusion, rights, jobs, surveillance) rather than catastrophic risk; safety-specific funding is one hub among 13 labs. Grants go mainly to Global South institutions through calls. Its budget depends on Canadian and UK aid policy.
tag_notes: Home: a single-programme funder, so under H4 it takes its programme's tradition: development research and responsible-AI policy, i.e. law_policy (public-interest, ELSI and development funding); economics (African Growth and AI Network, labour) and peace (the safety, peace and security hub) are secondary. It is not on the K list of generalist funders. Ring: kept bridge (E3; an old institution with a new AI-safety line), since its 2025 expansion explicitly added 'safety, peace, security' and it funds UCT's AI-safety hub. Transfer: into_institutions (J, funders coded by the work they fund: policy hubs, observatories, governance capacity). Standpoint neither (O): a Canadian host's programme run from Ottawa, even though its focus is the Global South.

name: Alexander von Humboldt Institute for Internet and Society (HIIG): AI & Society Lab and Public Interest AI
summary: The AI & Society Lab is a research group at HIIG, a Berlin institute for internet and society research founded in 2011 by Humboldt University, the Berlin University of the Arts and the WZB. It runs the Public Interest AI work, led by Theresa Züger. That work sets six conditions for AI that serves the public rather than profit: justification, equity, participatory design, technical safeguards, openness to validation and sustainability. The group also maintains publicinterest.ai, with a global project map and stakeholder index, and built prototypes such as the Simba text simplifier and a claim-spotting tool for fact-checkers.
why_it_matters: It gives a worked, testable definition of public-interest AI, plus a dataset of AI projects that claim to serve democracy. These are concrete templates for a public option and participatory governance, which the safety field mostly leaves to others. It is also an established research partner close to int/a's Berlin community.

key_work.title: publicinterest.ai: six conditions for public-interest AI, project map and stakeholder index
Simba text simplifier and Claimspotting fact-checking prototypes
Can AI strengthen democracy? A data collection on AI projects aiming to serve democratic processes (98 projects)
Blind spot sustainability: Making AI's environmental impact measurable

people: Theresa Züger (Head of Research, Societal Values, Transformation and AI; leads the AI & Society Lab)
Wolfgang Schulz (HIIG research director and board)
funding: Public Interest AI was funded by Germany's Federal Ministry of Education and Research (FKZ 01IS20058) from October 2020 to September 2024. HIIG began in 2011 with €4.5M of start-up funding from Google over three years. It is now funded by German federal ministries, the DFG, Stiftung Mercator and Horizon 2020 (Wikipedia).
status_evidence: 13 Jul 2026: HIIG blog post by Youssef, Züger and Winter presenting a dataset of 98 AI projects that claim to serve democracy. Lab workshops are listed for October 2025.
engage: Submit a public-interest AI initiative to the project map on publicinterest.ai
Attend AI & Society Lab workshops, roundtables and open talks in Berlin (sessions listed for March and October 2025)
HIIG public events, e.g. an ideathon on barriers to AI entrepreneurship (26 November) and a symposium on EU digital law (3 December)
caveats: The Public Interest AI project's dedicated federal funding ended in September 2024. The work continues inside the lab, but on a smaller dedicated budget. HIIG's founding money came from Google. The lab works on public benefit, democracy and rights, with no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing.
tag_notes: Home: a multidisciplinary internet-and-society institute whose public-interest framework comes from political theory, STS and participatory design (H2), so law_policy, with democracy as secondary for its participatory design patterns and its democracy dataset. Ring: a sustained AI programme on public benefit and democracy with no safety or catastrophic framing, so it stays adjacent (E3). Transfer: its main outputs are governance templates (six conditions, design patterns for participatory governance), so into_institutions (J3). Org type: a research group in an academic research institute; HIIG is a non-university gGmbH, so academic was chosen over programme.

name: Bertelsmann Stiftung: reframe[Tech] – Algorithms for the Common Good (now Digitalisierung & Gemeinwohl)
summary: A digital-policy programme of the Bertelsmann Stiftung, the large German operating foundation founded in 1977. It writes analyses and policy proposals to steer digital technology towards the common good, for policymakers, public administrations and civil society. Recent work covers a European public AI option, practical implementation and simplification of the EU AI Act, interoperability standards, decentralised social media, and public attitudes to platform power. Its old domain, reframetech.de, now redirects to a site called Digitalisierung & Gemeinwohl.
why_it_matters: It argues for a public AI option and against dependence on a few private AI companies, and it reaches EU and German policymakers in a way most AI-safety groups do not. Its surveys of German public opinion on platform power give evidence on the structural, power-concentration side of the AI transition.

name: SUPERRR Lab
summary: A Berlin non-profit (Superrr Lab SL gGmbH) founded in 2019 by Julia Kloiber and Elisa Lindinger. It works on feminist digital policy and futures under the line 'digital policy is social policy'. Its AI work includes 'AI Mythbusting: The Zine' (July 2026), drawn from 13 public events in Berlin libraries, and 'Data Workers United' (September 2026, with DAIR), which links data-worker movements in Kenya, Nigeria, Venezuela, the US, Germany and Spain. It also runs feministtechpolicy.org.
why_it_matters: It brings the people behind AI training data, and feminist and futures methods, into the question of whose futures AI serves. The safety field rarely looks at the data-labelling workforce or at how the public understands AI. Its Berlin public events on AI power and myths are a ready local partner for int/a Berlin.

name: FIfF – Forum InformatikerInnen für Frieden und gesellschaftliche Verantwortung (Forum of Computer Professionals for Peace and Social Responsibility)
summary: A German association (e.V.) of computer scientists and IT professionals, founded in 1984 out of the peace movement, with Joseph Weizenbaum among its co-founders. It is based in Bremen and has about 700 members. It publishes the quarterly FIfF-Kommunikation, with AI issues in 2024 and 2025. It runs the Cyberpeace campaign against cyberweapons and armed drones, a working group on armed drones and AI targeting, and the Grüne Bits project on the environmental costs of AI data centres. It awards the Weizenbaum Study Prize and Medal, holds an annual conference (Berlin, 30 October to 1 November 2026, 'Resilience in the Polycrisis'), and is the legal host of the Bits & Bäume alliance.
why_it_matters: It carries a 40-year tradition of computing professionals taking responsibility for military and social uses of their work, from Weizenbaum onwards. That is a model of conscience among builders which AI-safety culture rarely draws on. Its AI work places autonomous weapons, surveillance and resource use inside a polycrisis frame.

Into_builders was considered, because it cultivates conscience among IT professionals, but its members are not specifically AI builders.

name: Bits & Bäume
summary: A German alliance of 13 environmental, climate, digital-rights, development, union and research organisations, plus a grassroots community, working for sustainable and socially just digitalisation. Members include CCC, FSFE, Germanwatch, Deutscher Naturschutzring, BUNDjugend, DGB, Brot für die Welt, Wikimedia Deutschland, IÖW, Konzeptwerk Neue Ökonomie, the Weizenbaum Institute, the Berlin Ethics Lab and FIfF. It formed in 2017, held conferences in Berlin in 2018 and 2022 with 2,000-2,500 participants, and has had a coordination office since 2023. Its AI work campaigns on generative AI's energy and climate costs and on gas plants built for data centres, and runs policy labs on community-run computing infrastructure.
why_it_matters: It treats AI as part of the ecological crisis and of Big Tech's infrastructure power. It brings environmental and degrowth groups, unions and hackers into AI debates that the safety field does not reach. Its Berlin policy labs and community are a direct way in for int/a Berlin.

name: Café IA (France)
summary: A French national programme of free, informal public conversations about AI, held in libraries, workplaces, schools and community spaces by volunteer hosts. Hosts use open (CC BY-SA) facilitation kits on what AI is, AI and work, AI and the environment, and AI and information. It was launched nationwide in 2024 at the President's request by the Conseil national du numérique, renamed the Conseil de l'IA et du numérique in 2025. It is now an independent state project hosted by the Directorate General for Enterprise (DGE) at the Ministry of the Economy. It reports more than 800 hosts, about five cafés a day (80% outside Paris), and aims to reach 2 million people by the end of 2027.
why_it_matters: It is working infrastructure for mass public conversation and AI literacy at national scale, a form of democratic participation the AI-safety field seldom builds. Its open kits could be adapted for discussing AI-transition questions, and int/a Paris could host cafés directly.

Its aim is literacy and conversation, not critique or safety. Participation figures are self-reported and vary by page: more than 50,000 in the first year on the English page, more than 150,000 over 18 months on the press page. The cafés produce discussion, not decisions handed to policymakers.
tag_notes: Home: popular public deliberation on AI through citizen-hosted cafés, so dem_deliberation. Ring: a sustained national programme on public understanding of AI with no safety or catastrophic framing, so it stays adjacent (E3). Transfer: it brings its constituency, the French public, into the AI conversation through literacy and dialogue, so convening (J5). Framing: flourishing is the closest fit for its empowerment aim ('informed and conscious decisions'). Org type: a programme hosted in the DGE (I). Status kept active rather than changed: the host moved but the name and mission continue.

name: Current AI
summary: A Paris-based non-profit (French loi 1901 association) launched at the AI Action Summit in February 2025 to build a 'public option for AI'. It brings together governments, philanthropies and companies. It funds community projects, builds open-source AI infrastructure such as the Suno Sutra offline translation device with India's Bhashini, the AlphaChat open chatbot and a Gap Map of the open AI stack, and convenes a wider public-interest AI movement. It reports $404M pledged towards a five-year goal of $2.5B, and has committed $11.3M in grants across two 2026 rounds, starting with a $3.2M pilot cohort announced in June 2026.
why_it_matters: It is a large new funder outside the AI-safety funding circuit, working on power concentration and on who builds and owns AI, including community control over language data. For new funders and founders it is one of the few sizeable pools aimed at public and open AI alternatives.

name: ILINA Program
summary: An African-led nonprofit that works on catastrophic risk from frontier AI through research, engagement with African governments and multilateral bodies, and an annual field-building programme. It runs a 12-week seminar on AI and global catastrophic risks, held online and in person in Nairobi, and a paid Junior Research Fellowship with governance and technical tracks. Recent outputs include a report on monitoring AI impacts in Africa (May 2026), a paper on Africa-centric safety evaluations, and input to Kenya's national AI policy and the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance.
why_it_matters: It is one of very few organisations putting African policy, legal and development perspectives into frontier-AI-safety governance, and it trains African graduates for the field. It shows how catastrophic-risk arguments are translated for Global South policymakers, a perspective the Anglo-American safety community mostly lacks.

name: Cape Institute for Safe AI (CISAI), formerly AI Safety South Africa (AISSA)
summary: A Cape Town nonprofit that runs a co-working hub, an in-house research lab and talent programmes on risks from advanced AI and on d/acc (defensive, decentralised technology). It is the 2026 successor of AI Safety South Africa, which Leo Hyams and Benjamin Sturgeon founded in 2024. AISSA ran Africa's first Cooperative AI Research Fellowship (10 fellows, Jan–Apr 2026, with the Cooperative AI Foundation, Principles of Intelligence and UCT). CISAI will host the PIBBSS/Principles of Intelligence fellowship from November 2026 to February 2027. Its in-house research is mainly capability evaluations, built with UK AISI and Apart Research, plus HumanAgencyBench, which tests whether AI assistants support human agency.
why_it_matters: It is one of very few AI-safety hubs in Africa, with a cooperative-AI and multipolar orientation. It states openly that it does not endorse racing or any single actor acting for humanity. Hosting the Princint fellowship makes Cape Town a site where interdisciplinary alignment research is done outside the US and UK.

MISFIT: the in-house evaluations are mainstream ML, which the taxonomy doesn't treat as a tradition.

name: Beijing Institute of AI Safety and Governance (Beijing-AISI)
summary: A Beijing research institute launched on 3 September 2024, with backing from Beijing municipal departments and the Mentougou District government. It was co-founded by the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Automation ethics centre and the AI Institute of CAICT, and its founding dean is Yi Zeng. It builds AI safety evaluation benchmarks and a leaderboard, publishes governance indices with Zeng's Center for Long-term AI (AGILE Index, Global Index for AI Safety), runs an AI ethics committee and assessment centre, and co-chairs a China–France dialogue on AI safety and red lines. Its stated aim is 'harmonious symbiosis' between humans and AI. Its research reframes superalignment as human–AI co-alignment towards a 'sustainable symbiotic society' and includes brain-inspired, empathy-driven moral agents.
why_it_matters: It is one of the most prominent Chinese institutions arguing publicly that superintelligence poses existential risk and should be prohibited until it can be made safe. It brings a value framework grounded in Chinese thought ('symbiosis', intrinsic morality rather than external rules) into international safety diplomacy. For int/a it is a rare non-Western alignment target, joined to an explicit call to slow down.

name: Hong Kong Catastrophic Risk Centre (HKCRC), Lingnan University
summary: A research centre in Lingnan University's philosophy department, established in January 2022, that studies the ethical and theoretical foundations of global catastrophic and existential risk, with AI as a main strand. It runs a seminar series (in person and on Zoom) and workshops with Japanese partners (Kobe University's Project Innovative Ethics, Mimir, Genoa). It also offers a free eight-module online course on ethics and global catastrophic risks, and hosts a humanities-based MA in AI and the Future. Its 2025–26 seminars covered AI welfare and moral status, power-seeking theorems, cognitive enfeeblement and free speech for language models.
why_it_matters: It describes itself as the first catastrophic-risk research centre in Asia, and it links x-risk philosophy to East Asian ethics networks. Its AI welfare and moral-status work and its MA give the field a humanities training route outside the UK and US.

It is arguably bridge as a unit of a philosophy department. Transfer convening: its outputs are scholarship, seminars and teaching for academics and students. Standpoint neither (Hong Kong, O).

name: Observatorio de Riesgos Catastróficos Globales (ORCG)
summary: A science-diplomacy nonprofit working on global catastrophic risk management in Spanish-speaking countries (Latin America and Spain). It connects decision-makers with experts and publishes evidence-based reports. Its four areas are AI risk, pandemics, global food crises (abrupt sunlight reduction) and risk-management systems. Its AI work includes input to the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, a peer-reviewed paper on the securitisation of AI (2025), a report on AI and the life sciences, and the AI Risk Explorer (AIRE). AIRE is a continuously updated platform that tracks frontier-model evaluations, AI-enabled cyber incidents and risk levels for policymakers.
why_it_matters: It is the main Spanish-language voice on AI catastrophic risk and governance, and it argues for Latin America's place in global AI governance. It treats AI alongside biosecurity and food-system resilience, which gives a cross-risk view. AIRE is a public, maintained evidence base on dangerous capabilities that decision-makers can use.
