name: Local Contexts
summary: An Indigenous-governed nonprofit, incorporated in the Navajo Nation in 2022, that grew from a project Jane Anderson and Kim Christen started in 2010. It provides Traditional Knowledge (TK) and Biocultural (BC) Labels, which Indigenous communities customise to attach provenance, protocols and permissions to their data and collections, and Notices, which institutions and researchers use to flag Indigenous interests. These are managed through the Local Contexts Hub, a web platform with an API. In September 2026 it published guidance with Creative Commons on using the Labels alongside CC licences.
why_it_matters: Its Labels and Hub are a working, machine-readable protocol for Indigenous consent and provenance over data. AI training-data pipelines could honour it, which is a concrete answer to how models absorb cultural knowledge without permission. Its Indigenous-led governance and reparative subscription model are templates for community authority over data.

Local Contexts Hub and API

name: European Group on Ethics in Science and New Technologies (EGE)
summary: An independent, multidisciplinary advisory body of ethicists, lawyers and scientists, founded in 1991, that advises the President of the European Commission where ethics, society and fundamental rights meet science and technology. The current group was appointed on 26 January 2025. Its AI-related advice includes a 2018 statement on AI, robotics and 'autonomous' systems, the opinion 'Democracy in the digital age' (2023) and 'Governing neuro-AI' (September 2026). The Commission has said it will request three further AI opinions in 2027: AI in science, fair digital futures, and AI in the energy system. Its secretariat also runs an international dialogue linking national ethics councils from 97 countries.
why_it_matters: It is the EU's highest-level ethics advisory body, and its rights-based, infrastructural analyses go straight to the Commission President. Its neuro-AI opinion treats neural data as a political-economic resource and raises concerns about concentration and dual use, a framing the AI-safety field rarely brings into EU policy.

key_work.title: Governing neuro-AI (statement)
Democracy in the digital age (opinion)
Statement on Artificial Intelligence, Robotics and 'Autonomous' Systems

engage: Members are appointed by the Commission President, with candidates found by an identification committee
Its research support project, SAEGE, holds public sessions, e.g. at a technology-ethics conference on 4 Nov 2026
caveats: AI is one topic among many; its other recent opinions cover nature, the just green transition, solar geoengineering and ultra-processed foods. Its advice is non-binding and framed around fundamental rights and democracy, not catastrophic risk.

Ring adjacent (E3): a sustained line of AI advice (2018, 2023, 2026, three opinions planned for 2027) framed around rights, democracy and sovereignty, not safety or catastrophic risk. Transfer into_institutions: its advice goes to Commission policy. Org_type public: an expert body established by Commission decision (I). Framing structural: it warns of erosion of democracy, concentration and dependency rather than single catastrophes.

name: UNESCO Ethics of AI programme (Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, Global Forum on the Ethics of AI)
summary: UNESCO's AI-ethics work, based in its Social and Human Sciences sector, centres on the 2021 Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, adopted by all 193 member states. Tools that came out of the Recommendation include a Readiness Assessment Methodology (more than 70 countries have used it or are using it), an Ethical Impact Assessment, and the Global AI Ethics and Governance Observatory with its country profiles. It also runs expert and peer networks: Women4Ethical AI, AI Ethics Experts Without Borders, a Global Network of AI Supervisory Authorities, a civil-society and academia network, and a coalition on linguistic diversity. Since 2022 it has held a Global Forum on the Ethics of AI; the fourth was in Riyadh from 14 to 17 September 2026.
why_it_matters: It is the only AI-ethics instrument every UNESCO member state has adopted, and one of the few global AI norms that names environmental and ecosystem flourishing, and cultural and linguistic diversity, as values. Its readiness assessments give it working channels into ministries across the Majority World, which AI-safety policy work rarely reaches.

key_work.title: Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
Readiness Assessment Methodology (RAM, now RAM 2.0), used by more than 70 countries
Global AI Ethics and Governance Observatory

status_evidence: Sep 2026: 4th Global Forum on the Ethics of AI held in Riyadh (14–17 Sep), co-hosted with SDAIA and ICAIRE; Globethics reported on it on 21 Sep 2026.
engage: Global Forum on the Ethics of AI: the 4th edition was in Riyadh, 14–17 Sep 2026, with public livestreams

caveats: The Recommendation is non-binding soft law, so implementation depends on each member state and is uneven. The United States announced its withdrawal from UNESCO in July 2025. The programme's framing is human rights and present harms; 'AI safety' appeared in 2026 only as one forum topic among many. The work also extends to neurotechnology, under a separate 2025 Recommendation.
tag_notes: Home: its outputs are an intergovernmental normative instrument plus readiness and impact-assessment tools for governments, aimed mainly at development contexts, so Law (law_policy). Philosophy is secondary because the programme sits in UNESCO's bioethics and ethics-of-science section (B13: ethics councils). Ring: it has a sustained AI programme framed around human rights, bias, diversity and the environment, with no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing, so the roster's adjacent stands. Transfer: its primary products are governance instruments (the Recommendation, RAM, the supervisory-authorities network), so into_institutions. Org type: A1/I, a unit inside an intergovernmental body, so Programme. Assurance is secondary for the Ethical Impact Assessment and the supervisory-authorities network.

name: Globethics
summary: Globethics is a Geneva-based international ethics NGO, founded in 2004 by the ethicist Christoph Stückelberger with 29 ethics experts from 21 countries. It holds ECOSOC consultative status and runs training, consulting, publishing (an open research library and journals) and conferences through regional centres in Accra, Bangalore, Buenos Aires, Cape Town, Nairobi, Tunis and Yogyakarta. 'Ethics of AI and Emerging Technology' is one of its three focus areas. Under it, Globethics runs the Emerging Leaders in Ethical AI Governance Fellowship (14 fellows in 2026, chosen from 1,660+ applications), chairs a UNESCO subgroup on empowering citizens and civil-society organisations in AI governance, and facilitates a UNESCO course for civil society.
why_it_matters: It brings two decades of applied-ethics training, multi-faith and church networks, and Global South regional centres into AI governance. In 2026 it co-hosted the first AI for Good panel on religious perspectives, with the Muslim Council of Elders. It offers a route for plural, non-Western ethical voices to reach civil society and policy forums that the AI-safety field rarely engages.

key_work.title: Emerging Leaders in Ethical AI Governance Fellowship (Geneva residency during Geneva Digital Week)
Chairing UNESCO's subgroup on Empowering Citizens and CSOs in AI Governance; course 'Empowering CSOs to Lead the Way in Advancing AI Ethics'

Global Ethics Forum 2026 on ethics, AI and governance (Bali, hybrid)

engage: Emerging Leaders in Ethical AI Governance Fellowship: 14 fellows in 2026; applications for the 2027 cohort 'will open soon'
Open Track webinars with the 2026 fellows, online, 26 May–16 Dec 2026
Global Ethics Forum 2026, Bali and hybrid, 20–22 Oct 2026
'Before the Tool: What Must Change Inside Organizations for Responsible AI in Crisis Contexts', Geneva, 14 Oct 2026
Online courses (classroom.globethics.net), a jobs page and an AI Ethics and Governance newsletter
caveats: Its website does not disclose funders. Besides its NGO work it sells consulting and advisory services, including to multinational businesses. Its roots are in Protestant ecumenical ethics (the founder and board president are theologians), though it presents itself as a non-confessional ethics organisation. When it says 'safe' AI it means inclusive, rights-based governance, not catastrophic risk.
tag_notes: Home: applied ethics, ethical-leadership training and character formation are its method, so Philosophy (phil_bioethics). Religion is secondary for its theologian founders and board and its formal faith partners (the Muslim Council of Elders, the All-Africa Conference of Churches, Jesuit Worldwide Learning); under B1 it is not Religion, because it does not speak for a tradition. Law is secondary for its human-rights framing of AI governance. Ring: it has a standing AI programme (fellowship, UNESCO subgroup, courses) centred on inclusion and civil-society voice, with no x-risk framing, so adjacent. Transfer: its main effect is to bring its own network of civil society, faith groups, Global South institutions and young leaders into AI-governance conversations through education and dialogue, so convening. Into_builders was considered for the fellowship but is not its main purpose. Framing: its AI page warns of 'deepening inequality and eroding trust', so structural. Standpoint is coded Neither because it is led from Geneva, though its regional centres and stated aims centre the Global South.

name: The University of Osaka Research Center on Ethical, Legal and Social Issues (ELSI Center)
summary: An interdisciplinary university centre, set up in April 2020, that studies the ethical, legal and social issues (ELSI) of emerging technologies. It works through three divisions: general, practice (industry co-creation) and collaborative (public engagement). Its AI work includes a Value and Privacy Impact Assessment (VPIA) process used for data at Expo 2025 Osaka, an AI risk-assessment methodology developed with the Japanese Standards Association, generative-AI risk assessments with Mitsubishi Electric, and studies of public values on AI in healthcare. It publishes the ELSI NOTE series, whose recent notes cover AI child-abuse risk assessment and the governance of AI agents (No. 77, September 2026), and it is a partner in the Horizon Europe AIOLIA project on operationalising AI ethics.
why_it_matters: It offers a worked Japanese model for building humanities and social-science review into R&D together with companies and standards bodies, from impact-assessment processes to risk-assessment methods. Its September 2026 note on keeping governance in step with AI agents shows it beginning to engage with agentic systems.

key_work.title: ELSI NOTE No. 77: 'Can governance keep up with AI agents? Redesigning harnesses and human involvement' (in Japanese)
VPIA: Value and Privacy Impact Assessment for responsible data use at Expo 2025 Osaka (ELSI NOTE 65)

Industry co-creation partners include Mercari, NTT, Mitsubishi Electric, PwC and the Japanese Standards Association.

Much of its AI work is co-created with and funded by companies, which raises questions about independence. It is one of several university ELSI centres set up in Japan's recent 'ELSI boom'.

Philosophy is secondary for its applied-ethics faculty; Safety is secondary because its director's background is risk research and it is building AI risk-assessment methods with the Japanese Standards Association. Transfer: its main products are assessment processes and governance methods for companies and government, so into_institutions. Way of knowing: its distinctive output is practitioner co-creation with industry (VPIA, PIA, risk assessment), so practice rather than interpretive. Standpoint: Japan is coded Neither in v1 (rule O).

name: Doublethink Lab (Taiwan)
summary: A Taipei-based nonprofit, founded in September 2019, that investigates authoritarian (mainly PRC) influence and information manipulation. Its Digital Intelligence team traces AI-generated and cross-platform influence operations with a coalition of OSINT analysts, fact-checkers and journalists, and builds its own AI tools for investigators. Its Global Research team runs the China Index (99 indicators of PRC influence across 101 countries) and the China In The World network. Its Social Engagement team runs audience surveys and focus groups on how propaganda lands in Taiwan. In 2026 it analysed the leaked GoLaxy documents on PRC AI-driven influence operations and a network of 549 fake Threads accounts.
why_it_matters: It produces hard evidence on how states already use AI for influence operations, together with OSINT methods and a whole-of-society resilience framework (Taiwan POWER). AI-safety work on persuasion, epistemic security and misuse could draw on all three.

key_work.title: The Rise of AI in PRC Influence Operations: Nine Takeaways from the GoLaxy Documents
Assessing the Borderless Group's Activity on Threads (549 fake accounts)
China Index 2024: Mapping PRC Influence Across 101 Countries
Taiwan POWER: a model for resilience to foreign information manipulation and interference

funding: USAID grants of about US$1.35 million, reported in Taiwanese media in February 2025. Its site lists no other funders.
status_evidence: Apr 2026: published the analysis of the GoLaxy documents (2 Apr) and of the Borderless Group's 549 fake Threads accounts (28 Apr).
engage: Research published on Medium (medium.com/doublethinklab)
The China In The World network connects civil-society researchers in 101 countries through an annual Summit and a Community Fund
caveats: Its work is politically charged and centred on the PRC. In 2025 Taiwanese opposition figures attacked its US funding. Its former chair resigned in February 2025 after a sexual-harassment complaint, which Taipei labour authorities upheld; the organisation publicly apologised for how it handled the investigation. AI is one line of its work, studied as a tool of state influence rather than as a risk in itself.
tag_notes: Home: it frames information integrity as defence against authoritarian states ('digital defence', FIMI), so Peace rather than Democracy, by the Peace boundary rule ('information integrity to Democracy unless framed as security'). Sub-tradition peace_arms (security studies) was chosen over peace_diplomacy despite its China-studies flagship. MISFIT: FIMI/OSINT investigation has no sub-tradition of its own. Democracy is secondary for its fact-checker coalition and counter-disinformation toolkits. Ring: the Digital Intelligence team traces AI-generated influence operations and builds AI tools, a sustained AI line framed around authoritarian influence rather than AI safety, so adjacent. Transfer: it defends Taiwanese and partner societies from AI-enabled manipulation, so protecting; into_institutions was considered but it does not produce instruments for governing AI. Standpoint: Taiwan is coded Neither in v1 (rule O). No engagement keys are coded because its own site lists no jobs, calls or open events.

name: The Pranava Institute
summary: A New Delhi think tank on emerging technology, policy and society, founded in 2020 by Shyam Krishnakumar and Titiksha Vashist, that works from what it calls an 'India-first' perspective. Its 'Feeling Automated' project, whose report launched in February 2026, studies the legal and societal side of social AI (companions and emotionally responsive chatbots). It combined a literature review, multi-stakeholder consultations and tests of selected systems using personas designed with psychologists, then made policy and design recommendations. Other work includes 'Design Beyond Deception', a manual on dark patterns for designers; a responsible-AI fitness check for India's public sector; the Youth Digital Cultures Lab and its Youth for Tech Futures Fellowship; and tech-geopolitics reports.
why_it_matters: It brings an Indian, design-aware view of manipulation by companion and emotional AI (addictive design, deceptive anthropomorphism, sycophancy and emotional dependency) and ties dark-patterns practice to regulation, a perspective from outside the US and UK.

key_work.title: Feeling Automated: Ethical Development of Emotional & Interactive AI Systems (report and panel)
Design Beyond Deception: a manual of ethical UI/UX principles against deceptive design
Youth Digital Cultures Lab and Youth for Tech Futures Fellowship (with the University of Leeds)
Responsible AI Deployment in the Public Sector (Notre Dame–IBM Tech Ethics Lab project)

The YTF Fellowship is run with the University of Leeds and supported by UKRI and INCLUDE. The French Consulate in Bengaluru and others supported its January 2026 event. Core funding not disclosed.

Its site doesn't state its legal form, and LinkedIn lists it as 'Privately Held', so it may not be a nonprofit. Independent coverage is thin; most details come from its own website and LinkedIn. Its social-AI work is framed around present harms and user safety, not catastrophic risk.

Arts is secondary for its design-research method (Design Beyond Deception, participatory and speculative design in the Youth Digital Cultures Lab). Psych is secondary because its system tests used personas designed with psychologists. Ring: Feeling Automated and the public-sector AI work are sustained AI programmes on present harms without x-risk framing, so adjacent. Transfer: its outputs are policy pathways and design principles for regulators and designers, so into_institutions (J3, ahead of protecting). Org type is coded nonprofit on the basis of its think-tank self-description; legal form unverified.

name: Tattle Civic Technologies (Tattle)
summary: An Indian open-source civic-tech group of technologists, researchers and artists that builds tools and datasets against inaccurate and harmful online content. It started in 2019 with a grant from the AI Ethics Initiative and is registered as a private limited company. Its products include Uli, a browser plugin and crowdsourced slur dataset for responding to online gender-based violence in Indian languages, and the collaboration platform behind the Deepfakes Analysis Unit's WhatsApp tipline. It also runs an 'AI Safety research and consulting' line: it wrote 2,000 Hindi safety prompts for MLCommons' AILuminate benchmark, built the open-source Kaapi Guardrails for NGO chatbots with Project Tech4Dev, and red-teams deployed chatbots, using participatory, multilingual methods.
why_it_matters: It shows how participatory, community-sourced and multilingual methods can produce safety benchmarks, evaluations and guardrails for non-English settings. This fills a gap in English-centric AI-safety evaluations, and it does so for deployments that actually reach low-income users in India.

key_work.title: Hindi safety-benchmark prompts (hate; sex-related crimes) for MLCommons AILuminate
Kaapi Guardrails: open-source safety guardrails for social-sector LLM chatbots (with Project Tech4Dev)

Safety is secondary for its evaluation, red-teaming and guardrail methods. Indigenous & decolonial is secondary for the feminist participatory method behind Uli, which it calls a feminist AI project. Ring changed from adjacent to bridge (rule E3): it runs an explicitly named 'AI Safety research and consulting' programme (MLCommons AILuminate prompts in 2024, Kaapi Guardrails in 2025–26, chatbot red-teaming), though the framing is deployment safety, not x-risk. Transfer: its safety work produces benchmarks, evaluations and guardrails aimed at model behaviour, so into_model. Org type: legally a private limited company (CIN U72900HR2019PTC079285), though it runs as an open-source project. Badge fractal: it contributes to a global safety benchmark while staying rooted in Indian-language communities and grassroots NGOs.

name: <A+> Alliance for Inclusive Algorithms and the Feminist AI Research Network (f<a+i>r)
summary: A global feminist coalition founded in 2019 by Women at the Table (Geneva) and Ciudadanía Inteligente after the 'Affirmative Action for Algorithms' declaration; it has been co-led since 2025 by Women at the Table and Code for Africa. Its Feminist AI Research Network (f<a+i>r), co-led with Instituto Tecnológico de Costa Rica from 2021 to 2024 with IDRC support, produced a body of feminist AI research and prototypes from Latin America, Africa, the Middle East and Asia. Its current Gender & AI Innovation Collective (February 2026 to June 2027) takes African women's rights organisations through a rights-based bootcamp. Selected teams then build prototypes in an AI Innovation Sandbox of open-source models and a curated feminist knowledge base, and keep ownership of what they build.
why_it_matters: It is a Majority-World feminist coalition that has moved from critiquing AI to building it with affected communities. Its replicable paper → prototype → pilot method and user-owned sandbox are a model for participatory, ownership-preserving AI development, which AI safety rarely engages with.

The current programme is time-limited and focused on Africa. Its framing is gender equality and human rights, not AI safety or catastrophic risk.
tag_notes: Home: feminist and decolonial epistemology is its core contribution: 'Feminist AI 101 and decoloniality' bootcamps, a curated feminist knowledge base, and building feminist AI with affected communities. By B8 it therefore stays in Indigenous & decolonial (ind_decolonial) rather than moving to Law. Law is secondary for its human-rights methodology (HUDERIA, rights-based lifecycle tools). Ring: it has a sustained AI programme on gender equality and inclusion with no safety framing, so adjacent. Transfer: like Te Hiku (worked example 6), it equips and defends the women's rights organisations and communities it serves, including tools against tech-facilitated gender-based violence, so protecting. Power is secondary because organisations keep ownership of the AI tools they build. Region: no single headquarters (co-leads in Geneva and Africa, hubs in Latin America and MENA), so Global. Standpoint: its research corpus and current programme centre the Majority World. Grants is coded for the open call offering seed-funded prototypes to eligible African organisations.

name: Neely Center for Ethical Leadership and Decision Making (USC Marshall), with the Psychology of Technology Institute
summary: A behavioural-science centre at USC's Marshall School of Business that studies social media, AI and mixed reality. It runs the Neely Indices, nationally representative longitudinal surveys of people's experiences with these technologies (an AI index since June 2023), and turns the findings into design codes for platforms. It is closely tied to the Psychology of Technology Institute, a network of behavioural scientists and technologists founded in 2016 that runs an annual research conference.
why_it_matters: It measures how people actually experience AI over time, and it has a record of turning behavioural evidence into design codes that the centre says have informed Minnesota policy and Ofcom's online-safety work. Its Knight-funded programme now applies that approach to chatbots. The Psychology of Technology Institute's 2026 conference is co-organised with Berkeley's Center for Human-Compatible AI, so it links social psychology to the AI-safety community.

Psychology of Technology conference: 'Promoting Human Flourishing Through Purpose-Driven AI' (UVA Darden, Nov 2025)
Neely Design Code for Social Media

Claims that the Design Code was adopted into Minnesota law and Ofcom's code come from the centre's own description ('influencing policy'), not checked independently. Most index output still concerns social media rather than AI. It frames AI by present harms and human flourishing, not catastrophic risk.
tag_notes: Home psych/psych_social: led by social and moral psychologists (Fast, Iyer, Schroeder); its AI outputs are behavioural surveys and design codes built on them (H1). Ring adjacent (roster kept): it has a sustained AI programme (AI index since 2023, $4M Knight initiative 2025) framed around wellbeing, harms and 'purpose-driven AI', not safety or catastrophic risk (E3). Transfer into_institutions: its main levers are design codes and policy testimony adopted by regulators, which come before protecting in rule J. Democracy is secondary for its social-cohesion and bridging work. Not on the classic map.

name: Institute for Family Studies (IFS): Family First Technology Initiative
summary: The technology programme of the Institute for Family Studies, a family-policy think tank in Charlottesville, Virginia. It researches how technology affects family life, writes model policy, and campaigns, at first on children's online safety and now increasingly on AI. Its AI outputs include the March 2025 report 'Protecting the Family in the Age of Artificial Intelligence', the Feb 2025 report 'A Future for the Family: A New Technology Agenda for the Right', and a June 2026 Supreme Court amicus brief backing Texas's app-store age law.
why_it_matters: It brings a socially conservative, family-centred constituency into AI governance, and it has a proven route into US state law: IFS says its youth online-safety policy work has produced more than a dozen state laws (2024 Heritage Innovation Prize). AI-safety funders (FLI, SFF) now back it, which shows them trying to widen the political coalition for AI governance beyond tech-policy circles.

key_work.title: Protecting the Family in the Age of Artificial Intelligence (Toscano and Hayden)
A Future for the Family: A New Technology Agenda for the Right (Toscano, Littlejohn, Waters, Morell, Askonas)
Supreme Court amicus brief supporting the Texas App Store safety law

people: Michael Toscano (Senior Fellow and Director, Family First Technology Initiative)
Jared Hayden (Policy Analyst, Family First Technology Initiative; co-author of the AI report and amicus brief)
funding: FLI 2025 grant of $550,000 for the 'Pro-Family, Pro-Human AI' project; SFF 2026 recommendation of $295,000 to IFS (general support, Freedom track; funded by Jaan Tallinn).
status_evidence: Jun 2026: filed a US Supreme Court amicus brief supporting the Texas App Store safety law; Jun 2026: published 'Simulated Spirituality: How AI Is Shaping Religious Practice'.
caveats: IFS is a socially conservative think tank, and one report is explicitly framed as an agenda 'for the Right', so many potential partners will find its positions on family and gender contested. The SFF 2026 grant is general support to IFS, not earmarked for the initiative. Its AI framing is family protection and human flourishing, not catastrophic risk. The founding years of IFS and of the initiative were not confirmed.
tag_notes: Home law/law_legal: its main outputs are model legislation, state-law campaigns and amicus briefs on children's online safety and AI (H1, B9: children's-rights law goes to Law). Religion is secondary for its Christian social-thought collaborators and its work on AI and religious practice. MISFIT: socially conservative family-policy thought has no tradition key. Ring adjacent (roster kept): it has a sustained AI line (two 2025 reports, a funded FLI project) framed around family protection, not safety or catastrophic risk (E3), although its AI-safety funders put it on the bridge seam. Transfer protecting: the work exists to defend families and children from technology's effects (J4). Not on the classic map.

name: Hybrid Intelligence Centre
summary: A ten-year Dutch research consortium (NWO Gravitation programme, 2020-2029), based at VU Amsterdam, on AI that augments human intellect instead of replacing it. Seven universities take part: VU, Amsterdam, TU Delft, Groningen, Leiden, Utrecht and Twente. It works on four themes: collaborative, adaptive, responsible and explainable hybrid intelligence. That covers human-agent teams, value inference by language models, and building ethics into system design.
why_it_matters: It treats human-AI teaming, mutual explainability and value alignment as one research problem, drawing on multi-agent systems, cognitive science and ethics, and it trains a large group of PhD researchers to work this way. Its work on keeping human agency central bears on human oversight and on avoiding humans being sidelined as AI agents spread.

key_work.title: Developing Guidelines for Human-LLM Agent Teams: A Multi-Stakeholder Lens (AAMAS 2026 Best Paper)
NWO Veni grant to Enrico Liscio for value alignment in multi-turn language-model interaction
Responsible HI toolkit: responsible research practices, socio-technical reflection exercises, ProtoStrategos game

Frank van Harmelen (Executive Board, community building; VU Amsterdam)
Birna van Riemsdijk (lead contact, Responsible HI)

status_evidence: Aug 2026: Best Student Paper award at ICCC 2026; Jul 2026: NWO Veni grant to Enrico Liscio for value-alignment research; May 2026: AAMAS 2026 Best Paper.
engage: PhD and postdoc positions (more than 20 recruited from 2025, with some expected late 2025 to early 2026; see the recruitment page)
caveats: This is mainstream academic AI research with a responsible-AI emphasis, not AI-safety work; it does not use catastrophic-risk framing. Funding ends in 2029. The grant amount and headcount were not confirmed.
tag_notes: Home psych/psych_cognitive: its AI work rests on human-machine teaming, theory of mind and mutual understanding between agents and people (H2, B5). Philosophy is secondary for the Responsible HI theme and the TU Delft ethics projects. Ring adjacent (roster kept): it is a sustained AI programme framed as augmenting rather than replacing humans and as responsible AI, without safety, catastrophic-risk or alignment framing at programme level, though individual projects study value alignment (E3). Transfer into_model: it designs agents, LLM teams and value-inference methods (J1). Org type programme: a time-limited research-council consortium (I). Not on the classic map.

name: Weizenbaum Institute (Weizenbaum-Institut e.V.)
summary: A Berlin research institute on the networked society, founded in 2017 as a consortium of FU, HU, TU and UdK Berlin, the University of Potsdam, WZB and Fraunhofer FOKUS. It is funded by the federal research ministry and the State of Berlin. Its four focus areas cover digital technologies in society, platform markets and public spheres, organising knowledge (including a 'Working with Artificial Intelligence' group) and digital infrastructures in democracy. Recent AI work covers generative AI and society, democratic control of AI and gendered disinformation, and it continues Joseph Weizenbaum's tradition of computer criticism.
why_it_matters: It brings STS, communication science and labour sociology to questions of who controls AI and what it does to democracy and the public sphere. It also offers a critical view of industry narratives, such as its Sept 2026 analysis of the interests behind calls to slow AI, which the safety field rarely examines. It is a large, well-funded research hub in Berlin, close to int/a's community there.

key_work.title: Weizenbaum Conference 2026: 'Generative AI and Society: What is at stake?'
Workshop 'The Rulers and the Commons: AI and the Question of Democratic Control' with Cecilia Rikap (23 Oct 2026)
'60 years of ELIZA, 50 years of computer criticism' programme
GENDIS: research project with TUM on gender-specific disinformation

people: Christoph Neuberger (Scientific Managing Director and Spokesperson)
funding: Federal Ministry of Research (BMBF, now BMFTR) about EUR 36m and State of Berlin about EUR 3.5m for 2022-2025 (German Wikipedia).
status_evidence: Sep 2026: interview 'Was steckt hinter dem Ruf nach einer Verlangsamung der KI-Entwicklung?' (24 Sep) and launch of the GENDIS project (21 Sep); workshop with Cecilia Rikap scheduled for 23 Oct 2026.
engage: Weizenbaum Conference (annual; 2026 edition on generative AI and society, 10-11 Jun 2026)
Public lectures, book presentations and workshops in Berlin (e.g. Distinguished Lecture by Zizi Papacharissi, 16 Sep 2026)
caveats: Its stance on AI is critical and sociological; it does not use catastrophic-risk framing, and some of its analysis is sceptical of industry calls to slow AI. The 'large' scale is inferred from its budget and 21 research groups in the setup phase. Funding figures after 2025 were not confirmed.
tag_notes: Home law/law_sts: its AI work comes from STS, sociology, communication science and critical computing (H1; the taxonomy's law_sts example). Democracy and economics are secondary for its public-sphere and labour/platform-economy groups. Ring adjacent (roster kept): a sustained AI research line on democracy, work and platforms with no safety or catastrophic-risk framing (E3). Transfer into_institutions: its research and convening aim at democratic governance of digital infrastructures and AI (J3). Org type academic: a publicly funded joint research institute of Berlin universities and research organisations (I). Not on the classic map.

name: Deutscher Ethikrat (German Ethics Council)
summary: Germany's statutory national ethics council, set up on 11 April 2008 under the Ethics Council Act as successor to the National Ethics Council of 2001. Its 26 members, appointed by the President of the Bundestag, come from law, medicine, theology, philosophy and the social sciences. It issues opinions and recommendations and holds public hearings and conferences. Its main AI output is the March 2023 opinion 'Humans and Machines: Challenges of Artificial Intelligence', on whether AI expands or diminishes human authorship and responsible action in medicine, schools, public communication and administration. In June 2026 it issued an ad hoc statement on children and adolescents in the digital world.
why_it_matters: It shows a pluralist, statutory process for public ethical deliberation on AI, bringing together law, theology, medicine and philosophy, of a kind the AI-safety field has few equivalents for. Its lens of human authorship and responsible agency gives a philosophical-anthropological vocabulary for loss of human agency as AI spreads.

key_work.title: Humans and Machines: Challenges of Artificial Intelligence (Opinion)
Ad hoc statement on protection, participation and empowerment of children and adolescents in the digital world
Web event 'Power and Images: AI and Political Opinion Formation'

funding: Public (federal) funding under the Ethics Council Act; amount not found.
status_evidence: Jun 2026: ad hoc statement on children and adolescents in the digital world (11 Jun); plenary 17-18 Sep 2026 and autumn conference in Leipzig 11 Nov 2026 scheduled.
engage: Public annual and autumn conferences (2026 annual conference on protecting and strengthening democracy; autumn conference 11 Nov 2026, Leipzig)
Public web events and hearings on its topics (AI events in Dec 2023 and Jun 2024)
caveats: AI is one of many topics. Its dedicated AI output is thin after the 2023 opinion: a 2024 web event and a 2026 statement on children's digital lives whose AI content was not confirmed. Members are appointed and change over time. Only the council's own site was checked.
tag_notes: Home philosophy/phil_bioethics: ethics councils go to Philosophy (B13; the taxonomy's own example), and its AI opinion is philosophical-anthropological argument about authorship and responsibility. Law is secondary because the chair and many members are lawyers. Ring adjacent (roster kept, borderline): AI and digital topics recur as a publication and convening line (opinions in 2020 and 2023, events in 2023 and 2024, a 2026 statement on children in the digital world) without safety or catastrophic framing (E3); if 2025-26 AI activity is judged too thin, this would drop to potential. Transfer into_institutions: its opinions advise the Bundestag and federal government (J3). Org type public: statutory council (I). Not on the classic map.

name: IEEE Global Initiative 2.0 on Ethics of Autonomous and Intelligent Systems
summary: An IEEE Standards Association Industry Connections activity (IC16-002), renewed in 2023. It builds on the original Global Initiative, which produced Ethically Aligned Design and led to the IEEE 7000 series of standards. The 2.0 plan aims to move AI governance 'beyond risk framing' towards a safety-first, safety-by-design principle. It has four workstreams: new standards for generative AI and large language models, sector toolkits linked to IEEE conformity assessment, an 'AI Safety Champions' community, and wider use of the 7000-series standards.
why_it_matters: It is a route by which ethical principles become engineering standards and certification. Its predecessor's Ethically Aligned Design included a chapter on classical and non-Western ethical traditions and fed into wellbeing-metric standards. For the int/a map it shows how pluralist ethics can enter technical standards, though current activity is hard to verify.

key_work.title: Ethically Aligned Design, First Edition (predecessor initiative's report)
IEEE 7000 series of standards on ethical concerns in system design
Planned report: 'Beyond Risk Framing in AI Governance' (not yet published)

funding: Hosted by the IEEE Standards Association; no separate budget found.
status_evidence: No dated 2024-26 output from the 2.0 activity found: its group site lists no upcoming events, and the planned 'Beyond Risk Framing' report is unpublished. The wider IEEE SA AI programme is active (IEEE AI Standardization and Responsible AI Assurance workshop, Melbourne, 7 Sep 2026).
engage: Participation open to anyone involved in researching, designing or deciding on intelligent systems, via the interest form on the activity page
caveats: Activity is unverified: the activity page describes the 2.0 plan agreed in 2023, but no 2024-26 deliverables, meetings or AI Safety Champions outputs were found. It is not listed among current Industry Connections activities, nor among closed ones. 'Safety' here means engineering and product safety, not catastrophic risk. The 2019 date for Ethically Aligned Design 1e and the 2016 founding rest on the predecessor initiative and its IC16 code.
tag_notes: Home philosophy/phil_bioethics: phil_bioethics explicitly includes engineering-ethics initiatives, and its core contribution is applied ethics (Ethically Aligned Design) carried into standards. Safety is secondary for standards and certification work. Ring adjacent (roster kept): its stated aims use 'safety-first' and 'safety by design' language, which by E3 could make it bridge, but no sustained 2024-26 programme activity could be verified, so it is not upgraded. Transfer into_institutions: its outputs are standards and toolkits that govern how people build systems (J3). Region by IEEE SA headquarters (O). Status unverified because the public activity site is minimal.

name: RInCA (Responsible Innovation with Conscience and Agility), JST-RISTEX
summary: A public R&D funding programme of the Japan Science and Technology Agency's Research Institute of Science and Technology for Society (RISTEX), running since FY2020. It funds research on the ethical, legal and social implications (ELSI) of emerging science and technology, and models of responsible research and innovation. Since then it has supported 25 R&D projects (about JPY 6-12m a year each in direct costs) and 28 feasibility studies. AI-related projects include Kyoto University's 'Autonomy and Affinity in AI Development and Use' (2021-2025) and a 2023 project on the ELSI of intimate relationships between humans and 'co-habitant' robots.
why_it_matters: It is a non-Western public funder that has built ELSI and responsible-innovation research into a standing programme. Its AI projects pair philosophers, lawyers and engineers on human autonomy and human-robot intimacy. It offers new funders a model of anticipatory, co-creative ELSI funding, and a route to Japanese perspectives on AI and society.

key_work.title: Autonomy and Affinity in AI Development and Use (PI Usami Makoto, Kyoto University; Oct 2021-Mar 2025)
Transdisciplinary Study on the ELSI of Building Intimate Relationship between Humans and 'Co-Habitant' Robots (PI Inatani Tatsuhiko, Kyoto University)
RInCA Journal #06

people: Kaori Karasawa (Programme Supervisor; Professor Emerita, University of Tokyo)
Makoto Usami (PI, AI autonomy project; Kyoto University)
funding: Japanese government via JST-RISTEX; R&D projects about JPY 6-12m a year each (direct costs), feasibility studies about JPY 3m per half-year.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: RInCA Essay #30 published; Apr 2026: RInCA Journal #06; Sep 2025: two new projects selected for FY2025.
engage: Annual funding calls for R&D projects and feasibility studies (open to Japan-based researchers; FY2025 projects selected Sep 2025)
RInCA Journal and essay series
caveats: AI is a minority strand: of 25 projects, only a few concern AI, robots or data (AI autonomy 2021-25, co-habitant robots 2023, educational data 2022, automated driving 2020). Most concern biomedicine, infectious disease and environmental technology. Calls are for researchers in Japan. No independent source was checked beyond JST's own pages.
tag_notes: Home law/law_policy: a one-programme ELSI/RRI funder, so its home is the tradition of the work it funds (H4; law_policy explicitly covers ELSI funders). Philosophy is secondary because its AI project is led by legal, moral and political philosophers. Ring adjacent (roster kept, borderline): it has funded AI and robot ELSI projects continuously since 2021 without safety or catastrophic framing (E3); since AI is a small share of its portfolio, potential would also be defensible. Transfer into_institutions: the funded work produces RRI practice models and conduct guidelines for AI development (J3, funders by the work they fund). Framing flourishing per its mission of technology creating value in harmony with people and society (L). Standpoint neither (Japan, O).

name: FEST – Forschungsstätte der Evangelischen Studiengemeinschaft
summary: The interdisciplinary research institute of Germany's Protestant church, founded in Heidelberg in 1958 and funded mainly by the EKD, its regional churches, the Kirchentag and the Protestant academies. Its four departments cover peace, sustainable development, religion, law and culture, and theology and natural science. Its AI-related output is thin: a digital-theology research field (digital church, computational theology, the Cursor_ platform) and a 2026 peace-ethics working paper on unmanned weapons.
why_it_matters: It holds German Protestant 'just peace' and military ethics and a long theology–science dialogue, and could bring church-backed ethical reasoning on autonomous weapons and human personhood into AI security debates. Through the EKD it also reaches a large church constituency that AI-safety work rarely addresses.

key_work.title: Unbemannte Waffen und ihre ethischen Implikationen: Betrachtungen revisited (Heidelberger Forum zur Friedensethik, Working Paper 8, ed. Ines-Jacqueline Werkner)
Digital theology research field (digital church, computational theology, Cursor_, SysLex, Global Network for Digital Theology)

people: Ines-Jacqueline Werkner (peace research; editor of the unmanned-weapons working paper)
funding: Core funding from the members of its sponsoring association (EKD, the EKD regional churches, the German Protestant Kirchentag and the Protestant academies), plus third-party project funding.
status_evidence: 2026: published Heidelberger Forum zur Friedensethik Working Paper 8 on unmanned weapons; FEST Briefing on democracy scheduled for 5 Oct 2026; Newsletter 2/2026.
engage: No AI programme: outreach would go to the Peace department (just peace, military and peace) or the Religion, Law and Culture department (digital theology)
FEST Briefing public events (e.g. democracy, 5 Oct 2026; climate-neutral church, 2 Nov 2026), with no AI strand
caveats: AI engagement is light: the digital-theology pages do not mention AI, and the 2026 working paper concerns unmanned weapons generally rather than AI specifically. No dedicated AI project found. Staff size not published.
tag_notes: Home peace, changed from provisional religion: its only dated AI-adjacent output (2026 working paper on unmanned weapons) is church-founded peace ethics, which B11 places in Peace; religion is kept as secondary for the theology and digital-theology work (A2). Ring potential (kept): no standing AI programme in 2024-26, only one weapons-ethics paper and a digital-theology field that does not address AI. Transferable method: Protestant just-peace and military ethics plus theology–science dialogue on personhood, applicable to autonomous weapons and human dignity alongside AI. Transfer convening (J5): its outputs feed EKD peace ethics and church debate rather than models or governance instruments.

name: Institut de recherche et d'innovation (IRI), Centre Pompidou
summary: A Paris research association created at the Centre Pompidou in 2006 on the initiative of the philosopher Bernard Stiegler, independent since 2008. It works on 'digital studies', contributory research and annotation software (Lignes de temps), and runs the annual Entretiens du Nouveau Monde Industriel (ENMI). ENMI 2025 was devoted to generative AI ('artificial synthesis and human contribution'), arguing that models depend on human contribution and calling for a contributory economy of knowledge; ENMI 2026 ('La clinique des objets') includes sessions on physical AI, robotics and computing.
why_it_matters: It carries Stiegler's 'pharmacological' philosophy of technology, which analyses how automation erodes human knowledge and attention ('proletarianisation') and proposes a contributory economy in response, a line of thought almost absent from AI-safety discourse. It also convenes philosophers, designers and economists in Paris every year.

key_work.title: ENMI 2025: Synthèse artificielle et contribution humaine (CNAM, Paris, 16–17 Dec 2025)
ENMI 2026: La clinique des objets (Cité des sciences, Paris, 14–15 Dec 2026), with a session on physical AI and robotics
ENMI préparatoires 2026 seminars (ENSCI, 25–26 June 2026)

funding: Independent research association since August 2008, whose board (administrators) included the Centre Pompidou, CCCB Barcelona, Microsoft France, Goldsmiths, the University of Tokyo, Institut Télécom and ENSCI; most research projects are funded through ANR, FUI and European calls.
status_evidence: Jun 2026: ENMI préparatoires seminars at ENSCI, Paris; ENMI 2026 scheduled for 14–15 Dec 2026 with registration open.
engage: ENMI 2026, 14–15 Dec 2026, Cité des sciences et de l'industrie, Paris, with remote participation
ENMI preparatory seminars each June in Paris, joinable remotely via BigBlueButton
caveats: Founder Bernard Stiegler died in 2020; current leadership is from Wikipedia and may be out of date, and the website's project and team pages are sparse. Its AI work is critical of the AI industry's extractive model rather than framed around safety. Ring changed from the roster's potential to adjacent.
tag_notes: Home philosophy (phil_technology): ENMI's AI sessions are built on Stiegler's pharmacology and Simondon; arts secondary for its design-school partners (ENSCI, EnsadLab) and annotation tools, economics for the contributory-economy line (C). Ring changed from potential to adjacent: ENMI 2025 was entirely about generative AI and ENMI 2026 continues with AI and robotics sessions, a repeated convening in 2025-26 (E2), with no safety or catastrophic framing (E3). Transfer convening (J5): it brings continental philosophers, designers and economists into the AI conversation through its annual conference.

name: FBK Center for Religious Studies (FBK-ISR), Fondazione Bruno Kessler
summary: A non-confessional research centre on religion in Trento, founded in 1975 and part of the Fondazione Bruno Kessler since 2007; it is financed mainly by the Autonomous Province of Trento and has a team of about 15 (ten researchers plus fellows, a PhD student and an intern) under director Massimo Leone. Its AI work is occasional: a 2020 response to the EU AI White Paper and a 2021 policy paper on religious and belief actors in AI policy, a 2026 seminar cycle and conference on solitude that treat chatbots as a new 'technique of solitude', and a project with Georgetown on faith-based healthcare that discusses AI in medicine.
why_it_matters: Its religious-studies and ethics research on solitude and communion bears directly on AI companionship and loneliness, which AI-safety work treats mostly as a product-harm issue. It has also worked on how religious and belief actors can take part in EU AI policy.

key_work.title: Policy paper: Shaping the AI Transformation: The Agency of Religious and Belief Actors
International conference 'The Lonesome Meaning' (Trento, 15–18 Dec 2026), with a strand on chatbots and AI
Seminar 'Techniques of Solitude: From Ascetics to Artificial Intelligence' (Solitude and Communion in Religion and Ethics cycle)
Global Faith-Based Healthcare Systems meeting, with Georgetown University

funding: Financed mainly by the Autonomous Province of Trento through FBK; the 2026 solitude seminar cycle and conference are supported by the Italian Ministry of Culture.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: Boris Rähme spoke on religion and AI at the University of Urbino; 19 Oct 2026 seminar on techniques of solitude and AI; conference scheduled for 15–18 Dec 2026.
engage: 'The Lonesome Meaning' conference, Trento, 15–18 Dec 2026
Solitude and Communion in Religion and Ethics seminar cycle, held in hybrid format
Conference grants for doctoral researchers in religious studies and related fields
caveats: AI is one strand among many, and its dedicated AI-policy work dates from 2020–21. The faith-based healthcare project's countries (Bangladesh, Kenya, India) come from the roster and were not confirmed on the project page.
tag_notes: Home religion (H1): its method is religious studies and ethics; philosophy secondary for the moral-philosophy seminar cycle. MISFIT: there is no sub-tradition for non-confessional academic religious studies; rel_interfaith is the closest. Ring potential (kept): in 2025-26 AI appears as one strand of a solitude seminar cycle and conference, in a single talk and in a healthcare meeting, not as a standing programme (E2). Transferable method: religious-studies and ethical analysis of solitude, communion and spiritual practice, applicable to AI companionship and loneliness. Transfer convening (J5). Org type academic (rule I: unit of a public research foundation). Framing flourishing is a low-confidence call: the work treats AI-mediated solitude as ambivalent rather than mainly as harm.

name: Omidyar Network
summary: A philanthropic investment firm (foundation plus LLC) founded in 2004 by Pierre and Pam Omidyar, which has committed more than $1.9bn and organises its work around the culture, governance and business of technology. Its AI grantmaking funds groups challenging concentrated tech power, worker voice and online safety (e.g. AI Now, Americans for Responsible Innovation, TechEquity), and it is one of ten founding partners of Humanity AI, a $500m five-year pooled fund. It endorsed New York's RAISE Act and California's 2025 AI bills, and condemned the December 2025 executive order against state AI regulation.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few public-interest technology funders that has also publicly backed frontier-safety legislation, so it links the power-and-accountability side of AI governance with safety policy. For new funders it is an established route into political-economy, labour and civil-society work on AI.

key_work.title: Founding partner of Humanity AI ($500m five-year pooled fund); May 2026 announcement of $18m in grants
Endorsement of New York's RAISE Act
Statement condemning the Trump executive order on state AI regulation
Humanity AI $10m open call for community-led projects

funding: Endowed by Pierre and Pam Omidyar; more than $1.9bn committed since founding (2026). Founding partner of Humanity AI ($500m over five years), which in May 2026 announced $18m: $8m to nine inaugural grantees and Data & Society/DPLA, plus a $10m open call.
status_evidence: 10 Sep 2026: announced Humanity AI's $10m open call; 11 Mar 2026: appointed Michele L. Jawando CEO.
engage: Humanity AI open call: $10m for US nonprofits working on education, labour and economy, or humanities, arts and culture; deadline 21 Oct 2026 (administered by Humanity AI)
Staff roles: https://omidyar.com/who-we-are/our-team/join-our-team/
caveats: Its own site lists Anthropic among the shareholdings in its Business of Tech portfolio, a possible conflict for safety-policy positions. The May 2026 $18m was granted through Humanity AI, the pooled fund, not by Omidyar alone. Wikipedia reports it ended its India operations in 2024 after government investigations. It took a new CEO in March 2026.
tag_notes: Home economics (H4, econ_power): its governance and business-of-tech lines fund 'groups challenging the concentration of tech power' and worker voice; law secondary for rights and accountability grantees (CDT, AI Now, Data & Society), democracy for AI Civics and democratic safeguards (C). Ring adjacent (kept): sustained AI grantmaking framed around public interest and shared power; endorsing the RAISE Act is advocacy, not a safety programme (E3). Transfer into_institutions (J3, funders by the work they fund): legislation, enforcement and governance. Flag for rule K: broad AI portfolio and Humanity AI founding partner, so a possible generalist-funder candidate.

name: Responsible AI UK (RAi UK)
summary: A UK research network hosted at the University of Southampton and funded by a £30.7m EPSRC grant running from April 2023 to June 2028. It funds and connects multidisciplinary research on responsible AI: keystone projects such as PHAWM (participatory harm auditing) and PROBabLE Futures (AI in law enforcement), plus enterprise fellowships, skills programmes, research sandpits and international partnerships. Its leaders also publish policy commentary, including a 2026 piece calling for legal powers to require frontier-model assessment after, as the piece reports, Anthropic declined a UK AISI evaluation.
why_it_matters: It is a large, publicly funded socio-technical network with participatory auditing methods and expertise in law, social science and HCI. Its leadership has begun commenting on frontier-AI assessment, so it could connect the UK's responsible-AI and AI-safety communities.

key_work.title: PHAWM: Participatory Harm Auditing Workbenches and Methodologies (keystone project)
PROBabLE Futures: probabilistic AI systems in law enforcement (keystone project)
Anthropic's AISI refusal heralds the end of the road for mutual collaboration on frontier AI assessment

name: WASP-HS (Wallenberg AI, Autonomous Systems and Software Program – Humanity and Society)
summary: Sweden's largest research programme on AI and society, funded by the Wallenberg Foundations as the humanities and social-science counterpart to the WASP engineering programme. It funds nine multi-university research environments (among them AI, Power and Politics; The AI Welfare State; The Rule of AI; Child Development in the Age of AI; Agentic AI for Humanistic Futures), a graduate school with over 100 PhD students from 19 Swedish universities, guest professorships, and postdoctoral scholarships at MIT and Stanford.
why_it_matters: It provides large, long-term humanities and social-science funding on AI, with themes on power, the welfare state and agentic AI that overlap with gradual-disempowerment concerns. Its 100+ PhD students are a pipeline of social scientists and humanists who know AI.

name: Project Liberty Institute
summary: The research and policy arm of Frank McCourt's Project Liberty: an independent 501(c)(3), formerly the McCourt Institute, led by president Tomicah Tillemann. It backs the Decentralized Social Networking Protocol (DSNP), promoted the Digital Choice Act on data portability and interoperability (enacted in Utah and South Dakota, and extended to AI in Virginia), and runs a responsible-AI investment process with more than 200 investors, which it presented at the OECD in 2026. It also publishes reports on digital infrastructure for 'middle power' governments and on data cooperatives in South-East Asia.
why_it_matters: It works against AI-era lock-in and loss of human agency through levers already in use: enacted state law, an open protocol, and steering investment towards a 'pro-human AI stack'. This is concrete counter-power-concentration work that x-risk governance seldom touches.

name: Future of Life Institute (FLI)
summary: Nonprofit founded in 2014 to steer transformative technologies away from extreme, large-scale risks. It does this through policy advocacy, public campaigns, events and grantmaking. Its recent grant rounds go well beyond technical safety: 16 grants (about $1.46M, decided May 2026) went to faith projects across Christian (Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, evangelical, Latter-day Saint), Jewish, Muslim and Hindu traditions to set moral red lines against an AGI race. Other rounds cover multistakeholder engagement (14 grants) and AI-driven power concentration (13 grants). Its Futures Program, led by Emilia Javorsky, uses worldbuilding, scenarios and creative contests to picture good futures with AI.
why_it_matters: FLI is the x-risk funder most visibly moving money into religion, family and child-wellbeing groups, journalism, creators and political economy. That makes it the clearest existing route from AI-safety money into the adjacent traditions this map covers. Its Religious Projects round sets a template that other funders could copy for other traditions.

Its endowment came from a single crypto donation.

Secondary traditions are the areas it funds most: law and civil society (multistakeholder engagement), psych (Institute for Family Studies, Common Sense Media), arts (Futures Program, Digital Media Accelerator, Bureau of Investigative Journalism) and economics (power-concentration grants). name: Coefficient Giving (CG; formerly Open Philanthropy)
summary: Grantmaking foundation in San Francisco, funded mainly by Dustin Moskovitz and Cari Tuna's Good Ventures. Founded in 2011 as GiveWell Labs, it was known as Open Philanthropy until it renamed itself in November 2025 and opened to other donors as a set of multi-donor funds. It is the largest funder of AI-safety and governance work. Project Tailwind backs founders of new AI-safety organisations at three stages: pre-seed ($200k to $2M), seed ($2M to $20M) and scale ($20M to $200M). It also runs an RFP on AI for forecasting and sound reasoning, and lists 'AI for decision-making' as a Tailwind target area.
why_it_matters: Most of the money for founding new AI-safety organisations comes from CG, and nothing public suggests Project Tailwind looks beyond ML and policy for founders. A legible list of problems from adjacent fields is exactly the input that could widen what it funds.

name: Schmidt Sciences
summary: Science philanthropy funded by Eric and Wendy Schmidt, spun out of Schmidt Futures in 2024. AI and advanced computing is one of its five centres. Its AI programmes include AI2050 fellowships (28 fellows announced on 1 October 2026, up to $16M), Science of Trustworthy AI, AI interpretability, multi-agent AI and a multi-agent safety RFP of up to $1M run with Google DeepMind, ARIA and CAIF, and AI at Work. It also runs the Humanities and AI Virtual Institute (HAVI), which gave $11M to 23 teams in December 2025.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few large AI-safety funders that also pays humanists and social scientists, through AI2050 fellows such as Alondra Nelson and David Danks, and through HAVI. That makes it a natural home for proposals that bring humanistic or social-science methods to AI going well. But HAVI so far funds mainly AI tools for humanities research, not humanities insight into AI.

name: OpenAI Foundation
summary: The nonprofit that controls OpenAI Group PBC, renamed and recapitalised on 28 October 2025. It holds about 26% of the company's equity and appoints the company's board. It has committed $25B to curing diseases and AI resilience, and planned at least $1B of spending over the year from March 2026. That spending covers four areas: life sciences, jobs and economic impact, AI resilience, and community support. AI resilience is led by OpenAI co-founder Wojciech Zaremba and covers biosecurity, cybersecurity, AI model behaviour and effects on young people; more than $130M of grants were being finalised in June 2026.
why_it_matters: A very large new funder whose AI-resilience remit explicitly includes institutional coordination and societal safeguards, not technical alignment alone. Youth effects, jobs and civil society are int/a territory, if proposals can reach it. Its closeness to OpenAI's commercial interests is the main question for anyone seeking or assessing its funding.

name: CIFAR: Canadian AI Safety Institute (CAISI) Research Program
summary: The research arm of the Canadian AI Safety Institute, which was announced in November 2024. It is led by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) and administered by CIFAR, the Toronto research institute founded in 1982. It funds AI Safety Catalyst Grants, three-year cross-sector Solution Networks, and Canadian projects in the UK-led Alignment Project. By early 2026 it was funding projects on disinformation, companion-chatbot risks, AI-generated fake evidence in courts, dialect bias in language models, Indigenous data sovereignty, and political persuasion by AI.
why_it_matters: A public AI-safety funder outside the UK and US that treats safety as sociotechnical. Its funded teams combine computer science with sociology, law, psychology, political science and Indigenous governance. That makes it a working model of the interdisciplinary safety funding int/a wants to see more widely.

name: G20 Interfaith Forum (IF20)
summary: A platform, run by the G20 Interfaith Forum Association from Washington DC, that has met each year since 2014 alongside the G20 host country. In September it published the policy paper 'AI Innovation and Human Dignity' for the US G20 presidency.

name: KAICIID International Dialogue Centre
summary: Intergovernmental organisation founded in 2012 by Saudi Arabia, Austria and Spain, with the Holy See as founding observer. Its board is made up of religious leaders from Christianity, Islam, Judaism, Buddhism and Hinduism, and it moved from Vienna to Lisbon in 2022. It uses interreligious dialogue for conflict prevention, peacebuilding and social cohesion. Its work includes a Fellows Programme (since 2015), regional platforms such as the Interreligious Platform for Dialogue and Cooperation in the Arab World (IPDC), and e-learning. Its AI engagement so far is a May 2026 webinar on ethics, empathy and AI, and the IPDC's adoption of social media and AI as a priority in September 2026.
why_it_matters: It has more than a decade of experience mediating between rival religious communities and training faith leaders in dialogue, which are methods relevant to polarisation and AI-driven hate speech. It has a direct line to senior Muslim and Christian leaders and to the Holy See. It has only begun to touch AI.

name: Fundación Vía Libre
summary: An Argentine nonprofit, founded in Córdoba in 2000, that defends fundamental rights wherever information technology shapes daily life. Its work covers privacy, free expression, electronic voting, access to culture and AI, and it has been the Creative Commons affiliate for Argentina since 2011. Its AI work includes EDIA, an open no-code tool (2022) that lets social scientists probe stereotypes in Spanish- and English-language models. It also scrutinises Buenos Aires's facial-recognition system, wrote a UNESCO-commissioned paper on digital and AI sovereignty (2026), and runs public events on AI and democracy.
why_it_matters: It speaks for Latin American digital rights and free culture, and is an informed sceptic of x-risk discourse. That makes it useful for seeing how AI-safety framings land in the Global South. EDIA is a working model of putting model audits in the hands of domain experts rather than ML engineers.
