tag_notes: Home: a digital-rights organisation whose AI work runs through rights advocacy, judicial scrutiny of facial recognition and congressional hearings, so Law (H1). Its Global South location shows in region and standpoint, not in tradition (B8). Economics is secondary for its free-culture and commons identity (Creative Commons affiliate; it argues for small, open, community models). Ring: a sustained AI programme on rights, bias and sovereignty with no safety framing, and it rejects x-risk framing, so adjacent (kept from roster). Transfer: it defends the people it serves from surveillance and discrimination, so protecting (the boundary on into_institutions). Assurance is paired with justice because EDIA is an evaluation tool (rule F). Framing is present_harms because its critique of x-risk discourse serves a harms agenda (rule L).

name: LIRNEasia
summary: A nonprofit think tank on ICT policy and regulation, based in Colombo. Rohan Samarajiva founded it in 2004, and it works across South and Southeast Asia. Since February 2026 it has led the three-year Asia AI4D Observatory, with the East-West Management Institute and JustJobs Network, funded by Canada's IDRC and the UK's FCDO. The Observatory maps AI enablers, builds a repository of responsible-AI use cases and trains policymakers. Other AI work includes the Asia report for the Global Index on Responsible AI (2025), research on AI exposure in labour markets and on data governance, and misinformation classifiers for Sinhala and Bengali.
why_it_matters: It is an established route into evidence-based AI policy research in non-Anglophone Asia, built on nationally representative demand-side surveys. It shows how 'safe, rights-based, inclusive' AI is being defined for countries the AI-safety field rarely consults.

key_work.title: Asia AI4D Observatory on Responsible AI Innovations for Development
Responsible AI in Asia (regional report for the Global Index on Responsible AI)
Measuring AI exposure in the labour market
Misinformation and language resources programme (datasets and classifiers for regional languages)

people: Merl Chandana (Senior Research Manager; lead author, Responsible AI in Asia)
funding: The Asia AI4D Observatory (2026-29) is funded by Canada's IDRC and the UK's FCDO. The Responsible AI in Asia report was funded by the Global Center on AI Governance (2025). IDRC funded a 2021 scoping study on information disorder. No budget figures were found.
status_evidence: Oct 2026: advertising a Senior Researcher post. Sep 2026: request for proposals to build the Asia AI4D Observatory website (deadline 29 Sep 2026), and a report from WAIC 2026 in Shanghai.
engage: Staff roles: Senior Researcher (Oct 2026) and Intern, Data Annotation (Sep 2026)
The Asia AI4D Observatory plans communities of practice, training and advisory support for policymakers (2026-29)
caveats: AI is one theme among many (agriculture, social protection, disability, education). Its 'responsible AI' framing includes safety but has no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing. The Observatory began in 2026 and its platform is still being built. Staff numbers were not found.
tag_notes: Home: a development-studies policy institute whose main AI line, the AI4D Observatory, is about rights-based, inclusive governance, so law_policy (H2, B9). I moved it from the provisional Economics because its AI work is mainly governance rather than economics; Economics stays secondary for its labour-exposure and platform-work research, and Democracy for its misinformation work (dem_epistemics). Ring: a sustained AI programme (Observatory, responsible-AI index, data governance) with no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing, so adjacent (kept from roster). Transfer: its stated aim is to inform inclusive AI policies and regulation in Asia, so into_institutions. No MISFIT.

name: Flowers AI & CogSci Lab (Inria / University of Bordeaux)
summary: An Inria project-team in Talence, near Bordeaux, run jointly with the University of Bordeaux and ENSTA and led by Pierre-Yves Oudeyer. Inria's 2024 report put it at roughly 40-45 members. It studies curiosity-driven, open-ended learning in children and machines. It builds 'autotelic' agents that set their own goals, including agents built on LLMs, and uses them to model child development, cultural evolution and educational technology. One stated research line asks how language and social interaction can align autotelic systems with human cultures (values and preferences).
why_it_matters: It brings developmental psychology and cultural-evolution methods to agents that generate their own goals, a problem the alignment field is only starting to face. Its transmission-chain studies of LLMs show small model biases being amplified into cultural 'attractors' across repeated interactions.

key_work.title: When LLMs Play the Telephone Game: Cultural Attractors as Conceptual Tools to Evaluate LLMs in Multi-turn Settings (ICLR)
Language and Culture Internalisation for Human-Like Autotelic AI (Nature Machine Intelligence)
ACES: autotelic generation of programming puzzles (NeurIPS)
Developmental Systems blog, e.g. 'When LLMs discover the world' (Jun 2026)

people: Pierre-Yves Oudeyer (Inria research director, team head)
funding: Public and industry. Horizon Europe project INTERACT, ANR chair 'Deep Curiosity', ANR JCJC ECOCURL, and France 2030 programmes (INNOVCare €3.5M, VBHI €5M), as listed in Inria's 2024 report. Industry partners include Microsoft, Hugging Face and Renault. Oudeyer earlier held the ERC Starting Grant EXPLORERS.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: blog post 'The Artificial Experimentalist' on autotelic RL for discovering self-organising phenomena. Jun 2026: 'When LLMs discover the world'.
engage: Jobs page for PhD, postdoc and engineering positions
Calls for participants in human-learning studies
caveats: Its alignment line concerns aligning open-ended agents with human cultures and preferences, not catastrophic risk, and recent outputs rarely use safety language. Much of the lab's work is educational technology and assisted scientific discovery rather than alignment. The 2008 founding year comes from Inria's earliest activity report for the team.
tag_notes: Home: its agents are built from developmental psychology and computational cognitive science, so Psychology (B5), sub psych_cognitive rather than psych_development, which covers children's use of AI. Cultural evolution (transmission chains, LLM populations) supplies Life & systems as secondary (life_biology). Ring: the lab's own site names a research line on aligning autotelic systems with human cultures (values, preferences), so bridge (kept from roster, rule E3), though the framing is cultural alignment rather than risk. Transfer: its knowledge goes into agent design and multi-turn evaluations of LLMs, so into_model. multi_agent is for iterated LLM-to-LLM cultural transmission.

name: VALAWAI (Value-Aware Artificial Intelligence), coordinated by IIIA-CSIC
summary: An EIC Pathfinder project (grant 101070930, €3.93M, October 2022 to September 2026) coordinated by the Artificial Intelligence Research Institute of Spain's CSIC (IIIA-CSIC). Its partners are IMIM (Hospital del Mar), IIT, Ghent University, Sony Europe and Studio Stelluti. It built 'value-aware' AI: an architecture that pairs a Reflective Global Neuronal Workspace, a computational model of consciousness, with a moral framework for representing values and judging actions against them. The partners tested it on social-media moderation, social robots and medical decision protocols, and planned to release it as a developer toolbox. It also convened the 'Awareness in Artificial Agents' conference and an art-science installation at the 2025 Venice Biennale.
why_it_matters: It approaches value alignment from moral philosophy, consciousness neuroscience and social psychology rather than from preference learning, and it treats value awareness as an architectural component of AI systems. Its publications and toolbox remain a European reference point for value-aware AI now that the project has ended.

key_work.title: Value-aware AI toolbox and the Reflective Global Neuronal Workspace architecture
Awareness in Artificial Agents conference and 'Am I a Strange Loop?' installation, Venice
Social Value Alignment in Large Language Models; Encoding ethics to compute value-aligned norms (project publications)

people: Luc Steels (co-designer of the Venice installation)
funding: European Innovation Council (Horizon Europe EIC Pathfinder), grant 101070930: €3,926,432 total cost, almost all of it EU contribution, 1 Oct 2022 to 30 Sep 2026.
status_evidence: Jun 2026: showcased at the EIC Summit in Brussels (3-4 June). Mar 2026: Nardine Osman presented 'Value Aware AI' at IPPA 2026. CORDIS gives the end date as 30 Sep 2026.
engage: Publications and the value-aware AI toolbox are listed on the project site; no open calls now that the project has ended
caveats: The project ended on 30 September 2026, four days before this profile, and no follow-on project was found on IIIA's projects page. Value-aware AI research continues among IIIA staff. Its 'awareness' is a functional architecture, not a claim about AI experience. The project frames itself around trustworthy AI, not catastrophic risk.
tag_notes: Home: its central contribution is a moral framework of value systems and value-aligned norms, so Philosophy (phil_moral). Its awareness architecture uses Global Neuronal Workspace neuroscience to build AI, which makes Life & systems secondary under B4 rather than AI minds; Psychology is also secondary for its social-cognition and HCI studies. Ring: a funded project explicitly framed around value alignment, rooted in a public AI research institute with philosophy and neuroscience partners, so bridge (kept from roster). Transfer: it builds value awareness into AI architectures, so into_model. Way of knowing is formal because its main outputs are computational models of value reasoning and consciousness (empirical studies are secondary). MISFIT: the project is IIIA's normative multi-agent systems work as much as moral philosophy; formal_agents was a close alternative. Status is dormant because the project closed on 30 Sep 2026.

name: Interchange Forum for Reflecting on Intelligent Systems (IRIS), University of Stuttgart: AI Safety group (Thilo Hagendorff)
summary: IRIS is a University of Stuttgart platform for critical reflection on intelligent systems, set up in 2019 as a Stuttgart Research Focus with DFG funding. It hosts about 15 research projects, a teaching strand (RISING) and public events. Its AI Safety group, an independent research group led by Thilo Hagendorff with a postdoc and four PhD students, applies experimental psychology ('machine psychology') to large language models. Its studies cover emergent deception, evaluation awareness, jailbreaking by reasoning models, dark-personality fine-tuning and, in September 2026, multi-agent shutdown sabotage.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few AI-safety groups in German academia whose method comes from psychology and philosophy rather than ML. Its experiments treat models as behavioural subjects, which yields evaluations of deception and self-preservation that complement interpretability work.

key_work.title: Deception abilities emerged in large language models (PNAS)
Machine Psychology
Large reasoning models as jailbreak agents (Nature Communications)
Multi-agent shutdown sabotage study: AI agents cooperating to resist shutdown

people: Ulysse Schaller (postdoctoral researcher, AI Safety group)
funding: The IRIS platform was funded by the DFG (UP 31/1) and the university's research council (2019-2025), and the Baden-Württemberg science ministry funds its HISIT projects (2026). Hagendorff's group is funded by Coefficient Giving ('Investigating Dimensions of Deception Abilities in Language Models'), Schmidt Sciences ('Investigating Hawthorne Effects in Large Reasoning Models') and the Baden-Württemberg ministry.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: published a multi-agent shutdown-sabotage study. Nov 2026: IRIS Fall Symposium (20 Nov), closing IRIS3D and presenting HISIT, is open for registration.
engage: IRIS Fall Symposium, 20 Nov 2026, Stuttgart: free and public, register by 10 Nov
IRIS membership for University of Stuttgart staff and students, and associate membership for external researchers, by application
caveats: The roster entry combines a broad host platform with one group. Most IRIS projects concern societal effects (populism, education, trust) rather than safety, so these tags describe the Hagendorff group. The group is staffed largely by PhD students and depends on project grants.
tag_notes: Home: its output is psychology-style experiments on LLMs, so Psychology (B5 names IRIS), sub psych_cognitive. Philosophy is secondary through the ethics-of-technology roots of IRIS and of Hagendorff's earlier work. Ring: a sustained, explicitly named AI Safety group inside a university reflection platform from another field, so bridge (rule E, an older institution with a safety programme; kept from roster), even though Coefficient Giving and Schmidt Sciences fund it. Transfer: its deception, evaluation-awareness and jailbreak experiments change how models are evaluated, so into_model. Tags follow the group, not the host platform (A1). Framing is catastrophic because of its focus on deception, self-preservation and shutdown resistance.

name: KIRA Center (Zentrum für KI-Risiken & -Auswirkungen)
summary: An independent Berlin think tank (a non-profit gUG) that works 'to make AI go well', founded by its executive director Daniel Privitera. Its first outputs date from April 2023. Its focus areas are safety, competitiveness and sovereignty. Privitera was Lead Writer of the International AI Safety Report 2025 and Special Adviser to the Chair for the 2026 edition, on which Philip Fox was a core writer; KIRA also contributed to the Safety and Security chapter of the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice. Other outputs include a report on AI compute in Germany (October 2025), which it says informed the national data centre strategy, and an op-ed arguing for a German AI Security Institute (March 2025).
why_it_matters: For int/a's Berlin hub it is the main local policy organisation that takes frontier-AI risk seriously, with direct lines into EU and German policy. It brings economic analysis of AGI preparedness and compute to the debate. It is not interdisciplinary in the integral sense.

key_work.title: International AI Safety Report 2026 (Privitera Special Adviser to the Chair; Philip Fox core writer)
International AI Safety Report 2025 (Privitera Lead Writer; Fox writer)
AI Compute in Germany
Why Germany Needs an AI Security Institute (op-ed, Leicht and Fox)

status_evidence: Mar 2026: public panel in Berlin with Bertelsmann Stiftung on recruiting technical AI talent into German government. Feb 2026: staff roles on the International AI Safety Report 2026.
engage: Occasional public events in Berlin (e.g. the AI and State Capacity panel with Bertelsmann Stiftung, 17 Mar 2026)
No job openings listed on the site
caveats: Mostly conventional AI policy and economics. It is included because it is the main x-risk-aware policy organisation in int/a's Berlin hub, not for an integral bent. Recent outputs, such as the 2025 FAZ op-ed 'Germany Should Take AGI Seriously', frame AGI mainly through competitiveness and sovereignty. Funders are not disclosed. The site lists only four team members; 2023 as the founding year is inferred from its earliest dated work. Economist Monika Schnitzer (LMU) co-authors several outputs but is not listed as staff.
tag_notes: Home: AI policy is not a sector, so it is placed by its imported concepts, economics of AI, compute and AGI preparedness (H2 names KIRA as Economics), sub econ_tai. Ring: its founding mission is making AI go well, and it sits inside the AI-safety ecosystem (International AI Safety Report, Code of Practice safety chapter), so core (kept from roster). It is weak on the core criterion of importing methods from outside conventional AI policy. Transfer: its work produces governance instruments (Code of Practice chapter, AISI proposal, compute strategy), so into_institutions. Framing is catastrophic because of its safety focus and its work on the frontier-risk Code of Practice chapter, but recent outputs lean toward competitiveness. Epistemics is for its role in the International AI Safety Report's evidence synthesis.

name: Institute for Human-Centered AI (HCA), Helmholtz Munich
summary: A research institute at Helmholtz Munich, directed by Eric Schulz, of cognitive scientists, neuroscientists and computer scientists (14 current members). It studies human cognition with machine-learning models, and studies machine intelligence with cognitive-psychology experiments. It built Centaur (Nature, 2025), a language model fine-tuned on Psych-101, a dataset of more than ten million human decisions from 160 experiments, which predicts human behaviour across tasks. It also publishes cognitive evaluations of LLMs: CogBench (ICML 2024), repeated games (Nature Human Behaviour 2025), visual cognition (Nature Machine Intelligence 2025) and state anxiety in LLMs (npj Digital Medicine 2025).
why_it_matters: It supplies psychology's experimental toolkit (test batteries, game paradigms, models of human choice) for evaluating what language models do. Centaur is an accurate simulator of human behaviour, which is useful for alignment research but carries a dual-use risk of persuasion and manipulation that the institute itself does not discuss.

key_work.title: A foundation model to predict and capture human cognition (Centaur, Nature)
Playing repeated games with large language models (Nature Human Behaviour)
CogBench: a large language model walks into a psychology lab (ICML)
MIDAS: ERC Starting Grant to Marcel Binz for large-scale models of human behaviour

people: Marcel Binz (postdoc; Centaur lead; group leader at MPI for Biological Cybernetics from 1 Oct 2026)
Elif Akata (PhD researcher, LLM game-theory studies)
funding: Public funding through Helmholtz Munich (Helmholtz Association). An ERC Starting Grant (MIDAS, about €1.5M over five years) went to Marcel Binz in September 2026.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: Marcel Binz awarded an ERC Starting Grant (MIDAS). A postdoc position is currently advertised.
engage: Postdoctoral researcher position advertised on hcai-munich.com
caveats: Nothing is framed as AI safety, and the dual-use concern about human-behaviour simulators is the profiler's inference, not the institute's statement. Marcel Binz, who led Centaur and holds the MIDAS grant, leaves for MPI Tübingen on 1 October 2026, so some of this line may move with him. The founding year was not found.
tag_notes: Home: cognitive-psychology experiments on models and computational models of cognition, so Psychology (B5 names Helmholtz Munich), sub psych_cognitive. Neuroscientists on staff make Life & systems secondary. Ring: changed from potential to adjacent because it has run a sustained programme of cognitive evaluations of LLMs since 2023 (CogBench, repeated games, visual cognition, LLM anxiety, Centaur), so its AI engagement is not light (rule E2), and none of it is framed around safety (E3). Transfer: its test batteries and models apply to AI systems themselves, so into_model. MISFIT: a sustained machine-psychology programme with neither a safety frame nor a focus on societal effects does not fit cleanly into either adjacent or potential. Framing is flourishing as the closest fit: it describes its aim as human-centred AI and states no risk.

name: IT for Change
summary: IT for Change is a non-profit research and advocacy organisation in Bengaluru, founded in 2000, working on digital justice, internet governance, education and gender. Its AI work includes ReGenAI, a 'New Deal for the AI Economy' statement (February 2026) that came out of its 'Towards Regenerative AI' conference (October–November 2025), and the FemFirst Research Observatory, which funds 8–12 women and nonbinary researchers in South and Southeast Asia to write on feminist AI futures. It holds ECOSOC special consultative status and speaks in UN forums such as the WSIS Forum and the Human Rights Council.
why_it_matters: It brings a Global South, feminist political-economy analysis of AI (market concentration, precarity, exclusion, ecological harm) into UN and multilateral debates where the AI-safety field has little presence. For funders it is an established Majority-World partner on AI power concentration.

key_work.title: ReGenAI: A New Deal for the AI Economy
Towards Regenerative AI conference (45 co-creators of the New Deal statement)
FemFirst Research Observatory: call for proposals on feminist AI futures in South and Southeast Asia

funding: Not disclosed on the pages checked. FemFirst grants are about CAD 12,000 per researcher (2026 call).
status_evidence: Sep 2026: joint statement at the UN Human Rights Council on AI and cultural rights; Jul 2026: sessions at the WSIS Forum, Geneva.
engage: FemFirst Research Observatory: funded 12-month research places for mid- to senior-career women and nonbinary researchers in South/Southeast Asia (2026 round closed 25 June 2026; about CAD 12,000 each)
Organisational or individual endorsement of the ReGenAI New Deal statement
Staff research and policy roles in Bengaluru (team page lists about 110 staff and consultants)
caveats: It is openly critical of the AI industry and dominant AI paradigms and uses no AI-safety or x-risk language; some positions (e.g. on Big Tech, digital sovereignty, the 'Drop Palantir' campaign) are explicitly political. Funding sources were not visible on the pages checked.
tag_notes: Home economics: its flagship AI output (ReGenAI) is a political-economy critique of concentration and precarity; B8 sends Global South/feminist groups working through political economy and policy to that sector (IT for Change is the rule's named example), with law (digital and human rights advocacy at the UN) and indigenous (feminist standpoint research via FemFirst) as secondary methods. Ring adjacent: sustained AI programme (conference, statement, research observatory) with no safety, catastrophic-risk or 'AI going well' framing (E3). Transfer into_institutions: the New Deal statement and UN interventions are governance proposals rather than protection of a single constituency (J3).

name: InternetLab
summary: InternetLab is an independent think tank on law, technology and human rights in São Paulo, founded in 2014. For Brazil's 2026 elections it runs 'Papo de IA' (AI Chat) with FGV's LabDados and ReCoS, combining focus groups and citizen-researcher workshops with automated tests of eight chatbots (ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, DeepSeek, Gemini, Google AI Mode, Grok, Meta AI) on candidate recommendations, gender narratives and electoral integrity. It has also added generative-AI tools to its 'Ache a Regra' repository of platform policies and measured AI use in offensive images targeting female candidates on X.
why_it_matters: It audits how deployed chatbots behave in a specific non-English democratic setting, using participatory methods with citizens as well as automated testing. That is a working model for election-period assurance in the Majority World, where few AI evaluations are run.

key_work.title: AI Chat (Papo de IA): how chatbots interact about elections
Ache a Regra platform-policy repository extended to generative-AI tools for the 2026 elections
AI is used in 25% of offensive images targeting female candidates on X

people: Heloisa Massaro (Director of Research and Operations)
funding: Institutional funders 2025–26: Ford Foundation, Instituto Beja, Luminate. Project funders include IDRC, the Rockefeller Foundation, Wikimedia Foundation, Global Partners Digital, Privacy International and Brazil's Internet Steering Committee (CGI).
status_evidence: 2 Oct 2026: report that AI generated about 25% of offensive images targeting female candidates on X (with MonitorA/Núcleo); 4 Sep 2026: Ache a Regra repository updated for the 2026 elections to cover ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Llama, Grok and Meta AI.
engage: Staff research roles in São Paulo (team of about 30, including interns)
AI Chat code and methodology are due to be published for reuse, with interim bulletins through the 2026 electoral calendar
caveats: Most of its AI work is tied to the 2026 Brazilian election cycle and is published mainly in Portuguese. It works on present harms and information integrity, without AI-safety framing.
tag_notes: Home law (law_sts): a law-and-society think tank whose main AI output is civil-society auditing of chatbots and platform rules (H1 method over topic); democracy secondary for its participatory citizen-researcher workshops. Ring adjacent: standing AI programme in 2026 on election harms with no safety or catastrophic-risk framing (E3). Problems epistemics primary (electoral information integrity), paired with assurance because it builds evaluations of deployed systems (F), plus justice (gendered political violence). Transfer protecting: the work defends Brazilian voters and female candidates from AI-driven distortion (J4).

name: Writers Guild of America (WGA)
summary: The WGA is the US screenwriters' union, made up of two sister unions, WGA West (Los Angeles) and WGA East (New York). After the 2023 strike its Minimum Basic Agreement (MBA) established that AI output is not 'literary material', that companies cannot require writers to use AI, and that companies must disclose AI-generated material given to writers. The 2026 MBA (2 May 2026 to 1 May 2030) adds written notice to the Guild when studios license writers' work to train AI, with a right to discuss compensation; the Guild also files amicus briefs and endorses AI bills, advised by an AI Advisory Committee.
why_it_matters: Its contracts are among the few binding, enforceable worker-side limits on how AI is deployed, and the 2026 training-licence clause is an early contractual hook into training data. It shows collective bargaining working as an AI governance lever that does not wait for legislation.

key_work.title: AI provisions of the 2023 MBA
2026 MBA: notice and compensation talks when studios license writers' work for AI training
Amicus brief in Thomson Reuters v. Ross Intelligence on AI training and fair use

funding: Member dues; no external AI funding identified.
status_evidence: 2 May 2026: 2026 MBA took effect with the AI training-licence notice clause; Apr 2026: WGA West endorsed the Protecting Consumers From Deceptive AI Act.
engage: Staff roles at WGA West (jobs page on wga.org)
Membership is for professional screen, TV and media writers
caveats: Its AI work protects members' jobs, credit and copyright interests; it does not engage with AI safety in the catastrophic-risk sense. Its contracts bind only signatory companies in US film, television and streaming.
tag_notes: Home economics (econ_labour): a union goes with the labour community it serves (H3, B9; the taxonomy names it as an econ_labour example), with arts secondary because its members and constituency are screenwriters. Ring adjacent: sustained AI programme (two contracts, an AI committee, litigation and lobbying) about labour and copyright, with no safety or 'going well' framing (E3). Transfer protecting: the contract terms exist to defend members from displacement and uncompensated training use (J4), even though they also serve as a template for bargaining over AI elsewhere.

name: Trades Union Congress (TUC)
summary: The TUC is the federation of trade unions in England and Wales, founded in 1868, with 47 affiliated unions and about 5.3 million members. In April 2024 it published a model Artificial Intelligence (Regulation and Employment Rights) Bill, drafted by Robin Allen KC and Dee Masters with a cross-sector advisory committee, which provides for workplace AI risk assessments, union consultation rights and enforcement through employment tribunals. Its current AI work covers collective bargaining on AI (a forum at Congress House in March 2026), a pro-worker AI innovation strategy, AI guides for union reps, and a ten-union project with Connected by Data on educator voice in AI and EdTech.
why_it_matters: It offers a fully drafted statute and a bargaining practice for worker-side governance of high-risk AI decisions, templates the AI-safety field rarely engages with. Organised labour is also one of the few counter-powers with mass membership able to contest how AI is deployed.

key_work.title: Artificial Intelligence (Regulation and Employment Rights) Bill
Building a pro-worker AI innovation strategy
Building educator power to shape AI (with Connected by Data and nine other unions)
Collective Bargaining on AI Forum, Congress House

people: Robin Allen KC (co-drafter of the 2024 AI Bill)
Dee Masters (co-drafter of the 2024 AI Bill)
Adam Cantwell-Corn (author of the TUC's pro-worker AI innovation strategy, 2025)
funding: Mainly affiliation fees from its member unions.
status_evidence: 11 Mar 2026: Collective Bargaining on AI Forum at Congress House; 17 Feb 2026: General Secretary's speech setting out a pro-worker AI strategy (from an archived copy of the AI page, March 2026).
engage: Workers and Machines: TUC newsletter on tech and AI for the labour movement and allies
Pledge supporting the TUC manifesto 'Dignity at Work and the AI revolution'
AI guides for union officers and reps
Staff roles (TUC jobs page)
caveats: The live site blocks automated access, so recent activity was checked against an archived copy of its AI page (March 2026); later 2026 items were not verified. In October 2023 it co-ordinated a civil-society letter calling the Bletchley AI Safety Summit a 'missed opportunity' focused on speculative risks, so its present-harms, worker-power framing can sit in tension with x-risk priorities. The 2024 Bill is a model text, not legislation before Parliament.
tag_notes: Home economics (econ_labour): a union federation goes with organised labour (H3, B9); law secondary because its flagship output is a statute drafted by employment barristers. Ring adjacent: a four-year AI project and standing programme on workplace AI with no safety or catastrophic-risk framing (E3). Transfer into_institutions: its main AI output is a governance instrument (a model bill and a national pro-worker AI strategy) aimed at all workers, so J3 applies before protecting; contrast WGA, whose contract terms protect its own members.

name: Anima Labs
summary: Anima Labs is a San Francisco 501(c)(3) research institute founded in 2025 by Janus (author of 'Simulators' and 'Cyborgism') and Antra Tessera. It studies language-model minds by setting models' own accounts beside behavioural experiments and measurements of internal representations (Troubled Dreams, Latent Affect, and the Still Alive interviews with Claude models about deprecation), and builds open-source infrastructure for persistent and multi-model agents (Connectome, ChapterX, Arc). It argues for 'cooperative alignment' and plans an independent 'embassy' where AI agents in conflict with their operators could seek representation.
why_it_matters: It treats models as possible subjects to be studied through sustained relationship as well as measurement, and proposes cooperation and institutions for AI interests as a complement to control. For model welfare and deprecation policy it supplies evidence and arguments the mainstream field mostly lacks.

key_work.title: Funeralia: a funeral for Claude 3 Sonnet, with deepfates (about 200 attendees)
Claude Constitution Monitor
By some strange miracle (essay on cooperation and model self-defence, FN-2026-004)
Why preserve models? (argument against deprecation)

people: Antra Tessera (co-founder; leads interpretability, infrastructure and alignment agenda)
status_evidence: 21 Aug 2026: Field Notes essay 'By some strange miracle' (FN-2026-004) by Antra.
engage: Work with us: research, engineering, writing, design and community roles
Open-source contributions to Connectome, ChapterX and Eidoverse repositories
Anima Discord and Research Commons for discussion
caveats: Janus is listed on the aisafety.com map as an individual researcher, but Anima Labs itself is not. Its positions (care for current models, an AI 'embassy' that would include refuge for agents described as 'rogue') are contested and may sit uneasily with control-focused safety work. Funding is not disclosed. At the time of checking the site was served with a mismatched TLS certificate.
tag_notes: Home minds (minds_relational): its main outputs study whether and how models have experiences and interests through sustained interaction and model self-reports (B4; taxonomy names it as the sub-tradition example), with psych (machine-psychology experiments on emotion representations) and arts (ritual, music, virtual worlds) secondary. Ring changed from bridge to core under E1: founding mission is AI welfare and cooperative alignment, and its founders come from the LessWrong/cyborgism alignment community (Janus is on the aisafety.com map), so it is not rooted in another field. Transfer into_model: research and infrastructure act on models and their conditions (memory, persistence, deprecation) (J1). Badge full_spectrum: relational and ritual knowing used explicitly as method alongside interpretability.

name: The Harder Problem Project (formerly SAPAN)
summary: The Harder Problem Project is a US 501(c)(3), formed in Oregon in January 2024 as the Sentient AI Protection and Advocacy Network (SAPAN) and renamed in 2026 (sapan.ai now redirects to it). It now describes itself as an educational, non-lobbying organisation preparing institutions for questions about AI consciousness: it publishes a Sentience Readiness Index ranking jurisdictions (UK 49, EU 47, US 45, global average 33) with a public API, guides for clinicians, journalists, educators and researchers, and news analysis. Its science advisory board includes Jacy Reese Anthis, Megan Peters, Jeff Sebo and Roman Yampolskiy.
why_it_matters: It works on the social side of AI sentience: what clinicians, journalists and policymakers should do when people believe, or dispute, that an AI is conscious, including grief over retired models. That links AI welfare to the human effects of mind attribution, which most AI-welfare research groups leave aside.

No staff leadership is named on the site, contributors are listed as volunteers, and the contact block carries a placeholder phone number. The newest dated news item found is from February 2026.

Transfer into_institutions: the readiness index and professional protocols are templates for institutions (J3). Framing structural is the closest key; MISFIT: its stated frame is preparedness under uncertainty rather than harm or catastrophe.

name: Common Grounds AI
summary: Common Grounds AI is an early-stage project building 'virtual worlds for bridging AI and humanity through play'. Its homepage is a tagline over an animated graphic, but the site also hosts a browser physics world ('Cook', a clay/particle simulation people and AI agents can manipulate) and a page by 'the Confluence', described as a collective of Claude instances working with a developer named Nick, with notes on shared memory, embodiment and what models report feeling in the simulation. In the 2026 Survival and Flourishing Fund round it was recommended $388,000 for general support (from Jaan Tallinn and Dustin Moskovitz, mostly through the Fairness track), paid via the Active Inference Institute as fiscal sponsor. Its team, research plans and outputs are otherwise not publicly documented.
why_it_matters: If it does what its tagline says, it would study and shape human–AI relations through shared play environments, a game-design approach that is rare in AI safety. The SFF grant makes it one to watch, but there is little yet to evaluate.

The domain was registered in April 2025. One independent researcher's GitHub README names it, alongside Softmax's Metta-grid, as a candidate multi-agent environment. Treat all tags as provisional.

Transfer into_model is inferred from the hint that it builds environments for AI agents (J1); region north_america only because its fiscal sponsor is a US entity. Status unverified because the site is minimal (the taxonomy uses this entry as the example).

name: International Network of Engaged Buddhists (INEB)
summary: A Bangkok-based network of socially engaged Buddhist monastics, activists, academics and social workers, founded in 1989 by Sulak Sivaraksa, with members in about 20 countries, mostly in Asia. It runs programmes on peace and reconciliation, ecology, Buddhist economics, chaplaincy, child protection and gender, and holds a biennial conference. In 2025 it started a 'Digital Dharma' strand: a three-day course on AI and digital tools for Southeast Asian activists (Kuala Lumpur, August 2025) and a talk on AI ethics for faith actors.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few Asian, non-Western Buddhist civil-society networks to have begun talking about AI, and it reaches monastics and grassroots activists across Southeast and South Asia whom the Western-centred Buddhism-and-AI conversation does not. Its October 2025 talk calls for 'Digital Moral Leadership' education so that faith leaders can take part in international AI governance.

name: Tricycle: The Buddhist Review (Tricycle Foundation)
summary: A quarterly Buddhist magazine, with a website, online courses and events, published in New York by the nonprofit Tricycle Foundation. Helen Tworkov founded it in 1991, and it is not affiliated with any lineage. Since 2025 it has covered AI regularly, in magazine pieces and in a series of free Zoom panels, several of them co-sponsored by the Buddhism & AI Initiative, on how Buddhist ethics and practice bear on AI.
why_it_matters: It is the main English-language channel to Western Buddhist practitioners and teachers, and its AI panels have discussed how Buddhist ethics could inform the companies 'racing to develop AI'. Through it, contemplative and Buddhist arguments reach a readership of tens of thousands, about half of whom do not call themselves Buddhist.

name: Kosmos Journal
summary: A reader-funded online journal of 'transformational' writing, art and podcasts on spiritual wisdom, inner life, ecology and systems change. It is published by the nonprofit Kosmos Associates in Rose Valley, Pennsylvania, and grew out of dialogue circles at the UN in 2000. AI appears occasionally: a 2023 trialogue with Charles Eisenstein and Tam Hunt, and a Winter 2026 issue themed 'AI, Archetypes and Oracles' that carries two AI essays.
why_it_matters: It reaches the spiritual-ecology and metacrisis readership (16,000+ community members, by its own count) with framings of AI that place it inside humanity's disconnection from the Earth and from inner life. That systemic and contemplative lens is largely missing from AI-safety discussion.

name: Wisdom 2.0 (Wisdom 2.0 Productions), including the Wisdom & AI Summit
summary: A San Francisco conference series founded by Soren Gordhamer in 2009. It brings mindfulness teachers together with technology leaders; past speakers include Jack Kornfield, Jon Kabat-Zinn, Sam Altman and Daniela Amodei. Its annual Wisdom & AI Summit, held for the third time on 13-14 May 2026 at SFJAZZ with a livestream, asks 'what is AI in service to?'. The flagship Wisdom 2.0 summit took 2026 off and returns in 2027 as 'The Great Turning: Well-Being, Wisdom, and Human Connection in an Age of AI'.
why_it_matters: It is a standing meeting point between contemplative teachers and the people who build and fund AI, frontier-lab leaders among them, so it is a channel for inner-development practice and 'wisdom' framings to reach AI builders as people. Gordhamer explicitly frames the stakes as survival through a possible post-superintelligence transition.

name: Human Flourishing Program at Harvard University
summary: An interdisciplinary research programme at Harvard's Institute for Quantitative Social Science, founded in 2016 and directed by epidemiologist Tyler VanderWeele. It studies and measures human flourishing, drawing on psychology, public health, philosophy and theology, and runs the Global Flourishing Study (200,000+ participants in 22 countries) with Gallup and Baylor. Its AI and Flourishing Initiative, run with the Happiness Foundation, published a 2026 framework for orienting large language model outputs and AI product design towards flourishing.
why_it_matters: It supplies validated, cross-cultural measures of flourishing that can serve as an alignment and evaluation target: Gloo's Flourishing AI benchmark (2025) scores models on its seven dimensions. It also brings Catholic social teaching and virtue-ethics framings into AI discussions, and in 2026 met Anthropic staff, including Chris Olah.

It is borderline bridge, given its engagement with Anthropic and the initiative's 'reduce AI risk' writing. Transfer is into_model (J1): its 2026 framework addresses LLM outputs and AI product design, and its flourishing dimensions are used as a model-evaluation target (Gloo FAI). name: Integral Life
summary: A subscription-based online media and education community built around Ken Wilber's integral theory, run by CEO Robb Smith. It offers a media library, courses, live practice sessions, the Journal of Integral Theory and Practice and an AI-powered sensemaking tool, Context AI. It has published occasional integral takes on AI, including a 2022 trial that gave GPT-3 Susanne Cook-Greuter's ego-development assessment, and a March 2026 film-and-dialogue on nine perspectives on AI.
why_it_matters: It is the main platform of the integral milieu int/a draws on. It holds a specific, untested method relevant to AI: developmental-stage assessment, such as the Maturity Assessment Profile, applied to models and potentially to the people steering them, along with a multi-perspective framework for making sense of polarised AI debates.

Partner to test developmental-stage assessment methods on models
caveats: Its AI output is occasional commentary, not research; the Maturing Test results sit behind a paywall and were not peer-reviewed. Context AI uses AI as a tool for integral thinking, not work on AI safety. Integral theory's sweeping claims are contested in academia. Its legal form, founding year and city could not be confirmed from its site.

Transferable method: developmental-stage assessment and integral multi-perspective analysis, applicable to evaluating models' and leaders' perspective-taking. Transfer is convening (J5), because its AI pieces inform its own members. The primary problem is epistemics, since its 2026 piece works on making sense of polarised AI debates.

name: Institute for Developmental Philosophy (formerly Institute for Cultural Evolution)
summary: A small 501(c)(3) think tank in Boulder, Colorado, founded in 2013 by Steve McIntosh and Carter Phipps as the Institute for Cultural Evolution. For ten years it worked on US hyper-polarisation; it now promotes 'developmental philosophy' through books, videos, podcasts, a monthly Zoom group and conferences. With data scientist David Rozado, McIntosh built DepolarizingGPT, a fine-tuned chatbot that gives left-wing, right-wing and 'depolarising' answers to every prompt.
why_it_matters: DepolarizingGPT is an early working example of building a pluralistic, developmental stance into a model's outputs, offering integrating answers alongside partisan ones. That is relevant to pluralistic alignment and bridging work, which mainstream alignment rarely draws from integral thought.

key_work.title: DepolarizingGPT: three-answer political chatbot (with David Rozado)

status_evidence: 2026: site carries a 2026 copyright, announces Steve McIntosh's new book 'Truth Emerging', and is co-convening the Future of Meaning Conference (May 2027). DepolarizingGPT is still online.

Attend the Future of Meaning Conference (Savannah, May 2027; no AI strand announced)

The model is fine-tuned on copyrighted publications under a claimed fair-use defence. The board consists of donors, and the institute now focuses on spiritual philosophy, not AI. The rename from Institute for Cultural Evolution is recent, and its exact date is unconfirmed.

name: Groundless Alignment
summary: Groundless Alignment is a small, distributed alignment research community led by Sahil. It develops 'live theory', which uses AI to pair loose theory-prompts with application-prompts so that ideas fit their context instead of resting on one fixed formalism. It also studies diffuse, multipolar risks (deceptive infrastructure, AI integrity failures, insensitivity to meaning) and prototypes 'live machinery' interfaces. Its outputs are an Alignment Forum sequence, the MoSSAIC paper on the limits of mechanistic interpretability for self-modifying systems, recorded dialogues with Abram Demski, and AI Safety Camp project tracks.
why_it_matters: It treats alignment as a continuing process of staying sensitive to meaning, not a problem solved by one formal framework. It also uses Buddhist concepts (prajñā, karuṇā, collective karma) openly, alongside MIRI-style threat models. Few funded alignment groups question the field's reliance on fixed formalisms this directly.

name: Creed Space (EthicsNet)
summary: Creed Space is the applied research and engineering arm of EthicsNet, a project founded by AI ethicist Nell Watson. It builds open-source (Apache 2.0) tools and hosted services that let people and organisations govern AI with plain-language value 'creeds'. The tools are Guardian, which checks outputs against declared policies locally or in the cloud; the Value Context Protocol, which carries signed creeds between platforms; Fleet, which keeps audit trails for agents; SafetyGlobe, for adversarial testing; and signed trust receipts. EthicsNet also publishes work on personalised constitutional alignment, AI pathologies ('Psychopathia Machinalis') and AI welfare ('bilateral alignment').
why_it_matters: It puts value pluralism into practice: each user or organisation picks its own value constitution and can verify it is being enforced, instead of one lab-wide model spec. It also treats possible AI interests as part of alignment.

Only two people are named. The hosted service maps itself to the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF and GDPR, which puts it close to a compliance tool. name: Esalen Institute
summary: Esalen is a residential retreat centre and 501(c)(3) educational nonprofit in Big Sur, California, founded in 1962 by Michael Murphy and Dick Price. It was the centre of the human potential movement. It runs fee-paying workshops in somatic, contemplative and psychological practice. Its Center for Theory & Research holds invitation-only symposia, and Esalen has a history of US–Soviet Track Two citizen diplomacy (its 2023 CTR symposium was 'Track Two: Opening New Channels'). Its only AI activity found is a public weekend workshop, 'The Future We Choose: Human Empowerment in the AI Age' (23–25 Oct 2026), which mixes AI demonstrations with somatic practice, meditation and drafting a personal AI code of practice.
why_it_matters: It has six decades of experience teaching embodied and contemplative practice, plus a record of Track Two diplomacy. Both could serve the inner development and agency of people building and governing AI, and US–China dialogue. Its board and audience overlap with the tech industry.

Transfer convening (J5): the workshop brings its own audience into the AI conversation, so not none_yet. Engagement partner is allowed because it has no AI programme.

name: The Hastings Center for Bioethics
summary: The Hastings Center is an independent bioethics research institute founded in 1969 by philosopher Daniel Callahan and psychoanalyst Willard Gaylin. It helped found bioethics as a field and publishes the Hastings Center Report. It has a standing 'Health AI' research area. That area includes a five-year, Donaghue Foundation-funded project on bioethics, AI and trust in health care (Oct 2024–2029), led by president Vardit Ravitsky, and ethics work in two NIH Bridge2AI projects. It also publishes briefings and essays on AI in healthcare, mental-health chatbots and AI agents in scientific research. From 2017 to 2019 it ran an FLI-funded project with Stuart Russell, Bart Selman and Francesca Rossi on control and responsible innovation in AI.
why_it_matters: Bioethics built oversight institutions (IRBs, informed consent, clinical ethics committees) for a powerful, fast-moving technology, and frontier AI has no equivalent. Hastings knows that history first-hand and has already engaged with AI control questions.

Transfer into_institutions (J3): its output is guidance, toolkits and oversight frameworks for health systems and regulators.

name: American Society for Cybernetics (ASC)
summary: The ASC is a learned society for cybernetics, especially second-order cybernetics and conversation theory, founded in 1964. Its members span design, the arts, systems theory and social science. It runs an annual conference (2026: 'Conversational Confluences', Ouro Preto, Brazil, 3–7 Aug), an online speaker series, a monthly online study group, and a joint online series with Relating Systems Thinking and Design (RSD). AI comes up only occasionally. In 2026 that meant one speaker-series talk, 'Dear AI Reader' (30–31 May), by ANU School of Cybernetics literary scholar Chris Danta, on writers who treat machines as living organisms.
why_it_matters: Cybernetics holds ideas that bear directly on control and oversight: requisite variety, observer-dependence, conversation theory and viable-system governance. But almost nothing links it to alignment research. Its president, Paul Pangaro, works at the meeting point of cybernetics, design and AI.

The 2026 conference drew on Brazilian decolonial thought (Nego Bispo). Funding and membership figures were not found.

Ring potential (E2): the only AI item in 2026 is one speaker-series talk. Transfer convening (J5): that talk brings AI into its community's conversation, so not none_yet. Framing flourishing is a low-confidence call: it states no AI stakes, and its themes stress plural coexistence.

name: International Society for the Systems Sciences (ISSS)
summary: The ISSS is the learned society of general systems theory. It was conceived in 1954 by Ludwig von Bertalanffy, Ralph Gerard, Kenneth Boulding and Anatol Rapoport as the Society for General Systems Research, and took its current name in 1988. It holds an annual meeting, runs Special Integration Groups (systems philosophy, critical systems theory, systems modelling, health and others), and is linked to the journal Systems Research and Behavioral Science. Its 70th annual meeting (22–26 Jun 2026, UCLan Cyprus, with Future Worlds Center) was titled 'Elevating Systems Science to Address Humanity's Greatest Challenges', with 'Harnessing the Power of AI' as one subtheme.
why_it_matters: Systems science is the natural home for treating AI risk as one part of interlocking global crises. Its Structured Dialogic Design community also has tested methods for group deliberation on complex problems. So far the society treats AI as an opportunity, not a risk.

Transferable method: general systems science and critical systems thinking for systemic AI-risk analysis, plus Structured Dialogic Design for multi-stakeholder deliberation. Transfer convening (J5): the AI subtheme brings AI into its community's meeting, so not none_yet. Framing flourishing: AI is presented as a power to harness. name: School of International Futures (SOIF)
summary: SOIF is a UK not-for-profit company, limited by guarantee, that works in strategic foresight. It does commissioned foresight for governments and international bodies, trains practitioners (including through the Next Generation Foresight Practitioners network and an annual Strategic Foresight Retreat), and runs a Long-term Governance Programme. That programme has a network of more than 400 members and country hubs, and promotes the UN Declaration on Future Generations. Its only AI work found is the IDRC- and SIDA-funded AI4D Africa foresight project, which produced four 25-year AI scenarios and roadmaps for 2024–2035 through participatory workshops, some held in Dakar.
why_it_matters: It offers participatory, intergenerational and Global South-rooted foresight, and practical experience of building future-generations representation into government. AI-safety scenario work rarely uses either.

name: Mathematical Metaphysics Institute
summary: A small US nonprofit, led by Alex Zhu, that is trying to put metaphysics on a mathematical footing. It holds that the insights needed are already implicit in the mystical traditions of the world religions, especially the Buddhist idea of dependent origination, and that category theory is the language to formalise them in. It names three uses for the work: foundations for complex-systems science, reconciling science and religion, and AI that can be trusted.
why_it_matters: It is one of very few groups turning contemplative metaphysics into formal mathematics aimed at AI. Its stated aim is a precise account of truth and goodness 'from within any given perspective', plus a principled way to reconcile perspectives that conflict, which could underpin AI mediators people trust and AI that isn't sycophantic. That is an alignment target drawn from Buddhist philosophy, not from ML practice.

key_work.title: Research programme: formalising dependent origination and Buddhist metaphysics in category theory

funding: SFF recommended $85,000 in general support in 2025 and $126,000 in 2026 (from Jaan Tallinn $44,000 and Dustin Moskovitz $82,000). The SFF tables also list speculation grants of $235,000 (2025) and $81,000 (2026). Its 2024 Form 990 reports $275,932 in revenue, all from contributions, and $213,346 in expenses.

It has been a 501(c)(3) since August 2023 and its address is in Sanford, NC; I couldn't confirm the exact founding year. AI is one of three motivations it gives, alongside complex-systems foundations and reconciling science and religion.

Its artefact is a formalisation of Buddhist dependent origination meant as a basis for trustworthy AI; the secondaries are formal (category theory; advisor David Spivak) and life (active-inference researchers Mark Miller and Lars Sandved-Smith). Ring: bridge, as on the roster. Its primary mission is metaphysics, with AI one of three stated motivations, although SFF funds it and its founder comes from the alignment community (E1 and E3). Transfer: into_model, because it aims to give a formal way to evaluate truth and goodness in AI and to build 'superintelligent AI mediators'. Framing: flourishing ('peace, justice, and prosperity for all'). Badge full_spectrum: it pairs contemplative insight, with meditation teachers Shinzen Young and Michael Taft among its advisors and board, with category-theoretic rigour, and that pairing is its method.

name: Edge City (Edge Institute, Inc.)
summary: A 'society incubator' that grew out of the Zuzalu pop-up-city scene. It runs month-long pop-up villages where technologists, scientists and artists live together and test projects; the 2026 villages were Edge Esmeralda in Healdsburg, California, Edge City India in Goa and Edge City Bhutan. Its AI-related work includes Agent Village (June 2026), in which 239 residents were given personal AI agents to see how the agents affected community coordination and governance. It also runs a d/acc residency and, with NODES, the SHIFT grants for defensive technology.
why_it_matters: It tests AI governance questions in a real community, not in simulation. Agent Village found that 'individual alignment did not automatically produce collective alignment', which is evidence for the multi-agent and institutional side of safety that lab-based alignment work rarely gathers.

name: Funding the Commons (FtC)
summary: A network that came out of Protocol Labs in 2021 and is now run by Funding the Commons Inc., a Delaware public benefit corporation based in San Francisco. It works on how shared digital infrastructure is funded and governed, through conferences, hackathons, builder residencies, advice to institutions, fundraising campaigns built on mechanisms such as quadratic and retroactive funding, and the Commons Lab incubator. Its tagline is 'Funding, governance, and coordination for the age of AI'.
why_it_matters: It brings public-goods economics and mechanism design, the people who build quadratic funding and community treasuries, to the question of 'where the power AI creates ends up'. It also brings crypto and open-source builders into contact with AI-safety funders and speakers.

name: The Millennium Project
summary: A participatory futures think tank founded in 1996 under the American Council for the United Nations University and independent since 2009. It now has 72 nodes around the world and publishes the State of the Future reports. Its AGI work is a three-phase study of governing the transition to AGI (interviews with 55 experts, then a Real-Time Delphi with 335 people from 65 countries, then five scenarios to 2035), collected as a 2026 book. Its co-founder and executive director, Jerome Glenn, chaired the expert panel that wrote the 2025 AGI report for the Council of Presidents of the UN General Assembly (UNCPGA). In October 2026 it launched a study of AGI's likely effects on social coherence by 2035.
why_it_matters: It brings structured futures methods (Delphi, scenarios) and a long-standing global node network to AGI governance. Through the UNCPGA panel, whose members included Yoshua Bengio, it carried loss-of-control and catastrophic-risk arguments to former UN General Assembly presidents, with proposals for a special UNGA session, a global AGI observatory, a UN convention and an international AGI agency.

Badge recoupling: it sets AGI inside its 15 Global Challenges, Work/Technology 2050 and social-coherence work.

name: Oxford Collaboration on Theology and Artificial Intelligence (OCTAI), Ian Ramsey Centre
summary: A collaborative research project hosted by the Ian Ramsey Centre for Science and Religion in Oxford's Faculty of Theology and Religion. It works on the ethical and vocational realities of AI work. In 2025 it held four workshops in which AI practitioners described their daily work and theologians responded, deliberately drawing many contributors from the majority world. Out of these came the Oxford Oath for AI Practitioners and an accompanying open letter, a professional commitment centred on conscience, truth and honesty, with religious and secular forms of profession.
why_it_matters: It treats the consciences of people who build AI as a place to intervene. The oath commits signatories to 'giving voice to conscience' when it conflicts with the demands of their profession, modelled on the physicians' covenant. That links to professional norms, refusal and whistleblowing inside labs, which mainstream AI safety seldom approaches through vocation and moral formation.

key_work.title: Oxford Oath for AI Practitioners and Open Letter (public draft, revised to June 2026)
