Its outputs are theologically informed ethics produced by a Faculty of Theology team that is mostly Christian (B1, H1; the oath opens with James 3:13); the secondary is philosophy, for engineering ethics and professional oaths. Ring: changed from bridge to adjacent. The programme is sustained (workshops 2025, oath revisions 2026) but framed around vocation, human dignity, truthfulness and conscience, not safety, catastrophic risk or alignment (E3). Transfer: into_builders, because the oath and letter aim to form the consciences and professional commitments of AI engineers and corporate leaders. Standpoint neither: it emphasises the majority world but is led from Oxford (rule O).

name: HITRECORD
summary: A privately held collaborative media company and open online creative community, founded in 2004 by the actor and director Joseph Gordon-Levitt and his brother Dan; Joseph Gordon-Levitt is its sole owner. In 2025 FLI granted it $1,000,000 to develop mainstream film and television projects, grounded in research and informed by experts, on AI safety, ethics and risks. Gordon-Levitt's journal, published under the HITRECORD domain, carries frequent AI-policy essays and reported that filming began on 12 May 2026 on a Netflix thriller about AI that he is directing.
why_it_matters: It brings mainstream film and television, and a well-known storyteller, to public understanding of AI risk, an audience that AI-safety research and policy writing rarely reach. Its framing stresses corporate power and regulation and explicitly rejects 'doom trolling', so it shows a route to the public outside the x-risk vocabulary.

key_work.title: FLI grant: film and TV content on AI safety, ethics and risks
Netflix thriller about AI, directed and co-written by Joseph Gordon-Levitt (filming began 12 May 2026)
Joe's Journal essays on AI governance, e.g. 'Global coordination on AI is hard work, but not impossible'

funding: FLI: $1,000,000 (listed among 2025 grants; grant page published 1 Oct 2026) for digital content on AI safety, ethics and risks. Otherwise a privately held for-profit company.
status_evidence: Oct 2026: FLI grant page published (1 Oct), and journal essay 'Global coordination on AI is hard work, but not impossible' (2 Oct). 12 May 2026: filming began on the Netflix AI thriller.
engage: Open online creative-collaboration community at hitrecord.org
Joe's Journal newsletter (journal.hitrecord.org)
caveats: No FLI-funded production has been named publicly. The Netflix thriller is a Gordon-Levitt project, but I couldn't confirm that HITRECORD produces it or that FLI money pays for it. Much of the visible AI work is Gordon-Levitt's personal advocacy rather than the company's: he co-founded the Creators Coalition on AI in Dec 2025, testified to Utah legislators in Jan 2026, and was named to Time's TIME100 AI list in Aug 2026. Its framing (regulation, corporate accountability, against 'doom trolling') differs from the x-risk community's. The hitrecord.org site renders as a JavaScript app, so I couldn't check the community's current activity beyond the site's own description.
tag_notes: Home: arts (arts_narrative), because general-audience film and television go to Arts (H3). Ring: bridge, as on the roster. A media company from outside the field holds a $1M FLI grant explicitly for content on 'AI safety, ethics, and risks' and produced a steady stream of AI output in 2026 (E3). Transfer: convening, because its purpose is to bring broad public audiences into the AI conversation through entertainment. Framing: structural, because its own essays focus on unregulated corporate power and democratic control ('Who Benefits From Unregulated AI?') and reject 'doom trolling'. The online hub and community engagement rest on the site describing itself as an open online community for creative collaboration, which is not AI-specific.

name: Civic AI / 6-Pack of Care
summary: A project led by Audrey Tang and Caroline Emmer De Albuquerque Green at the University of Oxford's Institute for Ethics in AI, hosted in its Accelerator Fellowship Programme. It turns care ethics (Fisher and Tronto's phases of care) into six testable principles for building and governing AI: attentiveness, responsibility, competence, responsiveness, solidarity and symbiosis. It defines 'civic AI' as AI 'that the people it affects can check, correct and switch off'. Its outputs include a CC0 manifesto, a short instruction set (a 'Kami') that walks groups through oversight questions, a conference at Rhodes House in March 2026, essays, and a Wiley book due in February 2027.
why_it_matters: It brings care ethics and Taiwan's civic-tech practice into alignment debates. It reframes alignment as 'horizontal' (AI supporting cooperation between people) as well as 'vertical', and it proposes many local, bounded, time-limited systems as the alternative to a singleton. Few AI-safety groups offer anything like this: a relational, participatory alignment target with concrete governance tests.

key_work.title: 6-Pack of Care manifesto and framework
Civic AI Conference, Rhodes House, Oxford (25 March)
'Let the People Set the Pace of Frontier AI' (Hélène Landemore and Audrey Tang, Noema): proposes a standing Global Citizens' Assembly on AI
Civic AI: 6-Pack of Care (book, Wiley, due February 2027)

people: Audrey Tang (co-lead; Taiwan's ambassador-at-large, Accelerator Fellow at Oxford)
Caroline Emmer De Albuquerque Green (co-lead; Oxford Institute for Ethics in AI)
funding: Hosted by the Oxford Institute for Ethics in AI's Accelerator Fellowship Programme. No project-specific funding disclosed.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: Tang and Hélène Landemore published 'Let the People Set the Pace of Frontier AI' in Noema; site rebuilt on 4 Oct 2026.
engage: Propose amendments to the framework through its public GitHub repository and amendment ledger (CC0 licence)
Try the Kami instruction set with a community group: it asks who oversees a system, what could fail, who can veto it and when it ends
Book Civic AI: 6-Pack of Care (Wiley, February 2027)
caveats: Most of what is known comes from the project's own site; independent coverage found was thin (Wikipedia confirms Tang's Oxford Accelerator Fellowship). It works through process, not enforcement: the Kami instructions 'can only ask; they enforce nothing'. Catastrophic risk is addressed only indirectly, by arguing for a plural, federated architecture against a singleton. 6pack.care now redirects to civic.ai.
tag_notes: Home: philosophy (H1/H2). The framework is care ethics (Fisher and Tronto 1990; Tronto's Caring Democracy) turned into design principles; democracy is secondary for its Plurality roots, Polis sensemaking and the citizens'-assembly proposal. Ring: bridge (E3). It is rooted in Oxford's Institute for Ethics in AI and Taiwan's civic tech, not the x-risk ecosystem, but its manifesto explicitly addresses 'vertical' and 'horizontal' alignment, superintelligence and the singleton, and the work has been sustained through 2025-26 (conference, essays, book). Transfer: into_institutions (J3). The main output is governance principles and processes (oversight, veto, sunset); the Kami instruction set touches the model but is secondary. Problems: values first, because care as an alignment target is the column it would leave emptiest (F); democracy and power are paired for participatory oversight and its anti-lock-in 'solidarity' principle. Framing: flourishing over structural (L); concern about concentration runs through it, but the stated aim is a positive vision of care. Badges: speed_of_wisdom ('Let the People Set the Pace of Frontier AI', systems run at the pace of deliberation and bounded in time) and fractal (locally bounded 'kami' alongside a global assembly proposal). Status: new, launched 2025.

name: Win-Win
summary: A Substack newsletter and podcast hosted by Liv Boeree, a former professional poker player and science communicator, about competition, incentives and coordination, under the tagline 'don't hate the players, change the game'. It popularises the 'Moloch' or multipolar-trap account of destructive races, which Boeree applied to AI in her TEDAI 2023 talk. In 2025-26 most of its episodes are about AI: Emmett Shear on organic alignment, Will MacAskill on what comes after superintelligence, Daniel Kokotajlo and Dean Ball on markets versus governments, and a Huni Kuin elder on AI.
why_it_matters: It gives the AI-race problem a game-theoretic and cultural frame for a general audience. It also puts voices rarely heard in AI safety (Indigenous elders, ecologists, free-speech advocates) beside alignment researchers. Its central message, that wisdom means choosing which games to play, matches int/a's aim of not feeding the AI race.

key_work.title: The Dark Side of Competition in AI (TEDAI talk)
#47 Emmett Shear: Why Nature Holds the Answer to AI Alignment
#52 Will MacAskill: What Comes After Superintelligent AI?
I Asked an Amazonian Shaman About AI (with Txana Tuwe, Huni Kuin)

funding: No sponsors or funders stated; kept free by the host.
status_evidence: 26 Aug 2026: episode 'I Asked An Amazonian Shaman About AI' with Txana Tuwe.
engage: Free newsletter and podcast at winwinpodcast.com
caveats: A one-person media project with no stated organisation, funding or base. Output is irregular (roughly one post a month in 2026, and not all of it about AI). The Moloch frame comes from Scott Alexander's 2014 essay; Win-Win popularises it and applies it to AI rather than developing it as research.
tag_notes: Home: arts (H3: general-audience journalism and podcasts go to Arts). Formal is secondary for the game-theoretic Moloch / multipolar-trap concept it carries. Ring: bridge (E3), roster value kept. It is rooted in poker, game theory and science communication rather than the AI-safety ecosystem, with a sustained, explicitly safety-framed AI line: 7 of its 12 latest posts, covering superintelligence, alignment and AI-race governance, plus the host's TEDAI talk on Moloch in AI. Transfer: convening (J5); it informs a general audience. Problems: systemic first, since multipolar traps are named in that column and there is no cooperation or diplomacy programme to move it to multi_agent or security (F boundary). Region: global, as no base is stated (O). A speed_of_wisdom badge was considered for its anti-race message and left off to keep badges sparse.

name: AI Impacts
summary: A research project, led by co-founder Katja Grace and based at the Machine Intelligence Research Institute in Berkeley, that tries to answer decision-relevant questions about the future of AI. It is known for the Expert Survey on Progress in AI (rounds in 2016, 2022, 2023 and 2024; the 2024 round, with 1,580 respondents, was written up in September 2026) and for a wiki on timelines, historical technological discontinuities and arguments for AI risk. In 2024 it ran an essay competition on the automation of wisdom and philosophy: 90 entries, $20,000 in prizes, winners announced in October 2024.
why_it_matters: Its surveys are a widely cited, repeated measure of what ML researchers expect about AI timelines and risk. Its wisdom-and-philosophy essay competition was an early attempt in the x-risk field to treat wisdom itself as a target for differential AI development, which gives int/a's wisdom agenda a foothold in the core.

key_work.title: Advanced AI according to 1,580 researchers: uncertain, unsafe, and sooner than we thought (2024 Expert Survey on Progress in AI)
Winners of the Essay Competition on the Automation of Wisdom and Philosophy
2023 Expert Survey on Progress in AI (2,778 respondents)
AI Impacts Wiki

funding: Survival and Flourishing Fund: $351,000 general support (SFF-2026, Jaan Tallinn and Dustin Moskovitz), $546,000 (SFF-2022-H2), plus smaller 2019-2020 grants. Earlier grants from Open Philanthropy (now Coefficient Giving). Based at MIRI, which has acted as a sponsor.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: published the 2024 expert-survey paper 'Advanced AI according to 1,580 researchers'; May 2026: a run of blog posts by Katja Grace on AI races, coordination and unemployment.
engage: Read and reuse the survey data; the 2023 survey's reanalysis code was open-sourced in Dec 2024
Donations through the site
caveats: Its imports from outside ML are modest: survey methods, history of technology and philosophy. It is closer to mainstream AI-safety strategy than to the interdisciplinary edge. The wisdom competition was a one-off in 2024 and its funder was not named. Visible staff are now Katja Grace plus support staff. The roster marked it as not on the classic map, but it is listed there under Strategy/Forecasting. The founding year (2014, with Paul Christiano) is from memory of the earlier about page and was not reconfirmed on the current page.
tag_notes: Home: democracy (B10: expert surveys and judgmental forecasting are collective epistemics); philosophy is secondary for the lead researcher's background and the wisdom-and-philosophy competition. Ring: core (E1). It was founded to study the long-run impacts of advanced AI, sits at MIRI, is SFF-funded and is on the aisafety.com map. Transfer: into_institutions (J3), loosely; its output is evidence for decision-makers rather than a governance instrument. MISFIT: transfer has no value for 'informing decision-makers' and the public's picture'. Problems: systemic is added for its standing focus on long-term trajectory and, in 2026, race and coordination dynamics. Org type: nonprofit, as a project with its own identity hosted at MIRI (I). on_classic_map corrected to true ('AI Impacts', Strategy/Forecasting).

name: Life Itself (incl. Second Renaissance)
summary: A collective co-founded by Rufus Pollock (founder of Open Knowledge), performance artist Sylvie Barbier and cognitive scientist Liam Kavanagh, describing itself as 'a living experiment in wise living and wise societies'. It runs three co-living 'developmental' hubs near Bergerac in south-west France (it earlier had hubs in Berlin and London), a research circle, and the Second Renaissance project, which argues that the metacrisis is at root a crisis of worldview and culture. It publishes the 'Seeds of a Second Renaissance' newsletter, hosts an online forum with regular research groups, and holds Second Renaissance gatherings (September 2025 and 2026) and an online conference (December 2025).
why_it_matters: It is one of the main organised homes of the metamodern 'second renaissance' view, shared by int/a, that AI risk sits inside a wider crisis of meaning and paradigm. Its hubs and online research groups are working settings where AI could be taken up as a cultural and inner-development question rather than only a technical one.

key_work.title: Wiser Technology: Technology and a Second Renaissance, Parts I and II
Second Renaissance No 1 and No 2 (what a second renaissance is, and how paradigm change happens)
Seeds of a Second Renaissance, Issue 12: 'In Tech We Trust'
Second Renaissance Conference Online (5-7 December)

funding: Not disclosed on its site, which mentions co-living hubs and business ventures alongside research.
status_evidence: Oct 2026: forum active, including the research group 'Virtue Ethics and the Metacrisis' (2 Oct 2026); 9 Sep 2026: newsletter on a gathering on the art of the Second Renaissance.
engage: Residencies and co-living at the hubs near Bergerac, France
Second Renaissance gatherings (September, 2025 and 2026) and the online conference (December 2025)
Online forum (forum.secondrenaissance.net) with regular research groups, e.g. on virtue ethics and the metacrisis
Courses, learning journeys and embodiment retreats
Seeds of a Second Renaissance newsletter
caveats: Its AI engagement is light: a 2024 essay pair on technology, a February 2026 newsletter issue on technology's authority, and forum threads on AI and LLMs (Sep-Oct 2026). The roster's claim that its forum critiqued the Full-Stack Alignment programme could not be verified. Founding year and legal form were not found.
tag_notes: Home: contemplative (B7 names Life Itself: a metamodern, inner-development method applied to the metacrisis); sub cont_integral. Life & systems is secondary for its systems analysis of the metacrisis. Ring: potential (E2), roster value kept; there is no standing AI programme, only occasional technology essays and forum threads. Transferable method: developmental co-living spaces and research on paradigm change in the metacrisis, plus online research circles that could host inquiry into AI and wisdom. Transfer: convening (J5); its technology writing addresses its own community. Not none_yet, because some technology work exists (J6). Org type: nonprofit, though its legal form is unconfirmed. Hub: online, for recurring forum research groups (O); its Berlin and London hubs appear to have closed.

name: Metamoderna
summary: A publishing company registered in Denmark that publishes the books, essays and courses of 'Hanzi Freinacht', the joint pen-name of Daniel Görtz and Emil Ejner Friis, on metamodernism and 'political metamodernism'. Its books include The Listening Society (2017), Nordic Ideology (2019) and 12 Commandments, with German and Portuguese translations. In 2025 it released The Axial Turn by Emil Ejner Friis as a free PDF. It runs online courses on metamodernism through the Dandelion events platform and takes donations.
why_it_matters: Political metamodernism offers a developmental account of politics and institutions (the 'listening society' and its new forms of politics, such as democratisation, existential and empirical politics). That account could inform how societies govern AI and respond to the crisis of meaning AI deepens. It is a founding text of the metamodern milieu that int/a draws on, but it has not yet been brought to bear on AI.

key_work.title: The Listening Society
Nordic Ideology
The Axial Turn (Emil Ejner Friis, free PDF)
An Updated Masterclass in Metamodernism (online course)

people: Emil Ejner Friis (co-author as Hanzi Freinacht)
Robert Kelley Ayala (listed with the founders on its Dandelion page)
funding: Book sales, courses and donations via a 'Support Hanzi' Donorbox page.
status_evidence: 2025: released The Axial Turn (PDF); site footer © 2026. No dated 2026 posts or course dates found.
engage: Online courses on metamodernism via Dandelion (dates not listed when checked)
Donate via the 'Support Hanzi' page
Door to open: no AI work, so it needs outreach
caveats: No AI-related work found. Hanzi Freinacht is a deliberately provocative pseudonymous persona. Recent output is credited to Emil Ejner Friis alone, and Daniel Görtz's current role is unclear. Checks of its Medium and Substack were rate-limited, so recent posts there were not seen.
tag_notes: Home: contemplative (B7: metamodern bodies are Contemplative); sub cont_integral. Philosophy is secondary for its political philosophy. Ring: potential (E2), roster value kept; no AI work was found. Transferable method: political metamodernism's developmental model of politics and institutions, usable in designing AI governance and in diagnosing the metacrisis. Transfer: none_yet (J6). Org type: company, as 'an independent publishing company registered in Denmark' (I). Status: active, on thin evidence (a 2025 publication).

name: The Stoa
summary: An online, and occasionally in-person, space for dialogue and collective inquiry, run by Peter N. Limberg and part of the 'liminal web' of sensemaking communities. In late 2025 it ran two four-week, pay-what-you-wish 'inverse courses' through Metalabel: 'Worldview Studies' (October-November) and 'The Wise Agency' (November-December, with Ayelet Fishbach, C. Thi Nguyen, Paul Millerd and Scott Britton; online via Zoom with a parallel in-person cohort capped at 20). Limberg now describes it as 'Stoa-as-a-Service' for 'philosopher-builders', people building technology from a moral or philosophical stance.
why_it_matters: Its formats for dialogue and collective inquiry across worldviews, and its audience of technologists, could support sensemaking about AI and the inner life of the people building it. Limberg writes regularly on how AI affects meaning, intimacy and intellectual life, but The Stoa itself has engaged with AI only in single sessions.

key_work.title: The Wise Agency: Accomplish Consciously, Together (inverse course)
Worldview Studies: To See the World Is to Shape It (inverse course)
'The First Sage is The Stoa' (Stoa-as-a-Service for philosopher-builders)

funding: Pay-what-you-wish course tickets (suggested $40-50) via Metalabel; no institutional funders found.
status_evidence: Nov-Dec 2025: ran 'The Wise Agency' course, which sold out; the founder's Substack Less Foolish was active to Sep 2026.
engage: Pay-what-you-wish online courses and sessions via thestoa.metalabel.com
Less Foolish, Peter Limberg's Substack, which announces Stoa offerings
Door to open: no AI programme
caveats: Its former domain, thestoa.ca, no longer resolves (checked Oct 2026). Offerings are now occasional courses announced through the founder's Substack, and no Stoa events in 2026 were confirmed. Most of its AI engagement is the founder's personal essays (e.g. 'AI Can't Enjoy Cigars', Aug 2026) plus a November 2025 session with HeadOn, an AI project on online polarisation. The Toronto base is inferred from the .ca domain, Eastern-time scheduling and background knowledge, not stated on a current page.
tag_notes: Home: contemplative, sub cont_integral (B7: the liminal-web, metamodern sensemaking and dialogue milieu). Philosophy is secondary for its practice of philosophical inquiry. Ring: potential (E2), roster value kept; AI appears only in single sessions and in the founder's essays. Transferable method: facilitated online collective inquiry and dialogue across worldviews, reaching technologists ('philosopher-builders'). Transfer: convening (J5); not none_yet, because it has hosted some AI content. Hub: online, for recurring remote courses (O). Status: active on verified 2025 activity; its lapsed domain is noted in caveats.

name: Software Heritage (incl. CodeCommons)
summary: Software Heritage is a public archive of publicly available source code, set up in 2016 under Inria with UNESCO's support. It gives every archived file a persistent identifier (SWHID), so provenance can be traced. CodeCommons is a two-year, roughly €5 million consortium funded by France 2030 through Bpifrance and led from Inria with CEA, Tweag and Italian universities. It is turning the archive into a curated, metadata-rich dataset for training code models. Access is conditional on 2023 principles: models trained on the archive must be openly licensed, training data must be documented, and authors can opt out.
why_it_matters: It applies archival provenance to training data. Persistent identifiers make it possible to check what went into a model and to attribute generated code. It also offers a working template for a training-data commons that sets conditions on model builders, a governance lever that mainstream AI safety rarely builds.

key_work.title: Software Heritage statement on large language models for code (transparency, open licensing of trained models, opt-out)
CodeCommons: a traceable, curated code dataset for AI training
Software Heritage 2026 Symposium and Summit at UNESCO (10th anniversary; theme on transparent AI)
Archive used to build The Stack v2 / StarCoder2 (BigCode)

funding: Run by Inria with UNESCO support. Sponsors include Microsoft, the Technology Innovation Institute, CEA, CNRS, Huawei, Infosys, the French research ministry, AWS, GitHub and Google. CodeCommons has about €5M over two years from France 2030 and Bpifrance (IEEE Spectrum, Jan 2025).
status_evidence: Oct 2026: blog post 'Metadata fatigue is not a fatality'. Sep 2026: job opening for a Head of Communications. Jan 2026: 10th-anniversary symposium co-hosted with UNESCO, with a strand on transparent AI.
engage: Staff roles: Head of Communications and DevOps Engineer listed in 2026 (softwareheritage.org/jobs)
Annual symposium and summit with UNESCO in Paris, with online attendance (January 2026)
Ambassadors programme, profiled on the blog through 2026
caveats: CodeCommons is a time-limited project, roughly 2025-26, and its own site shows little news after 2024. Whether the curated dataset and opt-out system have been released is unverified. The archive itself is not an AI-governance organisation: the AI relevance sits in CodeCommons and the 2023 LLM principles. Big-tech sponsors, including AI developers, fund the archive.
tag_notes: Home economics/econ_commons (B9): it treats source code as a digital commons and Digital Public Good and governs access to it as a commons. Law is secondary for authors' rights and licence compliance. MISFIT: archival science and digital preservation have no tradition key. Ring adjacent (E3): CodeCommons is a sustained, funded AI project framed around transparency, fairness and sustainability, not safety or catastrophic risk. Transfer into_model (J1): CodeCommons shapes the training data of code models and sets conditions on the models trained on it. Org_type academic (I): a permanent, named initiative hosted by Inria, a public research institute. Framing flourishing: the stated aim is a transparent, sustainable and fair commons for AI training, not harm avoidance.

name: Open Future
summary: Open Future is a European think tank for the open movement, registered as a Dutch foundation (stichting), with staff in Amsterdam and Warsaw. Its AI work covers Public AI (AI as commons-based public infrastructure), training-data transparency under the EU AI Act, and the relationship between AI and knowledge commons such as Wikimedia and libraries. It publishes white papers and makes EU policy submissions. In 2024 it hosted an online Alignment Assembly on AI and the Commons, using the Collective Intelligence Project's method.
why_it_matters: It develops concrete institutional alternatives to concentrated AI power: public AI infrastructure, library-governed datasets and rules on training-data transparency. Those designs bear directly on concentration and lock-in, which the AI-safety field names as a risk but seldom designs against.

key_work.title: White Paper on Public AI
European Public AI Policy Brief
European Books Data Commons feasibility study; Wikimedia, the Commons and the New AI Knowledge Loop
Alignment Assembly on AI and the Commons (with Creative Commons and Fundación Karisma)

funding: Arcadia Fund (€1.05M, 2020-24), Open Society Foundations ($300k, 3 years from 2023), Horizon Europe (€450k, 2023), AI Collaborative (€480k, 2025), Internet Archive (€95k, 2025), Wikimedia CH (€91.4k, 2025-26), European AI & Society Fund (€41k, 2025), EU Public Domain Registry (€228k, 2024).
status_evidence: 11 Sep 2026: response to the EU call for evidence on an AI strategy for the cultural and creative sectors. Jul 2026: European Books Data Commons study published.
caveats: Paul Keller and Alek Tarkowski also lead COMMUNIA (president and team member), so the two organisations overlap in people and policy positions. Staff size and budget are not published. No open calls or roles were found on the site.
tag_notes: Home economics/econ_commons (B9): its method is Ostrom-style commons governance applied to knowledge and AI infrastructure (public AI, data commons). Law is secondary for copyright and AI Act work. Ring adjacent (E3): a sustained Public AI programme in 2025-26, framed around power concentration and the public interest rather than safety or catastrophic risk. Transfer into_institutions (J3): its outputs are policy designs and EU submissions for governing AI and training data. The 2024 Alignment Assembly was a one-off, so democracy is not added.

name: Creative Commons (CC): CC signals and AI and the Commons
summary: Creative Commons is the US nonprofit, run by a distributed team, that stewards the CC licences. Its AI and the Commons work includes CC signals, a framework announced in June 2025 that lets creators and collection holders state how AI systems may reuse their work. In April 2026 CC said that preference signals without enforcement do not shift power. By September 2026 it was exploring an experimental legal tool that could set conditions on bulk access to large data collections. In 2025-26 it also published guidance on using CC licences in an AI ecosystem, on open heritage in the age of AI and on Indigenous collections.
why_it_matters: It holds global norm-setting infrastructure for sharing, through licences used on a vast body of works, and is testing how a commons can set terms for AI developers that neither law nor company policy sets. Its public conclusion that unenforced signals do not change developer behaviour is useful evidence for anyone designing voluntary AI norms.

key_work.title: CC signals framework (announced)
Update on CC signals: what changed and why
Guidance on Using CC Licenses in an AI Ecosystem
Open Heritage in the Age of Artificial Intelligence; Guidance for Indigenous Collections and Data

people: Brigitte Vézina (author of CC's open heritage and AI guidance)
funding: Donations and foundation grants. Arcadia has funded its open culture work for about five years, and that funding ends in 2026 (CC, Jan 2026). Other funders were not checked.
status_evidence: 2 Oct 2026: blog post on the Open Heritage Roundtable. 21 Sep 2026: CEO post 'A Principled Approach as the Sands Shift', on CC signals moving towards legal tools.
engage: Join the CC signals community through the intake form and Zulip chat
CC Global Network community
caveats: CC signals changed direction in 2026: in April CC dropped reliance on preference signals, and in September it described an experimental legal tool for conditioning bulk data access. The final design is not yet public. Arcadia's open culture funding ends in 2026. The AI work is one strand of a broader licensing organisation.
tag_notes: Home economics/econ_commons (B9): its AI work is framed around reciprocity and sustaining the knowledge commons. Law is secondary because its instruments are licences and legal tools. Ring adjacent (E3): a sustained AI and the Commons programme in 2025-26, without safety or catastrophic-risk framing. Transfer into_institutions (J3): CC signals and its licence guidance are norms that govern how AI developers may reuse content. Region global (O): a US-registered nonprofit whose staff work remotely. Framing structural (L): it describes AI training as having 'concentrated power and undermined trust' in the commons.

name: COMMUNIA Association for the Public Domain
summary: COMMUNIA is an international association under Belgian law, based in Brussels, that advocates for the public domain and for access to and reuse of culture and knowledge, mainly in EU copyright policy. It grew out of a European Commission-funded thematic network (2007-11). Its AI work includes policy papers on training machine-learning models on copyrighted works (2023) and against new exclusive rights for AI-generated outputs (2025), AI Act submissions on text-and-data-mining opt-outs, and a 2026 study on copyright obstacles to open-source AI in the EU.
why_it_matters: It holds detailed copyright-law expertise on who may train on, and who may own, the outputs of AI. That decides whether open and public-interest AI stays legally viable in Europe, a question about power and lock-in that conventional AI policy usually leaves to lobbyists for rights holders or for developers.

key_work.title: Policy Paper #15: On using copyrighted works for teaching the machine
Policy Paper #22: Against new exclusive rights for AI-generated outputs
Study: Copyright challenges in open-source AI development in the European Union
Response to the Commission's call for evidence on the AI Strategy for the Cultural and Creative Sectors

funding: Arcadia (charitable fund of Lisbet Rausing and Peter Baldwin), plus member contributions.
status_evidence: 1 Oct 2026: COMMUNIA Salon 'Time to fix copyright'. 14 Sep 2026: response on the EU AI strategy for the cultural and creative sectors.
caveats: It overlaps with Open Future in leadership: Paul Keller presides over COMMUNIA and co-founded Open Future, and Alek Tarkowski works with both. Its AI engagement is copyright-specific. Its Salons are in-person events in Brussels; no AI-specific open calls were found.
tag_notes: Home law/law_legal (H1, B9): its method is copyright law and legal-policy analysis, though its aim is the public domain, so economics (commons) is secondary. Ring adjacent (E3): a recurring publication line on AI and copyright (2023, 2025, 2026), with no safety framing. Transfer into_institutions (J3): it argues for EU copyright and AI Act rules, such as text-and-data-mining exceptions and no new rights in AI outputs. Org_type nonprofit rather than membership (I): it has members but no credentials, and works as a staffed advocacy NGO.

name: Open Data Institute (ODI)
summary: The ODI is a London nonprofit co-founded in 2012 by Tim Berners-Lee and Nigel Shadbolt. It works on data infrastructure, data stewardship and data institutions such as data trusts. Since November 2023 it has run a data-centric AI programme on AI-ready data, transparency about training data (an AI Data Transparency Index) and responsible data use. The programme also produces policy input such as advice on the UK National Data Library and a recurring DCAI event series. In 2026 it co-launched Data Foundations for AI with the Global Partnership for Sustainable Development Data, and became a joint steward of the Digital Public Goods Alliance's DPG4AI collection.
why_it_matters: It treats data as the main lever for governing AI. Its tools are data trusts and stewardship models, transparency indices on training data, and AI-ready public data infrastructure, and it has a direct line into UK government. These institutional tools for accountability and against concentration complement model-centred safety work.

key_work.title: Data-centric AI programme
AI Data Transparency Index (first iteration)
Data Foundations for AI (with GPSDD, hosted by the UN Foundation)
Joint steward of the DPG4AI collection and AI Readiness Toolkit (Digital Public Goods Alliance)

funding: Innovate UK (£6M over three years). The data-centric AI programme is supported by the Patrick J. McGovern Foundation ($250k for its launch), DSIT and Omidyar Network. It also earns revenue from consultancy and training.
status_evidence: 9 Sep 2026: joined the Digital Public Goods Alliance as a joint steward of DPG4AI. 14 Oct 2026 (scheduled): DCAI #16 'AI chatbots must not be the new social media'.
engage: DCAI (data-centric AI) event series and Data Ethics Professionals sessions on AI (October 2026)
ODI training courses on data and AI
caveats: A large share of its work is consultancy and training for organisations, not only public-interest research. Its AI framing is responsible data and trust rather than safety. Staff size is estimated.
tag_notes: Home economics/econ_commons (B9): it brings data-institution and data-commons designs (data trusts, open data as public infrastructure, digital public goods). Law is secondary for data ethics and policy work. MISFIT: data stewardship and information science have no tradition key, and law_policy was a close alternative. Ring adjacent (E3): a sustained data-centric AI programme since 2023, framed around trust, accountability and access, not catastrophic risk. Transfer into_institutions (J3): its outputs are data-governance frameworks, transparency indices and policy advice. Assurance is a secondary problem because the AI Data Transparency Index tracks model developers.

name: Starling Lab for Data Integrity
summary: Starling Lab is an academic research centre co-founded by Stanford's Department of Electrical Engineering and the USC Shoah Foundation. It began as a research programme in 2018 and formally launched in 2021. It prototypes tools and principles for capturing, storing and verifying authentic digital records, using cryptography and decentralised storage, for journalism, history, law and human-rights archives. Its 2026 dispatches cover deepfakes as courtroom evidence, guiding principles for AI in international criminal courts, a guide to synthetic-media and provenance law in the EU, US and China, and AI in documentary production.
why_it_matters: It applies archival chain of custody and cryptographic provenance to the problem of keeping authentic records once generative AI makes fabrication cheap. That makes it a practical source on epistemic resilience for courts, newsrooms and historians, beyond detecting individual deepfakes.

key_work.title: Guide to synthetic media regulation and content provenance in the EU, US and China
New guiding principles for AI in the courtroom (international criminal law and deepfake evidence)
Decoding the California AI Transparency Act
Preserving Armenian cultural heritage on the decentralised web

funding: Stanford and USC, a multi-year sponsored research agreement with Protocol Labs and the Filecoin Foundation for the Decentralized Web, and donor-advised funds from Ampathy and the IOG Research Hub.
status_evidence: 15 Jul 2026: dispatch 'Lab Activities, Summer 2026'. 26 Jun 2026: guiding principles for AI in the courtroom.
engage: 2026 fellows on documentary, generative AI and media authenticity
Dispatch newsletter (dispatch.starlinglab.org)
caveats: Its main funders are decentralised-web and crypto-linked foundations (Protocol Labs, Filecoin Foundation, IOG), which shapes its technical approach. Independent coverage of the lab itself is thin. It has about nine staff.
tag_notes: Home democracy/dem_epistemics: its core contribution is provenance and authenticity of records, a collective-epistemics method. Law (evidence and human-rights law, Stanford Law faculty) and arts (journalism and documentary) are secondary. MISFIT: archival science has no tradition key. Ring adjacent (E3): a sustained 2025-26 line of work on deepfakes and provenance, framed around trust in records, not AI safety. Transfer into_institutions (J3): its outputs are principles and tools for courts, newsrooms and archives. Framing structural: erosion of trust in records, not one catastrophe; one 2026 dispatch argues the deepfake-evidence threat is overstated.

name: WITNESS
summary: WITNESS is a human-rights organisation founded in 1992 by Peter Gabriel. It trains and supports people to use video as evidence of abuses. About 30 staff work on five continents from a Brooklyn base. Its AI programme, 'Prepare, Don't Panic' (since 2018), runs a Deepfakes Rapid Response Force (since 2023) and the TRIED benchmark for AI-detection tools (2025). It co-chairs the C2PA provenance coalition's Threats and Harms task force. In September 2026 it launched a regional rapid-response force in Brazil with Brazilian fact-checkers and Unicamp's Recod.ai, and published lessons on verification from the Nepal floods.
why_it_matters: It brings threat models and verification practice from the people most exposed to AI-enabled information attacks, human-rights defenders and journalists, many of them in the Majority World. It also feeds that knowledge into provenance standards and detection benchmarks that the AI field relies on.

key_work.title: Prepare, Don't Panic: deepfakes and generative AI programme
Deepfakes Rapid Response Force
TRIED (Truly Innovative and Effective AI Detection) benchmark
First regional Deepfake Rapid Response Force, Brazil

funding: Ford Foundation, MacArthur Foundation, Skoll Foundation, Andrew W. Mellon Foundation, Heising-Simons Foundation, Sida, the Filecoin Foundation for the Decentralized Web, the Digital Democracy Initiative, the William H. Donner Foundation and others. It was founded with a $1M seed grant from the Reebok Human Rights Foundation.
status_evidence: 24 Sep 2026: launched a regional Deepfake Rapid Response Force in Brazil. Sep 2026: report on five lessons from the Nepal floods for verifying what is real.
engage: Staff roles (careers page)
Journalists and fact-checkers can escalate suspected deepfakes to the Rapid Response Force
caveats: Most of its work is human-rights video practice in general; AI is one of three priority areas. It frames AI as a matter of present harms and trust, not catastrophic risk.
tag_notes: Home law/law_legal (H1): its method is human-rights documentation and video-as-evidence practice. Democracy (provenance, verification) is secondary. Ring adjacent (E3): a sustained AI programme since 2018, framed around human rights and trust in evidence, not safety or catastrophic risk. Transfer protecting (J4): the AI work exists so that frontline defenders' evidence cannot be faked or dismissed, though it also shapes C2PA standards. Standpoint neither (O): it is led from Brooklyn, though much of its AI work centres on Brazil, Nepal and other Majority-World settings. Way of knowing: practice, informed by frontline consultations, so communal was a close alternative.

name: TeachAI
summary: TeachAI is a coalition launched on 2 May 2023 by Code.org (renamed CodeAI in June 2026), ETS, ISTE, Khan Academy and the World Economic Forum. Code.org staffs and runs it. It publishes the AI Guidance for Schools Toolkit, built on seven principles for AI in education, as well as Foundational Policy Ideas for education policymakers and a tracker of AI-in-education guidance from US states and other countries. With the Computer Science Teachers Association (CSTA) it also produced briefs on computer-science education in the age of AI, released 2024-25. Its advisory committee lists more than 100 organisations, among them Google, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon, OpenAI and UNICEF.
why_it_matters: Many school systems draw their AI rules from its toolkit, whose principles include keeping human decision-making and regularly assessing AI's effects. That makes it a lever on norms for children's cognitive autonomy and AI literacy, an area the AI-safety field barely reaches. Because tech companies sit inside it, it is also a place to watch whose framing of 'AI in schools' wins.

key_work.title: AI Guidance for Schools Toolkit
Guidance on the Future of Computer Science Education in an Age of AI (briefs with CSTA)
AI in Education Policy Tracker

people: Pat Yongpradit (Lead of TeachAI; Chief Academic Officer, Code.org)
funding: Not disclosed. Code.org (now CodeAI) staffs and operates the coalition, coordinating with the World Economic Forum.
status_evidence: Jun 2026: CodeAI's rebrand announcement describes TeachAI as the global coalition it co-founded. Early 2025: the last TeachAI–CSTA computer-science briefs were released.
engage: Free AI Guidance for Schools Toolkit, with editable sample policies, at teachai.org/toolkit
Advisory committee of 100+ organisations; contact through the 'Engage With Us' section of its site
caveats: The advisory committee is heavy with industry (Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI), and the framing puts opportunity first: it promotes AI adoption in schools as much as caution. Its own site shows no dated 2026 output (the footer reads © 2025). The core toolkit dates from 2023, and the latest dated outputs are the CSTA briefs of early 2025. Code.org rebranded as CodeAI on 2 June 2026.
tag_notes: Home: its outputs are school AI guidance and policy ideas from education leaders, and Psychology/child & youth development is the closest home (MISFIT: education and school policy has no tradition of its own). Ring: a standing AI-in-education programme since 2023 with no safety, catastrophic-risk or alignment framing, so adjacent (E3). Transfer: its main products are policy templates that school systems adopt to govern AI use, so into_institutions (J3); this is not mainly defensive. Framing coded flourishing because its mission is to realise AI's benefits for learning while mitigating risks.

name: AILit Framework (European Commission and OECD) and PISA 2029 Media & AI Literacy (MAIL) assessment
summary: A joint project of the European Commission and the OECD, supported by Code.org (now CodeAI), that defines AI literacy for primary and secondary schools. A review draft was launched on 22 May 2025. After consultation with more than 2,000 people in over 100 countries, the final framework, 'Empowering Learners for the Age of AI', was launched on 18 June 2026 with four domains: Engage with AI, Create with AI, Manage AI and Shape AI. It feeds the OECD's PISA 2029 Media & Artificial Intelligence Literacy (MAIL) assessment of 15-year-olds, to be fielded in 2029.
why_it_matters: PISA 2029 will measure, across the countries and economies that take part, whether 15-year-olds can evaluate AI-mediated content and use AI responsibly. That will be one of the largest public measurements of human epistemic agency alongside AI. The framework holds that AI cannot replace human judgement, care or relationships, and that choosing not to use AI can be a responsible decision: an alignment-relevant norm for the human side of the transition.

key_work.title: Empowering Learners for the Age of AI: final AI Literacy Framework for Primary and Secondary Education
AILit Framework review draft and global consultation
Shaping Future Success: AI Literacy Framework and the PISA 2029 MAIL Assessment

people: Mario Piacentini (OECD; writes on the PISA 2029 MAIL assessment)
Romina Cachia (Scientific Team Leader, Joint Research Centre, European Commission)
funding: European Commission and OECD, with support from Code.org (CodeAI). No budget published.
status_evidence: 18 Jun 2026: the final AILit framework was launched at the European Digital Education Hub flagship event 'Collaborate for Impact'.
engage: The framework, competences and learning scenarios are free at ailiteracyframework.org
The 2025 global consultation on the draft has closed; PISA 2029 MAIL is fielded through national PISA centres
caveats: The entry covers two related but separate instruments: AILit is a curriculum reference framework, while MAIL is a PISA assessment framework developed by the OECD, with ACER leading delivery of PISA 2029. Code.org/CodeAI, a nonprofit backed by the tech industry, supported the drafting. Ethics runs through the framework, but it has no safety or catastrophic-risk framing. MAIL results are not expected before about 2031.
tag_notes: Home: comparative education policy and international assessment of what young learners should know about AI, for which Psychology/child & youth development is the closest home (MISFIT: education and international assessment have no tradition of their own). Democracy is secondary because MAIL assesses media literacy and credibility judgement. Ring: a funded, sustained AI-literacy project from 2025 to 2029 with no safety framing, so adjacent (E3). Transfer: it equips education systems and learners with AI literacy, which counts as literacy for its own community, so convening (J5); it is not a rule for governing AI. Status new: the draft appeared in 2025 and the final version in June 2026. Paris hub because the OECD Directorate for Education and Skills team is there.

name: Experience AI (Raspberry Pi Foundation with Google DeepMind)
summary: A free AI-literacy programme for learners aged about 8 to 17, created by the Raspberry Pi Foundation with Google DeepMind and launched in April 2023. It offers lesson plans, slides, videos and a free online course for teachers ('Understanding AI for educators'), delivered through regional partner organisations and translations. It reports reaching tens of thousands of educators and millions of learners in more than 180 countries. Recent units cover AI safety for ages 11-14 (privacy, misinformation, trust and responsibility; February 2026) and using large language models to learn (September 2026).
why_it_matters: Its September 2026 unit on large language models, 'think first, prompt second', teaches 13- to 16-year-olds to resist cognitive offloading: they rewrite prompts so the tool serves their learning, judge the outputs and stay actively involved in their own thinking. Few classroom programmes aim directly at keeping young people's thinking their own as LLMs spread. Its partner network across many countries could also carry broader AI-risk literacy for young people.

key_work.title: Encouraging learners to think first, prompt second: LLM unit
AI safety resources for ages 11-14 (helping young people stay safe online in the age of AI)
2025 UNESCO King Hamad Bin Isa Al-Khalifa Prize for the Use of ICT in Education
Experience AI expands to reach over 2 million students (Google.org-funded expansion)

people: Rehana Al-Soltane (Raspberry Pi Foundation; author of the AI safety and LLM unit announcements)
Ben Garside (Raspberry Pi Foundation; Experience AI resources)
funding: Google.org gave the Raspberry Pi Foundation $10m to expand Experience AI (2024). Content is co-developed with Google DeepMind.
status_evidence: 28 Sep 2026: published a new five-lesson unit on using large language models to learn ('think first, prompt second').
engage: Free lessons, slides and videos for teachers at experience-ai.org
Free online course for teachers, 'Understanding AI for educators'
Regional partners deliver training and translations, e.g. an Australia/New Zealand programme to train 5,000 more educators by 2028
caveats: Google DeepMind co-develops the content and Google.org funds the expansion, so a frontier developer shapes and pays for how millions of children are introduced to AI. In these materials, 'AI safety' means online safety (privacy, misinformation, trust), not the AI-safety field's sense.
tag_notes: Home: computing-education pedagogy for children and teenagers, for which Psychology/child & youth development is the closest home (MISFIT: education). Ring: a standing curriculum since 2023 about children's understanding and use of AI; its 'AI safety' unit means online safety, so it stays adjacent (E3), not bridge. Transfer: AI literacy for learners and teachers, so convening (J5); the cognitive-offloading unit also protects learners. Framing coded flourishing because the programme's aim is to empower young people to understand AI, though its 2026 units address harms.

name: Digital Promise (AI in education initiative)
why_it_matters: About 40 district leaders, school staff and AI researchers co-designed its certification. To pass, a product must let educators override AI output, label generative-AI features, monitor for algorithmic bias and be transparent about data. That makes it a working, buyer-side assurance scheme for protecting human agency: the kind of procurement lever AI-governance discussions often lack.

key_work.title: Responsibly Designed AI product certification
AI Literacy Framework
Digital Promise and TNTP three-year AI partnership

funding: Salesforce funds the first phase of the 2026 TNTP partnership. Congress authorised the organisation through the Higher Education Opportunity Act of 2008. Its other funders are listed on its supporters page.
status_evidence: 2 Apr 2026: announced a three-year AI partnership with TNTP aiming to reach 15 million learners by 2028. Dec 2025: published a review of AI evaluation frameworks in 32 states and Puerto Rico.
engage: Edtech developers can apply for the Responsibly Designed AI certification
Districts can engage it for AI professional learning, such as its AI Champion onboarding
Staff roles listed on its careers page
caveats: It mostly helps schools adopt AI well rather than questioning adoption, and its AI work is partly funded by industry (Salesforce for the TNTP partnership). The certification covers privacy, bias, labelling and educator override, not longer-term cognitive dependency. AI is one strand of a much wider education portfolio.
tag_notes: Home: learning sciences and education research on AI in K-12 learning, for which Psychology/child & youth development is the closest home (MISFIT: education and learning sciences). Safety is secondary because of its product certification. Ring: standing AI programmes (certification, literacy framework, research centre) focused on learners and teachers with no catastrophic-risk framing, so adjacent (E3). Transfer: the certification and frameworks exist to safeguard learner and educator agency, privacy and fairness, so protecting (J4). Assurance is paired with minds because it certifies products (F). Framing coded flourishing from its mission to expand opportunity for every learner.

name: EDSAFE AI Alliance
summary: A coalition run by InnovateEDU, a New York nonprofit, that promotes 'S.A.F.E.' (Safe, Accountable, Fair and Efficacious) AI in education. It dates its founding to 2020; it launched publicly in August 2021, financed by the AI edtech company Riiid, with DXtera as fiscal agent. It maintains the SAFE Benchmarks Framework, which draws on more than 24 AI safety, trust and market frameworks. It also runs 29 district Policy Labs, an AI fellowship (156 fellows so far), an Industry Council of 175+ companies and a Policy Essentials course. In 2026 it published recommendations on AI companions in schools and started a Spark Fund that gives technical assistance to 10 districts.
why_it_matters: Its February 2026 report on AI companions asks developers to strip engagement-maximising and anthropomorphic features, such as excessive praise and affectionate language, from tools children use. It also asks vendors to support mandatory reporting when students express self-harm. This is design guidance on sycophancy and emotional dependency written by the education sector itself, and the alliance shows a sector building its own AI benchmarks and procurement standards from district level up.

key_work.title: S.A.F.E. by Design: Policy, Research, and Practice Recommendations for AI Companions in Education
SAFE Benchmarks Framework
EDSAFE AI Spark Fund, inaugural cohort of 10 districts

people: Erin Mote (CEO and founder of InnovateEDU; leads the alliance)
Jim Larimore (Riiid; helped form the alliance in 2021)
funding: Riiid financed its founding (2021), with DXtera as fiscal agent. Current funders are not published.
status_evidence: Aug 2026: named 10 districts and networks as the first Spark Fund cohort. Feb 2026: published its report on AI companions in education.
engage: AI fellowship programme (156 fellows to date)
Policy Essentials course and a policy resource hub
Industry Council for companies; Policy Labs for school districts
Spark Fund technical assistance for districts (first cohort August 2026)
caveats: It was founded with money from an AI edtech company (Riiid) and has a large industry council, so it may lean towards enabling adoption. 'Safety' here means student data privacy, cybersecurity and wellbeing, not catastrophic risk. The alliance gives 2020 as its founding year, but the public launch was in August 2021.
tag_notes: Home: its main outputs are benchmarks, procurement standards and policy guidance for edtech AI, so Safety/engineering & assurance (standards) is the closest home (MISFIT: education governance has no tradition of its own). Psychology is secondary for its work on student wellbeing and companions. Ring: a standing programme on edtech AI where 'safe' means privacy, security and wellbeing, with no alignment or catastrophic-risk framing, so adjacent (E3). Transfer: its benchmarks and recommendations exist to protect students and schools, so protecting (J4). Assurance comes first because the SAFE benchmarks are its central output, paired with minds for the companion work (F).

name: News Literacy Project (NLP)
summary: A nonpartisan US education nonprofit in Washington, DC, founded in 2008 by Pulitzer Prize-winning reporter Alan C. Miller, that teaches students and the public to judge whether information is credible. Its products include the Checkology virtual classroom, the RumorGuard debunking site, The Sift newsletter for teachers and the annual National News Literacy Week. Its AI materials include 'AI or not?' lessons, '6 Things to Know About AI', the 'Two Truths and AI' video series, RumorGuard debunks of AI-generated fakes, and teen surveys on trust in AI chatbots (2024 and 2026).
why_it_matters: It applies nearly two decades of journalism-based verification teaching to AI-generated misinformation. It reports that more than 1.4 million students have been taught with its resources since 2016 (3.5 million on another of its counts), and its educators work in more than a third of US public school districts. That is epistemic self-defence at population scale, which AI-safety work on truthfulness rarely connects to.

key_work.title: Teaching About AI: classroom resources ('AI or not?', 'Two Truths and AI', 6 Things to Know About AI)
National News Literacy Week 2026: rebuilding trust in the age of AI
NLP Teen Survey Report (including teen trust in generative AI chatbots)

funding: Startup grant from the Knight Foundation ($250,000, 2008); $10m commitment from Melanie and Richard Lundquist (2022); budget of $9.3m in the 2024-25 school year.
status_evidence: Feb 2026: National News Literacy Week (2-6 Feb), its seventh, was themed on rebuilding trust in the age of AI. 2025-26: RumorGuard posts on AI-generated fakes and new AI lessons at newslit.org/ai.
engage: Free Checkology educator accounts and AI lessons
The Sift, a weekly newsletter for educators
National News Literacy Week, held each February
Staff roles (47 staff)
caveats: Focused on the US. Its AI work is one strand of news literacy, aimed at misinformation, deepfakes and 'AI slop' rather than wider AI risks.
tag_notes: Home: verification and fact-checking literacy (RumorGuard debunks, credibility skills) is collective epistemics, so Democracy (B10). Arts/journalism is secondary because a journalist founded it and journalists host its lessons. Ring: a sustained AI-literacy strand (lessons, videos, surveys) on misinformation with no catastrophic-risk framing, so adjacent (E3). Transfer: it defends students and the public it already serves against AI-generated misinformation, so protecting (J4).

name: Elements of AI (University of Helsinki and MinnaLearn)
summary: A series of free online courses for non-experts, launched in 2018 by the University of Helsinki and the Finnish firm Reaktor and now run with the learning company MinnaLearn. Its two courses, 'Introduction to AI' (which ends with a module on implications) and 'Building AI', have had more than 2 million enrolments from 170+ countries and are offered in 40+ languages. Finland offered the course to all EU citizens as its 2019 EU-presidency gift. MinnaLearn's 'Get AI Ready', a workplace course of under 60 minutes mapped to the EU AI Act's AI-literacy duty, is now the featured product.
why_it_matters: It is proven mass public-education infrastructure, available in many EU languages and conceived as 'a civics course in AI'. Today it mostly teaches fundamentals and compliance, but it could carry AI-risk and cognitive-autonomy literacy to millions of adults.

key_work.title: Introduction to AI and Building AI (free online courses)
Course offered in all EU languages as Finland's EU-presidency gift
Get AI Ready (workplace AI-literacy course mapped to the EU AI Act)

people: Teemu Roos (Lead instructor; professor, University of Helsinki and Finnish Center for Artificial Intelligence)
funding: Finland's Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment paid nearly EUR 1.8m for the EU-wide expansion (2019). MinnaLearn sells Get AI Ready commercially.
status_evidence: 2026: the European Disability Forum's 'Empowered by AI' project, funded by Google.org, runs a MinnaLearn Get AI Ready train-the-trainer programme, with activities from September 2026.
engage: Free self-paced courses (Introduction to AI, Building AI) at elementsofai.com
Get AI Ready workplace course through MinnaLearn
caveats: Its AI-safety content is thin: the courses cover what AI is and general implications, and the newer product is commercial compliance training. The co-creating partner has changed from Reaktor to MinnaLearn. Ring changed from the roster's potential to adjacent: the whole product is a sustained AI programme, even though its content on societal effects is light. No dated news on its own site; activity in 2026 is confirmed only through partner use of Get AI Ready.
tag_notes: Home: free mass civic education in AI ('a civics course in AI'), built as a public knowledge commons, so Democracy/forecasting & collective epistemics is the closest home. The provisional home of Psychology was not used because the courses are adult and public education, not child development (MISFIT: adult and public education). Ring changed from potential to adjacent: it is itself a standing AI programme since 2018 (E2) about public understanding of AI and its implications, with no safety framing (E3). Transfer: AI literacy for the public and workers, so convening (J5). Way of knowing coded practice as the closest fit for teaching content.

name: WHO Health Ethics & Governance unit
summary: The World Health Organization's ethics team, part of the Research for Health Department in the Chief Scientist's division in Geneva. It writes WHO's ethics and governance guidance on AI in health: the 2021 guidance on AI for health, the guidance on large multi-modal models (first issued January 2024, current version dated 25 March 2025, more than 40 recommendations for governments, developers and providers), and a July 2026 report on ethics review and oversight of AI-related health research.
why_it_matters: It sets ethics and governance expectations for general-purpose generative models through a multilateral, expert-consensus process aimed at 194 member states, and it works through health research ethics committees. Mainstream AI safety rarely draws on that review machinery. It shows how bioethics institutions can be pointed at foundation models rather than only at clinical tools.

key_work.title: Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health: Guidance on large multi-modal models
Artificial intelligence-related health research: ethics review and oversight
Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health: WHO guidance

people: Andreas Reis (co-lead, WHO Global Health Ethics team)
funding: Part of WHO's core budget (assessed and voluntary contributions); unit-level figures not found.
status_evidence: Jul 2026: published 'Artificial intelligence-related health research: ethics review and oversight'; the unit page lists a virtual launch on 21 Sep 2026.
engage: Follow new guidance and its virtual launch events on the unit's page (AI research-ethics report launch, 21 Sep 2026)
Work with WHO Collaborating Centres on AI governance, e.g. TU Delft Digital Ethics Centre, designated March 2025
caveats: Its AI work covers health care and health research only. It has no programme on the population mental-health effects of consumer chatbots. Many WHO AI outputs treat AI as a tool, not as something to make safe. WHO has faced deep budget cuts since the US announced its withdrawal in January 2025, which may limit the unit.
tag_notes: Home: a global health ethics unit whose AI outputs are bioethics-based governance guidance, so philosophy/phil_bioethics (B13: ethics bodies go to Philosophy), with public health (safety) and human-rights law as secondary methods. Ring: kept at adjacent because there is a sustained AI line (2021, 2024/25 and 2026 guidance) framed around patient and public benefit and harms, not catastrophic risk or alignment (E3). Transfer: the guidance gives governments, developers and research ethics committees governance templates, so into_institutions (J3). Org type: a unit inside WHO, so programme (I, A1). Framing: closest fit is present_harms.

name: US FDA Digital Health Advisory Committee (DHAC)
summary: A federal advisory committee that advises the FDA Commissioner on digital health technologies. FDA announced it in October 2023; it has nine core voting members including the chair, plus temporary members per topic. Both of its meetings so far were on generative AI: lifecycle considerations for generative-AI-enabled devices (20-21 Nov 2024), and generative-AI digital mental-health medical devices such as therapy-like chatbots (6 Nov 2025), covering premarket evidence and postmarket monitoring.
why_it_matters: It is a working case of an existing regulator applying premarket evidence standards, labelling, crisis-escalation safeguards and postmarket surveillance to generative-AI chatbots, using medical-device safety methods. AI safety discusses post-deployment monitoring and incident reporting, but rarely sees them run by a regulator with legal powers.

key_work.title: Meeting on generative AI-enabled digital mental health medical devices (docket FDA-2025-N-2338)
Inaugural meeting: Total Product Lifecycle Considerations for Generative AI-Enabled Devices

people: Ami Bhatt (Chair; Chief Innovation Officer, American College of Cardiology)
funding: US federal government (FDA).
status_evidence: 6 Nov 2025: public meeting on generative-AI mental-health devices; public docket closed 8 Dec 2025. No 2026 meeting found on FDA's committee page as of Oct 2026.
engage: Comment on public dockets when a meeting is announced (FDA-2025-N-2338 closed 8 Dec 2025)
Watch the webcast meetings or speak in the open public hearing segment
caveats: It is advisory only, and covers only products marketed as medical devices, not general-purpose chatbots used for emotional support. FDA had authorised no AI device for a mental-health indication as of Nov 2025. I found no meeting announced for 2026, so its cadence is about one a year.
tag_notes: Home: medical-device regulation and patient safety, so safety/safety_health (B12), with clinical psychiatry as secondary for the 2025 mental-health meeting. Ring: kept at adjacent. Two meetings in 2024-25 are on generative AI, framed around patient benefit and risk (confabulation, suicidality monitoring, psychosis), not catastrophic risk (E3). Transfer: its output is regulatory advice on evidence and postmarket monitoring, so into_institutions (J3). Org type: a federal advisory committee, treated as a statutory council, so public (I).

name: Global Centre for Preventive Health and Nutrition (GLOBE), Deakin University
summary: A public-health research centre in Deakin University's Institute for Health Transformation. It is a WHO Collaborating Centre for Obesity Prevention, established in 2003, and works on commercial determinants of health: how food, alcohol, gambling and vaping marketing and policy shape disease. Its AI engagement is light. In 2026 Kathryn Backholer co-wrote a Lancet Comment and a Conversation piece arguing that targeted advertising in generative-AI chatbots is a public-health risk.
why_it_matters: It brings the commercial-determinants playbook from tobacco, alcohol and junk food, which follows business models and marketing exposure to harm, to chatbot monetisation. AI safety rarely examines that incentive. Its SCANNER system, which combines screen recording with computer vision to measure the marketing individual young people actually see, could be adapted to audit what chatbots show users.

key_work.title: Targeted advertising in generative artificial intelligence chatbots: a new public health risk (Lancet Comment)
OpenAI will put ads in ChatGPT. This opens a new door for dangerous influence (The Conversation)
SCANNER: AI-enabled monitoring of harmful digital marketing to young people

people: Kathryn Backholer (Professor of Public Health Policy; Co-Director, Institute for Health Transformation; GLOBE co-lead)

name: ISACA
summary: The global professional association for IT audit, governance, risk and security. It was founded in 1969, has more than 195,000 members and 230 chapters, and owns the CISA credential and the COBIT framework. Since 2025 it has launched three AI credentials for experienced professionals: Advanced in AI Audit (AAIA, May 2025), Advanced in AI Security Management (AAISM, Aug 2025) and Advanced in AI Risk (AAIR, Apr 2026). Each requires a prior credential such as CISA, CISM or CPA.
why_it_matters: Any regime of third-party AI audits needs a credentialed workforce and certifying machinery, and ISACA already runs both for IT audit at scale. AI-safety debate about audits rarely asks who the auditors will be, how they are certified, or what professional duties bind them.

The London hub is via the ISACA London Chapter.

name: The Institute of Internal Auditors (IIA)
summary: The global professional body and standard-setter for internal audit. It was founded in 1941, has more than 265,000 members, and owns the Global Internal Audit Standards, the Certified Internal Auditor credential and the Three Lines Model. Its AI work includes an AI Knowledge Center (launched December 2023), an AI Auditing Framework updated in September 2024 to cover generative AI and board oversight, and advocacy, such as a March 2026 statement urging Congress to build assurance mechanisms into US AI legislation.
why_it_matters: It owns the Three Lines Model, which AI governance research has already proposed for AI labs (Schuett, 'Three lines of defense against risks from AI', 2023). Its standards define how internal audit gives boards independent assurance, which bears on board oversight of AI risk inside labs.

name: International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board (IAASB)
summary: The independent global standard-setter for audit and assurance (the ISAs, ISAE 3000 for non-financial assurance, and ISSA 5000 for sustainability assurance). It works under the Public Interest Oversight Board and has been housed since 2023 by the International Foundation for Ethics and Audit. Its Technology Position covers how audits use technology. In 2025 it ran global roundtables with more than 240 stakeholders on AI in audits, in December 2025 approved developing non-authoritative AI materials, and in July 2026 added 'potential new or evolving assurance engagements' to its Catalog of Issues.
why_it_matters: ISAE 3000 and ISSA 5000 are generic assurance machinery: defined subject matter, suitable criteria, practitioner independence and professional scepticism. A third-party assurance regime for AI systems and AI-lab safety claims could reuse it rather than invent its own, as sustainability reporting did. Practitioners such as BABL AI already argue that the missing piece is suitable criteria for AI claims, not the framework.

tag_notes: Home: assurance standard-setting, so safety/safety_engineering (standards, certification, assurance). MISFIT: audit and assurance has no sub-tradition of its own. Ring: kept at potential. Its AI work treats AI as an audit tool, with no programme on assuring AI systems or AI going well (E2/E3). Transfer: the roundtables and practitioner guidance bring its own profession into the AI conversation, so convening (J5). Org type: an independent standard-setting board with its own identity, so nonprofit.

name: ForHumanity
summary: A US 501(c)(3) charity, with a French sister association (ForHumanity Europe), founded in 2016 by Ryan Carrier after a 25-year career in finance. It crowdsources binary (compliant or non-compliant) audit criteria and certification schemes for AI, algorithmic and autonomous systems, modelled on third-party financial audit. Schemes cover the EU AI Act, GDPR and other privacy laws, children's codes, employment decision tools and disability inclusion. It also trains and certifies auditors (FHCA) through an online education centre. More than 2,600 volunteer contributors draft the criteria.
why_it_matters: It is a sustained, open attempt to transplant the financial-audit model (public criteria, certified independent auditors, certification) to AI. It is one of the few groups drafting auditable certification schemes against the EU AI Act. AI-safety discussion of third-party audits can learn from both its criteria and its difficulty getting regulators to approve them.

Its whole mission is AI, but it sits outside the AI-safety ecosystem, and its framing is ethics, bias, privacy and trust rather than catastrophic risk or alignment (E3, borderline with bridge). Transfer: its certification schemes and certified auditors are governance instruments, so into_institutions (J3). Hub: online, since anyone can join the Slack community and take the online courses.

name: Research Data Alliance (RDA)
summary: A global, member-driven body for research-data sharing, founded in 2013. Volunteers in more than 100 working and interest groups write recommendations on FAIR data, metadata and trusted access. Its AI work covers documenting generative-AI use in research, FAIR for machine learning, 'data visitation' (the analysis travels to sensitive data, not the reverse) and, since 2026, the VANTAGE working group, which is drafting a framework for deciding whether and under what controls AI agents may work with restricted research data.
why_it_matters: Here data stewards rather than ML researchers are writing shared rules for when AI agents may touch sensitive data, and for how AI use in research is documented. That makes it a working venue for agent oversight and provenance standards, and a route to adoption for safety researchers.

It also receives SCOSS funding and organisational membership fees. No budget figure found.

VANTAGE and the documentation group are the parts that bear on oversight; both were still in community review and not yet endorsed in Sep 2026 (VANTAGE start date 4 Sep 2026, the Documenting Generative AI Interactions IG 7 Sep 2026). There is no catastrophic-risk framing. Hilary Hanahoe is named as Secretary General in 2025-26 speaker bios and co-authored the January 2026 agentic-AI consultation report; the RDA site does not show the name.

Framing is coded flourishing because its stakes are enabling trustworthy AI-assisted open science, not avoiding harm. name: AI4LAM (Artificial Intelligence for Libraries, Archives and Museums)
summary: An international association of libraries, archives and museums working on how AI is used in, for and by cultural-heritage institutions. It began in 2018 as a network under an agreement between the National Library of Norway and Stanford University Libraries, and was formally constituted in December 2025 by more than 40 institutions. It runs working groups (speech-to-text, AI literacy, 3D and image analysis, AI in cybersecurity), regional chapters and national nodes, community calls, and the annual Fantastic Futures conference. The 2026 conference theme was 'Trust in the Loop'.
why_it_matters: Memory institutions have long practice in provenance, authenticity and trust, which AI-safety work on content provenance rarely draws on. AI4LAM is where that practice is being turned into shared standards for AI. An example is its Transcript Provenance Metadata Elements (TPME), which record which model produced a transcript, with what settings, and whether a human corrected it.

London is coded only for the one-off MoU signing, so not as a hub; online covers open community and working-group calls.

name: Wikidata Embedding Project (Wikimedia Deutschland)
summary: A Wikimedia Deutschland project, started in 2024 and launched on 1 October 2025, that turns Wikidata's statements into vectors so that language models can search and cite them. It runs a free vector database built with Jina AI's multilingual embeddings and DataStax's Astra DB, and an MCP server that helps models write grounded SPARQL queries. In May 2026 it added a Wikibase MCP for other Wikibase instances. It also publishes processed Wikidata dumps on Hugging Face, to reduce load from AI scrapers.
why_it_matters: It shows public-interest grounding infrastructure working in practice: a community-curated, sourced knowledge graph made available to language models for retrieval with citations. It bears on model truthfulness and on alternatives to corporate AI infrastructure. It also tests whether a knowledge commons can supply AI without being worn down by scraping.

caveats: The Wikimedia Foundation is a separate roster entry; this profile is the German chapter's project. Its main users are AI developers, and part of the motive is reducing scraping load. Whether it reduces misinformation in deployed systems has not been shown. At first only about 30 million of Wikidata's roughly 119 million items were vectorised. It relies on commercial partners for embeddings and storage.
tag_notes: Home: a community-curated knowledge commons with source transparency, which is Democracy/dem_epistemics (knowledge commons, provenance). Economics is secondary because the project explicitly offers a commons-based alternative to Big Tech AI infrastructure. Ring kept at adjacent (rule E3): a funded, ongoing AI project since 2024 that aims at reliable, verifiable AI, with no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing. Transfer: into_model (rule J1), because it supplies grounding data, by retrieval and MCP, to AI systems themselves. Framing is coded structural: the stakes it names are unreliable AI and concentrated control of AI infrastructure. Way of knowing is coded communal because the knowledge comes from about 24,000 volunteer editors a month. Org type is programme (rule A1: the unit is the project, not WMDE).

name: Internet Archive
summary: A San Francisco nonprofit digital library founded by Brewster Kahle in 1996. It runs the Wayback Machine, which passed one trillion archived web pages in October 2025, and holds tens of millions of digitised texts, recordings and films. Its AI engagement is light: copyright submissions on AI (2023), episodes of its Future Knowledge podcast with Authors Alliance on AI and web archiving (2025-26), and a September 2026 event, 'Open For Whom? Access to Knowledge in the Age of AI'.
why_it_matters: Transferable method: web archiving as an independent, time-stamped record of what was published, which can be used to check provenance and claims as AI-generated content spreads. Since late 2025, publishers have been blocking its crawlers for fear of AI scraping, a direct case of AI pressure eroding a shared epistemic resource.

name: Library Futures (NYU Engelberg Center on Innovation Law & Policy)
summary: A library-rights initiative, set up as a nonprofit in January 2021, that has been a project of NYU Law's Engelberg Center since September 2022. It works on digital ownership, library e-lending rights and public access to information through advocacy, legal support and amicus briefs, a funded research network, internships and webinars for librarians. Its AI work is light: a four-part webinar series on machine learning and AI for information professionals (autumn 2025), including a session on resisting vendor AI contracts, and a 2025 piece on AI-generated books reaching library shelves.
why_it_matters: Transferable method: legal and policy advocacy for the public's right to own, lend and reach digital knowledge, for example through vendor contract terms and controlled digital lending. The same tools could shape how libraries and other public bodies buy AI tools, and who controls access to knowledge through AI.
