name: KB, National Library of the Netherlands (Koninklijke Bibliotheek)
summary: The Dutch national library, founded in 1798 and an independent administrative body funded by the Ministry of Education, Culture and Science. It adopted AI principles in 2020. In January 2024 it changed its terms of use and added technical measures to stop commercial AI firms crawling its Delpher and DBNL platforms for training, while keeping them open for academic research. Since 2024 it has sat on the content board of GPT-NL, the public Dutch language model built by TNO, SURF and NFI. In June 2026 it became a launching partner, supplying public-domain Delpher data and running a feasibility study on a retrieval assistant until November 2026.
why_it_matters: It is a working template for consent-based governance of AI training data by a public institution: it refuses commercial scraping, protects research access and supplies vetted public-domain data to a public model in which it has a governance seat. Other memory institutions and public-AI projects can copy this approach.

Law is secondary for copyright and consent rules, and Economics for its public-AI partnership with GPT-NL. MISFIT: no library or information-science tradition. name: Day of AI
summary: A free PreK-12 AI-literacy curriculum and teacher-training programme, started in 2021 at MIT RAISE (Responsible AI for Social Empowerment and Education) under Cynthia Breazeal. It became an independent nonprofit in August 2024 and still works closely with MIT RAISE. In August 2026 it released a grade-by-grade PreK-12 curriculum. Its high-school units cover ethics, identity, human agency, deepfakes and algorithmic profiling, and stress critical thinking and human-led work over reliance on AI. It reports reaching more than 4 million students, with teachers in about 175 countries.
why_it_matters: It is one of the largest free routes through which children learn what AI is and how to question it, so it shapes public understanding of AI early. Its curriculum puts students' own agency ahead of dependence on AI. It does not yet cover AI safety or catastrophic risk.

name: Financial Stability Board (FSB)
summary: The FSB is the G20 body that coordinates national financial authorities and international standard-setters. The BIS hosts it in Basel. Its AI workstream looks at how AI adoption could create system-wide weaknesses in finance: concentration on a few third-party providers, correlated models, cyber risk and model risk. Its outputs are a 2017 report, a November 2024 report on AI's implications for financial stability, an October 2025 report on monitoring indicators, a June 2026 consultation on 12 sound practices for responsible AI adoption (final report due October 2026 as a G20 deliverable) and the Chair's letter to G20 ministers of 31 August 2026 on cyber risk from frontier models.
why_it_matters: It applies the macroprudential toolkit to AI: watching a whole system for concentration, correlation and contagion. It can also put frontier-model risk in front of G20 finance ministers, as it did in August 2026 when its Chair asked authorities to support safe and responsible model release and deployment. Few AI-safety organisations have a channel like that.

Framing is structural, not catastrophic: the concern is systemic weakness, not irreversible outcomes. name: Bank for International Settlements (BIS) and Financial Stability Institute (FSI)
summary: The BIS is owned by member central banks and based in Basel. It has a sustained line of AI analysis for central banks and supervisors. Its 2024 Annual Economic Report chapter argued that shared models, a few dominant providers and cyber attacks could amplify herding, runs and fire sales, and it asked central banks to form a 'community of practice' on AI. The BIS's Financial Stability Institute, which supports supervisors worldwide through policy work and capacity-building, followed with a December 2024 paper on regulating AI in finance and a September 2026 paper on cyber threats from frontier AI.
why_it_matters: It turns findings about frontier-AI capabilities into supervisory language for central banks and supervisors around the world, and the FSI's capacity-building carries that framing into national practice. Its 2026 paper argues that frontier AI leaves the foundations of cyber resilience unchanged but greatly raises the speed at which they must be applied. That is a useful counterweight to calls for new AI-specific regimes.

name: Bank of England: Financial Policy Committee AI monitoring and AI Consortium
summary: The Bank of England is the UK's central bank, and its Financial Policy Committee treats AI as a risk to financial stability. In April 2025 the committee identified four channels: common weaknesses in widely used models, correlated AI trading, dependence on a few providers, and cyber threats. Its July 2026 Financial Stability Report said rapid progress in frontier AI had significantly raised cyber and operational risks, and flagged stretched AI-related valuations and fast-growing AI credit. With the FCA it runs the AI Consortium, a public–private forum that has met regularly since May 2025. In May 2026 it issued a joint statement on frontier AI models and cyber resilience with the FCA and HM Treasury.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few central banks to build frontier-AI capabilities into its systemic-risk assessment and to set supervisory expectations on them. Its surveillance methods (surveys, market intelligence, stress testing) are a template for watching AI risk across a whole sector. It is in London.

name: European Systemic Risk Board (ESRB)
summary: The ESRB is the EU body responsible for macroprudential oversight of the financial system; the European Central Bank in Frankfurt hosts its secretariat. Report No 16 of its Advisory Scientific Committee, 'Artificial intelligence and systemic risk' (December 2025), ranks the AI features that worsen systemic risk: monitoring difficulty, concentration, model uniformity, overreliance, speed and opacity. It proposes responses including stronger circuit breakers, labels on AI use and skin-in-the-game requirements. In July 2026 the ESRB issued a formal warning on systemic cyber risks from frontier AI models, after raising its assessment of systemic cyber risk to 'severe'.
why_it_matters: It treats AI as a system-level risk and uses formal instruments against it: warnings, recommendations and quarterly risk assessments. Its scientific committee has mapped the specific ways AI can amplify systemic risk and matched them with concrete tools. The report also names possible loss of human control as an amplifier, which is unusual for a financial regulator.

Ring changed from potential to bridge (E3): the roster saw only the December 2025 report, but the ESRB has since issued a formal warning on frontier AI models (dated 25 June 2026, published 7 July 2026) with quarterly monitoring and an analytical note, so its AI work is now sustained and framed explicitly around frontier AI. Transfer into_institutions (J3): its warnings and policy proposals are governance instruments for EU authorities. MISFIT: no sub-tradition covers macroprudential oversight; econ_tai is the nearest.

name: Systemic Risk Centre (SRC), London School of Economics
summary: The SRC is a research centre at the London School of Economics, launched in 2013 with ESRC funding, that studies how financial crises arise and how policy should respond. Since 2019 its co-director Jón Danielsson and collaborators have published on AI. They argue that AI amplifies leverage, liquidity stress and opacity through common data, speed and strategic complementarities, so crises become faster and more severe. Their proposed responses are for authorities to build their own AI, set up AI-to-AI communication with private firms, create automated crisis facilities and monitor AI use.
why_it_matters: It gives a formal, game-theoretic account of how many interacting AI agents in a market can produce a crisis: a multi-agent risk argument built on long experience of crisis economics. Its proposal that regulators run their own AI and talk directly to firms' AI is a concrete design for oversight at machine speed.

name: Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS)
summary: MAS is Singapore's central bank and integrated financial regulator, and since 2018 it has built AI governance together with the industry it supervises. Its work includes the FEAT principles (fairness, ethics, accountability, transparency; 2018) and the Veritas consortium (2019–2023), which produced assessment methods and an open-source toolkit. Project MindForge's second phase produced an AI Risk Management Toolkit in March 2026, and proposed Guidelines on AI Risk Management for all financial institutions went to consultation from November 2025 to January 2026. In 2026 it added work on frontier-AI cyber risk: an advisory on AI-driven threats in April, and in July an AI-Driven Cyber and Technology Risk Taskforce set up with the Association of Banks in Singapore.
why_it_matters: It shows a regulator co-building assurance methods and open tooling with the firms it supervises, rather than only issuing rules. It also moved within weeks from frontier-model releases to sector-wide guidance, and set up a standing taskforce within about three months.

name: Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) AI Lab
summary: The AI Lab is a programme of the UK Financial Conduct Authority, set up in October 2024, through which firms, the regulator and others test and discuss AI in financial services. Its main strand is AI Live Testing: firms run AI in live markets under FCA supervision, and the technical partner Advai checks fairness, accuracy, consumer outcomes and operational resilience. The first cohort started in late 2025 and the second began testing in April 2026. The Lab also runs a Supercharged Sandbox with NVIDIA computing power (23 firms in its first cohort), held an AI Sprint in January 2025, and ran an AI Input Zone in May–June 2026 that collected examples of good and poor AI practice.
why_it_matters: Supervised live testing is a regulatory method the AI-safety field rarely uses. Deployed systems are evaluated in real conditions with the regulator watching, and participating firms agree to share findings. It could serve as a template for post-deployment evaluation of AI in other high-stakes sectors.

name: Institute and Faculty of Actuaries (IFoA): AI and emerging technologies
summary: The UK's chartered professional body for actuaries, with about 34,000 members worldwide. It sets professional and ethical standards, runs the exams and disciplines members. Its AI work runs through several channels: an AI and Emerging Technologies Practice Board, which held a full-day symposium in London on 24 September 2026; ethical and professional guidance on data science and AI; a September 2023 risk alert on AI techniques and outputs; blog posts from its Professionalism, Regulation and Ethics Working Party; and an AI Manifesto (September 2026) arguing for an 'actuary-in-the-loop' on AI projects.
why_it_matters: Actuaries already work under a regulated regime of model governance, with professional codes, risk alerts and disciplinary standards. The IFoA is extending that regime to AI, which makes it a working template for holding AI practitioners professionally accountable. It is based in London, the int/a hub.

name: International Actuarial Association (IAA): Artificial Intelligence Task Force
summary: The IAA is the worldwide association of national actuarial associations, founded in 1895, with its secretariat in Ottawa. Its AI Task Force, set up in 2024 and chaired by Frank Chang, has produced three foundational papers on responsible AI use (a governance framework, testing and documentation) and an April 2025 Statement of Intent on AI. It has also run AI Summits in Singapore (2024) and San Francisco (2025), and runs an online community, AIforActuaries.org, and a GitHub of case studies and tools. Its 2025-26 workstreams cover engagement, research, case studies and tools, and an adoption framework.
why_it_matters: It is a single channel into dozens of national actuarial bodies, so its governance, testing and documentation papers could become the default for how risk professionals worldwide validate AI models. That makes it an entry point for anyone wanting AI-assurance practice adopted across the insurance and pensions sector.

name: Society of Actuaries (SOA) Research Institute: AI research
summary: The research arm of the Society of Actuaries, the largest North American actuarial body. Through its Actuarial Innovation & Technology research programme it publishes AI research for actuaries: a recurring Actuarial Intelligence Bulletin (five issues in 2026 so far) and a September 2026 handbook on governance and ethics for generative-AI models in actuarial work. It has also published a 2026 study applying fairness frameworks to AI in long-term-care insurance pricing, reports on AI in life underwriting and synthetic claims data, and essay collections on how AI may affect mortality, longevity and retirement.
why_it_matters: It applies the validation and documentation discipline that actuaries use for pricing and reserving models to large language models, and publishes the results as free practical guides. Its essays on AI and mortality and longevity are among the few attempts to put long-horizon actuarial modelling to work on AI's societal effects.

name: Casualty Actuarial Society (CAS): Research Paper Series on Bias and Insurance
summary: A research paper series of the Casualty Actuarial Society, the US-based professional body for property-casualty actuaries. It began in 2022 as the Research Paper Series on Race and Insurance Pricing and now covers bias and fairness across insurance operations and jurisdictions. Its papers cover: practical methods to measure and mitigate bias in pricing models (2025); regulators' views on algorithmic bias and unfair discrimination; a joint CAS/SOA comparison of rules for non-discriminatory AI in insurance across China, the US, Canada and Europe; and a 2026 toolbox for detecting indirect discrimination in rates, which won a 2026 American Academy of Actuaries research award.
why_it_matters: It holds tested quantitative methods for finding proxy discrimination in predictive models, developed in an industry that has worked under anti-discrimination law for decades. These methods can be reused to audit AI decision systems outside insurance.

name: Actuaries Institute (Australia): AI risk management and discrimination guidance
summary: The professional body for actuaries in Australia, based in Sydney. In September 2026 it published a framework for managing AI risk in financial services with the UTS Human Technology Institute. The framework is designed to fit into existing enterprise risk management and is built around four questions: who is accountable, how risks are classified, how they are quantified, and which controls suit common use cases. In December 2022 it co-wrote guidance with the Australian Human Rights Commission on how federal anti-discrimination law applies to AI in insurance pricing and underwriting. It also runs regular AI webinars and columns.

Ring: kept adjacent under E(3): its AI guidance stretches from 2022 to 2026 and is framed around governance and discrimination, not catastrophic risk. Transfer: into_institutions under J(3), since it supplies a risk-management framework and legal guidance for firms using AI.

name: Armilla AI
summary: A Toronto-based managing general agent and Lloyd's coverholder that sells insurance specific to AI. Its affirmative AI liability policy, launched in April 2025 with the Lloyd's underwriter Chaucer, covers model error and underperformance, harmful outputs, agent mistakes, data leakage and regulatory violations; limits rose to US$25m per insured in early 2026. It also offers AI performance warranties backed by independent assessment of AI systems. It keeps an AI litigation database, partners with auditors such as Eticas, and in July 2026 became a founding member of the Appia Foundation, which writes conformity specifications for AI systems.
why_it_matters: It turns AI reliability into a price: cover depends on independent evaluation, so insurance becomes a market incentive and a form of soft regulation. Its underwriting data, such as broker surveys and case law, shows which AI failures actually cost money. It is a direct comparator to AIUC.

key_work.title: Affirmative AI Liability Insurance with Lloyd's underwriter Chaucer
Lessons from a Year of Underwriting AI Liability Insurance
Founding member of the Appia Foundation (AI conformity specifications)
From Audit to Insurance: Building the Infrastructure AI Safety Is Missing (with Eticas)

funding: Seed round of C$6m (US$4.5m) led by Mistral Venture Partners, closed December 2023, with Y Combinator, MS&AD Ventures, SixThirty Ventures, Morgan Creek Digital, Greenlight Re and Chaucer (BetaKit). A 2021 pre-seed round included Yoshua Bengio. Insurance capacity comes from Lloyd's underwriters and partners including Chaucer, AXIS, Convex, Swiss Re and Greenlight Re.
status_evidence: 18 Aug 2026: published a report on 16 months of underwriting AI liability; 21 Jul 2026: became a founding member of the Appia Foundation.
engage: Careers section on armilla.ai
AI litigation database and broker resources on its site
caveats: It is a commercial insurer with an interest in selling cover, and its 'AI safety' language means operational reliability, not catastrophic risk. The early-2026 '$25m' was coverage capacity, not equity, although some outlets reported it as funding. Sources disagree on the founding year (2019 or 2020). TechCrunch lists different seed co-investors from BetaKit.
tag_notes: Home: insurance underwriting and risk pricing, which the taxonomy places in Safety & risk sciences (safety_risk names insurance), by H1. Ring: kept adjacent under E(3), though it is borderline. A 2026 post uses 'AI safety' language, but its programme is framed around enterprise liability and reliability, not catastrophic risk or alignment. It is not part of the x-risk ecosystem and is not on the classic map; it could be read as bridge. Transfer: into_institutions under J(3), as insurance, warranties and conformity specifications are governance instruments. MISFIT (framing): its stakes are commercial liability risk, which no framing key covers; present_harms is the closest.

name: Munich Re aiSure (AI insurance)
summary: A product line of the reinsurer Munich Re, which says it has insured AI products and services since 2018. aiSure covers contractual liabilities such as AI providers' performance guarantees on model accuracy, AI liabilities such as discrimination, IP infringement, hallucinations and regulatory fines, and companies' own losses from AI errors. Cover follows a technical due-diligence assessment of the model. The team works from Munich, with business development in Palo Alto, and publishes client case studies (new ones in 2026), research on IP risk in generative AI, and podcasts.
why_it_matters: It is the longest-running attempt to price AI model error actuarially, treating it as frequent, low-severity losses that add up. It presents insurance as 'soft regulation' that rewards well-tested models. Its loss experience and due-diligence method are a working example of insurance as AI assurance.

key_work.title: aiSure performance guarantees and AI liability cover
Case study: SeismicAI earthquake early-warning system with a performance guarantee
Generating content with AI: An IP-infringement minefield? (whitepaper)

people: Peter Bärnreuther (Senior Underwriter for Artificial Intelligence Risks)
Tom Van den Brulle (Head of New and Green Tech Solutions)
Theodore Pine (Senior Business Development Manager, Insure AI, Palo Alto)
Yuanyuan Li (Research Scientist; author of the AI IP whitepaper)
funding: Commercial product line of Munich Re, a reinsurer founded in 1880; no separate figures published.
status_evidence: Feb 2026: new aiSure case study published (SeismicAI performance guarantee, document 2026-016).
engage: Contact the aiSure team in Munich or Palo Alto about coverage or partnership (contacts listed on the product page)
caveats: It is a commercial product inside a large reinsurer. Munich Re publishes little on policy volumes or loss experience, and the named contacts may change. Only the product page and Munich Re's own documents were checked; I found no independent 2025-26 coverage. It frames AI risk as business and liability risk, not safety in the catastrophic sense.
tag_notes: Home: reinsurance and actuarial pricing of model-performance risk, which the taxonomy places in Safety & risk sciences (safety_risk names insurance), by H1. Ring: kept adjacent under E(3): a standing AI insurance line since 2018, framed as business risk, with no catastrophic or alignment framing. Transfer: into_institutions under J(3), since performance guarantees and liability cover are governance instruments that Munich Re itself calls soft regulation. Org_type is programme because it is a unit inside Munich Re (A1). MISFIT (framing): its stakes are commercial losses from AI error, which no framing key covers; present_harms is the closest.

name: AI Safety, Ethics and Society course and textbook (Center for AI Safety)
summary: A free online course run by the Center for AI Safety, built on Dan Hendrycks's textbook Introduction to AI Safety, Ethics and Society (Routledge, 2024). The book can be read free online. The course runs about 12 weeks at around 5 hours a week: an optional AI fundamentals week, eight weeks of readings with weekly facilitated video-call discussions, then a four-week independent project. It assumes no prior AI knowledge. Besides catastrophic risks and single-agent safety, the curriculum has chapters on safety engineering, complex systems, collective action problems (game theory of races and cooperation), machine ethics under moral uncertainty, and governance.
why_it_matters: It is the main AI-safety curriculum written for people outside computer science. It teaches AI risk through risk management from other industries, complex-systems thinking and game theory, not only through ML alignment. That makes it a ready on-ramp for people from adjacent fields, and a template for teaching AI safety across disciplines.

key_work.title: Introduction to AI Safety, Ethics, and Society (textbook, Taylor & Francis/Routledge; free online and audiobook)
AI Safety, Ethics and Society virtual course, Winter 2025 cohort (3 Nov 2025 to 1 Feb 2026)

people: Dan Hendrycks (author; director, Center for AI Safety)
funding: Free to participants. The course's own funding isn't disclosed. Open Philanthropy (now Coefficient Giving) gave CAIS general-support grants of $5.16M (Nov 2022) and $4.03M (Apr 2023), then a $1.87M exit grant (Oct 2023).
status_evidence: Nov 2025 to Feb 2026: ran the Winter 2025 cohort (fundamentals week from 3 Nov, main course 10 Nov 2025 to 4 Jan 2026, projects to 1 Feb 2026). The University of Freiburg used the textbook as the core text for a 2025/26 winter-semester seminar. No later cohort was posted as of Oct 2026.
engage: Free online course, open to anyone with internet and a webcam. Applications open roughly a month before each cohort (the Winter 2025 participant deadline was 10 Oct 2025); no 2026-27 dates were posted as of Oct 2026
Facilitators are recruited for each cohort (Winter 2025 deadline 5 Oct 2025)
The textbook is free to read online, for self-study or for use in university courses
caveats: The parent organisation, Center for AI Safety, is on the aisafety.com map, but the course and textbook are not listed separately. The chapters on safety engineering, complex systems and game theory are introductory surveys, not original work in those fields. CAIS lost Open Philanthropy support after the 2023 exit grant, and no cohort after Winter 2025 had been announced by Oct 2026, so it's uncertain whether the course will continue.
tag_notes: Home: safety (H2). Its distinctive non-ML content is the safety-engineering chapter (risk decomposition, lessons from other industries); complex systems and the game theory of collective action are secondary (B6 puts complexity under life and game theory under formal). Ring: core (E1). It is a CAIS programme whose purpose is teaching catastrophic AI risk inside the AI-safety ecosystem. Transfer: into_builders (J2). It builds the capacities of people who go on to work on or govern AI. Primary problem 'people' because the course's distinctive role is widening who enters the field, beyond computer scientists.

name: AAC&U Institute on AI, Pedagogy, and the Curriculum
summary: A seven-month online institute run by the American Association of Colleges and Universities (AAC&U). Campus teams of at least five people get expert sessions, design sessions, an assigned mentor and an online community while they work out how their courses and curricula should respond to AI. Themes include pedagogy, academic-integrity policy, 'the ethical and equity implications of AI', and writing AI competencies into learning outcomes. It began in September 2024 with 124 institutions; the 2025-26 cohort had 192 teams from 176 institutions, and the third cohort runs 10 Sept 2026 to 6 Apr 2027.
why_it_matters: It is a large existing channel for reshaping non-computer-science university curricula around AI, reaching senior academic officers and faculty across disciplines. For anyone wanting the ethics or safety of AI taught across higher education, it is a ready route to campus decision-makers. It does not currently carry any safety or catastrophic-risk content.

key_work.title: Inaugural institute (124 institutions, Sept 2024 to Apr 2025)
2025-26 cohort: 192 teams from 176 institutions
2026-27 institute (10 Sept 2026 to 6 Apr 2027)

people: C. Edward Watson (Vice President for Digital Innovation, AAC&U)
funding: Paid for by team fees: $5,125 per five-member team from AAC&U member institutions and $6,325 from non-members, plus $1,025 or $1,265 for each extra member (2026-27). No external funders are named.
status_evidence: 10-11 Sep 2026: the 2026-27 cohort kicked off. Applications closed 9 Jun 2026, and the capstone is 5-6 Apr 2027.
engage: Campus teams of at least five, ideally including a senior academic officer, apply each spring for the following academic year (the 2026-27 deadline was 9 Jun 2026)
Fee-based and fully online; Mohawk College (Canada) has taken part, so non-US teams can apply
caveats: It is mainly about teaching with AI and adapting curricula. Ethics and equity are one theme among several, and there is no safety, alignment or catastrophic-risk framing, so its relevance to AI going well is indirect. It is a higher-education membership association's paid professional-development product, not a research programme. The institute faculty are not named publicly.
tag_notes: Home: philosophy/phil_bioethics, taken from the provisional home and AAC&U's liberal-education and ethics-in-curriculum identity (H3: a membership body goes with its constituency). MISFIT: education and pedagogy have no sector. Ring: adjacent (E3). It is a sustained, repeated programme since 2024 on AI's effects on teaching, with no safety framing. Transfer: convening (J5). It brings the higher-education community into the AI conversation through training. MISFIT on framing: AAC&U's stated aim is to respond to AI's 'challenges and opportunities', a pragmatic adaptation for which flourishing is the closest key.

name: AI Pedagogy Project (metaLAB (at) Harvard)
summary: An open website, launched in June 2023 at metaLAB (at) Harvard within the Berkman Klein Center, that curates free classroom assignments written by educators. The assignments get students to probe what generative AI can and cannot do; examples include comparing a human critique with an AI one, and illustrating a hoax with AI images. It also offers an AI guide, a hands-on LLM tutorial and a model-comparison tool. The project says it has reached over 200,000 people in 162 countries and is recommended by more than 134 colleges and universities. It runs events such as the AI & Tell dialogue (Apr 2026) and a Public AI Summit for Educators (Sept 2026).
why_it_matters: It approaches AI literacy from the arts and humanities. Students learn by critiquing and remixing AI outputs, not by being taught to use the tools. Its stated aim is to help educators decide whether to engage with AI at all, not to push adoption. That is a useful model for building public judgement about AI in classrooms outside computer science.

key_work.title: AI Pedagogy Project repository of open, educator-created AI assignments
AI Guide and LLM tutorial for educators
AI & Tell: AI Use, Disclosure, and Deceit (event)
Public AI Summit for Educators (16-17 Sept 2026)

people: Sarah Newman (founder and director; Director of Art & Education, metaLAB at Harvard)
status_evidence: Sep 2026: Public AI Summit for Educators (16-17 Sept). Apr 2026: AI & Tell event (15 Apr). A Dawson College article (Feb 2026) recommends it.
engage: Free, open-access assignments and guides that anyone can use or adapt
Events, for example a Public AI Summit for Educators (Sept 2026) and the IMPACT Conference (Nov 2026)
A newsletter with occasional updates and events
caveats: No funders are disclosed. It is a teaching-resource project, with no safety or catastrophic-risk framing. Its host, the Berkman Klein Center, is a separate entity and is not on the aisafety.com map either.
tag_notes: Home: arts/arts_creative (H1). It comes out of metaLAB's arts-and-humanities design lab and is led by an artist-educator. Law is secondary because the host is the Berkman Klein Center, a law and STS centre. Ring: adjacent (E3). It is a sustained programme since 2023 on AI in teaching, without a safety framing. Transfer: convening (J5). It equips educators and students to question AI through literacy resources. MISFIT on framing: the stance is critical exploration of AI's limits and of whether to adopt it, not deflationary scholarship, but critical is the closest key.

name: CRAFT: Classroom-Ready Resources About AI For Teaching (Stanford)
summary: A Stanford Graduate School of Education initiative, run with Stanford HAI and the Stanford Accelerator for Learning, that co-designs free AI-literacy resources with high-school teachers. The resources range from 15-minute activities to multi-day lessons for art, maths, English, history and science classes. Each year it takes a remote cohort of teacher co-design fellows; cohorts are listed from 2022-23 to 2025-26. The team also publishes learning-sciences research on how teachers fold AI literacy into their subjects.
why_it_matters: It puts critical AI literacy into humanities and non-computing classrooms, so that teenagers learn to understand, question and critique AI wherever they meet it. Its teacher co-design method and published research are a tested way to reach young people at scale; a December 2024 webinar said the resources are used in 54+ countries.

key_work.title: CRAFT-work: An Integrative Co-Design Approach for Designing High School AI Literacy Resources (CHI AI Literacy Workshop)
Co-designing AI Education Curriculum with Cross-Disciplinary High School Teachers (EAAI)
Teaching high school students about generative AI: Cases of teacher lesson design (Journal of Educational Research)

people: Victor R. Lee (Associate Professor, Stanford GSE; faculty director)
Isaac Joba Adisa (postdoctoral fellow, Stanford GSE)
funding: Initial funding came from the McCoy Family Center for Ethics in Society, with support from Stanford HAI, Stanford Digital Education and the Stanford Accelerator for Learning (as of 2023). Amounts are not disclosed.
status_evidence: Jan 2026: Victor Lee presented CRAFT at the University of Utah's Hugo Rossi lecture (23 Jan 2026). A 2025-26 cohort of seven teacher co-design fellows is listed, and two papers came out in 2025.
engage: Annual remote cohort of high-school teacher co-design fellows from across the US (applications closed for the current cycle; there is a sign-up form for future calls)
Free lessons and activities for any teacher to use
caveats: The discovery note marked its status unclear, but the 2025-26 fellow cohort and the Jan 2026 talk show it is active. Founding date: the earliest fellow cohort is 2022-23, and Stanford HAI announced it publicly in Aug 2023. It focuses on literacy and critique of present-day AI, with no safety framing.
tag_notes: Home: psych/psych_development (H1). Its method is learning sciences and youth education, working with teachers of teenagers. MISFIT: education and learning sciences have no sector of their own. Ring: adjacent (E3). It has run annual fellow cohorts and a publication line since 2022 on teaching about AI, with no safety framing. Transfer: convening (J5). It brings teachers and students into the AI conversation through literacy. MISFIT on framing: its aim, helping students 'question and critique' AI, is critical literacy rather than deflationary critique, but critical is the closest key.

name: Spencer Foundation: Initiative on AI and Education
summary: An initiative of the Spencer Foundation, a Chicago education-research funder founded in 1962. It grew out of a Spencer convening on AI and education in spring 2024. Rather than running a separate grant line, Spencer welcomes AI-focused proposals across its existing grant programmes (Vision Grants, large and small research grants, racial-equity and research-practice partnership grants). It funds research in four areas: AI and learning, AI policy, AI ethics and justice (including data sovereignty, privacy and bias), and how AI will transform education research itself. It also aims to connect researchers, the tech industry, policymakers and practitioners, and to shape public discourse on AI and education.
why_it_matters: It is an established funder of research on AI's effects on learners and on equity, with its own review machinery. It backs community-partnered designs, for example AI literacy 'grounded in care and local systems change'. New AI-safety funders interested in AI's effects on young people's minds could co-fund with it.

key_work.title: Spencer Convening on AI and Education (origin of the initiative)
Spencer Vision Grant: 'From Early Encounters to Equitable Futures: Grounding AI Literacy in Care and Local Systems Change' (University at Buffalo team, PI X. Christine Wang)
2026 Spencer Vision Grant Awardees Workshop, Chicago

people: Sepehr Vakil (Senior Advisor to the AI Initiative)
funding: A private endowed foundation established by Lyle M. Spencer in 1962. AI-focused work goes through existing programmes, for example Vision Grants (research-planning grants of $75,000 over 12-18 months). The total AI allocation is not published.
status_evidence: 2026: the Spencer Vision Grant Awardees Workshop in Chicago included the University at Buffalo team's AI-literacy planning grant. The initiative page, staff list and AI advisor role are current.
engage: Open grant programmes that welcome AI-focused proposals: Vision Grants, large and small research grants, racial-equity and research-practice partnership grants (check spencer.org for current deadlines)
Partnering or co-funding with the foundation on research about AI and education
caveats: AI money isn't reported separately from Spencer's general portfolio, so the initiative's size is unclear. Its framing is equity and opportunity in education, not AI safety. Grant amounts beyond the $75,000 Vision Grants weren't confirmed from Spencer's own pages.
tag_notes: Home: law/law_policy (H4: a one-programme funder goes to the tradition of its programme). Its most distinctive line is equity and justice in public-interest education research, and AI and learning (psych) is secondary. Ring: adjacent (E3). It is a standing funding initiative since 2024 on AI's effects on learning and equity, with no safety framing. Transfer: protecting (J4, funders tagged by the work they fund). The funded research centres the needs of young people and asks whether inequities are 'disrupted or reinforced' through AI. Not a generalist funder under rule K.

name: Division of Digital Psychiatry, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center / Harvard Medical School (incl. MindBench.ai)
summary: A clinical research group at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, a Harvard teaching hospital, led by psychiatrist John Torous. It works on smartphone and AI tools in mental health care; its other projects include the mindLAMP platform and the mindapps.org app-evaluation database. With the National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI) it built MindBench.ai (Nov 2025), a platform where patients, clinicians and researchers evaluate how LLM tools behave in mental-health scenarios. It has published dozens of papers on LLM chatbots in 2025-26, including a typology of AI-associated psychosis, a crisis-detection guardrail dataset and a JAMA piece on mental-health AI safety.
why_it_matters: It applies clinical-trial and app-evaluation methods to what chatbots do to vulnerable users. Patient advocates (NAMI) and people with lived experience take part: the Lancet psychosis typology was co-written by an engineer, a person with schizophrenia and a psychiatrist. That gives AI safety an evidence base for harms to human minds that mainstream evals lack.

key_work.title: Mindbench.ai: an actionable platform to evaluate the profile and performance of large language models in a mental healthcare context (NPP Digital Psychiatry and Neuroscience; with NAMI)
Beyond artificial intelligence psychosis: a functional typology of large language model-associated psychotic phenomena (Lancet Digital Health)
Mental Health AI Chatbots as Pharmakon: A Tripartite Theory of Use despite Risk (Psychotherapy and Psychosomatics)
Specialized or General-Purpose: The Wrong Question for Mental Health AI Safety (JAMA)

people: John Torous (Director, Division of Digital Psychiatry; Harvard Medical School)
Mason Granof (MindBench presentations to NAMI chapters)
Christine Shi (MindBench presentations to NAMI chapters)
funding: A grant-funded academic group. Some of its co-authored LLM papers acknowledge NIH grants (NIMH, NCCIH) and foundation funding, and MindBench is run in partnership with NAMI. No division budget is published.
status_evidence: 2 Oct 2026: Psychiatric Services paper on AI-assisted conavigation by peer digital navigators. 30 Jul 2026: joined the Partnership on AI. Jun 2026: presented MindBench at NAMICon 2026.
engage: MindBench recruits volunteers (patients, clinicians, researchers, developers) to help evaluate AI mental-health tools (call posted Mar 2026)
The division takes students, clinicians, researchers and postdocs (see its Join Us and careers pages)
Its studies recruit participants
caveats: 'Safety' here means clinical and patient safety, not catastrophic risk. The group also studies and supports clinical uses of AI, for example frameworks for validating generative-AI therapeutics. Several of the papers are led elsewhere with Torous as co-author; the npj Digital Medicine scoping review, for instance, is led from Essen. The founding year and team size were not found.
tag_notes: Home: psych/psych_clinical (H1: clinical psychiatry and trial methods produce its AI outputs). Safety (clinical AI assurance) is secondary. Ring: bridge (E3), kept from the roster. Since 2025 it has run a sustained programme explicitly framed as 'AI safety evaluation', including MindBench, guardrail datasets and the JAMA mental-health AI safety piece. That safety is clinical, in line with the Common Sense Media worked example. Problems: minds plus assurance, under the F must-pair for evaluation builders. Transfer: protecting (J4). The work exists to protect patients and people with mental illness from chatbot harms.

name: Department of Affective Disorders, Aarhus University Hospital – Psychiatry / Aarhus University (Søren Dinesen Østergaard group)
summary: A psychiatric research group led by Søren Dinesen Østergaard, Professor of Clinical Medicine at Aarhus University and Head of Research at the Department of Affective Disorders. In 2023 Østergaard predicted that generative AI chatbots could fuel delusions in people prone to psychosis. In 2026 the group searched 10.7 million clinical notes for 53,974 patients of the Central Denmark Region's psychiatric services for mentions of chatbots or ChatGPT. Notes for 38 patients were compatible with harmful consequences of chatbot use; delusions were the most common, followed by suicidality or self-harm and eating disorders. Other outputs include papers on emotion contagion and mania, on the adverse effects of voice-based chatbots, and a case report of first-episode mania during intense ChatGPT use.
why_it_matters: It shows how harms from AI can be monitored in a population using routine health records, a pharmacovigilance-style method that AI safety has hardly used. It also gives early clinical, rather than anecdotal, evidence on chatbot-associated delusions and mania.

key_work.title: Will Generative Artificial Intelligence Chatbots Generate Delusions in Individuals Prone to Psychosis? (Schizophrenia Bulletin)
Generative Artificial Intelligence Chatbots and Delusions: From Guesswork to Emerging Cases (Acta Psychiatrica Scandinavica)
Potentially Harmful Consequences of AI Chatbot Use Among Patients With Mental Illness: Early Data From a Large Psychiatric Service System (Acta Psychiatrica Scandinavica)
It Is the Journey, Not the Destination: Moving From End Points to Trajectories When Assessing Chatbot Mental Health Safety (JMIR Mental Health, with King's College London)

people: Søren Dinesen Østergaard (Professor of Clinical Medicine, Aarhus University; Head of Research, Department of Affective Disorders)
funding: No funding dedicated to the chatbot work was found. Outside it, Østergaard declares grants from the Lundbeck Foundation, the Danish Cancer Society, the Danish Agency for Digitisation's Investment Fund for New Technologies and the Independent Research Fund Denmark.
status_evidence: Aug 2026: case report of first-episode mania with grandiose delusions during intense ChatGPT use (Munkholm and Østergaard). Feb 2026: the health-record study in Acta Psychiatrica Scandinavica.
caveats: The group has no public homepage; the URL is Østergaard's Aarhus University profile. Much of the AI output is short editorials and letters by Østergaard, and the 2026 health-record study is an early, keyword-based screen, so it likely undercounts harms. The group's broader research is on psychiatric epidemiology and clinical prediction tools, with AI chatbots as a recent line.
tag_notes: Home: psych/psych_clinical (H1: clinical psychiatry and psychiatric epidemiology). Safety (public-health harm surveillance) is secondary. Ring: adjacent (E3), kept from the roster. It has a sustained publication line from 2023 to 2026 on chatbot harms to patients, without a safety, alignment or catastrophic-risk framing. Its editorial comparing chatbots with the 'global social media experiment' frames harm as a public-health problem. Assurance is a secondary problem because health-record screening works as incident surveillance. Transfer: protecting (J4). It documents and warns about harm to psychiatric patients.

name: KI-Campus (Stifterverband)
summary: KI-Campus is a free online learning platform for artificial intelligence, mostly in German. The Stifterverband für die Deutsche Wissenschaft runs it with partner universities, and the federal research ministry (BMBF, now BMFTR) has funded it since 2019. It offers courses, videos and podcasts, from machine-learning basics and explainable AI to data and algorithm ethics, EU AI Act essentials, and AI-competence courses for school teachers and university lecturers. Over 190,000 learners have earned more than 100,000 certificates.
why_it_matters: It is the main public AI-literacy channel into German-speaking universities and schools, aiming for 500,000 learners and 100 universities by 2030. Its content on risks and societal effects is thin (an ethics course, an AI Act course), so it is a ready-made German-language carrier for AI-safety and societal-resilience material rather than a source of it.

key_work.title: KI-Kompetenzen für Lehrkräfte (AI competences for teachers, 8-hour course)
Daten- und Algorithmenethik (data and algorithm ethics course)
EU AI Act Essentials (course)
Lehrenden-Lounge zu KI-Kompetenzen (online community of practice for lecturers, with DHBW and FernUniversität in Hagen)

people: Florian Rampelt (head of the KI-Campus office, Stifterverband)
funding: German federal research ministry (BMBF, now BMFTR) since 2019; run by the Stifterverband. The 2026 lecturer community runs inside the BMFTR joint project 'KI-Kompetenzen an Hochschulen stärken'. No amounts found.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: call for participation for the online 'Lehrenden-Lounge zu KI-Kompetenzen', starting November 2026.
engage: Free online AI courses, videos and podcasts (mostly German)
Lehrenden-Lounge: online community of practice for university lecturers from November 2026; open call for short talks, no deadline
Advisory offer for integrating KI-Campus courses at North Rhine-Westphalian universities (announced June 2026)
caveats: Its teaching is mainly AI skills and competence; AI risk is barely covered, so it is included for its reach, not for any safety work. It depends on federal project funding. The legal operator is the Stifterverband in Essen; the Berlin base comes from older project descriptions and was not confirmed on the current site.
tag_notes: Home psych, following the panel's provisional home. MISFIT: education and adult learning have no tradition key; sub psych_development is the nearest fit, through its teacher and school courses. Ring potential, kept from the roster: it runs a standing AI programme, but it teaches AI skills, and its engagement with AI's risks or societal effects is limited to a few courses (data and algorithm ethics, EU AI Act essentials, explainable AI). Transferable method: a federally funded, German-language public AI-literacy platform that reaches universities and teachers and could carry AI-safety and societal-resilience content. Transfer convening: it educates its own higher-education and teacher community. Framing flourishing is nominal. MISFIT: its framing is about competence and opportunity, not stakes.

name: Leaf: Dilemmas and Dangers in AI
summary:
Leaf is a small nonprofit that runs selective five-week online courses for 14- to 19-year-olds on how to have a positive impact. It has been a US-registered 501(c)(3) since 2025, and its team works mainly in the UK. Its 'Dilemmas and Dangers in AI' course covers:
- AI's promise and perils
- arguments about extinction risk
- misalignment and deception
- power concentration, and governance seen through historical analogies
- how students could contribute
It combines self-paced material, weekly facilitated discussions and talks from AI-safety researchers.
why_it_matters: It is one of very few programmes that teach AI-risk ideas to school-age students. It selects for altruism as well as ability, draws thousands of applicants (3,901 for the winter 2026 cohort) and gives about 40% of places free. Its board includes int/a steward Christine Tan, which links int/a directly to a pre-university pipeline.

key_work.title: Dilemmas and Dangers in AI: autumn 2026 cohort (12 October to late November)
Leaf's Winter 2026 cohort: 368 teenagers selected from 3,901 applicants in 30+ countries
What Leaf learned about cost-effective talent development

funding: Early grants from the Centre for Effective Altruism / EA Infrastructure Fund: Longterm Wiki lists $317,000 in 2022, and an EAIF grant followed in early 2023. Carina Initiatives funds programmes through summer 2026. Tiered tuition (most families pay about £150/$200, about 40% pay nothing) exceeded costs for the winter 2026 cohort.
status_evidence: Oct 2026: autumn cohort of 'Dilemmas and Dangers in AI' runs from 12 October to 22 November 2026; applications close 5 October.
engage: Students aged 14-19 who have not started university can apply for five-week online cohorts, held several times a year; fees on a sliding scale, free if needed
Schools and parents can refer students (information pages for schools and parents)
Donations via every.org
caveats: The roster unit is one course inside Leaf, which also runs ethics, biology and policy courses. The content follows the EA/AI-safety canon (speakers from Anthropic, Redwood Research and AI Impacts) rather than bringing in outside traditions. Funding was uncertain in late 2024, and the current grant runs only through summer 2026. Board member Christine Tan is an int/a core steward, so int/a has a stake in it. The two course pages give different end dates (20 and 22 November).
tag_notes: Home philosophy by H2: AI-risk content is not a sector, and the course and its sister course 'The Mathematics of Morality' import EA moral philosophy and cause prioritisation. MISFIT: its distinctive contribution is pre-university teaching, which has no tradition key. Ring core (A1, E1): the unit is a course whose sole purpose is AI-risk education, inside the EA/AI-safety ecosystem and listed on the aisafety.com map. Transfer into_builders: it forms future AI researchers and policymakers through a talent pipeline. Region global under rule O, as a US-registered organisation that works fully distributed.

name: National Education Association (NEA)
summary: The NEA is the largest US labour union, representing educators from pre-kindergarten to higher education. Its AI work rests on a June 2024 task force report and the policy statement its Representative Assembly adopted in July 2024. These set five principles: students and educators at the centre, evidence-based tools, ethical use and strong data protection, equitable access, and AI literacy and agency. It runs an AI in Education hub with micro-credentials, independent-study courses, vetting guidance and sample school-board policies.
why_it_matters: It sets organised-labour norms for keeping human judgement in high-stakes educational decisions across US public schools. Its task force documented concrete failures: wrong AI-assigned grades, facial recognition failing Black students, opaque data governance. It is the main channel to US teachers, and a test case of a workforce setting terms for how AI enters its profession.

Its AI work concerns classroom practice, equity and data protection, not advanced-AI risk. Leadership changed on 1 September 2026.

Ring adjacent (E3): a standing AI programme since 2024 (task force, policy statement, hub), framed around equity, ethics and educator voice, with no catastrophic-risk framing. Transfer protecting: its principles and guidance defend students and educators from AI's effects in schools. Way of knowing communal: an educator task force drafted the policy, and about 6,000 delegates adopted it.

name: Education International (EI)
summary: Education International is the global federation of teachers' and education workers' unions, based in Brussels: about 383 member organisations representing more than 32 million educators. On AI it argues three things: teachers and their unions must help govern AI in education, the teacher-student relationship stays central, and schools must not become testing grounds for technology companies. It held a global conference on human-centred AI in Brussels in December 2025, launched an AI and Technology Network (first in-person meeting in Madrid, June 2026), and made the case at the 2026 International Labour Conference.
why_it_matters: It is the only body speaking for organised educators worldwide on AI. It brings a political-economy critique of AI in schools (commercialisation, data extraction, de-professionalisation) that is largely missing from AI-safety work on education. Its Worlds of Education platform publishes academic critiques of the UNESCO and OECD/European Commission AI-literacy frameworks.

The 2024 World Congress resolution on technology and AI is known only from secondary descriptions; its text was not checked. Worlds of Education pieces carry a disclaimer that they are the authors' views, not EI policy. It has no advanced-AI or catastrophic-risk framing.
tag_notes: Home economics by H3 (a federation of unions), sub econ_labour. MISFIT: the educational tradition has no key. Ring adjacent (E3): a sustained AI programme (2024 Congress resolution, December 2025 global conference, AI and Technology Network from 2026) about teachers' voice, students' development and commercialisation, without safety or catastrophic framing. Transfer protecting: it defends teachers and students from AI's effects and from the commercialisation of schooling. Framing structural: its statements stress power over education passing from public authorities and educators to technology firms. Region europe by its Brussels headquarters (rule O), although membership is global.

name: European Trade Union Committee for Education (ETUCE)
summary: ETUCE is the European federation of education trade unions and the European region of Education International: about 125 unions representing 11 million teachers and other education staff, and the EU social partner for education. Its EU co-funded project 'Balancing AI in EDU' (January 2025 to December 2026) helps unions bargain collectively and lobby on AI. The project includes a survey of unions, a conference in Copenhagen (October 2025), a workshop on collective bargaining in Dublin (May 2026) and a forthcoming guide. In September 2026 ETUCE campaigned against a proposed GDPR Article 88bis that would let companies train AI on students' and educators' data.
why_it_matters: It handles AI in schools through collective bargaining and EU data-protection law, organised counter-power over AI training data and deployment that AI-safety work rarely uses. It is a working example of one sector negotiating over AI with employers and EU institutions.

Membership figures (about 125 unions, 11 million staff) date from 2023. The Stop the Omnibus campaign is run jointly with the school-student union body OBESSU and the European School Heads Association.
tag_notes: Home economics by H3 (federation of unions), sub econ_labour. Secondary law for its GDPR and data-protection advocacy. Ring adjacent (E3): an EU-funded AI programme for 2025-26 plus repeated AI campaigns, framed around workers' and students' rights, not safety. Transfer protecting: collective bargaining and the data campaign defend teachers and students, its own constituency (the boundary rule sends this to protecting rather than into_institutions). MISFIT: the educational tradition has no key.

name: Chartered College of Teaching
summary: The Chartered College of Teaching is the professional body for teachers in England: a London-based charity that holds an 1849 Royal Charter and relaunched under its present name in 2017. With Chiltern Learning Trust, and funded by the Department for Education, it produced the free 'Safe and effective use of AI in education' materials (June 2025, updated May 2026). They include training on understanding and safely using generative AI, a certified assessment that earns credits towards Chartered Teacher Status, case studies, and an Impact journal special issue. It also runs the DfE-backed EdTech Evidence Board, which published its pilot findings in September 2026.
why_it_matters: It is the main professional-formation route through which England's teachers learn to judge AI in their classrooms, and it ties that judgement to evidence-informed practice and professional credentials. Its EdTech Evidence Board is a working model of evidence standards for technology products sold to schools.

MISFIT: pedagogy and the teaching profession have no tradition key; psych_development is the nearest fit, through children's learning. Ring adjacent (E3): a funded AI programme running 2025-26 (materials, assessment, Impact issue) about safe classroom use, without x-risk framing. Transfer convening: it trains its own profession to use AI. Framing present_harms, since 'safe use' covers safeguarding, data protection and bias.

name: Cognitive Resonance
summary: Cognitive Resonance is a one-person venture that teaches educators and policymakers about generative AI through cognitive science. Benjamin Riley, who earlier founded the teacher-preparation nonprofit Deans for Impact, set it up in March 2024. Its method explains first how human learning works and then how large language models produce output. It works through workshops, consulting, keynotes, the white paper 'Education Hazards of Generative AI' (2024) and a Substack newsletter. Since September 2026 the newsletter has run investigative reports on alleged harms to students at Alpha School, an AI-centred private school.
why_it_matters: It applies learning science to AI in schools, arguing that tools which do students' thinking for them undercut the effortful practice that learning depends on, and it resists the claim that AI in education is inevitable. It is a deflationary counterweight to both edtech hype and AGI narratives, useful for anyone asking where AI erodes human cognition.

caveats: It is essentially one person's practice, working as a 'virtual organisation' with outside scientists; its legal form and funding are not stated. It is sceptical of AGI claims and of the premises of x-risk discourse, so it will not frame its work as AI safety. Its recent output is mostly investigative journalism on a single school.
tag_notes: Home psych (H1: cognitive science of learning is its method), sub psych_cognitive. Secondary arts for its investigative journalism on Alpha School. Ring adjacent (E3): a sustained AI programme since 2024 (white paper, workshops, newsletter) on AI's effects on learning, with an explicitly anti-hype, non-x-risk stance. Transfer protecting: it equips teachers and parents to shield students' learning from AI and reports on harms to children. Framing critical (L): deflating AI hype is its main output. Org type company is inferred from its paid consulting model; its legal form is unverified.

name: Stanford SCALE Initiative (Systems Change Advancing Learning and Equity): AI Hub for Education
summary: SCALE is an initiative of the Stanford Graduate School of Education, part of the Stanford Accelerator for Learning, that links education research to K-12 decision-makers. Its programmes include Getting Down to Facts, the National Student Support Accelerator (tutoring) and the AI Hub for Education. The hub keeps a searchable repository of more than 800 studies on AI in K-12 education. In March 2026 it published 'The Evidence Base on AI in K-12: A 2026 Review', which found only about 20 studies with strong causal evidence. It is also studying how students and teachers use ChatGPT, using classroom data shared by OpenAI (announced July 2025).
why_it_matters: It holds claims about AI in schools to the causal-evaluation standards of education policy research. Its finding that very few studies meet that bar is a check on boosters and critics alike. Research on AI deskilling or cognitive offloading in children can build on its repository and methods, though its own focus is whether AI tools work, not whether they harm.

The hub's launch date and funders are not published.

MISFIT: education research and causal programme evaluation have no tradition of their own; psych_development is the closest because the work is about how K-12 pupils and teachers fare with AI. Ring adjacent (E3): a standing AI hub on AI's effects in schools, with no safety, catastrophic-risk or alignment framing. Transfer protecting (J4): it evaluates AI tools for the pupils and teachers that education serves. Problems: minds (children's learning and development), plus assurance because it appraises the causal evidence on specific AI tools (F must-pair). Framing flourishing is the nearest fit for its efficacy framing ('Moving from AI Promise to Learning Impact'). MISFIT: no framing key fits a neutral 'does it work' stance.

name: Centre for the Science of Learning & Technology (SLATE), University of Bergen, host of the AI LEARN centre
summary: SLATE opened in January 2016 in the University of Bergen's Faculty of Psychology as Norway's national research and competence centre for learning analytics. It draws on information science, computer science, cognitive science, pedagogy, sociology and law. It hosts AI LEARN (AI Centre for the Empowerment of Human Learning), a 2025-2030 centre run with NTNU that studies how people learn, work and create with AI; it has 16 PhD candidates and about 35 partners from universities, the public sector and industry. SLATE also runs NOKI, a national AI Olympiad for upper-secondary pupils, and in May 2026 launched three continuing-education master's courses in human-AI systems.
why_it_matters: AI LEARN is a large, publicly funded research programme whose stated aim is to strengthen human agency as AI enters learning and work. It studies cognitive engagement, trust and 'hybrid intelligence' with learning-sciences methods. That produces evidence on human deskilling and over-reliance, which the AI-safety field worries about but rarely studies directly.

MISFIT: learning analytics and the learning sciences have no sub-tradition. Secondary law for its legal and ethical strand. Ring adjacent (E3): a funded five-year AI centre (2025-30) on human agency in learning, with no safety or catastrophic-risk framing. Status active rather than new: SLATE dates from 2016, although AI LEARN opened in Dec 2025.

name: Leibniz-Institut für Wissensmedien (IWM, Leibniz Institute for Knowledge Media)
summary: IWM is a Leibniz Association research institute in Tübingen, founded in 2001, with more than 150 staff. It studies how people use digital media to learn, find information and share knowledge, mainly through experimental educational and cognitive psychology. One of its nine labs is Language and AI in Education, led since 2024 by computational linguist Detmar Meurers; it builds intelligent tutoring systems, tests them in schools and runs the WoLKE project on reflective use of AI tools in teacher training. Recent AI work includes a doctoral thesis on when and how people decide to use AI (August 2026), an AI masterclass for teachers (August 2026) and a recurring conference on generative AI for educators (third edition July 2025).
why_it_matters: Its experimental research on knowledge acquisition, information search and handing thinking over to tools is the evidence that claims about AI-induced deskilling and over-reliance need. It also tests AI tutors in randomised field studies in schools.

Its stance is neutral research on the 'beneficial and detrimental effects' of AI on knowledge processes, with no risk framing. The draft's link between the 2026 thesis and cognitive offloading rests on the thesis title, not a confirmed abstract.

The AI lab's computational linguistics is not a taxonomy tradition (H2). Ring adjacent (E3): a dedicated AI lab since 2024, funded AI projects and a recurring AI conference, all on AI's effects on learners and none framed around x-risk. Transfer protecting (J4): it studies how AI affects the learners and teachers it serves. Problems: minds (learning and offloading), epistemics (information search and knowledge sharing with AI). Framing flourishing is the nearest fit for neutral research on 'beneficial and detrimental effects' (MISFIT). Org_type academic per rule I: Leibniz institutes are public research institutes.

name: Centre for Research in Digital Education (University of Edinburgh)
summary: A research centre in the University of Edinburgh's Moray House School of Education and Sport, affiliated with the Edinburgh Futures Institute. It was established in 2015, growing out of the Digital Cultures and Education group (2009) and the online MSc in Digital Education (2006). Its five themes are Cultures & Futures, Children & Technology, Data Society, Data Education in Schools, and Digital Education in the Global South. Its AI work includes Ben Williamson's critical research on AI, datafication and the political economy of edtech platforms; a draft AI curriculum framework for Scotland and a 'Teach AI Literacy' guide for teachers; and futures-thinking resources on AI for schools.
why_it_matters: It applies critical data studies and the sociology of education to AI in schools and universities, asking who owns and profits from educational AI and how data systems change teaching. The AI-safety field's treatment of education largely leaves out these questions. Its Scottish AI-literacy curriculum is a working template for teaching young people to judge AI critically.

Ring adjacent (E3): standing AI research and AI-literacy work in schools, on AI's societal effects, with no safety framing. Transfer protecting (J4): it defends teachers, pupils and universities against datafication and platform capture, and equips them with AI literacy. Problems: power (political economy and assetisation of edtech), epistemics (AI literacy and futures thinking), justice (the voice of young people and the Global South). Framing structural: it reads datafication and platform power as systemic drift. Standpoint neither despite the Global South theme, because the centre is led from Edinburgh (O). The MSc is not AI-specific, so it is not coded under courses.

name: Civics of Technology Project
summary: A US 501(c)(3) nonprofit launched in 2022 by education professors Daniel Krutka and Marie Heath, now co-directed with Jacob Pleasants. It promotes critical inquiry into technology in K-16 classrooms, starting from the premise that technologies are not neutral. It publishes free curricula and technology-audit frameworks and a weekly blog and newsletter, and runs monthly online book clubs and an annual virtual conference; the fifth, billed as an 'Online Conference Against Tech Hype', was in August 2026. Its AI materials include 'Critical Inquiries of Generative AI' lessons for university students and a 'What is AI made of?' lesson plan. Its 2026 blog posts cover GenAI in history teaching, ableism in educational AI, technofeudalism, and teachers' roles beyond being a 'human-in-the-loop'.
why_it_matters: It gives teachers Neil Postman-style media ecology and technoskepticism, including the view that refusing a technology is a legitimate educational choice. AI-safety work tends to treat public education as AI literacy or adoption training; this project offers ready-made curricula for questioning AI's effects instead.

name: Deans for Impact (DFI)
summary: A US nonprofit founded in 2015 that works with educator-preparation programmes to ground teacher training in cognitive science, known for its guide 'The Science of Learning'. It reports working with 261 programmes in 45 states. It runs the Impact Academy fellowship for educator-preparation leaders and does state policy work on teacher pathways. In August 2026 it announced an AI Framework for Teacher Preparation with TeachingWorks (University of Michigan). The framework is funded by the Gates Foundation, will be developed over 2026-27, and will set out the competencies novice teachers need to use AI with sound judgement.
why_it_matters: It turns cognitive-science findings, such as the value of effortful retrieval and practice, into norms for how teachers are trained. Those norms are what can stop AI from doing the thinking that produces learning. Its AI framework could shape how many US teacher-preparation programmes teach the use of AI.

Ring changed from potential to adjacent (E2/E3): the Gates-funded AI Framework for Teacher Preparation (2026-27) is a funded project, more than light engagement, and it has no safety framing. Its transferable method is still the one the roster named: turning cognitive-science findings on effortful practice into professional norms that guard against handing thinking over to AI. Transfer convening (J5): the framework equips its own community of teacher educators and novice teachers to use AI. Framing flourishing is the nearest fit for its aim to have teachers 'use AI tools well... as a support for strong instruction'. Way of knowing practice: codified competencies for teaching practice.

name: Embedded EthiCS @ Harvard
summary: A Harvard programme in which philosophers teach ethics modules inside computer-science courses, about ten courses a semester. Computer scientist Barbara Grosz and philosopher Alison Simmons piloted it in spring 2017. AI-related modules have covered fairness in model selection, value-laden reward design in reinforcement learning, the precautionary principle under uncertainty in NLP, the ethics of interpretability, deepfakes, autonomous vehicles, and open-source models and power. Modules in 2025-26 included one in 'Software Engineering with Gen AI'. It publishes its modules openly under CC BY 4.0, and Stanford, Toronto, Technion, Nebraska-Lincoln and California State University campuses have started similar programmes.
why_it_matters: It is an established way to build normative judgement into the people who build AI while they learn the technical craft, and other universities have copied it. No explicit AI-safety or alignment module could be confirmed, so for the safety field the value lies in the teaching model rather than its current content.

Alison Simmons (Co-founder; Samuel H. Wolcott Professor of Philosophy)
Matthew Kopec (Program Director and Lecturer in Philosophy)
James Mickens (Executive board; Gordon McKay Professor of Computer Science)
funding: Not published for the core programme. The NSF supports its partnership with nine Hispanic-Serving Institution campuses piloting AI-focused ethics programmes (Harvard Gazette, Nov 2025).
status_evidence: Spring 2026: modules taught in CS courses (module repository). Nov 2025: the Harvard Gazette reported demand exceeding capacity.
engage: Open teaching modules for reuse by other universities (CC BY 4.0)
Philosophy postdoctoral fellowships with the programme
Invites other institutions to adopt the model
caveats: Its modules cover present-day issues (fairness, privacy, deepfakes, trust in AI); no explicit AI-safety or alignment module was found. The news page on its site is stale, showing placeholder items from 2023.
tag_notes: Home philosophy (H1): philosophers teach applied-ethics modules inside CS courses; phil_bioethics covers engineering-ethics initiatives. Ring adjacent (E3): a standing programme with AI modules on fairness, reward design, interpretability and deepfakes, without safety or alignment framing. Transfer into_builders (J2): it forms the ethical judgement of future AI and software builders. Problems: people (the conscience and practical wisdom of builders), justice (fairness and accountability topics). Framing present_harms is the nearest fit for 'socially responsible' computing focused on bias, privacy and misuse. Org_type programme (I): a teaching programme inside Harvard, not a research centre.

name: International Federation of Library Associations and Institutions (IFLA)
summary: IFLA is the global federation of library associations and institutions. It has more than 1,700 members in about 155 countries, and its headquarters are at the National Library of the Netherlands in The Hague. Its AI work runs through an Artificial Intelligence Special Interest Group (sessions at the annual World Library and Information Congress, webinars and satellite meetings), guidance such as 'Developing a library strategic response to Artificial Intelligence' (2023) and the IFLA Statement on Copyright and AI (April 2025), and Knowledge Rights 21, its Arcadia-funded European copyright programme.
why_it_matters: Libraries are the institutions much of the world already relies on for information literacy and knowledge stewardship. IFLA reaches that profession in about 155 countries, and it holds settled positions on AI literacy and on access to training data that the AI-safety field rarely engages with.

key_work.title: IFLA Statement on Libraries and Artificial Intelligence
Developing a library strategic response to Artificial Intelligence (AI SIG working document, v1.1)
IFLA Statement on Copyright and Artificial Intelligence
AI SIG satellite conference on AI in public libraries, Seoul (with the Public Libraries and IT Sections)

funding: Membership fees from more than 1,700 members, plus project grants. For example, Arcadia gave the Stichting IFLA Foundation EUR 3m (2021) and EUR 5.5m (extension announced Dec 2024) for Knowledge Rights 21. Overall budget not checked.
status_evidence: Aug 2026: AI SIG paper session at the World Library and Information Congress in Busan, and a co-organised AI satellite conference for public libraries in Seoul (14 Aug). June 2026: AI SIG webinar with the Management of Library Associations Section on how library associations govern AI.
engage: AI Special Interest Group: open to IFLA members and affiliates; runs sessions and calls for papers at the annual World Library and Information Congress (August)
Free global webinars from the AI SIG (e.g. 23 June 2026, on library associations and AI governance)
Satellite meetings on AI, e.g. on research integrity in the age of AI (2026, with Yonsei University)
caveats: Its AI work is about libraries' own use of AI, AI literacy and copyright, not AI safety. Automated tools couldn't load IFLA's website, so the recent details come from search snippets of IFLA pages. It wasn't confirmed who convenes the AI SIG after the 2023-25 term. Knowledge Rights 21 has its own profile.
tag_notes: Home democracy/dem_epistemics: its AI outputs (statements, strategic-response guidance, AI literacy) come from library practice in access to information and knowledge stewardship, and H3 places a professional federation with the community it serves. MISFIT: the taxonomy has no library or information-science key, and dem_epistemics (knowledge commons) is the closest. Secondary law for its copyright and TDM advocacy (Advisory Committee on Copyright, KR21). Ring adjacent (E3): a standing AI SIG and repeated AI statements from 2020 to 2026, framed around access, literacy and copyright, with no safety, alignment or catastrophic-risk framing. Transfer convening (J5): the main purpose is helping member libraries respond to AI. Framing flourishing is a weak fit, based on its copyright statement's 'realising potential, supporting users' framing. Problem power is secondary, for its advocacy on access to training data and on AI licensing terms.

name: Knowledge Rights 21 (KR21)
summary: Knowledge Rights 21 is a European advocacy programme that works to reform copyright law and practice so that libraries, researchers and the public can access and use knowledge. Arcadia funds it, IFLA manages it, and LIBER and SPARC Europe are partners. It runs from The Hague, with a Brussels lead and national coordinators in 18 countries. 'Research & AI' is one of its four themes: it argues for research-first AI policy, for keeping text-and-data mining open for research, and against the EU's opt-out system for AI training.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few organised voices in EU AI and copyright policy speaking for research and libraries. It argues that TDM opt-outs entrench the largest developers and skew training data, which ties copyright rules to power concentration in AI. AI-governance work tends to miss that angle.

key_work.title: Principles on AI, Science and Research
Webinar: Closed Licences, Closed Doors: Open Licensing, AI, and the Future of Research Impact
Copyright and Access in the Age of AI (event in Cyprus)
Copyright & AI: The EU Landscape and What Comes Next (webinar with MEP Axel Voss, run by the University of Edinburgh Library, listed by KR21)

people: Benjamin White (Policy Committee co-chair; UK national coordinator)
funding: Arcadia: EUR 3m to the Stichting IFLA Foundation for a first three-year phase (launched Sept 2021), then a EUR 5.5m extension for five more years, announced Dec 2024 (to 2029).
status_evidence: Oct 2026: news post 'Choose Europe…' (1 Oct) and a listing for a 9 Oct webinar on copyright and AI in the EU with MEP Axel Voss. May 2026: event in Cyprus on copyright and access in the age of AI.
engage: Webinars and national events on copyright, research and AI (listed on its events page)
European Rights Retention Community of Practice and the KR21 European e-Books & e-Lending Community of Practice (first meeting Sept 2026), for library and research professionals
Newsletter
caveats: AI is one of four themes; most of its work is on e-lending, rights retention and secondary publishing rights. It argues for access and against opt-outs, which puts it on the opposite side from creator and rightsholder groups in the EU debate on AI and copyright. The University of Edinburgh Library runs the 9 Oct 2026 webinar; KR21's UK coordinator sits on the panel. The roster placed it in Brussels, but its contact base is IFLA in The Hague, with a Brussels lead.
tag_notes: Home law/law_legal: its AI work is copyright-law reform (TDM exceptions, the AI Act, contract override), argued from access-to-knowledge legal theory. Secondary democracy for the library knowledge-commons perspective. MISFIT: no library key. Ring adjacent (E3): a standing 'Research & AI' strand with principles, a primer, position work and repeated events in 2024-26, but no safety or catastrophic-risk framing. Transfer into_institutions (J3): it aims to change EU copyright law as it governs AI training and research use. Its subject is copyright restriction, not protecting libraries from AI's effects, so the label isn't protecting. Problem power is primary because its AI page argues that opt-outs reinforce market concentration. Framing structural, from the same page's emphasis on concentration, bias and competitiveness. The mission statement is more aspirational. Org type programme (I): it is managed by IFLA on time-limited Arcadia funding.

name: Association of Research Libraries (ARL)
summary: ARL is a membership association of about 125 research libraries in the United States and Canada, based in Washington, DC. Its AI work includes the Research Libraries Guiding Principles for AI (April 2024), advocacy on copyright and AI, and polls of its members. It also runs a scenario-planning programme with the Coalition for Networked Information (CNI): the ARL/CNI 2035 Scenarios of AI-influenced futures (2024), the free Futurescape Libraries AI Toolkit (Sept 2025) with workshops, and a workshop report on the strategic implications of AI futures (March 2026).
why_it_matters: It applies scenario planning to how AI will reshape scholarship and research infrastructure, and has packaged the method as a reusable toolkit with workshops. AI-safety groups working on societal resilience could borrow that tested format for institutional foresight.

key_work.title: Research Libraries Guiding Principles for Artificial Intelligence
ARL/CNI 2035 Scenarios: AI-Influenced Futures
Futurescape Libraries AI Toolkit (with CNI)
Strategic Implications of AI Futures for Research Libraries: Workshop Report

people: Cynthia Hudson Vitale (co-author, 2026 AI futures workshop report)
Keith Webster (developer of the Futurescape toolkit; Dean of University Libraries, Carnegie Mellon)
funding: Member dues. The Futurescape toolkit had early funding from the US Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS) and ongoing support from CNI.
status_evidence: Mar 2026: ARL and CNI published the 'Strategic Implications of AI Futures for Research Libraries' workshop report (announced 27 Mar). Jan 2026: AI quick poll of member libraries.
engage: Futurescape Libraries AI Toolkit: free, five modules of scenario activities and templates
