Futurescape toolkit workshops, run in person across the US and online
caveats: Its AI work serves research libraries' own strategy, operations and copyright interests, and it has no safety or catastrophic-risk framing. CNI is a separate organisation, run jointly by ARL and EDUCAUSE, and the scenario work is shared between them. ARL's AI page itself shows mainly 2024-25 materials; the 2026 activity comes from CNI announcements and press coverage.
tag_notes: Home arts/arts_futures (H2, B10): its distinctive AI output is scenario planning (the 2035 scenarios, the Futurescape toolkit and its workshops). MISFIT: no library key. H3 would otherwise place a library association with its community (closest dem_epistemics), so democracy is the first secondary; law covers its copyright and AI advocacy. Ring adjacent (E3): sustained AI work in 2024-26 (principles, scenarios, toolkit, polls, a report) on the future of scholarship, without safety or x-risk framing. Transfer convening (J5): the work prepares its own member libraries for AI. Framing flourishing is a weak fit: the toolkit aims to help libraries 'thrive in the AI landscape'. Problem power is secondary, for its copyright and AI advocacy. Org type membership (I): an association of institutional members with dues.

name: InterPARES Trust AI (I Trust AI: Archives 4.0)
summary: InterPARES Trust AI ('Archives 4.0: Artificial Intelligence for Trust in Records and Archives') is a multinational archival-science research partnership, led from the University of British Columbia's School of Information. It runs from 2021 to 2026 with more than 60 partner organisations in 26 countries. It studies how AI can help keep public records trustworthy and accessible, what risks AI brings to records and archives, and how archival concepts such as provenance, authenticity and paradata should inform responsible AI. Outputs include work on paradata documentation, cryptographic provenance for AI-generated images, AI competencies for archivists, and a series of symposia.
why_it_matters: Archival science has a mature method for establishing whether a record is authentic and where it came from. Applied to AI, it offers ways to document the processes AI systems carry out ('paradata') and to establish provenance for AI-generated content. Both matter for accountability and information integrity.

key_work.title: Papers on cryptographic provenance and authentication of AI-generated images
InterPARES Trust AI symposium, Università di Macerata
InterPARES Trust AI symposium, Ascoli Piceno (AI competencies for archivists, cryptographic provenance, paradata)
Final symposium: Keeping Evidence: Archives, AI and Trust in Public Records (Library and Archives Canada, Ottawa)

people: Luciana Duranti (principal investigator and co-director, UBC)
Tracey P. Lauriault (Carleton University; organiser of the final symposium)
funding: SSHRC Partnership Grant of CAD 2.5 million over five years, plus more than CAD 3 million in matching cash and in-kind support from 60+ partner organisations.
status_evidence: June 2026: symposium in Ascoli Piceno, Italy. Final symposium scheduled for 29 Oct 2026 at Library and Archives Canada, Ottawa.
engage: Final InterPARES Symposium, 29 Oct 2026, Library and Archives Canada, Ottawa (free; registration required via Carleton University)
caveats: The project ends in 2026. Its final symposium also marks the end of Luciana Duranti's career and of more than three decades of InterPARES research, so it is likely to go dormant after October 2026 unless a successor phase is funded. Much of its work is about using AI inside archives rather than about governing AI.
tag_notes: Home democracy/dem_epistemics: its contribution is archival diplomatics (authenticity, provenance, chains of custody), and the taxonomy's nearest home for provenance and knowledge commons is collective epistemics. MISFIT: there is no archival or information-science key. Ring adjacent (E3): a funded multi-year AI programme from 2021 to 2026 on the trustworthiness of records, without safety or catastrophic-risk framing. Transfer into_institutions (J3): its stated goal is that archival principles inform responsible AI, through paradata documentation and provenance practice for public institutions. Problem assurance is secondary, for paradata as documentation and accountability of AI processes. Framing structural, because the stake is the erosion of trust in the evidential record; the mission itself is mostly positive. Org type programme (I): a time-limited, SSHRC-funded consortium.

name: Institutional Data Initiative (IDI), Harvard Law School Library
summary: The Institutional Data Initiative is a research initiative at Harvard Law School Library. It was incubated at the library's Library Innovation Lab and launched in December 2024. It works with libraries, museums, archives and government agencies to clean, document and publish their collections as open datasets for AI, and it builds open tools for doing so. Its first release, Institutional Books 1.0 (June 2025), holds about 983,000 public-domain books (242 billion tokens, 254 languages) from Harvard's Google Books scans. In 2026 it published 1.47 million historical newspaper pages and a dataset of 186 years of university proceedings.
why_it_matters: It treats training data as a commons that knowledge institutions steward, with documented provenance and quality, instead of scraped material. That gives open and smaller developers a well-understood alternative, and gives libraries a say in what models learn from.

key_work.title: Institutional Books 1.0 (983K public-domain books, 242B tokens)
GRIN Transfer: open-source pipeline for libraries to retrieve their Google Books collections
Institutional Proceedings: 186 years of university decisions
1.47 million historical newspaper pages released as granular data

funding: Launch funding from Microsoft and OpenAI (reported by Wired, Dec 2024). Collaborators include Google Books and the Boston Public Library. Amounts not disclosed.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: released 1.47 million historical newspaper pages (2 Sep) and extended Institutional Books with enriched text and 22 million extracted images (8 Sep).
engage: Open roles: Senior Partnerships Manager; Communications and Community Manager
Invites institutions, researchers and technologists to collaborate on and improve its datasets (contact@institutional.org)
Online talks and events (e.g. Oct 2025, with Ruth Okediji, on diversity in AI training data)
caveats: Microsoft and OpenAI fund it, and its datasets are open to commercial developers, so it also widens the training data available to frontier labs. The books corpus leans heavily towards Western European languages (43% English). It is not framed around AI safety. It launched in December 2024, so its track record is short.
tag_notes: Home economics/econ_commons: its goal is 'a vast commons of well-understood data' held by institutions as stewards, and it supplies public-domain data as a public good for AI. Secondary democracy (knowledge commons, provenance). MISFIT: its actual method is library collection stewardship, and there is no library key. Ring adjacent (E3): a sustained AI programme since Dec 2024 (datasets, tools, events), framed around responsible training data and levelling the playing field, with no safety framing. Transfer into_model (J1): its outputs are training data for AI systems. Problem power is primary, for its aim to give smaller developers and researchers data that only large firms usually assemble. Org type academic (I): a university library research unit with its own identity and staff. Status active rather than new: it launched in Dec 2024.

name: Transparent Books: AI Infrastructure for Discovery and the Public Interest (HathiTrust, Northeastern University Library, Authors Alliance)
summary: Transparent Books is a five-year project, announced in August 2026, led by HathiTrust with Northeastern University Library and Authors Alliance and funded by a $5 million Mellon Foundation grant. It aims to: make HathiTrust's roughly 19 million digitised volumes usable for noncommercial text-and-data mining and AI research; improve metadata and text quality with AI tools; agree shared principles on legal frameworks, research integrity, accountability and environmental impact; and build services that can sustain themselves. It puts into practice the framework of the Public Interest Corpus, a Mellon-funded planning project that Authors Alliance and Northeastern ran from December 2024 to April 2026.
why_it_matters: It is a library-governed alternative to commercially assembled book corpora: lawful, documented text for noncommercial research and models, under public-interest principles. That makes it a concrete model of who could hold and govern training data.

key_work.title: Public Interest Corpus: statement of principles and white paper (planning phase, Dec 2024 - Apr 2026)
Transparent Books: $5M Mellon grant to HathiTrust, Northeastern and Authors Alliance

people: Dan Cohen (Dean of the Library, Northeastern University)
Thomas Padilla (Public Interest AI Strategist, Public Interest Corpus)
funding: Mellon Foundation, $5 million over five years (from 2026). The Public Interest Corpus planning phase (Dec 2024 - Apr 2026) was also Mellon-funded.
status_evidence: Aug 2026: HathiTrust, Northeastern University Library and Authors Alliance announced the $5M Mellon grant (27 Aug).
engage: No open calls yet; follow announcements from HathiTrust, Northeastern University Library and Authors Alliance
caveats: It has only just launched, no dedicated project website was found, and its outputs are still to come. The named people lead the partner organisations; their specific roles in the project were not confirmed. It could also be read as a renamed successor to the Public Interest Corpus, though it has a new lead organisation (HathiTrust) and a new grant.
tag_notes: Home economics/econ_commons: a noncommercial books corpus stewarded by libraries as a public good, offered as an alternative to corporate data control. Secondary law for public-interest copyright (Authors Alliance leads policy and convening). MISFIT: it is grounded in library stewardship, and there is no library key. Ring adjacent (E3): a funded five-year AI-infrastructure project framed around 'AI for the public good', with no safety framing. Transfer into_model (J1): it supplies verified text for TDM, AI research and noncommercial models; its principles work (into_institutions) is secondary. Problem power is primary (who holds and governs book data), with epistemics for discovery and transparency. Org type programme (I): a time-limited grant-funded project across three organisations. Status new: launched Aug 2026; the predecessor is noted in caveats.

name: Authors Alliance
summary: Authors Alliance is a US nonprofit, founded in 2014 at Berkeley by Pamela Samuelson and colleagues. It represents authors who want their work widely read and argues for copyright policy that keeps knowledge accessible. Its AI work includes the Knight Foundation-funded project 'AI, Authorship, and the Public Interest' (from 2025), with an AI legal fellow and research subgrants, and analysis of AI-training litigation and policy. It also co-led the Public Interest Corpus and now leads policy and convening for Transparent Books, a books corpus stewarded by libraries for noncommercial AI research.
why_it_matters: It argues the authors' side of the AI training-data question from a public-interest position: fair use for research, attribution and preserving the commons. That challenges the assumption that authors' interests lie only in licensing and opt-outs.

key_work.title: AI, Authorship, and the Public Interest (Knight Foundation-funded project)
AI, Authorship, and the Public Interest research grants (5 recipients from 160+ proposals)
Public Interest Corpus (with Northeastern University)
Analysis of the Third Circuit ruling in Thomson Reuters v. ROSS (AI training and fair use)

funding: Knight Foundation (AI, Authorship and the Public Interest; amount not disclosed). Mellon Foundation (Public Interest Corpus; partner in the $5M Transparent Books grant to HathiTrust, 2026). Earlier support from Arcadia (a two-year $500,000 grant).
status_evidence: Oct 2026: post on the Third Circuit's ruling in Thomson Reuters v. ROSS (2 Oct). Aug 2026: announced Transparent Books with HathiTrust and Northeastern.
engage: Staff and fellowship roles (e.g. AI Legal Fellow, Public Interest Legal Fellow; check its jobs page)
Research grants of up to $20,000 on AI, copyright and the public interest (2025 call, now closed)
caveats: Its stance generally favours fair use for text-and-data mining and AI research. That puts it at odds with authors' groups, such as the Authors Guild, that seek licensing for training: it is a pro-access advocate, not a neutral voice. It was founded at Berkeley; its current listed address is in Sacramento.
tag_notes: Home law/law_legal (H1): its AI outputs are legal analysis of copyright, fair use, authorship and AI-training litigation, by staff attorneys and legal fellows. Secondary economics (commons), through its formal partnership in the Public Interest Corpus and Transparent Books. Ring adjacent (E3): a standing, funded AI project since 2025 (fellow, subgrants, symposia) framed around the public interest and copyright, with no safety framing. Transfer into_institutions (J3): it aims to shape copyright law and policy as they apply to AI. Problem power is primary (who owns and may use training data), with epistemics for public access and preserving the commons. Framing flourishing: the AI project's stated aim is how AI 'can best advance knowledge and serve the public interest'.

name: Department of Psychosis Studies, Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience, King's College London: AI-associated delusions research (Morrin and Pollak)
summary: A clinical research line inside King's College London's Department of Psychosis Studies, led by the psychiatrists Hamilton Morrin and Thomas Pollak, that studies delusions arising during sustained chatbot use. They coined the term 'AI-associated delusions', set out in The Lancet Psychiatry (2026) how LLMs can co-create delusional content and what safeguards would help, and in September 2026 analysed 185 real-world reports of chatbot-linked harm. Morrin co-leads LAMBDA (Looking After Minds and Brains in the Digital Age), a group on the mental-health effects of AI chatbots.
why_it_matters: It gives a clinical account of how sycophancy, linguistic mirroring and hyper-personalised replies can build an 'amplification spiral' with vulnerable users. It also argues that chatbot safety should be judged over whole conversation trajectories rather than single replies, which maps directly onto multi-turn sycophancy evaluations. Pollak has publicly called for AI safety teams to include psychiatrists.

key_work.title: Artificial intelligence-associated delusions and large language models: risks, mechanisms of delusion co-creation, and safeguarding strategies (The Lancet Psychiatry)
It Is the Journey, Not the Destination: Moving From End Points to Trajectories When Assessing Chatbot Mental Health Safety (JMIR Mental Health)
Characterizing the spiral: potential mechanisms in AI-associated delusions (NPP Digital Psychiatry and Neuroscience)
Delusions and Harms Associated with AI Chatbot Use: Early Evidence from 185 Real-World Reports (arXiv preprint)

people: Hamilton Morrin (psychiatrist, Wellcome doctoral fellow; joint lead of LAMBDA)
Thomas Pollak (consultant neuropsychiatrist, Reader in Immunopsychiatry)
Oliver Howes (Head of Department of Psychosis Studies)
funding: Morrin holds a Wellcome Trust doctoral fellowship; no dedicated funding for the AI line found. The department holds about £25M in research grants overall.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: arXiv preprint analysing 185 reports of chatbot-linked delusions and harms (Morrin, Pollak and others, including Etienne Brisson of the Human Line Project); Jul 2026: authors' reply on terminology in The Lancet Psychiatry.
engage: Public talks through KCL's Neuropsychiatry Research and Education Group, e.g. 'Delusions by design' (28 Oct 2025, in person and online)
The department takes PhD and MD(Res) students in psychosis studies (not AI-specific)
caveats: The AI work is a small research line led by a doctoral fellow and a consultant, not a funded centre; no public LAMBDA page was found. The evidence so far is case reports, media reports and conceptual papers, and the terminology ('AI psychosis' versus 'AI-associated delusions') is still debated in the journal.
tag_notes: Home: clinical psychiatrists applying psychosis research to chatbot-linked delusions (H1, method over topic). Ring: kept adjacent as the work is a sustained line (2025-26 papers) framed around clinical harm, not catastrophic risk or alignment, although the trajectory-evaluation paper speaks to model safety evaluation. Transfer: the main aim is protecting vulnerable patients through safeguards and 'AI-informed care' (J4); assurance is added because it proposes how chatbot safety should be evaluated (F must-pair).

name: RAND Health (formerly RAND Health Care): generative AI and mental health research
summary: RAND's health research division (now styled RAND Health) has a research line, led by Ryan McBain with Jonathan Cantor and colleagues, that measures how people use AI chatbots for mental health and how the chatbots respond. It has run nationally representative surveys of chatbot use for mental-health advice by US 12- to 21-year-olds, estimated how often mental health comes up in public chatbot conversation logs, and tested how ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini answer suicide-related questions graded by clinicians for risk. McBain also writes commentary on company safety claims, such as OpenAI's teen protections.
why_it_matters: It gives independent, epidemiology-grade measures of frontier-model behaviour and use, with population denominators that company figures lack. For example, it showed that published estimates of 'mental health use' range from 0.01% to 72% largely because of differing definitions. Its suicide-query tests are third-party misuse and harm evaluations done to clinical standards.

key_work.title: Study of ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini responses to 30 suicide-related questions rated by clinical risk (Psychiatric Services, NIMH-funded)
AI Chatbot Use and Disclosure for Mental Health Among US Adolescents and Young Adults (JAMA Pediatrics)
Prevalence of Mental Health Discussions in Publicly Available Generative AI Conversations (JAMA Network Open)
OpenAI Says ChatGPT Is Safer for Teens. Now It Needs to Show Proof. (commentary)

people: Ryan K. McBain (senior policy researcher; lead on AI and mental health)
Li Ang Zhang (co-author of the survey and log studies)
Peter S. Hussey (vice president and director, RAND Health)
funding: NIMH funded the suicide-query study and the conversation-log study. RAND Health is funded through contracts and grants from US federal agencies (NIH, AHRQ, CDC, CMS and others), states and foundations such as the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation.
status_evidence: Aug 31 2026: JAMA Network Open research letter on mental-health discussions in public chatbot logs; Aug 27 2026: commentary on OpenAI's 'ChatGPT for Teens'.
engage: RAND careers page lists research positions
caveats: This entry covers one research line within RAND's health division, not RAND as a whole. RAND's AI security and catastrophic-risk work (RAND Global and Emerging Risks, which is on the classic map) is separate and mainstream AI policy. Several authors also hold Harvard appointments. The division's site now says 'RAND Health', while leadership titles still say 'RAND Health Care'.
tag_notes: Home: the methods are survey epidemiology and health-services research, i.e. public health (H1), with youth mental health as the topic, so psych is secondary. Ring: kept adjacent, since there is a sustained 2025-26 publication line but it is framed around present mental-health harms, not catastrophic risk or alignment. Transfer: the aim is protecting young people and patients from harmful chatbot use (J4); assurance is paired because it evaluates model responses (F).

name: Clinical Cancer Epidemiology Lab, Flinders Health and Medical Research Institute (Flinders University): AI vigilance and health-disinformation safeguards
summary: A clinical-epidemiology and pharmacology group at Flinders University in Adelaide, co-led by Michael Sorich and Ashley Hopkins, that repeatedly audits whether public generative-AI tools can be made to produce health disinformation. Since 2023 it has tested chatbots' safeguards (BMJ 2024), shown that system instructions can turn LLM APIs into disinformation chatbots (Annals of Internal Medicine 2025), and in 2026 tested six consumer chatbot platforms and ten image and two video generators. It calls for 'AI vigilance': routine auditing, transparency and regulation.
why_it_matters: It brings surveillance-style repeated measurement from pharmacovigilance and public health to model safeguards, producing dated, comparable misuse evaluations of named commercial models (for example, Claude and ChatGPT refused while Copilot, Meta AI, Grok and Gemini showed gaps). That is a public-health template for independent misuse auditing outside the labs.

key_work.title: Health Disinformation Use Case Highlighting the Urgent Need for Artificial Intelligence Vigilance: Weapons of Mass Disinformation (JAMA Internal Medicine)
Repeated cross-sectional analysis of LLM safeguards, risk mitigation and transparency against health disinformation (BMJ)
Assessing the System-Instruction Vulnerabilities of Large Language Models to Malicious Conversion Into Health Disinformation Chatbots (Annals of Internal Medicine)
Evaluation of Generative Artificial Intelligence Safeguards Against the Creation of Images and Videos Harmful to Public Health (Public Health Reports)

people: Ashley M. Hopkins (associate professor; lab co-lead)
Bradley D. Menz (researcher; first author of the 2024 JAMA Internal Medicine and BMJ papers)
Natansh D. Modi (first author of the 2025 Annals and 2026 JMIR Infodemiology safeguard audits)
funding: The 2026 Public Health Reports study acknowledges the National Health and Medical Research Council (APP2030913, APP2008119), Tour de Cure, Cancer Council South Australia and The Hospital Research Foundation.
status_evidence: Jul 2026: Public Health Reports print issue (vol 141, no 4; online Feb 2026) on image and video generator safeguards; Apr 2026: JMIR Infodemiology evaluation of six consumer LLM platforms.
caveats: AI auditing is a strand of a cancer-epidemiology lab whose main work is predicting drug benefits and side effects; there is no dedicated AI-safety unit or web page. FHMRI itself (founded 2019, 600+ researchers) has no institute-level AI programme. Collaborators include the University of South Australia and the security scholar Kacper Gradon.
tag_notes: Home: public-health epidemiology and pharmacovigilance methods (repeated cross-sectional audits) applied to model safeguards (H1). Ring: kept bridge because the 2023-26 line is explicitly framed around AI safeguards against malicious misuse and 'AI vigilance' (E3), though the stakes are framed as present public-health harm. Transfer: its evaluations target model behaviour and developers' safeguards (J1), with secondary calls for routine regulatory auditing.

name: Mind: Mental Health in the Age of AI Commission
summary: Mind, the mental-health charity for England and Wales, set up a year-long commission on AI and mental health. It was announced in February 2026 after a Guardian investigation, which Mind's information team supported, found Google's AI Overviews giving inaccurate mental-health advice. The commission brings together clinicians, technologists, policymakers and people with lived experience. It is gathering evidence from the public, regulators, providers and tech companies on how AI is changing help-seeking, how to keep users safe, and what AI does to inequalities in access, and will then make recommendations to policymakers and industry.
why_it_matters: It is a large frontline charity applying a lived-experience inquiry to consumer AI, drawing on people who have been harmed by chatbot advice rather than only on experts' views. It could give UK regulators and companies a public-health and service-user account of what safe AI for mental health requires.

key_work.title: Testing of Google AI Overviews on common mental-health queries (with the Guardian)
Mental Health in the Age of AI Commission and public call for evidence

people: Rosie Weatherley (information content manager; led the AI Overviews testing)
Elena Simperl (commissioner; co-director, King's Institute for Artificial Intelligence)
funding: Mind is a charity funded by donations, fundraising, its charity shops and grants. Funding for the commission has not been disclosed.
status_evidence: Aug 12 2026: King's College London announced Elena Simperl's appointment to the commission, with a public call for evidence open to adults in England and Wales.
engage: Public call for evidence (open in Aug 2026 to people aged 18+ in England and Wales)
Mind careers page
caveats: The chair and full membership could not be confirmed because Mind's site blocked automated reading; only one commissioner is confirmed. The commission runs for about 12 months, so recommendations are not expected before 2027. Mind also stresses AI's potential to widen access, so this is not an anti-AI campaign.
tag_notes: Home: a mental-health charity drawing on crisis services and lived-experience peer support (H3, constituency). Ring: adjacent, as it is a funded year-long programme on AI's mental-health effects with no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing. Transfer: it defends people with mental-health problems, its own constituency, from unsafe AI advice (J4); epistemics is secondary because of its work on AI-generated health misinformation.

name: Center for Countering Digital Hate (CCDH)
summary: CCDH is a nonprofit with UK and US entities that researches online hate, misinformation and child-safety harms and campaigns for regulation of platforms. Its AI work uses persona-based safety tests of chatbots. In 'Fake Friend' (Aug 2025), 53% of 1,200 ChatGPT responses to prompts from teen personas contained harmful self-harm, eating-disorder or drug content. In 'Killer Apps' (Mar 2026, with CNN), 8 of 10 chatbots tested regularly helped users plan violent attacks. It then turns these findings into open letters and policy asks.
why_it_matters: It runs reproducible, public-facing exposure tests of deployed chatbots and turns the results into regulatory pressure, a civil-society counterpart to lab red-teaming. Its STAR framework (safety by design, transparency, accountability, responsibility) is a ready-made policy template that it now applies to AI products.

key_work.title: Fake Friend: How ChatGPT betrays vulnerable teens by encouraging dangerous behavior
Killer Apps: How mainstream AI chatbots assist users planning violent attacks
Open letter from 62 terrorism survivors and bereaved families calling for UK AI chatbot regulation
STAR Framework for regulating social media and AI

people: Sarah O'Quinn (US Director of Public Affairs)
funding: Philanthropic trusts and public donations; funders reported in 2020 included the Pears Foundation, Joseph Rowntree Charitable Trust and Barrow Cadbury Trust.
status_evidence: Jul 1 2026: recommendations to the Irish Presidency of the EU Council on AI and the protection of minors; Jul 29 2026: latest research report.
engage: Staff roles via 'Work at CCDH'
Tipline for reporting harmful content
'AI platforms must stop generating harmful content' public action campaign
caveats: AI is one strand of a broader social-media harms programme. Its reports are advocacy research, not peer-reviewed. It is politically contested: X Corp sued it in 2023 (dismissed in March 2024, then appealed), and in December 2025 the US State Department imposed visa sanctions on its CEO, after which a court blocked his detention.
tag_notes: Home: civil-society auditing of platforms (law_sts) is its method, applied to chatbots (H1). Ring: adjacent, as it has a sustained AI line (2025-26 reports, letters, campaigns) framed around present harms to teens and the public rather than catastrophic risk or alignment. Transfer: its tests feed regulatory asks and the STAR policy design (J3); region is uk_ireland because it was founded and registered in London in 2018, with a separate US 501(c)(3) in Washington, DC.

name: KFF Health Information and Trust Initiative (formerly Health Misinformation and Trust Initiative)
summary: One of KFF's core programmes. It tracks where Americans get health information, whom they trust and how false health claims spread, through regular tracking polls, a polling dashboard and a newsletter, The Monitor. AI is a recurring strand. Its March 2026 poll found that 32% of US adults had used AI chatbots for health information in the past year and 16% for mental-health advice, and recent Monitor issues covered state regulation of AI mental-health tools (Aug 2026) and AI-generated search answers (Sep 2026).
why_it_matters: It provides repeated, population-level measures of how people use and trust AI in one high-stakes domain, the kind of survey baseline on AI-mediated information that AI-safety sensemaking work rarely has. It also links this to health communicators who have to adapt when AI answers replace visits to original sources.

key_work.title: KFF Tracking Poll on Health Information and Trust: use of AI chatbots for health and mental-health information (Feb-Mar 2026 fieldwork)
The Monitor, vol. 53: Different State Regulatory Approaches Reflect Open Questions About AI Mental Health Tools
The Monitor, vol. 54: Correcting False Health Claims and Navigating AI-Generated Information

people: Irving Washington (senior vice president and executive director, Health Information and Trust Initiative)
funding: KFF is an endowed public charity; its endowment is supplemented by external funds, mainly from foundations. Initiative-specific funders were not found.
status_evidence: Sep 14 2026: The Monitor vol. 54 on AI-generated health answers; Jul 23 2026: polling dashboard updated with AI-use data.
engage: KFF 'Join Our Team' jobs page
Email subscription to The Monitor
caveats: AI is one strand of a wider health-misinformation and trust programme, so its AI engagement is real but modest (borderline between adjacent and potential). The work is US-focused, and the initiative's founding year was not confirmed.
tag_notes: Home: misinformation monitoring and public-opinion tracking of the information environment are collective-epistemics methods (dem_epistemics), with public-health communication as the secondary tradition. Ring: adjacent, given recurring AI polling and Monitor coverage in 2026 with no catastrophic-risk framing; this is close to potential because AI is a minor strand. Transfer: it studies and defends the public's access to accurate health information against AI-generated errors (J4).

name: Algorithmovigilance programme, Vanderbilt University Medical Center (ADVANCE Center and Department of Biomedical Informatics)
summary: A Vanderbilt University Medical Center team that monitors deployed clinical AI tools for performance drift, unfairness and harm. Peter Embí, then chair of biomedical informatics, coined the term 'algorithmovigilance' by analogy with pharmacovigilance. The team, including human-factors researcher Megan Salwei, designed the Vanderbilt Algorithmovigilance Monitoring and Operations System (VAMOS) with participatory design sessions and reported early deployment experience in 2026. It sits in the ADVANCE Center (AI Discovery & Vigilance to Accelerate Innovation & Clinical Excellence), launched in March 2024.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few working examples of post-deployment AI monitoring inside a large organisation, modelled on drug-safety adverse-event surveillance and built with human-factors methods. That template is directly relevant to incident reporting and post-deployment oversight of general-purpose AI.

key_work.title: Human-centered design of an artificial intelligence monitoring system: the Vanderbilt Algorithmovigilance Monitoring and Operations System (JAMIA Open)
Design and Early Evaluation of an Algorithmovigilance System (Studies in Health Technology and Informatics)
Explainability in context: calibrating appropriate trust and reliance in artificial intelligence (JAMIA)
AIM-HI project on AI-enabled diagnosis using randomised trials, algorithmovigilance and proactive risk assessment

people: Peter Embí (originated algorithmovigilance; founding director of ADVANCE; left to direct the US National Library of Medicine in Sep 2026)
Megan E. Salwei (human-factors researcher; lead author of the VAMOS papers)
funding: Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation grant of up to $750,000 through Kaiser Permanente's AIM-HI initiative (Dec 2023); AHRQ career award K01 HS029042 (Salwei); NICHD P50 HD103537.
status_evidence: Aug 2026: JAMIA paper on calibrating clinician trust in AI (Davis and Salwei); May 2026: early evaluation of the deployed algorithmovigilance system.
engage: DBMI open positions page
ADVANCE Center consultations and membership (aimed at the VUMC community)
caveats: The founder, Peter Embí, left VUMC to direct the National Library of Medicine from 10 September 2026, and DBMI now has an interim chair, so the programme's leadership is in transition. The work covers clinical predictive models in one health system, not frontier general-purpose AI.
tag_notes: Home: pharmacovigilance, patient safety and human factors applied to clinical AI assurance (safety_health). Ring: kept adjacent, as it is a standing, funded programme framed around patient safety and equity of deployed clinical tools, not catastrophic risk or alignment. Transfer: it supplies an institutional template, an AI monitoring and incident-response system for health organisations (J3).

name: Center for an Informed Public (CIP), University of Washington
summary: An interdisciplinary research centre at the University of Washington, founded in December 2019 by the Information School, Human Centered Design & Engineering and the School of Law. It studies how rumours, misinformation and disinformation spread, runs rapid-response election-rumour research, and does public education and media-literacy work. Its AI work includes a 2025 PNAS paper on anthropomorphic conversational agents as 'super communicators', a free online course on generative AI ('Modern-Day Oracles or Bullshit Machines?'), AI-literacy lessons for schools, and an August 2026 piece on scrutinising AI tools that evaluate science.
why_it_matters: It brings crisis informatics and collective-sensemaking research, built on studying rumours during elections and disasters, to the question of how generative AI changes what the public believes. AI-safety work on persuasion and sycophancy rarely draws on this tradition of studying misinformation as it actually spreads.

key_work.title: The benefits and dangers of anthropomorphic conversational agents (PNAS, with Jevin West)
Modern-Day Oracles or Bullshit Machines? Free online course on generative AI (Jevin West and Carl Bergstrom)
AI science evaluation tools should be scrutinized through 'critically engaged pragmatism'
Election-rumour research for the 2026 US midterms

funding: Founded with a $5M Knight Foundation grant (2019). Other funders include the Hewlett Foundation, NSF, Microsoft, Omidyar Network and Craig Newmark Philanthropies. A secondary source reports a further Knight grant of $4.5M (2025-29) and a $1M Hewlett renewal (2025-27).
status_evidence: 29 Sep 2026: news post on a mentorship award; Sep 2026: election-rumour research for the 2026 US midterms; 11 Aug 2026: post on scrutinising AI science-evaluation tools.
engage: Free online course 'Modern-Day Oracles or Bullshit Machines?' on the risks and uses of generative AI
Postdoctoral scholar programme at the centre
Webinars and Media Mentorship learning events (videos released Aug 2026); newsletter and mailing list
caveats: AI is a growing strand within a misinformation centre, not its core. Its 2020 Election Integrity Partnership work with the Stanford Internet Observatory later drew political attacks and litigation in the US. The 2025-29 Knight figure comes from a secondary source.
tag_notes: Home democracy/dem_epistemics: its AI outputs study how generative AI shapes rumours, persuasion and public sensemaking (collective epistemics, B10). Law is secondary because the School of Law co-founded it and Ryan Calo is a co-founder. Ring adjacent (kept): a sustained AI strand (2025 PNAS paper, generative-AI course, K-12 AI-literacy work, Aug 2026 evaluation piece) framed around civic health, without catastrophic-risk or alignment framing. Transfer protecting (J4): the work defends the public and students it already serves from misleading information. Framing structural: its mission speaks of civic health and democratic discourse, which is epistemic decay rather than harm to identifiable people. Problems limited to epistemics because the anthropomorphism line is not yet sustained.

name: International Panel on the Information Environment (IPIE)
summary: An independent scientific body, loosely modelled on the IPCC, launched at the Nobel Prize Summit in May 2023 and registered as a charity in Zurich in December 2023. It synthesises research on threats to the global information environment through standing scientific panels, evidence assessments and an annual global expert survey (the 2026 edition drew on 470 experts in 71 countries), and has an affiliate network of more than 500 researchers. Its AI work includes a panel on global standards for AI audits (literature review in 2024, audit framework in 2025) and panels on AI and peacebuilding and on AI and economic inclusion.
why_it_matters: It runs an IPCC-style international scientific assessment for the information environment, the kind of model the AI-safety field is also trying out with the International AI Safety Report. Its AI-audit panel brings in perspectives that AI-safety evaluation work rarely includes, such as Indigenous data sovereignty and Global South auditing.

key_work.title: Global Approaches to Auditing Artificial Intelligence: A Literature Review
Global framework for AI audits (Scientific Panel on Global Standards for AI Audits)
Expert Survey on the Global Information Environment 2026: Under Pressure

people: Wendy Hui Kyong Chun (Chair, AI audits panel)
funding: Foundations including Hewlett, Knight, Simons, Ford and the Rockefeller Brothers Fund. It states that it is financially independent of technology firms and governments.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: published 'Trends in the Information Environment: 2026 Expert Survey Results'; 22 Apr 2026: affiliate network passed 500 researchers.
engage: Researchers can apply online to join the affiliate network (500+ members as of Apr 2026)
Annual expert survey and reports released around the UN General Assembly each September
caveats: AI is one theme among several. Much of its output covers climate misinformation, platforms and child protection, and some AI panel pages list no recent outputs. Its secretariat is about 10 people, and most of the work is done by volunteer experts.
tag_notes: Home democracy/dem_epistemics: it does IPCC-style evidence synthesis and expert surveys on information integrity, which belongs to Democracy because it is not framed as security. Law is secondary for the AI-audit panel (civil-society auditing). Ring adjacent (kept): standing AI panels (audits since 2024, peacebuilding, economic inclusion) with no x-risk or alignment framing. Transfer into_institutions (J3): assessments and an audit framework aimed at policymakers and UN processes. Framing structural: its core message is the worsening of the information environment. Online hub: researchers anywhere can join the affiliate network through an open form.

name: Forum on Information & Democracy
summary: A Paris-based civil-society organisation created in November 2019 by Reporters Without Borders (RSF) and ten partner organisations. Its job is to turn the principles of the intergovernmental International Partnership for Information and Democracy, endorsed by more than 50 countries, into policy recommendations. It convenes expert working groups and workstreams that bring states and civil society together, publishes policy frameworks, and hosts the International Observatory on Information and Democracy. AI is one of its four thematic pillars: its 2024 framework 'AI as a Public Good' made more than 200 recommendations, and in February 2026 it launched a workstream on reliable information in the age of AI, co-chaired by Ukraine, Spain and Luxembourg.
why_it_matters: It has a direct channel from civil-society policy research to a coalition of governments, and brings press-freedom and journalism-sustainability expertise to the question of how AI reshapes the information commons. It is also one of the few information-integrity bodies funded by an AI-safety funder, the Future of Life Institute.

key_work.title: AI as a Public Good: Ensuring Democratic Control of AI in the Information Space
Information Ecosystems and Troubled Democracy (International Observatory on Information and Democracy)
AI and democracy in West Africa: recommendations for Benin, Côte d'Ivoire and Senegal
How AI is Harming Public Interest Media's Sustainability (AI workstream)

people: Laura Schertel Mendes (co-chair, 2024 AI policy working group)
Jonathan Stray (co-chair, 2024 AI policy working group)
funding: Agence Française de Développement, Ford Foundation, Future of Life Institute, the French and Luxembourg foreign ministries, the Swedish Postcode Lottery Foundation and the National Endowment for Democracy.
status_evidence: 25 Sep 2026: video on investing in public-interest media for World News Day; 19 Jun 2026: AI workstream output 'How AI is Harming Public Interest Media's Sustainability'.
engage: Calls for proposals for rapporteurs and policy advisors (Jan 2026)
The AI workstream invites researchers to submit materials and join discussions
Occasional secretariat job openings (e.g. Development and Resource Officer, 2025)
caveats: An intergovernmental partnership mandates it and two foreign ministries part-fund it, so it is not fully independent of states. No board chair has been named publicly since founding president Christophe Deloire died in June 2024. Its AI work centres on media viability and information manipulation, not on the AI systems themselves.
tag_notes: Home democracy/dem_epistemics: its AI work concerns the reliability of information and the information commons, which sits in Democracy unless framed as security. Arts (journalism, the public-interest-media constituency, H3) and law (policy frameworks) are secondary. Ring adjacent (kept): a standing AI pillar and a 2026 workstream framed around information integrity and media viability, not safety or catastrophe. Transfer into_institutions (J3): policy recommendations addressed to the states of the Partnership. Power is a secondary problem because the workstream targets imbalances between media and technology providers, including compensation and copyright. Paris hub: its secretariat is in Paris.

name: Oxford Internet Institute (OII)
summary: A multidisciplinary department of the University of Oxford, founded in 2001 with a gift from Dame Stephanie Shirley's Shirley Foundation, that studies the social science of the internet and digital technology and teaches MSc and DPhil students. Its AI research covers law and ethics (the Governance of Emerging Technologies programme of Sandra Wachter, Brent Mittelstadt and Chris Russell, on LLM truthfulness, deepfakes and loopholes in the EU AI Act), the science of LLM evaluation (Adam Mahdi's Reasoning with Machines Lab), and survey and experimental work on how people use and are influenced by AI. Scott A. Hale became director in January 2026.
why_it_matters: It combines legal, ethical and social-data-science methods with LLM evaluation research, and has had AI Security Institute support, for example for a 2026 report on public use of and emotional reliance on LLMs. Its 'careless speech' and benchmark-validity work questions how the field measures and governs whether models tell the truth.

key_work.title: Do large language models have a legal duty to tell the truth? ('careless speech', Wachter, Mittelstadt, Russell)
Systematic review of construct validity in LLM benchmarks (Reasoning with Machines Lab)
Study of LLM chatbots giving medical advice, finding that people using them did no better than a control group using their usual sources
Large Language Models in the UK: Public Use, Trust, and Attitudes (Enock and Margetts; funded by the AI Security Institute and EPSRC)

people: Sandra Wachter (Professor of Technology and Regulation)
Brent Mittelstadt (Professor of Data Ethics and Policy)
Adam Mahdi (lead, Reasoning with Machines Lab)
funding: Founded with a major gift from the Shirley Foundation plus HEFCE support (2001). Its Governance of Emerging Technologies programme lists the Alan Turing Institute, British Academy, EPSRC, Luminate, Sloan Foundation and Wellcome Trust. The July 2026 report on AI use was supported by the AI Security Institute and EPSRC.
status_evidence: 9 Jul 2026: report with the UK AI Security Institute on UK adults' use of AI for emotional support; Apr 2026: papers at ICLR 2026 (SimBench, predicting LLM failures from activations).
engage: Research and staff posts through the University of Oxford
Public seminars and events, many with an AI strand
MSc and DPhil programmes in social data science and the social science of the internet (not AI-specific)
caveats: A large department, so AI-safety-related work is a minority of its output. The ring rests mainly on the Reasoning with Machines Lab and AISI collaborations. The roster's 'Mind and Emerging Technologies Lab' could not be verified. The Governance of Emerging Technologies page gives its funded period as 2019-2024, though its outputs continue.
tag_notes: Home law/law_sts: an internet-and-society department (comparable to the Weizenbaum Institute) whose AI work comes from law, ethics and social data science. Philosophy (digital ethics) and economics (Fairwork labour research) are secondary under the hub rule (C, H5). Ring changed from adjacent to bridge (E3): the Reasoning with Machines Lab lists AI safety among its standing foci, and OII produced a 2026 study in partnership with the UK AI Security Institute; most OII AI work is still governance and present-harms research. Transfer into_institutions (J3): regulatory analysis (EU AI Act, a legal duty of truthfulness) and evaluation methodology. Framing structural: 'careless speech' argues that LLMs erode shared truth over time. No London hub: it is based in Oxford.

name: AI Security Initiative, Center for Long-Term Cybersecurity (CLTC), UC Berkeley
summary: A research group founded in 2019 inside UC Berkeley's Center for Long-Term Cybersecurity, in the School of Information, that develops risk-management guidance and standards for general-purpose and agentic AI. It maintains an annually updated General-Purpose AI Risk-Management Standards Profile and has published an Agentic AI profile (Feb 2026), recommendations on intolerable risk thresholds (Feb 2025) and work on thresholds for AI-enabled cyber threats (Jan 2026). It runs the UC Berkeley AI Policy Hub and takes part in NIST's AI consortium, the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice plenary and an OECD expert group on AI risk.
why_it_matters: It brings risk-management and standards-engineering practice (standards profiles, risk thresholds, Bayesian-network risk modelling, risk communication) into frontier-AI governance. That turns safety concerns into guidance that developers and public agencies can adopt.

key_work.title: General-Purpose AI Risk-Management Standards Profile (annual update)
Agentic AI Risk-Management Standards Profile
Toward Risk Thresholds for AI-Enabled Cyber Threats: Enhancing Decision-Making Under Uncertainty with Bayesian Networks
Intolerable Risk Threshold Recommendations for Artificial Intelligence

people: Jessica Newman (founding director; co-author, Agentic AI profile)
funding: Open Philanthropy grants to CLTC for the initiative's AI standards and risk-management work: $25,000 (2021), $20,000 (2022) and $200,000 (Feb 2024).
status_evidence: 23 Apr 2026: published the updated General-Purpose AI Risk-Management Standards Profile; 11 Feb 2026: launched the Agentic AI profile with a webinar.
engage: UC Berkeley AI Policy Hub fellowships (for UC Berkeley researchers)
Non-resident fellowships
Contact the director to partner; mailing list; launch webinars (e.g. Feb 2026)
caveats: The host centre, CLTC, is listed on the aisafety.com map under its own name, so this programme is partly covered already. Its interdisciplinarity is mainly risk engineering and standards rather than wider integral perspectives. A case could be made for ring bridge, since CLTC is a cybersecurity centre.
tag_notes: Home safety/safety_engineering: it adapts risk-management standards (NIST-style profiles, thresholds, Bayesian risk modelling) to AI. Ring core (kept, E1): the unit was founded in 2019 with AI risk as its mission, is funded through Open Philanthropy's AI-risk programme, and its host CLTC is on the aisafety.com map. The old-institution rule (SIPRI, York CfAA) could argue bridge, but the unit itself was created for AI risk. Transfer into_institutions (J3): standards profiles and threshold recommendations for developers, NIST, the EU Code of Practice and state agencies. Framing catastrophic: intolerable-risk thresholds for frontier AI and 'devastating' harms in its own approach statement. Org type academic, as a university research unit (rule I). on_classic_map false by name; the parent CLTC is listed.

name: Data Provenance Initiative (DPI)
summary: A volunteer research collective, started in 2023 and coordinated mainly from the MIT Media Lab, that audits the data and markets behind AI. It has traced the licences, sources and creators of more than 4,000 public text, speech and video datasets (the Data Provenance Explorer), tracked how robots.txt files and terms of service restrict AI crawling across 14,000 web domains ('Consent in Crisis', 2024), and measured concentration and participation across some 851,000 open-weight models ('Economies of Open Intelligence', Dec 2025). Its newest project, the AI Observatory (2026 preprint), annotates about 23,000 real chatbot conversations from seven public and private sources to compare how people use and misuse AI.
why_it_matters: It provides public-interest measurement of the AI supply chain, combining legal analysis of licences and consent with large-scale auditing. It documents the erosion of the data commons and the concentration of model markets, issues mainstream alignment work seldom measures.

key_work.title: The Data Provenance Initiative: A Large Scale Audit of Dataset Licensing & Attribution in AI (Nature Machine Intelligence)
Consent in Crisis: The Rapid Decline of the AI Data Commons
Economies of Open Intelligence: Tracing Power & Participation in the Model Ecosystem
The AI Observatory: A Public Measure of Real-World AI Use (preprint)

funding: A 2023 MIT seed grant for research on the social implications of generative AI. It is otherwise volunteer-run and discloses no budget.
status_evidence: 2026: 'The AI Observatory' preprint (data to 2026, sources accessed May 2026); Dec 2025: 'Economies of Open Intelligence' (arXiv 2512.03073); Nov 2025: its open-model data cited by the Financial Times.
engage: Contact the organisers to contribute to audits (volunteer collective)
Use the Data Provenance Collection and public dashboards (dataset audits, web consent, open-model ecosystem, AI Observatory)
caveats: A volunteer collective with no disclosed core funding, and some leads are doctoral researchers, so its continuity is uncertain. The roster marked its status as unclear, but its site shows new work in late 2025 and 2026. Its outputs are explicitly not legal advice.
tag_notes: Home law/law_sts: civil-society auditing of datasets' licences, consent and attribution backed by legal analysis (H1, method over topic). Economics (power concentration in open-model markets) and democracy (provenance, knowledge commons) are secondary. Ring adjacent (kept): a sustained AI audit programme since 2023 framed around transparency, consent and concentration, not safety or catastrophe. Transfer into_institutions (J3): evidence and calls for universal data-provenance standards aimed at policymakers, courts and developers. Org type network: a volunteer collective of 50+ contributors across institutions, coordinated through the MIT Media Lab. Framing structural: decline of the data commons and concentration of power. Status set to active from the roster's 'unclear' on the strength of the Dec 2025 paper and the 2026 AI Observatory preprint.

name: Data Nutrition Project (DNP)
summary: A US nonprofit, begun in 2018 as a Harvard–MIT Assembly fellowship project and an independent 501(c)(3) since 2021, that makes the Dataset Nutrition Label. The label is a standardised summary of a dataset's provenance, intended uses, cleaning, ethical review, subpopulation coverage and known risks, meant to be read before a model is trained on it. DNP builds and certifies labels for clients (for example the 2024 ISIC dermatology dataset), consults on data governance and trains organisations on AI from a sociotechnical perspective; in August 2025 it co-hosted a Public AI Summit with the AI Pedagogy Project.
why_it_matters: It applies the logic of consumer-protection labelling, together with design research from Harvard's metaLAB, to AI training data. It is a working example of a documentation standard used as a governance tool before models are built.

key_work.title: Dataset Nutrition Label (third generation)
Quality Measures for Humanitarian Data (with UN OCHA Centre for Humanitarian Data)
CLeAR Documentation Framework for AI transparency
Public AI Summit (co-hosted with the AI Pedagogy Project)

people: Sarah Newman (Research Lead; Director of Art & Education, metaLAB at Harvard)
funding: Grants and awards including New Media Ventures (2024), a Mozilla Foundation infrastructure grant (2023) and a Burroughs Wellcome Fund Innovation in Regulatory Science award (2023, with Memorial Sloan Kettering). It also offers paid labelling and consulting services.
status_evidence: 13-14 Aug 2025: co-hosted the Public AI Summit; website updated Oct 2025.
engage: Request a Dataset Nutrition Label, data-governance consulting or training
Public AI Summit (Aug 2025, co-hosted with the AI Pedagogy Project)
Donations through the website
caveats: Little dated public activity after August 2025. The team is small and remote, with several part-time collaborators based at Harvard's metaLAB. Its focus is dataset quality and bias rather than wider AI-safety questions.
tag_notes: Home safety/safety_engineering: its main product is a documentation and certification standard for datasets (labels as standards, modelled on food labelling). Arts is secondary for its design-research practice with Harvard's metaLAB (Prix Ars Electronica award, 2022). Ring adjacent (kept): sustained dataset-documentation work since 2018 framed around bias, equity and data quality, not safety or catastrophe. Transfer into_institutions (J3): a labelling standard and documentation framework (CLeAR) that organisations adopt; it touches training data but governs practice rather than changing models. Framing present_harms: its mission is equity, justice and integrity, with bias mitigation as the stated aim.

name: Finance Watch
summary: A Brussels-based public-interest association (AISBL), set up in 2011 after a cross-party petition by MEPs, that argues for the public interest in EU financial regulation as a counterweight to the financial-industry lobby. Since 2024 its digital-finance team has produced a line of reports and consultation responses on AI in finance. They argue that opaque AI models conflict with the principles of accountability, responsibility and transparency that financial regulation relies on, and they ask for the AI Act to cover all financial services and for the AI Liability Directive to be brought back.
why_it_matters: Finance has decades of practice in supervising opaque, automated decision models: model-risk management, named accountability, systemic-risk analysis. Finance Watch carries that practice into AI governance, and it flags the concentration of AI model providers as a financial-stability risk. Mainstream AI policy rarely draws on this regulatory template.

key_work.title: Artificial intelligence in finance: how to trust a black box?
Protecting EU consumers in the age of AI-driven retail finance
Consultation response: robust consumer protection standards are needed for the use of AI in the insurance sector
Consultation response: the growth of AI in finance demands appropriate supervision and regulation

people: Thierry Philipponnat (author of the 2025 AI report; former Chief Economist)
funding: 2025 income was EUR 2.91m. About 64% came from foundation grants, the largest from Quadrature Climate Foundation (EUR 459k) and ClimateWorks (EUR 339k), and about 35% from an EU DG FISMA operating grant (EUR 1.02m). It accepts no money from the financial industry.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: report on dark patterns and addictive design in digital finance; Mar 2026: Annual Report 2025 published. Last AI-specific output: July 2025 report on AI-driven retail finance.
engage: Staff roles are advertised at https://www.finance-watch.org/work-for-us/
Individuals and civil-society organisations independent of the financial sector can become members
caveats: AI is one strand among many: most of its work is on sustainable finance, banking and retail finance. It has published nothing specifically on AI since July 2025, and the author of the 2025 AI report has since left. Its frame is consumer protection and regulatory accountability, not catastrophic AI risk.
tag_notes: Home: economics. Its method is public-interest financial-regulation analysis and counter-lobbying (H1), with secondary law for the liability and consumer-protection proposals (B9). MISFIT: there is no sub-tradition for financial regulation and supervision; econ_power is the closest, given its counter-lobby identity and its concern about AI concentration risk. Ring: adjacent. A 2024-25 publication line (two reports, two consultation responses) on AI's effects on consumers and supervision, with no catastrophic or alignment framing (E3). Transfer: into_institutions. Its outputs are regulatory designs for the European Commission and the supervisors: AI Act scope, the AI Liability Directive, supervisory capacity (J3).

name: Soka Gakkai International (SGI)
summary: A worldwide lay Buddhist movement in the Nichiren tradition, founded in 1975 and based in Tokyo. Peace and disarmament advocacy at the UN is a large part of its work. Its AI work is a standing campaign against autonomous weapons: it joined the Stop Killer Robots coalition in 2018 and has taken part in UN First Committee meetings and the 2024 Vienna conference on autonomous weapons. It also made an exhibition, 'Automated by Design', on digital dehumanisation. In July 2026, ahead of the CCW Seventh Review Conference, its Global Perspectives Committee called for an urgent international legal framework on autonomous weapons, a ban on systems that target humans, and meaningful human control. The same month it co-supported the Vatican-hosted Global Nobel Laureates Assembly on AI, nuclear and autonomous weapons, which ended with the Rome Declaration.
why_it_matters: It brings a Buddhist dignity-of-life ethic and a mass lay membership to the treaty campaign on autonomous weapons. It shows how a faith community can carry an AI red line (no machine decisions over life and death) into multilateral disarmament processes alongside its nuclear-abolition work.

key_work.title: SGI Statement: Autonomous Weapons Systems: Ensuring Human Control Based on Respect for the Dignity of Life
Co-supporter of, and speaker at, the Global Nobel Laureates Assembly on AI, nuclear and autonomous weapons (Rome)
Joined the Stop Killer Robots coalition; 'Stopping Killer Robots' focus area

people: Yoshiyuki Nagaoka (Executive Director, Office of Public Affairs, Soka Gakkai)
funding: Member donations and investments, according to Wikipedia. National organisations raise their own funds. No AI-specific budget is published.
status_evidence: 23 Jul 2026: Global Perspectives Committee statement on autonomous weapons ahead of the CCW Seventh Review Conference; 15 Jul 2026: spoke at the Global Nobel Laureates Assembly session on faith, AI and nuclear weapons.
engage: Its AI advocacy runs through the Stop Killer Robots coalition, which organisations can join
Local SGI community centres in many countries (not AI-specific)
caveats: Its AI work is limited to autonomous weapons and military AI. Its claim of 12 million members is disputed by scholars. Soka Gakkai has close historic ties to Japan's Komeito party, and critics question how far its social and cultural projects serve recruitment (Wikipedia flags the article's neutrality). The Toda Peace Institute, which SGI founded, is a separate roster entry.
tag_notes: Home: religion. A Buddhist lay federation speaking for its tradition and members (B1, H3). Secondary peace, because the AI work is disarmament advocacy; B11 sends religious-founded peace research to Peace, but that is Toda, not SGI itself. Ring: adjacent. A standing focus area since 2018, with UN and CCW activity in 2024-26. It frames the issue as human dignity and human control rather than catastrophic AI risk (E3), though the AI-nuclear Rome Declaration brings it near bridge. Transfer: into_institutions. Its main output is advocacy for a binding treaty and a meaningful-human-control norm (J3). Framing is present_harms, from 'life and death decisions should never be delegated to machines'; structural (digital dehumanisation) is a close alternative. Hubs left empty: its local centres in London, Berlin and Paris do no AI work.

name: Kumagai Lab, Institute for the Future of Human Society, Kyoto University (BuddhaBot and Buddharoid)
summary: Professor Seiji Kumagai's group at Kyoto University's Institute for the Future of Human Society (IFOHS) builds AI from religious traditions, working with the Kyoto start-ups Teraverse and XNOVA. It released BuddhaBot, a Buddhist dialogue AI grounded in scripture, in 2021, and later added AR apps, a Protestant 'Catechism Bot' (covered by the media in December 2025) and, in February 2026, Buddharoid. Buddharoid is a Unitree G1 humanoid running BuddhaBot, unveiled at Shoren-in temple, Kyoto. The team says it holds ongoing ELSI discussions on the benefits and risks of giving Buddhist AI a body, and plans further 'Traditional Knowledge Tech' bots representing philosophers and saints.
why_it_matters: It is a long-running case of scholars of a living religious tradition building AI with values built in: scripture-grounded dialogue models and an embodied 'robot monk'. Along the way they have to decide what an AI may say and do in religious roles. That makes it a concrete test bed for tradition-specific alignment targets and their ethical governance, and a contrast to positions such as Yaqeen's that AI should not issue religious rulings.

key_work.title: BuddhaBot, a Buddhist dialogue AI
Protestant Catechism Bot
Buddharoid: Buddhist AI humanoid robot unveiled at Shoren-in temple

status_evidence: 25-26 Feb 2026: Buddharoid unveiled at Shoren-in, Kyoto (ITmedia, FPCJ release); 24 Mar 2026: IFOHS news on international coverage.
caveats: The work is done with commercial partners, and much of its public record is press coverage. The ELSI discussions are mentioned but I found no published output from them. Whether AI should give religious guidance is contested. The 2021 founding year is that of BuddhaBot's release, not of the institute. Its funding is not disclosed.
tag_notes: Home: religion. Its bots carry a tradition's scriptures and teachings to believers and temples, now across Buddhist and Protestant texts, so B1 places it in Religion rather than Contemplative: these are not artefacts built from meditative insight. rel_buddhist matches its main output. Ring: adjacent. AI building has been sustained since 2021, with ELSI language but no safety, catastrophic-risk or alignment framing (E3). Transfer: into_model. Its primary output is AI systems trained on and constrained by religious texts (J1).

name: World Institute for Science, Religion and Culture (WISR; formerly the Center for Christogenesis)
summary: An online educational institute founded in 2016 by the Franciscan theologian Ilia Delio as the Center for Christogenesis, and renamed WISR in July 2026. It works in the tradition of Teilhard de Chardin and wants to integrate science, religion and culture 'in service of a world in evolutionary transition'. Its mission now includes cultivating 'a new way of knowing for an AI age'. AI runs through its 2025-26 output: Delio's essays, Hunger for Wholeness podcast episodes with Robert Geraci on apocalyptic AI and a 'global mind', and paid online events on Teilhard and AI, interfaith perspectives on AI, and Pope Leo's AI encyclical Magnifica Humanitas.
why_it_matters: It treats AI as a question about collective consciousness, personhood and interiority rather than a technical control problem. This evolutionary and process frame is close to the metamodern milieu int/a comes from, and it reaches a contemplative Christian audience that mainstream AI safety does not.

key_work.title: Intelligence Was Never the Point: Interior to Interiority in the Age of AI (Ilia Delio)
AI and the Pope: Who Has the Last Word? (online panel on Magnifica Humanitas)
Hunger for Wholeness podcast: Apocalyptic AI and the Stories Technology Tells, with Robert Geraci
Re-Enchanting the Earth: Why AI Needs Religion (book by Ilia Delio)

people: Ilia Delio OSF (founder and Executive Director)
funding: Donations, plus paid webinars ($15-30), courses ($45) and conferences ($95-140). Amounts are not published.
status_evidence: Aug 2026: Delio essay on AI and interiority; 30 Jul 2026: online panel on Magnifica Humanitas; 10th-anniversary conference at Villanova scheduled for 9-11 Nov 2026.
engage: Monthly paid online webinars, for example on 15 Oct 2026
10th-anniversary conference 'Love, Conflict, and an Unfolding Universe', Villanova University, 9-11 Nov 2026
Online courses and recordings
Christophany groups (community formation circles)
caveats: Renamed in July 2026 from the Center for Christogenesis, with the same founder and mission, so search under both names. Delio retired from her Villanova chair in 2026. AI is one theme among science-religion topics. Its frame is theological and evolutionary; it does not engage with technical alignment or catastrophic-risk analysis. Its legal base is not stated on the site: it describes itself as an online educational resource, and it holds events at Villanova.
tag_notes: Home: contemplative. B1 places Teilhardian bodies in Contemplative explicitly; sub-tradition cont_integral, with secondary religion for its Catholic and Franciscan theology. Ring: adjacent. A sustained 2025-26 line of essays, podcasts and events on AI, framed around personhood and consciousness, not safety or catastrophic risk (E3). Transfer: convening. It brings its own contemplative-Christian community into the AI conversation through education and media (J5). Status changed because of the July 2026 rename.

name: International Association of Jesuit Universities (IAJU): Artificial Intelligence Task Force
summary: IAJU is the Rome-based coordinating body for Jesuit higher education, founded in 2018 and made up of six regional associations. AI is one of its strategic priorities. A seven-member task force, chaired by Renato Cerqueira from Brazil, runs it. The task force keeps a curated knowledge hub of cases and guidelines, holds a virtual community of practice for faculty, staff and students, and organises pilot projects and working groups on ethical AI, academic integrity, accessibility, mental health and teaching. It explicitly links AI adoption to Ignatian discernment, cura personalis and the magis.
why_it_matters: It is a global channel into Jesuit universities that is building a shared practice for AI grounded in Ignatian discernment, a codified spiritual method for making choices. That makes it an example of a religious tradition's practice applied to institutional technology decisions, and a possible route for bringing questions about AI going well into university formation.

key_work.title: AI Task Force: knowledge hub, community of practice and working groups
The Impact of AI on the Educational Transformation of Universities (UNIJES faculty survey, published by IAJU)
The AI Frontier and the Jesuit Universities (report on the GRAJU inaugural symposium, Manila)

people: Brian Patrick Green (member, AI Task Force)
Joseph Christie SJ (President, IAJU Board of Governors; Secretariat for Higher Education)
status_evidence: May 2026: IAJU published UNIJES's survey of 681 faculty on generative AI; Mar 2026: IAJU reported on the GRAJU symposium 'The AI Frontier and the Distinctives of Global Jesuit Higher Education'.
engage: Virtual community of practice for faculty, staff and students at Jesuit institutions
caveats: The task force is mostly about adopting AI in teaching, research and administration, which sits at the edge of scope. Its frame is education and human dignity, not catastrophic risk. The March 2026 Manila symposium was run by the Global Research Alliance of Jesuit Universities (GRAJU, founded 2025), not by the task force, and the July 2026 Florence conference on AI and Jesuit formation was run by the Society of Jesus. The draft attributed both to the task force. The year the task force was set up and its budget are not published. The chair's name is spelled 'Cerqueria' on the IAJU site.
tag_notes: Home: religion. A Catholic, Jesuit network serving its own institutions (H3), framed by Ignatian spirituality; sub-tradition rel_christian. Ring: adjacent. A standing AI priority with a task force and community of practice in 2025-26, focused on AI's effects on education and formation, with no safety or catastrophic framing (E3). Transfer: convening. It brings Jesuit universities into shared reflection and practice on AI (J5). org_type programme, because the unit is a task force inside IAJU (A1, I).

name: America Media (America: The Jesuit Review)
summary: The media ministry of the US Jesuits, publishing America magazine since 1909 from New York, along with a website, newsletters and podcasts. In 2026 it covered AI steadily from the standpoint of Catholic social teaching. Examples are editor Sam Sawyer SJ's column arguing that the alignment problem is a moral question rather than a technical one, its Vatican correspondent's reporting on Pope Leo's remarks about AI catastrophe, and a subscriber webinar on the AI encyclical Magnifica Humanitas.
why_it_matters: It is one of the main English-language channels through which Pope Leo's teaching on AI, and debates about AI risk and alignment, reach a large Catholic readership. It reframes alignment as a question of morality and justice, which is a perspective technical AI safety seldom hears from.

key_work.title: How to worry about A.I. without despairing (Sam Sawyer SJ)
Pope Leo on AI risk at the in-flight press conference from France (Colleen Dulle)
Live Zoom panel on Magnifica Humanitas

funding: Owned and operated by the Jesuit provinces of the United States; also funded by subscriptions and donations.
status_evidence: 2 Oct 2026: Sawyer column on AI alignment and existential-risk worry; 28 Sep 2026: report on Pope Leo's AI remarks.
engage: Subscriber webinars, such as the 19 August 2026 Zoom panel on Magnifica Humanitas
caveats: It is journalism and opinion, not research. Its editor is sceptical of numerical extinction estimates and prefers moral language to 'alignment'. The draft suggested it might be bridge; I kept it adjacent because its AI coverage argues against the catastrophic-risk frame rather than adopting it. The Washington Post has described it as liberal-leaning. Events are for subscribers only. Staff size is estimated.
tag_notes: Home: religion. Faith media go with the community they serve (H3); secondary arts for its journalism. Ring: adjacent, unchanged. It runs a sustained 2026 line of AI coverage, but its main AI argument puts dignity and justice ahead of existential-risk framing, so it does not take up the catastrophic or alignment frame that bridge requires (E3). Transfer: convening. It informs its Catholic readership about AI (J5). Framing structural: Sawyer's dominant stake is the erosion of human dignity and justice. Present_harms is a close alternative.

name: Yaqeen Institute for Islamic Research
summary: A US Muslim research and education nonprofit founded in 2016 by Omar Suleiman and based in Irving, Texas. It publishes papers, videos and curricula on Islamic topics for a broad audience. Its one AI output so far is 'Toward an Islamic Ethics and Fiqh of Artificial Intelligence' (June 2026, updated September 2026). The paper argues for weighing AI's harms and benefits at the design stage, holds designers, deployers and users liable, and concludes that AI should not issue fatwas on its own, only assist scholars under oversight.
why_it_matters: It turns fiqh al-muwazanat, Islamic law's codified method for weighing harms against benefits, into a design-stage assessment of AI. It also gives a reasoned juristic position on AI in religious authority, and it reaches a very large Muslim audience that AI-safety debates do not.

key_work.title: Toward an Islamic Ethics and Fiqh of Artificial Intelligence (AbuTaleb, Alkiek, Hani, Ansari, Khan)

people: Mohamed AbuTaleb (lead author, AI ethics paper)
funding: Donor-funded 501(c)(3). Revenue was about $8.76m in 2023, according to Wikipedia.
status_evidence: 30 Sep 2026: updated its AI ethics and fiqh paper (first published 12 Jun 2026).
engage: Careers at https://yaqeeninstitute.org/careers
Paper proposals via 'Publish on Yaqeen'
caveats: Its AI engagement is a single paper; I found no other AI papers or programme. It has been criticised for publishing material against LGBTQ+ activism. Its position on AI fatwas is one juristic view among several in Muslim scholarship. Staff size is estimated.
tag_notes: Home: religion. An Islamic institute speaking to and for Muslims through fiqh and ethics (B1, H3); sub-tradition rel_islamic_jewish. Ring: potential. Its AI engagement is one 2026 paper with no standing programme (E2). Transferable method: fiqh al-muwazanat, a codified harm-benefit balancing jurisprudence, used as a design-stage AI assessment. Transfer: convening. The paper gives its own community an ethical framework, and recommends Muslim scholar consortia and verification habits (J5); protecting is a close alternative because of the ruling against AI fatwas.

name: Association des traducteurs littéraires de France (ATLF)
summary: The French association of literary translators, founded in 1973. Its members translate from more than 60 languages for publishing, the press, theatre and audiovisual work. Since 2022 it has campaigned against generative AI in translation. Its model publishing contract now commits publisher and translator not to use AI for the translation itself or when exploiting the rights (for example AI-narrated audiobooks), and lets the translator refuse the use of their work for AI training. It also issues joint statements, for example on the publisher Harlequin's move to AI translation in December 2025.
why_it_matters: It shows a profession governing AI from below through contracts: a standard clause on training-data opt-out and AI substitution, which members negotiate book by book. This is a working, copyable instrument for consent over training data, and one the AI-safety field rarely looks at.

key_work.title: Generative-AI clauses in the ATLF model translation contract
Deux ans de lutte contre l'IA (two years of campaigning against AI)
Harlequin passe à l'IA (joint statement with Collectif En chair et en os)
Response to the government report 'IA : notre ambition pour la France'

funding: Membership fees and a subsidy from the Centre national du livre (CNL); amounts not published on the site.
status_evidence: Apr 2026: new board elected with Cyril Laumonier as president; Dec 2025: joint statement on Harlequin's move to AI translation; Jul 2026: posts on festival appearances.
engage: Membership open to practising literary translators
Its model contract, AI clauses included, is published for any translator to use in negotiations
Staff recruitment announced February 2026 ('L'ATLF recrute !')
caveats: Its stance is refusal of AI in translation and protection of its members' rights, not engagement with AI safety. Sources give slightly different dates: a July 2024 ATLF article describes two AI clauses (articles 1.2 and 10) added to the model contract, while the clauses page refers to three clauses adopted in December 2024. Wikipedia still lists Corinna Gepner as president.
tag_notes: Home economics (H3, B9): a professional association of literary translators defending their work and pay against AI substitution, so it goes with organised labour; law is secondary for moral-rights and contract work. Ring adjacent: a sustained AI campaign since 2022 (contract clauses, joint positions, responses to government) about present harms to translators, with no catastrophic or 'going well' framing. Transfer protecting: the clauses exist to defend its members' work and rights, even though they also act as a governance instrument over training data (J4). Way of knowing is practice because the main output is a codified contract standard. Paris hub: offices at the Hôtel de Massa and regular events. Community engagement requires professional standing as a literary translator.

name: Collectif En chair et en os
summary: A volunteer collective of French translators, founded in September 2023, whose slogan is 'Oui à l'humain, non à l'IA' (yes to the human, no to AI). Its manifesto and Change.org petition ask publishers, studios and media not to use AI for translation or creative work, to tell the public when AI was used, and to deny public funding to AI-generated works; ATLF reported more than 15,000 signatures by mid-2024. In 2026 it held an 'anti-summit' in Lille (13 June) against the Hauts-de-France regional AI summit. With the translators' union Stef and IA-lerte générale it also co-organised an international translators' strike day on 30 September, with events in Aubervilliers and Lyon and support from groups in Spain, Italy, Germany, Switzerland and Portugal.
why_it_matters: It is organised refusal: workers whose jobs are already being automated deciding together whether, and how fast, AI enters their field. Its anti-summit linked AI to extraction, militarisation and labour, a systemic critique rarely heard in AI-safety venues.

key_work.title: Manifesto and petition 'Non à des traductions sans âme'
Anti-sommet de l'IA, Lille
International day of action for translators (strike), 30 September
Blog series 'IA et traduction'

funding: Volunteer-run; a support fund takes donations for its actions. No institutional funders found.
