status_evidence: Sep 2026: international translators' strike day on 30 September (programme posted 7 Sep 2026); Jun 2026: anti-summit on AI in Lille, report posted 3 Jul 2026.
engage: Sign the manifesto petition on Change.org
Attend its public events (Lille anti-summit, June 2026; strike-day workshops, September 2026)
Donate to the support fund for its actions
caveats: Its site names no spokespeople and gives no figures for membership. The collective rejects generative AI outright rather than seeking to shape it, so it is a counter-voice to the AI-safety field rather than a partner within it. Evidence comes mainly from its own site and from ATLF, which works with it.
tag_notes: Home economics (H3, B9): organised translators acting together against AI replacing their work (petition, strike, joint statements with a union); arts is secondary because its members are literary, film and game translators. Ring adjacent: sustained AI campaigning 2023-26 (manifesto, blog series, anti-summit, strike) framed around harms to workers and culture, not catastrophic risk. Transfer protecting: it defends translators and cultural work from AI substitution. Framing is present_harms rather than critical, because its critique serves an organising agenda (L). Paris hub left empty: events in Aubervilliers, but regular activity in Paris is not verified. Considered for the speed_of_wisdom badge as a slow-technology refusal stance, but not given, as it is a blanket refusal rather than discernment about pace.

name: Rising Voices (Global Voices)
summary: Rising Voices is the outreach initiative of Global Voices. It was founded in 2007 and supports digital activism in Indigenous, endangered and marginalised languages through microgrants, mentoring, regional networks and reporting. Since 2025 it has worked on AI with Indigenous language activists in Mexico. It co-organised an AI+Indigenous Languages Forum in Mexico City (March 2025: 47 activists, more than 20 languages). It then ran a hybrid peer-learning programme on AI accountability and Indigenous self-determination for 15 Mayan-language activists in Chiapas (online in April, in person on 5-7 May 2026), with First Languages AI Reality (FLAIR) and the Canada Research Chair in Digital Indigeneities. It also publishes reporting on AI's language gaps.
why_it_matters: It puts the question 'who decides if and how AI enters a language?' to the speakers themselves, and its Chiapas participants argued for pausing to reflect before adopting AI and against narratives of inevitability. That is a working model of community discernment about AI. The field mostly treats language coverage as a data gap to be filled, and has nothing like it.

key_work.title: AI+Indigenous Languages Forum, Mexico City
Artificial intelligence, accountability and Indigenous self-determination (hybrid programme, Chiapas)
Who decides if and how AI is used? Self-determination should be the priority, say Mayan activists from Chiapas
Africa has 2,000 languages. AI content moderation covers fewer than 20

people: Kiado Cruz (Zapotec communicator, facilitator of the AI programme)
Genner Llanes-Ortiz (Maya anthropologist, Canada Research Chair in Digital Indigeneities, facilitator)
funding: Started in 2007 with a Knight News Challenge award. The 2026 AI programme is supported by the W.K. Kellogg Foundation and the Pulitzer Center. The 2025 forum was also supported by the Embassy of Canada in Mexico, the Wikimedia Foundation and the Centro Cultural de España en México.
status_evidence: Jul 2026: report on the Chiapas AI accountability workshop (held 5-7 May 2026); May 2026: Mayan Languages Digital Activism Summit, Chiapas.
engage: Open calls for its peer-learning programmes (the 2026 AI programme was for up to 15 Indigenous activists in Chiapas)
Public events such as the Mayan Languages Digital Activism Summit (Chiapas, May 2026)
Contribute writing to the Rising Voices and Global Voices blogs
caveats: The AI work so far is concentrated in Mexico and depends on project funding (Kellogg, Pulitzer Center). Rising Voices is a programme of Global Voices, which is not itself Indigenous-led; the AI programme was facilitated by Indigenous researchers and communicators.
tag_notes: Home indigenous (B8): the AI work rests on Indigenous self-determination and data sovereignty and is run with Indigenous facilitators; arts is secondary for Global Voices' citizen-media method. Ring adjacent: a sustained AI line in 2025-26 (forum, funded peer-learning programme, reporting) about rights and self-determination, with no catastrophic-risk framing. Transfer convening (J5): its main purpose is AI literacy and dialogue within Indigenous language communities, so that they can decide for themselves; protecting is a close alternative. Region global because Global Voices is a distributed network; standpoint majority_world because the programme is centred on and led from Mexico's Indigenous communities. Badge speed_of_wisdom: the 2026 programme explicitly argued for pausing before adoption and against inevitability narratives. MISFIT: language-rights activism has no sector of its own.

name: Welsh Language Commissioner (Comisiynydd y Gymraeg)
summary: The statutory regulator for the Welsh language, created under the Welsh Language (Wales) Measure 2011 and operating since April 2012. It enforces Welsh language standards on public bodies and other organisations in Wales. In July 2025 it published a regulatory policy statement on AI. Organisations that use AI to deliver services must still meet their Welsh-language duties, test AI systems specifically in Welsh and be transparent about how those systems work. They must also follow principles of linguistic fairness, accuracy and naturalness of language, and data security. The Commissioner calls this a precautionary approach.
why_it_matters: It is a working template for holding AI deployment to a minority-language rights regime. It works through existing statutory duties rather than new AI law, which shows how a rights regulator can extend its remit to AI without waiting for AI-specific legislation.

key_work.title: Artificial intelligence and the Welsh language: the Welsh Language Commissioner's regulatory policy statement
Managing AI within Welsh language standards (announcement and National Eisteddfod panel)
Response to inquiry on artificial intelligence and the Welsh economy

people: Efa Gruffudd Jones (Welsh Language Commissioner, since 2023)
funding: Funded by the Welsh Government; about 39 full-time-equivalent staff in 2024-25.
status_evidence: Aug 2025: announced its AI policy and discussed it at a panel at the National Eisteddfod; Jul 2025: AI regulatory policy statement published.
caveats: The AI policy is a single regulatory statement (July 2025) with no announced follow-up found, though it binds every organisation subject to Welsh language standards. The roster placed it in Cardiff; the headquarters is in Caernarfon.
tag_notes: Home law (H1): its AI output applies statutory minority-language rights to AI deployment. Ring adjacent: a standing regulatory policy on AI (2025), plus earlier evidence to an inquiry on AI and the Welsh economy, focused on language rights without safety or catastrophic-risk framing. Transfer protecting: the statement exists to defend Welsh speakers' rights, though it also serves as a governance template (the J3/J4 boundary is decided by its primary purpose). Problems include assurance because it requires Welsh-specific testing of AI systems. Org type public (I: statutory commissioner). MISFIT: language regulation and planning has no sector; law is the closest.

name: Språkrådet (Language Council of Norway)
summary: Norway's state language agency under the Ministry of Culture, established in 2005. It manages the official Bokmål and Nynorsk written standards and oversees state bodies' compliance with the Language Act 2021. Its language technology and AI work does four things. It sets language requirements for public-sector digital products and their procurement, shares Bokmål and Nynorsk language data for building models, advises schools and agencies on AI writing tools, and tests AI output; a September 2026 evaluation found that at least one in three machine-translated Nynorsk sentences needed correcting. In 2026 it also set quality requirements for Nordic language models and warned against Norway's dependence on US AI providers.
why_it_matters: It treats AI as a question of linguistic sovereignty and public-sector quality assurance for a small language and its minority written standard, and it acts on models' training data and outputs. It gives the field a state-level example of protecting a language community from homogenising AI.

key_work.title: Language requirements for digital solutions (Krav til språk i digitale løysingar)
Er maskin-nynorsken god nok? (evaluation of machine and AI translation into Nynorsk)
Kunstig intelligens og ugunstig avhengighet (AI and unhealthy dependence)
Norden sammen for bedre språkmodeller (requirements for Nordic language models)

funding: State agency funded through the Ministry of Culture and Equality (Kultur- og likestillingsdepartementet); 47 employees in 2025.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: published an evaluation of machine-translated Nynorsk (17 Sep) and requirements for Nordic language models (14 Sep).
engage: Organisations can contribute Bokmål and Nynorsk language data through its 'Bidra med data' page
Its guidance on AI writing tools for schools and the public sector is publicly available
caveats: Åse Wetås, director since 2015, left in 2026; Nina Teigland is acting director. Much of the AI work is guidance and advocacy; the binding force comes from the Language Act, which applies to state bodies.
tag_notes: Home law (H1): its AI work applies language law (Language Act 2021) and language planning to AI products and procurement. Ring adjacent: a standing language technology and AI programme with a steady stream of AI publications 2025-26 (tests, requirements, op-eds), framed around language quality and sovereignty, not catastrophic risk. Transfer protecting: the requirements and tests exist to protect Norwegian and Nynorsk users; into_model is a close second, given its language-data sharing and requirements on language models. Framing structural: it stresses the gradual weakening of a small language and dependence on foreign providers. Org type public (I). MISFIT: linguistics and language planning have no sector; law is the closest.

name: SIL Global
summary: SIL Global (formerly SIL International, originally the Summer Institute of Linguistics, founded in 1934) is a faith-based organisation working with minority-language communities on field linguistics, literacy and Bible translation. Its AI and NLP team builds tools and datasets for low-resource languages. These include projects such as Serval and Scripture Forge, which are used for machine-assisted Scripture translation, and the Bloom multimodal datasets in more than 300 languages, released for research. In April 2024 it published an AI ethics statement built on being 'Just, Kind, Humble', committing to informed consent for language data, benefit and self-determination for language communities, and not personifying AI.
why_it_matters: It has long field experience of collecting language data with minority communities, and a written consent and community-benefit protocol for using that data in AI. Both bear on how developers handle low-resource-language data. Its missionary purpose and history mean the protocol should be read critically rather than adopted wholesale.

key_work.title: AI Ethics Statement
Bloom Library: Multimodal Datasets in 300+ Languages (EMNLP 2022)
SIL AI and NLP projects (Serval, Scripture Forge, AQuA and others)

people: Jon Hirst (chief innovation officer; on the AI ethics task force, 2024)
Joshua Nemecek (data scientist leading AI development, 2024)
funding: Donor-funded faith-based nonprofit. Its AI work won an Amazon Web Services IMAGINE Grant in 2022. Overall budget not checked.
status_evidence: Oct 2026: active commits to its Serval and SILNLP machine-translation repositories on GitHub; May 2025: new executive director appointed.
engage: Its AI and NLP code (Serval, SILNLP) is open source on GitHub
The Bloom and eBible datasets are available for research
caveats: Most of its AI work is applied NLP serving Bible translation, close to an 'AI for good' application. Its relevance here rests on its work on linguistic diversity in AI and on its consent protocol. SIL's missionary work in Indigenous communities has drawn long-standing criticism from anthropologists and some Indigenous organisations. The roster dated the ethics statement to about 2022-23; SIL announced it in April 2024. The executive director is based in Nairobi, though the legal base is Dallas.
tag_notes: Home religion (H3): a Christian mission organisation whose AI work serves Scripture access and whose ethics statement draws on 'Just, Kind, Humble' (Micah 6:8). Field linguistics, its working method, has no sector (MISFIT). Ring changed from potential to adjacent (E2/E3): it runs a standing AI and NLP programme (eight projects, datasets, papers, an ethics statement, active code in 2026) focused on bringing minority languages into AI, without safety framing. Transfer into_model: its datasets and machine-translation systems change what AI systems cover. Framing flourishing, after its own language of 'people flourishing in community' and 'digital flourishing'. Standpoint neither, by its Dallas legal base, despite a Nairobi-based executive director and largely Majority-World work.

name: Foundation for Endangered Languages (FEL)
summary: A UK charity, founded in 1996, that supports the documentation, protection and promotion of endangered languages. It does this through small grants of about US$1,000, an annual conference with published proceedings, and the newsletter Ogmios. Its 30th conference, held with INALCO in Paris on 3-5 November 2026, is titled 'Endangered Languages and Innovative Technologies: Documentation, Processing and Revitalisation'. The theme statement notes that digital systems are built mostly on data from a few dominant languages, and calls for tools developed with language communities that respect their data sovereignty.
why_it_matters: It connects scholars and community language workers, many from the Majority World, who know how to document and revitalise languages with consent. Their documentation ethics is a ready method for how AI builders should collect and use minority-language data.

Ring potential (E2): no standing AI programme, only the 2026 conference on language technologies. Transferable method: consent-based, community-led documentation and revitalisation practice for minority-language data, applicable to how AI developers collect low-resource-language data. Transfer convening, not none_yet, because the 2026 conference brings its community into the technology conversation. The Paris conference is a one-off, so no hub. Partner is included because it has no AI programme.

name: Cambridge Language Sciences Interdisciplinary Research Centre
summary: A University of Cambridge Interdisciplinary Research Centre: a virtual network linking language researchers in linguistics, psychology, neuroscience, computer science, education and Cambridge University Press & Assessment. It awards small incubator and workshop grants. From 2024 to 30 September 2026 it ran the AI@Cam-funded project 'Improving language equity and inclusion through AI', which paid for workshops and symposia on AI in aphasia recovery, human-AI collaboration in language assessment, computational methods for language-learning technology, and the conceptual blind spots of automated hate-speech detection.
why_it_matters: It brings psycholinguistic, clinical and sociolinguistic methods for asking whose speech and language AI systems handle well or badly: people with aphasia or hearing loss, language learners, speakers of non-standard varieties. Mainstream AI evaluation rarely measures this.

Ring changed from potential to adjacent: a two-year funded AI@Cam project with repeated workshops in 2024-26 is a sustained programme (E2), framed around equity and inclusion, not safety (E3). Transfer: the work studies and defends the people language science serves (people with aphasia or hearing loss, learners, minority speakers), so Protecting (J4).

name: Humans, Machines, Language (HuMaLa), BAAL Special Interest Group
summary: A special interest group of the British Association for Applied Linguistics, founded in March 2024 as successor to the EU COST network 'Language In The Human-Machine Era' (LITHME, 2020-24). It studies how language technologies, from AI assistants and machine translation to conversational agents and AR/VR, change language teaching, policy, translation, intercultural communication and literacies. Membership is free through a JISCMail list, and an elected committee runs annual events: a conference in Granada (June 2025), a machine-translation and GenAI literacy event in Granada (2-3 June 2026), and the HUMIC workshop on conversational AI at the University of Surrey (16 June 2026).
why_it_matters: It brings sociolinguistics, translation studies and intercultural pragmatics to the question of how LLMs and conversational agents reshape human language, rapport and translators' work. The AI-safety field rarely looks at AI's effects on human communication.

name: Royal Statistical Society (RSS): AI Task Force
summary: The RSS is the UK's learned society and professional body for statistics, founded in 1834 and based in London. Its AI Task Force, formed in June 2024 and chaired by Donna Phillips, plans the society's AI work through subgroups on communications, policy and ethics, evaluation of AI models, and practitioners. In 2026 it published 'AI is Statistics' (2 March) and 'AI regulation needs statistics' (8 July). The papers argue that regulating AI is largely a matter of statistically evaluating models in deployment, through uncertainty quantification, subgroup analysis and testing under distribution shift, and the RSS has followed up with sector regulators in health, education and finance.
why_it_matters: It offers an established discipline of inference, uncertainty and experimental design as the basis for evaluating and overseeing AI, and a professional community that could do that work. AI evaluation is often short on this kind of statistical rigour.

tag_notes: Home: statistics (inference, uncertainty quantification, experimental design) applied to AI evaluation, placed under Formal; MISFIT: no statistics sub-tradition, so formal_maths is the nearest. Ring kept as bridge (E): a standing task force since June 2024 with a subgroup on evaluating AI models and 2026 papers explicitly about safe use and regulatory evaluation (E3), though borderline with adjacent because the focus is sector regulation. Transfer: its papers offer regulators a common statistical framework for evaluating AI, so Into institutions (J3); the education role reflects public statistical-literacy work (William Guy lectures, schools).

name: American Statistical Association (ASA)
summary: The US professional society for statisticians, founded in Boston in 1839 and based in Alexandria, Virginia. Its board issued a statement on the role of statistics in data science and AI (August 2023) and the 'Statement on Ethical AI Principles for Statistical Practitioners' (8 October 2024). The 2024 statement sets trustworthiness as the overall goal, with accountability, transparency and fairness as principles, and says practitioners should be able to audit, monitor and evaluate AI and make sure its risks are assessed and mitigated. The ASA also co-sponsors the Annual Symposium on Risks and Opportunities of AI in Pharmaceutical Medicine, held since 2022; the 2026 edition at UC Berkeley (13-14 October) is themed on agentic AI in drug development.
why_it_matters: It holds codified professional ethics and the validation, auditing and model-governance methods that AI evaluation and assurance could borrow. Its members already audit models in regulated industries such as pharmaceuticals.

The ASA site shows no standing AI task force, so the ring sits between adjacent and potential. Scale reflects its membership; staff numbers were not checked.
tag_notes: Home: statistical practice and professional ethics (auditing, validation, model governance), placed in Formal as a professional body serving statisticians (H3); MISFIT: no statistics sub-tradition. Ring changed from adjacent to potential (E2): the annual symposium is about applying AI in drug development (AI-for-health application, excluded as qualifying work), so its engagement with AI going well is two board statements (2023, 2024), which is light. Transferable method: statistical validation, auditing and model-governance practice that its members already use in regulated industries. Transfer: the ethics statement informs its own practitioners, so Convening (J5); fairness is a stated principle, hence justice as secondary problem.

name: Centre for AI Measurement, National Physical Laboratory (NPL)
summary: A national centre led by NPL, the UK's National Metrology Institute, to develop the measurement science for testing, evaluating, validating, verifying and monitoring AI systems, including defining what is measured and quantifying uncertainty. It has three pillars (measurement science and research; applied assurance and industry support; community building) and is part of the UK government's programme to grow a third-party AI assurance market, following DSIT's Trusted Third-Party AI Assurance Roadmap (Sept 2025). It ran a call for evidence on AI testing, evaluation and assurance from 1 September to 9 October 2026 and launches officially at Teddington on 10 November 2026. NPL also co-leads the UK AI Standards Hub with BSI (it was set up in 2022 with the Alan Turing Institute; UKAS has since joined as a partner).
why_it_matters: It brings metrology's discipline of traceability, uncertainty quantification and comparability to AI evaluation, where results are often hard to reproduce or compare. As a national laboratory it can turn evaluation practice into good-practice guides and pre-standards.

Ring kept as bridge (E): an old institution with a standing, government-backed AI assurance centre framed around safe and trustworthy AI (E3, 'old institutions with new AI-safety programmes are bridge'). Transfer: it supplies testing methods, standards and assurance infrastructure for governing AI, so Into institutions (J3). Framing set to present_harms as the nearest key for reliability of deployed systems; the centre's own language is 'trust' and 'confidence'. London hub because Teddington is in Greater London.

name: PTB Competence Centre AI and Metrology (AI-Met)
summary: A competence centre set up on 17 January 2025 at the Physikalisch-Technische Bundesanstalt (PTB), Germany's national metrology institute. It pulls together PTB's AI work and acts as its contact point, coordinated by Maik Liebl in department 9.4 (Metrology for the Digital Transformation) at PTB's Berlin institute. With Fraunhofer IAIS and DIN it led DIN SPEC 92007 (June 2026), general requirements for AI test datasets, which responds to the AI Act's Article 15 call for benchmarks; it also took part in DIN SPEC 92006 on requirements for AI test tools (Feb 2026). With Argentina's INTI it published U-TraCE (Jan 2026), a conformal-prediction method that gives a formal upper bound on a black-box model's error probability, and it hosted the MAITRE 2025 workshop in Berlin.
why_it_matters: It applies metrology's reference standards, traceable uncertainty and conformity assessment to AI benchmarks and test data. The EU AI Act needs this measurement infrastructure, and most AI-safety evaluation lacks it.

name: IEEE Reliability Society TRUE AI Initiative
summary: A cross-disciplinary initiative of the IEEE Reliability Society on Trustworthy, Robust, Understandable and Explainable (TRUE) AI for reliability-critical, safety-critical and mission-critical systems, announced around January 2026. It is chaired by Ruolin Zhou, with George Pallis as co-chair. Its focus areas include AI for reliability assessment and prognostics, robust and fault-tolerant ML, verification, validation and assurance of AI models, secure and self-recovering AI, human-AI teaming, and standards and metrics for AI reliability. Planned outputs are workshops and tutorials at IEEE conferences, a roadmap, position papers, a TRUE AI column in Reliability Magazine and special issues of IEEE Transactions on Reliability.
why_it_matters: It links AI assurance to reliability engineering's long practice of failure analysis, prognostics and fault tolerance in aerospace, defence, energy and healthcare, and to IEEE's standards machinery.

Framing present_harms is the nearest key for dependable deployed systems.

name: Nishan Forum on World Civilizations (Nishan World Center for Confucian Studies)
summary: A state-backed international forum on dialogue between civilisations, held near Qufu, Shandong (Confucius's birthplace) since 2010. The Nishan World Center for Confucian Studies organises it with Chinese central and provincial government bodies. AI became one of six sub-topics in 2025 (the 11th forum, July 2025, 'the development of AI and the trajectory of human civilisation') and again in late September 2026 ('Artificial Intelligence and Universal Harmony', overall theme 'Civilization · Order · Justice', 340+ guests from 40+ countries). There, Confucian and Daoist scholars and Tsinghua's Xue Lan argued for Confucian ethics as a basis for responsible AI and global AI governance.
why_it_matters: It is the main recurring venue where Confucian and Daoist scholars, Chinese officials and foreign academics discuss AI ethics and governance together. That makes it a window on how Chinese relational ethics (ren, 'do not impose on others what you do not desire') is being put forward as an input to global AI norms, and a possible channel for East-West dialogue on what AI should serve.

The forum's own pages give different dates for the 2026 edition (28-29 or 29-30 Sep), and the edition numbering after the 11th (2025) is unclear.
tag_notes: Home: the AI sessions apply Confucian (and some Daoist) philosophy to technology and civilisation ('technology is the vessel, civilisation is the way'), so this is Chinese philosophy of technology (phil_technology). Religion is secondary for the Daoist and Confucian-institution participants and the forum's interreligious history. Ring changed from potential to adjacent under E(2)/(3): AI was a named sub-topic in two consecutive editions (Jul 2025, Sep 2026), which counts as repeated convening, and the framing is civilisational harmony and ethics, not catastrophic risk. It is borderline potential, since AI is one of six sub-topics. Transfer: convening, because the forum's primary purpose is bringing its Confucian-studies community and invited guests into the AI conversation (J5). Its stated aim of supplying 'Confucian value guidance' for global AI governance is aspirational, with no instrument yet. Transferable method: Confucian relational ethics and civilisational dialogue applied to AI governance norms. Standpoint is Neither per O (China).

name: European Association for the Study of Science and Technology (EASST)
summary: Europe's learned society for science and technology studies (STS), founded in 1981 and registered as an association in the Netherlands. It holds a biennial conference (jointly with 4S every four years), publishes the open-access EASST Review and, with the Finnish STS association, the journal Science & Technology Studies, and gives awards and small EASST Fund grants. EASST2026 (Kraków, 8-11 Sept 2026, 'More Than Now: Exploring resilient futures') had at least 13 AI panels, including 'The politics of machine learning (ML) evaluation', 'Ground truths and the epistemology of AI' and 'AI cold war and AI nationalism between signals, sovereignty, and imagination'.
why_it_matters: STS has well-developed methods for studying how evaluations, benchmarks, 'ground truth' and stories about the future actually work in practice. AI safety depends on all of these and rarely examines them. EASST is the European entry point to the people who use those methods.

name: Society for Social Studies of Science (4S)
summary: The main international learned society for science and technology studies, founded in 1975 and incorporated as a 501(c)(3) nonprofit in Virginia. It publishes Science, Technology, & Human Values and the open-access journal Engaging Science, Technology, and Society, runs the Backchannels blog, prizes and small Global Outreach grants, and holds an annual meeting. The 2026 meeting (Toronto, 7-10 Oct, 'TechnoPower · Technoscientific Futures', sold out) has 26 of 244 accepted open panels with 'AI' or 'artificial intelligence' in the title (31 counting machine learning, algorithms and generative models), among them 'Polycentric Futures: Governing AI Beyond Monocentric Control' and 'Contesting AI Futures'. A plenary includes a talk on how AI is framed, including existential-risk discourse.
why_it_matters: 4S is the largest gathering of scholars trained to study how sciences make knowledge, claims and futures. They could study AI-safety communities, evaluations and forecasts the way STS has studied physics, biomedicine and climate science, and serve as reflexive critics and collaborators.

name: EPIC (Ethnographic Praxis in Industry Community)
summary: A nonprofit (501(c)(3), incorporated in Oregon) and global membership network of ethnographers and other interpretive social scientists working in companies and organisations. ken anderson and Tracey Lovejoy, then social scientists in technology-company R&D, founded it in 2005. It runs an annual conference, a members' virtual Learning Week, paid trainings and a video and paper library. Its recent output leans heavily on AI: an Automation collection, papers such as 'Grounded Models: The Future of Sensemaking in a World of Generative AI' and 'Decolonizing LLMs: An Ethnographic Framework for AI in African Contexts', and the EPIC2026 conference (Chicago, 26-28 Oct) on 'Modeling, predicting, and interpreting context'.
why_it_matters: Its members are practising ethnographers inside technology companies, so EPIC holds both the method and the access needed to study AI labs and deployment settings from the inside. It also argues that AI systems need contextual, lived-experience grounding that model-centric work misses.

caveats: The site blocks automated access, so details come from archived copies (Jan-Sep 2026). Publication years for the featured AI papers could not be confirmed.
tag_notes: Home: applied anthropology and ethnography, so Law, rights & society / STS (H1, B9). Arts is secondary for the design-research practitioners among its members. Ring changed from potential to adjacent under E(2)/(3): it has a sustained AI line in 2024-26 (Automation collection, repeated AI papers and talks, and an AI- and computation-themed EPIC2026), framed around context, work and responsible innovation with no safety framing. Transfer: convening, because it mainly equips its own practitioner community to engage with AI through its conference, trainings and library (J5). Its influence on AI products through members inside companies is indirect. MISFIT (framing): EPIC frames stakes as professional and business value ('innovate responsibly, manage risk, and generate value'); flourishing is the nearest key. Region is global per O: US-incorporated, volunteer-run, with a worldwide network.

name: Committee on the Anthropology of Science, Technology and Computing (CASTAC), American Anthropological Association
summary: A committee of the American Anthropological Association's General Anthropology Division for anthropologists who study science, technology and computing. It was founded in 1991 as the Committee for the Anthropology of Computing. It runs the Platypus blog (since 2012, about 30 contributing editors), the Platypod podcast, the Assemblage member directory, mentorship, AAA Annual Meeting sessions, and the Diana Forsythe and David Hakken prizes. Its AI output is occasional: tagged Platypus essays such as 'Automating Language, Losing Relationality: Feminist Reflections on African Language AI' (Jul 2026) and 'The Kids Are AI-right' (Aug 2026), and a 2026 series, 'An African Studies Approach to AI'.
why_it_matters: It is the organised home of US anthropologists of computing, the community best equipped to do fieldwork on AI labs, AI-safety cultures and everyday AI use. Platypus is an open venue for that work.

key_work.title: Series: An African Studies Approach to AI (Platypus)
Automating Language, Losing Relationality: Feminist Reflections on African Language AI (Mpho Primus, Siri Lamoureaux)
Platypus blog, AI tag

Attend CASTAC-organised sessions at the AAA Annual Meeting
caveats: A volunteer-run committee with no budget or staff found. AI is one topic among many, and no CASTAC work on AI safety or AI-lab cultures was found.

Ring kept at potential under E(2): its AI engagement is a handful of blog posts and one small 2026 series, not a standing programme. Transfer: convening, since the blog brings its own anthropologists into the AI conversation (J5). Transferable method: ethnography of computing cultures, applicable to AI labs and AI-safety communities. Org type is programme per I, as a committee inside the AAA's General Anthropology Division. The URL is set to castac.org, the committee's homepage; the Platypus blog is at blog.castac.org.

name: University Research Priority Program (URPP) Digital Religion(s), University of Zurich (incl. MEEET Lab)
summary: A cross-faculty research consortium at the University of Zurich, with about fifty staff, that studies how digitalisation changes religious practice, communities and institutions. It is directed by practical theologian Thomas Schlag, with anthropologist of AI Beth Singler as co-director. Its AI work includes Singler's project 'Religion in the post-AI age', Schlag's '(Post-)digital religious education and the challenges of AI', a Templeton Religion Trust–funded project on adolescents' resilience and wellbeing through religion-related AI (from Sept 2025), a digital spiritual care project (2026), and the 'Church & AI' conference (Zurich, 15-18 June 2026). The associated MEEET Lab at UZH's Digital Society Initiative (funded 2023-2026) hosted the 2025 conference 'AI Hopes, Fears, and Realities'.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few institutional homes for studying AI apocalypticism, AI as religion, religious chatbots and beliefs about superintelligence. That includes AI-risk discourse itself, which helps AI-safety people see how their narratives circulate and how religious communities will meet advanced AI.

Ring kept at adjacent under E(3): it runs standing AI projects and repeated convenings in 2025-26 on AI's religious and cultural effects; it studies AI-risk discourse but does not frame its own work around safety. Transfer: convening, since much of its AI work brings churches, religious educators and spiritual-care practitioners into the AI conversation (Church & AI, religious education), alongside academic research (J5). MISFIT (sub_tradition): an academic multi-religion research consortium (Christian theology plus Islam, Buddhism and others); rel_interfaith is the nearest key. MISFIT (framing): mostly descriptive scholarship, with constructive projects on spiritual care and adolescent wellbeing; flourishing is the nearest key.

name: Science, Technology, and Social Values Lab (ST&SV Lab), Institute for Advanced Study
summary: A social-science lab at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, led by Alondra Nelson (Harold F. Linder Professor; former acting director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy). It studies science and technology through civil, political and social rights. Its AI work includes the AI Policy and Governance Working Group, which Nelson co-founded; its members range from Helen Toner, Dan Hendrycks, David Krueger, Miles Brundage and Jaan Tallinn to Deborah Raji and Rumman Chowdhury, and it sent recommendations to NTIA and the UN Tech Envoy in 2023. The lab also runs SINAI, on sociotechnical imaginaries and narratives of generative AI (with SFU's Digital Democracies Institute), the AI Democracy Projects with Proof News, which tested chatbots on election information in 2024, and, in 2026, a call for chapters on the global political economy of AI.
why_it_matters: Its working group is a rare standing forum that brings people focused on catastrophic risk and people focused on present harms to rough consensus on policy. SINAI applies STS and narrative methods to how hopes and fears about AI, including x-risk stories, shape legislation and markets.

key_work.title: AI Policy and Governance Working Group: recommendations to the UN Secretary-General's Envoy on Technology on global AI governance
AI Democracy Projects report: Seeking Reliable Election Information? Don't Trust AI (with Proof News)
SINAI: Sociotechnical Imaginaries and Narratives of AI
CFP: Global Political Economy in the Age of AI (edited volume)

tag_notes: Home: Nelson's sociology and STS of science and social rights, so Law, rights & society / STS (H1). Arts is secondary for SINAI's narrative methods (reading fiction, memoir and chatbot outputs) and the journalism partnership. Ring kept at bridge under E(3): an STS lab rooted in social science runs a standing working group that explicitly names 'catastrophic outcomes' and 'neglected risks on the horizon' alongside present harms, with leading AI-safety figures as members. Transfer: into institutions, since the main AI outputs are governance recommendations to NTIA and the UN plus policy panels (J3). Framing is structural because the mission centres justice and democracy, and the working group pairs present harms with long-run risks and the erosion of democratic trust; the framing is mixed.

name: Harding Center for Risk Literacy
summary: A research centre for risk literacy and evidence communication, founded in 2009 with Gerd Gigerenzer at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development in Berlin. It has been part of the University of Potsdam's Faculty of Health Sciences since 2020, and also of the Brandenburg Medical School Theodor Fontane (MHB) since 2026. It studies how people understand risks, and builds tools such as fact boxes for doctors, patients and journalists. Its AI line, 'algorithmic decision environments', tests whether AI in healthcare and chatbots such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Le Chat meet evidence-based standards. That work includes the EB-LLM study on cancer-screening information and a systematic review of patient-relevant outcomes.
why_it_matters: It judges AI by the standard of evidence-based medicine: does the AI improve decisions and outcomes that matter to patients, not just benchmark accuracy? Its 2025 review found that AI tools for clinicians are rarely evaluated on patient-relevant outcomes. That gives a concrete template for outcome-based AI assurance and for risk communication about AI.

Evaluating evidence-based health information from generative AI using a cross-sectional study with laypeople seeking screening information (npj Digital Medicine 8, 343)

2026 David Sackett Prize (German Network for Evidence-Based Medicine) for research on the evidence for AI in healthcare

caveats: AI is one strand among its health-risk communication projects. The site now lists EB-LLM under 'Finished Projects'. The work concerns health information, with no catastrophic-risk framing. The centre has two addresses, in Potsdam-Golm and in Neuruppin.
tag_notes: Home: Gigerenzer-school psychology of judgement and risk literacy produces its AI outputs, through lay comprehension studies and fact-box standards (H1), so psych_social, with safety_health as secondary for clinical-AI evaluation. Ring: a sustained AI line in 2024-26 (EB-LLM, systematic review, prize-winning publications) on AI's effects on patients' information and decisions, with no safety or x-risk frame, so adjacent (E3). Transfer: the primary purpose is informed decisions for patients and lay health consumers, its existing constituency, so protecting (J4). It also builds evaluations, so epistemics is paired with assurance (F).

name: INFORMS Decision Analysis Society (DAS)
summary: The decision-analysis subdivision of INFORMS, with more than 1,000 members. It was founded in 1980 as the ORSA Special Interest Group on Decision Analysis and took its present name in 1996. It covers subjective expected utility, Bayesian inference, multi-attribute utility, risk analysis, elicitation and behavioural decision research. It publishes the journal Decision Analysis, gives the Frank P. Ramsey Medal and other awards, and runs the Advances in Decision Analysis conference and a webinar series. Its engagement with AI is light: AI appears as a conference topic, in one webinar and in journal papers on LLMs and human-in-the-loop advice.
why_it_matters: Decision analysis offers formal tools that AI governance mostly handles informally: value of information, multi-attribute trade-offs, structured expert elicitation and sensitivity analysis. They could apply to deployment go/no-go decisions and safety-case thresholds. The society's members include established risk analysts such as Vicki Bier and Elisabeth Paté-Cornell, who have barely been engaged on AI.

Webinar: Sensitivity Analysis for Decision Making: From Decision Trees to Artificial Intelligence (Emanuele Borgonovo, 8 Oct 2025)
LAMDA: Large Language Model as Decision Analyst (Decision Analysis, ahead of print)

funding: Runs within INFORMS on membership; no budget figures found.

Submit to the journal Decision Analysis
caveats: No AI-safety or governance programme. Its AI content mostly treats AI as a tool for decision analysis, not as something to govern. Most of the site's discussion areas need an INFORMS login.

Ring: AI appears only as a conference topic, one webinar and a few papers, with no standing programme, so potential (E2), as on the roster. Transferable method: formal decision analysis and structured elicitation for AI deployment and safety-threshold decisions. Transfer: its AI activity brings its own community into AI topics, so convening (J5; none_yet excluded because some AI work exists). MISFIT: framing, because DAS states no AI stakes; flourishing reflects its positive aim of better decisions. Society subdivision, so org_type membership (I).

name: Society for Decision Making Under Deep Uncertainty (DMDU Society)
summary: A volunteer-run, multidisciplinary professional society for decisions under deep uncertainty: cases where the parties cannot agree on system models, probabilities or how to weigh consequences. Its methods include robust decision making, exploratory modelling, scenario discovery, info-gap theory and dynamic adaptive pathways, in the RAND and TU Delft lineage. It holds an annual meeting (the first in 2013 in Washington DC), runs a summer school, and has regional groups such as DMDU-Asia. Its application areas are climate, water, energy, health and infrastructure. AI comes up only in meeting themes: the 2025 London meeting asked how DMDU should integrate AI, and the 2026 call cites the rapid adoption of AI.
why_it_matters: AI governance is a textbook case of deep uncertainty, where experts cannot agree on probabilities. DMDU offers stress-testing of policies across many plausible futures and adaptive plans with signposts and triggers. These complement the probabilistic forecasting already strong on the AI-safety map.

Scenario discovery and adaptive pathways draw on futures practice, so arts is secondary (B10 noted; quantitative modelling dominates). Ring: AI appears only in the themes of the 2025 and 2026 meetings, so potential (E2). Transferable method: robust and adaptive decision methods for AI governance where probabilities are contested. Transfer: its AI activity convenes its own community on AI, so convening (J5). Framing: the 2025 polycrisis and 'fractured future' theme gives structural. Region global: there is no single base, and leadership spans Mexico, the US and Kenya. The online hub rests on the annual meeting's online option and the DMDU-Asia webinars; the 2025 London meeting was a one-off and does not count for london.

name: European Network for Business and Industrial Statistics (ENBIS)
summary: A European society for applied and industrial statistics, launched in Amsterdam in December 2000 and registered in the Netherlands. It covers design of experiments, statistical process control, reliability and measurement uncertainty. Individual membership is free and companies pay a fee. ENBIS runs an annual conference, spring meetings, courses and webinars, and has local networks and special interest groups, including Reliability and Safety, and Measurement Uncertainty. Its AI engagement is growing but light: a 2026 webinar on certified robustness in reinforcement learning, ML courses, and a Spring Meeting 2027 on Statistics and Explainable AI at JKU Linz.
why_it_matters: Industry uses these statisticians' methods to validate and monitor production systems: designed experiments, control charts and reliability analysis. They map directly onto AI evaluation design and post-deployment monitoring, which the AI-safety field often reinvents. The 2027 meeting already lists DoE for AI validation, explainability methods in safety-critical systems and the EU AI Act.

Transfer: the 2027 meeting and webinars bring its own community into explainability and AI validation, so convening (J5). MISFIT: framing, because ENBIS states no stakes; its language of trustworthiness and accountability is closest to present_harms. The online hub rests on the recurring webinar series. Society with members, so membership (I).

name: EURAMET European Metrology Network for Mathematics and Statistics (EMN Mathmet)
summary: One of EURAMET's twelve European Metrology Networks. It links 14 national metrology institutes, among them NPL, PTB, LNE, INRiM, VSL and METAS, on mathematical and statistical methods for measurement science. It provides guides, quality-assurance tools for software, measurement-uncertainty training, a strategic research agenda (2023-2033) and an international conference. Its AI theme asks how metrology can raise the quality of AI: characterising training data (uncertainty, mislabelling), testing robustness, making model outputs traceable, and evaluating uncertainty. Related projects include uncertainty-aware machine learning (A3SmartML, 2025-28) and medical-imaging AI.
why_it_matters: Metrology has a mature framework for stating how far a number can be trusted and tracing it back to reference standards (GUM uncertainty evaluation, SI traceability). AI evaluations lack anything comparable. The network's institutes already sit in standards bodies, so they could make AI benchmarks comparable and auditable.

tag_notes: Home: mathematical and statistical metrology (uncertainty evaluation, modelling) is its method, so formal_maths, as provisional; measurement standards and quality assurance make safety secondary. MISFIT: metrology has no sub-tradition. Ring: the AI theme is a position page and related projects are sector-specific, with no standing AI-safety or AI-quality programme, so potential (E2). Transferable method: measurement-uncertainty and traceability frameworks for ML evaluation. Transfer: its AI outputs target training data, robustness and model-output traceability, so into_model (J1). MISFIT: framing, because it states trustworthiness and quality rather than harms; present_harms is closest. Way of knowing is practice: codified metrology standards (GUM). Hubs: member institutes NPL (Teddington, London) and LNE (Paris, which holds the secretariat). Network of institutes without individual members, so network (I).

name: Bayesian AI Section of the International Society for Bayesian Analysis (BayesAI-ISBA)
summary: A section of the International Society for Bayesian Analysis that links Bayesian statisticians with AI researchers. Its stated aims are to scale Bayesian methods to large AI models and to extend them to reasoning, decision-making and online learning. It organises the 'Bayesianism in the Age of Modern AI' workshop series, which began at Dagstuhl in 2024 and met at MBZUAI in 2025. The section organises the series itself for the first time in 2026, in Edinburgh. It also runs sessions and a tutorial at the ISBA World Meeting, endorses other events, and funds travel support and prizes from income from the community's Bayesian Deep Learning book.
why_it_matters: Calibrated uncertainty, a model knowing when it does not know, underpins reliable evaluation, oversight and robustness to distribution shift. This section is where the Bayesian community organises its engagement with modern AI. It has no safety framing, but its 2026 workshop already centres uncertainty quantification, trustworthiness and robustness.
