The section's webinar page currently shows another ISBA section's listings, so it has no visible webinar series of its own yet. Its work is ML methodology; safety relevance comes through uncertainty quantification, not a safety mission.
tag_notes: Home: Bayesian statistics and the theory of learning under uncertainty, so formal_maths, as provisional. Ring kept at potential, as on the roster. MISFIT: it works wholly on AI, but as a methods community with no safety framing and no focus on societal effects, so neither bridge nor adjacent fits (E3). Transferable method: calibrated Bayesian uncertainty quantification and decision theory for evaluation and oversight. Transfer: its methods apply to AI models themselves (uncertainty, priors, robustness), so into_model (J1). MISFIT: framing, because it states reliability and trustworthiness, not harms; present_harms is closest. Region global: officers are in the US, France, Germany, UK and Greece. The online hub rests on the Google group community. Launched about 2025, so status new.

name: Hokkaido University Center for Human Nature, Artificial Intelligence, and Neuroscience (CHAIN)
summary: An interdisciplinary research and graduate-education centre at Hokkaido University in Sapporo. It brings philosophy, especially phenomenology and the Kyoto School thinker Tanabe Hajime, together with neuroscience and AI, around four questions: consciousness, self, sociality and rationality. Since July 2020 it has run a graduate education programme with summer and winter schools; 33 students joined in 2026. It also runs a long seminar series (#63 in Sept 2026). In September 2026 it hosted the international symposium 'Rethinking Humanity in the Age of AI', with Shannon Vallor, David Gunkel and Anna Puzio, on how generative AI changes creativity, communication and moral judgement.
why_it_matters: It approaches human nature in the age of AI through Japanese and continental philosophy (phenomenology, enactivism, Tanabe) working alongside neuroscientists and AI researchers. It trains graduate students across these fields. That gives a non-Anglophone lens on meaning, embodiment and moral judgement, and a convening point for AI ethics in East Asia.

key_work.title: International symposium 'Rethinking Humanity in the Age of AI' (4-5 Sept 2026; keynotes Vallor, Gunkel, Puzio, Miyazono)
CHAIN graduate education programme integrating humanities, neuroscience and computer science (since July 2020)
Two AI for Science (SPReAD) grants: AI robot birds for songbird vocal communication; an AI partner for an embodied Turing test

people: Hayate Shimizu (Specially Appointed Assistant Professor; symposium organiser)
funding: Hokkaido University, with competitive grants (e.g. JST AI for Science SPReAD awards in 2026; a JSPS-NWO bilateral seminar in 2025). The Uehiro Foundation on Ethics and Education supported the 2026 symposium. No budget figures found.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: hosted 'Rethinking Humanity in the Age of AI' (4-5 Sept) and CHAIN Seminar #63 (8 Sept). 29 Sep 2026: news post on the director's contribution to a Mainichi feature on Tanabe Hajime.
engage: Public seminars and international symposia (in person, Sapporo)
Graduate education programme (open to Hokkaido University master's and PhD students)
Visiting researcher and partner-institution links
caveats: No AI-safety framing. The AI work spans ethics events, embodied cognition and AI-for-science projects rather than one AI programme. Hokkaido University established CHAIN in July 2019 (inaugural ceremony 23 July 2019); the graduate programme began in July 2020, and CHAIN became a permanent department in April 2024. In Aug 2026 CHAIN warned that a cryptocurrency (memecoin) was misusing its name; it has no connection to the centre.
tag_notes: Home: its AI outputs come from phenomenology, Kyoto School and continental philosophy of technology, as in the AI-ethics symposium, so phil_technology. Neuroscience and embodied-AI research (life) and consciousness studies (minds) are secondary. Ring: a sustained programme in 2024-26 (graduate programme, seminar series, 2026 international AI symposium, AI grants) on what AI means for human nature, creativity and moral judgement, with no safety or x-risk frame, so adjacent (E3), as on the roster. Transfer: it brings philosophers, scientists and students into the AI conversation through education and convening, so convening (J5). Framing: no harm or risk framing; the 'rethinking humanity' orientation is closest to flourishing. Standpoint neither: Japan is coded Neither in v1 (O).

name: médialab, Sciences Po
summary: An interdisciplinary research laboratory at Sciences Po in Paris where sociologists, engineers and designers study digital society with digital methods. It also builds open-source research tools: Hyphe, minet and xan, and Spinosa, a local framework for working with LLMs. Its 'Technological Futures' line studies AI from an STS perspective. Projects cover situating AI in the worlds that produce it, LLMs in ordinary work practice (EL2MP), sociologically aware language models, the political and democratic biases of generative AI, and generative AI in citizen participation.
why_it_matters: It brings Latourian controversy mapping and large-scale digital methods, which could map how AI-risk debates themselves form, spread and settle. It also does empirical work on how LLMs reshape everyday work and democratic participation. It is in Paris, where int/a has a community.

key_work.title: Situer l'intelligence artificielle (situating AI beyond excessive discourse)
Écologies des pratiques LLMs (EL2MP): LLMs in ordinary work practice
Spinosa, a local LLM research framework with sub-agents
How do recommendation systems learn our political opinions? (Faverjon, Cointet, Ramaciotti, PLOS One)

funding: A research unit of Sciences Po; its site does not itemise project funders.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: published a PLOS One study on how recommender systems learn users' political opinions (29 Sep) and co-hosted the seminar 'Towards Agentic Economies: Eight Cases of New Commerce under AI' with Koray Caliskan and Donald MacKenzie (11 Sep). Its Spinosa repository was updated on 4 Oct 2026.
engage: Public research seminars in Paris (e.g. 6 Oct 2026)
Jobs section on its website lists openings
Open-source tools on github.com/medialab
caveats: AI is one of four research lines, not the lab's whole focus. Its stance is to situate AI 'beyond excessive discourse', so it is sceptical of hype in both directions and does not frame its work around safety. The founding year comes from general knowledge, not from its own site.
tag_notes: Home: law_sts, because its AI work is STS, sociology and digital methods (H1); arts is secondary for its staff designers and design-research methods. Ring: adjacent, from several standing AI projects (Situer l'IA, EL2MP, SALM, Communs Démocratiques), none framed around safety or catastrophic risk (E3). Transfer: into_institutions. The work on generative AI in participatory democracy and on the democratic biases of LLMs supplies templates for governing and debating AI, though much of the output is academic. Framing is structural (democratic bias, recommender systems shaping opinion, AI in work), not harm documentation.

name: Shaping AI (Shaping 21st-Century AI: Controversies and Closure in Media, Policy and Research)
summary: A three-year comparative social-research consortium (Feb 2021 to Feb 2024), funded through the European Open Research Area scheme. It mapped how AI was built up as a scientific paradigm and a contested political issue in the UK, France, Germany and Canada. Teams at Warwick's Centre for Interdisciplinary Methodologies, Sciences Po médialab, ZeMKI Bremen with HIIG Berlin, and Concordia/INRS analysed a decade of AI controversies across media, policy, research and public participation.
why_it_matters: It offers a tested method and comparative data for studying how AI controversies form and close, which could be applied to AI-safety and x-risk debates themselves. The French team had already begun, with a paper titled 'Shoggoth with Smiley Face' (named after a meme from AI-safety circles) and one on the Galactica model's withdrawal.

key_work.title: 'Shifting AI Controversies' conference, WZB Berlin
Reclaiming AI accounts: a plea for a participatory turn in AI inquiries (Gourlet, Ricci, Crépel, Big Data & Society)
Galactica's dis-assemblage (Chartier-Edwards, Grenier, Goujon, AI & Society)
(de)Stabilizing Diffusions exhibition and (un)Stable Diffusions symposium on AI's publics

people: Christian Katzenbach (consortium lead, ZeMKI, University of Bremen)
Donato Ricci (French PI, Sciences Po médialab)
funding: European Open Research Area (ORA) scheme for the social sciences, Feb 2021 to Feb 2024. Grant amounts are not published on the site.
status_evidence: Jan 2024: 'Shifting AI Controversies' conference at WZB Berlin (29-30 Jan). The publication list ends with items forthcoming in 2024, and funding ended Feb 2024.
engage: None current: the project ended in Feb 2024. Its publications and event records remain on shapingai.org, and the partner teams (médialab, HIIG, Warwick CIM, ZeMKI) continue related work.
caveats: A closed, time-limited project. It stays in because its method and outputs are reusable and its teams remain active. Overlaps with the médialab entry, which was its French partner.
tag_notes: Home: law_sts. Its method is STS controversy analysis and media studies (H1); arts is secondary for the design-led French team and its exhibition work. Ring: adjacent. It was a funded AI programme running into 2024 with no safety or catastrophic-risk framing (E3), and status dormant records that it has closed. Transfer: convening. It brought the STS community into the AI conversation through conferences, an EASST-4S panel and publications, and did not produce governance instruments. Framing is critical because its main output analyses AI discourse and its closure. Region is set by the consortium lead in Bremen. No hubs are coded because the project has ended, although HIIG (Berlin) and médialab (Paris) were partners.

name: AIMODELS: The Culture of Algorithmic Models (ERC project, Ca' Foscari University of Venice)
summary: An ERC Consolidator project (2024 to 2028) on the historical epistemology of AI, based in the Department of Philosophy and Cultural Heritage at Ca' Foscari University of Venice and led by Matteo Pasquinelli. It writes a history of AI through its algorithmic models and models of intelligence, builds a comparative epistemology with the psychology of learning, and studies how large foundation models affect the automation of work and digital culture. It holds yearly symposia: Chat Token Vector in 2025, and The World Algorithm, Dysphoria Mundi and Adversarial Poetry in 2026. It publishes open-access volumes and papers.
why_it_matters: It argues that what matters about AI is its epistemic difference from human reason, not its similarity, which directly challenges the anthropomorphic assumptions in much AI-risk talk. It is a source for tracing where the field's ideas of intelligence, and of measuring intelligence, come from.

key_work.title: Operativism: Labor, Automation, Agitation (eds Pasquinelli and Vogman)
Machine, Organism, and Language: A Comparative Epistemology of AI Models (Pasquinelli)
The Algorithm and the Antichrist: Political Theology and the Sunset of Silicon Valley (Cesarale and Pasquinelli)
Adversarial Poetry: Critical Humanities and the Limits of Artificial Intelligence (symposium)

funding: ERC Consolidator Grant (grant agreement 101088645), EU contribution €1,927,573, Jan 2024 to Dec 2028.
status_evidence: Oct 2026: held the symposium 'Adversarial Poetry: Critical Humanities and the Limits of Artificial Intelligence' (1-2 Oct). This followed 'Dysphoria Mundi: Making and Breaking World Models' (28-29 Sep 2026).
engage: Symposia and book presentations in Venice (next listed: Algomedia book presentation, 9 Dec 2026)
Project newsletter (sign-up on the project site)
caveats: Its perspective is critical theory with roots in the political economy of labour. It is sceptical of anthropomorphic and Silicon Valley framings of AI and does not share AI-safety premises, so expect productive disagreement rather than alignment. The project ends in Dec 2028.
tag_notes: Home: philosophy. Its method is historical epistemology from a philosophy department (H1). MISFIT: there is no history-of-science tradition, so it goes under phil_technology rather than law_sts. Economics is secondary for its labour political economy ('Vectors for Workers', tokenisation as a measure of labour, Operativism). Ring: adjacent. It is a funded five-year AI project with no safety framing and explicitly rejects anthropomorphism (E3). Transfer: convening. It brings critical humanities into the AI debate through symposia and open-access books. Primary problem is agency, since its central output is an account of what AI models are epistemically. Framing is critical (CORDIS objective, rule L).

name: Histories of Artificial Intelligence: A Genealogy of Power (Mellon Sawyer Seminar, Cambridge HPS)
summary: An 18-month Mellon Sawyer Seminar in the University of Cambridge's Department of History and Philosophy of Science. It examined the history of AI and its ties to politics, power and control through four threads: hidden labour, encoded behaviour, disingenuous rhetoric and cognitive injustice. It ran a reading group, methods and critical-issues training, community research seminars, 14 fellowships and research awards, a virtual summer school (July 2021) and a winter symposium (December 2021). It published a model graduate syllabus and a community bibliography.
why_it_matters: Its syllabus, bibliography and network of AI historians are a ready resource for anyone writing a history of AI-risk ideas or testing the field's assumptions against a longer view of whom AI has served. The seminar has ended, so this is a resource rather than a partner.

key_work.title: Model Syllabus v1 (Penn, Charbonneau, Moran)
Community bibliography v1
Winter Symposium, Homerton College
BJHS Themes vol. 8: Histories of Artificial Intelligence: A Genealogy of Power (special issue)

funding: Andrew W. Mellon Foundation, through its Sawyer Seminar programme. The amount is not published on the site.
status_evidence: 2023: its special issue, BJHS Themes vol. 8 'Histories of Artificial Intelligence: A Genealogy of Power', was published (papers workshopped at the Dec 2021 Homerton symposium). No activity found since. The site remains online with its outputs.
engage: The site lists a mailing list and a Slack channel; whether they are still active is unknown
caveats: Closed: no activity after the 2023 BJHS Themes special issue, and the site does not give a start date. It stays in for its reusable outputs and network; drop it if the map lists only live organisations. Some organisers have moved institutions (e.g. Stephanie Dick).
tag_notes: Home: law_sts. Its method is critical history and genealogy of science and technology (H1). MISFIT: there is no history-of-science tradition. Secondary values: indigenous (ind_decolonial threads such as cognitive injustice, data colonialism and race, through organisers like Syed Mustafa Ali) and philosophy (an HPS department). Ring: adjacent, because it was a sustained AI programme with no safety framing (E3). Strictly, E2 would make it potential, since it was inactive in 2024-26; here ring records what it was and status dormant records that it has closed. Transfer: convening. It brought historians into the AI conversation through training, a syllabus and a summer school. Framing is structural: AI's entanglement with systems of power and control.

name: Center for Genetics and Society (CGS)
summary: A Berkeley-area nonprofit, founded in 2001 by Richard Hayes and Marcy Darnovsky. It works to put social justice, human rights and democratic governance at the centre of debates on human genetic and reproductive technologies: heritable genome editing, assisted reproduction and the resurgence of eugenics. It runs the Missing Voices Initiative on heritable genome editing, an anti-eugenics network of scholars and advocates, the Surrogacy360 resource and an assisted-reproduction working group of 150+ members. It publishes the Biopolitical Times blog and a monthly newsletter, and is a fiscally sponsored project of Tides Center.
why_it_matters: It has two decades of civil-society experience pressing for democratic limits on a powerful technology, notably against heritable human genome editing. It also tracks the eugenic and transhumanist ideas that run through some AI-future visions. Its AI commentary is occasional and sceptical of x-risk narratives.

key_work.title: Is AI the End of the World as We Know It? (Pete Shanks, Biopolitical Times)
Missing Voices Initiative on heritable genome editing
Confronting Eugenics to Build a Just Future

people: Marcy Darnovsky (co-founder; executive director 2012-2025, now emeritus)
funding: A fiscally sponsored project of Tides Center (501(c)(3)); its site does not list funders.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: Biopolitical Times published 'Is AI the End of the World as We Know It?' (Pete Shanks, 24 Sep), alongside posts that month on gene-editing start-ups and the history of eugenics.
engage: Door to open: no AI programme yet; its anti-eugenics and Missing Voices networks are the natural point of contact
Monthly newsletter, Biopolitical News & Views
Webinars and events on human biotechnology (not AI-specific)
caveats: Its AI output is light and mostly reposted news plus occasional commentary. That commentary criticises 'AI doomer' narratives as a distraction from concrete harms and corporate power, so it would be a critical partner. The core staff is very small (executive director, coordinator, intern, plus fellows and consultants). The site's address is not stated; the location comes from the roster and its 510 (East Bay) phone number.
tag_notes: Home: law_policy, as a public-interest, human-rights and social-justice advocacy organisation on biotechnology governance (B9; its leader is a sociologist, not a bioethicist). Ring: potential, since its AI engagement is occasional blog commentary and reposted news with no standing AI programme (E2). Transferable method: civil-society campaigning for democratic limits on a dual-use technology (heritable genome editing), with inclusive 'missing voices' engagement and critique of eugenic and transhumanist ideology. Transfer: convening, not none_yet, because it does some AI commentary aimed at its own network of readers. Framing is critical, from its AI output (scepticism about doomer narratives); its biotech mission would read as present harms.

name: Deutsches Museum Research Institute (Forschungsinstitut für Technik- und Wissenschaftsgeschichte)
summary: The research institute of the Deutsches Museum in Munich, a Leibniz research museum. It works on the history of science, technology and the environment, collection-based and education research, conservation science and digital projects. Two DFG-funded projects in its digital-technology strand touch AI. One is a feminist revision of the ethics of autonomous vehicles (Liliia Zemnukhova). The other, 'Artificial Vision at Work' (2024 to 2027), is a history of how human vision became an information-processing problem and was automated at work. Since January 2026 it has also hosted the Munich office of 'Edition Wissenschaftliche Software', a 21-year academy project to archive and edit scientific software from 1950 to 2010.
why_it_matters: It offers a historian's long view of safety-critical automation, a feminist-epistemology analysis of how ethics enters autonomous-vehicle engineering, long-term archival care for software, and a major museum's public reach. None of this is yet framed around advanced-AI safety.

key_work.title: Feministische Revision einer Ethik der autonomen Fahrzeuge (DFG)
Artificial Vision at Work (DFG, Jun 2024 to Jun 2027)
Edition Wissenschaftliche Software, Munich office (2026 to 2046)

people: Rudolf Seising (PI, Artificial Vision at Work)
Ulf Hashagen (project director, Edition Wissenschaftliche Software, Munich)
funding: The Deutsches Museum belongs to the Leibniz Association. The autonomous-vehicle ethics and Artificial Vision projects are DFG-funded. Edition Wissenschaftliche Software is funded through the academy programme of the Union of German Academies of Sciences (2026 to 2046).
status_evidence: Jan 2026: the Munich office of Edition Wissenschaftliche Software started (the project runs 2026 to 2046). Artificial Vision at Work runs from Jun 2024 to Jun 2027.
engage: Scholar-in-residence programme: stipends with apartments, plus senior-researcher and guest-scientist routes
Door to open: no AI-safety programme yet; approach the digital-technology researchers directly
caveats: Its AI work is two individual research projects in a large history-of-technology institute, which puts it on the boundary between potential and adjacent. Research leadership is currently acting. Most of the site is in German, and the institute's founding date is not stated on it.
tag_notes: Home: law_sts. History of technology is closest to STS (H1). MISFIT: there is no history-of-science or history-of-technology tradition. Philosophy is secondary for its philosophy-of-science and feminist-epistemology methods. Ring: potential, kept from the roster. The institute's AI engagement is two individual DFG projects inside a broad history institute, not a standing AI programme. Under E2 a funded project could argue for adjacent, so this is a boundary case. Transferable method: historical analysis of safety-critical automation and of how ethics enters engineering practice, plus long-term archiving of scientific software. Transfer: convening, since its light AI work reaches scholarly and museum audiences rather than models or governance instruments. Framing is present harms: the autonomous-vehicle project starts from the first pedestrian death. Org type: academic, as a unit of a Leibniz public research institution (rule I).

name: BlackboxNLP: Workshop on Analyzing and Interpreting Neural Networks for NLP
summary: An annual workshop on interpreting and explaining language models, held since 2018 alongside a major ACL conference (EMNLP in all years but 2019). Its call invites methods from machine learning, psychology, linguistics and neuroscience to assess what representations and computations models learn and what inductive biases they have. The ninth edition is on 29 October 2026 in Budapest at EMNLP 2026, with a reproducibility challenge. The 2025 edition in Suzhou ran a shared task on circuit and causal-variable localisation using the MIB benchmark.
why_it_matters: It is the standing venue where computational linguists and cognitive scientists study language-model internals, bringing linguistic and psycholinguistic analysis to interpretability, a core AI-safety agenda. It does not describe its work as safety research, so the overlap with safety-motivated interpretability lies in the substance, not in its stated aims.

key_work.title: BlackboxNLP 2026, ninth edition at EMNLP 2026, Budapest
BlackboxNLP 2026 Reproducibility Challenge
Shared task on circuit localisation and causal-variable localisation (MIB leaderboard)
Workshop proceedings in the ACL Anthology

funding: Sponsored by NDIF (National Deep Inference Fabric) in 2026 and by the Association for Computational Linguistics in 2025. No budget is published.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: published the accepted papers for the 29 Oct 2026 Budapest workshop (15 Sep) and announced keynotes by Ivan Titov, Sheridan Feucht and Michael Hahn (9 Sep).
engage: Attend the workshop at EMNLP 2026, Budapest, 29 Oct 2026
Submit papers or enter the yearly reproducibility challenge (2026 deadlines were in July)
Join its Discord server
caveats: It belongs to the NLP and ML research community, so it is closer to mainstream ML than most entries on this map. It has no safety framing; the ring was changed from the roster's bridge to adjacent for that reason. MISFIT: the taxonomy has no linguistics tradition.
tag_notes: Home: psych (psych_cognitive), for linguistic and psycholinguistic probing and experiments on models (H2, B5). MISFIT: no linguistics tradition. No secondary tradition is coded, because the neuroscience and ML inspirations in its call are not distinct methods (rule C excludes ML). Ring changed from bridge to adjacent: its 2025-26 site makes no reference to safety, alignment, trust or risk, so E3's 'explicitly framed' test fails. MISFIT: the adjacent definition assumes work on societal effects, whereas this is work on model internals. Transfer: into_model, since its knowledge is about the internals and inductive biases of AI systems. Framing: MISFIT, as there is no value for neutral scientific understanding; flourishing is the least misleading of the five. Region is global because it moves with EMNLP and its organisers are spread across institutions. Hub online, for the open Discord community.

name: Rede Latino-Americana de Estudos sobre Vigilância, Tecnologia e Sociedade (LAVITS)
summary: A network of Latin American researchers, activists and artists, founded in 2009, that studies surveillance, technopolitics, algorithms and AI from a critical and decolonial standpoint. It holds an international symposium: the seventh, in Rio de Janeiro on 26-28 August 2026, drew 350 participants and presented 141 papers chosen from over 300 submissions. It also runs research projects (digital gender violence, public-security technologies, digital peripheries) and publishes commentary under themes including 'Algoritmos & Política' and 'Inteligência Artificial'. A 'Conselho Ciborgue' (Cyborg Council) admits members and decides who speaks for the network.
why_it_matters: It brings Latin American surveillance studies and the critique of data colonialism to AI, for example the argument that AI's environmental footprint is structural and falls mostly on the Global South. The AI-safety field's work on power concentration rarely draws on these perspectives. A council member put them before the first UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance in July 2026.

key_work.title: VII International LAVITS Symposium: 'Tramar o presente: tecnopolíticas dissidentes e ecologias do Comum'
Jamila Venturini at the 1st UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance (Geneva): manipulative design and AI's environmental footprint
Big techs e eleições (Rafael Evangelista)
'Algoritmos & Política' theme, incl. 'Imperialismo, IA e meio ambiente'

people: Fernanda Bruno (founding member; UFRJ professor; coordinated the VII Symposium)
Jamila Venturini (Conselho Ciborgue member; co-executive director of Derechos Digitales)
funding: Its site lists the Ford Foundation, CNPq and FAPERJ as supporters (2026). No amounts published.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: published its report on the VII International Symposium (26-28 Aug 2026, Rio de Janeiro, 350 participants). Aug 2026: launched a new website and newsletter.
engage: Newsletter, launched Aug 2026
Membership: researchers, activists and artists apply to the Conselho Ciborgue; members coordinate by email lists and Telegram
Ciclo LAVITS event series, launched June 2026
Symposium calls for papers (the 2026 call opened Feb 2026)
Communications coordinator post advertised May 2026
caveats: AI is one theme among broader surveillance and technopolitics topics. The network's stance is critical of Big Tech and it does not engage with the AI-safety community. Six symposia ran from 2009 to 2019, then nothing until 2026. The site names few staff. Most sources are its own site.
tag_notes: Home: critical surveillance studies and STS from communication, sociology, anthropology and law scholars (H1, B8: its core contribution is STS critique; decolonial framing is secondary, so it stays in Law), with indigenous/decolonial and arts as secondary traditions (symposium strands on decolonial struggles and Indigenous technological knowledge, seven artistic practices, artists as members). Ring: kept adjacent. It has a sustained AI and algorithms line (themes, symposium, UN input) but no safety, catastrophic-risk or alignment framing (E3). Transfer: its main purpose is exchange between Latin American researchers, activists and artists, bringing that community into AI debates (J5). Framing is structural: surveillance capitalism, data colonialism and imperialism rather than individual harms. No hub: it is Brazil-based with no London/Berlin/Paris presence, and no open online programme could be verified.

name: Data Privacy Brasil
summary: A São Paulo nonprofit that began as a data-protection training school in 2018 and added a research association in 2020; the two were merged in 2026. It researches and advocates on data protection, platform and digital-market regulation and AI governance. Its AI projects cover rights-based AI regulation in Brazil ('IA com Direitos', 'Onde canta o sabIA'), AI in classrooms and, with Aláfia Lab, an Observatory of AI in the Elections, which logged 413 AI uses in political content before the 2026 campaign, over 80% of them deepfakes. It has trained over 6,000 professionals, including staff of government, the judiciary and Brazil's data protection authority, and runs the annual Data Privacy Global Conference.
why_it_matters: It brings human-rights and data-protection law, plus Global South civil-society positioning, to AI governance. Its work includes empirical tracking of AI deepfakes during a live national election and co-leading a working group whose proposals feed the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance. That is Latin American regulatory experience the AI-safety governance field seldom draws on.

key_work.title: IA na pré-eleição: deepfakes, desinformação e novos desafios para a integridade das eleições de 2026
Observatório IA nas Eleições (with Aláfia Lab)
One year of ECA Digital: materials on age assurance and manipulative design
Data Privacy Global Conference, 5th edition

funding: Internews is the only funder named on its site (DIRECT project on data protection law). It publishes an ethical and transparent financing policy but does not list other funders.
status_evidence: Oct 2026: observatory case entries dated 3 Oct 2026. Sep 2026: pre-election AI report (15 Sep) and ECA Digital materials (17 Sep).
engage: Data Privacy Global Conference, 7-8 Dec 2026 (5th edition)
Submit AI election content to the Observatório IA nas Eleições reporting channel
Training through its Data Privacy school and Data Governance School
Newsletter
caveats: The training school (2018) and research association (2020) had separate identities until they merged in 2026, so founding dates vary by source. Most output is in Portuguese. It has no catastrophic-risk framing, and its funding is largely undisclosed on its site.
tag_notes: Home: data-protection and human-rights law is its method (H1, B9). Secondary traditions: economics, for its standing platform and antitrust lines (Observatório das Fusões Digitais), and democracy, for the election observatory, which is fact-checking and provenance work. Ring: kept adjacent. It runs sustained AI regulation and election-integrity programmes framed around rights, not safety or catastrophic risk (E3). Transfer: its primary aim is rights-based AI regulation and global governance proposals (J3). Minds is a third problem because of its child-protection and manipulative-design work under ECA Digital. Region and standpoint follow its São Paulo base and Global South leadership (O).

name: Laboratório de Políticas Públicas e Internet (LAPIN)
summary: A Brasília nonprofit founded in 2016 that researches and advocates on internet regulation and digital rights. It works on four axes: digital surveillance, AI and emerging technologies, disinformation, and data governance and the digital economy, with dedicated AI and surveillance working groups. Its recent AI work addresses the material footprint of AI. With O Joio e O Trigo and the Heinrich Böll Foundation it held a seminar on AI, environment and socio-environmental justice, reported in February 2026. In June 2026, with IDEC, it sent evidence on AI data centres to the UN Special Rapporteur on climate change and human rights. In August and September 2026 it opposed Brazil's REDATA tax regime for data centres.
why_it_matters: It connects the AI infrastructure build-out to water, energy, land and the rights of Indigenous and traditional communities, and calls for free, prior and informed consultation of affected people. AI-safety governance seldom models this resource and territorial side of the AI transition.

key_work.title: Report: I Seminário Inteligência Artificial, Meio Ambiente e Justiça Socioambiental
Input to the UN Special Rapporteur on climate change and human rights: the case of AI data centres (with IDEC)
Statement against the approval of REDATA (data-centre tax regime)

funding: Not disclosed on its site. The Heinrich Böll Foundation partnered on the AI and environment seminar (report Feb 2026).
status_evidence: Sep 2026: statement against the approval of REDATA (2 Sep 2026). Aug 2026: public note against the REDATA vote.
engage: Newsletter sign-up on lapin.org.br
Contact form for partnerships and joint projects
caveats: Funding is undisclosed. The AI and environment line is recent (2025-26). It has no catastrophic-risk framing, and its output is mostly in Portuguese. The profile rests on its own site, with no independent source found because search was unavailable.
tag_notes: Home: digital-rights and internet public-policy advocacy argued through human rights (H1, B9, B8: Global South rights advocacy goes to Law). Ring: kept adjacent. It has a standing AI working group and sustained AI-environment advocacy, with no safety or catastrophic-risk framing (E3). Transfer: regulatory submissions and statements on REDATA, the UN rapporteur and AI regulation (J3). Systemic is the second problem because of its planetary-resource line on data centres. MISFIT: environmental justice and political ecology have no tradition key, so this AI-environment work sits under Law. Engagement is left empty because no 2025-26 courses, events or calls could be confirmed on its site.

name: Instituto de Tecnologia e Sociedade do Rio (ITS Rio)
summary:
A Rio de Janeiro nonprofit research institute founded in 2013 by Ronaldo Lemos, working on law and technology, democracy and technology, education and innovation. Its AI work includes:
- a postgraduate specialisation in AI and technology regulation with UERJ and CEPED (third cohort August 2026), plus short AI courses
- an operational AI sandbox in Rio's Public Defender's Office
- 'Boca de IA', which tests how chatbots recommend votes in the 2026 election
- a September 2025 design, with CEBRI, for a Brazilian Institute for AI Safety and Opportunities
It also publishes commentary on AI, such as a September 2026 column on AI companions.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few Global South institutes to have designed a national AI safety institute. It pairs that with AI-regulation teaching for Brazilian lawyers and officials and with tests of chatbot behaviour in elections, so it could carry AI-safety governance ideas into Brazil.

key_work.title: An AI Safety and Opportunities Institute for Brazil: A Design of Features, Functions, and Potential Challenges (with CEBRI)

It has wide tech-industry partnerships (its site lists Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft and others as partners) and runs a Google policy fellowship. The team page did not render, so leadership roles beyond Lemos are not confirmed on the site.

Democracy is secondary for its democracy and technology line (Boca de IA, public consultations). Ring: kept adjacent. Its sustained AI programme is regulation and rights-focused; the AI safety institute design (2025) is one safety-framed output and would move it to bridge if it became a standing line (E2/E3). Transfer: regulatory models, a justice-sector sandbox and an institute design (J3). Framing: its mission stresses regulation that protects privacy, free expression and access to knowledge, which is harm-avoidance, not flourishing (L).

name: Centro de Estudios en Tecnología y Sociedad, Universidad de San Andrés (CETyS)
summary: An interdisciplinary centre at the Universidad de San Andrés in Buenos Aires (founded 2007, according to its site) that works on internet governance, the political economy of digital technology and emerging technologies, with a Latin American focus. Its AI line covers AI ethics and governance in the region and AI adoption by courts. It led the GuIA research network, launched in 2020 with support from the IDB's fAIr LAC and Meta. Its court work includes a study of judicial AI readiness in Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Mexico and Uruguay, submissions to the Buenos Aires Supreme Court on AI in justice, and the 'Redes de justicIA' workshop on 26 August 2026. It also teaches diplomas in internet governance, data protection and digital regulation, plus executive courses such as one on digital competition and antitrust (August 2026).
why_it_matters: It offers Latin American evidence on how public institutions, especially courts, actually adopt generative AI, and it convenes a regional network of AI-governance researchers. That is practical knowledge of AI oversight in states with weak regulatory frameworks, which AI-safety governance work rarely has.

Redes de justicIA: del diagnóstico a la adopción responsable (workshop)

Economics is secondary for its standing competition and antitrust line (B9). Ring: kept adjacent. It has sustained AI research on governance and judicial adoption, framed as responsible adoption rather than safety or catastrophic risk (E3). Transfer: its outputs are recommendations and consultation submissions for judicial AI policy (J3). Way of knowing is empirical because its main recent AI output is a multi-country readiness study. Framing: 'responsible adoption' is harm-avoidance, so it takes the nearest harm framing (L).

name: The Shift Project: digital and AI programme (Numérique)
summary: The digital programme of The Shift Project, a Paris think tank founded in 2010 by a group of experts including Jean-Marc Jancovici to plan the decarbonisation of the French economy. Since its 2018 'Lean ICT' report the programme has measured the energy and carbon footprint of digital technology. Its final report on AI, data and computing (October 2025) projects that data-centre electricity use could triple between 2023 and 2030. It argues that current AI deployment is incompatible with carbon budgets whatever the technical progress, and recommends binding carbon-energy trajectories for AI infrastructure with expansion conditional on them. An April 2026 report on controlling data-centre deployment in France followed.
why_it_matters: It treats AI deployment as a problem of physical limits, rebound effects and planning within carbon budgets. AI-safety and compute-governance work rarely makes that systems connection. Its quantitative trajectories for data-centre energy could inform compute governance.

key_work.title: Intelligence artificielle, données, calculs : quelles infrastructures dans un monde décarboné ? (final report)
Réussir la transition dans l'incertitude : maîtriser le déploiement des centres de données

Its 2025 crowdfunding campaign raised over €4.6m from 36,552 contributors (per Wikipedia). Sponsors of the AI project: ADEME, AXA, Caisse des Dépôts, Davidson, Devoteam, Institut Norsys and Le CNAM.

Economics is secondary for its economy-wide transformation plan (PTEF). Ring: kept adjacent. It has a standing digital programme with AI reports in 2025-26 framed around carbon budgets, not safety or catastrophic risk (E3). Transfer: it proposes binding carbon-energy trajectories and conditions on infrastructure deployment (J3). Tagged as a programme per A1 and I. The recoupling badge was considered and not awarded: the analysis links AI to planetary limits but covers a single domain (carbon and energy) and does not treat AI risk on its own (P).

name: Pause IA
summary: A French association (loi 1901), launched in mid-2024 as the national group of the PauseAI movement, that campaigns for a global, coordinated moratorium on training the most powerful AI systems until they can be made safe. It has local groups in cities including Paris, Lyon, Toulouse and Bordeaux and a monthly newsletter. Its campaigns target French and international decision-makers: G7 2026, an international treaty at the UN Global Dialogue in Geneva, a 'loss of control' campaign from September 2026, and one on AI and jobs. It also runs 'La Fresque des risques de l'IA', a free, CC BY-SA, 2.5-hour card workshop for 2-8 people, adapted from CeSIA material and modelled on the Climate Fresk.
why_it_matters: It takes the Climate Fresk's participatory, card-based workshop format, proven in French climate education, into AI-risk literacy. It also holds an explicit position in favour of slowing the AI race.

key_work.title: La Fresque des risques de l'IA (collaborative AI-risk workshop)
Campaign: 'Nous sommes au bord de la perte de contrôle' (loss of control)

Roughly 55% came from individual donations, 12% from an earmarked conference donation, 12% from a €10,000 launch grant from Stichting PauseAI (July 2024), 10% from memberships and 7% from crowdfunding. The executive director's salary was initially covered by PauseAI Global, out of its Future of Life Institute funding. It spent €21,198 in its first financial year (June 2024-Nov 2025). A single donor gave over a third of first-year income. It states that it takes no money from AI companies or from states in the AI race.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: launched the 'loss of control' campaign and held an action week in seven French cities, covered by 20 Minutes (29 Sep 2026) and France 3 (24 Sep 2026).

MISFIT: no tradition key covers climate-movement organising and education methods. Ring: kept core. Its founding mission is AI x-risk advocacy within the PauseAI ecosystem, which is funded by Stichting PauseAI and FLI (E1). Transfer: its primary aim is a governance instrument, a global moratorium or treaty (J3). Problems are security (treaty and red lines), epistemics (public AI-risk literacy through the Fresque) and power (its standing AI and jobs campaign). Speed-of-wisdom badge: an explicit pause position against the AI race. Hubs: HQ and a local group in Paris, and online Fresque sessions.

name: Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL): Ethics Committee and Responsible NLP Research Checklist
summary: The ACL is the international learned society for computational linguistics and natural language processing. It was founded in 1962 and runs the field's main conferences. In March 2020 it adopted the ACM Code of Ethics as its own. Its Ethics Committee (co-chairs Min-Yen Kan, Aurélie Névéol and Zhijing Jin) maintains ethics-review guidelines, reviewer training and teaching materials. Every paper submitted through ACL Rolling Review must complete the Responsible NLP Research Checklist, first developed for NAACL 2022 and revised for the October 2024 cycle. It asks authors about malicious or unintended harms, dual use, risks to marginalised groups, data practices and their use of AI assistants. Papers that are flagged get a separate ethics review.
why_it_matters: Ethics review is built into the publication pipeline of the field that produces language models. That makes it a working model of field-wide harm review before publication, which AI-safety venues could copy or extend. It is also the main institutional door into the linguistics community, though that community is now heavily ML-dominated.

key_work.title: ACL Code of Ethics (adoption of the ACM Code)

status_evidence: 2026: the ACL portal lists the current Ethics Committee and a separate Publication Ethics Committee. The checklist remains mandatory for ARR submissions; it was last revised for the October 2024 cycle.
engage: Volunteer as an ethics reviewer for ACL Rolling Review (training on ethics.aclweb.org)
Teaching materials on NLP ethics for BSc, MSc and PhD levels on the ACL ethics site
ACL membership and conferences, which include ethics review
caveats: Computational linguistics now overlaps heavily with mainstream ML, so the ACL sits close to the AI mainstream. What is distinctive here is the research-ethics apparatus, not linguistic knowledge. The checklist covers research practice (harms, data, reproducibility), not catastrophic risk or alignment. The committee's site gives no founding date; a past co-chair served from 2021 to 2025.
tag_notes: Home is philosophy/phil_bioethics (H1): its AI-relevant output is a research-ethics code, an ethics review process and a responsible-research checklist, which is engineering and research ethics rather than linguistic method. Ring adjacent (kept): a sustained programme since 2020-21, framed around harms, dual use, fairness and privacy, with no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing. Transfer into_builders (J2): the code and checklist act on NLP researchers' own conduct before publication. Org type membership (rule I: learned society); the profiled unit is its Ethics Committee and the ARR checklist (A1), so scale is recorded as programme. MISFIT: there is no linguistics tradition in the taxonomy, and computational linguistics now largely overlaps with mainstream ML.

name: International Federation of Translators (FIT)
summary: FIT is the international federation of professional associations of translators, interpreters and terminologists. It was founded in 1953 under UNESCO auspices and has its secretariat in Paris. It has about 110 regular member associations, representing some 67,500 professionals. Its AI work consists of position papers on the use of AI in interpreting (August 2024) and on machine translation in the age of AI (June 2025); the interpreting paper opposes replacing human interpreters with unsupervised machine interpreting. In August 2026 its Working Group on AI Ethics, chaired by Adriana Zúñiga Hernández, published a report with six principles: accessibility, accountability, accuracy, confidentiality, fairness and transparency. The report calls for shared responsibility for AI errors and for labels that show whether a translation was produced by a human, by a machine, or by a machine and then reviewed.
why_it_matters: Translators and interpreters have long managed errors that change meaning in courts, hospitals and diplomacy. FIT turns that practice into norms on human oversight, labelling and liability for machine translation and interpreting. It shows a profession setting assurance terms for an AI deployment.

key_work.title: FIT Position Paper on the Use of AI in Interpreting
FIT Position Paper on Machine Translation in the Age of AI
Ethics of AI in Translation and Interpreting (Working Group on AI Ethics)

people: Adriana Zúñiga Hernández (chair, Working Group on AI Ethics; chair, Standards Committee)
status_evidence: 28 Sep 2026: news of the Working Group on AI Ethics report (dated 31 Aug 2026), published by ITI. International Translation Day 2026 campaign on FIT's own site.
engage: Individuals take part through a national member association (in the UK, for example, ITI or CIOL)
Position papers and the AI ethics report are free to read
caveats: The AI papers mainly defend the role of human professionals, which is partly a labour interest. The Working Group on AI Ethics is not among the 2025-2028 standing committees on FIT's site; its report was found through ITI. ITI dates the machine-translation paper June 2026, while FIT's own page says June 2025.
tag_notes: Home is arts/arts_narrative (H3: a professional federation goes with the translation community it serves). MISFIT: the taxonomy has no translation, interpreting or linguistics tradition, so FIT is placed under communications. Ring adjacent (kept): position papers in 2024 and 2025 and a working-group report in 2026 are framed around ethics, quality and human oversight, not catastrophic risk. Transfer protecting (J4): the papers defend professional translators, and the people who depend on accurate translation, against unsupervised machine translation; the 2026 principles on labelling and shared liability could also be read as into_institutions. Org type membership (rule I: federation). Hub paris: the secretariat is in Paris.

name: Chartered Institute of Linguists (CIOL)
summary: CIOL is the UK's Royal Charter professional body for linguists. It was founded in 1910 and has over 5,000 members, more than 1,200 of them Chartered Linguists. Its associated charity, IoLET, runs CIOL Qualifications such as the Diploma in Translation and the Diploma in Public Service Interpreting. Its AI work is a standing hub (the CIOL AI Voices white papers, AI Updates and Linguists' Voices) plus commissioned research. A University of Bristol study led by Lucas Nunes Vieira surveyed 2,500 frontline public-service workers. It found that a third use AI translation, often on personal devices, including for medical consent forms and child-protection work. The study was presented to the APPG on Modern Languages on 23 June 2025.
why_it_matters: The public-services study is rare empirical evidence of unsupervised generative-AI use in high-stakes settings. CIOL argues for governance, training and clear accountability rather than bans. It is a concrete case of deployment risk documented by the profession that used to carry that responsibility.

key_work.title: AI translation in UK public services (University of Bristol research commissioned by CIOL)
CIOL AI Voices 2025
Joint ITI-CIOL response to the UK copyright and AI consultation

people: Lucas Nunes Vieira (University of Bristol; led the commissioned public-services study)
status_evidence: 1-3 Oct 2026: news items on CIOL's homepage. The AI Updates hub links a May 2026 papal encyclical on AI and Anthropic's paper on recursive self-improvement.
engage: CIOL membership (grades up to Chartered Linguist)
Conference Season 2026 presentations and resources
Free login for AI Voices and Linguists' Voices resources; monthly eUpdates
caveats: The AI work is mostly curation and advocacy for the profession. The research was carried out by University of Bristol researchers on CIOL's commission. The London office is not open for visits, and staff work remotely or hybrid.
tag_notes: Home is arts/arts_narrative (H3: the professional body of linguists goes with that community). MISFIT: no linguistics tradition. Ring adjacent (kept): in 2025-26 it ran a standing AI hub, published AI Voices white papers and commissioned research on public services, all framed around risk, quality and the role of human linguists rather than catastrophic risk. Transfer convening (J5): the hub's main job is to inform linguists; the Bristol study adds a strand on safeguards in public services. Way of knowing is empirical because the main output is the survey of 2,500 workers. Hub london: registered office on the Strand, though staff work remotely or hybrid.

name: Institute of Translation and Interpreting (ITI)
summary: ITI is a UK professional membership association for translators and interpreters. It was founded in 1986, is based in Milton Keynes and has about 2,600 members. Its board-level AI policy holds that humans remain essential to accurate and ethical translation. It curates AI resources and endorses the FIT and European Language Council AI papers. In 2025-26 it ran Translation and AI and Interpreting and AI courses with the University of Surrey (184 attendees over five cohorts). It wrote to the UK Government on AI policy in October 2025 and filed a joint copyright and AI consultation response with CIOL in February 2025.
why_it_matters: ITI holds codes of professional conduct and a system for assessing qualified members in work where errors change meaning. These are ready-made norms for human oversight of AI translation. Its member surveys also document how AI is reshaping a skilled profession.

key_work.title: ITI policy on artificial intelligence
Translation and AI and Interpreting and AI courses with the University of Surrey
Joint ITI-CIOL response to the UK copyright and AI consultation

status_evidence: 28 Sep 2026: published its support for FIT's AI ethics report. Its 2025-26 annual review records AI courses, letters to Government on AI policy (Oct 2025) and the EX:CHANGE 2026 conference (1-2 July 2026).

Translation and AI and Interpreting and AI courses with the University of Surrey
Webinars and CPD on AI and emerging technologies
42 networks, including a London Regional Group
caveats: The AI work is mainly member education and advocacy for human translators, which is partly a labour interest. The courses teach the use of AI tools rather than AI governance. A member survey found many attributing falling work to AI.
tag_notes: Home is arts/arts_narrative (H3: a professional association goes with the community it serves). MISFIT: no translation or linguistics tradition. Ring changed from potential to adjacent (E2): the 2025-26 annual review shows a standing AI line: a board AI policy, recurring Translation and AI and Interpreting and AI courses with Surrey (five cohorts), letters to Government on AI policy in October 2025 and a joint copyright consultation response. It is framed around the human role and livelihoods, not catastrophic risk. Transfer convening (J5): it mainly educates and informs members. Problem power comes first because work availability and pay are its main AI concern. Hub online: webinars and on-demand courses for members.

name: European Language Council (CEL/ELC)
summary: CEL/ELC is a European association of universities and other higher-education institutions working on language policy, multilingualism and the education of translators and interpreters. Its secretariat is at the Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore in Milan, its president is Maria Teresa Zanola, and it publishes the European Journal of Language Policy. Its Special Interest Group on AI in translation and interpreting is coordinated by Maurizio Viezzi and Kris Peeters. In November 2025 it published 'AI for Translation and Interpreting: A Roadmap for Users and Policy Makers', and on 20 April 2026 it held an online seminar, '(De)Generative AI and Multilingual (Mis)Communication'.
why_it_matters: The roadmap explains to lay users and policymakers how LLMs communicate differently from humans, and which side effects to weigh against the benefits. It also covers how translators and interpreters should be trained alongside AI. This is a language-policy view of communication risk that AI governance rarely draws on.

name: Interpreting SAFE AI Task Force (Stakeholders Advocating for Fair and Ethical AI in Interpreting)
summary: An independent US-based group of stakeholders, formed in June 2023 and launched in September 2023 with Bill Rivers as interim chair. Its stakeholder assembly of more than 50 members includes interpreter and translator associations (among them the American Translators Association and RID), certifying bodies, language-service companies, technology vendors, hospitals, standards bodies and researchers. It ran perception surveys of interpreters and of end users in ten spoken languages and ASL (2023-24). In July 2024 it published guidance on AI and interpreting services, built on four principles: end-user autonomy, evidence of safety and wellbeing, transparency of quality, and accountability for errors and harm. In August 2025, with CoSET, it released Part A of an AI Interpreting Solutions Evaluation Toolkit, with checklists on organisational readiness, setting-specific risks, vendor assessment and procurement.
why_it_matters: It treats AI interpreting as a sociotechnical system: evaluation covers the human participants, the legal or medical setting and liability, not only model accuracy. It is an assurance and procurement framework for a high-stakes deployment, written by the profession affected, a perspective AI assurance work rarely gets.

AI Interpreting Solutions Evaluation Toolkit, Part A (with CoSET)

MISFIT: no interpreting tradition. Ring adjacent (kept): sustained since 2023 and framed around the fair, ethical and safe deployment of AI interpreting for end users, not AI safety in the x-risk sense. A product-safety reading (cf. Common Sense Media, worked example 4) could justify bridge. Transfer into_institutions (J3): the guidance and the evaluation toolkit are governance instruments for organisations buying AI interpreting. Region north_america: the group is distributed within the US.

name: Coalition for Sign Language Equity in Technology (CoSET)
summary: A US coalition of Deaf people, sign-language interpreters, researchers and technologists. It was formerly called the Advisory Group on AI and Sign Language Interpreting, and is pending incorporation as a 501(c)(3) nonprofit. It grew out of three webinars hosted at Brown University in autumn 2023, with about 300 participants, which fed its #DeafSafeAI report and the 2024 paper 'Deaf-Safe AI: A Legal Foundation for Ubiquitous Automatic Interpreting'; a symposium at Brown followed in April 2024. With the SAFE AI Task Force it co-wrote the AI Interpreting Solutions Evaluation Toolkit (Part A, 2025). It runs an on-demand course, 'A Risk Framework for Interpreting in the Age of AI', in ASL, Spanish and English.
why_it_matters: Deaf signers are a linguistic minority for whom failures of AI interpreting are hard to detect and costly. CoSET brings co-design with signers and interpreters, failure modes gathered from the community and a legal basis for accountability. It shows the knowledge of an affected community entering AI assurance.
