name: ICT4Peace Foundation
summary: A Geneva foundation, set up in 2003 by the former Swiss ambassador Daniel Stauffacher, that works on ICTs for peacebuilding and crisis management, and since 2007 on norms and confidence-building for a peaceful cyberspace. Since 2025 its main AI line has been a 'Global Compact on Extreme AI Risks' workstream: op-eds, interviews and policy papers arguing for binding minimum standards on frontier models, aimed at the Swiss-hosted Geneva AI Summit in June 2027. It also works on autonomous weapons in the UN GGE, AI and disinformation, and digital sovereignty.
why_it_matters: It brings two decades of cyber-norms diplomacy (norms of responsible state behaviour, confidence-building measures, proposals for a state peer-review mechanism and an independent attribution mechanism) to frontier-AI governance. It is one of the few long-standing Geneva peace NGOs that explicitly frames its AI work around extreme risks, and it has a direct line into Swiss preparations for the 2027 summit.

key_work.title: Global Compact on Extreme AI Risks (workstream)
Co-hosted the Geneva launch of the Strategic Foresight Group report 'The Essential Convergence: Global Compact on Extreme AI Risks' (with IFRC and GCSP)
NZZ op-ed: 'When It Comes to the Extreme Risks of Artificial Intelligence, Switzerland's Hour Has Come'
Policy paper on sovereignty, access and extreme AI risks

people: Paul Meyer (Senior Advisor; Chair, International Advisory Board)
funding: Supported by governments and philanthropic foundations (Wikipedia); no funder names or budget published on its site.
status_evidence: 3 Oct 2026: statement on the Swiss National Council motion (2 Oct) asking the Federal Council to use the 2027 Geneva AI Summit to set minimum safety standards for the most powerful AI models.
caveats: A small foundation whose AI output centres on its founder's advocacy (op-eds, interviews, speeches) rather than peer-reviewed research. Its own site gives 2003 as the founding year, while Wikipedia gives 2004 (the concept came out of WSIS 2003 and was endorsed in the 2005 Tunis Commitment). Funding is not disclosed. ICT4Peace Academy trainings found were tailored cyber workshops for governments, not open courses.
tag_notes: Home: its AI work applies cyber-diplomacy practice (UN OEWG/GGE norms, CBMs) to frontier AI, so Peace, sub Track II and diplomacy; secondary Law for the international-law advisers on staff (Géry, Roguski) and its human-rights line. Ring: bridge under E(3); an older peace institution with a sustained 2025-26 programme explicitly on extreme AI risks (Global Compact workstream, IASEAI affiliate since Jan 2026, summit advocacy). Transfer: into_institutions (J3), because it proposes governance instruments (minimum standards, a 'three-layer architecture' for international AI governance). Framing catastrophic: it names bio, chemical and cyber misuse and loss of control. Badge speed_of_wisdom: it argues explicitly for 'pacing' frontier models, not only regulating them. Engagement left empty because no open calls, courses or events were found on its site.

name: DiploFoundation (Diplo), incl. humAInism and the DiploAI ecosystem
summary: A non-profit foundation set up by the governments of Malta and Switzerland. It grew out of a 1992 ICT-and-diplomacy project and became a foundation in 2002. It trains diplomats and officials, mostly online, in digital diplomacy and global governance, and runs the Geneva Internet Platform and its Digital Watch observatory, which tracks AI-governance processes. Its humAInism project (since 2019) works on aligning AI with human values, rights and dignity. Diplo also builds its own 'bottom-up' AI tools (reporting assistants, a GraphRAG chatbot, custom assistants) and teaches a nine-week AI Apprenticeship course.
why_it_matters: It reaches diplomats from small and developing states, who are otherwise thinly represented in AI governance, and gives them AI literacy and hands-on tool-building. Its 'bottom-up AI' argument, for community-built models on curated local knowledge as a counter to knowledge monopolies, is a practical alternative to centralised AI that the safety field rarely engages with.

key_work.title: humAInism project
AI Apprenticeship online course
The DiploAI ecosystem (reporting assistant, Diplo chatbot, MyDepartment)
Jovan Kurbalija, 'To foster human freedom and prosperity, artificial intelligence must be developed bottom-up' (updated Aug 2026)

people: Stephanie Borg Psaila (Director of Digital Policy)
Vladimir Radunović (Director of Cybersecurity and Diplomacy)
hq: Malta (offices in Geneva, Belgrade and Washington DC)
funding: Established by the governments of Malta and Switzerland; course fees (e.g. AI Apprenticeship EUR 990) and project partners. No budget figures found.
status_evidence: 1 Oct 2026: DiploNews issue 548; Sep 2026 blog posts on AI-driven futures and physical AI; online courses starting 2 Nov 2026.
engage: Diplo Academy online courses, incl. the 9-week AI Apprenticeship (EUR 990; scholarships for professionals from developing countries)
Courses online and in Geneva, with new cohorts starting 2 Nov 2026
Diplo/GIP events at IGF, AI for Good and WSIS
DiploNews and Digital Watch newsletters
caveats: humAInism is framed around human-centred values and rights, not catastrophic risk, and Diplo's leadership argues against centralised AI rather than for AI-safety framings. The discovery draft said Diplo is 'organising' the 2027 Geneva AI Summit. I could only confirm that it tracks the summit on Digital Watch and features it on its homepage; the summit is a Swiss government event. Staff count (about 48 on the staff page) includes consultants.
tag_notes: Home: diplomatic training and practice is its method (H1), so Peace, sub Track II and diplomacy (UN and multilateral diplomacy); secondary Philosophy for humAInism's humanities lens and 'AI philosophy' strand. Ring: adjacent (roster value kept, E3); a sustained AI programme on governance and human values with no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing. Transfer: convening (J5), because its primary purpose is bringing diplomats into the AI conversation through education and tools. Problems: justice first, from its stated mission to raise the role of small and developing states; power from the bottom-up-AI argument against knowledge monopolies. Framing structural, from the knowledge-concentration critique. Standpoint neither: led from Malta and Switzerland, though it serves the Majority World substantially.

name: IFSH (Institute for Peace Research and Security Policy at the University of Hamburg): Arms Control and Emerging Technologies
summary: IFSH is a Hamburg peace-research institute founded in 1971. Its Arms Control and Emerging Technologies area, funded by the German Federal Foreign Office since 2019, studies arms control, verification and escalation, with a growing strand on military AI. The AI work covers autonomous weapons governance at the CCW, AI and nuclear escalation, public opinion on autonomous weapons, and AI assurance in chemical-weapons verification. A separate project, 'Algorithms and Artificial Intelligence as Game Changers?', is funded by the German Foundation for Peace Research (DSF). Through its Berlin office it briefs Bundestag members and ministries.
why_it_matters: It brings arms-control expertise in verification, norm-building and escalation dynamics to military AI, and puts it in front of German parliamentarians. Its work on why the CCW talks on autonomous weapons have stalled is directly useful to anyone designing international AI agreements.

key_work.title: Anja Dahlmann, 'Contesting control: Mechanisms of norm stagnation in the CCW debate on autonomous weapon systems', Contemporary Security Policy
Alexander Keller, 'Artificial Intelligence Assurance for the OPCW: Governing Trustworthy AI in CWC Implementation', CBWNet Working Paper 20
Algorithms and Artificial Intelligence as Game Changers? (DSF-funded project)
Arms Control and Emerging Technologies project (Federal Foreign Office)

people: Ulrich Kühn (Head, Arms Control and Emerging Technologies)
Anja Dahlmann (Head of the Berlin office; autonomous weapons)
Christian Alwardt (researcher, 'Algorithms and AI as Game Changers?')
funding: Institute core-funded by the City of Hamburg (science authority, BWFG). The Arms Control and Emerging Technologies project has been funded by the German Federal Foreign Office since 2019, in two phases running to at least 2026. The 'Game Changers' project is funded by the Deutsche Stiftung Friedensforschung (DSF).
status_evidence: Sep 2026: Dahlmann on CCW norm stagnation (23 Sep), Keller on AI assurance for the OPCW (14 Sep) and Łabuz et al. on LLMs as psychotherapists (23 Sep).
engage: Research and PhD positions (IFSH careers page and PhD programme)
Public events and IFSH Briefings at the Berlin office
Parliamentary briefings for Bundestag members and staff (by invitation)
caveats: AI is one strand inside a broader arms-control programme dominated by nuclear issues. The work on AI and nuclear escalation puts it near the bridge line, but its own framing is arms control and norm research, not AI safety. The LLM-psychotherapy paper sits outside the arms-control work. The team size (about 12 core researchers) is for the whole Arms Control and Emerging Technologies project, not just AI. The DSF 'Game Changers' project page gives no dates; the latest related news item found is from 2021, so it may be finished. Keller's OPCW paper appeared in the CBWNet series, a joint project in which IFSH is one partner.
tag_notes: Home: peace and conflict research on arms control and verification (H1), so Peace, sub arms control and IHL. Ring: adjacent (roster value kept, E3); a sustained, funded military-AI strand framed around arms control and norms rather than catastrophic risk or alignment. Borderline with bridge because of the AI-nuclear work. Transfer: into_institutions (J3), from arms-control and verification templates for CCW and OPCW. Assurance added for the OPCW AI-assurance paper. Framing structural: erosion of arms control and rivalrous dynamics, not a single catastrophe. Org type academic (I): a publicly funded research institute affiliated with the University of Hamburg. Berlin hub: its Berlin office has run since 2019, houses the Arms Control and Emerging Technologies staff and holds regular events.

name: PRIF Emerging Disruptive Technologies research group, with the Cluster for Natural and Technical Science Arms Control Research (CNTR)
summary: A research group set up in 2023 at PRIF, the Leibniz peace-research institute in Frankfurt, jointly led with PEASEC at TU Darmstadt. It combines political science with natural and computer science to study the military use of AI and machine learning, autonomous weapons, drones, cyber operations and other emerging technologies, and how arms-control verification could work for them. It sits within CNTR, a Federal Foreign Office-funded cluster whose annual CNTR Monitor covered AI in military use, verification, chemistry and biological design in its 2025 edition.
why_it_matters: It works on a question AI governance will need answered: how compliance with limits on military AI, and on AI more broadly, could be verified technically. Its mix of physicists, computer scientists and political scientists is a working model for verification research on international AI agreements.

key_work.title: CNTR Monitor 2025: how the materialisation of AI is reshaping global security risks and governance
Niklas Schörnig, 'Warfare at Machine Speed: The Growing Use of AI in the Military'
Thomas Reinhold, blog post on autonomous AI cyberattacks as a security-policy warning
Crisis Talk: Using Military AI Responsibly and Rethinking Regulation (Brussels, 270+ attendees)

people: Thomas Reinhold (Research Fellow; cyber, AI and arms control)
Malte Göttsche (CNTR; Science for Nuclear Diplomacy)
funding: CNTR is funded by the German Federal Foreign Office from Jan 2023 to Dec 2026, with partners TU Darmstadt and JLU Giessen. PRIF is a publicly funded Leibniz institute.
status_evidence: 23 Jul 2026: Reinhold's PRIF blog post on automated AI cyberattacks; Jun 2026: PRIF Spotlight 8/2026 on LLMs and cybersecurity and a CNTR fact sheet on human enhancement.
engage: PRIF Crisis Talks and public panels on military AI
Research positions via the PRIF careers page
CNTR Monitor and PRIF blog
caveats: CNTR's current funding period ends in December 2026, and I found no confirmation that it continues. The CNTR Monitor 2025 introduction explicitly dismisses 'rogue superintelligence' framings in favour of present security and proliferation risks, so the group is not AI-safety-aligned in framing. The group itself is small (two heads, two fellows, one associate).
tag_notes: Home: peace research on arms control and verification (H1, B12), so Peace, sub arms control and IHL; secondary Safety for PEASEC's IT-security and cyber methods. Ring: adjacent (roster value kept, E3); a standing, funded programme on military AI and verification whose framing explicitly rejects superintelligence narratives. Transfer: into_institutions (J3), from verification and arms-control designs. Assurance added for the work on verification of military technology and AI in verification. Framing structural: acceleration of warfare, erosion of human control and arms-race dynamics. Way of knowing empirical, from natural-science and technical verification research. Org type academic (I): a unit of a public research institute.

name: PAX (Netherlands)
summary: The largest Dutch peace organisation, based in Utrecht, formed by the 2007 merger of Pax Christi Netherlands and the Interchurch Peace Council (IKV) and renamed PAX in 2014. Most of its work is civilian protection, justice and peacebuilding in conflict areas. It has long campaigned against autonomous weapons as a founding member of the Stop Killer Robots coalition. Its 2026 AI outputs include a report with Privacy International on Big Tech becoming military suppliers, investor guidelines against financing autonomous weapons, and advocacy for binding rules on 'digital dehumanisation and automated harm'.
why_it_matters: PAX brings humanitarian-disarmament campaigning experience, the coalition model behind the landmine, cluster-munition and nuclear-ban treaties, to military AI. It also uses a lever the AI field rarely touches: research on companies and pressure through investors and financial institutions.

key_work.title: When Algorithms Go to War (with Privacy International): tech companies' convergence with arms manufacturers
Preventing Investments in Autonomous Weapons: guidelines for financial institutions
Developing rules to counter digital dehumanisation and automated harm
Don't be evil? A survey of the tech sector's stance on lethal autonomous weapons

funding: Revenue of about EUR 17.3 million in 2023, of which about EUR 0.84 million came from individual donations (Wikipedia). The Dutch Postcode Lottery is a displayed supporter.
status_evidence: 2 Sep 2026: event and publication on rules to counter digital dehumanisation, timed with CCW talks in Geneva; 21 Aug 2026: investor guidelines on autonomous weapons.
engage: Staff vacancies (paxforpeace.nl/who-we-are/vacancies)
Supports the Stop Killer Robots campaign, which has its own coalition membership
caveats: AI is a small part of a large, mostly non-AI peace organisation. Its autonomous-weapons work runs through the Stop Killer Robots coalition, which is already on the roster. The founding year is ambiguous: PAX dates itself from Pax Christi Netherlands (1948); IKV dates from 1966; the merged organisation from 2007; and the PAX name from 2014. Staff size not found.
tag_notes: Home: humanitarian disarmament and civilian-protection advocacy (H1), so Peace, sub arms control and IHL; secondary Law for its business-and-human-rights and corporate-accountability work. Ring: adjacent (roster value kept, E3); a sustained autonomous-weapons programme framed around dehumanisation and civilian harm, not catastrophic risk or alignment. Transfer: into_institutions (J3), because it seeks binding international rules and investor standards. Power added for the 2026 report on tech-arms convergence and corporate power concentration. Framing present_harms: 'machines making decisions over life and death' and harm to civilians. Way of knowing interpretive: normative argument grounded in IHL and human-rights law, backed by company research.

name: Berghof Foundation
summary: A Berlin-based conflict-transformation NGO, founded in 1971 by Georg Zundel, that works on mediation, dialogue support, peace education and research. Examples include high-level dialogue channels in Yemen, national dialogues and insider mediators. Its digitalisation theme says AI is reshaping armed conflict and names autonomous weapons and digital surveillance, but its digital projects target misinformation, conspiracy narratives and online polarisation (for example Digital.Truth and DesINFORMIERT!). It has no dedicated AI project.
why_it_matters: Transferable method: mediation, insider mediation and conflict-transformation practice, which could inform de-escalation of the US-China and lab-to-lab AI race and help bridge polarised AI-risk debates. It sits in int/a's Berlin hub, which makes it a plausible partner for a pilot.

key_work.title: Digitalisation theme: digital technologies, AI and peacebuilding
Digital.Truth: workshops for parents and teachers on conspiracy narratives and misinformation
Supporting social media influencers in Lebanon to counter sectarian messaging
Berghof Foundation Annual Report 2025

funding: German Federal Foreign Office, BMZ, the EU and the Berghof Stiftung endowment (own site). No budget figures found.
status_evidence: 17 Sep 2026: International Day of Peace feature on insider mediators; 28 Jul 2026: Annual Report 2025 published.
engage: Staff roles, tenders and training courses listed on its site (not AI-specific)
Door to open: no AI programme yet, so engagement would need outreach and a partnership proposal
caveats: No AI-specific project or publication found. Its only AI content is a framing statement on the digitalisation theme page, and its digital projects (2021-24) are about misinformation and polarisation. Inclusion rests on the transferable method, not on current AI work.
tag_notes: Home: conflict transformation, mediation and dialogue facilitation (H1), so Peace, sub peacebuilding and mediation. Ring: potential under E(2); no AI project in 2024-26, and the digital work addresses misinformation, not AI. Transferable method: mediation and conflict-transformation practice applied to de-escalating the AI race and polarised AI-risk debates. Transfer: none_yet (J6), because no AI work has moved yet. Problems are what the method would bear on: security (race de-escalation), then epistemics (its existing polarisation and disinformation work). Framing structural, from its digital theme's concern with polarisation and epistemic erosion. Berlin hub: its headquarters is in Berlin.

name: TUM Institute for Ethics in Artificial Intelligence (IEAI)
summary: An AI-ethics institute founded in 2019 at the Technical University of Munich, now part of its School of Social Sciences and Technology and directed by the business ethicist Christoph Lütge. It runs interdisciplinary projects on AI and human rights, the psychological impacts of interactive systems (PSAIS), AI-mediated civic participation, and AI for policymakers. It coordinates alignAI, a Horizon Europe doctoral network of 16 PhDs on aligning LLMs with human values in education, mental health and news. It publishes quarterly research briefs and hosts The Responsible AI Forum (TRAIF), the Global AI Ethics Consortium and the RAIN-Africa network.
why_it_matters: alignAI pairs a social-science or humanities PhD with a technical PhD on each use case. This is a concrete training model for bringing value questions into LLM alignment work, which the safety field mostly treats as a technical problem. Its work on the psychological effects of chatbots, and on human rights as limits on state use of AI, adds normative depth.

key_work.title: alignAI: Horizon Europe doctoral network on aligning LLMs with human values
Research brief Q3 2026: 'Human Rights as Negative Obligations in the Age of AI' (Julia Howard)
TRAIF 2026: The Responsible AI Forum (19-20 May)
PSAIS: psychological impact assessment of interactive systems

people: Auxane Boch (Associate Research Director; lead researcher, PSAIS)
Julia Howard (Program and Event Manager; author of the Q3 2026 research brief)
funding: Launched with a US$7.5 million grant from Facebook, announced in January 2019 (German Wikipedia). It now draws on corporate partners (Meta, Fujitsu, IBM, Munich Re, TÜV SÜD), Horizon Europe (alignAI), BMBF, TUM and the Bavarian government.
status_evidence: 30 Sep 2026: Q3 2026 research brief on human rights and AI; Sep 2026: 2025-26 Annual Report; Oct 2026 speaker series with Aditya Johri.
engage: Job openings (ieai.sot.tum.de/jobs)
Speaker series and The Responsible AI Forum (TRAIF)
Thesis projects for TUM students
Global AI Ethics Consortium and RAIN-Africa networks (institutional)
caveats: Founded with Facebook money. Press coverage of the leaked contract, cited by German Wikipedia, reported that Facebook could stop funding after the first US$1.5 million without giving reasons, and that replacing the director needed Facebook's written consent. Critics called it marketing for Facebook; Lütge called the arrangement a 'win-win'. Corporate funding continues. Its framing is responsible AI, not AI safety, and 'alignment' in alignAI centres on fairness and explainability in applied use cases.
tag_notes: Home: applied and business ethics led by a philosopher-ethicist director (H1, B13 ethics), so Philosophy, sub applied ethics; secondary Psychology (PSAIS, chatbot-bonding work) and Law (human-rights research). Ring: adjacent (roster value kept, E3); a responsible-AI framing focused on societal effects. alignAI's 'alignment of LLMs with human values' is a borderline bridge signal, but it is framed as fairness and explainability in applications, not AI safety. Transfer: into_institutions (J3), from its mission to produce guidelines for the ethical development and use of AI. Problems: values first (alignAI is its largest funded line), then minds and justice. Framing present_harms, because its outputs mainly guard against rights and psychological harms despite an upbeat mission statement (L).

name: La Quadrature du Net (LQDN)
summary: A Paris digital-rights association that defends civil liberties online against censorship and surveillance by states and companies. Its AI-related work investigates and litigates against automated systems used by French administrations: the CNAF welfare risk-scoring algorithm, which it is challenging before the Conseil d'État with 24 other organisations, France Travail's profiling of unemployed people, predictive policing and algorithmic video surveillance. It also campaigns against online identity and age verification and runs the Technopolice project on urban surveillance.
why_it_matters: It shows, case by case, how machine-learning decision systems are already used against the poorest people in a European state. It also has the tools to contest them: document leaks, freedom-of-information requests, analysis of source code and strategic litigation on data protection and non-discrimination. That is accountability practice the frontier-focused AI-safety field rarely has.

key_work.title: Conseil d'État case against the CNAF discriminatory risk-scoring algorithm (filed Oct 2024 by 15 groups; 10 more joined Jan 2026)
France Travail deploys an algorithmic profiling tool for job-search checks (with Radio France's investigation unit)
Predictive policing in France: against opacity and discrimination, the need for a ban
Algorithmic videosurveillance is spreading in Europe: let's fight back together

funding: About EUR 500,000 a year (Wikipedia gives EUR 540,154 for 2025). About 78% comes from individual donations. The rest comes from foundations: Fondation Charles Léopold Mayer, Un Monde Par Tous, Limelight, Digital Freedom Fund, Open Society Foundations and Civitates.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: published a review of the RIPOST security law (9 Sep). Jul 2026: published the France Travail profiling investigation (20 Jul).
engage: Volunteer: subtitling, translation review, software development, graphics, contacting MPs during campaigns (laquadrature.net/qui-sommes-nous)
Donate (the association is mostly funded by individual donors)
caveats: An activist and adversarial organisation. Its framing is civil liberties and present harms; it does not engage with AI x-risk. Most material is in French. It was an unregistered collective until 2013.
tag_notes: Home: its AI outputs are strategic litigation (Conseil d'État case on the CNAF algorithm on data-protection and non-discrimination grounds) and rights advocacy. That is law_legal (H1). Its algorithm investigations also touch law_sts civil-society auditing. Ring: a sustained programme since about 2023 on scoring algorithms, predictive policing and algorithmic video surveillance, all framed as present harms with no safety or catastrophic framing, so adjacent (E3). Transfer: protecting (J4). It defends the people targeted by state algorithms (welfare claimants, unemployed people, people under surveillance) rather than designing governance templates. Democracy is secondary for its civil-liberties work. Engagement is limited to what its own site shows (the volunteering page).

name: Comité consultatif national d'éthique du numérique (CCNEN), formerly CNPEN
summary: France's statutory advisory committee on the ethics of digital technology and AI. Decree no. 2024-463 of 23 May 2024 created it as the successor to the Comité national pilote d'éthique du numérique (CNPEN), which had worked under the aegis of the bioethics committee CCNE since December 2019. It issues formal opinions, on its own initiative or at the request of government and other institutions. Earlier opinions covered chatbots (2021), autonomous vehicles (2021), AI in medical diagnosis (2023), generative AI (2023), facial and behavioural recognition (2024) and the metaverse (2024). In 2026 it issued a joint opinion with the CCNE on digital neurotechnologies, and the higher-education ministry asked it to examine AI in scientific research.
why_it_matters: It is a working model of a standing, pluralist national ethics council for AI. Its 21 members include judges from the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation, scientists and civil-society representatives, and it borrows its method from bioethics. Its opinions on emotional manipulation by chatbots, cognitive liberty and neurotechnology, and youth and social media cover human-mind harms that AI-safety policy work seldom addresses.

key_work.title: Avis 150 du CCNE & Avis 10 du CCNEN: digital neurotechnologies
CNPEN Avis 7: Systèmes d'intelligence artificielle générative, enjeux d'éthique
CNPEN Avis 3: Agents conversationnels, enjeux d'éthique
Referral from the Ministry of Higher Education, Research and Space on AI systems in scientific research

people: Claude Kirchner (president since February 2025; emeritus research director, Inria)
funding: A state-created statutory committee. No budget figure found.
status_evidence: 9 Sep 2026: announced the ministry's referral on AI systems in scientific research. 7 Apr 2026: Avis 10 on neurotechnologies, jointly with the CCNE. 23 Feb 2026: joint CCNE-CCNEN declaration on young people and social networks.
engage: Public events, e.g. 'Contrôler ou libérer nos cerveaux ?' on neurotechnologies (registration opened Sep 2025)
Anyone can follow its opinions and agenda at ccnen.fr
caveats: Renamed and reconstituted: CNPEN (pilot, 2019-2024) became CCNEN by the May 2024 decree, and members were appointed in September 2025. It is advisory only, with no binding power. Its working-groups page is out of date (it still describes 2021-22 work).
tag_notes: Home: a statutory ethics council in the bioethics mould, so phil_bioethics (B13: ethics councils go to Philosophy). Law is secondary because members from the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation sit on it. Ring: ten opinions since 2020, mostly on AI and digital technology, with no catastrophic or alignment framing, so adjacent (E3). Transfer: its opinions advise government on how to govern AI and neurotech, so into_institutions (J3). The minds problem comes first because chatbots, neurotechnology and youth and social media are its most sustained thread. Status is changed because CNPEN was renamed CCNEN and reconstituted under a new decree.

name: Council of Europe: Framework Convention on AI, HUDERIA and CDNET (formerly the Committee on Artificial Intelligence, CAI)
summary: The Council of Europe's AI work centres on the Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law, the first legally binding international AI treaty. It was adopted on 17 May 2024 and opened for signature in Vilnius on 5 September 2024. The Convention requires risk and impact assessments, transparency, remedies and the option of bans or moratoria ('red lines'). It covers public authorities and private actors, but exempts national security and defence. The Committee on Artificial Intelligence (CAI, 2022-2025, preceded by CAHAI from 2019) drafted it and developed HUDERIA, a methodology for assessing AI's impact on human rights, democracy and the rule of law. A new Steering Committee for New and Emerging Digital Technologies (CDNET) succeeded the CAI in December 2025.
why_it_matters: It is the only binding multilateral AI treaty, and it is open to non-European states. The US, UK, Canada, Japan, Israel and Uruguay have signed, and Argentina, Australia, Mexico, Peru, Costa Rica and the Holy See took part in drafting. That makes it a treaty-law route for AI governance that the AI-safety field mostly bypasses. HUDERIA is a ready-made template for assessing sociotechnical impact, and a Conference of the Parties will monitor implementation once the treaty is in force.

key_work.title: Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (CETS 225)
HUDERIA risk and impact assessment methodology for AI systems
Establishment of the Steering Committee for New and Emerging Digital Technologies (CDNET), successor to the CAI

people: Mario Hernández Ramos (chair of the CAI)
funding: Council of Europe budget (contributions from its 46 member states). No budget figure found for the AI programme.
status_evidence: Dec 2025: the Committee of Ministers set up CDNET to succeed the CAI (19 Dec), and Bosnia and Herzegovina signed the Convention (10 Dec). A July 2026 archived copy of the Convention page lists 21 signatories, with the EU listed as a Party.
caveats: coe.int blocks automated fetches (403), so the current status comes from Wayback Machine copies (Jan, Jul and Aug 2026) and Wikipedia. Not yet in force: it needs five ratifications, including three CoE member states. German Wikipedia reported no ratifications as of October 2025. The draft entry's '50+ signatories' conflates the states that drafted the treaty with those that signed it; the actual count was about 21 in mid-2026. The CAI's mandate ended in 2025 and CDNET replaced it with a broader remit. Critics point to the national-security exemption and the option for parties to apply the treaty to private actors only indirectly.
tag_notes: Home: international human-rights and rule-of-law treaty-making, so law_legal (H1). Ring: a standing AI programme since 2019 (CAHAI, CAI, now CDNET) framed around human rights, democracy and the rule of law, with no catastrophic or alignment framing, so adjacent (E3). Transfer: it produces a binding treaty and an impact-assessment methodology, governance instruments, so into_institutions (J3). Assurance is a secondary problem for HUDERIA. Org type is public because it is an intergovernmental body (rule I). Status is changed because the CAI named in the roster entry was succeeded by CDNET in December 2025, while the Convention work continues. No individual engagement routes were verified, as the site could not be fetched directly.

name: Laboratoire national de métrologie et d'essais (LNE): AI evaluation and LEIA
summary: France's national metrology and testing laboratory is a public industrial and commercial establishment (EPIC) under the Ministry of Industry, with about 1,000 staff. It runs an AI evaluation laboratory, LE.IA, with several test platforms (including robotics, autonomous vehicles, drones and generative AI). It reports more than 1,500 AI systems evaluated over 15 years, in fields such as medicine, defence, video surveillance and autonomous vehicles. It offers a certification framework for AI processes, built against the EU AI Act, and ISO 42001 certification. It is one of the four bodies federated in INESIA, the French AI evaluation and security institute set up in January 2025 alongside ANSSI, Inria and PEReN.
why_it_matters: It brings measurement science (traceability, reproducible protocols, qualified reference datasets, independent benchmarking) to AI evaluation. That is the metrological basis that much AI eval work lacks. Through INESIA it links that practice to France's equivalent of an AI safety institute.

key_work.title: LE.IA AI evaluation laboratory and test platforms
Certification framework for AI processes
Founding member of INESIA, the national institute for AI evaluation and security
ROSE challenge: evaluating agricultural weeding robots (with IRSTEA, funded by ANR and AFB)

people: Thomas Grenon (director general since 2016, per Wikipedia; not confirmed for 2026)
funding: A public establishment (EPIC) under the Ministry of Industry that also earns revenue from testing and certification for about 5,000 clients. About 1,000 staff (2025), with 25% of its budget spent on research in 2025. No budget figure found for its AI work.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: news on fire-behaviour regulation (11 Sep). Its homepage features the AI evaluation platform and links it to job openings, and it marks 125 years in 2026.
engage: Job openings at nousrejoindre.lne.fr; the homepage links AI evaluation to recruitment
Commercial AI evaluation, benchmarking and certification services for developers
caveats: Much of its AI work is commercial testing and compliance certification, so the rule excluding compliance consultancies is a near miss. It stays in because it is a public metrology institute and part of INESIA. INESIA is a federation of existing bodies, not a separate legal entity, and has no regulatory power. Wikipedia gives 1900 as the founding year; LNE itself says 'since 1901'.
tag_notes: Home: metrology, testing and certification applied to AI systems, so safety_engineering (rule I and the Safety definition: certification and standards). Ring: an institution founded in 1901 running a standing AI evaluation programme framed around reliability and safety, and a member of INESIA, France's counterpart in the international network of AI safety institutes. That makes it bridge (E: old institutions with new AI-safety programmes are bridge). Transfer: its certification framework, benchmarks and evaluation protocols are assurance templates, so into_institutions (J3), as with York CfAA. Way of knowing is empirical because measurement and testing are its core output. Framing is nominal: it speaks of reliability, security and trust rather than harms, and present_harms is the closest key.

name: Science of Intelligence (SCIoI), Cluster of Excellence, TU Berlin and HU Berlin
summary: A Berlin Cluster of Excellence, funded by the DFG since 2019 and renewed for 2026-2032, that looks for principles of intelligence shared by animals, humans and machines. Its 'analytic-synthetic loop' pairs behavioural biology, psychology and neuroscience with robotics and computer science: principles found in biological systems are built into robots and models to test whether they generalise. It reports 145 researchers, 52 projects and nine candidate principles of intelligence. TU Berlin and HU Berlin lead it, with Charité, FU Berlin, Potsdam and the Max Planck Institute for Human Development as partners.
why_it_matters: It studies intelligence comparatively across substrates (fish swarms, plants, fungi, humans, robots). That gives an empirical account of what agency and intelligence are, close to the agenda of Principles of Intelligence (PIBBSS), but it has no safety framing yet. Being in Berlin, it is an obvious partner for int/a's Berlin community.

caveats: No AI-safety, alignment or societal-impact research programme was found. Its ethics work is an oversight structure for its own research (an Ethics Advisory Board, an internal committee and an ethics research team), not public-facing AI ethics. German Wikipedia says its aim includes helping to design 'safe and ethically responsible technologies', but no outputs on that were found.
tag_notes: Home: comparative and synthetic study of intelligence anchored in behavioural biology and collective behaviour, with robots as test beds, so life_biology (B5: organisms go to Life & systems). Psychology is secondary because cognitive science and psychology groups are core members. Ring: it builds artificial agents, but has no programme on AI safety, AI's societal effects or 'AI going well', so potential (E2). Transferable method: the analytic-synthetic loop, which extracts principles of intelligence from biological systems and tests them in artificial agents, applicable to the science of agency and to alternative agent design. Transfer: into_model, since its principles are put into artificial agents; it is not none_yet because the work itself involves AI. Framing is nominal (MISFIT): no statement of stakes beyond 'responsible' and 'safe' technology, so flourishing is the closest key. Partner (door to open) applies because it has no AI-safety programme.

name: Dezentrum
summary: A Zurich 'think and do tank for digitalisation and society'. Legally it is an association (Verein) that owns Dezentrum GmbH, run by five partners under Sociocracy 3.0. It uses scenario techniques, speculative objects and 'future experiments' (for example no1s1, a self-owning blockchain building prototyped with ETH Zurich). It also runs workshops, a game against youth radicalisation (Radical Choices) and internet-safety workshops. Its AI work is a participatory service that helps NGOs, public bodies, schools and SMEs write their own AI guidelines, plus blog essays on AI literacy and AI-generated 'workslop'.
why_it_matters: Its tools (speculative design, scenarios, participatory guideline-writing) help organisations and publics make sense of AI together. Those are methods the AI-safety field rarely uses outside expert circles. It shows how to turn abstract AI governance into norms co-written by the people affected, inside ordinary organisations.

Democracy is secondary because of its participatory processes and its TA-SWISS work on digital democracy. Transferable method: participatory futures and speculative design for collective sense-making about AI, and co-written organisational AI norms. Transfer: the AI offer produces organisational guidelines, so into_institutions rather than none_yet. Framing: its mission, 'a digital transformation that serves society', is aspirational, so flourishing. Partner applies because it has no substantive AI programme.

name: Center for Subjectivity Research (CFS), University of Copenhagen
summary: A University of Copenhagen research centre in the Department of Communication, directed by the phenomenologist Dan Zahavi. It was founded in 2002 as a Danish National Research Foundation Centre of Excellence, funded until 2012. It works on consciousness, selfhood, empathy, intersubjectivity and collective intentionality, combining phenomenology with analytic philosophy and working with psychiatry, developmental psychology and the social sciences. Current projects include 'Who Are We?' on we-identity and 'Mapping Perceptual Presence'. It is co-organising Models of Consciousness 2026 in Copenhagen, which has a theme on AI, LLMs and consciousness science.
why_it_matters: Debates on AI consciousness, moral status and people's attribution of minds to chatbots lean on functionalist assumptions. CFS has spent two decades on the first-person structure of experience, on empathy and on what it takes to be a 'we'. That is a phenomenological check on claims about machine minds and human-AI relationships, which AI-welfare work rarely draws on.

It sits on the seam with Philosophy: B13 sends philosophy of mind to AI minds only when it is mainly about AI. It is placed in minds because its relevance and its MoC 2026 role are in consciousness science. Philosophy and psychology (psychiatry and developmental psychology collaborations) are secondary. Ring: no AI programme, only co-organising one conference with an AI theme, so potential (E2). Transferable method: phenomenological analysis of selfhood, empathy and intersubjectivity, as a check on claims about machine consciousness and on human mind attribution to AI. Problems pair ai_status with minds (F must-pair: attribution plus status). Transfer: convening, because co-hosting MoC 2026 brings phenomenologists into AI-consciousness debates; none_yet would apply if that event were left out. Framing is nominal (MISFIT): no AI statement was found, and critical reflects its long-standing anti-reductionist programme. Way of knowing: interpretive, because its output is philosophical argument and Husserl scholarship, though phenomenology also borders on experiential.

name: Centre for Philosophy and AI Research (PAIR), FAU Erlangen-Nürnberg
summary: A philosophy-of-AI research centre at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg, set up with Vincent C. Müller's Alexander von Humboldt Professorship in Theory and Ethics of AI. About a dozen researchers work on what AI is, could be and should be, across philosophy of mind and science, epistemology, ethics and political philosophy, and the centre runs a weekly research seminar and workshops (responsibility gaps, agentic AI, AI and mental health). It is linked to the Society for the Philosophy of AI, which Müller chairs, with its diamond open-access journal Philosophy of AI and the biennial conference series (PT-AI).
why_it_matters: Müller edited the 2016 collection Risks of Artificial Intelligence and ran an early expert survey on AI timelines and risk with Nick Bostrom, but has since argued (Ratio, 2022) that the standard singularity-plus-orthogonality argument for existential risk is unsound. That makes PAIR a source of informed philosophical scrutiny of the concepts AI safety rests on (intelligence, goals, responsibility), and its society, journal and conference are a meeting point for philosophers of AI that the safety field rarely uses.

Müller's AI-risk publications (2014 JETAI special issue, 2016 edited volume, 2016 expert survey with Bostrom) mostly predate PAIR, and his 2022 paper with Michael Cannon is sceptical of the standard existential-risk argument. The 2026 Nature item is a Correspondence, not a research paper. The PhAI journal is hosted by the University of Cologne library.
tag_notes: Home philosophy (phil_technology): its outputs are philosophy of AI (what AI is, could be and should be) across mind, science, epistemology and ethics. Ring adjacent kept (E3): a standing AI-centred programme framed as 'a positive vision for the role of AI in society', not around catastrophic risk; the director's AI-risk work is largely pre-2024 and partly deflationary, so not bridge. Transfer convening (J5): the PhAI society, journal and conference bring the philosophy community into AI questions. Framing flourishing from the mission statement (L). Problems: agency (nature of AI and agentic AI), justice (responsibility gaps), minds (AI in education and mental health workshops).

name: Center for Science and Thought (CST), University of Bonn
summary: An interdisciplinary centre in the University of Bonn's philosophy department, directed by the philosopher Markus Gabriel and the physicist Ulf-G. Meißner, that puts philosophy in dialogue with physics, neuroscience, biology and computer science. Its AI work includes the philosophy sub-project of Certified AI (ethical requirements for certifying AI systems, with Fraunhofer IAIS under North Rhine-Westphalia's KI.NRW flagship), Desirable Digitalisation (with Cambridge, funded by Stiftung Mercator) on designing AI for social justice and ecological sustainability, and Polyglot, which builds open foundation models for low-resource languages. It also runs 'AI at a Crossroads', an online seminar series with partners in Brazil, India and Greece on AI in death, intimacy, care and counselling.
why_it_matters: It joins philosophy of technology to concrete standard-setting: its catalogue of ethical requirements for AI certification fed into Germany's AI standardisation roadmap. Its partnership with Cambridge's Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence and its seminar series with Brazilian and Indian partners bring continental, feminist and non-Western perspectives into AI governance.

name: Munich Center for Mathematical Philosophy (MCMP), LMU Munich
summary: A research centre for mathematical philosophy at LMU Munich, founded in 2010 by Hannes Leitgeb with an Alexander von Humboldt Professorship and now directed by Leitgeb, Stephan Hartmann and Christian List. It applies logic, probability, statistics, decision theory and social choice theory to philosophical problems, and lists philosophy of AI among its research areas. Its main AI work is Tom Sterkenburg's DFG Emmy Noether group 'From Bias to Knowledge: The Epistemology of Machine Learning' (2023-2029), and it hosts PhilML'26, the annual Philosophy of Machine Learning conference, on 6-9 October 2026.
why_it_matters: Formal epistemology, decision theory and social choice are the tools behind agent foundations and preference aggregation, and MCMP holds a large concentration of that expertise. It now has a funded group on what machine learning can justify, and PhilML'26 lists alignment, safety and mechanistic interpretability among its topics, so it is a natural partner for foundational alignment work that wants philosophical rigour.

Transfer convening (J5): PhilML brings philosophers and ML researchers together; nothing yet changes models or governance. MISFIT: framing has no stated stakes (foundational epistemology of ML); present_harms chosen only because PhilML's ethical strand centres fairness. MISFIT: the adjacent ring assumes work on societal effects, whereas this is foundational theory of learning.

name: Center for Advanced Internet Studies (CAIS)
summary: A non-profit research institute in Bochum, founded in November 2016 as a research college and expanded in April 2021 into an institute for digitalisation research. It is funded by the North Rhine-Westphalia Ministry of Culture and Science and sponsored by six universities and three other institutes. Two of its four research programmes are on AI: Design of Trustworthy AI (led by Hendrik Heuer; participatory co-design and user audits of AI systems on social media) and Educational Technologies and AI; it also runs third-party projects such as KIKI 2036 on childhood in the age of AI, and the CAIS College hosts residential fellows and working groups.
why_it_matters: It applies participatory software design, audits of recommender systems and design-fiction labs with children to AI, methods that give affected users a say in how AI systems are built and checked. Its residential fellowship college is a possible host for researchers working on AI's societal side.

name: Bavarian Research Institute for Digital Transformation (bidt)
summary: An institute of the Bavarian Academy of Sciences and Humanities, set up in 2018 and funded by the Free State of Bavaria, that researches digital transformation in three areas (economy and work, communication and society, law and ethics) and gives policy advice. Its research focus 'Humans and Generative AI: Trust in Co-Creation' funds four-year projects at Bavarian institutions, and it also funds interdisciplinary consortium projects and a graduate centre. Recent AI outputs include experiments on public trust in judges who draft rulings with generative AI, public courses on bias in chatbots and AI agents, and the bidt Digitalbarometer survey.
why_it_matters: It is a public funder and think tank running a multi-year line on how people come to trust, or over-trust, generative AI in shared work, including in courts, a question that bears on human oversight. Its directorate includes Julian Nida-Rümelin, a leading proponent of 'digital humanism', so it connects German philosophy and social science to AI governance.

name: AI, Media & Democracy Lab (AIM4DEM)
summary: An ELSA (ethical, legal and societal aspects) lab co-founded by the University of Amsterdam, the Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences and the Dutch national research institute for mathematics and computer science (CWI), which began in 2022 with Dutch Research Council (NWO) funding. Led by law professor Natali Helberger and communication scientist Claes de Vreese, its roughly 35 researchers study how AI affects news media and democracy, working with partners including the BBC, NPO, DPG Media, RTL and Bayerischer Rundfunk. Projects cover disinformation and Dutch law, newsrooms' dependence on big tech, AI disclosure labels, responsible recommender systems, and an advisory report for the Council of Europe on generative AI, media and elections.
why_it_matters: It tests AI in real newsrooms and recommender systems against democratic values and runs cross-national surveys of public attitudes, giving empirical grounding to the gradual erosion of the information ecosystem that AI-safety work mostly discusses in theory. Its Council of Europe report is a direct route into intergovernmental AI governance.

name: Danish Institute for Human Rights (DIHR): Technology and Human Rights
summary: The technology strand of the Danish Institute for Human Rights, Denmark's national human rights institution (founded 1987, government-funded, with UN 'A' status), run from its Human Rights, Business and Tech department. It develops rights-based tools and guidance for digital technology and AI: a guide to fundamental rights impact assessments for high-risk AI under the EU AI Act (with ECNL, December 2025), the Digital Rights Check for development projects, an online microlearning series on a human rights-based approach to AI, and the NHRI Digital Rights Alliance, a peer network of national human rights institutions. A 2025-26 project is drafting global legal principles for human rights in the digital space.
why_it_matters: It brings human rights impact assessment, a field-tested method from business and human rights, to AI deployment, and has written it up as a practical, phased guide for the EU AI Act's FRIA duty. That is a ready template for rights-based assurance and oversight, and its NHRI alliance reaches national oversight bodies worldwide.

name: Integrales Forum e.V.
summary: The Integrales Forum is a German nonprofit association that promotes integral theory, mainly Ken Wilber's work, in the German-speaking world. It began in 1998 as a Ken Wilber study group and became a registered association in 2006. It keeps a large German-language online archive, published the journal Integrale Perspektiven (print 2006–2018) and an online journal, makes podcasts, runs monthly regional groups in Leipzig, Dresden and Munich plus free online hubs, and co-organises the annual Flow to Future Festival. It has no AI programme; its July 2026 festival included two AI workshops.
why_it_matters: It is the established German-speaking home of the integral and developmental frameworks that int/a draws on, with salons, online hubs and a festival already in place. Its board has started to bring AI into its programme, so int/a Berlin could use it to reach a practitioner community that AI safety has never engaged.

Integral theory and the Spiral Dynamics stage model it relies on are criticised as esoteric or pseudoscientific (e.g. Metzler philosophy lexicon, as cited on German Wikipedia). The association is mid-renewal: it ended its old structures in 2024 and says its operative team is being rebuilt. The discovery entry said it had no AI strand; in fact there are a few 2015–16 essays on AI and the singularity and two 2026 festival workshops, which is still light engagement. Registered at the Berlin-Charlottenburg court, but its address is Lilienthal near Bremen and no Berlin group is listed.
tag_notes: Home: a Wilber-inspired integral network whose library, journal and festivals are integral theory and inner development, so contemplative/cont_integral (B1: integral bodies are Contemplative). Ring: potential, kept from the roster: there is no AI programme, only 2015–16 essays and two workshops at the 2026 festival (E2). Transferable method: integral (AQAL) and adult-development frameworks, plus a German-speaking practitioner network of salons, online hubs and festivals that could host inner-development work for people in AI. Transfer: convening, because its little AI activity brings its own community into the AI conversation (J5); not none_yet, since some AI work exists. Org type: membership, as a registered association with individual members (I). Way of knowing: interpretive, since its AI outputs are integral-theory essays and talks; its festival practice is experiential. Hubs: online only, because no Berlin group is listed.

name: Futurium
summary: Futurium is Berlin's 'House of Futures', a free-entry museum that opened in September 2019. It is run by Futurium gGmbH, a nonprofit company whose lead shareholder and main funder is the federal research ministry. It combines a permanent exhibition on possible futures of humans, nature and technology with a Forum for public talks and a Lab for hands-on workshops. Since September 2026 its thematic focus 'ON/OFF RELATIONSHIP' has looked at how people will share their lives with AI and other technology, through installations on AI-generated avatars, deepfakes and data extraction, a talk series and family labs.
why_it_matters: It reaches a mass public (nearly 670,000 visitors in 2025) with participatory, exhibition-based futures work, and it is now running a public programme on living with AI. Those are formats the AI-safety field rarely uses. For int/a Berlin it is a natural venue for bringing AI scenarios and questions of human agency to a general audience.

key_work.title: ON/OFF RELATIONSHIP: How we will share our lives with technology (thematic focus and exhibits)
The future of artificial intelligence: technological promises and the power of terminology (public talk, 12 Oct 2026)

Other shareholders include the Max Planck Society, Fraunhofer, Helmholtz and Leibniz associations, Leopoldina, acatech, DAAD and the Humboldt Foundation, plus a few companies.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: opened the ON/OFF RELATIONSHIP thematic focus (press preview 11 Sep 2026); AI talk scheduled for 12 Oct 2026; 'Robots, AI and more' family labs on 4 and 25 Oct 2026.
engage: Free public talks in the ON/OFF RELATIONSHIP series, starting with 'The future of artificial intelligence' on 12 Oct 2026 (German, recorded for YouTube)

caveats: Its AI work is public engagement and exhibition-making, not research, and ON/OFF RELATIONSHIP covers technology in general with AI as one strand. The AI talk is on 12 October 2026, not the 16 October given in the discovery entry. Its AI framing is partly deflationary: the talk page calls AI systems pattern processors 'nothing more' and treats superintelligence talk as discourse to examine. It depends almost entirely on federal funding: in December 2025 the Bundesrechnungshof (Federal Audit Office) concluded that its financing concept had failed, citing too little private participation (German Wikipedia). Staff numbers are not published. The October family-lab dates could not be confirmed on the Lab page.
tag_notes: Home: a futures museum whose method is exhibitions, art installations and participatory futures formats, so arts/arts_futures (H1). Ring: changed from potential to adjacent, because since September 2026 it has run a standing AI-themed focus (exhibits on AI avatars, deepfakes and data, plus a talk series and labs) on human-machine relationships, with no catastrophic-risk or alignment framing (E2, E3). Transfer: convening, because it brings its public into the AI conversation through exhibitions and talks (J5). Problems: epistemics first, since how publics picture and narrate AI futures and spot deepfakes is Sensemaking; minds second, for dependence and relationships with technology. Framing: flourishing, from its mission question 'How do we want to live?' (L), although the AI exhibits stress unease, manipulation and dependence. Org type: nonprofit, as a government-funded gGmbH (I).

name: Geneva Academy of International Humanitarian Law and Human Rights
summary: The Geneva Academy is a joint centre of the University of Geneva's law faculty and the Geneva Graduate Institute. Founded in 2007, it teaches and researches international humanitarian law, international criminal law and human rights. It runs LLM and executive master's programmes, summer courses and projects such as War Watch (conflict and civilian-harm tracking), IHL in Focus and Arms TRACK (assessments for the Arms Trade Treaty), and until 2025 RULAC, its classification of armed conflicts. Its AI work so far is a 2024 report on AI decision-support systems in military targeting, from an ICRC-funded project on the digitalisation of armed conflict (2020–2025), and an August 2026 consultation with Oxford's Institute for Ethics in AI on UN human-rights standard setting for AI.
why_it_matters: It holds deep, practice-tested expertise in IHL and in how UN human-rights standards are actually made: conflict classification, arms-trade assessment and treaty and Human Rights Council processes. That expertise bears directly on military AI and on any future international AI norms, and the AI-safety governance field mostly lacks it. It has started to apply it to AI, but has no standing programme.

The project that produced the 2024 military AI report ended in October 2025, and the 2026 item is an account of a small informal consultation, not a full report with findings. Governance changed in 2026: two co-presidents and an executive director replaced the single director. Its partner, Oxford's Institute for Ethics in AI, does not list the consultation in its own news. Scale is estimated from the roughly 70 people listed on its people page, which includes board, committee and visiting faculty.

Ring: potential, kept from the roster: its AI output is one 2024 report from a broader digitalisation project that has ended, plus one 2026 consultation, which counts as light engagement rather than a standing AI programme (E2). Transferable method: IHL and UN human-rights standard-setting expertise (conflict classification, arms-trade assessment, treaty and Human Rights Council processes) for military AI and international AI norms. Transfer: into_institutions, because its AI work aims at legal standards and IHL compliance (J3). Framing: present_harms, centred on civilian protection and rights (L). Org type: academic, as a university joint centre (I).

name: Chung-Ang University AI Humanities Research Institute (HK+ AI Humanities; 인공지능인문학연구소)
summary: A Chung-Ang University institute in Seoul that has carried the National Research Foundation of Korea's Humanities Korea Plus (HK+) agenda 'AI Humanities' since 2017. Its aim is to set up AI humanities as a new foundational humanities field. Research runs in five strands: AI relations and communication, AI ethics and norms, hermeneutics of humanities data, technology criticism, and AI society and culture. It publishes the KCI-listed Journal of AI Humanities three times a year (vol. 23, August 2026) and has co-published the international applied-ethics journal JAHR since 2021. It ran the International Conference on AI Humanities (ICAIH) every year from 2018 to at least 2024, and also holds domestic conferences and colloquia.
why_it_matters: It is a sustained institutional attempt to make AI a central object of the humanities, with a peer-reviewed publication line. It opens a channel into Korean philosophy, linguistics, media and cultural studies of AI, work that English-language AI-safety research rarely reads.

HK+ funding comes in time-limited phases, and the site does not say whether NRF support continues. The framing is human-centred AI ethics and technology criticism, without a catastrophic-risk focus.

name: NIAS Consciousness Studies Programme (with its offshoot Complex Systems Programme), National Institute of Advanced Studies
summary: An interdisciplinary programme at the National Institute of Advanced Studies on the IISc campus in Bengaluru. Philosopher Sangeetha Menon set it up with physicist B. V. Sreekantan after she joined NIAS in 1996, and it describes itself as India's first academic group to study consciousness with an interdisciplinary mandate. It combines Indian philosophy of self, phenomenology, Ayurveda and well-being studies with neuroscience and complexity measures of consciousness. Its main AI output is the 2024 Springer volume 'AI, Consciousness and the New Humanism'. Its offshoot, the NIAS Complex Systems Programme led by Nithin Nagaraj, develops chaos-based 'neurochaos learning' and in February 2026 posted DAIReS, a method for detecting hallucinations and backdoor triggers in language models.
why_it_matters: It brings first-person, Indian-philosophical accounts of consciousness and self, and complexity-based measures of levels of consciousness, to the question of machine minds. That Majority-World perspective is largely missing from AI-welfare and consciousness-indicator work.

key_work.title: AI, Consciousness and The New Humanism: Fundamental Reflections on Minds and Machines (Springer; eds. Menon, Todariya, Agerwala)
DAIReS: a unified syndrome-decoding approach for hallucination and backdoor trigger detection (Complex Systems Programme)
ChaosNet: a chaos-based artificial neural network architecture (start of the neurochaos learning line)

The technical AI work sits in the separate Complex Systems Programme and is mostly machine-learning methods research, with one dependability preprint. Some affiliated publications appear in venues outside mainstream consciousness science. The founding year is not stated precisely (late 1990s).

Ring changed from adjacent to potential: in 2024-26 the programme has no standing AI programme, only one edited volume, and the offshoot's neurochaos ML line is capability research, not a programme on AI's societal effects or safety (E2). Transferable method: first-person, Indian-philosophical accounts of self and consciousness, plus network-causality and complexity measures that distinguish levels of consciousness, applicable to AI consciousness and welfare assessment. Transfer: the book informs its own scholarly community, so convening (J5); the Complex Systems DAIReS preprint alone would be into_model. Merged with the Complex Systems Programme, which grew out of it (Nagaraj joined CSP in 2015).

name: Araya Inc. (株式会社アラヤ)
summary: A Tokyo company founded in December 2013 by neuroscientist Ryota Kanai, its CEO, with 92 employees as of September 2025. Its research arm states two aims: to understand consciousness and intelligence through neuroscience and mathematics in order to build conscious, intelligent machines, and to develop brain-machine interfaces. Its revenue comes mainly from AI development services such as visual inspection, construction automation and HVAC optimisation. Since October 2025, research team leader Manuel Baltieri has been co-PI on a UK ARIA 'Mathematics for Safe AI' project that formally links a system's physical description to goal-directed interpretations of it.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few organisations openly trying to build machine consciousness, and is led by a co-author of the 2023 'Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence' indicators report. For AI-welfare and digital-minds work it is both a source of expertise and a case for governance. Its ARIA project adds agent-foundations work grounded in dynamical systems and information theory.

key_work.title: Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Science of Consciousness (Kanai a co-author)
Combining Physical and Intentional Stance for Safe AI (ARIA Mathematics for Safe AI, Oct 2025 to Jun 2027)
Nikkei Science special feature 'AI, the Brain, and Consciousness' (Kanai, Nakai, Hamada)

people: Manuel Baltieri (research team leader; ARIA co-PI)
funding: Commercial revenue from AI development and consulting. Public research grants: UK ARIA (Mathematics for Safe AI, 2025-27), JSPS KAKENHI, JST FOREST, AMED-PRIME, Japan's defence-ministry Innovative Science and Technology Initiative for Security (2024-27), and the PwC Japan Foundation.
status_evidence: Jul 2026: Kanai and colleagues featured in Nikkei Science's 'AI, the Brain, and Consciousness' issue. Mar 2026: MOU with Fluent BCI on speech-decoding BCI. Dec 2025: ARIA grant announced.

One grant comes from Japan's defence-ministry security research programme (a recommendation-system project). The Consciousness Club Tokyo it hosted appears inactive.
tag_notes: Home: the stated research mission asks what could make artificial systems conscious, and Kanai co-authored the AI-consciousness indicators report, so AI minds/minds_science (B4: asking whether AI has experience goes to AI minds whatever the method). NeuroAI and BMI work gives Life & systems as a secondary tradition, and the ARIA agent-foundations project gives Formal. Ring changed from adjacent to bridge: the company is rooted in neuroscience and consciousness science, and it holds a funded project explicitly framed around safe AI (ARIA Mathematics for Safe AI, Oct 2025 to Jun 2027), which counts as sustained under E3. Transfer: its research is aimed at AI architectures and at tools to verify that an AI's actions match its intended purpose, so into_model (J1). Framing: the company presents an aspirational vision, so flourishing. MISFIT: none.

name: Japanese Society for Artificial Intelligence (JSAI) Ethics Committee (人工知能学会 倫理委員会)
summary: The ethics committee of the Japanese Society for Artificial Intelligence, Japan's main AI learned society. It was relaunched in 2014 under Yutaka Matsuo and deliberately includes outsiders: science-fiction novelists, journalists, legal scholars and philosophers. It wrote the JSAI Ethical Guidelines (approved February 2017), whose ninth clause says that an AI which becomes a member or quasi-member of society must abide by the guidelines too. It also runs the AI-ELSI Award, holds sessions at JSAI meetings and issues statements.
why_it_matters: It is an example of a professional society writing a researchers' code through open debate, with science-fiction writers as standing members, and it posed an early, deliberate question about AI as a moral agent bound by its own code. Its third award gave a special prize to the AI Alignment Network's superintelligence scenario contest, a sign that Japan's mainstream AI community is open to safety themes.

Its recent statements stress human-AI symbiosis, research competitiveness and security more than risk. Output is mostly in Japanese, and activity is periodic.

name: RIKEN AIP Science, Technology and Society Team (Osamu Sakura) and AI Utilization in Society and Legal System Team (Hiroshi Nakagawa)
summary: Two societal-implications teams at RIKEN's Center for Advanced Intelligence Project (AIP) in Tokyo. The Science, Technology and Society Team, led by Osamu Sakura (March 2017 to March 2026), studied public images of AI and robots in Japan and East Asia, including science fiction, and contrasted Buddhist and Judeo-Christian views of humans and machines. The AI Utilization in Society and Legal System Team, led by Hiroshi Nakagawa (October 2016 to March 2026), worked on AI ethics, privacy protection, explainability, accountability, trustworthiness and AI agents. Both closed in March 2026, along with AIP's whole AI in Society Research Group, leaving the centre with technical groups only.
why_it_matters: Their closure removes Japan's national-lab base for culturally specific East Asian research on how people relate to AI. The niche is open, and researchers such as Sakura, Nakagawa and Arisa Ema remain available to funders who want non-Western perspectives in AI governance.

name: Infinity Foundation
summary: A Princeton-based nonprofit founded in 1994 by Indian-American author Rajiv Malhotra, with an Indian arm, Infinity Foundation India. It applies what it calls a 'Dharma lens' to civilisational studies and argues against Western universalism through books, videos, grants and events. On AI, Malhotra wrote 'Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Power: 5 Battlegrounds' (Rupa, 2020). He also edited 'The Power of Future Machines', which includes the essay 'Artificial Intelligence as an Enabler of Western Universalism'. Its video output continues to cover AI, e.g. 'Ask Rajiv: AI, Youth Liability & Internal Colonization' (July 2026).
why_it_matters: It represents an influential Hindu-nationalist Indian view of AI as a contest over power, sovereignty and cultural identity, which matters for understanding how AI governance is argued in India. It is a voice to understand rather than an obvious partner.

key_work.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Power: 5 Battlegrounds (Rupa Publications)
The Power of Future Machines (edited volume, incl. 'Artificial Intelligence as an Enabler of Western Universalism')
Ask Rajiv: AI, Youth Liability & Internal Colonization (video)

Divya Reddy (trustee, Infinity Foundation India; co-author of the AI and Western universalism essay)
funding: Created by private endowment (per its site) and supported by donations. It says it has made over 400 grants for research, education and philanthropy.
status_evidence: Oct 2026: video on Swami Dayananda Saraswati and Malhotra. Jul 2026: 'Ask Rajiv: AI, Youth Liability & Internal Colonization'.
engage: Newsletter and YouTube channel linked from infinityfoundation.com
caveats: Wikipedia, citing scholars, describes Malhotra as a public proponent of Hindutva. His books are polemical (e.g. 'Breaking India', 'Academic Hinduphobia'), and in 2015 scholars alleged plagiarism in 'Indra's Net'. Its AI critique is framed as civilisational competition. Its AI engagement is mainly books (2020 and early 2020s) plus occasional videos. The taxonomy has no Hindu or Dharmic sub-tradition.
