MISFIT: no Hindu or Dharmic sub-tradition exists. rel_interfaith is chosen as closest because the foundation's 1997 mission covers integrating religion, science and psychology and bridging Eastern and Western thought. The AI frame is power and sovereignty (the '5 battlegrounds'), so Economics (political economy) is secondary. Ring: AI is a recurring theme (a 520-page book, an edited volume and 2026 videos) about AI's societal and cultural effects, with no safety framing, so adjacent is kept (E3), though 2024-26 AI output is thin. Transfer: the book aims to inform at-risk Indian publics so they demand a seat at AI policy tables, so convening (J5). Standpoint is majority_world because its mission centres on India and the Indian arm is led locally, although headquarters is in the US (O).

name: Center for Digital Society (CfDS), Universitas Gadjah Mada
summary: A research centre in the Faculty of Social and Political Sciences at Universitas Gadjah Mada in Yogyakarta, founded in 2015, which studies digital society in Indonesia: digital governance, the platform economy, digital literacy, cybersecurity and, increasingly, AI. Since December 2023 it has run an AI Policy and Skilling Lab with Google Indonesia and KORIKA, which has trained over 400 participants from 35 ministries, agencies, associations and communities. It publishes commentaries (for example on militarised AI, September 2025, and the gap between AI principles and practice, December 2025) and runs the DIFUSSION discussion series (no. 136, on data sovereignty, August 2026).
why_it_matters: A Southeast Asian social-science centre that trains government officials on AI and writes about data sovereignty, information operations and AI's environmental footprint from an Indonesian standpoint. It is a route into Global South policy communities that AI-safety governance work rarely reaches.

key_work.title: AI Policy and Skilling Lab series (with Google Indonesia and KORIKA)
Militarized AI in the New Age of Wars: Functionality and Geopolitical Contestation (commentary)
DIFUSSION 136: What 'Data Sovereignty' Actually Means in Indonesian Policy Circles
Fairwork Indonesia gig-work ratings (with the Fairwork Foundation)

funding: Universitas Gadjah Mada (FISIPOL). Project partners include Google Indonesia and KORIKA (AI Policy and Skilling Lab), Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung, Goethe-Institut, Tokopedia, the Pulitzer Center, ISIF-APNIC, ASEF and GIZ.
status_evidence: Sep 2026: posts on Indonesia's position on AI's material environmental effects and on AI and investigative journalism. Aug 2026: DIFUSSION 136 on data sovereignty. Jul 2026: 2025 annual report.
engage: DIFUSSION discussions, livestreamed on YouTube with free registration (mostly in Indonesian)
Free public Kecerdasan Digital (digital intelligence) online course series
Student internship programme
caveats: The AI policy training is co-run with Google Indonesia, which raises questions about independence. Much content is in Indonesian and written by research assistants. There is no catastrophic-risk framing.
tag_notes: Home: a multidisciplinary social-science public-interest centre (political science, IR, STS) working on digital policy, so Law/law_policy (B9). Recurring security themes (militarised AI, cyberspace, information operations, digital diplomacy) give Peace as a secondary tradition. Ring: a sustained AI line in 2024-26 (policy training, commentaries, discussion series) on societal effects, without safety framing, so adjacent is kept (E3). Transfer: its main AI activity is building government officials' capacity for AI governance, so into_institutions (J3). Framing: the work centres on concrete harms (labour conditions, harmful content, deepfakes, scams), so present_harms. Online hub: DIFUSSION is a recurring livestreamed series with registration, and the course series is open online (O). Indonesia gives standpoint majority_world.

name: Economics of Transformative AI Initiative (EconTAI), University of Virginia
summary: A University of Virginia research centre, launched in August 2025, that studies how AI matching or exceeding human ability would change growth, labour markets, inequality and public finance. Anton Korinek and Lee Lockwood lead it, with Basil Halperin as faculty adviser. It publishes papers on AI take-off, the automation of research and taxation under transformative AI, and co-organises scenario-planning workshops with the IMF, the Windfall Trust and the Stanford Digital Economy Lab.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few academic economics groups that takes transformative AI as a premise. It works out practical consequences that AI-safety policy rarely models, for example what happens to the tax base and public finances if labour income collapses. Its scenario workshops bring together labs, labour, the IMF and civil society to plan for more than one possible 2030.

key_work.title: Public Finance in the Age of AI: A Primer (Korinek and Lockwood, Brookings)
Measuring the AI Economy (Korinek and McKelvey, PIIE working paper)
Scenario Planning Workshop on Global Economic and Financial Implications of AI (co-organised with the IMF, with Windfall Trust)
Transformative AI, existential risk, and real interest rates (Chow, Halperin, Mazlish)

funding: UVA College of Arts & Sciences provided launch support. Korinek's CV lists a 2025 FLI grant for the economics of transformative AI. The site does not list any other funders.
status_evidence: 17 Sep 2026: Lee Lockwood presented 'Public Finance in the Age of AI' at the NBER Tax Policy and the Economy conference. Jul 2026: on the steering committee of the PAI/Windfall Trust Shaping Economic Futures workshop.
engage: Newsletter on the site (econtai.org/newsletter.html)
No open fellowships, jobs or public events were listed as of Oct 2026. Its workshops have been invitation-only, under the Chatham House Rule.
caveats: Launched in Aug 2025, so the track record is short. The core team is three economists and the website is sparse. Korinek's CV lists membership of Anthropic's Economic Advisory Council (2025–), which is a possible conflict of interest for work on lab-economy policy. Funding is not disclosed on the site.
tag_notes: Home economics (H1): growth, labour and public-finance models built by UVA economists; sub econ_tai. Ring bridge kept from roster (E3): a university economics unit with an explicit transformative-AI and 'shared prosperity' mission, part-funded by FLI. As a 2025 founding with a TAI-only mission it sits close to the core line, but its identity is academic economics. Transfer into_institutions (J3): its tax, public-finance and scenario work is aimed at policymakers (IMF, Brookings, NBER). Second problem epistemics, for repeated scenario-planning workshops and the use of real interest rates to forecast AI timelines. Framing structural (L): tax-base erosion and labour displacement, not a single catastrophe. Way of knowing formal: macro models of take-off and public finance.

name: Stanford Digital Economy Lab
summary: A research lab at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI, founded in 2020 by Erik Brynjolfsson. It studies how AI changes the economy through four streams: the economics of transformative AI, new measures of the economy (such as the GDP-B welfare metric), digital platforms, and AI agents (the Loyal Agents project with Consumer Reports). In August 2025 it ran a two-week course on the economics of transformative AI, funded by Open Philanthropy, that included sessions on AI safety and existential risk. In July 2026 it organised the 'We Must Act Now' statement from economists and Nobel laureates.
why_it_matters: It trains PhD economists in the theory of explosive growth and in weighing existential risk against growth. Its 'Canaries in the Coal Mine' series measures AI's effect on young workers' jobs, which the AI-safety field rarely tracks. Its Loyal Agents work sets duties of loyalty and care for AI agents acting for consumers, an approach to agent alignment taken from law and markets.

key_work.title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of AI (revised Aug 2026: 19% employment gap for young workers)
The Economics of Transformative AI summer course (48 participants; lectures on AI safety and existential risk vs growth)
'We Must Act Now' statement on preparing for AI's economic transformation
Loyal Agents (with Consumer Reports Innovation Lab)

people: Sandy Pentland (HAI Fellow and lead faculty)
funding: Funders listed on its site include NSF, Open Philanthropy (now Coefficient Giving), Schmidt Futures, the Russell Sage Foundation and Good Ventures. Corporate affiliates include ADP, Autodesk, Capgemini, Denso and Nasdaq, and Jerry Yang and Akiko Yamazaki are individual donors. Open Philanthropy grants: $120k for a TAI workshop (Nov 2023) and $165k for the TAI course (Mar 2025).
status_evidence: 12 Aug 2026: revised 'Canaries in the Coal Mine?' paper with an expanded dataset. 13 Jul 2026: 'We Must Act Now' statement (16 Nobel laureates among the signatories).
engage: Postdoctoral, research and fellowship openings on its careers page
Public seminars and research workshops
Corporate affiliate programme
Interest form for future TAI economics courses (the course will not run in summer 2026)
caveats: Most of the lab's work is mainstream productivity and labour economics. The TAI stream and course are the parts closest to AI safety, and the course is paused in 2026. It has industry ties through its corporate affiliates. Signatory counts for 'We Must Act Now' differ between sources.
tag_notes: Home economics (H1): labour, growth and welfare-measurement economics; sub econ_tai. Ring bridge kept (E3): a standing transformative-AI research stream, framed around AI 'resulting in widely shared prosperity and human flourishing', plus a 2025 course with existential-risk sessions funded by Open Philanthropy. It is borderline with adjacent, because most outputs concern present labour effects. Transfer into_institutions (J3): metrics (GDP-B, AI economic indicators) and policy calls aimed at governments. Second problem epistemics, for its measurement and early-warning indicators of AI's economic effects. Framing structural: job displacement and concentration ('Turing Trap'). Way of knowing empirical: employment data, surveys and new measures.

name: RadicalxChange Foundation (RxC)
summary: A US 501(c)(3) founded in 2018 by economist Glen Weyl, out of the ideas in the book Radical Markets. It now describes itself as an international nonprofit advancing participatory governance in the age of AI. It designs and pilots mechanisms such as plural (quadratic) voting, partial common ownership and data coalitions. Its AI-related work includes, with OpenMined, network-sourced AI infrastructure that lets news outlets control and price AI access to their reporting, deployed with AMSI's network of more than 500 outlets in Indonesia and with partners in Uruguay and Denmark. In 2026 it joined the coalition behind 'Reverse Alignment', a programme proposed by Glen Weyl and others that argues for redesigning institutions so that societies can absorb AI; RxC contributes on its democracy dimension.
why_it_matters: It brings mechanism design and participatory practice to the side of AI safety that most funding ignores: preparing institutions, economies and democracies to receive AI. It also gives communities such as news publishers and faith groups working tools for collective bargaining and a voice over AI.

key_work.title: Reverse Alignment (Noema paper by a coalition of 27 experts; RxC salon 24 Aug 2026)
Federated data bargaining / network-sourced AI for journalism (with OpenMined and IFPIM)
'Can AI See Me?' side event and Geneva Reflection principles submitted to the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance

funding: Revenue about $1.86m in 2024 ($1.56m in 2023), per Form 990 data on InfluenceWatch. Grants have come from the Omidyar Network, Rockefeller, Sloan, Hewlett, Kauffman and Robert Wood Johnson foundations, Microsoft, and an FTX Future Fund regrant. It also takes individual and crypto donations.
status_evidence: 10 Sep 2026: published 'On Reverse Alignment' (Noema paper and RxC salon on 24 Aug 2026). Jul 2026: co-convened a side event at the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance. Aug 2026: ASPIRE Canberra Policy Lab.
engage: Monthly open community call (first Wednesday, 9am ET / 3pm CET)
Autonomous local chapters in 30+ cities
Events such as Community Week NYC (May 2026) and online salons
Public input processes it runs, e.g. Colorado's climate preparedness roadmap (input open to 7 Oct 2026)
caveats: A broad movement organisation: much of its work, such as housing and health deliberations, is not about AI. It is associated with crypto (Buterin on the board, plural money pilots) and has received an FTX Future Fund regrant. The leadership changed in 2025, when Jess Scully succeeded Matt Prewitt. Reverse Alignment is a coalition effort, and RxC is one of its contributors.
tag_notes: Home economics, not democracy: the democracy facet's boundary sends mechanism design to economics (quadratic voting and funding, partial common ownership, data coalitions; B9 commons). Sub econ_commons for data cooperatives and public-goods funding mechanisms; democracy secondary for its deliberative and participatory processes. Ring bridge kept (E3): an explicit programme on 'participatory governance in the age of AI', plus Reverse Alignment, which is framed around societies harnessing AI safely. Transfer into_institutions (J3): its outputs are governance mechanisms and institutional designs. Framing structural: institutions unready for AI, 'productivity without prosperity'. Way of knowing communal: its main recent outputs are participant-authored (Geneva Reflection principles, resident deliberations), although its roots are formal mechanism design. Region global (O): a distributed organisation with chapters and an executive director in Sydney, though registered in California.

name: Stripe Economics of AI Fellowship
summary: A fellowship launched by Stripe in March 2025, led by UVA economist Basil Halperin with Stripe's Emily Glassberg Sands. It gives graduate students and early-career economists a grant of at least $10,000, a conference in San Francisco, a community and possible access to Stripe data. It prioritises research on the economics of transformative AI, meaning AI that brings change on the scale of the industrial revolution. The first cohort of 24 fellows was announced in 2025.
why_it_matters: It is one of very few pipelines that bring PhD economists into research on transformative AI. Several 2025 fellows work directly on the economic theory of AI safety, AI-driven growth or software-only take-off. That builds economics capacity the AI-safety field otherwise lacks.

key_work.title: 2025 cohort of 24 fellows (e.g. Eric Chen on the economic theory of AI safety, Parker Whitfill, Zach Mazlish, Lindsey Raymond)
Fellows' conference in San Francisco

people: Basil Halperin (lead and fellowship adviser; UVA)
Emily Glassberg Sands (fellowship adviser; Head of Data & AI, Stripe)
funding: Funded by Stripe. Each fellow gets at least $10,000, with more available for data purchases or teaching buyouts.
status_evidence: 2025: applications closed on 15 Apr 2025, and the first cohort of 24 fellows was announced in summer 2025. As of Oct 2026 the page still shows only the 2025 cohort, and no 2026 call was found.
engage: Fellowship for graduate students and early-career researchers (the 2025 round is closed; no 2026 round announced)
Contact: basilh@virginia.edu
caveats: Whether it continues is unclear: no second cohort or 2026 call could be found, and the page still describes the 2025 round. It is a corporate programme, and part of its offer is access to Stripe and customer data. The roster's '15-20 fellows' was the original plan; 24 were selected.
tag_notes: Home economics (H4): a one-programme funder for academic economics; sub econ_tai, because it explicitly prioritises the economics of transformative AI. Ring bridge kept (E3): a fellowship framed around transformative AI and promoted to the AI-safety community, with several fellows working on AI-safety economics. Borderline with adjacent, since 'safety' is not stated. Transfer convening (J5): its purpose is to bring economists into AI research. Framing structural, weakly grounded: the programme states no stakes beyond economic transformation. Way of knowing empirical: most funded projects are empirical labour, IO and growth studies. Status new: launched in 2025, with continuation unconfirmed. Org type programme (I): a strand inside Stripe.

name: OpenMined Foundation
summary: A 501(c)(3), founded in 2017 by Andrew Trask, that builds open-source privacy-enhancing software (PySyft, SyftBox, Syft Space). The software lets parties run approved computations on data, models or benchmarks without handing them over. Its main AI-safety use is external evaluation of AI models. In 2026 PySyft ran the first double-blind evaluations of a proprietary frontier model (Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite, with Google DeepMind, AVERI, Singapore AISI and MLCommons), and the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) signed a research agreement with it. It also develops 'attribution-based control' and network-sourced AI, which keep data owners in control of, and paid for, how AI uses their data.
why_it_matters: It brings cryptography and structured transparency to a central problem in AI oversight: evaluators and labs both have reasons not to show their assets. Its attribution-based control is a technical counterweight to the concentration of data and AI rents, and was the largest grantee in FLI's power-concentration programme.

key_work.title: PySyft used for first double-blind evaluation of a proprietary, frontier-class AI model
CRADA with NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation for secure AI evaluations
Introduction to Attribution-Based Control (ABC)
Network-sourced AI for journalism (with RadicalxChange; 500+ outlets in Indonesia, Uruguay, Denmark)

funding: Coefficient Giving (Open Philanthropy): about $6m (2023) for AI-audit software and about $10.9m over two years (Jun 2025) for PySyft and secure enclaves for frontier-model evaluations. FLI's AI-driven power concentration programme gave $1,661,750. Sloan Foundation gave $648k (2021). It also takes donations.
status_evidence: 19 Sep 2026: blog post on scaling embedded AI evaluators. 27 Aug 2026: announced the double-blind evaluation of Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite. 27 Mar 2026: CAISI CRADA.
engage: Staff openings on its careers page (remote)
Open-source contribution to PySyft and related tools (400+ contributors to date)
Research partnerships via the NAIRR Pilot and federated-learning co-design programme
Newsletter
caveats: It depends heavily on Coefficient Giving. Trask has been affiliated with Google DeepMind, and DeepMind's model was the subject of the 2026 double-blind pilot. Claims for attribution-based control (e.g. unlocking '6+ orders of magnitude' more data) are ambitious and unproven at scale. Its product line has been renamed and rebuilt several times (PySyft, SyftBox, Syft Space).
tag_notes: Home safety (H1/H2): cryptography and privacy-enhancing technologies are information-security methods; sub safety_risk. Economics secondary for its data-ownership and per-query payment designs aimed at power concentration (FLI grant). Ring bridge kept (E3, 'older institution from another field'): founded in 2017 as a privacy-tech community, it now runs a sustained, explicitly safety-framed programme on frontier-model evaluation. Transfer into_institutions (J3): it supplies infrastructure for third-party audit and evaluation regimes (CAISI, AISIs), not changes to model behaviour. Problems assurance first, then power for attribution-based control. Framing structural: its stated concern is who holds power over AI and data. Way of knowing practice: engineering and deployment know-how. Region global (O): a remote US 501(c)(3).

name: Cooperative AI Foundation (CAIF)
summary: A UK charity, backed by a $15m commitment from Macroscopic Ventures, that funds and convenes research on the cooperative capabilities of AI systems and on risks from interacting agents (miscoordination, conflict, collusion). It runs a PhD fellowship (14 fellows in 2026, from 240 applicants), an annual summer school (Toronto, 3–7 August 2026, 45 participants), a monthly online seminar series and research grants. In 2025 it published the 'Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI' report. In June 2026 it launched a fund of up to $10m for multi-agent safety with Schmidt Sciences, Google DeepMind, ARIA and Google.org.
why_it_matters: It sets the agenda for multi-agent safety, drawing on game theory, mechanism design, social choice and the science of cooperation rather than single-model alignment. It is also the largest dedicated funder of work on risks from ecosystems of interacting agents.

key_work.title: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI (CAIF Technical Report #1, led by Lewis Hammond with dozens of co-authors)
Up to $10m multi-agent safety funding call with Schmidt Sciences, Google DeepMind, ARIA and Google.org (tiers up to $300k and $1m; deadline 8 Aug 2026)
Cooperative AI Summer School 2026 (Victoria College, Toronto; prizes from the Schwartz Reisman Institute)
2026 Cooperative AI PhD Fellows (14 fellows)

people: Brigit Goebelbecker (CEO from Oct 2026; formerly UK AISI)
hq: Exeter, UK (registered charity, England and Wales)
funding: $15m philanthropic commitment from Macroscopic Ventures. Its 2026 multi-agent safety call (up to $10m) is co-funded with Schmidt Sciences, Google DeepMind, ARIA and Google.org. It also co-funded a 2026 Cape Town fellowship with AI Safety South Africa, alongside SFF and the AI Safety Tactical Opportunities Fund.
status_evidence: 8 Sep 2026: appointed its first CEO, Brigit Goebelbecker (starting Oct 2026). 10 Sep 2026: online seminar on multi-agent AI governance with IASEAI. 3–7 Aug 2026: summer school in Toronto.
engage: Cooperative AI PhD Fellowship (annual; up to $40k/yr top-up for CAIF Scholars)
Research grants, including the 2026 multi-agent safety fund (awards expected autumn 2026)
Annual Cooperative AI Summer School for early-career researchers (fees £275–£550, bursaries available)
Monthly online seminar series, open to the public
Partnerships supporting PIBBSS and MATS fellows, and the 2026 Africa cooperative AI fellowship with AI Safety South Africa
caveats: Most of its money comes from a single donor, Macroscopic Ventures, whose grantmaking officer Jesse Clifton is a CAIF trustee and also a CLR trustee. Google DeepMind staff sit on the board and DeepMind co-funds the 2026 call, which raises questions about independence from frontier labs. Its first CEO starts only in Oct 2026.
tag_notes: Home formal (B6 names CAIF): game theory of cooperation, bargaining and commitment; sub formal_agents. Economics secondary for mechanism design and social choice, life for evolutionary and collective-behaviour cooperation research and the science of agent networks. Ring core (E1): its founding mission is the cooperative intelligence of advanced AI, it sits inside the AI-safety ecosystem and is on the classic map. Transfer into_model (J1): the funded work targets the behaviour of AI agents and their ecosystems (testbeds, agent infrastructure, oversight); infrastructure work also touches institutions. Org type funder (I): its main activity is fellowships and grants, though it also does research and runs a school. Framing structural: miscoordination, collusion and destabilising multi-agent dynamics, rather than one decisive catastrophe; catastrophic is arguable. Way of knowing empirical (N): the funded work is mostly testbeds and agent experiments, with formal game theory alongside. Merged the $10m fund and the Summer School into this profile.

name: Center on Long-Term Risk (CLR)
summary: A London charity that works on worst-case (suffering) risks from advanced AI. It began in 2013 as a project of the Swiss Effective Altruism Foundation, first as the Foundational Research Institute, and became an independent UK charity at the end of 2021. It runs two research streams: an empirical Model Personas agenda on how malicious traits such as spite and sadism emerge and generalise in language models, and a conceptual agenda on Safe Pareto Improvements, bargaining changes meant to prevent catastrophic conflict between AI systems. It also makes grants through the CLR Fund and runs a paid summer research fellowship in London and online reading courses.
why_it_matters: It brings bargaining theory, decision theory and suffering-focused ethics to a risk that most of the field overlooks: conflict between AI systems and the resulting extreme suffering, including possible suffering of artificial minds. Its Safe Pareto Improvements agenda is one of the few concrete technical approaches to AI–AI conflict.

key_work.title: Safe Pareto Improvements research agenda (Anthony DiGiovanni)
Model persona research agenda
Emergent misalignment: narrow finetuning can produce broadly misaligned LLMs (Betley et al., led by Owain Evans's group; CLR researchers Daniel Tan and Niels Warncke co-authors)
SPI Fundamentals Program (4-week online course, Aug 2026)

people: Anthony DiGiovanni (Researcher; leads the SPI agenda)
funding: Individual donors and institutional donors including Macroscopic Ventures, Open Philanthropy (now Coefficient Giving), the Survival and Flourishing Fund and Community Foundation Ireland. Budgets back to 2013 are on its transparency page; 2023 was cut after a funding shortfall.
status_evidence: 21 Jul 2026: Summer Update 2026, covering five persona publications and an SPI workshop (Feb 2026). Aug 2026: SPI Fundamentals online course (3–28 Aug).
engage: Summer Research Fellowship: eight paid weeks in London (applications for 2027 open in March 2027)
Research Affiliates Program (open now)
CLR Fund: grants to individuals and organisations working on s-risks (rolling)
SPI Fundamentals and CLR Fundamentals online reading courses
Career coaching (always open); planned hiring for SPI research roles
caveats: Its suffering-focused priorities (s-risks, the view that extreme suffering is not easily outweighed by happiness) are a minority position, even within effective altruism. The team is small, it reports that limited capacity holds back the SPI agenda, and it is narrowing the persona work to malevolent personas. It shares a funder and a trustee (Jesse Clifton, Macroscopic Ventures) with CAIF. Its parent, the Effective Altruism Foundation, ceased operations in 2025.
tag_notes: Home formal (B6 names CLR): bargaining, open-source and evolutionary game theory and decision theory behind Safe Pareto Improvements; sub formal_agents. Philosophy secondary for the suffering-focused ethics that sets its priorities. Ring core (E1): its founding mission is worst-case risk from advanced AI, it sits inside the effective-altruism and x-risk ecosystem and is on the classic map. Transfer into_model (J1): SPI evaluations and persona research target the propensities and bargaining behaviour of models. Problems: multi_agent first (AI–AI conflict), agency second (how harmful propensities generalise in LLMs). Framing catastrophic (L): s-risks and catastrophic conflict, the taxonomy's own example. Way of knowing formal, for the SPI agenda it calls its main line on conflict, with a substantial empirical persona stream alongside. Hubs: a London office and fellowship, plus recurring online courses.
